Solutions Solution P1 · 2499, but read the product field 2499.0, the right number. The digits-only mask removed the comma the model wanted after "2", and the next best digits were "499". The same field shows what a mask cannot do, though. The constrained product value for that text is "Refurbished MacBook Pro 16 for 2,499 dollars, currently sold out. Condition: refurbished": the whole sentence. Nothing in a string mask marks the end of a product name. And in the XGrammar run on the same model, the MacBook is valid but "in_stock": true although it is sold out. Constrained decoding guarantees the shape of the answer, not its truth. Solution B1 · Give the model a way to say "unknown" If condition is required and must be one of new, used or refurbished, constrained decoding forces a choice even when the text never says. The model picks the likeliest option, usually "new", and the answer is valid, confident and invented. The from-scratch run shows how readily the forced choice goes wrong: for a Kindle the text calls "used", the constrained decoder wrote "new". Make "not stated" representable. Either make the field optional and nullable ( condition: Literal["new", "used", "refurbished"] | None = None ), or add an explicit value such as "unknown" . Then tell the model in the prompt to use it when the text is silent, and test that path with examples like this one. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure A classifier uses constrained decoding with a schema of two fields, answer and reasoning , in that order. The output is always valid JSON and the accuracy is worse than the free-text version was. What is wrong? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The field order. The model commits to the answer before it writes any reasoning, so the reasoning tokens never shape the answer, and you lose the gain that step-by-step gives. Put reasoning first and answer last; the schema stays valid, and no validator will ever flag the difference, because the order is logic and not formatting. The pitfall. The constrained decoding lesson calls it the pitfall that costs you. With answer first, the model writes the decision token at the first position where the grammar allows it, and the reasoning that follows is a story about a choice already made. With reasoning first, the chain comes before the decision, and the decision token is conditioned on it. Both documents validate. Only one is right. The lesson's skill refuses any design that puts an answer or decision field before the reasoning fields. Neighbors of the same mistake. Schema choice What goes wrong Fix A strict pattern for a value that can be missing, such as a date the model invents a value to satisfy the grammar allow null or a sentinel A field left optional that matters the model omits it when it is inconvenient make it required and allow null, so the absence is explicit Nesting four levels deep or more each level is one more place to lose the structure flatten An enum with thousands of options the grammar compiles slowly or times out predict a short list of candidates first, then constrain to it Why the unconstrained reply did better. A free-text reply tends to explain before it concludes, so it had the chain by accident. The constrained schema removed it. The fix restores it on purpose. Plausible wrong answers. "Constrained decoding guarantees a correct output." It guarantees the shape; the lesson shows valid JSON with a wrong answer. "Order does not matter in JSON." It does not matter to the parser; it matters to the model, which writes the fields in order. "Add a check that the reasoning supports the answer." That is an eval, not a fix; the fix is to generate the reasoning first. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why can no validator catch this? Expected: both orders are valid against the schema; the harm is in what the model has seen when it writes the answer token. (level 2) The schema forces a date pattern and the model fills in dates that are not in the text. Which related mistake is that? Expected: a grammar too strict for missing data; allow null or a sentinel so the model does not invent a value. (level 3) A field is optional and the model leaves it out when it matters. What do you change? Expected: make it required and allow null, so the model has to state that the value is missing. (level 3) The schema nests four levels deep and errors rise. What do you do? Expected: flatten, because each level of nesting is one more place to lose track of the structure. Where it is taught. The lesson constrained decoding names the field order pitfall and the strict grammar pitfall, and the lesson structured outputs covers nesting depth and optional fields. Explain the mechanism A teammate turned on the provider's JSON mode and says the extraction output is now guaranteed. What does JSON mode guarantee, what does it not, and what do you turn on instead? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. JSON mode guarantees that a finished output parses, nothing more; a response cut at the token limit can still fail, so check the finish reason first. It does not guarantee your keys, your types, your enum values or the absence of extra fields. Turn on the schema mode, where the provider takes a JSON Schema and constrains decoding to it, and keep a check on your side for the values that a schema cannot judge. Four levels of control. Level Guarantee Typical failure A prompt that says "respond in JSON" none; about 90 percent valid code fences, preamble text, truncation, wrong structure JSON mode valid syntax extra keys, wrong types, missing fields Schema mode the output conforms to your schema a wrong value with the right type, or a refusal Constrained decoding every token is valid for the schema the same as schema mode; this is how schema mode is built The constrained decoding lesson is blunt about it: pure JSON mode guarantees valid JSON, not JSON that is valid for your use case, so always provide a full schema. What strict schema mode asks of you. The structured output lesson lists the strict mode rules: every property appears in required , additionalProperties is false everywhere, and there is no unresolved reference. A schema that breaks these is rejected at request time with a 400. What stays with you. Under strict enforcement two failures disappear for a response that finishes, the parse error and the schema violation. A response cut at the token limit can still fail to parse, so check the finish reason before you read it. Two more remain. The model can refuse when the input does not fit the schema, which your code treats as a typed outcome. And the model can fill a field with a value that has the right type and the wrong content; no format layer sees that. Plausible wrong answers. "JSON mode means the keys match my model." It only guarantees syntax; extra keys, wrong types and missing fields still happen. "Adding 'respond in valid JSON' to the prompt is the same thing." A prompt-only approach is about 90 percent reliable and fails with fences, preambles and truncation. "With schema mode I can drop validation." A schema cannot catch a wrong value with the right type; keep a semantic check. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which failure remains under strict schema mode? Expected: a refusal, when the model decides the input does not fit the schema; handle it as a typed outcome, and route a response cut at the token limit to the error path. (level 2) What does strict mode demand of the schema? Expected: every property required, additional properties forbidden, no unresolved references; otherwise the request is rejected with a 400. (level 2) The output matches the schema and the price is wrong. Which layer failed? Expected: none of the format layers; the value is invented, and only a semantic check or an eval catches that. (level 3) A field is sometimes unknown in the source text. How do you write the schema? Expected: allow null or a sentinel; a grammar that forces a value makes the model invent one, such as a date. Where it is taught. The lesson structured outputs lays out the four levels, the lesson constrained decoding warns against JSON mode without a schema, and the lesson structured output gives the strict mode rules. Debug a failure An extraction pipeline with strict schema enforcement has reported zero validation errors for a month. A finance review finds that a share of the extracted invoice totals do not match the source documents, and that a status field often holds a value that is allowed by the enum and wrong for the document. The engineers say the schema guarantees correctness. What do you tell them, and what do you build? Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Schema enforcement guarantees shape, not truth. A total with the right type and the wrong number passes every format check, and an enum member can be allowed and still be the wrong one. Build a semantic eval: a labeled set of documents with gold records, exact match and field-level accuracy per field, plus a confidence signal from repeated extraction or token probabilities that sends low-confidence fields to human review. The failures a schema cannot see. The structured outputs lesson lists them even with enforcement on: Failure Example Why the schema passes it Invented value the text says one amount and the record holds another right type, wrong content Enum confusion the model picks an allowed member that does not fit the document the member is in the set Array length too many or too few line items not every provider enforces the item bounds at decode time Optional omission a field left out when it was inconvenient optional means allowed to be absent The constrained decoding lesson adds two causes that make the values worse: a grammar too strict for missing data, which pushes the model to invent, and a decision field placed before the reasoning. What to build. A labeled set. The lesson's exercise uses 50 documents with hand-labeled records. Label real invoices, including the hard cases. Field-level metrics. Exact match on the record, accuracy per field, and type compliance as a sanity row that should sit near 100 percent. A confidence per field. Run the extraction three times and measure agreement, or read the token probabilities, and flag the fields that disagree. A review queue. Low-confidence records go to a human before they reach accounting. Schema repairs. Put a reasoning field ahead of the status, give enum members descriptions that make their meaning explicit, and add a null or an "other" member if the source has cases that none of the members fit. Why size does not fix it. The structured output lesson notes that grammar enforcement lets a small model beat a much larger one on structured tasks, because the format is decoupled from the model size. The values are not. Only a labeled eval tells you how often they are right. Plausible wrong answers. "Zero validation errors means zero extraction errors." Validation checks shape; the review found value errors that no shape check can see. "Switch to a bigger model and the values will be right." Size changes the error rate, not the blind spot; without a labeled eval you cannot tell by how much. "Add a tighter pattern to the total field." A tighter grammar does not make the number true; a grammar too strict even pushes the model to invent one. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which failure can a schema never see? Expected: a value with the right type and the wrong content, such as a total copied from the wrong line. (level 3) How do you get a confidence per field without a new model? Expected: run the extraction three times and measure agreement, or read token probabilities, and flag fields that disagree for review. (level 4) The status enum has a member the model keeps picking wrongly. What are the candidate fixes? Expected: describe the members so their meaning is explicit, put a reasoning field before the status, and check whether the source has cases no member fits, which calls for a null or an "other" member. (level 4) What does the finished eval report look like? Expected: schema compliance near 100 percent as a sanity row, then exact match and field-level accuracy per field on the labeled set, with the hardest fields named. Where it is taught. The lesson structured outputs lists the failures that survive a schema and sets the labeled extraction eval, the lesson constrained decoding covers the strict grammar and field order causes, and the lesson structured output separates format reliability from model size. Check your understanding Q1 Why is getting structured JSON output from LLMs challenging? A JSON is too complex for LLMs B LLMs only output plain text C LLMs can't generate JSON D LLMs generate free-form text token by token and can produce invalid JSON (missing brackets, wrong types, extra text) at any point LLMs generate tokens autoregressively. They might add a trailing comma, forget a closing bracket, include markdown formatting around JSON, or hallucinate extra fields. Each token is independent, so structural validity isn't guaranteed. Q2 What is constrained decoding? A Limiting the model's vocabulary size B Using a smaller model C Compressing the output D Restricting which tokens the model can generate at each step to ensure the output conforms to a grammar or schema Constrained decoding masks out invalid tokens at each generation step. After an opening brace, only valid JSON keys are allowed. After a colon, only valid value tokens. This guarantees structural validity at the token level. Q3 What is the benefit of using Pydantic models for LLM output validation? A They define typed schemas that automatically validate, parse, and reject malformed LLM outputs with clear error messages B They make API calls faster C They reduce token usage D They improve model accuracy Pydantic enforces types, required fields, value constraints, and nested structures. When the LLM produces invalid output, Pydantic gives specific error messages that can be fed back to the model for self-correction. Q4 What should you do when the LLM returns invalid JSON despite instructions? A Switch to a different model B Manually fix the JSON C Implement a retry loop that sends the validation error back to the model as context for a corrected attempt D Increase the temperature A retry loop with error feedback works well: parse the output, catch validation errors, send the error message back as context ('Your output had this error: ... Please fix it'). Most models self-correct on the second attempt. Q5 When should you use the API's native JSON mode vs prompt-based JSON extraction? A Always use prompt-based extraction B Always use native JSON mode C Use native mode for guaranteed structure; use prompt-based for complex extraction where you need the model to reason about what to extract D They produce identical results Native JSON mode (OpenAI's response_format, Anthropic's tool_use) guarantees valid JSON structure. Prompt-based extraction is more flexible for complex reasoning about which fields to populate. Use native mode when structure matters most. a1104: Course home / Phase 11 · LLM Engineering Embeddings & Vector Representations Lesson 11.4 75 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Generate text embeddings using API providers and open-source models, and compute cosine similarity between them Explain why embeddings solve the vocabulary mismatch problem that keyword search cannot handle Build a semantic search index that retrieves documents by meaning rather than exact keyword match Evaluate embedding quality using retrieval benchmarks (precision@k, recall) and choose the right embedding model for your task Before you start Needs : Phase 11, Lesson 01 (Prompt Engineering) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Text is discrete. Math is continuous. Every time you ask an LLM to find "similar" documents, compare meanings, or search beyond keywords, you're relying on a bridge between these two worlds. That bridge is an embedding. If you don't understand embeddings, you don't understand modern AI. You just use it. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Embedding "Text to numbers" A dense vector where geometric proximity encodes semantic similarity Word2Vec "The OG embedding" 2013 model that learned word vectors by predicting context words; proved vector arithmetic encodes meaning Cosine similarity "How similar are two vectors" Cosine of the angle between vectors; 1 = identical direction, 0 = orthogonal, -1 = opposite HNSW "Fast vector search" Hierarchical Navigable Small World graph -- multi-layer structure enabling $O(\log n)$ approximate nearest neighbor search Bi-encoder "Embed separately, compare fast" Encodes query and document independently into vectors; enables pre-computation and fast retrieval Cross-encoder "Slow but accurate reranker" Processes query-document pair jointly through the full model; higher accuracy, no pre-computation Matryoshka embeddings "Truncatable vectors" Embeddings trained so the first N dimensions capture the most important information, enabling variable-size storage Binary quantization "1-bit embeddings" Converting float vectors to binary (sign bit only) for 32x storage reduction with Hamming distance search Chunking "Split docs for embedding" Breaking documents into 256-512 token segments so each can be independently embedded and retrieved Vector database "Search engine for embeddings" Data store optimized for storing vectors and performing approximate nearest neighbor search at scale Contrastive learning "Train by comparison" Training approach that pushes similar pair embeddings together and dissimilar pair embeddings apart MTEB "The embedding benchmark" Massive Text Embedding Benchmark -- 58 datasets across 8 task types in the original paper, since extended (MMTEB) to hundreds of tasks and languages; the standard leaderboard for comparing embedding models The problem In plain words first An embedding model turns a piece of text into a list of a few hundred or a few thousand numbers, a vector, trained so that texts with similar meanings get vectors pointing in similar directions. Search then becomes geometry: embed the query, and return the stored texts whose vectors are closest, usually by cosine similarity. That finds "transaction failed" for "my payment didn't go through" even though they share no words. This lesson builds the whole loop from scratch with a TF-IDF stand-in, then runs a real 33M-parameter embedding model on the lesson's support-ticket example, adds a cross-encoder reranker, and measures what compression (fewer dimensions, int8, single bits) and HNSW approximate search cost in recall on 3,000 Wikipedia paragraphs. No model is trained. You have 10,000 support tickets. A customer writes "my payment didn't go through." You need to find similar past tickets. Keyword search finds tickets containing "payment" and "didn't go through." It misses "transaction failed," "charge was declined," and "billing error." These tickets describe the exact same problem with completely different words. This is the vocabulary mismatch problem. Human language has dozens of ways to say the same thing. Keyword search treats each word as an independent symbol with no meaning. It cannot know that "declined" and "didn't go through" refer to the same concept. You need a representation of text where meaning, not spelling, determines similarity. You need a way to place "my payment didn't go through" and "transaction was declined" close together in some mathematical space, while pushing "my payment arrived on time" far away despite sharing the word "payment." That representation is an embedding. Idea 1 · What Is an Embedding? An embedding is a dense vector of floating-point numbers that represents the meaning of text. The word "dense" matters -- every dimension carries information, unlike sparse representations (bag-of-words, TF-IDF) where most dimensions are zero. "The cat sat on the mat" becomes something like [0.023, -0.041, 0.087, ..., 0.012] -- a list of a few hundred to a few thousand numbers depending on the model (384 for the small model used below, 1,024 to 4,096 for current large ones). These numbers encode meaning. You never inspect them directly. You compare them. Idea 2 · The Word2Vec Breakthrough In 2013, Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google published Word2Vec. The core insight: train a neural network to predict a word from its neighbors (or neighbors from a word), and the hidden layer weights become meaningful vector representations. The famous result: Copy Vector arithmetic on word embeddings captures semantic relationships. The direction from "man" to "woman" is roughly the same as the direction from "king" to "queen." This was the moment the field realized that geometry could encode meaning. Word2Vec produced 300-dimensional vectors. Each word got one vector regardless of context. "Bank" in "river bank" and "bank account" had the same embedding. This limitation drove the next decade of research. Idea 3 · From Words to Sentences Word embeddings represent single tokens. Production systems need to embed entire sentences, paragraphs, or documents. Four approaches emerged: Averaging : take the mean of all word vectors in the sentence. Cheap, lossy, surprisingly decent for short text. Loses word order entirely -- "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" get identical embeddings. CLS token : transformer models (BERT, 2018) output a special [CLS] token embedding that represents the entire input. Better than averaging but the [CLS] token was trained for next-sentence prediction, not similarity. Contrastive learning : train the model explicitly to push similar pairs together and dissimilar pairs apart. Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019) used this approach and became the foundation for modern embedding models. Given "How do I reset my password?" and "I need to change my password," the model learns these should have nearly identical vectors. Instruction-tuned embeddings : the current approach. Models expect a prefix or instruction that says what the text is for: "query: " and "passage: " for E5, "search_query: " and "search_document: " for Nomic, a task instruction for Qwen3-Embedding, and an optional "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: " before queries for BGE. Use exactly the prefixes the model card gives; the wrong prefix quietly costs accuracy. Idea 4 · Modern Embedding Models A sample of production options in November 2026, with the facts from each provider's documentation: Model Provider Dimensions Context Notes Gemini Embedding 2 Google 3,072 see docs multimodal (text, images and more) voyage-4, voyage-4-large, voyage-4-lite Voyage AI (MongoDB) 1,024 default; 256 to 2,048 32K the family shares one vector space; voyage-4-nano is open-weight text-embedding-3-large / -small OpenAI 3,072 / 1,536, shortenable 8,191 $0.13 / $0.02 per million tokens Qwen3-Embedding (0.6B, 4B, 8B) Alibaba up to 4,096, shortenable 32K open-weight, instruction-aware BGE-M3 BAAI 1,024 8,192 open-weight; dense, sparse and multi-vector outputs bge-small-en-v1.5 (used below) BAAI 384 512 open-weight, 33M parameters, runs on a laptop CPU MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) and its multilingual successor MMTEB rank models across retrieval, classification, clustering, reranking and more. Rankings move every few months and averages hide large differences by task and domain, so treat the leaderboard as a shortlist and benchmark on your own queries before committing. Idea 5 · Similarity Metrics Given two embedding vectors, three ways to measure how similar they are: Cosine similarity : the cosine of the angle between two vectors. Ranges from -1 (opposite) to 1 (identical direction). Ignores magnitude -- a 10-word sentence and a 500-word document can score 1.0 if they point the same direction. This is the default for 90% of use cases. ( a , b ) = ∥ a ∥ ⋅ ∥ b ∥ dot ( a , b ) ​ Dot product : the raw inner product of two vectors. Identical to cosine similarity when vectors are normalized (unit length). Faster to compute. OpenAI's embeddings are normalized, so dot product and cosine give the same ranking. ( a , b ) = i ∑ ​ a i ​ b i ​ Euclidean (L2) distance : straight-line distance in the vector space. Smaller = more similar. Sensitive to magnitude differences. Use when the absolute position in space matters, not just the direction. ( a , b ) = i ∑ ​ ( a i ​ − b i ​ ) 2 ​ When to use which: Metric Use when Avoid when Cosine similarity Comparing texts of different lengths; most retrieval tasks Magnitude carries information Dot product Embeddings are already normalized; maximum speed Vectors have varying magnitudes Euclidean distance Clustering; spatial nearest-neighbor problems Comparing documents of wildly different lengths The same idea as a formula For vectors : a ⋅ b ​ , ∥ a − b ∥ 2 = ∥ a ∥ 2 + ∥ b ∥ 2 − 2 a ⋅ b . If every vector is normalised to length 1, then = 2 − 2 cos ( a , b ) : cosine, dot product and Euclidean distance give the same ranking , which is why embedding models ship normalised vectors. Contrastive training (InfoNCE), which makes those geometries meaningful: for a query , its matching passage and the other passages ​ in the batch, ​ e c o s ( q , p j ​ ) / τ e c o s ( q , p + ) / τ ​ , with a temperature around 0.01 to 0.05. It pulls matching pairs together and pushes everything else apart. Worked example Unit vectors, three metrics, one ranking Two unit vectors at cosine 0.80: squared distance , distance 0.632. At cosine 0.60: , distance 0.894. Higher cosine, smaller distance, same order. Scale one vector by 3 without normalising: the cosine is unchanged, the dot product triples and the distance changes. Only cosine ignores length, which is why it is the safe default. Storage: 3,000 vectors × 384 dimensions × 4 bytes = 4.6 MB in float32; one bit per dimension is 48 bytes per vector, 144 KB. Check your mental model ✗ "An embedding search finds documents with the query's words." ✓ It finds documents whose vectors point the same way; they may share no words, and sharing words does not guarantee similarity (watch the "payment arrived on time" ticket below). ✗ "Cosine, dot product and Euclidean give different results." ✓ For unit-length vectors they give the same ranking; they differ only for unnormalised vectors. ✗ "Cutting an embedding to its first half keeps half the quality." ✓ Only for Matryoshka-trained models is the front of the vector the most informative part. Predict before you run For "my payment didn't go through", which ranks higher with TF-IDF: "Transaction failed when I tried to pay for my order", or "My payment arrived on time, thanks for the quick confirmation"? And with the neural embedding? (Solution P1.) Idea 6 · Vector Databases and HNSW A brute-force similarity search compares the query against every stored vector. At 1 million vectors with 1536 dimensions, that is 1.5 billion multiply-add operations per query. Too slow. Vector databases solve this with Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) algorithms. The dominant algorithm is HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World): Build a multi-layer graph of vectors Top layers are sparse -- long-range connections between distant clusters Bottom layers are dense -- fine-grained connections between nearby vectors Search starts at the top layer, greedily descending to refine Returns approximate top-k results in time instead of HNSW trades a small accuracy loss (typically 95-99% recall) for massive speed gains. At 10 million vectors, brute force takes seconds. HNSW takes milliseconds. Production options: Database Type Best for Max scale Pinecone Managed SaaS Zero-ops production Billions Weaviate Open source Self-hosted, hybrid search 100M+ Qdrant Open source High performance, filtering 100M+ ChromaDB Embedded Prototyping, local dev 1M pgvector Postgres extension Already using Postgres 10M FAISS Library In-process, research 1B+ Idea 7 · Chunking Strategies Documents are too long to embed as single vectors. A 50-page PDF covers dozens of topics -- its embedding becomes an average of everything, similar to nothing specific. You split documents into chunks and embed each one. Fixed-size chunking : split every N tokens with M-token overlap. Simple and predictable. Works well when documents have no clear structure. A 512-token chunk with 50-token overlap: chunk 1 is tokens 0-511, chunk 2 is tokens 462-973. Sentence-based chunking : split at sentence boundaries, grouping sentences until reaching the token limit. Each chunk is at least one complete sentence. Better than fixed-size because you never cut a thought in half. Recursive chunking : try splitting at the largest boundary first (section headers). If still too large, try paragraph boundaries. Then sentence boundaries. Then character limits. This is LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter and it works well for mixed-format corpora. Semantic chunking : embed each sentence, then group consecutive sentences whose embeddings are similar. When the embedding similarity drops below a threshold, start a new chunk. Expensive (requires embedding every sentence individually) but produces the most coherent chunks. Strategy Complexity Quality Best for Fixed-size Low Decent Unstructured text, logs Sentence-based Low Good Articles, emails Recursive Medium Good Markdown, HTML, mixed docs Semantic High Best Critical retrieval quality The sweet spot for most systems: 256-512 token chunks with 50-token overlap. Idea 8 · Bi-Encoders vs Cross-Encoders A bi-encoder embeds the query and documents independently, then compares vectors. Fast -- you embed the query once and compare against pre-computed document embeddings. This is what you use for retrieval. A cross-encoder takes the query and a document as a single input and outputs a relevance score. Slow -- it processes each query-document pair through the full model. But far more accurate because it can attend across query and document tokens simultaneously. The production pattern: bi-encoder retrieves top-100 candidates, cross-encoder reranks them to top-10. This is the retrieve-then-rerank pipeline. Reranking models: hosted ones from Cohere and Voyage, and open-weight ones such as the BGE rerankers, Qwen3-Reranker and the small MS MARCO cross-encoders (one is used below). Idea 9 · Matryoshka Embeddings Traditional embeddings are all-or-nothing. A 1536-dimensional vector uses 1536 floats. You cannot truncate to 256 dimensions without retraining. Matryoshka Representation Learning (Kusupati et al., 2022) fixes this. The model is trained so that the first N dimensions capture the most important information, like a Russian nesting doll. Truncating a 1536-d Matryoshka embedding to 256 dimensions loses some accuracy but remains functional. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small and text-embedding-3-large support Matryoshka truncation via the dimensions parameter; OpenAI reported that text-embedding-3-large shortened to 256 dimensions still beat its previous model (text-embedding-ada-002) at its full 1,536. Truncating a model that was not trained this way loses much more: the run below measures it. Idea 10 · Binary Quantization A 1536-dimensional embedding stored as float32 uses 6,144 bytes. Multiply by 10 million documents: 61 GB just for vectors. Binary quantization converts each float to a single bit: positive values become 1, negative values become 0. Storage drops from 6,144 bytes to 192 bytes -- a 32x reduction. Similarity is computed using Hamming distance (count differing bits), which CPUs can do in a single instruction. The accuracy hit is around 5-10% on retrieval recall. The common pattern: binary quantization for the first-pass search over millions of vectors, then rescore the top-1000 with full-precision vectors. This gets you 95%+ of full-precision accuracy at 32x less memory. Step 1 · Text Chunking We build a semantic search engine from scratch. No vector database. No external embedding API. Pure Python with numpy for the math. Copy Step 2 · Building Embeddings from Scratch We implement a simple dense embedding using TF-IDF with L2 normalization. This is not a neural embedding, but it follows the same contract: text in, fixed-size vector out, similar texts produce similar vectors. Two to three minutes on CPU, mostly embedding, so the output below was recorded. Copy Recorded output Copy Reading this output Truncating dimensions breaks this model. Keeping the first 192 of 384 dimensions finds only 53.1% of the true top 10, and the first 96 only 28.7%. bge-small was not trained with Matryoshka representation learning, so its information is spread over all dimensions. Models trained that way (OpenAI's text-embedding-3, Voyage 4, Gemini Embedding, Nomic and others) put the most important information first and are designed to be cut. Check the model card before truncating. int8 is nearly free. One byte per dimension instead of four, with a scale per dimension taken from the corpus, keeps 98.8% of the top 10. A quarter of the memory for about one result in a hundred. Binary is 32 times smaller and needs a second pass. One sign bit per dimension (48 bytes per vector) compared by Hamming distance finds only 41.8% of the top 10 on its own. Use it as a fast first pass: take its top 100, rescore those in float32, and agreement rises to 88.3%. The float vectors are still needed, but they can sit on disk because only 100 per query are read. HNSW: near-exact at small scale, and not yet faster. With efSearch=64 it returns 99.6% of the exact top 10, and 94.7% at 16. At 2,000 vectors exact search takes a fraction of a millisecond, so HNSW has nothing to save; at 64 it was even slower here. The point of HNSW is that its cost grows roughly with the logarithm of the corpus size, while exact search grows linearly. The gap appears at millions of vectors, not thousands. Break it on purpose Embed the 20 tickets with the BGE model but compare the query to them with the lesson's Euclidean distance on vectors you have not normalised ( normalize_embeddings=False ), then on normalised ones. Does the ranking change? Now index half the tickets with one embedding model and query with another. What happens? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Instruction-aware, multilingual, long-context embedders (Qwen3-Embedding, voyage-4, Gemini Embedding 2, BGE-M3), many open-weight, most with Matryoshka dimensions. Retrieve, then rerank is the default pipeline: a bi-encoder (often hybrid with BM25) for recall, a cross-encoder or LLM reranker for precision. Quantised vectors : int8 and binary storage with float rescoring is built into vector databases and libraries (Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, pgvector's halfvec and bit types, faiss). HNSW remains the default ANN index; disk-based indexes (DiskANN-style) for billions of vectors. Sources: Voyage 4 models , Gemini Embedding 2 , OpenAI text-embedding-3-large , Qwen3 Embedding paper , MTEB paper , Matryoshka Representation Learning , HNSW paper , faiss . Recap What to keep from this lesson An embedding is a vector whose direction encodes meaning; search is nearest neighbours. Normalise, and cosine, dot and Euclidean agree. Bi-encoders retrieve fast; cross-encoders rerank accurately. Compression (Matryoshka, int8, binary) trades recall for memory; rescoring wins most of it back. HNSW makes search sublinear at a small recall cost; tune it with efSearch. EV Cheat sheet · Embeddings and Vector Search Practice problem · Cosine similarity top-k search From the source repository: write the function, then press "Run the checks". They run as real Python in your browser (the first run loads Python, about 10 MB) and tell you which part is wrong and why. Hints open one at a time; the reference solution opens when every check passes. easy 15 min implement A vector search finds the documents whose embeddings point in the same direction as a query embedding. Cosine similarity measures that direction and ignores the length of the vectors. The retrieval step of a RAG system starts with this search. Task Write three functions. normalize_rows(X) returns a copy of X with each row divided by its L2 norm. cosine_similarity_matrix(Q, D) returns the cosine similarity of each query row against each document row. top_k(Q, D, k) returns, for each query, the indices of the k documents with the highest cosine similarity. The cosine similarity of vectors and is q ⋅ d ​ . Zero vector rule: a row with norm 0 has no direction. normalize_rows leaves it as a row of zeros. Its cosine similarity with any vector is 0.0 . Tie rule: top_k sorts the scores from high to low. When two documents have the same score, the document with the lower index comes first. Input and output Name Type Shape Meaning X float array (n, dim) any matrix of row vectors Q float array (n_queries, dim) one query embedding in each row D float array (n_docs, dim) one document embedding in each row k int scalar the number of documents to return for each query normalize_rows returns a new float array of shape (n, dim) . cosine_similarity_matrix returns a float array of shape (n_queries, n_docs) . Entry (i, j) is the score of query i against document j . top_k returns an int array of shape (n_queries, k) . Row i holds document indices, best first. Constraints 1 <= n_queries <= 64 , 1 <= n_docs <= 1000 and 1 <= dim <= 1024 . 1 <= k <= n_docs . Rows of Q and D can be zero vectors. Do not change the input arrays. Use numpy only. Examples Copy Copy Copy Copy Copy Copy For the second query, documents 0 and 1 have the same score. The tie rule puts document 0 first. Your code Run the checks Reset import numpy as np def normalize_rows(X): raise NotImplementedError def cosine_similarity_matrix(Q, D): raise NotImplementedError def top_k(Q, D, k): raise NotImplementedError Common mistakes the checks catch Takes the norm over axis 0, so it normalizes columns and not rows. Divides the input array in place, so the caller's vectors change. Divides by a zero norm, so a zero vector gives NaN and not 0. Sorts ascending and reverses the order, so equal scores put the higher index first. Drops the best match and returns ranks 2 to k + 1, as if it removed a self match. Hint 1 Use np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1, keepdims=True) to get one norm for each row, with shape (n, 1) . Hint 2 A zero norm gives a division by zero. Replace each zero norm with 1 before you divide. A zero row divided by 1 stays a zero row, so its scores are 0. Hint 3 After you normalize both matrices, one matrix product gives all the scores. The shape of the result is (n_queries, n_docs) . Hint 4 Sort the negated scores with np.argsort(..., axis=1, kind="stable") . A stable sort keeps equal scores in index order, so the lower index comes first. Then keep the first k columns. Reference solution and notes Copy Why normalize first After normalization every nonzero row has length 1. The dot product of two unit vectors is the cosine of the angle between them. One matrix product then scores every query against every document. Many vector indexes store normalized embeddings for this reason and search with the dot product. The zero vector A zero vector has no direction, so the cosine is not defined. The lesson function cosine_similarity returns 0 for this case. A zero embedding can come from an empty chunk or from a text with no known words. If you divide by its norm, you get NaN, and NaN breaks the sort. The tie rule Exact ties occur more often than you expect. Duplicate chunks give the same score, and so do zero vectors. A stable sort on the negated scores keeps index order inside a tie. The lesson gets the same order from the Python sort with reverse=True , which is also stable. Where this goes next The RAG lessons use this search as the first stage. A reranker or a fusion step with BM25 then reorders the top candidates. Solutions Solution P1 · TF-IDF picks the wrong ticket TF-IDF ranks "My payment arrived on time, thanks for the quick confirmation" first (0.376), because it shares "my" and "payment" with the query; "Transaction failed when I tried to pay for my order" shares only "my" and does not make its top 6. The neural embedding ranks the transaction-failed ticket second (0.754) and keeps the on-time ticket out of its top 6: it compares meanings, not words. Solution B1 · Unit vectors make the metrics agree; mixed models make nonsense Euclidean distance mixes direction and length: = ∥ a ∥ 2 + ∥ b ∥ 2 − 2 a ⋅ b . If the vectors are not unit length, a ticket can rank higher just because its vector is shorter or longer, so the ranking can differ from cosine. Once every vector is normalised the distance is ​ and the ranking is exactly the cosine ranking. Mixing models is worse: two embedding models place texts in unrelated coordinate systems. If the dimensions differ the dot product fails with a shape error; if they happen to match, it runs and returns numbers that mean nothing. Every vector in an index must come from the same model and version, and changing the model means re-embedding the whole corpus. Check your understanding Q1 What problem do embeddings solve that keyword search cannot? A Embeddings use less storage B Embeddings capture semantic meaning, matching 'payment didn't go through' with 'charge was declined' even though they share no words C Embeddings are faster D Embeddings work offline Keyword search treats words as independent symbols. Embeddings map text to high-dimensional vectors where semantic similarity = geometric proximity. Texts with the same meaning cluster together regardless of word choice. Q2 What does cosine similarity measure between two embedding vectors? A The angle between the vectors, indicating how similar their directions are regardless of magnitude B The Euclidean distance C The sum of their components D The number of matching dimensions Cosine similarity = dot(A,B) / (|A|*|B|). It ranges from -1 (opposite) to 1 (identical direction). Two texts with the same meaning will have vectors pointing in nearly the same direction, giving cosine similarity near 1. Q3 What is the typical dimensionality of modern text embedding models? A 2-10 dimensions B 768-3072 dimensions C 50-100 dimensions D 100,000+ dimensions Modern embedding models (OpenAI text-embedding-3, BGE, E5) produce vectors with 768 to 3072 dimensions. Higher dimensions capture more nuance but cost more to store and search. Q4 Why should you evaluate embedding quality using retrieval benchmarks rather than just inspecting similarity scores? A Similarity scores don't use cosine distance B Retrieval benchmarks are faster C Similarity scores are always wrong D Absolute similarity values vary by model; what matters is whether relevant documents rank higher than irrelevant ones (precision@k, recall) A cosine similarity of 0.85 might mean 'very similar' for one model and 'somewhat similar' for another. Retrieval metrics (precision@k, recall) measure what actually matters: does the right document come back? Q5 When would you use a local/open-source embedding model instead of an API-based one? A When you need data privacy, offline operation, lower cost at scale, or domain-specific fine-tuning B API models don't support batching C Local models produce higher quality embeddings D Local models are always better API embeddings (OpenAI, Cohere) are easy but send your data externally. Local models (BGE, E5, Nomic) keep data private, eliminate per-call costs at scale, and can be fine-tuned on domain-specific data. a1105: Course home / Phase 11 · LLM Engineering Context Engineering: Windows, Budgets, Memory, and Retrieval Lesson 11.5 90 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Calculate token budgets across all context window components (system prompt, tools, history, retrieved docs, generation headroom) Implement context window management strategies: truncation, summarization, and sliding window for conversation history Prioritize and order context components to maximize the model's attention on the most relevant information Build a context assembler that dynamically allocates tokens based on query type and available window space Before you start Needs : Phase 10 (LLMs from Scratch), Phase 11 Lesson 01-02 Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Prompt engineering is a subset. Context engineering is the whole game. A prompt is a string you type. Context is everything that goes into the model's window: system instructions, retrieved documents, tool definitions, conversation history, few-shot examples, and the prompt itself. The best AI engineers in 2026 are context engineers. They decide what goes in, what stays out, and in what order. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Context window "How much the model can read" The maximum number of tokens (input + output) the model can attend to in one request -- about 1M for the current Claude, GPT and Gemini flagships, 32K for the small open model used in this lesson Context engineering "Advanced prompt engineering" The discipline of deciding what goes into the context window, in what order, and at what priority -- encompasses retrieval, compression, tool selection, and memory management Lost-in-the-middle "Models forget stuff in the middle" Empirical finding that LLMs use information at the beginning and end of the context better than in the middle; 22 points lower for GPT-3.5-Turbo with 20 documents in the original study Token budget "How many tokens you have left" An explicit allocation of context window capacity across components (system prompt, tools, history, retrieval, generation) with per-component limits Dynamic context "Loading stuff on the fly" Assembling the context window differently for each query based on intent classification, relevant tool selection, and retrieval results History summarization "Compressing the conversation" Replacing verbatim old conversation turns with a concise summary, reducing token cost while preserving key information Tool pruning "Only including relevant tools" Classifying query intent and only including tool definitions that match, reducing tool token cost by 60-80% Long-term memory "Remembering across sessions" Facts and preferences stored in a database and retrieved at session start -- CLAUDE.md, ChatGPT Memory, and similar systems Episodic memory "Remembering specific past events" Past interactions stored as embeddings and retrieved when the current query is similar to a past conversation Generation budget "Room for the answer" Tokens reserved for the model's output -- if the context fills the window completely, the model has no room to respond The problem In plain words first Everything a model knows about your request has to be in its context window: instructions, tool definitions, retrieved documents, the conversation so far, and room for the answer. The window is large but not free: every token costs money and time on every call, and models use long contexts unevenly, finding facts at the start and end more reliably than in the middle. Context engineering is deciding what goes in, in what order, and what gets summarised or left out. This lesson builds a token budget, a reordering step, a history compressor and a tool selector, then measures two things on real models: how wrong the usual "words × 1.3" token estimate is for code, JSON and other languages, and where in a long context a 0.5B model can still find a fact. No model is trained. Claude Opus 5.5 has a 1M token window. OpenAI's GPT-6.2 models take 1.05M, Google's Gemini 4 Argon 1M, and some open models advertise more. These numbers sound enormous until you fill them, and pay for them on every call. Here is a real breakdown for a coding assistant. System prompt: 500 tokens. Tool definitions for 50 tools: 8,000 tokens. Retrieved documentation: 4,000 tokens. Conversation history (10 turns): 6,000 tokens. Current user query: 200 tokens. Generation budget (max output): 4,000 tokens. Total: 22,700 tokens. That is only 18% of a 128K window. But attention does not scale linearly with context length. A model with 128K tokens of context pays quadratic attention cost ( ) in vanilla transformers, though most production models use efficient attention variants). More importantly, retrieval accuracy degrades. The "Needle in a Haystack" test shows that models struggle to find information placed in the middle of long contexts. Research by Liu et al. (2023) showed that models answer best when the relevant information sits at the start or end of a long context and worst when it sits in the middle: for GPT-3.5-Turbo with 20 documents, 75.8% with the answer document first, 53.8% with it in the middle and 63.2% with it last. The effect varies by model and has shrunk in newer long-context models, but performance still falls as contexts fill up with distractors, so test your own model at your own lengths. The practical lesson: having 200K tokens available does not mean using 200K tokens is effective. A carefully curated 10K token context often outperforms a dumped 100K token context. Context engineering is the discipline of maximizing signal-to-noise ratio within the context window. Every token you put in the window displaces a token that could carry more relevant information. Every irrelevant tool definition, every stale conversation turn, every chunk of retrieved text that does not answer the question -- each one makes the model slightly worse at the task. Idea 1 · The Context Window is a Scarce Resource Think of the context window as RAM, not disk. It is fast and directly accessible, but limited. You cannot fit everything. You must choose. Each component competes for space. Adding more tool definitions means less room for conversation history. Adding more retrieved context means less room for few-shot examples. Context engineering is the art of allocating this budget to maximize task performance. Idea 2 · Lost-in-the-Middle The most important empirical finding in context engineering. Models attend better to information at the beginning and end of the context. Information in the middle gets lower attention scores and is more likely to be ignored. Liu et al. (2023) tested this systematically. They placed the document containing the answer among 20 documents at various positions and measured answer accuracy. For GPT-3.5-Turbo it was 75.8% with the document first, 63.2% with it last and 53.8% with it in the middle (position 10), below the 56.1% the model scored with no documents at all. This has direct engineering implications: Put the most important information first (system prompt, critical instructions) Put the current query and most relevant context last (recency bias helps) Treat the middle of the context as the lowest-priority zone If you must include information in the middle, duplicate the key point at the end Idea 3 · Context Components System prompt : sets the persona, constraints, and behavioral rules. This goes first and stays constant across turns. Coding agents and assistants ship many thousands of tokens of instructions and tool definitions. Keep it tight: every word in the system prompt is sent again on every API call (prompt caching, Lesson 11.15, makes the repeats cheaper, not free). Tool definitions : each tool adds 50-200 tokens (name, description, parameter schema). 50 tools at 150 tokens each is 7,500 tokens before any conversation happens. Dynamic tool selection -- only including tools relevant to the current query -- can reduce this by 60-80%. Retrieved context : documents from a vector database, search results, file contents. The quality of retrieval directly determines the quality of the response. Bad retrieval is worse than no retrieval -- it fills the window with noise and actively misleads the model. Conversation history : every previous user message and assistant response. Grows linearly with conversation length. A 50-turn conversation at 200 tokens per turn is 10,000 tokens of history. Most of it is irrelevant to the current query. Few-shot examples : input/output pairs that demonstrate the desired behavior. Two to three well-chosen examples often improve output quality more than thousands of tokens of instructions. But they cost space. Generation budget : the tokens reserved for the model's response. If you fill the window to capacity, the model has no room to answer. Reserve at least 2,000-4,000 tokens for generation. The same idea as a formula The budget. With a window of tokens and a reserve for the answer, the components must fit: ​ + T tools ​ + T retrieved ​ + T history ​ + T examples ​ + T query ​ ≤ W − R . What a token of context costs at inference. Every token in the window is stored in the KV cache of every layer: ​ × d head ​ × b , for layers, ​ key-value heads of size ​ and bytes per number (keys and values: the factor 2). Prefill attention work grows with for prompt tokens, so doubling the context roughly doubles the per-token cost of reading it. Billing. Input cost per request ​ × p in ​ : whatever you put in the window you pay for again on every call. Worked example Qwen2.5-0.5B, and the lesson's coding-assistant budget KV cache per token: bytes, 12 KB. A full 32,768-token context: 384 MiB per sequence. The lesson's budget: tokens, 17.7% of 128K. Measured below, one realistic tool definition is 131 Qwen tokens, so 50 tools are 6,550 tokens, sent on every request: over 3 million tokens a day at 500 requests. Sending only 5 relevant tools saves 5,895 tokens per request, 90% of the tool budget. Check your mental model ✗ "A 1M-token window means 1M tokens of context are equally useful." ✓ Accuracy falls as relevant facts get buried among distractors; a short, relevant context often wins. ✗ "Tokens are about 1.3 per word." ✓ For English prose, roughly. Code, JSON, logs and many languages take far more (measured below); count with the model's own tokenizer. ✗ "Put the most important document in the middle so the model sees it in context." ✓ Put it first or last; the middle is where models miss things. Predict before you run A 0.5B model must find one value among 75 key-value pairs (about 1,400 tokens). Will its accuracy depend on where the pair sits, and if so, will the middle be worst? (Solution P1.) Idea 4 · Context Compression Strategies History summarization : instead of keeping all previous turns verbatim, periodically summarize the conversation. "We discussed X, decided Y, and the user wants Z" in 100 tokens replaces 10 turns that took 2,000 tokens. Run summarization when history exceeds a threshold (e.g., 5,000 tokens). Relevance filtering : score each retrieved document against the current query and drop documents below a threshold. If you retrieved 10 chunks but only 3 are relevant, discard the other 7. Better to have 3 highly relevant chunks than 10 mediocre ones. Tool pruning : classify the user's query intent and only include tools relevant to that intent. A code question does not need calendar tools. A scheduling question does not need file system tools. This can reduce tool definitions from 8,000 tokens to 1,000. Recursive summarization : for very long documents, summarize in stages. First summarize each section, then summarize the summaries. A 50-page document becomes a 500-token digest that captures the key points. Idea 5 · Memory Systems Context engineering spans three time horizons. Short-term memory : the current conversation. Stored in the context window directly. Grows with each turn. Managed by summarization and truncation. Long-term memory : facts and preferences that persist across conversations. "The user prefers TypeScript." "The project uses PostgreSQL." Stored in a database, retrieved on session start. Claude Code stores this in CLAUDE.md files. ChatGPT stores it in its memory feature. Episodic memory : specific past interactions that might be relevant. "Last Tuesday, we debugged a similar issue in the auth module." Stored as embeddings, retrieved when the current conversation matches a past episode. Idea 6 · Dynamic Context Assembly The key insight: different queries need different context. A static system prompt + static tools + static history is wasteful. The best systems dynamically assemble context per query. Classify the query intent Select relevant tools (not all tools) Retrieve relevant documents (not a fixed set) Include relevant history turns (not all history) Add few-shot examples that match the task type Order everything by importance: critical first, important last, optional in the middle This is what separates a good AI application from a great one. The model is the same. The context is the differentiator. Step 1 · Token Counter You cannot budget what you cannot measure. Frontier models in 2026 are much better on such tests, but long-context benchmarks still show accuracy depending on position and on how many similar distractors surround the fact. What to do about it. Put the most important material (instructions, the best retrieved passages, the current task) at the start or the end of the context, not in the middle. Keep only what is needed, because every extra chunk is another distractor. Given a query, dynamically assemble the optimal context. Copy Use it: the same idea with real libraries Harness-Managed Context Coding agents such as Claude Code manage context in layers. The system prompt holds behavioral rules and tool definitions. When a file is opened, its contents are injected as context; when the agent searches, results are added. Long sessions are compacted: older turns are replaced by a summary. A CLAUDE.md file provides project memory that persists across sessions. The key engineering decision: Claude Code does not dump your entire codebase into the context. It retrieves relevant files on demand. This is context engineering in practice. Dynamic Context Loading Cursor indexes your entire codebase into embeddings. When you type a query, it retrieves the most relevant files and code blocks using vector similarity. Only those pieces go into the context window. A 500K-line codebase is compressed into the 5-10 most relevant code blocks. This is the pattern: embed everything, retrieve on demand, include only what matters. Assistant Long-Term Memory ChatGPT stores user preferences and facts as long-term memory. On each conversation start, relevant memories are retrieved and included in the system prompt. "The user prefers Python" costs 5 tokens but saves hundreds of tokens of repeated instructions across conversations. RAG as Context Engineering Retrieval-Augmented Generation is context engineering formalized. Instead of stuffing knowledge into the model's weights (training) or the system prompt (static context), you retrieve relevant documents at query time and inject them into the context window. The entire RAG pipeline -- chunking, embedding, retrieval, reranking -- exists to solve one problem: putting the right information in the context window. Break it on purpose In the full pipeline, set the history budget so small that the compressor drops the turn where the user stated a constraint ("only show results in EUR"). Then ask a follow-up. What does the assembled context lose, and how would you make that constraint survive compression? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Server-side compaction and context editing : Anthropic's API can summarise older turns for you (compaction, in beta) and clear old tool results or thinking blocks by rule (context editing); agent harnesses do the same client-side. Memory as files and stores : long-term memory lives outside the window (memory tools, CLAUDE.md-style project files, vector or key-value stores) and is loaded on demand. Tool search instead of all tools : agents with hundreds of tools load a few definitions per task through search, the dynamic tool selector of this lesson. Context rot : evaluations keep finding that accuracy falls as input grows, even on simple retrieval, so curated short contexts beat stuffing the 1M-token window. Sources: Liu et al. 2023 , Claude compaction , Claude context editing , Anthropic on context management , Claude models overview , OpenAI models . Recap What to keep from this lesson The window is a budget: system, tools, retrieval, history, examples, query, and a reserve for the answer. Count tokens with the real tokenizer; code and JSON cost far more than prose. Put critical material first and the query and best evidence last; the middle is weakest. Compress history, prune tools, filter retrieval: relevance beats volume. Keep long-term memory outside the window and load it when it matters. Instead of binary include/exclude, assign each tool a relevance score to the current query. Include tools in descending relevance order until the tool budget is exhausted. Compare task performance with 5, 10, 20, and 50 tools included. Build a multi-strategy context compressor. Implement three compression strategies (truncation, summarization, extraction of key sentences) and benchmark them on a set of 20 documents. Measure the tradeoff between compression ratio and information retention (does the compressed version still contain the answer to the query?). Solutions Solution P1 · Position mattered Yes, and the middle was worst. The value was found 90% of the time at the start and 95% at the end, but only 50% a quarter of the way in, 55% in the middle and 80% three quarters in. The context was about 1,400 tokens, well within the model's window. Position alone changed the result by 40 percentage points. Solution B1 · Constraints must be pinned, not summarised away The compressor summarises or drops old turns by age, not by importance, so "only show results in EUR" can disappear while greetings from the last two turns survive. The next answer then quietly uses dollars: nothing errors, the constraint is just gone. Make constraints survive explicitly: extract user preferences and hard constraints into a small pinned block (or a memory store) that is always included, outside the history budget; or summarise with a prompt that must keep every instruction and decision; and test it with conversations where the key fact sits in an early turn. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism You assemble a prompt from a system message, ten retrieved documents, the chat history so far and the user question. In which order do you place them, and what evidence decides it? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Put the system prompt and the critical instructions first, the current question and the most relevant context last, and the lowest-priority material in the middle. The evidence is the lost-in-the-middle finding: with one relevant document among 20, accuracy was 85 to 90 percent when it sat first or last and fell to 60 to 70 percent in the middle. If a key point has to sit in the middle, repeat it at the end. The finding. Models attend best to the start and the end of the context. The study placed one relevant document among 20 irrelevant ones and moved it. First or last, 85 to 90 percent accuracy. In the middle, 60 to 70 percent. The lesson generalizes it as a 10 to 20 percent drop for information at 40 to 70 percent of the way through the context. The budget. Component Typical size System prompt about 500 tokens Tool definitions 2K to 8K tokens Retrieved context 2K to 10K tokens Conversation history 2K to 20K tokens Few-shot examples 1K to 3K tokens User query 100 to 500 tokens Generation reserve 2K to 8K tokens Every token in the window displaces a token that could carry more signal. A 10K prompt that is 90 percent signal beats a 100K prompt that is 10 percent signal. Do not include all ten documents. Bad retrieval is worse than none; it fills the window with noise and misleads the model. Score each document against the query and drop those below a threshold. If you retrieved 10 chunks and 3 are relevant, keep the 3. The reorder. The lesson's function sorts the documents by score, sends the odd ranks to the front in order and the even ranks to the back in reverse, so the best sit at both ends and the weakest in the middle. Then the history, compressed into a summary when it passes a threshold, then the question last, with 2,000 to 4,000 tokens reserved for the answer. Plausible wrong answers. "The window is huge, more context is always better." A 10K prompt that is 90 percent signal beats a 100K prompt that is 10 percent signal; more context is more noise for attention to filter. "Put the question first so the model knows what to look for." The end of the context gets high attention too; the lesson places the current query last and the instructions first. "Order does not matter, attention sees everything." The measured drop in the middle is 10 to 20 percent. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why not include all ten retrieved documents? Check your understanding Q1 What is the difference between prompt engineering and context engineering? A Context engineering is about database design B A prompt is the user's query; context is everything in the model's window: system prompt, tools, retrieved docs, history, and the prompt itself C They are the same thing D Prompt engineering is more advanced Prompt engineering focuses on crafting the user instruction. Context engineering manages the entire input to the model: what goes in, what stays out, in what order, and how to allocate the limited context window. Q2 Why does context window order matter for LLM performance? A Order only matters for code B LLMs have recency and primacy biases, paying more attention to the beginning and end of the context window C Alphabetical order helps the model search faster D It doesn't -- LLMs process all tokens equally Research shows LLMs attend more to the start and end of the context window ('lost in the middle' phenomenon). Placing the most important information at the beginning or end of context improves utilization. Q3 A coding assistant uses 22,700 tokens of a 128K context window. Why is budget management still important? A Only the prompt matters B Token counting is inaccurate C 128K should be enough for any use case D Long conversations, large code files, and retrieved documentation can quickly fill the window; without budget management, critical context gets truncated 22,700 tokens is the baseline. A 50-turn conversation adds 30K+ tokens. Retrieving a large codebase adds 50K+. Tool call results add more. Without active management, the window fills and oldest context is lost. Q4 What is the sliding window strategy for conversation history? A Keeping only the N most recent turns in context and dropping older turns, optionally summarizing them first B Expanding the context window dynamically C Moving the model to a different server D Processing the conversation in fixed-size chunks Sliding window keeps the K most recent conversation turns in full context. Older turns are either dropped or replaced with a summary. This bounds memory usage while preserving the most relevant recent context. Q5 How should a context assembler allocate tokens across components? A Maximize retrieval context always B Equal allocation to each component C Minimize system prompt tokens D Dynamically based on query type: a simple question needs less retrieval context; a complex question needs more, with generation headroom always reserved A simple factual question might need 500 tokens of retrieved context. A complex analysis might need 10,000. A good context assembler adjusts allocation dynamically while always reserving headroom for the model's response. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Your LLM knows everything up to its training cutoff. It knows nothing about your company's docs, your codebase, or last week's meeting notes. RAG solves this by retrieving relevant documents and stuffing them into the prompt. It's the most deployed pattern in production AI. If you build one thing from this course, build a RAG pipeline. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means RAG "AI that reads your docs" Retrieve relevant documents, paste them into the prompt, and generate an answer grounded in those documents Embedding "Convert text to numbers" A dense vector representation of text where similar meanings produce similar vectors Vector database "Search engine for AI" A data store optimized for storing vectors and finding the nearest neighbors by similarity Chunking "Split docs into pieces" Breaking documents into smaller segments (typically 256-512 tokens) so each can be embedded and retrieved independently Cosine similarity "How similar are two vectors" The cosine of the angle between two vectors; 1 = identical direction, 0 = orthogonal, -1 = opposite Top-k retrieval "Get the k best matches" Return the k most similar chunks to the query from the vector store Context window "How much text the LLM can see" The maximum number of tokens the LLM can process in a single request; retrieved chunks must fit within this Augmented generation "Answer using given context" Generating a response using retrieved documents as context rather than relying solely on trained knowledge TF-IDF "Word importance scoring" Term Frequency times Inverse Document Frequency; weights words by how distinctive they are within a corpus Indexing "Preparing docs for search" The offline process of chunking, embedding, and storing documents so they can be searched at query time The problem In plain words first A model only knows what was in its training data, and your company's documents were not. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fixes that without touching the model: when a question arrives, search your documents for the most relevant passages, paste them into the prompt, and tell the model to answer from them and cite them. The documents can change daily, every answer can point to its source, and any model can be used. This lesson builds the pipeline from scratch (chunking, TF-IDF vectors, cosine search, prompt construction), then runs it for real: a small embedding model retrieves from an invented company handbook and a 0.5B model answers ten questions with no context, with the right passages, and with the wrong ones. No model is trained. You build a chatbot for your company. A customer asks "What's the refund policy for enterprise plans?" The LLM responds with a generic answer about typical SaaS refund policies. The actual policy, buried in a 200-page internal wiki, says enterprise customers get a 60-day window with pro-rated refunds. The LLM has never seen this document. It cannot know what it was not trained on. Fine-tuning is one solution. Take the LLM, train it on your internal docs, and deploy the updated model. This works but has serious problems. Fine-tuning costs thousands of dollars in compute. The model becomes stale the moment a document changes. You have no way to know which source the model drew from. And if the company acquires another product line next month, you fine-tune again. RAG is the other solution. Leave the model untouched. When a question comes in, search your document store for relevant passages, paste them into the prompt before the question, and let the model answer using those passages as context. The document store can be updated in minutes. You can see exactly which documents were retrieved. The model itself never changes. This is why RAG is the dominant pattern in production: it's cheaper, fresher, more auditable, and works with any LLM. Idea 1 · The RAG Pattern The entire pattern fits in four steps: Query -> Retrieve -> Augment prompt -> Generate. Every RAG system follows this pattern. The differences between production RAG systems are in the details of each step: how you chunk, how you embed, how you search, and how you construct the prompt. Idea 2 · Why RAG Beats Fine-Tuning Concern Fine-tuning RAG Cost From a few dollars (LoRA on a small model) to $100,000+ per run, repeated for every update A small charge per query for embedding and the longer prompt, plus indexing Freshness Stale until retrained Updated in minutes by re-indexing docs Auditability Cannot trace answer to source Can show exact retrieved passages Hallucination Still hallucinates freely Reduced when the right passages are retrieved; when retrieval misses, the model can still invent an answer (measured below) Data privacy Training data baked into weights Documents stay in your vector store Fine-tuning changes the model's weights permanently. RAG changes the model's context temporarily. For most applications, temporary context is what you want. The case where fine-tuning wins: when you need the model to adopt a specific style, tone, format or reasoning pattern that prompting cannot achieve. For adding factual knowledge, RAG usually wins: Ovadia et al. (2023) found retrieval beat unsupervised fine-tuning for injecting new facts, and the two combine well when you need both. Idea 3 · Embedding Models An embedding model converts text into a dense vector. Similar texts produce vectors that are close together in this high-dimensional space. "How do I reset my password?" and "I need to change my password" produce nearly identical vectors despite sharing few words. "The cat sat on the mat" produces a very different vector. Common embedding models (November 2026; Lesson 11.4 compares them): Model Dimensions Provider Notes text-embedding-3-small / -large 1,536 / 3,072, shortenable OpenAI $0.02 / $0.13 per million tokens Gemini Embedding 2 3,072 Google multimodal voyage-4 family 1,024 default, 256 to 2,048 Voyage AI 32K context; nano version open-weight Qwen3-Embedding up to 4,096, shortenable Alibaba (open-weight) 0.6B to 8B, 32K context BGE-M3 1,024 (dense + sparse + multi-vector) BAAI (open-weight) three views from one model bge-small-en-v1.5 (used below) 384 BAAI (open-weight) 33M parameters, CPU-friendly For this lesson, we build our own simple embedding using TF-IDF. Not because TF-IDF is what production systems use, but because it makes the concept concrete: text goes in, a vector comes out, similar texts produce similar vectors. Idea 4 · Vector Similarity Given two vectors, how do you measure similarity? Three options: Cosine similarity : the cosine of the angle between two vectors. Ranges from -1 (opposite) to 1 (identical). Ignores magnitude, only cares about direction. This is the default for RAG. ( a , b ) = ∥ a ∥ ⋅ ∥ b ∥ dot ( a , b ) ​ Dot product : the raw inner product. Larger vectors get higher scores. Useful when magnitude carries information (longer documents might be more relevant). ( a , b ) = i ∑ ​ a i ​ b i ​ L2 (Euclidean) distance : straight-line distance in the vector space. Smaller distance = more similar. Sensitive to magnitude differences. ( a , b ) = i ∑ ​ ( a i ​ − b i ​ ) 2 ​ Cosine similarity is the standard. It handles documents of different lengths gracefully because it normalizes by magnitude. When someone says "vector search," they almost always mean cosine similarity. Idea 5 · Chunking Strategies Documents are too long to embed as single vectors. A 50-page PDF might produce a terrible embedding because it contains dozens of topics. Instead, you split documents into chunks and embed each chunk separately. Fixed-size chunking : split every N tokens. Simple and predictable. A 512-token chunk with 50-token overlap means chunk 1 is tokens 0-511, chunk 2 is tokens 462-973, and so on. The overlap ensures you do not split a sentence at an unlucky boundary. Semantic chunking : split at natural boundaries. Paragraphs, sections, or markdown headers. Each chunk is a coherent unit of meaning. More complex to implement but produces better retrieval. Recursive chunking : try to split at the largest boundary first (section headers). If a section is still too large, split at paragraph boundaries. If a paragraph is still too large, split at sentence boundaries. This is the LangChain RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter approach and it works well in practice. Chunk size matters more than people think: Too small (64-128 tokens): each chunk lacks context. "It increased 15% last quarter" means nothing without knowing what "it" refers to. Too large (2048+ tokens): each chunk covers multiple topics, diluting relevance. When you search for revenue data, you get a chunk that's 10% about revenue and 90% about headcount. Sweet spot (256-512 tokens): enough context to be self-contained, focused enough to be relevant. Most production RAG systems start with 256-512 token chunks and some overlap, then tune chunk size on their own questions (Lesson 5.23 measures the strategies). Idea 6 · Vector Databases Once you have embeddings, you need somewhere to store and search them. Options: Database Type Best for FAISS Library (in-process) Prototyping, small to medium datasets Chroma Lightweight DB Local development, small deployments Pinecone Managed service Production without ops overhead Weaviate Open source DB Self-hosted production pgvector Postgres extension Already using Postgres Qdrant Open source DB High-performance self-hosted For this lesson, we build a simple in-memory vector store. It stores vectors in a list and does brute-force cosine similarity search. This is equivalent to FAISS with a flat index. It scales to maybe 100,000 vectors before getting slow. Production systems use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms like HNSW to search millions of vectors in milliseconds. Idea 7 · The Full Pipeline The indexing phase runs once per document (or when documents update). The querying phase runs on every user request. In production, indexing might process millions of documents over hours. Querying must respond in under a second. The same idea as a formula Retrieve. Rare words across the corpus get higher IDF. The product gives a vector where important, distinctive words have high values. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Hybrid retrieval and reranking as the baseline: BM25 plus dense vectors, fused, then a cross-encoder or LLM reranker (Lesson 11.7).
