Solutions Solution P1 · Context turned guesses into answers Closed book: 0 of 10 correct, and 0 times "I don't know": ten confident guesses. With the top 3 retrieved passages: 9 of 10 correct. With three passages that lack the answer: "I don't know" 5 times, a wrong answer 4 times (often a number lifted from an unrelated passage, such as "60-day monthly uptime"), and 1 counted correct. The instruction to abstain worked half the time, which is far better than never and far from reliable. Solution B1 · Without an exit, the model fills the gap Without an explicit way out, the model treats "answer using the context" as "produce an answer". Even with the line in place, 4 of 10 wrong-document answers were confident fabrications assembled from unrelated passages; remove it and expect most of the 5 "I don't know" replies to turn into answers of the same kind, moving the wrong-documents setting towards the closed-book result (all guesses). Run it to see the exact count for this model. The fixes are layered: keep the abstain instruction, check that the cited passage actually contains the answer (Lesson 11.12 covers groundedness checks), and gate on retrieval scores so very weak matches return "no relevant documents" before the model is called. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Weigh a trade-off A team is about to index a new document corpus and asks you to review the chunker. They picked semantic splitting, 1000 tokens per chunk and 20 percent overlap, because a blog post recommended it. What do you tell them? Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Start from the query type, not from a post. Factoid questions want 256 to 512 tokens, analytical or multi-hop questions 512 to 1024, and whole-section questions 1024 to 2048. Begin with recursive splitting at 512 tokens and no overlap, then measure recall at 5 on a 50-query set before you move any knob. Why size follows the question. A chunk must be large enough to hold the answer plus its local context, and small enough that the top k returns the answer and not noise. Too small, at 64 to 128 tokens, and a chunk says "it increased 15% last quarter" with no subject. Too large, at 2048 tokens and more, and one chunk is 10% about revenue and 90% about headcount, so its embedding points nowhere. Query type Chunk size Factoid 256 to 512 tokens Analytical or multi-hop 512 to 1024 tokens Whole-section comprehension 1024 to 2048 tokens What the measurements say. Recursive splitting at 512 tokens beat semantic splitting 69% to 54% in the chunking study. Overlap gave zero measurable benefit in the sparse retrieval study, and every overlapped token is embedded and stored again, so the index cost grows with the overlap. Response quality drops sharply around 2,500 tokens of context, so bigger chunks hit a cliff. Semantic splitting without a minimum size produces 40-token fragments that hurt retrieval. Pick a default without a benchmark. Three properties decide the first chunker: the document type, the paragraph length, and whether the format carries structure. Prose with no structure gets recursive splitting. Markdown and API docs get the header splitter. Code gets a syntax-aware splitter. When in doubt, recursive splitting is the strongest single baseline. Then measure. Build a 50-query eval set, stratified by query type, and read recall at 5 for each candidate. Clamp every chunker with a minimum and a maximum size. Never let a chunk span two documents. Plausible wrong answers. "Semantic splitting is best because it follows meaning." It lost to recursive splitting at 512 tokens in the measured study, and it makes tiny fragments unless you set a floor. "Overlap is a safety margin, keep it." The studies found that overlap often adds nothing, and it adds index cost in proportion to its size; justify any overlap with an ablation. "Bigger chunks give the model more context." Quality drops around 2,500 tokens of context, and a chunk that covers many topics dilutes its own embedding. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the chunk size depend on the kind of question? Expected: the chunk has to contain the answer with its context, and still be small enough that the top k is about the answer and not about the surrounding noise. (level 2) The corpus is markdown API documentation. What do you try first? Expected: the structural header splitter, because the format carries explicit structure; drop or merge header-only chunks. (level 3) Which two guards does every chunker need, whatever the strategy? Expected: a minimum and a maximum size, because chunks of 5 tokens or 5000 tokens both break retrieval. (level 3) You switch the embedding model later. What do you run again? Expected: the chunking eval, because the winner depends on the corpus and the model, and semantic splitting moves its boundaries when the model changes. Where it is taught. The lesson chunking strategies gives the size table and the measurements, the lesson RAG explains the too-small and too-large failures, and the lesson chunking comparison picks a default from three properties. Explain the mechanism You write the search step of a retrieval pipeline. A teammate wants to rank chunks by the raw dot product between the query vector and each chunk vector. What do you use instead, and when is the dot product the right choice? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Use cosine similarity, which is the dot product divided by the lengths of the two vectors. It measures only the angle, so a long chunk and a short chunk compete on direction and not on size. The raw dot product is right only when the vector length carries meaning that you want to reward. Three measures. Measure What it does Behavior Cosine the cosine of the angle between two vectors, from -1 to 1 ignores length, the default for retrieval Dot product the sum of the products of each pair of values longer vectors score higher L2 distance the straight-line distance between the two points smaller is closer, sensitive to length Cosine normalizes by length, so chunks of different sizes compare on direction alone. When someone says vector search, they almost always mean cosine. The code. Copy The guard returns zero when a vector has no length, so an empty chunk does not divide by zero. When the two agree. Many embedding models return unit-length vectors, or the caller asks for normalized output. The question-answering lesson encodes with normalization on and then ranks with a plain matrix product. With unit vectors the dot product equals the cosine, so the cheaper operation gives the same order. Plausible wrong answers. "The dot product and the cosine give the same order." Only when every vector has the same length; otherwise longer vectors win on the dot product. "A smaller cosine means a closer match." A larger cosine means a smaller angle; smaller is closer only for a distance such as L2. "Use whatever the vector store defaults to." The measure must match how the vectors were produced and normalized, so check the embedder before the store. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What do the values 1, 0 and -1 mean for cosine? Expected: the same direction, orthogonal, and opposite directions. (level 2) Your embedder returns unit vectors. Does the choice still matter? Expected: no, because with unit vectors the dot product and the cosine are equal, which is why the lesson normalizes and then uses a matrix product. (level 2) Why does L2 distance treat a long and a short chunk differently? Expected: it measures the straight-line distance, so a longer vector sits farther away even when it points the same way. (level 3) When would you keep the raw dot product on purpose? Expected: when the model was trained so that length carries a signal, such as more content in a longer document, and you want that signal in the rank. Where it is taught. The lesson RAG defines the three measures and the guard, and the lesson question answering ranks normalized vectors with a matrix product. Defend a design Design a question answering service over a company's internal documents: wikis, policies, contracts and support articles, a few hundred thousand pages, with weekly updates. Users are employees with different access rights. Walk through the pipeline, the evaluation, and the first three things you would measure in production. Level 3 of 4 · about 30 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Build two sides. The ingestion side parses each document, chunks it per document with a structure-aware splitter, embeds the chunks, and indexes dense vectors and a BM25 index with metadata and access labels on every chunk. The query side filters by access first, runs hybrid retrieval with rank fusion, reranks a candidate pool with a cross-encoder, and generates a cited answer with a refuse path. Prove it with a golden set labeled by domain experts and a retrieval eval that reports recall at k per query class, then measure retrieval quality weekly, faithfulness and citation correctness per turn, and cost per query in production. Requirements first. Freshness. Weekly updates mean re-indexing changed documents, not retraining a model. Access. Different rights mean per-chunk labels and a filter before retrieval. Audit. Answers must point at the passages they came from. Scale. Several hundred thousand pages do not fit any prompt; retrieval decides what the model sees. Ingestion. Parse each document into text and structure. Chunk per document. Start with recursive splitting at 512 tokens and no overlap; use the header splitter for markdown; clamp every chunk with a minimum and a maximum; never let a chunk span two documents. Attach metadata: source, date, version, category, author, role label, jurisdiction or business unit tag. Embed each chunk and write the vector with its payload. Build a BM25 index beside it with field weights so a title or code match counts more than a body match. Query. Filter the candidate space by the caller's role labels before any search. Run dense and BM25 retrieval in parallel and fuse by rank. Send the top 20 to a cross-encoder and keep the top 5, the funnel the production capstone uses. Build the prompt with the stable parts first: the system prompt and the static policies, then the reranked context, then the question. The capstone targets a cache hit rate of 60 to 80 percent on that prefix, which drops the cost per query by 3 to 5 times. Generate with instructions to cite every claim and to refuse when the snippets do not answer; gate on the reranker's rank-1 score before generation and drop uncited claims after it. Evaluation before launch. A golden set of 200 question and answer pairs with citations, labeled by a domain expert, as the capstone requires. Qrels in tiers: a smoke set of 20 queries in CI, a regression set of 200 nightly, a deep set of 2000 weekly. Retrieval metrics per query class: recall at k first, then MRR, then nDCG if relevance is graded. Answer metrics: faithfulness and relevance, judged by a model from another family. A red team of 50 adversarial prompts: jailbreaks, data extraction attempts, off-domain questions and cross-unit leaks. The first three production measurements. Retrieval quality on the golden set, weekly. The capstone alerts on a 5 percent drop. Slice it by document type and business unit. Faithfulness and citation correctness per turn. These catch the generator inventing or mis-citing while retrieval is fine. Cost and latency per query by stage. Cache hit rate, tokens per query, and the split between retrieval, in the lesson's range of 50 to 200 ms, and generation, in the range of 500 to 3000 ms. Plausible wrong answers. "Put every document into one long prompt." Hundreds of thousands of pages do not fit, and the lesson budgets 2,500 to 5,000 tokens of retrieved text per query for a reason. "Tune the model on the documents every week." It cannot cite, it goes stale between runs, and it cannot enforce access rights. "Vector search alone is enough." Exact identifiers, codes and names need the lexical side; run both and fuse. "Ship without a labeled set, the demo works." A demo on ten documents says nothing about hundreds of thousands of pages; label the golden set first. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Where does access control live? Expected: in the retrieval filter, as role labels on chunks applied before the similarity search, and never in the prompt text. (level 3) A document changes on Tuesday. What is stale and for how long? Expected: its chunks, until the next re-index; re-embed only changed documents, carry the version in the metadata, and watch the gap between source updates and index updates. (level 4) How do you keep the model cost down at this volume? Expected: a cache-friendly prompt with the system prompt and policies first, the reranked context next and the question last; the capstone targets a 60 to 80 percent hit rate and a 3 to 5 times lower cost per query. (level 4) The golden set passes and one department still reports bad answers. What do you do? Expected: slice the eval by document type and query class, add that department's real queries to the qrels, and check whether their documents are chunked by a splitter that fits their format. Where it is taught. The lesson RAG builds the two phases, the lesson advanced RAG adds hybrid search, reranking and metadata filters, the lesson end-to-end RAG composes the stages with a cited generator, the capstone production RAG sets the golden set, the red team and the cache targets, and the lesson RAG evaluation tiers the qrels. Weigh a trade-off Your chunker keeps a 100-token overlap between neighbor chunks. After the last corpus refresh the index size and the embedding bill both went up, and a teammate says the overlap must stay because it protects sentences that a boundary would cut in half. How do you settle it? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Settle it with an ablation, not an opinion. Run the same recall at 5 eval with the overlap at zero and at the current value on a stratified query set, and keep the overlap only if the number moves. The recent studies found that overlap often adds no measurable benefit, while it adds index cost in proportion to its size. Where overlap came from. The fixed-window baseline cuts every N tokens with no regard for sentences. The RAG lesson shows the classic layout: 512-token chunks with a 50-token overlap, so chunk 1 holds tokens 0 to 511 and chunk 2 holds tokens 462 to 973. The repeated tail makes sure a sentence cut at an unlucky point appears whole somewhere. Why it matters less now. A recursive splitter tries the paragraph break first, then the line break, then the sentence end, then the space. Its boundaries fall at natural breaks, so the problem that overlap solved mostly disappears. The chunking lesson lists overlap under cargo cult: the 2026 studies found zero measurable benefit in the measured case, and every overlapped token is embedded and stored twice. The test. Keep the chunker, the embedder and the query set fixed. Run recursive splitting at 512 tokens with overlap zero and with the current overlap. Compare recall at 5 per query slice, and compare chunk counts. Keep the overlap only where a slice shows a real gain, and record the ablation next to the setting. The chunker skill in the lesson sets overlap to zero by default and refuses an overlap above 20 percent without an ablation that shows it helps. Plausible wrong answers. "Overlap is free, embeddings are cheap." Every overlapped token is embedded and stored twice, so the index cost grows in proportion to the overlap. "A blog post says 20 percent overlap." The studies found no measurable benefit in the measured case; the answer depends on your corpus, so measure it there. "Remove it everywhere, no test needed." The ablation is cheap and the result is corpus dependent; a slice with real boundary losses would show up in it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why did the fixed-window splitter need overlap? Expected: it cuts at a fixed count whatever the text, so a boundary can split a sentence; the repeated tail puts that sentence whole into the next chunk. (level 2) What does a recursive splitter do instead? Expected: it splits on the paragraph, the line and the sentence separators in turn, so boundaries land on natural breaks. (level 3) What rule does the chunker skill apply to overlap? Expected: default zero, and refuse any overlap above 20 percent without an ablation. (level 3) The ablation shows a gain on one document type only. What do you ship? Expected: overlap for that type alone, with the ablation recorded, and a re-run when the corpus or the embedder changes. Where it is taught. The lesson chunking strategies reports the overlap studies and sets the skill rule, and the lesson RAG shows the fixed-window layout that overlap was built for. Explain the mechanism A product team wants an assistant that answers questions about the internal policy wiki. One engineer proposes to tune the model on the wiki pages. Another proposes to search the pages at question time and paste the matches into the prompt. Which do you pick, and in which case would you still tune the model? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Pick retrieval for knowledge. The model never changes, the document store updates in minutes, and you can show the passages behind each answer. Tuning fits when you need a style, a tone or a reasoning pattern that a prompt cannot reach, not when you need facts. Why retrieval wins on facts. The lesson lines the two up on five concerns: Concern Tuned model Retrieval Cost a training run costs from $1,000 to more than $100,000 a query costs $0.01 to $0.10 for the embedding and the model call Freshness stale until the next training run re-index the changed page and the next query sees it Audit no way to trace a fact to a page the retrieved passages are visible and can be returned Grounding the model still invents facts freely the prompt tells the model to answer only from the passages Privacy the pages are baked into the weights the pages stay in your own store Tuning changes the weights for good. Retrieval changes the context for one request. For facts, a temporary context is what you want. The one case for tuning. When the goal is how the model writes or reasons, and prompting does not get there, tuning is the right tool. A fixed voice, a house format or a reasoning habit lives in the weights better than in a long instruction. The shape of the system. Retrieval runs in two phases. The index phase chunks each page, embeds each chunk and stores the vectors with the text. The query phase embeds the question, finds the top k chunks, builds a prompt from them and calls the model. The lesson budgets k at 5 to 10 chunks and 2,500 to 5,000 tokens of retrieved text per query. Plausible wrong answers. "Tune the model, because then it knows the documents." The weights hold a copy that goes stale, and nothing in the output says which page a fact came from. "Retrieval is always better." A fixed style, a tone or a reasoning pattern is learned better by tuning than by a prompt. "Skip the search and put the whole wiki in the prompt." The lesson budgets 2,500 to 5,000 tokens of retrieved text per query; a whole wiki does not fit, and unrelated text dilutes the prompt. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) A policy page changes. What happens in each approach? Expected: with retrieval you re-index that page and the next answer uses the new text; with a tuned model the old fact stays until you train again. (level 2) A legal reviewer asks which page an answer came from. Which approach can show it? Expected: retrieval, because the passages that went into the prompt are known and can be returned with the answer. (level 2) Why is the privacy story different? Expected: with retrieval the pages stay in your store and only the matched chunks go to the model for one call; with tuning the content is inside the weights of the model you deploy. (level 3) The answer is wrong even though the right passage is in the store. Which stage do you check first? Expected: retrieval, with recall at k, because the model cannot use a passage that the search did not return. Where it is taught. The lesson RAG compares the two approaches and builds the index and query phases. Check your understanding Q1 What does RAG stand for and what problem does it solve? A Recurrent Attention Generation -- improving attention mechanisms B Retrieval-Augmented Generation -- giving LLMs access to external knowledge they weren't trained on C Reduced Architecture Generation -- making models smaller D Random Augmented Generation -- generating random outputs RAG retrieves relevant documents from an external knowledge base and adds them to the prompt. This gives the LLM access to up-to-date, domain-specific information without retraining. Q2 Why is RAG preferred over fine-tuning for most knowledge-grounded applications? A RAG is cheaper, instantly updatable when documents change, and provides source attribution -- fine-tuning is expensive and becomes stale B RAG produces better models C Fine-tuning doesn't work D RAG uses less memory Fine-tuning costs thousands of dollars, produces a static model that becomes stale as documents change, and offers no source attribution. RAG updates instantly (just update the document store), costs only embedding + storage, and can cite its sources. Q3 What is the correct order of steps in a basic RAG pipeline? A Chunk documents, embed chunks, store in vector DB, embed query, retrieve similar chunks, generate answer with context B Generate, retrieve, embed, chunk C Embed query, generate answer, retrieve documents D Store documents, query the LLM, add documents to response Ingestion: chunk documents -> embed chunks -> store in vector DB. Query time: embed the user's query -> retrieve top-K similar chunks -> add chunks to prompt -> generate answer grounded in retrieved context. Q4 What is a common failure mode in basic RAG systems? A The embeddings are too large B The vector database crashes C The retrieved chunks are semantically similar to the query but don't contain the actual answer (e.g., returning 'revenue strategy' when asked for 'Q3 revenue numbers') D The LLM refuses to answer Semantic search finds text that 'sounds like' the query, not necessarily text that 'answers' it. A query about revenue might retrieve chunks discussing revenue strategy rather than the chunk containing the actual number. Q5 How do you evaluate RAG quality? A By checking if the LLM produces any output B Using both retrieval metrics (did we find the right chunks?) and generation metrics (is the answer faithful to the retrieved context?) C By measuring response time only D By counting the number of retrieved documents RAG evaluation has two parts: retrieval quality (precision/recall of retrieved chunks against ground truth) and generation quality (faithfulness to context, relevance to query, no hallucination beyond retrieved information). Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Basic RAG retrieves the top-k most similar chunks. That works for simple questions. It falls apart for multi-hop reasoning, ambiguous queries, and large corpora. Advanced RAG is the difference between a demo that works on 10 documents and a system that works on 10 million. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means BM25 "Keyword search" A probabilistic ranking algorithm that scores documents by term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization Hybrid search "Best of both worlds" Running semantic (vector) and keyword (BM25) search in parallel, then merging results with rank fusion Reciprocal Rank Fusion "Merge ranked lists" Combining multiple ranked lists by summing 1/(k + rank) for each document across all lists Reranking "Second pass scoring" Using a more expensive cross-encoder model to re-score a candidate set from initial retrieval Cross-encoder "Joint query-document model" A model that takes a query and document as a single input, producing a relevance score; more accurate than bi-encoders but too slow for full corpus search Bi-encoder "Independent embedding model" A model that embeds queries and documents independently; fast because embeddings are precomputed, but less accurate than cross-encoders HyDE "Search with a fake answer" Generate a hypothetical answer to the query, embed it, and search for real documents similar to it Parent-child chunking "Small search, big context" Index small chunks for precise retrieval but return the larger parent chunk to provide sufficient context Metadata filtering "Narrow before searching" Filtering documents by attributes (date, source, category) before running vector search to reduce the search space Faithfulness "Did it stay grounded" Whether the generated answer is supported by the retrieved documents, as opposed to hallucinated from the model's training data The problem In plain words first Basic RAG finds passages whose embeddings sit close to the query, and close is not the same as useful. Keyword search finds exact terms (error codes, names, numbers) that embeddings blur; embeddings find paraphrases that keywords miss. Hybrid search runs both and merges the two rankings. A reranker, a slower model that reads the query and each candidate together, then reorders the shortlist. Query rewriting and HyDE fix vague questions, parent-child chunking retrieves small and returns big, and evaluation tells you which of these is actually helping. This lesson builds each piece, then measures BM25, dense retrieval, hybrid fusion and cross-encoder reranking on SciFact, a real benchmark with human relevance labels. No model is trained. You built a basic RAG pipeline in Lesson 06. It works for straightforward questions on a small corpus. Now try these: Ambiguous query : "What was revenue last quarter?" Semantic search returns chunks about revenue strategy, revenue projections, and the CFO's thoughts on revenue growth. All semantically similar to the word "revenue." None containing the actual number. The correct chunk says "$47.2M in Q3 2025" but uses the word "earnings" instead of "revenue." The embedding model thinks "revenue strategy" is closer to the query than "Q3 earnings were $47.2M." Multi-hop question : "Which team had the highest customer satisfaction score improvement?" This requires finding the satisfaction scores for each team, comparing them, and identifying the maximum. No single chunk contains the answer. The information is scattered across team reports. Large corpus problem : You have 2 million chunks. The correct answer is in chunk #1,847,293. Your top-5 retrieval pulls chunks #14, #89,201, #1,200,000, #44, and #901,333. Close in embedding space, but none containing the answer. At this scale, approximate nearest neighbor search introduces enough error that relevant results get pushed out of the top-k. Basic RAG fails because vector similarity is not the same as relevance. A chunk can be semantically similar to a query without being useful for answering it. Advanced RAG addresses this with four techniques: hybrid search (add keyword matching), reranking (score candidates more carefully), query transformation (fix the query before searching), and better chunking (retrieve at the right granularity). Idea 1 · Hybrid Search: Semantic + Keyword Semantic search (vector similarity) is good at understanding meaning. "How do I cancel my subscription?" matches "Steps to terminate your plan" even though they share no words. But it misses exact matches. "Error code E-4021" might not match a chunk containing "E-4021" if the embedding model treats it as noise. Keyword search (BM25) is the opposite. It excels at exact matches. "E-4021" matches perfectly. But "cancel my subscription" returns zero results if the document says "terminate your plan." Hybrid search runs both, then merges the results. BM25 (Best Matching 25) is the standard keyword search algorithm. It has been the backbone of search engines since the 1990s. The formula: Copy Where tf(t,d) is the term frequency of t in document d, IDF(t) is the inverse document frequency, |d| is the document length, avgdl is the average document length, k1 controls term frequency saturation (default 1.2), and b controls length normalization (default 0.75). In plain terms: BM25 scores documents higher when they contain query terms (especially rare ones), but with diminishing returns for repeated terms. A document with the word "revenue" 50 times is not 50x more relevant than one with it once. Idea 2 · Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) You have two ranked lists: one from vector search, one from BM25. How do you combine them? Reciprocal Rank Fusion is the standard approach. Copy Where k is a constant (typically 60) that prevents the top-ranked result from dominating. A document ranked #1 in vector search and #5 in BM25 gets: 1/(60+1) + 1/(60+5) = 0.0164 + 0.0154 = 0.0318 A document ranked #3 in vector search and #2 in BM25 gets: 1/(60+3) + 1/(60+2) = 0.0159 + 0.0161 = 0.0320 RRF naturally balances the two signals. A document that ranks highly in both lists gets the best score. A document that ranks #1 in one list but is absent from the other gets a moderate score. This is robust because it uses ranks, not raw scores, so differences in score distributions between the two systems do not matter. Check your mental model ✗ "Dense retrieval has made BM25 obsolete." ✓ On many benchmarks BM25 is still competitive, and it wins on exact identifiers; fusion usually beats either alone (measured below). ✗ "RRF needs the two systems' scores to be comparable." ✓ It uses only ranks, which is exactly why it works across BM25 scores and cosines. ✗ "A reranker can find documents the first stage missed." ✓ It only reorders the shortlist; recall is capped by what retrieval passed it. Predict before you run On SciFact (scientific claims against paper abstracts), which scores higher at nDCG@10: BM25 or a 33M-parameter dense model? Does RRF fusion beat both? How much does a cross-encoder rerank of the top 20 add? (Solution P1.) Idea 3 · Reranking Retrieval (whether vector, keyword, or hybrid) is fast but imprecise. It uses bi-encoders: the query and each document are embedded independently, then compared. The embeddings are computed once and cached. This scales to millions of documents. Reranking uses cross-encoders: the query and a candidate document are fed together into a model that outputs a relevance score. The model sees both texts simultaneously and can capture fine-grained interactions between them. A cross-encoder can understand that "What were Q3 earnings?" is highly relevant to a chunk containing "$47.2M in Q3" even if a bi-encoder missed the connection. The trade-off: cross-encoders are 100-1000x slower than bi-encoders because they process the query-document pair jointly. You cannot pre-compute cross-encoder scores for a million documents. The solution: retrieve a larger candidate set (top-50 from hybrid search), then rerank with a cross-encoder to get the final top-5. Common reranking models (late 2026): - Managed APIs: Cohere Rerank and Voyage rerank, multilingual, priced per search - Open-weight cross-encoders: bge-reranker-v2-m3, Qwen3-Reranker (0.6B to 8B), Jina rerankers - cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2: open-weight, 22M parameters, runs on CPU for prototyping (used below) - LLM rerankers: a general model asked to score or order the candidates; slower and costlier, sometimes better on reasoning-heavy queries - Late interaction (ColBERTv2, Jina-ColBERT): one vector per token, document vectors precomputed, so scoring a candidate is cheap while keeping token-level matching Idea 4 · Query Transformation Sometimes the problem is not retrieval but the query itself. "What was that thing about the new policy change?" is a terrible search query. It contains no specific terms. The embedding is vague. No retrieval system can find the right documents from this. Query rewriting : rephrase the user's query into a better search query. An LLM can do this: Copy HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) : instead of searching with the query, generate a hypothetical answer, embed that, and search for similar real documents. Copy Embed the hypothetical answer and search for real documents similar to it. The intuition: the hypothetical answer lives closer in embedding space to the real answer than the original question does. Questions and answers have different linguistic structures. By generating a hypothetical answer, you bridge the gap between "question space" and "answer space" in the embedding. HyDE adds one LLM call before retrieval. This increases latency by 500-2000ms. Worth it when retrieval quality is poor on raw queries. Idea 5 · Parent-Child Chunking Standard chunking forces a trade-off: small chunks for precise retrieval, large chunks for sufficient context. Parent-child chunking eliminates this trade-off. Index small chunks (128 tokens) for retrieval. When a small chunk is retrieved, return its parent chunk (512 tokens) for the prompt. The small chunk matches the query precisely. The parent chunk provides enough context for the LLM to generate a good answer. The query "enterprise refund?" matches child chunk C2 precisely. But the prompt receives the full parent chunk P, which includes the surrounding context about processing time and submission process. Idea 6 · Metadata Filtering Before running vector search, filter the corpus by metadata: date, source, category, author, language. This reduces the search space and prevents irrelevant results. "What changed in the security policy last month?" should only search documents from the last 30 days in the security category. Without metadata filtering, you search the entire corpus and might retrieve a 2-year-old security document that happens to be semantically similar. Production RAG systems store metadata alongside each chunk: source document, creation date, category, author, version. Vector databases support pre-filtering by metadata before similarity search, which is critical for performance at scale. Idea 7 · Evaluation You built a RAG system. How do you know if it works? Three metrics: Retrieval relevance (Recall@k) : for a set of test questions with known relevant documents, what percentage of relevant documents appear in the top-k results? If the answer to a question is in chunk #47, does chunk #47 appear in the top-5? Faithfulness : is the generated answer grounded in the retrieved documents? If the retrieved chunks say "60-day refund window" and the model says "90-day refund window," that is a faithfulness failure. The model hallucinated despite having the correct context. Answer correctness : does the generated answer match the expected answer? This is the end-to-end metric. It combines retrieval quality and generation quality. A simple faithfulness check: take each claim in the generated answer and verify it appears (in substance) in the retrieved chunks. If the answer contains a fact not in any retrieved chunk, it is likely hallucinated. Solutions Solution P1 · Dense won; fusion and reranking added little Dense beat BM25 at nDCG@10 (0.774 against 0.727), and on recall@10 (0.870 against 0.843). RRF fusion did not beat dense on nDCG (0.773) but raised recall@10 to 0.874, because the two methods miss different claims (18 and 23 of them). The cross-encoder rerank of the fused top 20 gave the best numbers, recall@10 0.893 and nDCG@10 0.776, for most of the run time: 501 s for 300 queries. On this benchmark each step added a little; none transformed the result. Solution B1 · Scores live on different scales BM25 scores are unbounded sums that grow with query length and term rarity, while cosine similarities lie between −1 and 1 and, for a model like bge-small, mostly in a narrow band well above 0. Added with equal weights, the BM25 term is many times larger and decides the order almost alone: the "hybrid" is BM25 with a little noise. To add scores you must first put them on one scale, for example min-max or z-score normalisation per query, and then tune the weight on held-out queries. RRF avoids the problem by using only ranks, , which is why it is the usual choice for hybrid search in search engines and vector databases. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism A retrieval pipeline uses one model to find candidate chunks and a second model to order them. Explain what each model sees as input, and why the second model does not run over the whole corpus. Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A bi-encoder embeds the query and each document on their own and compares the vectors, so every document vector is computed once at index time. A cross-encoder reads the query and one document together as a single sequence and outputs one relevance score, so it can see how the two texts interact. That score costs one forward pass for each pair, so the cross-encoder runs only on a short candidate list. Input shape. The bi-encoder maps a text to a vector. The query vector and the document vectors live in the same space, and the rank is the cosine between them. The two encodings never see each other, so the model has to compress all that is useful about a document into one vector without knowing the question. The cross-encoder takes [CLS] query_tokens [SEP] document_tokens [SEP] as one sequence. Attention runs across the join, so every document token can attend to every query token. The output at the first position goes into one linear head that gives one number. Cost. The bi-encoder embeds once and answers queries for ever. The cross-encoder runs once per pair. On a 10 million document corpus that is 10 million forward passes for one query, which no request budget allows. The advanced RAG lesson puts the gap at 100 to 1000 times slower than a bi-encoder. Staging. Retrieve the top N with the cheap model, then rerank N down to K with the expensive one. N is small, 50 to 200. The quality is the cross-encoder quality, capped by the recall of the first stage at N. A low N caps quality, not only latency. The production point is a cross-encoder of about 22M parameters. Larger rerankers are kept for offline work or for a very small K. Plausible wrong answers. "The cross-encoder is a better embedding model." It does not produce an embedding; it produces one score for one query and one document. "Run the cross-encoder over every chunk for the best quality." On a 10 million document corpus that is 10 million forward passes per query. "A larger reranker always wins." The 22M parameter class is the production point; larger models lose more latency than they gain and are kept for offline reranking or a very small K. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which of the two outputs can you compute before any query arrives? Expected: the bi-encoder document vectors; a cross-encoder score depends on the query. (level 2) What caps the quality of the two-stage pipeline? Expected: the recall of the first stage at N, because the reranker can only reorder what the retriever returned. (level 2) Does the order of the two texts in the pair matter? Expected: yes, the cross-encoder is not symmetric; feed the query first, or recall collapses. (level 3) A team promises a p95 under 100 ms with a 22M parameter reranker. What do you plan first? Expected: memory, because the weights take 88 MB at float32, and batching, because scoring the N candidates one by one multiplies the latency by N. Where it is taught. The lesson cross-encoder builds the two-stage pipeline, and the lesson advanced RAG gives the cost gap. Read the code Read these four lines of a BM25 scorer from the advanced retrieval lesson. Explain the + 1 inside the logarithm, say what k1 and b control, and describe what happens to a term that appears in more than half of the documents. python idf = math.log((self.n_docs - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5) + 1) numerator = tf * (self.k1 + 1) denominator = tf + self.k1 * (1 - self.b + self.b * doc_len / self.avg_dl) score += idf * numerator / denominator Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The + 1 inside the log is the smoothed inverse document frequency: without it a term that is in most of the documents gets a negative weight, and with it the weight stays positive. k1 sets how fast repeated occurrences stop adding score, and b sets how much a long document is penalized. A term in most documents gets a weight near zero, which is the right treatment for a stop word. The inverse document frequency. The ratio inside the log is the number of documents without the term, plus a half, over the number with the term, plus a half. When fewer documents contain the term than not, the ratio is above one and the log is positive. When the term crosses the half-corpus line the ratio drops below one and the log alone turns negative. The + 1 keeps it positive. The capstone lesson notes that this matters for stop words, which appear in most documents, and in small corpora where one common term can cross the line. Term frequency saturation. The term frequency factor is tf * (k1 + 1) over tf + k1 * (...) . As tf grows the factor approaches k1 + 1 , so a document that repeats a term 50 times is not 50 times more relevant than one that has it once. The advanced RAG lesson defaults k1 to 1.2; the capstone lesson uses 1.5 and calls it the published recommendation, with the advice not to move it without a benchmark. Length normalization. b scales the length term. At b of zero, document length is ignored. At b of one, the length penalty is full. Both lessons default to 0.75: longer documents are penalized, but not linearly. Field weights. The capstone implements field weighting as a multiplier on term counts at index time, for example the symbol name repeated above the body. The scoring code stays the same. Plausible wrong answers. "The +1 avoids a logarithm of zero." The ratio is never zero because of the half in the numerator; the +1 keeps the weight from going negative when the term passes half the corpus. "k1 is the number of results to keep." k1 is the term frequency saturation constant. "A higher b favors long documents." A higher b penalizes length more; b at zero ignores length. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) What is the weight of a term that appears in every document? Expected: df equals the document count, the ratio inside the log is near zero, the log of about one is near zero, so the term adds almost nothing. (level 3) A document repeats a query term 50 times. How does its score compare with one occurrence? Expected: it is not 50 times higher; the term frequency factor saturates toward k1 plus 1. (level 4) When would you move b ? Expected: up when long documents really say less per word, and down toward zero when document length has nothing to do with topic. (level 4) The two lessons default k1 differently. What do you do? Expected: keep the published default unless a benchmark on your own corpus says otherwise, and tune k1 and b by re-running the eval harness rather than by intuition. Where it is taught. The lesson advanced RAG gives this scorer, and the lesson hybrid retrieval explains the smoothed IDF, the defaults and field weighting. Estimate it A proposal replaces the vector retriever with a cross-encoder that scores every chunk in a 10 million chunk index, so that nothing is ever missed. Estimate the work for one question, and say what you propose instead. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. One forward pass per chunk means 10 million forward passes for one question, which no request budget allows. Keep a bi-encoder for the first stage, because its document vectors are computed once at index time, and run the cross-encoder on a pool of 50 to 200 candidates. The advanced RAG lesson puts the per-pair cost at 100 to 1000 times a bi-encoder comparison. The count. Stage Work at index time Work per query Bi-encoder one embedding per chunk, stored one embedding of the query, then one vector comparison per chunk Cross-encoder nothing can be stored, the score depends on the query one forward pass per pair, so one per chunk in the pool With the cross-encoder over the whole index, the pool is the index. An index of 10 million chunks means 10 million passes for one question. The staged shape. Retrieve a larger candidate set with the cheap stage, for example the top 50 from hybrid search, and rerank with the cross-encoder to the final top 5. The expensive model runs 50 times instead of 10 million, and its lift lands where it matters, in the final order. Two more numbers to plan. A production cross-encoder of about 22M parameters takes 88 MB at float32. Load it once and keep it resident. Run the N candidates as one batch. Scored one at a time, the latency multiplies by N. Plausible wrong answers. "Score everything, GPUs are fast." 10 million passes per question is not a latency a user waits for, and the lesson's model takes 88 MB before any batch. "Precompute the cross-encoder score for every chunk." The score depends on the query, so there is nothing to precompute. "Use a smaller cross-encoder over the whole corpus." Smaller rerankers lose quality faster than they save latency, and the pass count stays the same. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which part of the bi-encoder cost is paid once? Expected: the document embeddings, at index time; a query pays for one embedding and the comparisons. (level 2) Why does the expensive model pay for itself on the top 50? Expected: 50 passes fit a request budget and the lift is concentrated in the final order of the candidates. (level 3) The index doubles in size. Which stage grows in cost per query? Expected: the first stage, because it compares against every chunk; the reranker stays at N passes while N is fixed. (level 3) At this scale the first stage itself is not a brute-force scan. What does it use, and what does that cost? Expected: an approximate nearest neighbor index, which trades a little recall for speed; the advanced RAG lesson notes that at 2 million chunks the error can push a relevant chunk out of the top k. Where it is taught. The lesson cross-encoder counts the passes and sizes the model, and the lesson advanced RAG gives the cost gap and the top 50 to top 5 funnel. Defend a design Design a code search service that answers questions such as "how is the upload retry budget enforced" across 10 repositories with about 2M lines of code, and that stays fresh on every push. What is different from document retrieval, and where does it break? Level 4 of 4 · about 30 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Chunk at syntax tree nodes, functions and classes, not at fixed windows, and give each chunk three retrievable forms: a dense code embedding, BM25 terms with the symbol name weighted above the body, and a one-sentence natural-language summary. Retrieve hybrid, rerank with a cross-encoder, and synthesize with mandatory file and line citations that a post-filter enforces. Freshness is the hard part: a push triggers a symbol-level diff so that only changed chunks re-embed and only affected cross-file edges recompute. Why fixed windows fail on code. A fixed window cuts an identifier in half and separates a function body from its signature. The capstone parses each file with a syntax tree parser, extracts function and class nodes, and emits one chunk per node with its repository, path, start line, end line, symbol and body. The chunk boundary is the unit the user wants cited. Three representations per chunk. Form Catches Dense embedding of the code paraphrased questions about behavior BM25 with field weights, symbol name 4, summary 2, body 1 literal symbol names and "find the function named X" A one-sentence summary from a small cached model a user who says "authorized" when the code says check_permission Users ask in English about code that uses other words. The summary adds the modality that neither the code embedding nor the lexical index covers. The symbol graph. Record edges for imports, calls and inheritance across files and repositories. At query time, expand retrieval along the edges so that a question which crosses four repositories still finds the chain from the caller to the budget configuration. The query path. Retrieve dense and BM25 in parallel, de-duplicate by repository, path and symbol, rerank the top 50 and keep the top 10, synthesize with a cached system prompt, and require a repository, path and line range anchor on every claim. A claim without an anchor is flagged for a re-ask or dropped. Incremental freshness. A push triggers a diff of changed files and changed symbols. Only chunks whose text changed re-embed. The cross-file edges of the changed chunks recompute, which covers imports, calls and inheritance, so a changed call or base class does not leave a stale edge. A deleted file or symbol removes its chunks from the dense and lexical indexes and its edges from the graph, so search cannot return it after the push. The capstone's target is a 50-file push searchable in under 60 seconds on the 2M line fleet. Evaluation. Label 100 cross-repository questions with gold file and line answers. Measure MRR at 10, nDCG at 10, citation faithfulness as the fraction of claims with a verifiable anchor, and p50 and p99 latency. Re-run the set weekly and alert on an MRR at 10 drop above 5 percent. Where it breaks. Generated code. Boilerplate from code generators poisons retrieval with near duplicates; flag generated chunks in the payload and down-weight them. The capstone injects 20 percent generated code to show the effect. Monorepo duplication. Repeated utility code spreads the lexical signal over copies; de-duplicate by symbol. The long tail. Rarely imported symbols have weak embeddings; the lexical side and the summary carry them. A big push. A commit that retouches half the files is where the incremental path is tested; measure the push-to-searchable time, not only the average. Plausible wrong answers. "Chunk code every 512 tokens like prose." Fixed windows cut identifiers in half and separate a function from its signature; cut at syntax tree nodes. "Re-index the whole fleet on every push." Two million lines per commit never catches up; diff at the symbol level. "Citations are optional for code answers." The capstone rejects any claim without a file and line anchor; the post-filter drops or re-asks. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why three forms per chunk and not one good embedding? Expected: users ask how something is authorized while the code says check_permission ; the summary bridges a vocabulary gap that neither the code embedding nor BM25 covers. (level 3) What does the symbol graph buy at query time? Expected: expansion across repository boundaries, from a function to its callers and imports, so a question that spans several repositories finds the whole chain. (level 4) Generated boilerplate enters the corpus. What happens and what do you do? Expected: near-duplicate code poisons retrieval; flag generated chunks in the payload and down-weight them. (level 4) What is the freshness target and how do you hold it? Expected: a 50-file push searchable in under 60 seconds on the 2M line fleet, by re-embedding only changed chunks and recomputing only affected edges. Where it is taught. The capstone codebase RAG sets the syntax-aware chunks, the three forms, the symbol graph, the incremental re-index and the eval, and the lesson advanced RAG supplies hybrid search and reranking. Debug a failure Support agents search the knowledge base with the exact error code from a ticket, such as E-4021. The vector search returns articles about error handling in general and misses the one article that contains that code. What is happening, and what do you add? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The embedding model treats a rare code as noise, so the query vector lands near articles about errors in general and not near the one exact match. Add a lexical index with BM25 next to the vector index, run both for every query, and merge the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion. The exact token wins on BM25, and the fused list puts that article first. Two retrievers, two strengths. Semantic search understands meaning. "How do I cancel my subscription" matches "steps to terminate your plan" with no shared word. It misses exact matches, because a code such as E-4021 carries no meaning for the model to embed. Lexical search does the opposite. BM25 scores a document by summing, over the query terms, an inverse document frequency factor times a saturating term frequency factor with a length correction. A term that appears in few documents weighs most, so a rare code is exactly what BM25 is best at. It fails when the query and the document share no words. Hybrid search. Run both retrievers in parallel and fuse by rank: each document gets the sum of one over k plus its rank in each list, with k at 60. The capstone demo shows the three cases. The literal symbol query sits at BM25 rank 1 and dense rank 4, and fuses to rank 1. The paraphrased query sits at BM25 rank 6 and dense rank 1, and fuses to rank 1. The fusion wins on both query classes, so the fix for the error code does not cost the paraphrased queries. Two details that matter. Field weighting. If the codes live in a title or symbol field, repeat those tokens at index time so a title match counts more than a body match. The math stays the same. Out-of-vocabulary codes. A code present in the ticket and absent from every article gets zero from BM25, because its document frequency is zero, while the dense side still returns plausible-looking neighbors. De-duplicate by document so the empty lexical side adds no stray rank contributions. Rank fusion still scores the documents that only the dense side returns, so they stay in the fused list and can rank first. Check that a retrieved article contains the code, and when none does, say that no retrieved article contains it instead of answering from the neighbors. Plausible wrong answers. "Switch to a better embedding model." A rare code has no meaning to learn; the fix is a lexical signal next to the semantic one. "Lower the similarity threshold so more articles come back." More neighbors on the wrong topic do not include the one exact match. "Replace the vector search with BM25." Then the queries that share no words with the article fail; run both and fuse. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does BM25 give a rare code so much weight? Expected: the inverse document frequency factor; a term in few documents scores high and a term in most documents scores low. (level 2) The code is in the ticket but in no article at all. What does each retriever return? Expected: BM25 contributes nothing for that term, and the dense retriever still returns neighbors that look plausible and are wrong, and the fusion keeps them; check that a retrieved article contains the code, and when none does, say that no retrieved article contains it. (level 3) How do the paraphrased queries fare after you add the lexical index? Expected: they still win, because the fusion is rank based; in the demo the paraphrased query sat at BM25 rank 6 and dense rank 1 and fused to rank 1. (level 3) The codes live in a short title field and the body is long prose. What do you tune? Expected: field weighting, which repeats the title tokens at index time so a title match counts more. Where it is taught. The lesson advanced RAG contrasts the two retrievers, and the lesson hybrid retrieval shows the three query classes, field weighting and the out-of-vocabulary case. Defend a design A question asks what changed in the security policy last month. Your vector search returns a two-year-old security document because it is semantically close. Design the retrieval step so that this cannot happen, and say what else the same mechanism buys you in a regulated deployment. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Store metadata with each chunk, such as the source, the creation date, the category, the author and the version, and filter on it before the similarity search runs. For this question the filter is the security category and the last 30 days, so the old document is never a candidate. Under regulation the same pre-filter carries role labels and jurisdiction tags, so a user only retrieves chunks they are allowed to see. Pre-filter, not post-filter. A filter after the top k comes back can leave nothing: if every slot in the top k went to old documents, the right one never had a chance. A filter applied ahead of the search shrinks the space the similarity search runs over, which the advanced RAG lesson calls critical for performance at scale, and an excluded document cannot fill a slot. Vector stores support this as metadata pre-filtering. What to store. Field Used for Source document citations and per-document de-duplication Creation date and version time windows and stale-document control Category scope, such as security or billing Author provenance Role label who may see the chunk Jurisdiction tag which regulatory scope the chunk belongs to The regulated pipeline. The production capstone orders the query side as: filter by role and jurisdiction first, then parallel dense and BM25 retrieval, then rank fusion, then the top 20 to the reranker, then the top 5 to the generator. The labels are produced at ingestion, next to the chunk summaries, so nothing downstream has to guess them. Prove it. Access control that is not tested is a hope. The capstone runs a pre-release red team with cross-jurisdiction leak probes, and its exercise builds a second corpus slice under another jurisdiction and runs a 20-question cross-jurisdiction probe, scored pass or fail. Plausible wrong answers. "Put the date into the query text so the embedding reflects it." An embedding does not enforce a date; a semantically close old document still scores high. "Filter the results after the top k comes back." If the top k is all old documents the filter leaves nothing, and the right one never had a chance. "Tell the model not to use documents from another jurisdiction." Access control belongs in retrieval, before the text reaches the prompt. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why filter before the search and not after? Expected: the search space shrinks, which helps at scale, and an excluded document can never take a slot in the top k. (level 2) Which fields do you store with each chunk? Expected: source, date, category, author and version, plus role and jurisdiction labels in a regulated setting. (level 3) How do you test that the role filter holds? Expected: a probe set of cross-jurisdiction questions, which the capstone runs as a 20-question check scored pass or fail. (level 3) Where does the filter sit relative to the reranker and the generator? Expected: before retrieval; the capstone filters, then runs hybrid retrieval, then the reranker gets the top 20 and the generator gets the top 5. Where it is taught.
