Defend a design A regulated-domain assistant serves analysts in two jurisdictions from one index. In a red-team probe, a question asked under one jurisdiction returned a contract clause that belongs to the other. The reranker and the generator behave as designed. Where is the leak, how do you close it, and how do you prove that it stays closed? Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The leak is in retrieval: the jurisdiction tag was not applied as a pre-filter before the similarity search, so a semantically close chunk from the other jurisdiction entered the candidate pool, and nothing downstream is built to remove it. Close it by tagging every chunk with role and jurisdiction at ingestion and filtering on both before hybrid retrieval runs. Prove it with a cross-jurisdiction probe set in the red-team suite, scored pass or fail with a severity, and run before every release. Why downstream stages cannot save you. The reranker orders the candidates it receives by relevance, and the leaked clause is relevant. The generator cites what it is given. The output guard scrubs personal data and blocks forbidden topics; it does not know which jurisdiction a clause belongs to. Access control has to happen before the text reaches the prompt, and the only stage that sees the whole corpus is retrieval. The capstone order. Filter by role and jurisdiction first. Then run dense and BM25 retrieval in parallel, fuse by rank, send the top 20 to the reranker, the top 5 to the generator, then the guards, then cite and return. The tags come from ingestion, where each chunk receives a summary, a role label and a jurisdiction tag. Closing it. Tag at ingestion, and make ingestion refuse a chunk that has no tag. Filter before retrieval, not on the top k after it; a post-filter can leave an empty result and still lets an untagged chunk through. Treat the caller's jurisdiction as a request parameter, never as a hint in the prompt. Proving it. The capstone runs a pre-release red team of 50 adversarial prompts that include cross-jurisdiction leaks, scored pass or fail with a severity. Its exercise adds a second corpus slice under another jurisdiction and runs a 20-question cross-jurisdiction probe. Put that probe in the release gate for every change to ingestion or retrieval, and carry the leak count on the drift dashboard as a hard zero. Plausible wrong answers. "Add a sentence to the system prompt about the user's jurisdiction." The model cannot verify which jurisdiction a chunk belongs to; access control belongs in retrieval. "Separate indexes solve it, no tags needed." Role filtering still needs labels, shared documents get duplicated, and the probe is still needed to prove the split holds. "The red team passed once, so it is closed." One pass proves one build; the probe runs on every ingestion or retrieval change. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why can the reranker not catch the leaked clause? Expected: it only orders the candidates it receives, and a clause from the wrong jurisdiction is still relevant to the question. (level 3) Why is the output guard not the fix? Expected: it scrubs personal data and blocks forbidden topics; it cannot tell which jurisdiction a clause belongs to. (level 4) The tags exist and the leak persists. What do you check? Expected: whether the filter runs before retrieval or on the top k after it, and whether ingestion lets an untagged chunk in. (level 4) How do you keep the proof current? Expected: run the probe set in the red team on every change to ingestion or retrieval, and show the leak count on the drift dashboard with a zero threshold. Where it is taught. The capstone production RAG applies its access filter ahead of retrieval and probes it in its red team, and the lesson advanced RAG explains metadata pre-filtering. Read the code Read this retrieval function from the chunking lesson. What problem does the two-level layout solve, what does the seen set do, and how many parents can the function return? python def retrieve_parent(child_query, mapping, encoder, top_k=3): child_embs = encoder.encode([m["child"] for m in mapping], normalize_embeddings=True) q_emb = encoder.encode([child_query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0] scores = child_embs @ q_emb top = np.argsort(-scores)[:top_k] seen, parents = set(), [] for i in top: if mapping[i]["parent_idx"] not in seen: parents.append(mapping[i]["parent"]) seen.add(mapping[i]["parent_idx"]) return parents Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Small child chunks are indexed for a precise match and the larger parent is returned for context, which removes the trade-off between a precise hit and enough surrounding text. The seen set drops a parent that several top children map to, so the prompt does not receive the same text twice. For a mapping that is not empty and a positive top_k , the function returns between one and top_k parents, fewer when children share a parent; an empty mapping or a top_k of zero returns none. The layout. Standard chunking forces a choice: small chunks match precisely but lack context, large chunks carry context but cover many topics. The two-level layout indexes small children and stores the parent each child came from. The chunking lesson splits parents at 2048 and children at 256 by default, and the advanced RAG lesson draws a 512-token parent with four 128-token children. A query about one detail matches one child precisely, and the prompt receives the whole parent, including the lines around the detail. Walk the function. Encode every child and the query with normalization on, so the matrix product equals the cosine. Sort children by score and keep the top k indices. For each top child, look up its parent index; if that parent was not seen, append the parent text and mark it. Return the parents in the order of their best child. Why de-duplicate. Several children of one parent often match the same query, because they sit in the same section. Without the set, the prompt would receive the same parent twice or three times and waste its context budget. The lesson calls this the key insight of the pattern. What production changes. The function re-encodes every child on each call. A real index stores the child vectors once and only embeds the query. The two-level layout also degrades gracefully: a poor child match still returns a reasonable parent. Plausible wrong answers. "Return the parent of every top child, duplicates included." Several children map to one parent, and the repeated text wastes the context budget. "Make the child as large as the parent." Then there is no precision gain; the point is a small match unit and a large context unit. "The function always returns exactly top_k parents." It returns fewer when children share a parent. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why index the child and not the parent? Expected: a small chunk matches a specific question precisely, while a large chunk covers many topics and its embedding points nowhere in particular. (level 2) Why a plain matrix product and no cosine? Expected: the vectors are normalized at encode time, so the dot product equals the cosine. (level 3) What does this function do on every call that production code must not? Expected: it re-encodes all the children; store the child vectors once at index time and embed only the query. (level 3) Two parents each have one matching child, and a third parent has three matching children below the cut. What does the function miss? Expected: it ranks by the best child only; a parent with several good children gets no extra credit unless you aggregate child scores per parent. Where it is taught. The lesson chunking strategies gives this function and the de-duplication insight, and the lesson advanced RAG draws the parent and child layout. Weigh a trade-off Your pipeline offers three query rewriters: write a hypothetical answer and search with it, write several paraphrases and merge, or decompose it into sub-questions and merge. A user asks "what does our team do when uploads fail and the budget is gone?" Which rewriter fits, and when would each of the other two be the right pick? Level 2 of 4 · about 9 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Split it, because the question joins two topics with a conjunction, an upload failure and an exhausted budget, and no single chunk holds both. The hypothetical answer fits a jargon-heavy question whose words do not match the corpus vocabulary. Paraphrases fit a short question that could be asked in many equally good ways. The three, side by side. Rewriter What it does Wins when Loses when Hypothetical answer the model writes a passage in the corpus voice; its embedding replaces the query vector the query and the corpus use different words the model invents an identifier that is not in the index Paraphrases the model writes N rewrites; retrieve each; merge the lists by rank fusion any of several phrasings would have asked it better the rewrites all converge, so the merge equals one retrieval Sub-questions the model splits the question; retrieve each part; merge the question has conjunctions or two unrelated topics the question is atomic and gets split anyway Costs. Each rewriter adds one model call before retrieval, and the advanced RAG lesson puts the hypothetical answer at 500 to 2000 ms extra. The retrievals after the call run in parallel, so the model call is the floor. Cache the rewriter output by a hash of the query, because many queries repeat. Guards. Cap the hypothetical to two or three sentences; longer ones collect noise, shorter ones lose the lexical signal. Add an explicit diversity instruction to the paraphrase prompt, and drop near duplicates by Jaccard overlap. Check that the sub-questions are distinct before the fan-out, so an atomic question returns unchanged. Choosing per query. The end-to-end lesson picks a strategy from heuristics on query length, conjunctions and jargon ratio. The other option is to run all three in parallel and fuse the three result sets; the cost is three model calls and one fusion. Plausible wrong answers. "Always write the hypothetical answer, it is the strongest." It bridges a vocabulary gap and does nothing for a two-topic question; an invented identifier can also hurt the lexical side. "A rewriter fixes a weak retriever." It only moves the query closer to the corpus voice; a chunker that cut the answer still loses. "Split every query into sub-questions." Atomic questions get over-split and come back worse than the original. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What does a rewriter cost in latency? Expected: one model call before retrieval, 500 to 2000 ms for a hypothetical answer in the advanced RAG lesson, with the retrievals after it in parallel. (level 2) The paraphrases come back nearly identical. What happens and what do you change? Expected: the merged list equals one retrieval; add a diversity instruction and drop near duplicates by Jaccard overlap. (level 3) The splitter turns an atomic question into three parts. What is the damage and the guard? Expected: the same document comes back three times at a lower rank and the merge is worse; test that the parts are distinct before the fan-out. (level 3) How does the end-to-end system choose without a human? Expected: heuristics on length, conjunctions and jargon ratio, or run all three and fuse. Where it is taught. The lesson query rewriting builds the three rewriters and their failure modes, and the lesson advanced RAG gives the latency cost. Read the code Read this fusion function from the advanced RAG lesson. Explain the + 1 in the denominator, say what the function ignores on purpose, and describe what happens to a document that appears in only one of the lists. python def reciprocal_rank_fusion(ranked_lists, k=60): scores = {} for ranked_list in ranked_lists: for rank, (doc_id, _) in enumerate(ranked_list): if doc_id not in scores: scores[doc_id] = 0.0 scores[doc_id] += 1.0 / (k + rank + 1) fused = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) return fused Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. enumerate starts at zero, so the + 1 turns the index into a rank that starts at one, and the top document gets 1/61 as the published formula defines. The function drops the score that came with each document, because ranks are the comparable unit across retrievers. A document present in one list gets one contribution and no penalty for the other, so it can still place well if it ranked high where it appeared. Walk the loop. The outer loop visits each ranked list, for example the vector list and the BM25 list. The inner loop reads each entry as a pair and discards the second element, the retriever's own score. The contribution for a document at zero-based index rank is 1.0 / (k + rank + 1) , which is one over k plus the one-based rank. Contributions sum per document id across the lists. The result is sorted by the summed contribution, highest first. What the caller does. The hybrid search in the same lesson asks each retriever for three times the final top k, fuses the two lists and returns the first top k of the fused result. The deeper candidate lists let a document that is good in both retrievers reach the final list even when it is first in neither. The capstone version. The hybrid retrieval lesson adds a weights list with one multiplier per ranked list, applied to each rank contribution, and raises an error when the number of weights does not match the number of lists. It also keeps a map from document id to document so it can return documents instead of ids. The key. Fusion runs on the document id. Two chunks of the same document are two keys. The capstone lesson recommends de-duplication by document, because a term that is out of vocabulary for BM25 gives a zero and the dense retriever still returns noise; per-document fusion absorbs that. Plausible wrong answers. "The function averages the two scores." It never reads the scores; it sums a function of the ranks. "A document missing from one list is penalized." It gets no contribution from that list, which is not a penalty; it can still rank first if it was first in the other. "k is the number of results to keep." k is the decay constant in the denominator; the caller slices the fused list to the final top k. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What changes if you delete the + 1 ? Expected: the top document gets 1/60 instead of 1/61, the curve shifts a little, and the constant no longer matches the published definition. (level 2) Why does the caller fetch three times the final k from each retriever? Expected: a deeper list lets a document that ranks well in both retrievers reach the fused top k even when it is first in neither. (level 3) How does the capstone version let you favor one retriever? Expected: a weights list with one multiplier per ranked list, applied to the rank contribution, with an error when the lengths differ. (level 3) What is the fusion key, and why does that matter for chunks? Expected: the document id; chunks of one document are separate keys unless you de-duplicate by document, which the lesson recommends. Where it is taught. The lesson advanced RAG gives this function and its caller, and the lesson hybrid retrieval adds the weights and the de-duplication advice. Explain the mechanism You have a BM25 ranked list and a vector ranked list for the same query. An engineer proposes to merge them as alpha times the BM25 score plus one minus alpha times the cosine. What is wrong with that, and what do you do instead? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. BM25 scores are unbounded and change with the corpus, while a cosine sits between -1 and 1, so a weighted sum needs a new alpha every time you re-index. Reciprocal rank fusion merges by rank instead: each document gets the sum, over the lists, of one over k plus its rank, with k at 60. Ranks are comparable across the two retrievers, so nothing has to be calibrated. The formula and one worked case. A document at rank 1 in the vector list and rank 5 in the BM25 list gets 1/(60+1) + 1/(60+5) = 0.0164 + 0.0154 = 0.0318. A document at rank 3 and rank 2 gets 1/(60+3) + 1/(60+2) = 0.0159 + 0.0161 = 0.0320. The second document wins by a hair: a document that is good in both lists beats one that is first in one list and deep in the other. What k does. With k at 60, rank 1 contributes 1/61 and rank 10 contributes 1/70. The contribution decays slowly, so deep candidates still vote. A smaller k lets the top results dominate. A larger k flattens the curve. Why ranks and not scores. A linear combination of scores needs an alpha tuned per corpus, and it breaks on every re-index because the BM25 score spread moves. Ranks do not have a scale. The capstone lesson notes that the rank-based baseline has beaten score interpolation in every public TREC track since 2010, and that the production search engines that document hybrid search came to the same conclusion. A knob that keeps the method honest. If you have evidence that one retriever beats the other on your data, multiply its rank contribution by a weight. The rank decay shape stays and the method stays scale free. Plausible wrong answers. "Normalize both scores to a zero to one range and add them." The two distributions still differ per query and per corpus, so the tuned balance drifts after a re-index. "Take the document with the highest score in either list." One unbounded BM25 score then dominates every query; ranks are the comparable unit. "Fusion is only a tie-breaker between the two lists." In the demo it decides the top result on every query class; a document good in both lists beats one that is top in only one. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What does the constant k control? Expected: how fast the contribution decays with rank; at 60, rank 1 gives 1/61 and rank 10 gives 1/70, so deep candidates still count. (level 2) When would you lower k? Expected: when the top result of each list should dominate the fused order. (level 3) You know BM25 is better on your corpus. How do you express that? Expected: a per-list weight that multiplies the rank contribution of the BM25 list; the decay shape and the scale-free property both survive. (level 3) Why does the rank method survive a re-index when the weighted sum does not? Expected: ranks keep their meaning when the corpus changes, while BM25 scores and their spread move, so the tuned alpha no longer fits. Where it is taught. The lesson hybrid retrieval gives the published formula, the role of k and the case against score interpolation, and the lesson advanced RAG works the two-document example. Sources and further reading Robertson & Zaragoza, "The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond" (2009) -- the definitive reference for BM25, explaining the probabilistic foundations behind the formula Cormack et al., "Reciprocal Rank Fusion Outperforms Condorcet and Individual Rank Learning Methods" (2009) -- the original RRF paper showing it beats more complex fusion methods Gao et al., "Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels" (2022) -- the HyDE paper demonstrating that hypothetical document embeddings improve retrieval without any training data Nogueira & Cho, "Passage Re-ranking with BERT" (2019) -- showed cross-encoder reranking on top of BM25 significantly improves retrieval quality Khattab et al., "DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines" (2023) -- treats prompt construction and weight selection as an optimization problem over retrieval pipelines; read this for "program LLMs" instead of "prompt LLMs." Edge et al., "From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization" (Microsoft Research 2024) -- GraphRAG paper: entity-relation extraction + Leiden community detection for query-focused summarization; the global vs local retrieval distinction. Asai et al., "Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection" (ICLR 2024) -- self-evaluating RAG with reflection tokens; the agentic frontier past static retrieve-then-generate. LangChain Query Construction blog -- how to translate natural-language queries into structured database queries (Text-to-SQL, Cypher) as a pre-retrieval step. Check your understanding Q1 What is the limitation of basic top-k semantic search in RAG? A It requires GPU B It retrieves chunks that are semantically similar to the query but may not contain the actual answer, especially for ambiguous or multi-hop questions C It's too slow D It can't handle large documents Basic semantic search matches surface-level meaning. 'What was revenue last quarter?' retrieves chunks about 'revenue strategy' (semantically similar) instead of the chunk saying '$47.2M in Q3 2025' (which uses 'earnings'). Q2 What is hybrid search in the context of RAG? A Combining BM25 keyword matching with semantic vector search to capture both exact terms and meaning-based relevance B Using both CPU and GPU for search C Searching across multiple databases D Using two different LLMs BM25 catches exact keyword matches (e.g., '$47.2M' or 'Q3'). Semantic search catches meaning matches. Combining them with a reranker gives the best of both worlds: precision on specific terms plus recall on semantic variants. Q3 What does a cross-encoder reranker do in an advanced RAG pipeline? A It encodes documents into vectors B It generates the final answer C It splits documents into chunks D It takes (query, document) pairs and scores their relevance with higher accuracy than embedding similarity, reordering the initial retrieval results Bi-encoder similarity (used for initial retrieval) is fast but approximate. A cross-encoder processes the full query-document pair together with cross-attention, giving much more accurate relevance scores for reranking the top candidates. Q4 What is the HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embedding) query transformation technique? A Encrypting the query for privacy B Using the LLM to generate a hypothetical answer, then embedding that answer as the search query instead of the original question C Expanding abbreviations in the query D Hiding the query from the model The original query 'What was Q3 revenue?' might not embed close to the answer chunk. HyDE asks the LLM to generate a hypothetical answer ('Q3 revenue was approximately...'), then uses that as the search query, which embeds closer to actual answer-containing chunks. Q5 Why does parent-child chunking improve RAG over flat chunking? A It's faster to index B Small child chunks are used for precise retrieval, but the larger parent chunk is returned for context, preventing the 'lost context' problem C It reduces the number of chunks D It eliminates the need for embeddings Small chunks (200 tokens) embed precisely but lack context. Large chunks (2000 tokens) have context but embed imprecisely. Parent-child uses small chunks for search accuracy but returns the parent chunk for generation context. a1108: Course home / Phase 11 · LLM Engineering Fine-Tuning with LoRA & QLoRA Lesson 11.8 75 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Implement LoRA by injecting low-rank adapter matrices (A and B) into a pretrained model's attention layers Calculate the parameter savings of LoRA vs full fine-tuning: rank $r$ with $d_{\text{model}}$ dimensions trains $2 \cdot r \cdot d$ parameters instead of $d^2$ Fine-tune a model using QLoRA (4-bit quantized base + LoRA adapters) to fit within consumer GPU memory Merge LoRA weights back into the base model for deployment and compare inference speed with and without adapters Before you start Needs : Phase 10, Lesson 06 (Instruction Tuning / SFT) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Full fine-tuning a 7B model requires 56GB of VRAM. You don't have that. Neither do most companies. LoRA lets you fine-tune the same model in 6GB by training less than 1% of the parameters. This isn't a compromise -- it matches full fine-tuning quality on most tasks. The entire open-source fine-tuning ecosystem runs on this one trick. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means LoRA "Efficient fine-tuning" Low-Rank Adaptation: freeze base weights, train two small matrices A and B whose product approximates the full weight update QLoRA "Fine-tune on a laptop" Quantized LoRA: load the base model in 4-bit NF4, train LoRA adapters in fp16 on top, enabling 7B fine-tuning in 6GB VRAM Rank (r) "How much the model can learn" The inner dimension of the A and B matrices; controls expressiveness vs. parameter count Alpha "LoRA learning rate" Scaling factor applied to the LoRA output; $\alpha/r$ scales the adaptation's contribution to the final output NF4 "4-bit quantization" Normal Float 4: a 4-bit data type with quantization levels at normal distribution quantiles, optimal for neural network weights Adapter "The small trained part" The LoRA A and B matrices saved as a separate file (10-100MB), loadable on top of any copy of the base model Target modules "Which layers to LoRA" The specific linear layers (q_proj, v_proj, etc.) where LoRA adapters are injected Merging "Bake it in" Computing $W + (\alpha/r) \cdot BA$ and replacing the original weight, eliminating the adapter overhead at inference Paged optimizers "Don't OOM during training" Offloading optimizer states (Adam momentum, variance) to CPU when GPU memory is exhausted Catastrophic forgetting "Fine-tuning broke everything else" When updating all weights causes the model to lose previously learned capabilities The problem In plain words first Fine-tuning changes a model's weights to teach it a behaviour: a format, a style, a narrow task. Changing all of them needs memory for the weights, their gradients and the optimiser's statistics, about 16 bytes per parameter. LoRA freezes the original weights and learns a small correction for each weight matrix, written as the product of two thin matrices, so only a fraction of a percent of the parameters train. QLoRA also stores the frozen weights in 4 bits. This lesson builds LoRA from scratch on a toy network, then measures the real numbers without training anything: adapter sizes on the actual Llama 3.1 8B architecture, the memory each method needs, an exact merge check with the PEFT library, and NF4 against plain 4-bit quantization on real SmolLM2 weights. You have a base model. Llama 3 8B. You want it to answer customer support tickets in your company's voice. SFT is the answer. But SFT has a cost problem. Full fine-tuning updates every parameter in the model. Llama 3 8B has 8 billion parameters. In bf16, each parameter takes 2 bytes: 16GB just to load the weights. Standard mixed-precision training with AdamW also keeps gradients, an fp32 master copy of the weights and Adam's two fp32 moments: about 16 bytes per parameter, roughly 128GB for an 8B model before activations. No single 80GB GPU fits that; you shard it across several GPUs (Lesson 10.5) or cut the memory with 8-bit optimisers and offloading. Every experiment costs GPU-hours, and you need several to get the hyperparameters right. Scale this to Llama 3 70B and the numbers get absurd: 140GB for the bf16 weights alone, over a terabyte of training state. You need a cluster. There's a deeper problem too. Full fine-tuning modifies every weight in the model. If you fine-tune on customer support data, you might degrade the model's general capabilities. It's called catastrophic forgetting. The model gets better at your task and worse at everything else. You need a method that trains fewer parameters, uses less memory, and doesn't destroy the model's existing knowledge. Idea 1 · LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation Edward Hu and colleagues at Microsoft published LoRA in June 2021. The paper's insight: the weight updates during fine-tuning have low intrinsic rank. You don't need to update all 16.7 million parameters in a 4096x4096 weight matrix. The useful information in the update can be captured by a matrix of rank 16 or 32. Here's the math. A standard linear layer computes: Where is a ​ × d in ​ matrix. For a 4096x4096 attention projection, that's 16,777,216 parameters. Whether that matches full fine-tuning depends on the task and on where the adapters go (next sections): on small and medium instruction-tuning datasets, LoRA on all layers usually comes close. A is initialized with a random Gaussian. B is initialized to zero. This means the LoRA contribution starts at zero -- the model begins training from its original behavior and gradually learns the adaptation. Check your mental model ✗ "LoRA makes training much faster." ✓ Mostly it saves memory; the forward and backward passes still run through the whole model, so compute drops by about a third. ✗ "Adapting q_proj and v_proj is the standard best practice." ✓ It was the original paper's choice; later studies find all linear layers, especially the MLP, are needed to match full fine-tuning. ✗ "A merged LoRA model is an approximation." ✓ Merging is exact algebra; only rounding to bf16 or a quantized format changes the numbers. Predict before you run Llama 3.1 8B uses grouped-query attention, so k_proj and v_proj are 4 times narrower than q_proj. How many trainable parameters does r = 16 on q_proj and v_proj give, and what fraction of the model is that? (Solution P1.) Idea 3 · Where to Apply LoRA A transformer has many linear layers. You don't need to add LoRA to all of them. The original paper tested different combinations: Target Layers Trainable params, Llama 3.1 8B, r=16 (counted below) What studies found q_proj + v_proj 6.8M The original paper's default; clearly below full fine-tuning on harder tasks q_proj + k_proj + v_proj + o_proj 13.6M Better, still attention only All linear (attention + MLP) 41.9M Needed to match full fine-tuning (QLoRA paper; Thinking Machines' "LoRA Without Regret") The original LoRA paper adapted only the query and value projections, and many tutorials still do. Later work found that the MLP layers matter most: the QLoRA authors needed LoRA on every linear layer to match full fine-tuning, and Thinking Machines (2025) found attention-only LoRA underperforms MLP-only LoRA even at matched parameter count. Default to all linear layers; the extra parameters are still about half a percent of the model. Idea 4 · Rank Selection The rank controls the expressiveness of the adaptation: Rank Trainable Params (per layer) Best For 4 32,768 Simple classification, sentiment 8 65,536 Single-domain Q&A, summarization 16 131,072 Multi-domain tasks, instruction following 32 262,144 Complex reasoning, code generation 64 524,288 Diminishing returns for most tasks 128 1,048,576 Rarely justified Hu et al. showed that already captures most of the adaptation for simple tasks. and are the most common choices in practice. Going beyond rarely improves quality and starts to lose LoRA's memory advantage. Idea 5 · QLoRA: 4-Bit Quantization + LoRA Tim Dettmers and colleagues at the University of Washington published QLoRA in May 2023. The idea: quantize the frozen base model to 4-bit precision, then attach LoRA adapters in fp16 on top. This changes the memory equation dramatically: Method Weight Memory (7B) Training memory before activations (7B) GPU Required Full fine-tune (mixed precision, AdamW) 14GB ~112GB (16 bytes/param) several 80GB GPUs, sharded LoRA (bf16 base) 14GB ~15GB one 24-48GB GPU QLoRA (4-bit base) ~4GB ~5GB one 16-24GB GPU Activations come on top and grow with batch size and sequence length; gradient checkpointing (Lesson 10.34) keeps them in check. The run below computes these numbers for Llama 3.1 8B. QLoRA makes three technical contributions: NF4 (Normal Float 4-bit) : A new data type designed specifically for neural network weights. Neural network weights follow a roughly normal distribution. NF4 places its 16 quantization levels at the quantiles of a standard normal distribution. This is information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed data. It loses less information than uniform 4-bit quantization (INT4) or standard Float4. Double quantization : The quantization constants themselves take memory. Each block of 64 weights needs a fp32 scale factor (4 bytes). For a 7B model, that's an extra 0.4GB. Double quantization quantizes these constants to fp8, reducing the overhead to 0.1GB. Small but it adds up. Paged optimizers : During training, optimizer states (Adam's momentum and variance) can exceed GPU memory on long sequences. Paged optimizers use NVIDIA's unified memory to automatically page optimizer states to CPU RAM when GPU memory is exhausted, and page them back when needed. This prevents OOM crashes at the cost of some throughput. Idea 6 · The Quality Question Does reducing parameters or quantizing the base hurt quality? What the main studies report: QLoRA (Dettmers et al. 2023) : with NF4, double quantization and LoRA on all linear layers, 4-bit QLoRA matched 16-bit full fine-tuning on their GLUE and Super-NaturalInstructions experiments, and 16-bit LoRA on MMLU with LLaMA models from 7B to 65B. LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less (Biderman et al. 2024) : on large code and math training runs, LoRA trailed full fine-tuning, but kept more of the base model's other abilities. LoRA Without Regret (Thinking Machines 2025) : on small and medium post-training datasets LoRA on all layers matched full fine-tuning, with a learning rate about 10 times higher; it fell behind once the dataset outgrew the adapter's capacity, and in reinforcement learning even rank 1 was enough. Rule of thumb: LoRA is close to full fine-tuning for behaviour and format changes on modest data, and trails it when you try to pour in large amounts of new knowledge. Idea 7 · Real-World Costs Fine-tuning Llama 3 8B on 50,000 examples (3 epochs): Estimate the compute instead of trusting a price table (worked example below): training costs about floating-point operations for parameters and tokens with full fine-tuning, and about with LoRA (the frozen weights need no weight gradients, but the backward pass still runs through them). 50,000 examples of 512 tokens for 3 epochs on an 8B model is a few GPU-hours on one modern GPU either way. LoRA saves memory far more than time, which is what lets it run on a single consumer GPU, and why the open-weight fine-tuning community exploded in 2023. Idea 8 · The 2026 PEFT stack Framework What it is Pick when Hugging Face PEFT The canonical LoRA/QLoRA/DoRA/IA3 library You want raw control and your training loop is already on transformers.Trainer TRL HF's reinforcement-from-feedback trainers (SFT, DPO, GRPO, PPO, ORPO) You need DPO/GRPO after SFT; built on top of PEFT Unsloth Triton-kernel rewrite of the forward/backward pass You want its vendor-reported 2x-plus speedup and lower VRAM on supported model families (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and more) Axolotl YAML-config wrapper over PEFT + TRL + DeepSpeed + Unsloth You want reproducible, version-controlled training runs LLaMA-Factory GUI/CLI/API over PEFT + TRL You want zero-code fine-tuning; 100+ model families supported torchtune Native PyTorch recipes, no transformers dep Legacy only: its README says it is no longer actively maintained (development wound down in 2025) Rule of thumb: research use or one-off experiment → PEFT. Repeatable production pipeline → Axolotl with Unsloth kernels enabled. Throwaway prototyping → LLaMA-Factory. Idea 9 · Merging Adapters After training, you have two things: the frozen base model and a small LoRA adapter (typically 10-100MB). You can either: Keep them separate : Load the base model, load the adapter on top. Swap adapters for different tasks. This is how you serve multiple fine-tuned variants from one base model. Merge them permanently : Compute = W + ( α / r ) ⋅ B A and save the result as a new full model. The merged model is the same size as the original. No inference overhead. No adapter to manage. For serving multiple tasks (customer support adapter, code adapter, translation adapter), keep them separate. For deploying a single specialized model, merge. Advanced merging techniques for combining multiple adapters: TIES-Merging (Yadav et al. 2023): Trims small-magnitude parameters, resolves sign conflicts, then merges. Reduces interference between adapters. DARE (Yu et al. 2023): Randomly drops adapter parameters before merging and rescales the rest. Surprisingly effective at combining capabilities. Task arithmetic : Simply add or subtract adapter weights. Adding a "code" adapter and a "math" adapter often produces a model good at both. Idea 10 · When NOT to Fine-Tune Fine-tuning is the third option, not the first. First: prompt engineering. Write a better system prompt. Add few-shot examples. Use chain-of-thought. This costs nothing and takes minutes. If prompting gets you 80% of the way there, you probably don't need to fine-tune. Second: RAG. If the model needs to know about your specific data (documents, knowledge base, product catalog), retrieval is cheaper and more maintainable than baking it into weights. See Lesson 06. Third: fine-tuning. Use this when you need the model to adopt a specific style, format, or reasoning pattern that cannot be achieved through prompting. When you need consistent structured output. When you need to distill a larger model into a smaller one. When latency matters and you can't afford the extra tokens from few-shot prompting. Step 6 · Simulated QLoRA Quantization Copy This simulates 4-bit quantization by mapping weights into 16 discrete levels within blocks of 64. Production QLoRA uses the bitsandbytes library for true NF4 on GPU. See it drawn NF4 against uniform 4-bit, on real weights The 16 NF4 levels built from normal-distribution quantiles exactly as the QLoRA paper describes, then block-wise (64 weights per block) quantization of all 315 million weights in SmolLM2-360M's linear layers with NF4 and with 16 evenly spaced levels, and the scale overhead with and without double quantization. About 40 seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output NF4's levels follow the bell curve. They are packed near zero (−0.091, 0, +0.080) and spread out towards ±1, while INT4 spaces its 16 levels evenly. Trained weights are roughly normally distributed within each block, so the levels sit where the weights are. You can see it in the usage. With INT4 the outer levels each hold 1% of the weights and the central four hold more than half. With NF4 every level holds between 2% and 10%. Each of the 16 codes carries more information, which is what "information-theoretically optimal for normal data" means in practice. Lower error with the same 4 bits. The relative error falls from 0.1056 to 0.0934, about 12% less, on all 315 million weights. The gap is modest but free: same storage, same speed, a better choice of levels. That is why QLoRA stores the frozen base in NF4. The scales are not free, and double quantization fixes that. One fp32 scale per 64 weights adds 0.5 bits per weight, so "4-bit" would really be 4.5. Quantizing the scales themselves to 8 bits, with one fp32 scale per 256 of them, cuts the overhead to 0.127 bits. For a 7B model that saves 0.33 GB (0.44 GB against 0.11 GB), which matters when the goal is fitting on one GPU. The adapter is two thin matrices: A with 16 rows and 4,096 columns, and B with 4,096 rows and 16 columns. Each holds 65,536 values, so the adapter trains 131,072 parameters. The frozen matrix holds 16,777,216, so the adapter is 0.78 percent of it. A doubled rank doubles the adapter, because its size is linear in the rank. The count. Copy Why so few parameters work. The update that fine-tuning makes to a weight matrix has a low intrinsic rank. A rank of 16 or 32 captures most of it. The lesson reports LoRA at rank 16 within about one point of full fine-tuning on the benchmarks it lists. The rank table. Rank Parameters for one 4096 by 4096 matrix 4 32,768 8 65,536 16 131,072 32 262,144 64 524,288 Alpha. The scale alpha / r sets how much the adapter output counts. With alpha equal to the rank, the scale is one; a common convention sets alpha to twice the rank. Alpha changes the effective step size, not the parameter count. Which matrices. The count above is one matrix. Adapters on the query and value projections of every layer are the usual start. Adding the key and output projections and the MLP layers raises quality a little and, on the lesson's 7B table, raises the count from 9.4M to 37.7M. Plausible wrong answers. The LoRA lesson counts the adapter parameters and builds the layer in PyTorch. Take-home Take-home. A company wants a support assistant built from an open 8B base model. They have about 50,000 past support conversations with customer ratings, two 24 GB GPUs, and three weeks. Write the post-training plan on one page: the stages, the data for each stage, the settings you start from, what you measure after each stage, and the three failure modes you guard against. Level 4 of 4 · about 45 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Three stages: first, SFT with QLoRA on the top-rated conversations in one chat template with the loss masked to the assistant turns, at a low learning rate for one to three epochs with a few percent of raw text mixed in, measured by held-out instruction loss, raw-text drift and a sample read. Second, DPO against the SFT checkpoint as the frozen reference, on pairs built from high- and low-rated answers to the same prompt with a conservative beta, measured by a blind pairwise eval and the absolute chosen log-probability, not the training margin. Third, a release gate: a fixed prompt set rated blind, a refusal set, and a comparison with the base model on tasks the data never covered. The guards are catastrophic forgetting, length and agreement exploits in the ratings, and over-optimization of the preference proxy. Stage 0: data. Convert every conversation into one chat template, with a fixed system prompt. SFT set: the top-rated answers, filtered for length, vocabulary diversity and a clean instruction-to-answer ratio. Tens of thousands of clean examples are enough; the reference SFT stage in the lesson used about 27,000. Preference set: for prompts with both a high-rated and a low-rated answer, build prompt, chosen and rejected triples. Where the data is thin, sample the rejected side from the SFT model, so that the pairs are in-distribution for the reference. A rater or a judge must confirm that each sampled answer is worse than the chosen one before it becomes a pair, because the SFT model trained on top-rated answers and its samples can be as good. Aim for the 5,000 to 20,000 pairs where DPO works well. A blind eval set of prompts never used in training, plus a forgetting set of tasks outside support, such as short code and arithmetic. Stage 1: SFT with QLoRA. Two 24 GB cards cannot hold a full update of this model; a 7B full update needs about 56 GB with gradients and optimizer states. QLoRA keeps the base in 4-bit and trains adapters of rank 16 on the attention projections in about 6 GB, so each card runs its own experiment. Start from: the lesson's SFT learning rate of 2e-5 for a full update, with a higher rate for adapters as the LoRA lesson's trainer shows; one to three epochs; 2 to 5 percent raw pretraining text mixed into the batches. Measure: held-out instruction loss, raw-text loss before and after with a budget of a 10 to 15 percent rise, exact match on the templated tasks where it applies, and a read of fifty samples. Stage 2: DPO. Reference: the merged SFT checkpoint, frozen. Policy: a copy with fresh adapters. Beta in the 0.1 to 0.3 range, a few epochs, and the four log-probabilities per pair over the answer tokens only. Measure: a blind pairwise eval against the SFT model on the held-out prompts, the implicit reward margin, the absolute chosen log-probability, the response length by checkpoint, and the forgetting set again. Stop on the eval, not on the margin. Stage 3: release gate. A fixed prompt set rated blind by people, against the SFT checkpoint and the base. A refusal and safety set with the expected behavior written down. The forgetting set. Adapters kept separate for a rollback; a merge only for the shipped artifact. The three guards. Catastrophic forgetting: low rate, short training, a pretraining mix, and a raw-text loss budget. Exploits of the rating signal: raters liked long and agreeable answers, so watch the length and the agreement with the premise, and filter pairs where length alone separates them. Over-optimization of the proxy: the DPO ratio can be pushed off the data, so stop early on the blind eval and keep beta conservative. Schedule. Week one: data and SFT. Week two: DPO and the first blind eval. Week three: the gate, a second seed of the best configuration, and the rollback plan. Plausible wrong answers. "Skip SFT and run DPO on the base model." DPO needs a reference that already follows instructions; the single-stage loss is a different method, and the base model's pairs are out of distribution. "Fully fine-tune the 8B model across both GPUs." A full update of a model this size needs about 56 GB with the optimizer states; two 24 GB cards hold it only with adapters and a 4-bit base. "Use the star ratings as the reward and run PPO." A regression on absolute scores is the weak label the lessons warn about, and the full stack does not fit the compute or the timeline. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why DPO and not a reward model with PPO here? Expected: tens of thousands of pairs, two small GPUs and three weeks fit the DPO regime; a reward model and PPO need three loops and more memory. (level 4) The ratings are one to five stars on single answers, not pairs. What changes? Expected: build pairs only where one prompt has answers at both ends of the scale, or use the unpaired loss that works on good and bad labels and keep the pairs for the eval. (level 4) How do you prove that the DPO stage did not degrade the SFT behavior? Expected: the blind pairwise eval against the SFT checkpoint, the forgetting set, and the absolute chosen log-probability; a margin that grows while those fall is a stop signal. (level 4) What would make you add an RL stage with a verifier? Expected: a part of the task with a checkable answer, such as a correct order number or a passing code snippet, where a binary reward and group-relative advantages give a signal the ratings do not. Estimate it You have one GPU with 24 GB of memory and want to fine-tune a 7B model on your own instruction data. Walk me through the memory for a full update, for LoRA and for QLoRA, and say what makes the last one fit. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A full update of a 7B model needs about 56 GB: the weights in half precision, the gradients, and two optimizer states per parameter, all in half precision. LoRA keeps the half-precision weights but trains only small adapters, so the gradients and optimizer states shrink and the run takes about 18 GB. QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit, about 3.5 GB of weights, and trains the adapters in half precision, so the run takes about 6 GB and leaves room for activations on a 24 GB card. The memory table. Method Weights Training total Fits on Full update, FP16 14 GB about 56 GB before activations, which depend on the workload one 80 GB datacenter GPU LoRA on an FP16 base 14 GB about 18 GB one 40 GB GPU QLoRA, 4-bit base 3.5 GB about 6 GB one 24 GB consumer GPU The 56 GB comes from two bytes per weight, two bytes per gradient, and two optimizer states per parameter; activations come on top of that. This estimate keeps the optimizer states in half precision too. Standard Adam keeps its states in FP32, so a typical full update needs more memory than this, not less. The adapters remove the gradients and the states for every frozen weight, which is the large part. What QLoRA adds. NF4. A 4-bit type whose 16 levels sit at the quantiles of a normal distribution, which matches how weights are distributed and loses less than uniform 4-bit integers. Double quantization. Each block of 64 weights needs a scale in FP32, about 0.4 GB for a 7B model; quantizing the scales to 8 bits brings that down to about 0.1 GB. Paged optimizers. Optimizer states page to CPU memory when the GPU runs out, which trades some throughput for no out-of-memory crash from optimizer states. Activations stay on the GPU, so a long sequence can still run out of memory. What it costs in quality. The lesson's table puts LoRA at rank 16 within about one point of a full update, QLoRA at rank 16 a fraction behind that, and QLoRA at rank 64 level with the full update on the listed benchmarks. What it costs in time and money. On the lesson's cost table, QLoRA at rank 16 on a 24 GB consumer card took about 6 hours and about 5 dollars for 50,000 examples over three epochs. The full update took about 8 hours on two 80 GB datacenter GPUs and about 32 dollars. Fused kernels cut the QLoRA run to about 2.5 hours. Plausible wrong answers. "Quantize the whole model to 4-bit and fine-tune it directly." Gradients and optimizer states still need higher precision; the base stays frozen in 4-bit, and only the adapters train. "QLoRA halves the quality." The lesson's table shows a loss of a fraction of a point at rank 16 and parity at rank 64. "Load the base in 8-bit with LoRA; it is the same thing." Eight-bit weights take twice the memory of NF4, and the double quantization and paged optimizers are what make the 6 GB figure. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does LoRA cut training memory so much more than it cuts weight memory? Expected: the gradients and the two optimizer states exist only for the adapter parameters, which are a fraction of a percent of the model. (level 2) The adapters train in half precision while the base is 4-bit. Where does the forward pass compute? Expected: the base weights are dequantized block by block to the compute dtype for each matrix product, and the adapter path runs in half precision. (level 3) When would you still pay for the full update? Expected: when the task needs changes that a low-rank update cannot express, when you have the data and the GPUs, or when the eval shows a gap that a higher rank does not close. (level 3) How do you serve several QLoRA fine-tunes from one base? Expected: keep the adapters separate and load them on top of one base copy; merge only when you ship a single specialized model. Where it is taught. The LoRA lesson gives the memory and cost tables and explains NF4, double quantization and paged optimizers. Sources and further reading Hu et al., "LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models" (2021) -- the original paper introducing the low-rank decomposition method, tested on GPT-3 175B with rank as low as 4 Dettmers et al., "QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized Language Models" (2023) -- introduces NF4, double quantization, and paged optimizers, enabling 65B fine-tuning on a single 48GB GPU PEFT library documentation (huggingface.co/docs/peft) -- the standard library for LoRA, QLoRA, and other parameter-efficient methods in the Hugging Face ecosystem Yadav et al., "TIES-Merging: Resolving Interference When Merging Models" (2023) -- techniques for combining multiple LoRA adapters without quality degradation Rafailov et al., "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model" (NeurIPS 2023) -- DPO derivation; the preference-tuning stage that comes after SFT, no reward model needed. TRL documentation -- official reference for SFTTrainer , DPOTrainer , KTOTrainer , and the integration surface with PEFT/bitsandbytes/Unsloth. Unsloth documentation -- fused kernels that double fine-tuning throughput and halve memory; the performance layer under TRL. Axolotl documentation -- YAML-configured multi-GPU SFT/DPO/QLoRA trainer; the config-as-code alternative to hand-written scripts. Check your understanding Q1 What is the core insight behind LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)? A Smaller models are always better B Weight updates during fine-tuning have low intrinsic rank, so they can be approximated by two small matrices instead of updating the full weight matrix C Most weights don't matter D Fine-tuning only needs the last layer Aghajanyan et al. showed that fine-tuning updates occupy a low-dimensional subspace. LoRA exploits this by representing the update as W + BA where B (d x r) and A (r x d) have small rank r, typically 8-64. Q2 How much memory does LoRA save compared to full fine-tuning of an 8B model? A Only saves disk space B No savings C From ~56GB down to ~6GB by training <1% of parameters while keeping base weights frozen D 50% reduction Full fine-tuning needs gradients and optimizer states for all 8B parameters (~56GB). LoRA freezes base weights and only trains adapter matrices (~80M parameters at rank 16), needing ~6GB total. Q3 What is QLoRA? A A different fine-tuning algorithm B LoRA applied to quantized activations C Quantized LoRA: the base model is loaded in 4-bit precision while LoRA adapters train in 16-bit, combining memory savings from both techniques D A faster version of LoRA QLoRA (Dettmers et al.) loads the frozen base model in 4-bit (NF4 quantization) while training LoRA adapters in FP16/BF16. This allows fine-tuning a 7B model on a single consumer GPU with 6GB VRAM. Q4 What does the 'rank' parameter (r) in LoRA control? A The learning rate B The number of training epochs C The capacity of the adapter: higher rank captures more complex adaptations but uses more parameters and memory D The number of layers to fine-tune Rank r determines the size of adapter matrices A (r x d) and B (d x r). Rank 4 trains very few parameters (fast, cheap). Rank 64 trains more parameters (more expressive). Most tasks work well with rank 8-32. Q5 What happens when you merge LoRA weights back into the base model? A Merging is not possible B The model becomes larger C The model needs to be retrained D The adapter matrices are added to the base weights (W_merged = W_base + B*A), producing a standard model with no inference overhead Since LoRA adds W_base + B*A, you can compute B*A once and add it to W_base permanently. The merged model has the same architecture and inference speed as the original, with no adapter overhead. a1109: Course home / Phase 11 · LLM Engineering Function Calling & Tool Use Lesson 11.9 75 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Implement a function calling loop: define tool schemas, parse the model's tool-call JSON, execute functions, and return results Design tool schemas with clear descriptions and typed parameters that the model can reliably invoke Build a multi-turn agent loop that chains multiple function calls to answer complex queries Handle function calling edge cases: parallel tool calls, error propagation, and preventing infinite tool loops Before you start Needs : Phase 11 Lesson 03 (Structured Outputs) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line LLMs cannot do anything. They generate text. That is the entire capability. They cannot check the weather, query a database, send an email, run code, or read a file. Every "AI agent" you have ever seen is an LLM generating JSON that says which function to call -- and then your code actually calling it. The model is the brain. Tools are the hands. Function calling is the nervous system connecting them. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Function calling "Tool use" The model outputs structured JSON describing a function to invoke with specific arguments -- your code executes it, not the model Tool definition "Function schema" A JSON Schema object describing a tool's name, purpose, parameters, and types -- the model reads this to decide when and how to use the tool Tool choice "Calling mode" Controls whether the model must call a tool (required), may call a tool (auto), or must call a specific tool (named) Parallel calling "Multi-tool" The model outputs multiple tool calls in a single turn, reducing round trips -- GPT-4o and Claude both support this Tool result "Function output" The return value from executing a tool, sent back to the model as a message so it can use real data in its response Argument validation "Input checking" Verifying that model-generated arguments match the expected types, ranges, and constraints before executing the tool MCP "Tool protocol" Model Context Protocol -- the open standard (created by Anthropic, now under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation) for exposing tools via servers that any compatible client can discover and call Agent loop "ReAct loop" The iterative cycle of model-decides-tool, code-executes-tool, result-feeds-back until the model has enough information to respond Tool poisoning "Prompt injection via tools" An attack where tool results contain instructions that manipulate the model's behavior -- sanitize all tool outputs Rate limiting "Call budget" Setting a maximum number of tool calls per conversation to prevent infinite loops and runaway API costs The problem In plain words first A model cannot look anything up or do anything; it can only write text. Function calling gives it a structured way to ask: you describe your functions (name, purpose, typed arguments), and instead of answering the model may reply with a call such as get_weather(city="Tokyo") . Your code checks the call, runs the function, and sends the result back; the model then answers with real data. The model never executes anything, your code does, which is why validation and allow-lists matter. This lesson builds the loop with a simulated model, then runs it for real: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, whose chat template supports tools, picks tools, fills arguments, makes parallel calls and reads results for six questions. No model is trained. You build a chatbot. A user asks: "What's the weather in Tokyo right now?" The model responds: "I don't have access to real-time weather data, but based on the season, Tokyo is likely around 15 degrees Celsius..." That is a hallucination dressed in a disclaimer. The model does not know the weather. It never will. Weather changes every hour. The model's training data is months old. The correct answer requires calling the OpenWeatherMap API, getting the current temperature, and returning the real number. The model cannot call APIs. Your code can. The missing piece: a structured protocol that lets the model say "I need to call the weather API with these arguments" and lets your code execute it and feed the result back. This is function calling. The model outputs structured JSON describing which function to invoke with what arguments. Your application executes the function. The result goes back into the conversation. The model uses the result to produce its final answer. Without function calling, LLMs are encyclopedias. With it, they become agents. Idea 1 · The Function Calling Loop Every tool-use interaction follows the same 5-step loop. Step 1: the user sends a message. Step 2: the model receives the message along with tool definitions (JSON Schema describing available functions). Step 3: instead of responding with text, the model outputs a tool call -- a structured JSON object with the function name and arguments. Step 4: your code executes the function and captures the result. Step 5: the result goes back to the model, which now has real data to produce its final answer. The model never executes anything. It only decides what to call and with what arguments. Your code is the executor. Idea 2 · Tool Definitions: The JSON Schema Contract Each tool is defined by a JSON Schema that tells the model what the function does, what arguments it takes, and what types those arguments must be. Copy The description fields are critical. The model reads them to decide when and how to use the tool. A vague description like "gets weather" produces worse tool selection than "Get current weather for a city. Returns temperature in Celsius and conditions." The description is a prompt for tool selection. Idea 3 · Provider Comparison Every major provider supports function calling, but the API surface differs. Provider API Parameter Tool Call Format Parallel Calls Forced Calling OpenAI (GPT-6 family) tools function_call output items (Responses API), tool_calls[] (Chat Completions) Yes (multiple per turn) tool_choice="required" Anthropic (Claude Opus/Sonnet/Haiku 5.5) tools content[].type="tool_use" Yes (multiple blocks) tool_choice={"type":"any"} Google (Gemini) function_declarations functionCall Yes function_calling_config Open-weight (Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral) tools passed to the model's chat template Model-specific tags, e.g. <tool_call> JSON for Qwen (Hermes style) Model-dependent Serving engines (vLLM, SGLang) parse calls and support tool_choice The closed providers have converged on near-identical JSON-Schema-based formats. Open-weight models each define their tool format in their chat template, and serving engines translate it into the OpenAI shape. For shared tools across hosts, prefer MCP (Lesson 11.14) over inline function calling: the server is the same for all of them. Idea 4 · Tool Choice: Auto, Required, Specific You control when the model uses tools. Auto (default): the model decides whether to call a tool or respond directly. "What's 2+2?" -- responds directly. "What's the weather?" -- calls the tool. Required : the model must call at least one tool. Use this when you know the user's intent requires a tool. Prevents the model from guessing instead of looking up real data. Specific function : force the model to call a particular function. tool_choice={"type":"function", "function": {"name": "get_weather"}} guarantees the weather tool is called, regardless of the query. Use this for routing -- when upstream logic already determined which tool is needed. Idea 5 · Parallel Function Calling Current GPT, Claude and Gemini models, and many open-weight ones, can call multiple functions in a single turn. A user asks: "What's the weather in Tokyo and New York?" The model outputs two tool calls simultaneously: Copy Your code executes both (ideally concurrently), returns both results, and the model synthesizes a single response. This cuts round trips from 2 to 1; when an agent's calls are independent, the saving grows with their number (worked example below). The same idea as a formula Tool selection is next-token prediction. With tool schemas in the prompt, the model's first answer tokens choose between plain text and a call: The descriptions in are prompt text, which is why wording them well changes which tool gets picked. Latency of an agent turn with independent calls of latencies ​ , … , t k ​ and model round-trip time : ​ = k m + i ∑ ​ t i ​ , T parallel ​ = m + i max ​ t i ​ ( one model turn, calls run concurrently ) . Worked example Three independent lookups Model round trip s; tool latencies 0.3, 0.5 and 0.8 s. Sequential: s. Parallel: s, 62% less. The model still needs one more turn to read the results and answer, in both cases: add 1.2 s to each. Tokens: every tool schema is sent with every request; with three schemas this lesson's 0.5B model sees about 415 prompt tokens for a 10-word question (measured below), almost all of it schemas and the template's tool-use instructions. Check your mental model ✗ "The model calls the API." ✓ The model writes a request; your code decides whether to run it, runs it and returns the result. ✗ "If the model picked a tool, the arguments are safe." ✓ They are model-written text. Validate types, ranges and allow-lists before executing anything. ✗ "Errors should stop the loop." ✓ Return them as structured results; the model can often correct itself, or tell the user honestly. Predict before you run The 0.5B model sees three tools. For "Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?" will it answer directly or call a tool? For "What's the weather in Atlantis?" (a city the weather tool does not know), what will its final answer say? (Solution P1.) Idea 6 · Structured Outputs vs Function Calling Lesson 11.3 covered structured outputs. Function calling uses the same JSON Schema machinery, but for a different purpose. Structured outputs : force the model to produce data in a specific shape. The output is the final product. Example: extract product info from text as {name, price, in_stock} . Function calling : the model declares an intent to execute an action. The output is an intermediate step. Example: get_weather(city="Tokyo") -- the model is requesting an action, not producing the final answer. Use structured outputs when you want data extraction. Use function calling when you want the model to interact with external systems. Idea 7 · Security: The Non-Negotiable Rules Function calling is the most dangerous capability you can give an LLM. The model chooses what to execute. If your tool set includes database queries, the model constructs the queries. If it includes shell commands, the model writes them. Rule 1: Never pass model-generated SQL directly to a database. The model can and will generate DROP TABLE, UNION injections, or queries that return every row. Always parameterize. Always validate. Always use an allowlist of operations. Rule 2: Allowlist functions. The model can only call functions you explicitly define. Never build a generic "execute any function by name" tool. If you have 50 internal functions, expose only the 5 the user needs. Rule 3: Validate arguments. The model might pass a city name of "; DROP TABLE users; --" . Validate every argument against expected types, ranges, and formats before execution. Rule 4: Sanitize tool results. If a tool returns sensitive data (API keys, PII, internal errors), filter it before sending it back to the model. The model will include tool results in its response verbatim. Rule 5: Rate limit tool calls. A model in a loop can call tools hundreds of times. Set a maximum (10-20 calls per conversation is reasonable). Break infinite loops. Idea 8 · Error Handling Tools fail. APIs time out. Databases go down. Files do not exist. The model needs to know when a tool fails and why. Return errors as structured tool results, not exceptions: Copy The model reads this, adjusts its arguments, and retries. Models are good at self-correcting from structured error messages. They are bad at recovering from empty responses or generic "something went wrong" errors. Idea 9 · MCP: Model Context Protocol MCP is the open standard for tool interoperability that Anthropic created in 2024 and, in December 2025, donated to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. Instead of every application defining its own tools, MCP provides a universal protocol: tools are served by MCP servers, consumed by MCP clients (like Claude Code, Cursor, ChatGPT or your application). One MCP server can expose tools to any compatible client. A Postgres MCP server gives any MCP-compatible agent database access. A GitHub MCP server gives any agent repository access. The tools are defined once, used everywhere. MCP is to function calling what HTTP is to networking. It standardizes the transport layer so tools become portable. Step 1 · Define the Tool Registry Build a registry that stores tool definitions and their implementations. Each tool has a JSON Schema definition (what the model sees) and a Python function (what your code executes). Copy Step 2 · Implement 5 Tools Build a calculator, weather lookup, web search simulator, file reader, and code runner. Copy A substring blocklist reads the code as text, so it misses anything the string match does not literally spell. Parsing the code into a syntax tree and walking it lets the guard reject import statements, dunder attribute access (the __class__ and __globals__ chains that reach back to the real interpreter), and unsafe builtin names by structure rather than spelling. Even so, treat this as a teaching filter, not a real boundary. Any in-process guard shares the interpreter with the code it runs, and a determined caller can still find reachable objects. Production systems run untrusted code in a separate process or container (a subprocess with dropped privileges, gVisor, Firecracker, or a hosted code runner), where an escape lands the attacker in a throwaway box instead of your service. Step 3 · Register All Tools Copy Step 4 · Build the Function Calling Loop This is the core engine. It simulates the model deciding which tool to call, executes the tool, and feeds results back. Copy Step 5 · Argument Validation Build a validator that checks tool call arguments against the JSON Schema before execution. Copy Step 6 · Run the Demo Copy See it drawn The loop with a real model Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with three Python functions (weather, currency conversion, calculator), turned into JSON schemas by the chat template from their type hints and docstrings. For each question: the model's tool calls, the results your code returns (allow-listed and validated), and the model's final answer. Greedy decoding. About a minute. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Four of six questions went exactly right. Weather, currency and arithmetic each produced one well-formed call with the right arguments: (17 * 23) + 4 was written as an expression for the calculator instead of being computed by the model, and the answer 395 is correct. Your code, not the model, did the arithmetic and the conversion. Parallel calls work even at 0.5B. "Tokyo and Mumbai" produced two get_weather calls in one turn, and the final answer uses both results. The model also filled in units: "celsius" on its own, a default it read from the docstring. About 415 prompt tokens per request , for questions of about ten words. The three schemas and the template's tool instructions are sent every time, so tool definitions are a fixed cost per call. Fifty tools would cost thousands of tokens before the user has said anything (Lesson 11.5). Not calling a tool is also a decision, and here it went wrong. For "Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?" the model correctly made no call, then claimed it had no information. The answer is Jane Austen, which a 0.5B model usually knows without tools. Having tools in the prompt can make a small model hedge on questions it would otherwise answer. The error was returned, then misread. For Atlantis your code returned a structured error, CITY_NOT_FOUND . The model told the user it lacks access to real-time weather, which is not what the error said. Structured errors help, but you should still check what the model says about them. Some systems turn known error codes into fixed user-facing messages instead of letting the model paraphrase them. Use it: the same idea with real libraries OpenAI Function Calling Copy OpenAI's Chat Completions API returns tool calls as response.choices[0].message.tool_calls (the newer Responses API returns function_call items with a call_id ). Each call has an ID you must include when returning the result; the model uses it to match results to calls. A response can contain several calls: iterate and execute all of them. Anthropic Tool Use Copy Anthropic returns tool calls as content blocks with type: "tool_use" . The tool result goes in a user message with type: "tool_result" . Note the key difference: Anthropic uses input_schema for tool parameter definitions, while OpenAI uses parameters . MCP Integration Copy MCP decouples tool implementation from tool consumption. The Postgres server knows SQL. The GitHub server knows the API. Your agent just discovers and calls tools -- it does not need provider-specific code for each integration. Break it on purpose Give the calculator tool the description "Runs Python" and change its body to eval(expression) with no checks. Ask: "Calculate __import__('os').listdir('.') ". What does the loop do, and which of the five security rules would have stopped it? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Strict tool schemas : OpenAI and Anthropic can enforce tool arguments against the JSON schema ( strict: true ), so arguments always parse; validation of values stays your job. MCP as the tool layer : tools are packaged as MCP servers and shared across clients; the protocol is now governed by the Agentic AI Foundation. Tool search for large tool sets : agents load only the definitions they need per task instead of sending hundreds of schemas on every call. Server-side tools : providers run some tools themselves (web search, code execution, file search) inside the API call. Sources: Anthropic: donating MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation , MCP blog , Claude structured outputs (strict tools) , OpenAI function calling guide , Qwen function calling , Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard . Recap What to keep from this lesson The model proposes calls; your code validates, executes and returns results. Tool descriptions are prompts: they decide which tool gets picked. Independent calls can run in parallel in one model turn. Return errors as structured results; cap the number of calls. Allow-list tools and arguments; never execute model text as code or SQL.
