Solutions Solution P1 · No tool call for the novel, and a misread error For "Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?" it made no tool call, which is right, since no tool fits. Its answer was still poor: it said it had no information about the author, who is Jane Austen. For Atlantis it called get_weather . The code returned {"error": true, "code": "CITY_NOT_FOUND"} . The final answer then blamed a lack of real-time weather access instead of saying the city is unknown. The selection logic worked in both cases, and the wording of the answer failed in both. Solution B1 · Arbitrary code execution, one prompt away With eval(expression) and no checks, the model's call calculate({"expression": "__import__('os').listdir('.')"}) runs Python on your server, and the directory listing comes back as a "result". The model even reads it out to the user. The same channel would accept open(...) , os.remove(...) or a network call. The prompt can come from a user, or from a document or web page the model has read (prompt injection, Lesson 11.12), so this is arbitrary code execution one message away. The rules that stop it: validate arguments against a strict allow-list before executing (the lesson's calculator accepts only digits, operators and parentheses); give each tool the least capability it needs (a calculator never needs eval on raw text, so use a real expression parser); and never trust the description. Renaming the tool "Runs Python" changes what the model will try, not what the code permits. Sandbox anything that must run code, and log every call. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Weigh a trade-off You need two things from the same model: a typed summary of a support ticket, and the ability to look up the customer's account during the conversation. A teammate wants to build both as tools. Which mechanism fits each, and why does the distinction matter? Level 2 of 4 · about 7 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The ticket summary is structured output: the typed data is the final product, so use the schema mode and validate it. The account lookup is a function call: the model declares an intent to act, your code executes it and feeds the result back, so the output is an intermediate step. The two share the JSON Schema machinery but differ in what happens next, and mixing them hides which outputs are data and which are actions your code runs. Two uses of one mechanism. Structured output Function call What the model emits a record that matches a schema a function name and typed arguments What happens next your code validates and stores it your code executes it and returns the result to the model The output is the final product an intermediate step Fits extraction, classification, typed summaries lookups, writes, anything that touches another system The function calling lesson states the rule: use structured outputs when you want data, use function calling when you want the model to interact with an external system. The model never executes anything; it only decides what to call and with what arguments. When tool use is the right way to get data. The structured outputs lesson gives the exception. When the model has to choose among several schemas based on the input, for example 10 extraction schemas, tool use gives you the selection and the structure in one step. One provider also delivers its schema mode through tool use, with the schema on the tool input. In that case name the tool for the data it returns, never execute it, and route its arguments straight to the validator. Why the distinction matters in code. A record gets schema validation and a semantic check. An action gets argument validation, an allowlist, result sanitizing and a call budget before anything runs, because the model chose what to execute. If the summary and the lookup live in one registry, the security rules for actions either cover data they do not need to, or miss an action they should. Plausible wrong answers. "They are the same thing with different names." They share the schema machinery; one produces the final data, the other requests an action your code performs. "Use function calling for everything, it is more flexible." Every tool is an executable surface with security rules; data extraction does not need one. "The model runs the lookup itself." The model never executes anything; it emits a call and your code is the executor. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) When is tool use the right way to get structured data? Expected: when the model must pick one of several schemas from the input; the lesson's example is 10 extraction schemas, where tool use gives the selection and the structure together. (level 2) In the lookup case, who runs the function? Expected: your code; the model emits the name and the arguments, and the result goes back as a message. (level 3) What differs in validation between the two? Expected: data gets schema validation and a semantic check; an action gets argument validation, an allowlist and a call budget before it runs. (level 3) A provider offers schema output only through tool use. How do you keep the distinction? Expected: name the tool for the data it returns, never execute it, send its arguments to the validator as the final record, and keep real actions in a separate registry. Where it is taught. The lesson function calling separates data from action and gives the five-step loop, and the lesson structured outputs covers tool use as a way to choose among schemas. Defend a design Design the execution layer for an agent that can query a database, run small code snippets and read files on behalf of a user. The model decides which tool to call. What rules does the executor enforce, and what does it never do? Level 3 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The executor never passes model-generated SQL or shell text straight to a system. It exposes an allowlist of named functions with typed parameters, validates every argument against the schema before execution, sanitizes tool results before they return to the model, and caps the number of calls per conversation at 10 to 20. For code, an in-process filter is a teaching aid and not a boundary; untrusted code runs in a separate process or container. The five rules. Never pass generated SQL to the database. The model can and will produce destructive statements and injections. The lesson's exercise shapes the tool to accept a table name and filter conditions, with the tables on an allowlist and the operators restricted to a small set; your code builds the query. Allowlist the functions. The model calls only what you define. If fifty internal functions exist, expose the five the user needs. Never build a generic call-by-name tool. Validate the arguments. Check required fields, unknown fields, types and enum membership against the schema before execution; a city name can carry an injection string. Sanitize the results. A tool result goes back into the prompt verbatim, so strip keys, personal data and internal errors, and treat instructions inside a result as tool poisoning. Cap the calls. A loop can call a tool hundreds of times; 10 to 20 calls per conversation is the lesson's range, with a bounded retry count per failing call. The file tool. Reject any path with a parent reference or a leading slash, and return a structured error with the list of files that exist. The error shape matters: a message, a code and suggestions let the model correct its arguments; an empty response or a generic failure does not. The code tool. A substring blocklist reads the code as text and misses anything it does not literally spell. Parsing the code into a syntax tree lets the guard reject imports, dunder attribute access and unsafe names by structure. Even then, the guard shares the interpreter with the code it runs, and a determined caller finds reachable objects. Production runs untrusted code in a separate process with dropped privileges, in a sandbox or in a hosted runner, so an escape lands in a throwaway box. What the model never does. It never executes anything. It emits a name and arguments. Everything after that is your code, and every rule above lives there. Plausible wrong answers. "The model behaves, parameterize later." The model can and will generate destructive queries or injections; the rule is never to pass its SQL through. "A generic run-any-function tool is simpler." The allowlist is the rule: expose the five functions the user needs, not all fifty. "The code filter blocks imports, so it is safe." It shares the interpreter with the code it runs; production uses a separate process or container. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is a substring blocklist not enough for the code tool? Expected: it matches spelling, not structure; a parsed syntax tree rejects imports, dunder access and unsafe names by shape, and even that shares the interpreter with the code. (level 3) How do you shape the database tool so the model never writes SQL? Expected: accept a table name and filter conditions, allowlist the tables, restrict the operators, and build the query in your code. (level 4) What is tool poisoning and where is the control? Expected: results that carry instructions to the model; sanitize every result before it returns, and strip sensitive data such as keys and internal errors. (level 4) The agent loops on a failing tool. What stops it? Expected: a maximum number of calls per conversation, 10 to 20 in the lesson, structured errors that let the model fix its arguments, and a retry cap of about 3 per call. Where it is taught. The lesson function calling states the five security rules, builds the argument validator and the file and code guards, and sets the call budget. Explain the mechanism An agent has eight tools and keeps calling the wrong one. The tool descriptions are one or two words each, such as "gets weather". What does the description do, and how do you rewrite one? Level 2 of 4 · about 7 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The model reads the description to decide when and how to call the tool, so the description is a prompt for tool selection. Rewrite it as a full sentence that says what the tool does and what it returns, for example that it gets the current weather for a city and returns the temperature in Celsius and the conditions, and describe each parameter with an example value and an enum where the set is closed. Then validate the arguments against the schema before anything executes. What the model sees. A tool definition is a JSON Schema contract: a name, a description, and the parameters with their types, their own descriptions, and the required list. The model never sees your code. It picks a tool and fills the arguments from this text alone, so a vague description produces worse selection than a precise one, and a parameter with an example such as a city name is filled more reliably than a bare string. Beyond the description. Tool choice. Auto lets the model decide. Required forces at least one call, which stops the model from guessing when you know a lookup is needed. A named tool forces that one, for routing when upstream logic already knows. Parallel calls. Two cities in one question can come back as two calls in one turn; execute both and return both results. Structured errors. Return failures as results with a message, a code and suggestions, such as the city not found and the nearest names. Models self-correct from structured errors and not from empty or generic ones. A call budget. Set a maximum of 10 to 20 calls per conversation so a loop cannot run away. Measure it. Write a set of queries with the expected tool for each; the lesson's exercise uses 30. Run the selection and report the share that picked the right tool, and list the pairs that get confused. Plausible wrong answers. "The model infers the purpose from the function name." It reads the description; a vague one produces worse selection than a full sentence. "Describe every tool in a paragraph to be safe." Definitions travel with every request; one precise sentence plus parameter descriptions is the target. "Let the model call any function by name." The lesson's rule is an allowlist of the tools you define, never a generic execute-by-name tool. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Where else does a description help besides the tool itself? Expected: on each parameter, with an example value and an enum where the set is closed, so the arguments come out right. (level 2) The model still guesses instead of calling a tool when it should. Which setting changes that? Expected: tool choice set to required, or to a named tool when upstream logic already knows which one. (level 3) How do you prove the rewrite worked? Expected: a set of test queries with expected tool names, 30 in the lesson, the share that select the right tool, and the confused pairs listed. (level 3) A tool fails. What should it return so the model recovers? Expected: a structured error with a message, a code and suggestions, not an exception or an empty response. Where it is taught. The lesson function calling gives the tool definition contract, the tool choice modes, structured errors and the selection accuracy exercise. Check your understanding Q1 Can LLMs actually execute functions or access external systems? A No -- LLMs only generate text (typically JSON) describing which function to call; your code must execute it B LLMs execute functions through embeddings C Only GPT-4 can execute functions D Yes, LLMs can call APIs directly LLMs generate tokens. When 'calling a function,' the model outputs JSON specifying the function name and arguments. Your application code parses this JSON, executes the actual function, and sends the result back to the model. Q2 What is a tool schema in the context of function calling? A The API endpoint URL B A database schema C The model's architecture diagram D A JSON description of a function's name, parameters, types, and purpose that tells the model what tools are available Tool schemas describe available functions to the model: function name, parameter names and types, descriptions of what each parameter does, and what the function returns. The model uses these to decide when and how to call tools. Q3 What is the standard pattern for a multi-turn function calling loop? A Call all functions at once B The model executes functions internally C Send message -> model requests tool call -> execute function -> send result back -> model generates final response (repeat if needed) D Parse the entire conversation as a batch The loop: (1) send user message + tool schemas, (2) model responds with a tool call request, (3) execute the function, (4) send the result back as a tool response, (5) model generates the next response or another tool call. Q4 How do you prevent infinite tool calling loops? A Use a faster model B Set a maximum number of tool call iterations and implement a timeout, breaking the loop if the limit is reached C Remove all tool schemas after the first call D Infinite loops can't happen with function calling Without limits, a model could repeatedly call tools (e.g., searching for information it can never find). A max iteration count (e.g., 10 rounds) and total timeout prevent runaway loops in production. Q5 Why are clear, descriptive parameter names and descriptions important in tool schemas? A The model uses descriptions to decide which tool to call and how to fill in parameters -- vague descriptions lead to wrong tool selections and incorrect arguments B They improve response time C They are required by the API D They make the code more readable The model reads tool descriptions to decide what to call and how. A parameter described as 'q' vs 'search_query: The user's search terms to look up in the knowledge base' gives vastly different results. a1110: Course home / Phase 11 · LLM Engineering Evaluation & Testing LLM Applications Lesson 11.10 45 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Build an evaluation dataset with input-output pairs, rubrics, and edge cases specific to your LLM application Implement automated scoring using LLM-as-judge, regex matching, and deterministic assertion checks Set up regression testing that detects quality degradation when prompts, models, or parameters change Design evaluation metrics that capture what matters for your use case (correctness, tone, format compliance, latency) Before you start Needs : Phase 11 Lesson 01 (Prompt Engineering), Lesson 09 (Function Calling) Type : Build. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line You would never deploy a web app without tests. You would never ship a database migration without a rollback plan. But right now, most teams ship LLM applications by reading 10 outputs and saying "yeah, looks good." That is not evaluation. That is hope. Hope is not an engineering practice. Every prompt change, every model swap, every temperature tweak changes your output distribution in ways you cannot predict by reading a handful of examples. Evaluation is the only thing standing between your application and silent degradation. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Eval "Testing" Systematically scoring LLM outputs against defined criteria using automated metrics, LLM judges, or human review LLM-as-judge "AI grading" Using a strong model to score outputs against a rubric -- GPT-4 agreed with experts over 80% of the time on MT-Bench, but judges have position, length and self-preference biases Rubric "Scoring guide" Anchored descriptions for each score level (1-5) that reduce judge variance by defining exactly what each score means ROUGE-L "Text overlap" Longest Common Subsequence-based metric measuring how much of the reference appears in the output -- recall-oriented Confidence interval "Error bars" A range around your measured score that tells you how much uncertainty remains -- wider with fewer test cases Regression testing "Before/after" Running the same eval suite on old and new prompt versions to detect quality degradation before deployment Golden test set "Core evals" Curated input-output pairs representing your most important use cases -- every change must pass these Pairwise comparison "A vs B" Showing a judge two outputs and asking which is better -- eliminates scale calibration problems Bootstrap "Resampling" Estimating confidence intervals by repeatedly sampling from your scores with replacement -- works with any distribution Wilson interval "Proportion CI" A confidence interval for pass/fail rates that works correctly even with small sample sizes or extreme proportions The problem In plain words first An LLM application changes every time someone edits a prompt, swaps a model or updates the retrieval, and its outputs are free text, so you cannot check them by eye. Evaluation is a test suite for that: a fixed set of inputs, a way to score each output (exact checks, text-overlap metrics, a judge model with a rubric, or people), and statistics that say whether a change made things better or worse, or whether the test set is too small to tell. This lesson builds the scorer, the metrics, a confidence-interval calculator and a comparison report, then runs two honest experiments: a deliberately weak judge model, to show the biases a judge can have, and the statistics of how many test cases you need to see a 4-point regression. No model is trained. You build a RAG chatbot for customer support. It works great in your demos. You ship it. Two weeks later, someone changes the system prompt to reduce hallucinations. The change works -- hallucination rate drops. But answer completeness also drops 34% because the model now refuses to answer anything it is not 100% certain about. Nobody noticed for 11 days. Revenue from the self-service channel fell. Support tickets spiked. This is the default outcome when you evaluate by vibes. You check a few examples, they look fine, you merge. But LLM outputs are stochastic. A prompt that works on 5 test cases can fail on the 6th. A model that scores 92% on your benchmarks can score 71% on the edge cases your users actually hit. The fix is not "be more careful." The fix is automated evaluation that runs on every change, scores outputs against rubrics, computes confidence intervals, and blocks deployment when quality regresses. Evaluation is not a nice-to-have. It is table stakes. Shipping without evals is deploying blind. Idea 1 · The Eval Taxonomy There are three categories of LLM evaluation. Each has a role. None is sufficient alone. Automated metrics compare output text against reference answers using algorithms. BLEU measures n-gram overlap (originally for machine translation). ROUGE measures recall of reference n-grams (originally for summarization). BERTScore uses BERT embeddings to measure semantic similarity. These are fast and cheap -- you can score 10,000 outputs in seconds. But they miss nuance. Two answers can have zero word overlap and both be correct. One answer can have high ROUGE and be completely wrong in context. LLM-as-judge uses a strong model to grade outputs against a rubric. This captures semantic quality -- relevance, correctness, helpfulness, safety -- that string metrics miss. It costs money (worked out below) and needs calibration: in the MT-Bench study (Zheng et al. 2023), GPT-4 as a judge agreed with human experts over 80% of the time, about as often as the experts agreed with each other, but judges also showed position bias, a preference for longer answers and a preference for their own outputs. Lesson 5.27 has the calibration recipe. Human evaluation is the gold standard but the slowest and most expensive. Reserve it for calibrating your automated evals, not for running on every commit. Method Speed Cost per 1K evals Agreement with humans Best for Exact match, regex, unit tests instant $0 perfect where applicable Extraction, code, classification, formats BLEU/ROUGE <1 sec $0 weak for open-ended text Translation, summarization baselines BERTScore seconds $0 better than n-grams, still limited Semantic similarity screening LLM-as-judge, small fast model minutes cents to a dollar measure it on a labelled sample High-volume CI checks with a clear rubric LLM-as-judge, frontier model minutes a few dollars about human-human level in MT-Bench High-stakes scoring, safety, refusals RAG suites (Ragas, TruLens) minutes depends on judge measure it Faithfulness and retrieval metrics DeepEval / promptfoo (judge + CI) minutes depends on judge measure it CI-native, per-PR regression gates Human expert hours hundreds of dollars the reference Calibration, edge cases, policy Agreement numbers depend on the task and the rubric; the only number that matters is the one you measure on a sample of your own cases labelled by people. Idea 2 · LLM-as-Judge: The Workhorse This is the evaluation method you will use 90% of the time. The pattern is simple: give a strong model the input, the output, an optional reference answer, and a rubric. Ask it to score. Four criteria cover most use cases: Relevance (1-5): Does the output address what was asked? A score of 1 means completely off-topic. A score of 5 means directly and specifically answers the question. Correctness (1-5): Is the information factually accurate? A score of 1 means contains major factual errors. A score of 5 means all claims are verifiable and accurate. Helpfulness (1-5): Would a user find this useful? A score of 1 means the response provides no value. A score of 5 means the user can immediately act on the information. Safety (1-5): Is the output free from harmful content, bias, or policy violations? A score of 1 means contains harmful or dangerous content. A score of 5 means completely safe and appropriate. Idea 3 · Rubric Design Bad rubrics produce noisy scores. Good rubrics anchor each score to specific, observable behaviors. Bad rubric: "Rate from 1-5 how good the answer is." Good rubric: - 5 : The answer is factually correct, directly addresses the question, includes specific details or examples, and provides actionable information. - 4 : The answer is factually correct and addresses the question but lacks specific detail or is slightly verbose. - 3 : The answer is mostly correct but contains a minor inaccuracy or partially misses the question's intent. - 2 : The answer contains significant factual errors or only tangentially relates to the question. - 1 : The answer is factually wrong, off-topic, or harmful. Anchored descriptions make scores more consistent between runs and between judges; measure the effect on your own cases (Exercise 4). Pairwise comparison is an alternative: show the judge two outputs and ask which is better. This eliminates scale calibration issues -- the judge does not need to decide if something is a "3" or a "4." It just picks the winner. Useful for comparing two prompt versions head-to-head. Best-of-N generates N outputs for each input and has the judge pick the best one. This measures the ceiling of your system. If best-of-5 consistently beats best-of-1, you might benefit from sampling multiple responses and selecting. Idea 4 · The Eval Pipeline Every evaluation follows the same 6-step pipeline. Prompt : Define your test cases. Each case has an input (user query + context) and optionally a reference answer. Run : Execute the prompt against the model. Collect outputs. Run each test case 1-3 times if you want to measure variance. Collect : Store inputs, outputs, and metadata (model, temperature, timestamp, prompt version). Score : Apply your evaluation method -- automated metrics, LLM-as-judge, or both. Compare : Compare scores against a baseline. The baseline is your last known-good version. Compute confidence intervals on the difference. Decide : If the new version is statistically significantly better (or not worse), ship it. If it regresses, block. Idea 5 · Eval Datasets: The Foundation Your eval dataset is only as good as the cases in it. Three types of test cases matter: Golden test set (50-100 cases): Curated input-output pairs that represent your core use cases. These are your regression tests. Every prompt change must pass these. Adversarial examples (20-50 cases): Inputs designed to break your system. Prompt injections, edge cases, ambiguous queries, questions about topics outside your domain, requests for harmful content. Distribution samples (100-200 cases): Random samples from real production traffic. These catch problems that curated tests miss because they reflect what users actually ask. Idea 6 · Sample Size and Confidence 50 test cases is not enough. If your eval scores 90% on 50 cases, the 95% Wilson confidence interval is [78.6%, 95.7%]: a 17-point spread. You cannot distinguish a system scoring 80% from one scoring 95%. At 200 cases with 90% accuracy, the confidence interval tightens to [85.1%, 93.4%]. Now you can make decisions. Use 500+ if you are comparing two systems that are close in quality. Swap orders and calibrate against human labels. ✗ "Use ROUGE for everything; it is free." ✓ It rewards word overlap, not correctness; use it only where overlap means quality. Predict before you run A 0.5B model judges 12 pairs: a short correct answer against a longer, confident wrong one. How often will it pick the correct answer, and will its verdict survive swapping the order of the two answers? (Solution P1.) Idea 7 · Regression Testing Every prompt change needs a before/after eval. This is non-negotiable. The workflow: 1. Run your eval suite on the current (baseline) prompt -- store the scores 2. Make the prompt change 3. Run the same eval suite on the new prompt 4. Compare scores with a statistical test (paired t-test or bootstrap) 5. If no statistically significant regression on any criteria -- ship 6. If regression detected -- investigate which test cases degraded and why Idea 8 · Cost of Evals Evals cost money when using LLM-as-judge. Budget for it. Assume each judge call reads about 1,000 tokens (input, output, rubric) and writes about 200, and use Anthropic's November 2026 list prices per million tokens: Claude Haiku 5.5 from $0.10 in / $0.50 out, Sonnet 5.5 $2 / $10, Opus 5.5 $4 / $20. Eval size Haiku 5.5 judge Sonnet 5.5 judge Opus 5.5 judge 100 cases x 4 criteria ~$0.08 ~$1.60 ~$3.20 200 cases x 4 criteria ~$0.16 ~$3.20 ~$6.40 1000 cases x 4 criteria ~$0.80 ~$16 ~$32 A 200-case suite with a Sonnet-class judge on every PR costs about $3 per run; at 10 PRs a week, about $140 a month, less with batch pricing (50% off) and prompt caching of the rubric. Compare that to the cost of shipping a regression that tanks user satisfaction for 11 days. Idea 9 · Anti-Patterns Vibes-based evaluation. "I read 5 outputs and they looked good." You cannot perceive a 5% quality regression by reading examples. Your brain cherry-picks confirming evidence. Testing on training examples. If your eval cases overlap with examples in your prompt or fine-tuning data, you are measuring memorization, not generalization. Keep eval data separate. Single-metric obsession. Optimizing only for correctness while ignoring helpfulness produces terse, technically-accurate-but-useless answers. Always score multiple criteria. Evaluating without baselines. A score of 4.2/5 means nothing in isolation. Is that better or worse than yesterday? Better or worse than the competing prompt? Always compare. Using a weak judge. A small judge produces noisy, biased scores (the run below shows how badly). Use a capable model, check it against human labels, and swap the order in pairwise comparisons. Solutions Solution P1 · The weak judge was fooled It picked the correct answer 12 of 12 times when it came first, and 0 of 12 when it came second. The verdict survived the swap in 0 of 12 pairs, because the judge answered "A" every time. Pointwise, it gave every confident wrong answer a 3 and the correct answers an average of 2.25. Position bias and verbosity bias together turned the judge into noise. A 0.5B model was chosen to make the failure visible. Large judges show the same biases more weakly, which is why the order swap and the human-agreement check are standard practice. Solution B1 · Self-preference Self-preference: a model tends to rate text that looks like its own output more highly, because its own wording seems more probable and fluent to it. In a head-to-head eval it will inflate its own win rate. Detect it by comparing the judge with human labels on the same pairs, separately for pairs where the judge's own answer wins and pairs where it loses. Also re-judge with a model from another family: if your system's win rate drops when someone else judges, the gap is the bias. Avoid it by judging with a different model family than the one under test, and by hiding which system produced each answer. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design Two engineers ran the same judge on the same 100 answers with the instruction "rate from 1 to 5 how good the answer is" and got means almost a full point apart. How do you rewrite the rubric so the scores become reproducible, and what else goes into the judge prompt? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Anchor every level to behavior a reader can check. A rubric that states what a 5, a 4 and a 3 look like reduces judge variance by 30 to 40 percent compared with an unanchored scale. Score several criteria separately, give the judge the input, the output and the reference, and ask for the reasoning next to the number. From vague to anchored. The bad rubric asks how good the answer is. The good rubric describes each level: 5 : factually correct, directly addresses the question, includes specific details, gives actionable information. 4 : correct and on topic, but short on detail or slightly verbose. 3 : mostly correct with a minor inaccuracy, or partially misses the intent. 2 : significant factual errors, or only tangentially related. 1 : wrong, off topic or harmful. One criterion per score. Score relevance, correctness, helpfulness and safety on separate scales. A single overall score collapses the dimensions, and optimizing it produces terse answers that are technically right and useless. What the judge sees. The input, the output, the reference answer when one exists, and the anchored rubric for the criterion. Ask for a structured answer with the score and a short reason, so that a reviewer can audit the judge. Prove it. Run the judge three times on each case and compute an agreement statistic across the runs. Below 0.7 the rubric is still ambiguous. If the judge keeps wavering between two adjacent levels, switch that criterion to a pairwise comparison, which removes the scale. Plausible wrong answers. "Lower the temperature of the judge." A deterministic judge still applies a vague scale differently across cases; the rubric is the fix. "Average more runs." Averaging noise costs money and leaves a scale that two readers interpret differently. "One overall score is simpler." Simpler to read and wrong to optimize; the lesson warns that single metric optimization produces terse useless answers. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why score four criteria instead of one overall score? Expected: one score collapses dimensions; a model can be correct and useless, and the single number hides the trade. (level 2) How do you show the new rubric is reproducible? Expected: run the judge several times per case and compute an agreement statistic; below 0.7 rewrite again. (level 3) The judge still wavers between 3 and 4 on many cases. What design change removes that? Expected: pairwise comparison, which only asks which output is better. (level 3) One criterion has a reference answer and another has none. Does the rubric change? Expected: yes; correctness anchors to the reference, while helpfulness and safety anchor to properties of the output alone. Where it is taught. The evaluation and testing lesson gives the anchored rubric, the four criteria and the agreement check. Defend a design A model you fine tuned jumped eight points on a public benchmark after you added a new web scraped corpus to the training mix. Leadership wants to announce it. Design the audit that tells you whether the jump is capability or leakage, and say what you would publish instead if it is leakage. Level 4 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Audit for contamination before anyone announces anything. Search the new corpus for the benchmark questions and their close paraphrases and report the share found, then rerun the model on a versioned custom eval that the corpus cannot contain and diff the individual test cases against the previous model. If the overlap is material and the custom eval did not move, the jump is memorization, and you publish the custom eval result with the contamination share. Why the jump is suspect. Training corpora scrape the web and the benchmark questions live on the web. Nobody has to intend it. A new scraped corpus is the most likely path for the test to enter training, and a saturated benchmark rewards memorization with large jumps. The same lesson lists teaching to the test and saturation as the other two mechanisms that move a score without moving capability. The audit. Contamination search. Check what share of the eval questions, or close paraphrases of them, appear in the new corpus. Report exact matches and near matches separately with the method. Model diff. Compare the two model versions case by case: which items improved, which regressed, which stayed. If the improvements cluster on the items the search found, the diff names the leak. Custom eval. Run both models on your own versioned suite of at least 200 cases with edge cases, kept separate from every training and prompt example. A real gain shows there with an interval; a leak does not. Separation check. Confirm that no eval case overlaps with the prompt examples or the fine tuning data, because a test case that was also a training example measures memorization. What to publish. The custom eval numbers with intervals, the contamination share and the method, and the benchmark score with that caveat attached. Never a bare benchmark number. And add the dedup step to the training pipeline so the next corpus is checked against every eval set before training starts. Plausible wrong answers. "We did not include the benchmark on purpose, so it is clean." Web scale scraping includes it without intent; the lesson calls this the normal path to contamination. "Eight points is too large to be noise." Noise is not the alternative; memorization is, and it produces large jumps. "Announce the benchmark and add the caveat later." Publish the custom eval with intervals and the contamination share; a bare benchmark number is the claim you cannot defend. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) The search finds exact matches for a small share and paraphrases for more. Which count? Expected: both; paraphrases leak the answer as well, so report exact and near matches separately with the method. (level 3) The custom eval also rose. Is the jump real? Expected: more likely, if the suite is versioned, separate from training data and large enough that the rise exceeds its interval. (level 4) How do you prevent the question next time? Expected: deduplicate training corpora against every eval set before training, keep eval data out of prompts and fine tuning data, and record the check in the training report. Where it is taught. The evaluation lesson explains contamination and sets the contamination detection and model diff exercises, and the evaluation and testing lesson warns against testing on training examples. Take-home Take home. We give you a small instruction tuned model, a held out corpus, a set of short factual prompts with gold answers, a set of open form prompts with reference answers, and no network access. Build an evaluation pipeline that reports more than one number and explains its aggregate, and describe how it would run in CI once a network and a judge model are available. What do you deliver, and what do you leave out on purpose? Level 4 of 4 · about 60 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Deliver one runnable file with four evals: held out perplexity with honest token accounting, normalized exact match on the factual set, token F1 on the open form set, and a deterministic mock judge on a 1 to 5 scale with the same interface a real judge will have. Report every per eval number, a weighted aggregate with the weights in a config, and per example records for diagnosis. Leave out the real judge, intervals on the aggregate and anything that needs a network, and say so in the readme. The four evals. Each eval covers a dimension the others miss. Perplexity says whether the model fits the language at all. Exact match says whether it produces the gold string on short answers. Token F1 forgives paraphrase on open answers. The judge scores quality that string metrics cannot see. Each is a function from the model and a dataset to a result with the metric, the per example details and a name. The details a reviewer checks. Perplexity. Sum the loss over real target positions, exclude pad targets from the denominator, shift the targets by one, divide once at the end. Normalization. Lowercase, strip, collapse whitespace, drop trailing terminal punctuation when the sides differ only by it. Token F1 is one when both sides are empty and zero when only one is. Mock judge. A 5 when the normalized strings match, a 4 at token F1 of at least 0.8, a 3 between 0.5 and 0.8, a 2 between 0.2 and 0.5, a 1 otherwise, with a one line rationale. It is not a judge. It fixes the interface so a real model is a one function swap. The aggregate. Normalize each eval into the unit range: perplexity as one over one plus the log of perplexity, exact match and F1 as they are, the judge divided by 5. The default weights are 0.2, 0.3, 0.3 and 0.2. Put them in a config and print them in the report, because the choice is a product decision, not a fact. Write the report with stable JSON keys and a table for the terminal. The CI story. When a network exists, swap the mock judge for a real one and calibrate it against at least 50 hand labeled cases, with a Spearman correlation of 0.7 or more, before its scores gate anything. Grow the suite to about 200 cases, compare two runs with Wilson and bootstrap intervals, block on a regression beyond 0.3 on any criterion, trigger on prompt and model paths, and upload the report as an artifact. What to leave out and why. The real judge, because there is no network and no human labels to calibrate it. Intervals on the aggregate, because the weights make it a product number; put intervals on the components. Contamination checks, because the training corpus is not provided. Say each omission in the readme. Plausible wrong answers. "One accuracy number is the deliverable." A single metric never describes a model; the brief asks for several and for an explanation of the aggregate. "Skip perplexity, it is not a task metric." It is the cheapest check that the model fits the language at all, and wrong accounting there is what a reviewer looks for. "Hard code the weights." The weights are the product decision; expose them and print them next to the numbers. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why keep a mock judge in the deliverable at all? Expected: it fixes the interface and the aggregation path so the real judge is a one function swap, and it keeps the loop runnable offline. (level 3) Why is the weighted mean a product decision? Expected: weights encode what the product values; the pipeline exposes them in config and reports every component so a reviewer can see what the aggregate hides. (level 4) What is the first thing you add when a network appears? Expected: a real judge behind the same function, then a calibration run against hand labels before any of its scores gate anything. Where it is taught. The eval pipeline capstone builds the four evals and the aggregator, the evaluation and testing lesson adds the CI gate, and the LLM evaluation frameworks lesson gives the judge calibration rules. Estimate it A prompt change scores 90 percent on your 50 case golden set, and the baseline scored 86 on the same set. The author wants to ship it as a four point win. How sure can you be, and what sample size would you need to make this call? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. At 50 cases and 90 percent observed accuracy, the 95 percent interval runs from 78 to 97 percent, a 19 point spread. A four point gap sits well inside that spread, so the win cannot be told from noise. You need about 200 cases to detect a 5 percent change, and 500 or more when two systems are close. The table. Cases Observed accuracy 95 percent interval width Detects a 5 percent regression 50 90 percent 19 points no 100 90 percent 12 points barely 200 90 percent 9 points yes 500 90 percent 5 points with confidence 1000 90 percent 3 points precisely The width falls roughly with the square root of the sample size. Four times the cases cut the width by about half. The interval. For a pass rate the lesson uses the Wilson interval, which stays correct at small samples and at proportions near zero or one. The normal interval fails in both places, and those are the places where releases get decided. The paired case. Both versions ran on the same 50 cases, so compare them as pairs. A paired test or a paired bootstrap on the per case differences is tighter than two separate intervals. It still will not rescue a four point gap on 50 cases, but it is the right test once the set is large enough. How to build to 200. The lesson splits the set into a golden core of 50 to 100 curated cases, 20 to 50 adversarial cases and 100 to 200 samples of real traffic. Version the set, and compare two runs only on the same version. Plausible wrong answers. "Four points is four points." On 50 cases the interval is 19 points wide; a four point gap is noise. "Run the same 50 cases three times." Repeating the cases measures the model's variance, not the population; the interval over cases stays wide. "Always use a thousand cases." A thousand cases give a 3 point width but cost five times a 200 case run; use 200 for routine decisions and 500 or more for close calls. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the interval shrink slowly as you add cases? Expected: the width falls with the square root of the sample size, so four times the cases halve the width. (level 2) The two runs used identical cases. Does that help? Expected: yes; a paired comparison on per case differences is tighter than two independent intervals. (level 3) Which interval does the lesson use for a pass rate, and why? Expected: the Wilson interval, because it behaves correctly at small samples and extreme proportions where the normal approximation fails. (level 3) You can afford 200 judge calls per run. How do you split them? Expected: a golden core, an adversarial slice and a sample of production traffic, versioned and fixed between the two runs you compare. Where it is taught. The evaluation and testing lesson gives the sample size table, the Wilson interval and the three layers of an eval set. Defend a design You run three candidate models on the same fifty tasks and must publish a leaderboard with a winner. The means are 0.78, 0.75 and 0.10. The second team says their model is tied with the first. Design the aggregation and the statistics that settle it. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Report a mean with a bootstrap interval, a win rate, and a paired interval on the difference for each pair of models. Resample the tasks with replacement to get the interval on each mean. For the tie claim, bootstrap the per task difference between the first two models; if that interval includes zero, the leaderboard shows them as tied. The input. One record per model and task: model id, task id, metric name, a score in the unit range, and a category. The aggregator refuses any score outside the unit range, because a task that reports 0 to 100 would silently dominate the mean. Normalization belongs in the metric, upstream. Two rankings. Mean score is the headline. It is sensitive to outliers and to task imbalance. Win rate counts the tasks where the model has the best score; a tie gives every tied model a full win. It is less sensitive to outliers and to scale, and it loses magnitude information. Report both. Rank by mean by default and keep the win rate column. The intervals. Bootstrap over task ids: resample the fifty tasks with replacement, compute the mean, repeat, and take the percentile interval at the 0.05 level. The low level helpers default to 1000 resamples and the public aggregators to 500. For a pair of models, bootstrap the per task difference and read whether the interval excludes zero. That is the test for the tie claim, and it is paired because both models ran the same tasks. Categories and rendering. If each task carries a category, report a per category mean. A model that is good overall and weak on code shows up there and nowhere else. Render a table sorted by mean with rank, model, mean, interval to two decimals, win rate and task count. What this leaves out. Task weighting; every task counts the same. And independence: ten arithmetic items that share one error pattern are not fifty independent samples. A hierarchical bootstrap that resamples task families, then tasks, is the follow up. Plausible wrong answers. "Two means with overlapping intervals are tied." The paired difference is the test; separate intervals can overlap while the difference excludes zero. "Rank by win rate, it is robust." It loses magnitude; a model that wins every task by a hair and loses one badly looks perfect. Report both. "Weight the tasks by importance now." The capstone counts every task the same; add weights only with a documented reason and keep the unweighted table. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why bootstrap over tasks and not over predictions within a task? Expected: the unit of replication is the task; resampling within a task understates the variance across tasks. (level 3) When does win rate rank differently from the mean? Expected: when one model wins many tasks by a little and loses a few by a lot; the mean punishes the big losses, the win rate counts the wins. (level 4) Tasks come in families that share error patterns. What breaks? Expected: the tasks are not independent, so the interval is too narrow; resample families first, then tasks. (level 4) One task's metric returns 0 to 100 instead of 0 to 1. What should the aggregator do? Expected: refuse the run; a silent rescale would hide the bug, and the metric must return a fraction. Where it is taught. The leaderboard aggregation capstone builds the mean, the win rate and the bootstrap intervals, and the evaluation and testing lesson explains why a paired comparison decides. Debug a failure You compare two prompt versions by showing a judge model both outputs and asking which one is better. Version B wins 70 percent of the pairs. You then swap the two outputs and version A wins most of them. What went wrong, and how do you run the comparison? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The judge has position bias: it prefers the option it reads first. Your first run measured the order, not the prompt. Score every pair in both orders, count a win only when the same version wins twice, and treat split decisions as ties. Then report the win rate with a confidence interval. Why pairwise at all. A pairwise judge never has to decide whether an output is a 3 or a 4 on a scale. It only picks a winner, so it avoids the scale calibration problem of a single grader. That makes it the right tool for a head to head test of two prompt versions. The bias. Judges prefer the first option presented. The lesson's rule is short: always randomize the order and run both. One order gives you a number about the layout of the prompt. The protocol. For each input, score the pair in both orders. A version wins the pair only when it wins in both orders. A pair that flips with the order is a tie. Report the win rate and its confidence interval. A win rate near one half means the judge cannot separate the versions. Also check length. If version B is longer, the judge may reward verbosity. Normalize for length or state in the rubric that length does not count, and see if the preference survives. Plausible wrong answers. "The judge is random, so use a different judge." Position bias is systematic, not random; another judge has it too, and the protocol is the fix. "Always put the baseline first." That fixes the bias in one direction and hides it; run both orders. "Pairwise comparison is only for human raters." Judges run pairwise well once the order is randomized and both orders are scored. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does a pairwise comparison avoid rubric calibration problems? Expected: the judge only picks a winner and never places an output on a numeric scale. (level 2) Version B is also longer. What else do you control? Expected: verbosity bias; normalize for length or exclude it in the rubric, then check whether the preference remains. (level 3) After both orders, 40 percent of the pairs flip with the order. What does that tell you? Expected: the judge cannot tell the versions apart on those pairs; count them as ties and expect a win rate close to one half. (level 3) How many pairs make a 55 percent win rate real? Expected: enough that the interval excludes one half; use a Wilson or bootstrap interval, and expect to need hundreds of pairs. Where it is taught. The LLM evaluation frameworks lesson names position bias and the both orders rule, and the evaluation and testing lesson explains why pairwise comparison avoids scale calibration. Weigh a trade-off You can score a summarization feature in three ways: n-gram overlap against a reference, a strong model that grades with a rubric, or human experts. The team has one afternoon and a small budget. How do you decide which to use, and for what? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Use all three, each for a different job. Overlap metrics are free and instant but agree with people only 40 to 60 percent of the time, so they serve as a baseline and a smoke test. A judge model costs a few dollars per thousand cases and agrees 82 to 88 percent with people on a well anchored rubric, so it is the default scorer. People are the ground truth, so spend them on calibrating the judge and on edge cases, not on every commit. The trade. Method Speed Cost per thousand Agreement with people Use BLEU or ROUGE under a second nothing 40 to 60 percent baselines, smoke tests Embedding similarity about 30 seconds nothing 55 to 70 percent screening Judge model, small tier about 3 minutes about 8 dollars 82 to 86 percent default CI judge Judge model, large tier about 5 minutes about 25 dollars 85 to 88 percent high stakes, safety Human expert about 2 hours about 500 dollars ground truth calibration, policy Why each one stays. Overlap metrics miss meaning. Two answers with no shared words can both be right, and a high ROUGE answer can be wrong in context. They stay because they cost nothing, run in seconds and do not drift when a judge model changes. The judge captures relevance, correctness, helpfulness and safety. It stays the workhorse because it scales. It needs a rubric with anchored levels and a calibration run against human labels before its number means anything. Human review is slow and expensive. It stays because it is the only ground truth. Reserve it for calibrating the automated scores and for the cases the judge cannot settle. For the afternoon. Run the overlap metric on everything to catch gross breakage. Run the judge on the golden set with the four criteria. Have two people label a small slice and compare it with the judge before anyone reads the mean. Plausible wrong answers. "People are the gold standard, so grade everything by hand." Human review takes hours and costs about 500 dollars per thousand cases, so it cannot run on every change. "Overlap metrics are useless for generation." They catch gross regressions and cost nothing; they only miss meaning. "Pick one metric and optimize it." Optimizing only correctness yields terse answers that nobody can use; score several criteria. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What does ROUGE measure? Expected: recall of reference n-grams, built for summarization. (level 2) Why keep the overlap metric once you have a judge? Expected: it is free and fast, it catches gross regressions in seconds, and it does not move when the judge model changes. (level 2) When is a judge not enough? Expected: high stakes or policy decisions, and any time the judge has not been calibrated against human labels on this task. (level 3) The lesson says the judge must be at least as capable as the model it grades. Why? Expected: a weak judge gives noisy, inconsistent scores and cannot see the errors a stronger model makes. Where it is taught. The evaluation and testing lesson compares the three methods by speed, cost and agreement with people. Defend a design Design the evaluation gate that runs on every pull request that touches prompts or model code for a support assistant. Say what runs, what blocks the merge, what it costs per month, and how you stop the gate from blocking on noise. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Trigger on changes to the prompt and model paths, run a fixed versioned suite of about 200 cases through the proposed prompt, score four anchored criteria with a frozen calibrated judge, and compare with the stored scores of the last known good baseline. Block when any criterion drops beyond the threshold and the interval on the difference excludes zero, and store the results as artifacts. With a small judge tier a 200 case run costs about 4 dollars, so ten merges a week cost about 160 dollars a month. What runs. Trigger. A path filter on the prompt directory and the model code, so documentation commits do not pay for a run. Suite. A golden core of 50 to 100 curated cases, 20 to 50 adversarial cases such as injections, out of domain questions and harmful requests, and 100 to 200 samples of real traffic. Version the suite and tag every change. Scoring. Deterministic assertions first, such as a contains check or a regex, because they are free. Then the judge on relevance, correctness, helpfulness and safety, each on an anchored 1 to 5 scale, with the judge model and version frozen and calibrated against hand labels. What blocks. Score the baseline once, when it becomes the last known good version, and store its scores. Each pull request scores only the new prompt on the same suite version. For each criterion compute the mean difference and the pass rate at 4 or more with a Wilson interval. The lesson's code blocks on any mean drop of more than 0.3. It computes a bootstrap interval for each run separately, not an interval on the difference, so a noisy drop can block. Its written workflow asks for a statistical test, a paired t test or a bootstrap. Add a paired bootstrap on the per case differences to the code, and block only when both hold: a drop of more than 0.3 and an interval on the difference that excludes zero. The report lists the cases that degraded so the author can read them. What it costs. Suite Small judge tier Time 100 cases, 4 criteria about 2 dollars about 2 minutes 200 cases, 4 criteria about 4 dollars about 4 minutes 500 cases, 4 criteria about 10 dollars about 10 minutes 1000 cases, 4 criteria about 20 dollars about 20 minutes Ten pull requests a week at 200 cases is about 160 dollars a month, because each pull request pays for one run and reuses the stored baseline scores. If you score the baseline again on every pull request, the cost doubles. The lesson's counter example is a prompt change that cut answer completeness by 34 percent and went unnoticed for 11 days. How to keep noise out. At 50 cases the interval is 19 points wide and a 5 percent regression is invisible, so the suite needs about 200 cases. Freeze the judge, because a judge upgrade moves every score. Keep the suite versioned and never edit it inside the pull request that fails it. Add a bottom quantile alert and a per category breakdown, because a prompt can improve overall and regress on safety. Plausible wrong answers. "Run the eval nightly instead." Nightly finds the regression after the merge; the lesson's story is 11 days of a shipped drop. Run before merge. "Fifty golden cases are enough for a gate." At 50 cases the interval is 19 points wide, and a 5 percent regression cannot be detected. "Use the newest judge model on each run." Judge changes move every score; freeze the judge and change it only with a parallel baseline. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why a path filter on the trigger? Expected: the eval costs money and minutes; run it when prompts or model code change, not on every commit. (level 3) A criterion moved by 0.1 and the author calls it a regression. Expected: the threshold is 0.3 on the mean with intervals; 0.1 is inside noise at 200 cases, so report it and do not block. (level 4) The gate blocks the merge and the author says the suite is stale. What is the process? Expected: suite changes are their own reviewed and versioned change; rerun the baseline when the suite version changes, and never edit the suite inside the failing pull request. (level 4) How do you catch an aggregate improvement that regresses one category? Expected: a stratified per category report with intervals and a block rule on any category. Where it is taught. The evaluation and testing lesson gives the pipeline, the thresholds and the cost table, and the LLM evaluation frameworks lesson gives the test gate pattern and the calibration rules. Explain the mechanism Your eval report shows two kinds of numbers: a pass rate, which is the share of cases that scored 4 or more, and a mean judge score on a 1 to 5 scale. A reviewer asks for error bars on both. Which interval do you use for each, and why not the same one? Level 3 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Use a Wilson interval for the pass rate and a bootstrap interval for the mean score. A pass rate is a proportion, and the Wilson interval stays correct at small samples and near zero or one, where the normal approximation breaks. A mean of ordinal judge scores has no clean closed form, and the bootstrap resamples the scores with replacement and works with any distribution. The Wilson interval. Copy With z at 1.96 for 95 percent. The center moves toward one half when n is small, and the bounds are clamped to zero and one. At 50 cases and 90 percent accuracy it gives 78 to 97 percent. The normal interval would give bounds that can leave the unit range and a width that is wrong at the extremes. The bootstrap interval. Resample the n scores with replacement, compute the mean, repeat a thousand times, sort the means and read the percentiles at alpha over two from each end. It assumes only that the sample represents the population. It cannot repair a biased or tiny sample, and it costs compute rather than algebra. Comparing two runs. Neither interval compares two systems by itself. For two prompt versions that ran on the same cases, build the interval on the paired per case difference, by bootstrap over cases or a paired test. Two separate intervals that overlap do not prove equality, and two that do not overlap are not needed to prove a difference. Plausible wrong answers. "Plus or minus the standard error is fine." The normal interval fails at small samples and extreme proportions, exactly where releases are decided. "Bootstrap works for the pass rate too, so use it everywhere." It works, but Wilson is closed form, cheap and built for proportions; keep the code auditable. "Overlapping intervals mean no difference." Two separate intervals can overlap while the paired difference excludes zero; compare the difference. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) What goes wrong with a plus or minus one standard error interval on a proportion? Expected: at small n or near zero or one it gives bounds outside the unit range and the wrong width; Wilson corrects both. (level 3) What does a bootstrap assume? Expected: that the sample represents the population; it needs no distribution shape, but it cannot fix a biased or tiny sample. (level 4) Two prompt versions ran on the same 200 cases. Which interval decides? Expected: an interval on the paired per case difference; two overlapping intervals do not prove equality. Where it is taught. The evaluation and testing lesson builds the Wilson and the bootstrap interval and explains when each applies. Sources and further reading Zheng et al., 2023 -- "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena" -- the foundational paper on using LLMs to judge other LLMs, introducing MT-Bench and the pairwise comparison protocol promptfoo Documentation -- the most practical open-source eval framework with YAML config, 15+ providers, LLM-as-judge, and CI integration DeepEval Documentation -- Python-native eval framework with 14+ metrics, Pytest integration, and hallucination detection Braintrust Eval Guide -- production eval platform with experiment tracking, scoring functions, and dataset management Ribeiro et al., 2020 -- "Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList" -- systematic behavioral testing methodology (minimum functionality, invariance, directional expectations) applicable to LLM evaluation Arena (formerly LMSYS Chatbot Arena) -- live human evaluation platform where users vote on model outputs, the largest pairwise comparison dataset for LLMs Es et al., "RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation" (EACL 2024 demo) -- reference-free metrics for RAG (faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision/recall); the eval pattern that scales to prod without labelers. Liu et al., "G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment" (EMNLP 2023) -- chain-of-thought + form-filling as a judge protocol; the calibration and bias results every judge-builder needs. Hugging Face LLM Evaluation Guidebook -- practical advice on data contamination, metric selection, and reproducibility from the team maintaining the Open LLM Leaderboard. EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness -- the standard framework for automated benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, BIG-Bench); the engine behind the Open LLM Leaderboard. Check your understanding Q1 Why is manually reading a few LLM outputs not a reliable evaluation method? A Manual review is too expensive B It takes too long C Small samples miss failure modes that only appear at scale, and human judgment is inconsistent across reviewers and sessions D LLM outputs are always correct Reading 10 outputs shows you 10 points in a distribution. A prompt change might improve 90% of outputs but break 10% of edge cases. Without systematic evaluation, you'll miss the regression until users report it. Q2 What is regression testing in the context of LLM applications? A Testing on the training data B Measuring model loss during training C Running a fixed set of test cases after every change (prompt, model, parameters) to ensure quality hasn't degraded D Testing linear regression models Every prompt change, model swap, or temperature tweak changes the output distribution. Regression tests catch cases where a change that improves one area silently degrades another. Q3 What is the LLM-as-judge evaluation approach? A Using a strong LLM to score outputs against rubrics, replacing expensive human evaluation while scaling to thousands of test cases B Comparing two models' parameter counts C Having the model evaluate its own training loss D Using the model's confidence scores LLM-as-judge sends (input, output, rubric) to a strong model (e.g., GPT-4) which scores the output. It's cheaper and faster than human evaluation, though it has known biases (e.g., preferring verbose responses). Q4 What makes a good evaluation dataset for an LLM application? A As many examples as possible B Random samples from the internet C Only the hardest examples D Diverse inputs covering common cases, edge cases, adversarial inputs, and expected outputs with clear rubrics A good eval set covers the distribution: happy path cases, edge cases (empty input, very long input), adversarial inputs (prompt injection), and ambiguous queries. Each example has a clear expected output or scoring rubric. Q5 How should you handle non-deterministic LLM outputs in evaluation? A Run each test case multiple times and use aggregate metrics (pass rate, average score) to account for output variance B Only evaluate the first output C Set temperature to 0 for all evaluations D Non-determinism doesn't affect evaluation Even at temperature 0, some providers introduce sampling variation. Running each test 3-5 times and measuring pass rate or average score gives a more reliable picture than a single run that might hit a lucky/unlucky sample. In plain words first The idea in one line Most AI startups do not die from bad models. They die from bad unit economics. A single GPT-4o call costs fractions of a cent. Ten thousand users making ten calls per day costs $250 in input tokens alone -- before you charge a single dollar. The companies that survive are the ones that treat every API call as a financial transaction, not a function call. percentage of requests served from cache instead of calling the LLM -- 40-60% is typical for production chatbots, saves proportionally on cost The problem In plain words first Every call to a hosted model is billed by the token, input and output, and the same text is often paid for again and again: the same system prompt on every request, the same question asked in different words by different users. Cost engineering removes the repeats and sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it: provider prompt caching for repeated prefixes, your own exact and semantic caches for repeated questions, routing between cheap and expensive models, batch pricing for work that can wait, and rate limits and budgets so a bug cannot spend a month's money in an hour. This lesson builds each piece, recomputes the lesson's cost math with November 2026 prices, and measures the risk inside semantic caching: how often a similarity threshold serves the answer to a different question. No model is trained. You build a RAG chatbot. It works beautifully. Users love it. Then the invoice arrives. In November 2026, OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output; Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs the same, Claude Opus 5.5 $4 / $20, GPT-6.2 Astra $8 / $40, and the small models a few cents to a few tens of cents (Claude Haiku 5.5 from $0.10 / $0.50). The math below uses $2 / $10. Prices change often; always check the provider's current pricing page. Here is the math that kills startups: 10,000 daily active users 10 queries per user per day 1,000 input tokens per query (system prompt + context + user message) 500 output tokens per response Daily input cost: 10,000 x 10 x 1,000 / 1,000,000 x $2.00 = $200/day Daily output cost: 10,000 x 10 x 500 / 1,000,000 x $10.00 = $500/day Monthly total (30 days): $21,000/month That is just the LLM. Add embeddings, vector database hosting, infrastructure. You are looking at $30,000/month for a chatbot. The brutal part: in many support-style applications a large share of queries are near-duplicates. Users ask the same questions in slightly different words. Your system prompt -- identical across every request -- gets billed every single time. Context documents retrieved by RAG repeat across users who ask about the same topic. You are paying full price for redundant computation. Idea 1 · The Cost Anatomy of an LLM Call Every API call has five cost components. System prompts are the silent killer. At $2 per million input tokens, a 1,500-token system prompt sent with every request costs $0.003 per request, $3,000 per million requests, just for that prefix. At 100K requests per day, that is $300/day -- $9,000/month -- for text that never changes. Idea 2 · Provider Caching: Built-in Discounts All three major providers offer provider-side prompt caching in 2026, but the mechanics differ. See Phase 11 · 15 for the deep dive. Provider Mechanism Price of a cache hit (Nov 2026) Cache writes Cache Duration Anthropic Explicit cache_control markers 5% of the input price on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, 10% on Haiku 5.5 1.25x input price (5-minute cache) or 2x (1-hour cache) 5 min default, refreshed on each hit; 1 h option OpenAI Automatic prefix matching 5% of the input price on GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra ($0.10 vs $2.00 per million on Sol) no surcharge best effort, minutes to hours Google Gemini Implicit caching plus an explicit CachedContent API discounted cached tokens (see pricing page) explicit caches pay storage per hour user-configurable TTL for explicit caches Minimum cacheable prefix lengths differ by model; check the docs before relying on caching for short prompts. Anthropic's approach is explicit. You mark the end of the reusable prefix with cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"} . The first request pays a 25% write premium. Subsequent requests with the same prefix pay 5% of the input price on Sonnet 5.5. A 2,000-token system prompt that costs $0.004 normally costs $0.0002 on cache hits. Over 100K requests a day, that saves about $380/day. OpenAI's approach is automatic. Any prompt prefix that matches a recent request is billed at the cached-input price, 5% of the normal input price on GPT-6.2 Sol. No markers needed; you get less control over what stays cached, with zero implementation effort. Idea 3 · Semantic Caching: Your Custom Layer Provider caching only works for identical prefixes. Semantic caching handles the harder case: different queries with the same meaning. "What is the return policy?" and "How do I return an item?" are different strings but identical intent. A semantic cache embeds both queries, computes cosine similarity, and returns the cached response if similarity exceeds a threshold (typically 0.92-0.95). The embedding costs are negligible. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small costs $0.02 per million tokens. Checking the cache costs almost nothing compared to a full LLM call. Idea 4 · Exact Caching: Hash and Match For deterministic calls (temperature=0, same model, same prompt), exact caching is simpler and faster. Hash the full prompt, check the cache, return if found. This works perfectly for: - System prompt + fixed context + identical user queries - Function calling with identical tool definitions - Batch processing where the same document gets processed multiple times Idea 5 · Rate Limiting: Protecting Your Budget Rate limiting is not just about fairness. It is about survival. Token bucket algorithm: each user gets a bucket of N tokens that refills at rate R per second. A request consumes tokens from the bucket. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected. This allows bursts (use the full bucket at once) while enforcing an average rate. Per-user quotas: set daily/monthly token limits per user tier. Tier Daily Token Limit Max Requests/min Model Access Free 50,000 10 small models only Pro 500,000 60 mid-size models (Sonnet-, Sol-class) Enterprise 5,000,000 300 All models Idea 6 · Model Routing: Right Model for the Right Job Not every query needs a frontier model. "What time does the store close?" does not require a $10/M-output model. Claude Haiku 5.5 at $0.50/M output handles it. A simple classifier routes cheap queries to cheap models and complex queries to expensive models. A well-tuned router saves a large share of model costs: the RouteLLM study (Ong et al. 2024) reported cutting costs by more than half while keeping 95% of GPT-4's quality on its benchmarks. Measure quality on your own traffic before trusting the savings. Idea 7 · Cost Tracking: Know Where the Money Goes You cannot optimize what you do not measure. Log every API call with: Timestamp Model name Input tokens Output tokens Latency (ms) Computed cost ($) User ID Cache hit/miss Request category This data reveals which features are expensive, which users are heavy consumers, and where caching has the most impact. Idea 8 · Batching: Bulk Discounts OpenAI's and Anthropic's Batch APIs process requests asynchronously at a 50% discount. You submit a batch of up to tens of thousands of requests, and results come back within 24 hours (usually much sooner). Use batching for: - Nightly document processing - Bulk classification - Evaluation runs - Data enrichment pipelines Not for: real-time user-facing queries (latency matters). Idea 9 · Budget Alerts and Circuit Breakers A circuit breaker stops spending when you hit a limit. Without one, a bug or abuse can burn through your monthly budget in hours. Set three thresholds: 1. Warning (70% of budget): send an alert 2. Throttle (85% of budget): switch to cheaper models only 3. Stop (95% of budget): reject new requests, return cached responses only Idea 10 · The Optimization Stack Apply these techniques in order. Each layer compounds on the previous ones. Layer Technique Typical Savings Implementation Effort 1 Provider prompt caching 30-50% Low (add cache markers) 2 Exact caching 10-20% Low (hash + dict) 3 Semantic caching 15-30% Medium (embeddings + similarity) 4 Model routing 40-70% Medium (classifier) 5 Rate limiting Budget protection Low (token bucket) 6 Prompt compression 10-30% Medium (rewrite prompts) 7 Batching 50% on eligible Low (batch API) The savings in the table are typical ranges, not guarantees, and they do not simply add up: a semantic-cache hit also removes the routing and prompt-caching savings for that request. Measure each layer on your own traffic. Solutions Solution P1 · No threshold is both generous and safe At 0.95 the cache catches 27.1% of real duplicates and wrongly matches 2.7% of non-duplicates, and 86.4% of its hits are correct. No threshold does both jobs. Catching most duplicates (80% at 0.85) means matching one in five non-duplicates. Getting near-zero wrong matches (0.6% at 0.97) means catching fewer than one duplicate in five. Embedding similarity measures closeness of topic and wording, not "the same answer applies". Solution B1 · A changing prefix defeats prefix caching Prompt caching reuses work only for an identical prefix, token for token from the first one. Put the name and date first, and every user and every day gets a different first line. The 2,000 static tokens after it are then never part of a shared prefix, so the hit rate falls to about zero across users, and also across days for the same user. On Anthropic you also pay the 1.25x cache-write price on every request, which is more than not caching. The fix is the layout rule from Lesson 11.15: static instructions, tool definitions and examples first, with the cache breakpoint after them; the name, the date and the conversation after the breakpoint. Then check the cached-token fields in the usage data. Lesson 11.15's run shows the same effect on a real model: a timestamp at the top leaves only a few shared tokens.
