Add a tool registry (from Lesson 11.9 ) to the service. When a user asks a question that requires external data (weather, calculation, search), the pipeline should detect this, execute the tool, and include the result in the prompt. Add a tools_used field to the response. Build a cost alerting system. Track cost per user per day. When a user exceeds $0.50/day, switch them to gpt-4o-mini . When total daily cost exceeds $100, activate emergency mode: cache-only responses for repeated queries, gpt-4o-mini for everything else, reject requests over 2,000 input tokens. Test with a simulated traffic spike. Implement prompt versioning with rollback. Store all prompt versions with timestamps. Add an endpoint that shows quality metrics (latency, user ratings, error rate) per prompt version. Implement automatic rollback: if a new prompt version has 2x the error rate of the previous version over 100 requests, automatically revert. Add OpenTelemetry tracing. Instrument every component (cache lookup, guardrail check, LLM call, cost calculation) as a separate span. Each span records its duration. Export traces to the console. Show the full trace for a single request, with each component's contribution to total latency visible. Solutions Solution P1 · Jitter served everyone Without jitter, 150 of 200 are served and 50 give up: every retry wave arrives at the same instant (170 requests at the first retry against a capacity of 30), so only 30 get through per wave, and four retries are not enough. With full jitter all 200 are served, the largest retry burst is 24, and the last success comes after about one second instead of fifteen. Solution B1 · Timeouts shorter than the work multiply the cost Every attempt is cut off at 2 seconds, so all four attempts (the first plus 3 retries) fail and the user waits about 8 seconds plus backoff for an error message, longer than the 6 seconds the answer needed. You typically pay for all four partial generations, since providers still bill the tokens generated before the connection closed, and the provider sees four times the load. Set timeouts from measured latency (for example the 99th percentile plus a margin), stream so slow answers still show progress, and treat a timeout as a reason to fall back to a faster model, not to repeat the same slow request. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design A regression ships. One of your prompts starts to leak fake customer identifiers in about one answer in a hundred. Design the observability pipeline so that an alert reaches a person within five minutes of the first bad answer, and say what each stage adds to that clock. Level 3 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Instrument every model call with GenAI-convention spans and ship them over OTLP to a collector. Run a cheap pattern check on every output at the collector, run a judge over the sampled traces on a short schedule, write the scores back as eval spans, export the aggregates as metrics, and alert when the leak score crosses a threshold. The five minutes are the sum of the scrape interval, the judge batch window and the alert routing, so each stage has to be short, and the sampler must keep enough traffic to see a one-in-a-hundred event. The five-minute target covers only the leaks that the pattern flags or the sampler keeps. The stages and their share of the clock. Stage What it adds Time it costs instrumentation and OTLP export the span with the output seconds collector with tail sampling the decision to keep the trace seconds, plus the buffer wait pattern check on the output an instant flag for identifier shapes none worth counting judge over sampled traces a score for leaks the pattern misses the batch window eval spans and metrics export the aggregate the alert reads the scrape interval alert rule and routing the page the evaluation interval plus routing The capstone's eval job reads the last fifteen minutes of sampled traces. For a five-minute target, the judge has to run every minute on the newest traces, or the batch window alone eats the budget. Make the rare event visible. At one leak in a hundred, a sampler that keeps a tenth of the successes sees one leak in a thousand answers. At high volume that is fine, and at low volume it is blind. Run a pattern check for identifier shapes on every output at the collector, as the production application capstone does in its output guardrail, and keep every trace that the check flags. The judge then scores the paraphrased leaks on the sampled share only. A paraphrased leak in an unsampled trace gets no score and fires no alert. The alert chain. Eval scores land as eval spans linked to the parent trace. A metrics exporter aggregates them, an alert rule fires when the leak score in a window crosses the threshold, and the alert manager routes warnings to chat and critical breaches to the pager. Prove it. The capstone's regression probe injects a bug that leaks fake identifiers in one percent of answers and measures the time from deployment to the alert. Detection is the part of the recovery that the dashboard owns. The fix is the rollback, and that belongs to the release path. Plausible wrong answers. "Run the judge on every trace." At volume that costs more than the model calls. Sample, and filter with a cheap check first. "A daily eval report is enough." A day of leaked identifiers is the incident. The target is minutes. "The pattern check catches everything." Patterns miss paraphrases. The judge catches what the pattern misses, and the pattern keeps the judge affordable. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which stage usually dominates the five minutes? Expected: the judge batch window. A job that runs every fifteen minutes cannot meet a five-minute target. (level 3) The sampler drops nine of every ten successes. What happens to detection when the leak rate is one percent? Expected: it sees one leak in a thousand answers, so at low traffic the detection takes longer. Keep every trace that a cheap pattern check flags. (level 4) How do you prove the pipeline meets the target? Expected: inject the regression on purpose, as the capstone does, and measure the time from the deployment to the alert. Where it is taught. The observability dashboard capstone builds the ingest, eval and alert chain and measures detection time with an injected regression, and the production app lesson gives the pattern-based output guardrail. Read the code This function from the production app picks the prompt version for a request. Explain what it does, why it hashes the user id together with the experiment name, and what the number 10 in the experiment config means for one user over a week. python AB_EXPERIMENTS = { "general_chat_v2_test": { "template": "general_chat", "control": "v1", "variant": "v2", "traffic_pct": 10, }, } def select_prompt(template_name, user_id, variables): versions = PROMPT_TEMPLATES.get(template_name) if not versions: raise ValueError(f"Unknown template: {template_name}") version = "v1" for exp_name, exp in AB_EXPERIMENTS.items(): if exp["template"] == template_name: bucket = int(hashlib.md5(f"{user_id}:{exp_name}".encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 100 if bucket < exp["traffic_pct"]: version = exp["variant"] else: version = exp["control"] break template = versions.get(version, versions["v1"]) return template, template.template.format(**variables) Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The code hashes the user id plus the experiment name, takes the result modulo 100, and sends the users whose bucket falls below the traffic percentage to the variant. The hash is deterministic, so one user lands in the same arm on every request for the life of the experiment. The experiment name in the hash keeps the buckets of two experiments independent, so the users who saw the variant in one test are not the same users in the next. With a traffic percentage of 10, about a tenth of the users see the variant on every request all week, and the others never do. Line by line. The default version is v1 , so a template with no experiment always resolves. The loop finds the experiment for this template and stops at the first match. One experiment per template at a time. The bucket is a hash of user_id:exp_name , read as an integer and reduced modulo 100. That gives a value from 0 to 99. A bucket below traffic_pct gets the variant, and every other bucket gets the control. The template renders with the request variables. Why the hash is deterministic. The lesson is explicit: hash the user id, do not draw at random. A random draw per request would flip one user between the two prompts, so the user would see two behaviors and the per-user metrics would mix both arms. A stable arm per user also makes the exposure count a count of users, which the experiment analysis needs. Why the experiment name is in the key. Without it, the bucket of a user is the same in every experiment, so the same tenth of the users would be the variant group every time. Experiments would be correlated, and the effects of one would carry into the next. The experiment name acts as a salt that gives each experiment its own split. What to watch. The modulo 100 gives steps of one percent. A smaller share needs a larger modulus. The demo runs 1000 synthetic user ids through the selector and prints the control and variant shares. That is a cheap sample ratio check, and it belongs in a test. The break means that a second experiment on the same template never runs. The config shape makes that visible, but nothing warns you. Plausible wrong answers. "A random draw below the percentage would be simpler and the same." It assigns per request, so one user flips between arms and sees both prompts. "The hash function is weak, so the assignment is broken." The hash is not a security control here. It only has to be deterministic and well spread. "The percentage is the share of requests." It is the share of users, because the bucket is per user and stays fixed. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does a user stay in the same arm across requests? Expected: the hash of the same user id and experiment name gives the same bucket every time. (level 2) Two experiments are configured for the same template. What happens? Expected: the loop takes the first match and breaks, so the second experiment never assigns anyone. (level 3) Why not hash the user id alone? Expected: the same users would land in the variant of every experiment, so the experiments would be correlated and carry-over effects would mix the results. (level 3) How does the demo check the split, and what would you add? Expected: it runs 1000 synthetic ids through the selector and prints both shares. Add the same check on real exposure logs as a sample ratio check. Where it is taught. The production app lesson builds the prompt router with hash-based experiment assignment and checks the split in its demo. Debug a failure During a provider slowdown, the provider began to return rate-limit errors. Within minutes your own service ran out of memory and crashed, although your incoming traffic had not changed. Reconstruct what happened, and fix the retry policy. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The gateway retried every rate-limited call, and each waiting retry kept its connection, its buffers and its request state in memory. The retries multiplied the in-flight concurrency several times over the real traffic, and the memory went with it. Fix the policy with exponential backoff and jitter, a small fixed number of attempts, a cap on in-flight requests, and a fallback chain that fails over instead of waiting. The chain of events. The provider returns 429 for a share of the calls. The gateway retries each one. Each retry holds a connection, a buffer and the request state while it waits. In-flight requests become the traffic multiplied by the attempts. The chaos lesson names this retry-amplified concurrency. Memory follows the in-flight count, and the service that was healthy a minute ago runs out. The retry policy in the production application capstone. Exponential backoff with jitter: wait about 1 second, then 2, then 4, with a random spread added to each wait, and give up after 3 retries with a fallback response. The lesson's table separates the cases: Failure Retry Fallback 429, rate limit yes, with backoff queue the request and tell the user it is in progress 500, server error yes, 3 attempts switch to the fallback model timeout over 30 seconds yes, 1 attempt a shorter prompt or a smaller model The jitter matters as much as the backoff. Without it, every client retries at the same instant and the provider sees a wave on each cycle. Bound the concurrency, not only the attempts. Attempts bound the retries of one request. Nothing bounds how many requests wait at once. Add a cap on in-flight requests at the gateway and a retry budget as a share of traffic. When the cap is reached, fail fast into the queue or the fallback instead of holding memory. The fallback chain. Primary model, then a secondary model, then a cached response, then a short unavailable message. Each step trades quality for availability, and the user always gets something. Test it before the next slowdown. The chaos lesson's first model-specific experiment injects a provider rate-limit for a few minutes and watches the fallback. Most teams learn there that the fallback was never fully exercised. Plausible wrong answers. "Retry faster so the queue drains before memory runs out." Faster retries raise the request rate against a provider that is already limiting you. "Raise the maximum retries so users never see an error." Each attempt holds memory. More attempts multiply the in-flight state. "The provider caused the outage, there is nothing to fix here." The provider caused the errors. The retry policy turned them into an outage. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does backoff alone not stop the memory growth? Expected: backoff spreads the retries in time, and each waiting retry still holds its state. The fix needs a bound on in-flight requests. (level 3) What does a queue do that a retry does not? Expected: it stores the request without a connection or a worker, and it gives the user a progress message instead of a timeout. (level 4) The fallback model is cheaper and weaker. Who decides that it is acceptable, and how do you watch it? Expected: the product owner names the paths that may degrade. Log the fallback rate per path, and alert when it stays high. Where it is taught. The production app lesson gives the backoff, the retry limits and the fallback chain, and the chaos engineering lesson names the retry storm as the failure to test. Debug a failure An experiment assigns users evenly to control and variant. After a week the dashboard shows 47 percent of users in control and 53 percent in the variant, and the variant is ahead on the primary metric. What do you conclude, and what do you do next? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Do not read the result. A configured even split that delivers 47 to 53 over a week of traffic is a sample ratio mismatch, which means the assignment or the logging is broken and the two groups are no longer comparable. Find the cause in the assignment path, fix it, and start the experiment again. What the check says. An assignment hash puts each user into an arm. Over a week, the delivered split should sit very close to the configured one. When it does not, the lesson's answer is blunt: something is broken. Both experiment platform types in the lesson run this check for you, and it belongs in front of every readout. Why the win is void. Whatever lost users from one arm can be correlated with the outcome. If slow clients fail before they log an exposure in one arm, that arm looks faster and happier. The measured lift is then the dropout, not the variant. No correction after the fact restores the randomization. Where to look. The assignment function. The production application capstone assigns with a deterministic hash of the user id, so that one user stays in one arm. A random draw per request, or a hash on a field that changes, breaks the split. Exposure logging. One arm may drop events, for example when the variant path logs after a call that can fail. Client errors. A variant that crashes before it logs removes its users from the count. Bots and retries. A bot or a retry loop that lands in one arm inflates it. Caches. A cache in front of the assignment can serve one arm's decision to many users. Then. Fix the cause, discard the data, and restart. Pre-register the mismatch check so that it blocks the readout automatically, and nobody has to argue about a winning variant. Plausible wrong answers. "Three percent is within noise." Over a week of traffic, that gap under a fair split is very unlikely, and the mismatch check exists to flag exactly this case. "The variant wins by more than the gap, so ship it." The gap can be correlated with the outcome, so the lift can be the dropout itself. "Drop variant users until the groups match." Removing users after the fact adds a second bias on top of the first. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why hash the user id instead of drawing an arm at random on each request? Expected: the same user lands in the same arm on every request, so the experience is consistent and the exposure count is per user. (level 3) Name two causes that put more users in the variant than in control. Expected: a logging failure that drops control exposures, or a variant path that treats bots or retries differently. (level 3) Can you correct the mismatch statistically and keep the result? Expected: no. The mismatch shows that the groups are not comparable, and no correction restores the randomization. Where it is taught. The A/B testing lesson defines the sample ratio mismatch check, and the production app lesson hashes the user id to pick an arm. Defend a design A new version of a chat prompt looks better in a notebook. Design how it reaches users: the stages, how users are assigned, what you measure at each stage, and when it rolls back automatically. Level 2 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Run it in shadow first, on all traffic, logging its answers without showing them, and compare quality metrics with the current prompt. Then route a small share of users to it, 10% in the lesson, and widen in steps to 25%, 50% and 100% while the metrics hold. Assign by a deterministic hash of the user id so each user sees one version, and roll back automatically when the new version's error rate reaches twice the old one over a window of requests. Shadow mode. The new prompt runs on 100% of traffic but only its logs are kept. Nobody sees its output. This gives a full comparison of latency, cost per request, guardrail block rate and quality scores against the current version, and users never see a shadow answer. Shadow calls can share the provider quota with live calls, so give them a separate quota or key; otherwise a quota limit can slow or fail live requests. It is the same first stage that the ML design lesson calls shadow deployment for a model. Percentage rollout. Route 10% of traffic to the new version. If quality holds, raise it to 25%, then 50%, then 100%. If quality drops, switch back at once. Both versions stay deployed and the switch is configuration, so a rollback takes minutes, which is the lesson's rule for every stage. Deterministic assignment. Hash the user id combined with the name of the experiment and take it modulo 100. Buckets below the traffic share get the variant, the rest get the control. A user then sees the same version across requests inside one experiment, and the assignment can be recomputed later from the log. Random assignment per request mixes versions inside one conversation and makes the comparison noisy. What to measure. Per prompt version: latency percentiles, user ratings where they exist, error rate, guardrail block rate and cost per request. The eval logger records the template name and version with every request, so the metrics split by version without extra plumbing. Automatic rollback. The lesson's exercise sets the rule: when a new version shows 2x the error rate of the previous version over 100 requests, revert automatically. The window matters; a handful of requests is noise, and waiting for thousands lets a bad prompt run too long. A note on the business metric. Shadow and canary protect the user. Whether the new prompt improves the outcome that matters, such as task completion, needs a randomized split with enough traffic and time, which is the A/B stage from the ML design lesson. Plausible wrong answers. "Ship to everyone and watch the dashboard." A regression then hits every user before the dashboard moves. "Assign per request at random for a cleaner statistic." Users see both versions in one conversation and the logged metrics mix them. "Shadow mode is enough; skip the canary." Shadow mode never shows the output to a user, so it cannot measure user reaction. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why hash the user id and not pick randomly per request? Expected: a user then gets one consistent version across a session and the assignment is reproducible from the log. (level 2) What does shadow mode not tell you? Expected: how users react to the new answers; it only compares logged outputs and system metrics. (level 3) The new prompt costs more per request but scores higher. Who decides? Expected: a guardrail on cost per request decides whether it can ship at all; the quality gain against the cost is then a product decision with both numbers on the table. (level 3) How do you keep the control and the variant from sharing a cache entry? Expected: include the prompt version in the cache key, otherwise a hit returns the other version's answer and the comparison is corrupted. Where it is taught. The production LLM application lesson describes shadow mode, percentage rollout and hashed assignment for prompts, and the ML system design lesson gives the same three stages with the rollback rule for models. Defend a design Design the service behind a chat product with 10,000 daily active users who send about 5 queries each, with roughly 1,500 input tokens and 400 output tokens per query. Users must see a response start quickly, the tail must stay bounded, and the product has a unit cost target. Lay out the request path, the components, the budgets you hold each one to, and how you would scale it. Level 3 of 4 · about 25 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The request enters through a gateway that authenticates and rate limits per user, passes input guardrails, is matched against a semantic cache, and on a miss goes to the model with streaming, then through output guardrails, an eval logger and a cost tracker. The budgets are a median under 2s, a p99 under 10s, a cache hit rate above 30%, a guardrail block rate under 5%, and a cost per request under $0.01. At 50,000 queries a day this runs on a few async servers behind a load balancer; the servers are I/O bound, so a single async process holds a hundred or more concurrent requests and scaling means more servers, not more cores. The path. Gateway for authentication, rate limits of 10-50 requests a minute per user and CORS; input guardrails for injection patterns and personal data; a prompt router that picks the template and version; a semantic cache keyed by query embedding with a similarity threshold and a time to live; the model call with streaming and a fallback chain; output guardrails; an eval logger; a cost tracker; a server-sent events response. Seven components, each one a known piece; the engineering is the wiring and the budgets. Budgets. Metric Target Why Median latency Under 2s The typical experience p99 latency Under 10s The tail drives churn Cache hit rate Above 30% Direct cost savings Guardrail block rate Under 5% Higher means false positives Cost per request Under $0.01 Unit economics Streaming puts the first token inside the median budget even when the full answer takes seconds. Maximum token limits on input and output bound both the cost and the tail. Every external call has a timeout. Load and capacity. Traffic is 50,000 queries a day, and with the measured cache hit rate about 32,500 reach the model. Peak matters more than the average; size for the busiest minute. The servers wait on network I/O, so one async process serves 100+ concurrent requests and a box with four workers serves 400+. The lesson's scaling table puts this tier at a few async servers with a cache and a queue, for about $500 a month of infrastructure, with the model bill on top. Connection pooling to the provider avoids a new TLS handshake per request, which costs 100-200ms. Work that is not interactive, such as summarization, goes to a queue with workers and a job id the client polls. Observability. Every request writes one structured log line with the request id, the user, the template and version, the model, the input and output token counts, the latency, the cache result, the guardrail results and the cost. Traces across the components show where the time went. The five numbers in the table sit on one dashboard. If the model is self-hosted. The pipeline lesson's serving stage adds continuous batching, speculative decoding, and KV cache eviction, with quantized weights for serving and the eval gate rerun on the quantized model. The same gateway, cache and guardrails sit in front of it. Before launch. The deployment checklist has fifteen items; the ones people skip are per-user rate limits, maximum token limits, a health endpoint that reports dependency status, timeouts on every external call, and a load test with 100 concurrent users. Plausible wrong answers. "Scale the model servers first." The service is I/O bound at this traffic; the gateway, cache and async servers are the design, and the model is a dependency. "Skip the cache; the model is the product." A third of the traffic repeats, and the cache is the largest single saving in the bill. "The p99 is a vendor problem." Timeouts, maximum tokens, streaming and the fallback chain are what bound the tail on your side. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) A user pastes a document far longer than the context window. Where is that caught? Expected: at the maximum input token limit before the model call, with a clear error, not at the provider. (level 3) Why does cost per user matter when cost per request is already under target? Expected: a few heavy users dominate the bill; per-user tracking and a daily cap move them to a cheaper model or stop them. (level 4) The provider has a regional outage during the daily peak. Walk the request path. Expected: backoff and retries on the primary, fall through the chain to a second model, then cached answers for repeated queries, then an unavailable message; the cost tracker shows the fallback's price and the dashboard shows the step that answered. (level 4) How do you prove the service meets its budgets before the first user? Expected: a load test at 100 concurrent users against the staging stack with the dashboard metrics as pass criteria, plus a shadow run of the prompts on logged traffic. Where it is taught. The production LLM application lesson gives the architecture, the budgets, the scaling table and the checklist, and the complete LLM pipeline lesson describes the serving stage behind a self-hosted model. Explain the mechanism You built a small web demo of a model for reviewers. Three months later a colleague asks whether it is "production". How do you tell, and what changes when the answer is yes? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A demo serves known people in short sessions from one process. It has become a product when people outside the team use it every week, when someone asks for an uptime target or reports an outage, when users want to sign in or see history, when the weekly model cost is a budget line, or when the input is covered by a contract or a law. At that point the demo moves onto the production stack with authentication, fallback models, tracing, and cost tracking per user. The five signals. People outside your team use it every week. Someone asks for an uptime target, or reports an outage. Users ask to sign in, save results, or see their history. The weekly model cost is a line in a budget. The input includes data that a contract or a law covers. What changes. Property Demo Product Users Known people, short sessions Unknown people, daily use State None Accounts, history, saved results Availability Best effort, one process A written target, replicas, an on-call owner Cost control One daily usage cap Per-user quotas and billing Observability One log record per request Traces, metrics, and alerts What the demo already had. A good demo already had the small versions of these controls: an input limit, a per-client rate limit, a daily cap, and a log that keeps the input length and not the text. The product stack adds real authentication at the gateway, a fallback model chain for provider failures, traces across the components, and cost accounting per request and per user. The input limit and the log privacy carry over unchanged. Why the question matters. The dangerous state is the middle: a demo with product traffic and demo controls. One daily cap does not stop one tenant from using the whole budget, and one process has no replica to take over when it dies. Plausible wrong answers. "It is production when it runs on a server instead of a laptop." Where it runs does not decide; who depends on it does. "Add a disclaimer that it is a demo." A disclaimer does not stop traffic, cost or outages. "Keep the demo and build the product separately later." The signals mean the demo already carries product risk now. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which single signal is the strongest? Expected: an outage report, because it means someone depends on the demo and expects availability. (level 2) The weekly model cost appears in a budget. What control replaces the daily cap? Expected: per-user quotas and billing, so the total is attributed and limited per tenant. (level 2) Regulated data starts arriving in the input. What must the log do? Expected: keep no input text and no client address, with a retention period and access control on the records. Where it is taught. The model demo interfaces lesson lists the signals and the demo-to-product table, and the production LLM application lesson describes the stack the demo moves onto. Estimate it A chat feature expects 10,000 daily active users with 5 queries each, about 1,500 input tokens and 400 output tokens per query, at $2.50 per million input tokens and $10.00 per million output tokens. Measured cache metrics give a 35% hit rate. Walk me through the monthly estimate, and say which number you would attack first. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The traffic is 50,000 queries a day, and a 35% cache hit rate leaves 32,500 that reach the model. Over 30 days that is $3,656 of input and $3,900 of output, about $7,556 a month, against $11,625 without the cache, so the cache saves about $4,070. Output tokens cost four times more per token, so after the hit rate the output length is the number to attack, with a maximum output tokens limit and tighter prompts. The sheet. Variable Value Daily active users 10,000 Queries per user per day 5 Input tokens per query 1,500 Output tokens per query 400 Input price per million $2.50 Output price per million $10.00 Cache hit rate 35% Effective daily queries 32,500 Input: 32,500 queries a day times 1,500 tokens times 30 days, divided by a million, times $2.50 gives $3,656. Output: the same with 400 tokens and $10.00 gives $3,900. The total is $7,556 a month. Why the cache matters this much. The same traffic without caching costs $11,625. A 35% hit rate removes 35% of the model calls, so it removes 35% of the token cost. The cache is an embedding lookup with a similarity threshold and a time to live, so two differently phrased versions of one question return one answer. The hit rate is measured from the cache metrics, not assumed. Which number to attack. Hit rate first: every point of hit rate is a point off the whole bill. Output length second: output tokens are priced four times higher than input, and a maximum output tokens limit per template bounds the worst case. Input length third: the system prompt and retrieved context sit in every call; a provider-side cache of the fixed prefix and tighter retrieval cut it. Model routing last: a smaller model for simple templates cuts the per-token price, with an eval to prove quality holds. Where the estimate goes wrong. The averages hide a tail. A few users who paste long documents or run scripts can dominate the bill, which is why the production checklist tracks cost per user and per request, and why the cost alerting exercise moves a heavy user to a cheaper model past a daily threshold. The target in the lesson's dashboard is a cost per request under $0.01. Plausible wrong answers. "Multiply users by a cost per user from a vendor page." The bill comes from tokens per query, queries per user and the hit rate; each is measured. "Caching saves money only on exact repeats." A semantic cache matches similar queries by embedding, which is why the hit rate reaches a third of traffic. "Input tokens dominate because there are more of them." At these prices and lengths the output line is larger even though there are fewer output tokens. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which single metric on the dashboard tells you the estimate holds? Expected: cost per request, which combines token counts and prices and has a target under $0.01. (level 2) The cache hit rate drops to zero after a prompt template change. Why? Expected: the cache key is the query embedding and the response was generated with the old template; stale entries are invalid or the time to live cleared them. (level 3) How does prompt caching on the stable prefix change the input line? Expected: the system prompt and fixed instructions are billed at a discount when they repeat, so the effective input price per query falls without changing the token count. (level 3) What does a per-user daily cap protect that a per-request cost target does not? Expected: the total from one heavy user; many cheap requests still sum to a large bill. Where it is taught. The production LLM application lesson works through this cost projection and the metrics dashboard. Defend a design An engineering organization wants to ask questions across 10 repositories with about 2M lines of code and get answers that cite file and line. The index must stay fresh on every push. Design the ingestion, the retrieval, the answer step, the freshness path, and the evaluation, with the budgets you would commit to. Level 3 of 4 · about 25 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Parse each file into function and class nodes and chunk at those boundaries, give each chunk a dense embedding, sparse terms and a one-sentence summary, and store a graph of imports and calls between chunks. A query runs dense and sparse search in parallel, merges and deduplicates, reranks the top 50 with a cross-encoder to keep 10, and hands those to a long-context model that must cite every claim by file and line; uncited claims are dropped. A push triggers a symbol-level diff so only changed chunks re-embed, with a budget of under 60 seconds for a 50-file push. Quality is measured on 100 labeled cross-repo questions with MRR@10, nDCG@10, citation faithfulness and p50 and p99 latency. Ingestion. A push webhook starts a worker that collects the changed files. A parser with grammars for the languages in the fleet extracts function and class nodes with their full source span. Chunks follow node boundaries, not fixed token windows. Each chunk gets three representations: a dense code embedding, sparse terms in a field-weighted index with symbol names weighted 4, bodies 1 and summaries 2, and a one-sentence summary written by a small model with the system preamble cached. A symbol graph records imports, calls and inheritance across files and repositories, used at query time to expand retrieval across repo boundaries. The summary is the third retrievable modality: a user asks how something is authorized, the code says check_permission , and the summary says authorization. Retrieval and answer. Fire dense and sparse search in parallel, deduplicate by repository, path and symbol. Rerank the top 50 with a cross-encoder and keep the top 10. Call the synthesizer with the reranked chunks and a cached system prompt, requiring a file and line anchor on every claim. Parse the output and check each anchor against the span at the indexed commit; a claim without an anchor, or with a span that is missing or does not support it, is re-asked or dropped. Only verified claims return. Naive cosine search alone is poisoned by generated boilerplate, monorepo duplication and rarely imported symbols, which is why the hybrid search, the reranker and the graph exist. Freshness. On each webhook compute the symbol-level diff. Re-embed only the chunks whose text changed, recompute the import, call and inheritance edges of the changed symbols, and delete the chunks, summaries and edges of removed files and symbols from every store. The budget is a 50-file push searchable in under 60 seconds for the whole fleet, without reprocessing the 2M lines. Evaluation and budgets. Weight Criterion Measure 25 Retrieval quality MRR@10 and nDCG@10 on 100 held-out questions 20 Citation faithfulness Share of claims with a verifiable file and line anchor 20 Latency and scale p95 query latency at 10k QPS on the indexed corpus 20 Incremental indexing Time from push to searchable on a 50-file commit 15 Answer formatting Clickable citations, snippet previews, follow-up affordance A weekly rerun of the 100 questions with an alert on an MRR@10 drop above 5% catches drift in the index or the models. The service around it. The query path sits inside the production stack from the application lesson: a gateway with per-user limits, guardrails on input and output, streaming of the answer, structured logs per retrieval and synthesis step, and cost tracking that attributes the summary model, the embeddings, the reranker and the synthesizer separately. Plausible wrong answers. "A million-token context window replaces retrieval." Context helps but does not rank; cross-repo questions still need retrieval and citations. "Dense embeddings alone are enough for code." Exact symbol names need the sparse index, and the summary catches intent that the code text does not state. "Re-index the fleet on every push to keep it simple." Reprocessing 2M lines per commit blows the freshness budget; the diff keeps the index consistent at a fraction of the work. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why chunk at syntax nodes instead of fixed token windows? Expected: a window cuts functions in half and mixes neighbors; a node is one coherent unit with a stable symbol name to cite and deduplicate on. (level 3) What does the reranker add that the two retrievers cannot? Expected: it scores each query and candidate pair together, which is more accurate than cosine on separate embeddings, at a cost that only the top 50 can afford. (level 4) Generated boilerplate makes up a fifth of the corpus. What happens and what do you change? Expected: retrieval poisoning, where near-duplicate generated code crowds the results; flag generated chunks in the payload and down-weight them. (level 4) A question needs code from four repositories. Which component carries that? Expected: the symbol graph expands the candidate set across import and call edges, so the reranker sees chunks from repositories the first search missed. Where it is taught. The RAG over a codebase capstone gives the ingestion, the hybrid retrieval, the citation rule, the freshness budget and the rubric, and the production LLM application lesson gives the service around the query path. Defend a design Design the request path of a chat service that calls a hosted model. Users leave when nothing appears for a few seconds, the provider returns rate limits and server errors at night, and the vector store behind retrieval sometimes times out. Cover what the user sees, how you retry, and what happens when each part fails. Level 2 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Stream tokens over server-sent events so the first token appears in a few hundred milliseconds even though the full answer takes seconds. Retry provider failures with exponential backoff and jitter, capped at three retries, then fall through an ordered chain of models to a cached answer and finally a short unavailable message. Secondary systems degrade instead of failing the request: no retrieval context when the vector store is down, a direct model call when the cache is down, and a clear message when a guardrail blocks. Streaming. A response of a few hundred output tokens takes 3-8 seconds to finish. Without streaming the user watches a spinner for all of it. With streaming the first token arrives in 200-500ms, the total time is the same, and the perceived latency drops. Server-sent events are the default: one direction, over plain HTTP, consumed by the browser's event source or any HTTP client. Websockets are for two-way needs such as voice, and long polling is for clients that cannot do either. Three layers of failure. Layer Example Recovery Provider 429 rate limit, 500 server error, timeout Backoff with jitter, then the fallback chain Model Malformed JSON, invented function name Retry once with the error in the prompt Application Vector store slow, cache down, guardrail exception Degrade: skip the secondary system Backoff starts at one second, doubles on each attempt and adds random jitter so that many clients do not retry in step. Three retries is the cap; after that the request moves to the next model. Every external call has a timeout, with a default around 30s. The fallback chain. Primary model, then a cheaper or more available model, then a smaller one, then a cached response, then the unavailable message. Each step trades quality for availability. The user always gets something, and the log records which step answered so the cost tracker and the quality dashboard can attribute it. Degradation table. 429: retry with backoff; queue the request and tell the user it is processing. 500: retry up to three times, then switch model; transparent to the user. Timeout: one retry with a shorter prompt or a smaller model. Malformed output: retry with the error attached, else return the raw text. Guardrail block: no retry; explain why the request was blocked. Vector store down: no retry on the store; answer without retrieval context. Cache down: no retry on the cache; call the model directly. The user-visible contract. The dashboard targets are a median under 2s and a p99 under 10s. Streaming moves the first-token time inside the median target even when the full response does not. A streamed response has one trap: the status line is sent before the first token, so a failure after that must be sent as an error event inside the stream. Plausible wrong answers. "Retry until the provider answers." Unbounded retries pile up during an outage; cap them and fall through the chain. "If retrieval is down, fail the request so the answer stays grounded." A secondary system must not take down the primary flow; answer with reduced context and log it. "Buffer the whole response and send it at once for simplicity." The user sees nothing for seconds and leaves; the total time is the same either way. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why add jitter to the backoff? Expected: many clients that fail at once would otherwise retry at the same instants and reproduce the overload. (level 2) Why is a guardrail block not retried? Expected: the input is the problem; retrying the same input gives the same block and spends a call. (level 3) The fallback model has a different price. Where does that show up? Expected: in the cost tracker per request and per model, so the dashboard shows the cost of the outage, not only its rate. (level 3) The stream has started and the model fails. What can the server still do? Expected: send an error event inside the stream, because the HTTP status is already committed. Where it is taught. The production LLM application lesson gives the streaming protocols, the three failure layers, the backoff schedule and the fallback chain. Check your understanding Q1 What is the biggest gap between an LLM demo and a production LLM application? A The model quality B Infrastructure: error handling, streaming, cost tracking, rate limiting, fallbacks, observability, and graceful degradation under load C The choice of API provider D The prompt quality A demo calls an API and prints the response. Production must handle timeouts, provider outages, concurrent users, cost budgets, streaming delivery, logging, and graceful degradation. The model is the easy part. Q2 Why is streaming token delivery important in production LLM applications? A It improves model accuracy B It uses less memory C Users perceive the first token arriving quickly as faster, even if total generation time is the same -- reducing perceived latency from seconds to milliseconds D It reduces cost Without streaming, users wait 3-10 seconds seeing nothing before the full response appears. With streaming, the first token arrives in ~200ms and text flows continuously, making the experience feel responsive. Q3 What should happen when your LLM API provider has an outage? A Retry indefinitely until the provider recovers B Show users an error page C The application should automatically fall back to an alternative provider or return a graceful degraded response D Switch to a local model Production systems need fallback strategies: try Provider B if Provider A fails, serve cached responses for common queries, or return a helpful 'temporarily unavailable' message. Never let a provider outage crash your application. Q4 What observability metrics should a production LLM application track? A Only error counts B Only model accuracy C Request latency (P50/P95/P99), cost per request, error rates, token usage, cache hit rates, and quality scores from automated evals D Only monthly cost Comprehensive observability covers: latency percentiles (for SLA compliance), cost tracking (for budget management), error rates (for reliability), token usage (for optimization), and quality metrics (for regression detection). Q5 Why should you implement rate limiting in your LLM application? A To make the application seem exclusive B To prevent individual users from exhausting your API budget, protect against abuse, and ensure fair access during high traffic C To reduce model accuracy D Rate limiting is only needed for free tiers Without rate limiting, a single user (or bot) can exhaust your daily API budget in minutes. Rate limiting protects your costs, prevents abuse, and ensures all users get reasonable response times during peak load. a1114: Course home / Phase 11 · LLM Engineering Model Context Protocol (MCP) Lesson 11.14 75 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Distinguish an MCP host, client, server, transport, and server primitive. Build a JSON-RPC request with the metadata required by MCP 2026-07-28. Use server/discover to inspect versions, identity, and capabilities. Return typed and cache-aware results from tools, resources, and prompts. Explain how modern stateless MCP interoperates with handshake-era servers. Choose safe state, transport, and approval boundaries for a server. Before you start Needs : Phase 11 · 09 (Function Calling), Phase 11 · 03 (Structured Outputs) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line MCP gives an AI host one protocol for discovering and invoking tools, resources, and prompts. The 2026-07-28 revision makes that protocol stateless: capability and version context travels with every request, not in a connection-bound handshake. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means MCP "Tool protocol for LLMs" JSON-RPC protocol for server discovery, tools, resources, prompts, and extensions Host "The AI app" Owns the model and UI and mounts one or more MCP clients Client "The connector" Speaks MCP to one server on behalf of a host Stateless MCP "No session" Every request carries version and capabilities; no protocol state is keyed by a connection server/discover "Capability probe" Required server method advertising versions, capabilities, and identity resultType "Result state" Marks a result as complete or input_required State handle "Workflow id" Server-minted application identifier passed as an ordinary argument Streamable HTTP "Remote transport" One POST endpoint with JSON or request-scoped SSE responses MRTR "Ask and retry" Input request embedded in a result, followed by a retry of the original operation The problem In plain words first Every AI application needs to reach tools and data: databases, calendars, files, internal APIs. Without a shared protocol, every application writes its own adapter for every system. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is that shared protocol: a server describes its tools, readable resources and prompt templates in a standard JSON-RPC format, and any MCP client can discover and use them. The current revision, 2026-07-28, makes MCP stateless: there is no opening handshake or session, and every request carries its own protocol version and client capabilities. This lesson builds a server and client from the standard library, then runs the lesson's server as a real separate process over a stdio pipe and shows the actual messages, including what the server does with a request that has no metadata, an old protocol version, or the old handshake. Your application needs a database query, a calendar operation, and a file reader. Without a shared protocol, every AI host needs custom discovery, invocation, errors, transport, and authorization glue for those same capabilities. MCP reduces that integration matrix. A server publishes a standard JSON-RPC surface. A compliant client can discover the surface, present it to a model or user, invoke it, and interpret the result without a server-specific adapter. The important boundary is easy to miss. MCP standardizes communication. It does not decide which tool the model should call, make untrusted content safe, or turn a stateless request into durable application state. Your host and server still own those decisions. The idea Idea 1 · The three server primitives Tools are callable actions. Each tool has a name, description, JSON Schema input, and handler. Resources are named, URI-addressed content that a client can read. Prompts are reusable templates that a host can expose to a user. The host is the AI application. An MCP client inside that host speaks to one server. The transport carries JSON-RPC messages between them. Idea 2 · Stateless requests replace the handshake MCP 2026-07-28 removes initialize and notifications/initialized . It also removes protocol-level sessions. Every request carries the context needed to interpret it in params._meta : Copy The protocol version and client capabilities are required. Client identity is recommended. A missing _meta , a missing required field, or a required field with the wrong type is malformed and returns Invalid Params ( -32602 ). A well-formed version string that the server does not support returns UnsupportedProtocolVersionError ( -32022 ). A server can process a valid request without recovering a prior negotiation record. Stateless does not mean an application can never maintain state. It means that state is not hidden behind an MCP connection or Mcp-Session-Id . If a workflow needs continuity, the server mints an opaque handle and the client passes that handle as an ordinary tool argument on later calls. Authorization must still be checked on every request. Idea 3 · Discovery and version selection Every modern server implements server/discover . The result advertises supported versions, capabilities, and server identity: Copy A client may call another method directly and handle a version error, but discovery makes capability display and version selection explicit. An unsupported version returns UnsupportedProtocolVersionError with code -32022 . Its data contains supported , an array of server revisions, and requested , the rejected revision. On stdio, a dual-era client probes with server/discover . A discovery result or a recognized modern error such as UnsupportedProtocolVersionError identifies a modern server. Any error or timeout that is not recognized as modern permits fallback to the 2025-11-25 initialize flow. Legacy behavior is compatibility code, not the modern default. Idea 4 · Results are explicit Every core 2026-07-28 result has resultType : complete means the operation finished. input_required means the server needs another round trip through the Multi Round-Trip Requests pattern. Core servers may return it only from tools/call , resources/read , or prompts/get . Clients must treat a legacy result that omits resultType as complete. Servers should include io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo in every result's _meta . This identity is self-reported and is for display, logging, and debugging, not for security decisions. List and read results also carry ttlMs and cacheScope . A deterministic tools/list order plus a freshness hint lets clients cache discovery safely and improves prompt-cache stability. cacheScope: public permits shared caching; private confines reuse to the calling context. Idea 5 · The wire format and transport MCP uses JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio or Streamable HTTP. A request has jsonrpc , id , method , and params . A response has the matching id and either result or error . A notification has no id and expects no response. Modern Streamable HTTP exposes one endpoint that accepts POST. Each JSON-RPC message gets its own POST. A request POST receives either one JSON object or a request-scoped Server-Sent Events stream that ends with the final response. An accepted notification POST receives HTTP 202 with no response body; this core revision defines no client-to-server notifications over Streamable HTTP. There is no standalone MCP GET stream, DELETE session endpoint, Mcp-Session-Id , or Last-Event-ID replay in 2026-07-28. Long-lived change notifications use a subscriptions/listen POST whose response remains open as an SSE stream. The same idea as a formula Why a protocol pays off. With host applications and tool systems, point-to-point integration needs one adapter per pair; a shared protocol needs one client per host and one server per system: H × S ​ ​ ⟶ clients and servers with MCP H + S ​ ​ . A stateless request is a pure function of its own content: the server's reply depends on the method, the parameters and , plus whatever application state the server reads, never on an earlier handshake on the same connection. That is what lets any replica behind a load balancer answer any request. Validation order used by the demo server: missing or malformed _meta (Invalid Params); a well-formed but unsupported version ; otherwise the method runs. Worked example Five hosts, twenty systems, and the price of statelessness Point to point: adapters, each with its own discovery, errors and auth. With MCP: components. The metadata travels with every request: in the run below a tools/list without _meta is 65 bytes, with it 266 bytes, about 200 bytes more per message. At 1,000 tool calls a minute that is about 200 KB a minute of extra traffic, negligible next to the model tokens the results feed. In exchange, no server needs sticky sessions: a request can land on any instance. Check your mental model ✗ "MCP decides which tool the model should use." ✓ It standardises discovery and invocation; the host and the model decide, and the host enforces approval. ✗ "Stateless means an MCP server cannot keep state." ✓ It keeps application state behind explicit handles passed as arguments; it just keeps no protocol session. ✗ "Tool descriptions and resources from a server are trustworthy." ✓ They are untrusted input to the model, like any retrieved text (Lesson 13.15 covers tool poisoning). Predict before you run The lesson's server receives a tools/list with no _meta , then one that asks for protocol version 2025-11-25, then the old initialize handshake. Which error code does each get? (Solution P1.) Idea 6 · Client input without server-initiated requests Older revisions let a server send requests such as sampling/createMessage , roots/list , or elicitation/create over a stream. The current protocol uses Multi Round-Trip Requests instead. An eligible tool call, resource read, or prompt get returns resultType: input_required with at least one of inputRequests or requestState . The client gathers any requested input, retries the original method with a new JSON-RPC ID and the corresponding inputResponses , and echoes the exact requestState when one was provided. If no inputRequests were present, the retry omits inputResponses . Roots, Sampling, and Logging remain functional but are deprecated, so new implementations should not adopt them. Existing Roots or Sampling requests travel inside MRTR inputRequests , never as independent server-to-client JSON-RPC requests. Prefer explicit file or directory parameters, resource URIs, server configuration, and direct model-provider integration. Use stderr for stdio diagnostics and OpenTelemetry for production telemetry. Step 1 · register a server surface Registration stays simple even though the request contract changed: Copy The shipped implementation in code/main.py also registers a resource and prompt. It deliberately uses the standard library so you can see each envelope rather than delegating the protocol to an SDK. Step 2 · attach metadata to every request Copy Do not cache this metadata only in a connection object. The server validates it on each request. Step 3 · optionally discover before listing Call server/discover , choose a supported version, then call tools/list . A direct tools/list is also valid if you already know the version and can handle -32022 . The demo returns tool lists in name order and attaches ttlMs , cacheScope , resultType , and server identity. A tool call returns a complete, non-cacheable result because its output can depend on current state. See it drawn MCP over a real stdio pipe The lesson's MCPServer from code/main.py , launched as a separate Python process that reads one JSON-RPC message per line from stdin and writes replies to stdout (diagnostics go to stderr). The client sends discovery, a tool list, a tool call, a resource read, and three bad requests, and prints each reply as it comes back over the pipe. About a second. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The happy path. server/discover returns the supported versions (only 2026-07-28), the capabilities (tools, resources, prompts), instructions for the model, and the server's identity in _meta . tools/list returns the schemas sorted by name, tools/call returns {"sum": 42} wrapped in MCP's content format with isError: false , and resources/read returns the config resource. Every result carries resultType: "complete" : none of these needed a second round trip. The stateless contract. Nothing was negotiated first, yet every call worked, because each request carried its version and capabilities (about 200 bytes of _meta ). Drop the metadata and the server answers -32602 (Invalid Params). Ask for 2025-11-25 and it answers -32022 with supported and requested , enough for a client to pick a version it can speak. The old handshake. A legacy initialize request, which has no _meta , is rejected with -32602 like any other malformed request. A dual-era client therefore probes with server/discover first and falls back to initialize only for errors it does not recognise as modern. The pipe. The server ran as its own process; "server ready" went to stderr, so stdout carried nothing but protocol messages. Step 4 · map the same request to HTTP A remote tools/call POST includes headers that mirror the JSON-RPC body: Copy The MCP-Protocol-Version header must match the version in _meta . Mcp-Method is required on every JSON-RPC request and must match method . Mcp-Name is required only for tools/call , resources/read , and prompts/get , where it must match the tool name, resource URI, or prompt name. A missing required header or mismatch returns HTTP 400 with HeaderMismatch code -32020 . Step 5 · enforce safety outside protocol state Validate authorization and audience on every HTTP request. Bind local servers to localhost and validate Origin on Streamable HTTP. Mark mutating tools with destructiveHint: true and require host approval. Pass directory and file scope explicitly instead of depending on deprecated Roots. Treat resources and tool output as untrusted data. Keep stdout reserved for JSON-RPC under stdio; write diagnostics to stderr. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Run the lesson from its directory: Copy The first line should report discovery of demo-server at protocol 2026-07-28 . Then inspect MCPClient.request : it reconstructs _meta for every call. Remove the metadata from one request and observe the server reject it. Break it on purpose In the stdio launcher, add a print("server ready") to stdout instead of stderr, before the loop. What happens to the client's first readline() , and why does the specification reserve stdout for protocol messages? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) MCP 2026-07-28 (stateless): no initialize handshake or sessions, per-request _meta , required server/discover , resultType on every result, Multi Round-Trip Requests instead of server-initiated requests, subscriptions/listen for change notifications; Roots, Sampling and Logging deprecated. Governance : MCP was donated by Anthropic to the Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation) in December 2025. Adoption : MCP clients ship in Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code and most agent frameworks; the official MCP Registry lists public servers. Auth : OAuth 2.1 with Client ID Metadata Documents preferred over Dynamic Client Registration for remote servers. Sources: MCP 2026-07-28 key changes , MCP blog: the 2026-07-28 specification , MCP joins the Agentic AI Foundation , JSON-RPC 2.0 specification . Recap What to keep from this lesson MCP: hosts run clients; servers expose tools, resources and prompts over JSON-RPC. 2026-07-28 is stateless: version and capabilities in every request's _meta . server/discover advertises versions and capabilities; errors are explicit codes. stdio reserves stdout for messages; Streamable HTTP uses one POST endpoint. Approval, authorisation and trust stay with the host and server, not the protocol. Together they move from “the method works” to “the contract remains safe and diagnosable through deployment.” Exercises Add a subtract tool and confirm tools/list remains alphabetically ordered. Remove the protocol-version key and verify Invalid Params ( -32602 ). Then send the well-formed but unsupported version 2025-11-25 , verify -32022 , confirm requested echoes that revision, and choose from supported . Add a server-minted draftId to a create operation, then require it as an argument to update. Explain why that is application state rather than a protocol session. Return input_required from a tool that needs user confirmation. Retry the original call with a new ID, an inputResponses entry, and the exact requestState instead of inventing a server-to-client JSON-RPC request. Sketch a dual-era stdio client. Treat a result or recognized modern error as modern, and permit fallback to initialize only for an unrecognized error or timeout. Solutions Solution P1 · Two invalid-params errors and one version error No _meta : -32602 , "params._meta is required" (Invalid Params). Version 2025-11-25: -32022 , Unsupported protocol version, with data listing supported: ["2026-07-28"] and echoing requested: "2025-11-25" . The legacy initialize request also gets -32602 , because under 2026-07-28 it is simply a request without the required metadata: the handshake no longer exists. Solution B1 · One stray line breaks the protocol The client's first readline() returns "server ready", json.loads fails, and every later read is off by one line: the client pairs replies with the wrong requests or crashes. Over stdio the stream is the protocol, so a single stray print (a library warning, a debug line) corrupts it. That is why the specification reserves stdout for JSON-RPC messages and sends logs to stderr, and why stdio servers should configure logging to stderr before importing anything noisy. a1115: Course home / Phase 11 · LLM Engineering Prompt Caching and Context Caching Lesson 11.15 60 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 11 · 01 (Prompt Engineering), Phase 11 · 05 (Context Engineering), Phase 11 · 11 (Caching and Cost) Type : Build. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Your system prompt is 4,000 tokens. Your RAG context is 20,000 tokens. You send both with every request. You also pay for both — every time. Prompt caching lets the provider keep that prefix warm on their side and bill you 5-10% of the normal rate on reuse (Claude and GPT-6.2 models, November 2026). Used correctly, it cuts inference cost by 50–90% and first-token latency by 40–85%. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Prompt caching "Makes long prompts cheap" Reusing a provider-side KV-cache for matching prefixes; repeated input tokens billed at 5-10% of the normal price on current Anthropic and OpenAI models. cache_control "The Anthropic marker" Content-block attribute that declares "everything up to here is cacheable"; {"type": "ephemeral"} . Cache write "Paying the premium" The first request that populates the cache; billed at ~1.25x input rate on Anthropic, free on OpenAI. Cache read "The discount" Subsequent requests matching the prefix; billed at 5% (Anthropic Opus and Sonnet 5.5, OpenAI GPT-6.2) or 10% (Haiku 5.5) of the input price; Gemini discounted, see pricing. TTL "How long it lives" Seconds the cache stays warm; Anthropic 5m default (extendable 1h), OpenAI best-effort up to 1h, Gemini user-set. Extended TTL "1-hour Anthropic cache" {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"} ; 2x write premium but worth it for batch reuse. Prefix match "Why my cache missed" Caches only hit when every token from the start up to the breakpoint is byte-identical. Context caching (Gemini) "The explicit one" Google's named, storage-billed cache object; best for multi-day reuse of large corpora. The problem In plain words first Before a model writes its first word it processes the whole prompt (prefill) and keeps the result, the key-value (KV) cache, in memory. If the next request starts with exactly the same text (the same system prompt, tools and examples), that work can be reused instead of repeated. Providers sell this as prompt caching: the repeated part is billed at a small fraction of the normal price and the answer starts sooner. The catch is that only an identical prefix counts: one changed token near the top and everything after it is recomputed. This lesson covers the three providers' versions, the break-even arithmetic with November 2026 prices, and then does prefix caching by hand on a real 0.5B model: it times the first token with and without a cached prefix, checks the outputs match, and shows how a timestamp at the top destroys the cache. No model is trained. A coding agent sends the same 15,000-token system prompt to Claude on every turn of a conversation. Twenty turns at $2/M input tokens (Claude Sonnet 5.5) is $0.60 in input cost alone — before any of the user's actual messages. Multiply by 10,000 daily conversations and the bill hits $6,000/day for text that never changes. You cannot shrink the prompt without hurting quality. You cannot avoid sending it — the model needs it on every turn. The only move is to stop paying full price for a prefix the provider has already seen. That move is prompt caching. Anthropic shipped it in August 2024 (with a 1-hour extended-TTL variant in 2025), OpenAI automated it later that year, Google shipped explicit context caching alongside Gemini 1.5, and all three now offer it as a first-class feature on their frontier models. The idea The mechanic. When a request's prefix matches one from a recent request, the provider serves the KV-cache from the previous run instead of re-encoding the tokens. You pay a small write premium the first time and a large read discount every time after. Three provider flavors in 2026. Provider (Nov 2026) API style Price of a cache hit Write premium Default TTL Min cacheable Anthropic Explicit cache_control markers on content blocks 5% of input (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5), 10% (Haiku 5.5) 25% (5-minute cache), 100% (1-hour cache) 5 min, refreshed on each hit (1 hour optional) model-specific, see docs OpenAI Automatic prefix detection 5% of input on GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra none best effort model-specific, see docs Google (Gemini) Implicit caching, plus an explicit CachedContent API discounted cached tokens; explicit caches add a storage fee storage per token-hour (explicit) user-set for explicit caches model-specific, see docs Discounts have grown with each model generation (OpenAI's went from 50% on GPT-4o-era models to 95% now), so read the pricing page of the model you use. The invariant. All three cache prefixes only. If any token differs between requests, everything after the first differing token is a miss. Put the stable parts at the top, the variable parts at the bottom. Idea 2 · The break-even calculation Anthropic's 25% write premium (5-minute TTL) pays for itself on the first read, because a cache read costs 0.05x on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5. 1 write + 1 read averages 0.65x cost per request (saves 35%); 1 write + 10 reads averages 0.16x (saves 84%). The 1-hour TTL charges 2x for the write, so that block needs two reads to come out ahead. Rule of thumb: cache anything you expect to reuse at least 3 times within the TTL; that clears break-even on either TTL. Step 3 · OpenAI automatic caching OpenAI gives you nothing to configure. That is why providers keep caches for minutes, not forever, and charge for writing them. Pitfalls that still ship in 2026 Dynamic timestamps at the top. "Current time: 2026-04-22 15:30:02" at the top of the system prompt. Every request misses. Move timestamps below the cache breakpoint. Tool reordering. Serialize tools in a stable order — a dict reshuffle between deploys breaks every hit. Free-text near-duplicates. "You are helpful." vs "You are a helpful assistant." — one byte difference = full miss. Too-small blocks. Every provider has a minimum cacheable length (it differs by model). Smaller blocks silently do not cache; check the usage fields. Blind cost dashboards. Split "input tokens" into cached vs uncached. Otherwise a traffic drop looks like a cache win. Solutions Solution P1 · Much faster, and the same prediction In this run the first token came 57 times faster: 0.29 s instead of 16.76 s, because only the 14 tokens after the shared 2,346-token prefix had to be processed. The next-token prediction was identical (the logits match the full recomputation). Caching changes how much work is redone, not what the model computes. Solution B1 · Every deploy, every request misses Every deploy that reorders the tool list changes the prompt near its top. The cached prefix ends at the first changed token, so after each deploy every request misses until new cache entries are written, and the cost of the first request per prefix rises by the write premium. Worse, if the order changes per process or per request (a Python set of tool names, a dict built from an unordered source), different replicas send different prefixes, so the hit rate stays low all the time, not just after deploys. Serialise tools, examples and system text deterministically: sort tools by name, use a fixed JSON key order, and never put request-specific values above the cache breakpoint. Then alert on the cached-token share in the usage fields, so a regression shows up in a dashboard instead of in the bill. Estimate it Your provider charges a 25 percent premium to write a prefix into its cache, and it bills a cache read at a tenth of the normal input price. The cache lives for five minutes. A one-hour variant costs twice the normal input price to write. How many reads does each variant need to pay off, and what rule do you give the team? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. With the five-minute cache, one write and one read average 0.675 of the normal cost per request, a saving of about 32 percent, so the cache pays off on the first read. One write and ten reads average 0.205, about 80 percent saved. The one-hour cache charges 2x for the write, so that block needs two reads before it comes out ahead. The rule: cache anything you expect to reuse at least three times inside its lifetime. The arithmetic. A write costs 1.25 times the normal input price, and a read costs 0.1 times it. One write and one read: the two requests average 0.675 of the normal price. That is 32 percent saved on the first read already. One write and ten reads: the requests average 0.205 of the normal price, about 80 percent saved. The one-hour cache writes at 2 times the normal price. With one read the average sits above the normal price, and with two reads it falls below. The lesson says the one-hour block pays back fast on any batch that reuses the prefix more than five times. Three reuses inside the lifetime clear the break-even on either variant, which is the rule the lesson gives. What breaks the arithmetic. A prefix that differs by one token on every request, because of a timestamp, a request id or a reshuffled tool list. Every request writes and none reads. A block below the minimum cacheable size, which is 1,024 tokens on the provider in the lesson. A smaller block silently does not cache. Requests that arrive in parallel before the first write has landed. Each one pays the write premium, and none reads. Verify it. Read the usage fields on every response: the tokens written to the cache and the tokens read from it. In CI, assert that the second identical request reads more than zero. On the dashboard, split input tokens into cached and uncached, or a traffic drop will look like a cache win. Plausible wrong answers. "Caching always saves money." A prefix written once and never read costs 25 percent more than no cache. "Pick the one-hour cache, it lasts longer." It writes at twice the normal input price, so a block read once costs more than without the cache. "Mark the whole prompt as cacheable." The user message changes every time, so the match ends at the first differing token, and a block below the minimum size does not cache at all. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the five-minute cache pay off on the first read? Expected: the write premium is a quarter and the read saves nine tenths, so the two together already average below the normal price. (level 2) When does the one-hour cache make sense? Expected: a batch job that reuses the prefix across runs more than five minutes apart, more than five times. (level 3) Input tokens are down and the bill is flat. What is wrong with the dashboard? Expected: it does not split cached from uncached input, so a drop in traffic looks like a cache win. (level 3) Ten parallel requests share a prefix that nobody has cached yet. What happens to the arithmetic? Expected: all ten pay the write premium and none reads, so the cache costs more than no cache. Send one request first, then the rest. Where it is taught.
