Debug a failure An agent fans out ten tool calls at once for every user question. All ten share the same long system prompt, and prompt caching is on. The bill is several times what the cache should allow, and the usage fields show cache writes on nearly all calls and almost no cache reads. What is happening? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. All ten requests reach the provider before the first one has finished writing the prefix into the cache. Each one sees a miss, each one pays the write premium, and none of them reads. The fix is sequential-first: send one request alone, let its cache write land, then fan out the other nine. It adds about one write latency to the first tool call and removes the inflation. The mechanism. Cache writes happen per request. The lesson puts the first write at about 300 ms after the provider sees the prompt. Requests that arrive inside that window find nothing to read, so each of them writes. Ten writes and zero reads, on every user question that finds the prefix cold. A question that arrives while an earlier write is still inside the cache lifetime reads it, so the trap shows when the questions are further apart than that lifetime. The lesson reports a bill of 5 to 10 times the expected cached cost from this pattern alone. Read the usage fields. Each response reports the tokens written to the cache and the tokens read from it. In this incident the written count is high on every request and the read count is near zero. That is the signature. A later sequential request with the same prefix does read, which separates this case from a prefix that never matches. The fix. Send the first request alone and wait for it to return. Its write has landed by then. Fan out the remaining nine, and each of them reads. The cost is about 300 ms on the first tool call. The lesson's exercise asks for the same fix without adding end-to-end latency: warm the prefix with one call at the start of the session, before the first fan-out, so the first tool call already reads. Rule out the other cause. A prefix that carries dynamic text looks the same in the usage fields: writes on every request, no reads ever. The lesson's example has the time to the minute, a user id and a reshuffled example order inside the system prompt. One field report moved the hit rate from 7 to 74 percent by moving that text below the cache boundary. Check the prompt template before you blame the fan-out. Plausible wrong answers. "Caching is on, so the provider should deduplicate them." Writes are per request, and the cache can be read only after the first write has landed. "Shorten the system prompt." That lowers every bill a little and leaves ten writes and zero reads in place. "Turn caching off, it costs more." It costs more only because of the arrival pattern. Sequential-first turns ten writes into one write and nine reads. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) How do you tell the fan-out trap from dynamic text in the prefix? Expected: both show writes and no reads. After the fan-out trap, a later sequential request with the same prefix reads. With dynamic text, nothing ever reads. (level 3) How do you fix the fan-out without adding latency for the user? Expected: warm the prefix with one call when the session starts, so the first fan-out already reads. (level 3) Does a self-hosted prefix cache have the same trap? Expected: the lesson says the self-hosted caches follow the same prefix pattern at your own compute, so measure the cached tokens on a fan-out before you assume they are shared. Where it is taught. The caching economics lesson names the parallelization anti-pattern and its fix, and the prompt caching lesson shows the usage fields to read. Estimate it Your batch job sends the same 15,000-token rubric with each of twenty code reviews, spread over 40 minutes in uneven clusters, and some of the quiet stretches between clusters outlast the short cache. The provider bills a write at 1.25 times the input rate for a five-minute cache and at 2 times the input rate for a one-hour cache, and bills reads at one tenth of the input rate. Which cache do you pick, and show the break-even. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The five-minute cache pays for itself on the first read: a write costs 1.25 times and a read 0.1 times the normal input rate, so one write plus one read averages 0.675 times, a saving of 32 percent, and one write plus ten reads averages 0.205 times, a saving of 80 percent. Each read refreshes the five-minute lifetime, so the five-minute cache expires only in a gap longer than five minutes. This batch has such gaps, so the one-hour cache fits; its write costs 2 times the input rate and it needs only two reads to come out ahead, and twenty reviews give far more. The rule of thumb is to cache anything reused at least three times within the lifetime. The arithmetic. Case Cost per request against uncached One write, five-minute cache 1.25 One read 0.1 One write plus one read, averaged 0.675, a saving of 32 percent One write plus ten reads, averaged 0.205, a saving of 80 percent One write, one-hour cache 2, so two reads to break even The lifetime decides it. Each read refreshes the five-minute lifetime. If the reviews arrive steadily over 40 minutes, every gap stays inside five minutes, the entry never expires, and the five-minute cache wins with its cheaper write. If some gaps exceed five minutes, as in this batch, each of those gaps costs a new write at the premium, and the one-hour cache holds the whole batch for one write. If instead the reviews come as a burst of a few inside one minute followed by an idle hour, each burst fits the five-minute cache and the cheaper write wins. Pick from the gaps between requests, not from the total count. Prove it on the response. Read the usage fields: the lesson's first request reports 15,023 tokens written at 1.25 times, and the second reports the same count read at 0.1 times with zero written. In production, gate the deploy on a read fraction above 80 percent after warmup, and split the cost dashboard into cached and uncached tokens. Other provider shapes. The automatic provider gives 50 percent off reads with no premium, up to an hour on a best-effort basis, so the only job is a stable prefix. The explicit cache object on the third provider is storage-billed and reads at about 25 percent of the input rate; it fits reuse of one giant prompt across days. Plausible wrong answers. "Always pick the longer cache to be safe." Its write costs 2 times the input rate against 1.25; with reuse inside five minutes the shorter cache is cheaper. "The write premium makes caching a loss for short jobs." One write plus one read already saves 32 percent on the five-minute cache. "Cache the user message too." It differs on every request, so it never hits; the layout leaves it below the breakpoint. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the five-minute cache break even on the first read? Expected: the write costs 1.25 times and the read 0.1 times, so two requests average 0.675 times the uncached cost. (level 3) What does the one-hour cache need to come out ahead? Expected: two reads, because its write costs 2 times the input rate. (level 4) The reviews arrive in bursts of several within a minute, then nothing for an hour. Does the answer change? Expected: yes; each burst lives inside a five-minute cache, so the cheaper write wins, and the one-hour cache would pay the 2 times write for reuse that never comes. (level 4) How do you verify the saving in production rather than on paper? Expected: read the cache creation and cache read token fields on each response, gate the deploy on a read fraction above 80 percent after warmup, and split the dashboard into cached and uncached tokens. The usage field for cache reads stays at zero on every request, while cache creation tokens are charged every time. What do you look for, and in what order? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Something above the cache breakpoint changes on every request. Look first for a timestamp or a request id at the top of the system prompt, then for tool definitions serialized in a changing order, then for near-duplicate text that differs by a byte between code paths, and then for a block under the minimum cacheable size. The cache matches prefixes only, so the first differing token turns everything after it into a miss. The invariant. All the providers cache prefixes. When a request's prefix matches a recent one, the provider serves the stored key and value cache instead of encoding the tokens again, and bills a read at a fraction of the input rate. If any token differs, everything after it is a miss. The usage fields tell the story: a creation count every time and a read count of zero means the prefix never matched. The checklist, in order. A dynamic field at the top. A current time, a request id or a session id in the first lines of the system prompt misses on every request. Move it below the breakpoint with the other per-request fields. Tool reordering. Tools serialized from a dictionary can change order between deploys or between processes; serialize them in a stable order. Near-duplicate text. Two code paths that build the prompt with a one-byte difference produce two prefixes and no hits. Too-small blocks. The explicit cache has a floor of 1,024 tokens, 2,048 on the small model; a smaller block silently does not cache. On the automatic provider , a changed user field is part of the cache key, and the prefix must still be stable and above 1,024 tokens. The layout that hits. System prompt, then tool definitions, then few-shot examples, then retrieved documents if they are reused, then the history up to the last turn, then the current message, which is never cached because it is different every time. Turn it into a test. In CI, build two requests through the production prompt builder with the same user input, compare their cacheable prefixes, send both, and assert that the cache read token count is above zero on the second. Two hand-written identical bodies would skip the timestamp or request id that the builder adds. Expiry would show as writes after quiet periods, not on every request; the one-hour TTL also charges 2x for the write. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) How do you make this a test? Expected: two requests built by the production prompt builder with the same user input, with an assertion that the cache read tokens are above zero on the second; if they stay at zero the keys are drifting. Expected: nothing is cached and nothing is reported; the floor is 1,024 tokens, and 2,048 on the small model. (level 3) Input tokens fell after your change. Is that proof it works? The same loop written as an explicit graph is something you can checkpoint, interrupt, branch, and time-travel through. The agent hasn't changed. The harness around it has. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means StateGraph "The LangGraph graph" The builder object you add nodes and edges to before compile. Reducer "How the field merges" A function (old, new) -> merged applied when a node returns an update for that field; default is overwrite, add_messages appends. Thread "A conversation ID" A thread_id string that scopes all checkpoints for one session. Checkpoint "A paused state" A persisted snapshot of the full graph state after a node transition, keyed on (thread_id, checkpoint_id) . Interrupt "Pause for a human" interrupt() inside a node pauses and saves the state; resume with Command(resume=value) . Static interrupt_before / interrupt_after breakpoints are for debugging and resume with invoke(None, config) . Time-travel "Fork from a prior step" graph.invoke(None, config_with_old_checkpoint_id) replays from that checkpoint forward. Send "Parallel subgraph dispatch" A constructor a node can return to spawn N parallel executions of a target node. Subgraph "A compiled graph as a node" A compiled StateGraph used as a node in another graph; preserves its own state scope. The problem In plain words first An agent is a loop: the model reads the conversation, maybe asks for a tool, the tool runs, its result is added, and the model reads again. Written as a bare while True: loop, it cannot be paused for a person to approve a risky step, resumed after a crash, or rewound to try a different choice. Writing the same loop as an explicit graph fixes that: each step is a node, the arrows between steps are edges, and everything the agent knows lives in one state object that the runtime saves after every step (a checkpoint). LangGraph is the best-known library for this. This lesson builds the four-node agent graph, then runs a real one: a small local model handles a refund ticket, a human reviewer stops a wrong refund, the thread is rewound and replayed, and three short demos show the mistakes that silently lose data or repeat side effects. No model is trained. You ship a function-calling agent. It works for three turns, then something goes wrong: the model tries a tool that returns 500, the user changes their mind mid-task, or the agent decides to refund an order without a human signing off. The while True: loop has no hooks. You can't pause it, you can't rewind it, and you can't branch off into "what if the model had picked the other tool." The moment you ship this past a demo, the agent becomes a black box that either worked or didn't. The next step is obvious once you see it. The agent is already a state machine — system prompt plus message history plus pending tool calls plus the next action. Make the state machine explicit: nodes for "the model thinks," "a tool runs," "a human approves," and edges for the conditional transitions between them. Once the graph is explicit, the harness gets four things for free: checkpointing (save state between steps), interrupts (pause for a human), streaming (stream tokens and intermediate events), and time-travel (rewind to a prior state and try a different branch). The reference implementation of this abstraction is LangGraph. It is not an agent framework in the LangChain sense ("here is an AgentExecutor, good luck"). It is a graph runtime with first-class state, first-class persistence, and first-class interrupts. The agent loop is something you draw, not something you hand-write. The idea A StateGraph has three things. State. A typed dict (TypedDict or Pydantic model) that flows through the graph. Every node receives the full state and returns a partial update, which LangGraph merges using a reducer per field — operator.add for lists that should accumulate, overwrite by default. Nodes. Python functions state -> partial_state . Each is a discrete step: "call the model," "run tools," "summarize." Edges. Transitions between nodes. Static edges go one place. Conditional edges take a router function state -> next_node_name so the graph can branch on model output. You compile the graph. Compile binds the topology, attaches a checkpointer (optional but essential for production), and returns a runnable. You invoke it with an initial state and a thread_id . Every step of execution persists a checkpoint keyed on (thread_id, checkpoint_id) . Idea 1 · The four superpowers Checkpointing. Every node transition writes the new state to a store (in-memory for tests, Postgres/Redis/SQLite for prod). Resume by calling the graph again with the same thread_id . The graph picks up where it paused. Interrupts. Call interrupt(payload) inside a node and execution stops there. The checkpointer saves the state and the payload goes back to the caller, so your API can respond "awaiting approval." A later request to the same thread_id with Command(resume=value) resumes the run, and interrupt() returns value . Static breakpoints ( interrupt_before=[...] or interrupt_after=[...] at compile time) still exist, but the LangGraph docs recommend them for debugging, not for human approval; they resume with invoke(None, config) . Streaming. graph.stream(state, mode="updates") yields state deltas as they happen. mode="messages" streams the LLM tokens inside model nodes. mode="values" yields full snapshots. You pick what to surface in your UI. Time-travel. graph.get_state_history(thread_id) returns the full checkpoint log. Pass any prior checkpoint_id to graph.invoke and you fork from that point. Great for debugging ("what if the model had picked tool B instead?") and for regression tests that replay production traces. Idea 2 · Reducers are the point Every state field has a reducer. Most defaults are fine — a new value overwrites the old. But message lists need operator.add so new messages append instead of replacing. Parallel edges merge their updates through the reducer. If two nodes both update messages and you forgot the Annotated[list, add_messages] , the second wins silently and you lose half the turn. The reducer is the only subtle thing in the library; get it right and the rest composes. Idea 3 · The ReAct graph in four nodes A production ReAct agent is four nodes and two edges: agent — calls the LLM with the current message history. Returns the assistant message (which may contain tool_calls). tools — executes any tool_calls in the last assistant message, appends the tool results as tool messages. A conditional edge from agent that routes to tools if the last message has tool_calls, else to END . A static edge from tools back to agent . That is it. You get the full ReAct loop (Thought → Action → Observation → Thought → …) with checkpointing, interrupts, and streaming, in roughly 40 lines of code. Idea 4 · StateGraph vs Send (fanout) Send(node_name, state) lets a node dispatch parallel subgraphs. Example: the agent decides to query three retrievers at once. Each Send spawns a parallel execution of the target node; their outputs merge through the state reducer. This is how LangGraph expresses the orchestrator-workers pattern without threading primitives. Idea 5 · Subgraphs A compiled graph can be a node in another graph. The outer graph sees a single node; the inner graph has its own state and its own checkpoints. This is how teams build supervisor-worker agents: the supervisor graph routes user intent to a per-domain worker subgraph. The same idea as a formula A step. Step 1 · state and nodes Copy add_messages is the reducer that makes the message list accumulate instead of overwrite. Forgetting it is the most common LangGraph bug. Step 2 · run with a thread Copy Every update is a dict {node_name: state_delta} . Your frontend can stream these to the UI so users see "agent is thinking… calling search_web… got result… answering." Step 3 · add a human-in-the-loop interrupt Put an approval node on the edge into the side-effecting tools and call interrupt() inside it. Copy The state, the checkpoint, and the thread all persist across the interrupt. Nothing is in memory except during execution. Step 4 · time-travel for debugging Copy Passing None as the input replays from the given checkpoint; passing a value appends it as an update to that checkpoint's state before resuming. See it drawn Three mistakes the graph will not catch for you Three tiny graphs, no model: a list field with and without a reducer, three parallel Send branches writing the same field, and a side effect placed before interrupt() . Instant. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output 1. No reducer, lost history. Without a reducer, each node's {"log": [...]} replaces the field. Two steps later only ['tool ran'] is left: the user's request and the plan are gone, and nothing raised an error. With operator.add , all three entries survive. For messages, add_messages does the same and also lets a message with an existing id replace the old one. 2. Parallel writes without a reducer fail loudly. Three Send branches all write docs in the same step. With overwrite there is no correct winner, so LangGraph raises InvalidUpdateError and tells you to use an Annotated key. The "charge" ran once when the node first started and paused, and again when the node restarted on resume. One approval, two charges. Anything with an effect outside the graph goes after interrupt() , in a later node, or behind an idempotency key. Step 5 · swap the checkpointer for production Copy InMemorySaver is for tests. The SQLite and Postgres savers ship as separate packages ( langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite , langgraph-checkpoint-postgres ); Redis and other stores have their own packages. Anything that persists across restarts wants a real store. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) LangGraph 1.x (1.0 in October 2025): StateGraph , interrupt() and Command for human-in-the-loop, checkpointers for SQLite, Postgres and Redis, durable execution; LangChain 1.0's create_agent is built on it. Graph-shaped agent runtimes elsewhere : Pydantic AI's graphs, Google's Agent Development Kit workflow agents, Microsoft Agent Framework (successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel) workflows with checkpoints. Durable execution engines (Temporal and similar) used underneath long-running agents so a crash or deploy resumes a run. Approval gates on side effects in production agents: tool calls that move money, send messages or change data wait for a person, while reads run freely. Recap What to keep from this lesson An agent graph: state, nodes that return partial updates, edges and routers. Every list field that should grow needs a reducer ( add_messages , operator.add ). A checkpointer saves state after each step; a thread_id names the conversation. interrupt() pauses for a human; Command(resume=…) continues; the node re-runs from its top. Replay from any checkpoint to debug; it forks and keeps history. The Skill You build agents as graphs, not as while True loops. Before you reach for LangGraph, do a 60-second design: Name the nodes. Every discrete decision or side-effecting action is a node. "Agent thinks," "tool runs," "reviewer approves," "response streams." If you can't list them, the task is not agent-shaped yet. Declare the state. Minimal TypedDict with a reducer for every list field. Do not stuff everything into messages ; hoist task-specific fields (a working plan , a budget counter, a retrieved_docs list) to the top level. Draw the edges. Static unless the next step depends on model output. Every conditional edge needs a router function with named branches. Choose a checkpointer up front. MemorySaver for tests, Postgres/Redis/SQLite for anything else. Do not ship without one — no checkpointer means no resume, no interrupt, no time-travel. Decide interrupts before tools run, not after. Approvals go on the edge into a side-effecting node so you can cancel before harm; validation goes on the edge out of the model so you can reject bad calls cheaply. Stream by default. mode="updates" for the UI, mode="messages" for token-level streaming inside model nodes, mode="values" for full snapshots during eval. Refuse to ship a LangGraph agent that has no checkpointer. Refuse to ship one that interrupts after the side effect. Refuse to ship a messages field without add_messages as its reducer. Exercises Easy. Implement the four-node ReAct graph above with a calculator tool and a web-search tool. Verify that list(app.get_state_history(config)) returns at least four checkpoints for a two-turn conversation. Medium. Add a planner node that runs before agent and writes a structured plan: list[str] into state. Have agent mark plan steps as done. Fail the test if plan is lost across a checkpoint resume (wrong reducer). Hard. Build a supervisor graph that routes between three subgraphs ( researcher , writer , reviewer ) using Send . Each subgraph has its own state and checkpointer. Add an interrupt_before=["writer"] on the outer graph so a human can approve the research brief. Confirm that time-travel from a prior checkpoint re-runs only the forked branch. Solutions Solution P1 · One refund, and no learning from the correction One refund in total, and only on the replayed branch. In the main run the 0.5B model proposed issue_refund(A-1042, 50) without looking the order up. The reviewer rejected it with the correct amount, and the model ignored the correction: it asked for the order ID instead. No money moved. On the replay from step 0 the model proposed the same $50 refund (greedy decoding is deterministic). This time it was approved, and the fork records one refund of $50. The thread keeps both histories: 10 checkpoints. Solution B1 · Approved once, paid twice The refund is sent twice. The first pass through the node sends it and then pauses at interrupt() . On Command(resume="approve") LangGraph runs the node again from its first line, so it sends the refund again before interrupt() returns the approval. The third demo in the second visual shows the same thing with a card charge: ['charged card', 'charged card'] . A rejection would not help either, because the money moved before anyone was asked. Keep side effects after the interrupt, ideally in their own node ( tools here). Make them idempotent too, for example with a refund ID derived from the ticket, so a retry cannot pay twice. In plain words first The idea in one line Every framework sells the same demo (research agent builds a report) and hides the same bug (state schema fights with the orchestration layer). Pick the framework whose abstractions match the shape of your problem; everything else is glue you write twice. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Orchestration "How the agents coordinate" The layer that decides which node/role/agent runs next. Durable state "Resume after a restart" State that survives process death, attached to a checkpoint or session store. LLM-selected routing "Let the model decide" A planner LLM picks the next step each turn; flexible but pays tokens on every decision. Explicit routing "Developer decides" A Python function or static edge picks the next step; cheap and auditable. Crew "A CrewAI team" Roles + tasks + process (sequential or hierarchical) bound into a single runnable. GroupChat "AutoGen's multi-agent chat" A managed conversation between N agents with a speaker selector. Team (Agno) "Multi-agent Agno" Route / coordinate / collaborate mode over a set of agents. StateGraph "LangGraph's graph" Typed-state, node, conditional-edge, checkpointer abstraction. The problem In plain words first Agent frameworks are libraries that handle the plumbing around model calls: keeping state, deciding which step runs next, calling tools, retrying, logging. Each one is built around a different picture of an agent. LangGraph uses a graph of steps, CrewAI a team of roles, AutoGen a chat between agents, Agno a single agent with tools. A framework fits well when its picture matches your problem, and fights you when it does not. This lesson compares them on the questions that decide real projects: where state lives, who decides the next step, what you can observe, and what it costs. Then it measures two of those costs: letting a model choose every route against routing in plain code, and how much time the orchestration itself adds. No model is trained. You have a task that needs more than one LLM call. Maybe it is a research workflow (plan, search, summarize, cite). Maybe it is a code-review pipeline (parse diff, critique, patch, validate). Maybe it is a multi-turn assistant that books flights, writes emails, and files expense reports. You pick a framework. Three days later, you discover the framework's abstractions leak. CrewAI gives you roles but fights you when the "researcher" needs to hand a structured plan to the "writer." AutoGen gives you chat between agents but has no first-class state so your checkpoint is a pickle of a conversation log. LangGraph gives you a state graph but forces you to name every transition before you know what the agent will do. Agno gives you a single-agent abstraction that screams when you try to fan out to three concurrent workers. The fix is not "pick the best framework." It is to match the framework's core abstraction to the shape of your problem. This lesson draws that map. The idea Four frameworks show four different core abstractions. The 2026 landscape has more, and they follow the same patterns: the OpenAI Agents SDK, the Claude Agent SDK, Google's Agent Development Kit, Pydantic AI, and Microsoft Agent Framework. Agent Framework reached 1.0 in April 2026 as the successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel for new work; AutoGen itself receives bug fixes and security patches. Framework Core abstraction Best fit Worst fit LangGraph StateGraph — typed state, nodes, conditional edges, checkpointer. Workflows with explicit state and human-in-the-loop interrupts; production agents needing time-travel debugging. Loose, role-driven brainstorming where the topology is unknown. CrewAI Crew — roles (goal, backstory), tasks, process (sequential or hierarchical). Role-playing or persona-driven workflows with a short linear/hierarchical plan. Anything stateful beyond the crew's turn history; complex branching. AutoGen (maintenance; successor: Microsoft Agent Framework) ConversableAgent pair — two or more agents that speak in turns until an exit condition. Multi-agent dialogue (teacher-student, proposer-critic, actor-reviewer) where the thinking emerges from the chat. Deterministic workflows with a known DAG; anything needing durable state across restarts. Agno Agent — a single LLM + tools + memory, composable into teams. Fast-to-build single agents and lightweight teams; strong multi-modality and built-in storage drivers. Deep, explicitly-branched graphs with custom reducers. Idea 1 · What "abstraction" actually means A framework's core abstraction is the thing you draw on the whiteboard when you pitch the architecture. LangGraph → you draw a graph. Nodes are steps, edges are transitions, and the state object at every point is typed. The mental model is a state machine. CrewAI → you draw an org chart. Each role has a job description and a manager routes tasks. The mental model is a small team of specialists. AutoGen → you draw a Slack DM. Two agents message each other; a third joins if you need a moderator. The mental model is chat. Agno → you draw a single box with tools hanging off it. Put boxes next to each other for a team. The mental model is "agent with batteries included." Idea 2 · The state question State is where most framework choices break down in production. LangGraph. Typed state ( TypedDict or Pydantic model), per-field reducers, first-class checkpointer (SQLite/Postgres/Redis). Resume, interrupt, and time-travel are free. (See Phase 11 · 16.) CrewAI. Inside a crew, state flows as strings between tasks via the context field, or structured through output_pydantic . For durable, typed state use CrewAI Flows: a Pydantic state model, @start / @listen / @router steps, and @persist , which saves the state after each step and resumes a run by its ID. AutoGen. State is the chat history and any user-defined context . Conversation transcripts persist; arbitrary workflow state does not unless you write adapters. Agno. Built-in storage drivers (SQLite, Postgres, Mongo, Redis, DynamoDB) attached to an Agent via storage= — conversation sessions and user memories persist automatically. Not a full graph checkpointer; a session store. Idea 3 · The branching question Every non-trivial agent branches. Who decides the branch matters. LangGraph — you decide, via conditional edges. Routing is a Python function with named branches. Branches are first-class in the compiled graph; the checkpointer records which branch was taken. CrewAI — the manager decides in hierarchical mode; in sequential mode you decide at build time. Routing is implicit in the task list; there is no first-class "if" outside the manager's prompt. AutoGen — the agents decide via chat. Branching is emergent from who speaks next. GroupChatManager selects the next speaker; you can hand-write a speaker_selection_method but the default is LLM-driven. Agno — the agent decides by which tool to call next. Teams have a coordinator/router/collaborator mode; branching beyond that is the developer's responsibility. Idea 4 · The observability question LangGraph — OpenTelemetry via LangSmith or any OTel exporter. Every node transition is a trace span; checkpoints double as replayable traces. LangSmith is the first-party option; Langfuse/Phoenix also have adapters. CrewAI — first-class OpenTelemetry since late-2025; integrations with Langfuse, Phoenix, Opik, AgentOps. AutoGen — OpenTelemetry integration via autogen-core ; AgentOps and Opik have connectors. Tracing granularity is per-agent-message, not per-node. Agno — built-in monitoring=True flag plus OpenTelemetry exporters; tight integration with Langfuse for session traces. Idea 5 · Cost and latency All four frameworks add per-call overhead (framework logic, validation, serialization). Rough order of increasing overhead: Agno ≈ LangGraph < CrewAI ≈ AutoGen. The difference is dominated by how much extra LLM routing the framework does. CrewAI's hierarchical manager spends tokens deciding who goes next; AutoGen's GroupChatManager likewise. LangGraph only spends tokens where you write llm.invoke . Agno's single-agent path is thin. When cost per run matters, prefer explicit routing (LangGraph edges, AutoGen speaker_selection_method ) over LLM-selected routing. The same idea as a formula The price of letting the model route. A run with routing decisions, each made by a model call with a -token prompt and an -token answer, at input and output prices ​ and ​ per token: ​ + o c out ​ ) , extra latency ≈ D × t model call ​ . Explicit routing (a Python function or a static edge) costs about zero in both. A hybrid router uses the model only when the rules are unsure. If rules cover a share of inputs, the extra cost drops to ​ + o c out ​ ) , and accuracy becomes ​ + ( 1 − h ) ⋅ acc model on the rest ​ . Worked example A manager agent on 10,000 runs a day A hierarchical crew in which the manager makes routing decisions per run, each with a 1,500-token prompt (role descriptions plus history) and a 20-token answer, on Claude Sonnet 5.5 at \$2 / \$10 per million tokens. Per decision: $1{,}500 \times 2 \times 10^{-6} + 20 \times 10 \times 10^{-6} = \$0.0032$. Per run: $5 \times 0.0032 = \$0.016$. At 10,000 runs a day: \$160 a day, about \$4,800 a month, just to decide who goes next. At around a second per call, it also adds 5 seconds to every run. With rules covering 80% of decisions and the model handling the rest: \$32 a day and 1 second. Three function calls take about a microsecond. A LangGraph run adds under a millisecond for three steps: building the state, applying reducers, choosing edges. A checkpointer adds a few milliseconds more, because it serialises the state at every step (5 checkpoints for 3 steps: the input, the start, and one per node). One small-model routing decision on this CPU took far longer than the whole graph, checkpoints included. A hosted model call is typically hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. Choosing a framework for speed is rarely the right concern. What makes one framework expensive is the extra model calls it makes for you: a manager choosing the next speaker, a planner re-planning, a critic reviewing every turn. Count those. Idea 6 · Interoperability LangGraph ↔ LangChain tools, retrievers, LLMs. First-class MCP adapter (tools imported as MCP servers). CrewAI ↔ tools inherit from BaseTool ; LangChain tools, LlamaIndex tools, and MCP tools all adapt in. Crew-to-crew delegation via allow_delegation=True . AutoGen → FunctionTool wraps any Python callable; MCP adapter available. (AG2 is a separate, community-run fork of the original AutoGen; Microsoft Agent Framework supports MCP and is adding the A2A protocol.) Agno → @tool decorator or BaseTool subclass; MCP adapter; tools can be shared across agents and teams. The Skill You can explain, in one sentence, why a given framework is right for a given agent problem. Pre-build checklist: Draw the shape. Is this a graph (typed state, named transitions)? A role play (specialists hand off work)? A chat (agents talk until done)? A single agent with tools? Decide who branches. Developer-decided branching → LangGraph. Manager-agent-decided → CrewAI hierarchical. Chat-emergent → AutoGen. Tool-call-decided → Agno. Check the state budget. Do you need resume-from-checkpoint? Time-travel? Human interrupts mid-run? If yes, LangGraph is the default; Agno sessions cover conversation-scoped state. Check the cost budget. LLM-selected routing costs extra tokens per turn. If the agent runs thousands of times a day, prefer explicit routing. Budget the framework overhead. Every framework is another dependency. If the task is two LLM calls and a tool, write 30 lines of plain Python; no framework is cheaper than no framework. Refuse to reach for a framework before you can draw the graph, the org chart, the chat, or the agent box. Refuse to pick one that forces you to fight its state model for the thing you actually need. The Decision Matrix Problem shape Preferred framework Why Workflow DAG with typed state, human approvals, long-running LangGraph First-class state, checkpointer, interrupts, time-travel. Research / writing pipeline with distinct roles CrewAI (sequential) or LangGraph subgraphs Role-per-task is cheap to express in CrewAI; scale up with LangGraph when branching gets complex. Proposer-critic or teacher-student dialogue AutoGen, or Microsoft Agent Framework for new projects Agent-to-agent chat is its native shape (group chat and handoff orchestrations in Agent Framework). Single agent with tools, sessions, memory Agno Thinnest setup, built-in storage and memory. Thousands of parallel fanouts with reducers LangGraph + Send Parallel dispatch with per-field reducers for merging (others offer concurrent orchestration with less control over the merge). Quick prototype, no framework commitment Plain Python + provider SDK No framework is the fastest framework. Break it on purpose Switch a three-role crew from a sequential process to a hierarchical one, where a manager model decides who works next, without changing the tasks. What happens to the cost and the run-to-run consistency? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Graph and workflow runtimes : LangGraph 1.x, CrewAI Flows, Microsoft Agent Framework workflows (1.0 in April 2026, successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel), Google ADK workflow agents. Provider agent SDKs : the OpenAI Agents SDK (handoffs, guardrails, tracing) and the Claude Agent SDK (the harness behind Claude Code: tools, subagents, context management) put the loop next to the model. Protocols reduce lock-in : MCP for tools (Lesson 11.14) and A2A for agent-to-agent calls let parts built in different frameworks work together. OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions let traces from any framework land in the same observability backend. Sources: Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 (Visual Studio Magazine) , CrewAI, Mastering Flow State , LangGraph documentation , OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions , Anthropic, Building effective agents . Recap What to keep from this lesson Match the framework's core abstraction to the problem: graph, roles, chat, or single agent. Ask where state lives and whether a run can resume, pause for a human, and be replayed. Decide who branches: code (cheap, auditable) or a model (flexible, paid per decision). Orchestration overhead is milliseconds; extra model calls are the real cost. For two calls and a tool, plain Python is the cheapest framework. Exercises Easy. Take the same task — "research Anthropic's headquarters, write a 200-word brief, cite sources" — and implement it in LangGraph (four nodes: plan, search, write, cite) and in CrewAI (three roles: researcher, writer, editor). Report token cost per run and lines of code. Medium. Build the same task in AutoGen (researcher ↔ writer chat, editor joins via GroupChat ) and Agno (a single agent with search_tools and write_tools , plus a session store). Rank the four implementations on (a) cost per run, (b) ability to resume after a crash, (c) ability to inject a human approval before the write step. Hard. Build a decision-tree script pick_framework.py that takes a short problem description (JSON: {has_typed_state, has_roles, has_dialogue, has_parallel_fanout, needs_resume} ) and returns a recommendation with one-sentence justification. Verify it on six cases you design yourself. Solutions Solution P1 · Embeddings and rules beat the small model The embedding model and the hybrid tied at 22 of 24. The keyword rules got 20 of 24 (they abstain on 4 tickets), and the 0.5B model only 8 of 24, because it called almost everything "technical". Two caveats keep this honest. The rules were written by someone who had read the tickets. And a much larger model would route these easily, so the lesson is not that models cannot route. It is that model routing must be measured, it costs a call per decision, and cheap alternatives are often as good. Solution B1 · A manager is a model call on every handoff Every handoff now goes through a manager model call that reads the role descriptions, the task list and the work so far. A three-task sequential crew makes no routing calls. The hierarchical version makes at least three, often more when the manager delegates, checks and re-delegates. Each call carries a growing prompt. The worked example above puts five such decisions at about $0.016 per run on Claude Sonnet 5.5. Consistency also drops: a model choosing the order can choose differently on two runs with the same input, so the same request can follow different paths. That makes failures harder to reproduce and evaluations noisier. Use hierarchical mode when the order really cannot be known in advance, and log the manager's decisions so you can see where the tokens go. Covers 11.2 Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought, Tree-of-Thought Four patterns side by side Factor ReAct ReWOO Reflexion ToT / LATS Roles Thought, Action, Observation Planner, Workers, Solver Actor, Evaluator, Self-Reflector Policy, value function, search LLM calls One for each step One plan, one solve One run for each trial One for each node Observations In every step Not in the planner As reflections in the next trial Mixed into the value function Token cost Grows with depth About 5x fewer on HotpotQA Grows with the buffer 100-1000x CoT Paper result ALFWorld +34 points HotpotQA +4 accuracy Beats ReAct on ALFWorld Game of 24: 4% to 74% Main failure Loop length explosion Static plan Memory rot Noisy evaluator Use each pattern when ReAct : short tasks, unknown environment, reactive exception handling. ReWOO : structured tasks with known tools and parallel evidence. Plan-and-Execute : like ReWOO, with replanning after partial execution. Plan-and-Act : long horizon (>30 steps), web, mobile or computer use. Reflexion : a clear failure signal and a task class that repeats. ToT / LATS : a cheap, reliable value function. Correctness beats wall-clock. Self-Refine : no external verifier. One model generates and critiques. CRITIC : an external verifier exists: search, code, calculator, tests. ReAct loop: AgentLoop.run User : the message goes into the history as a user turn. LLM : respond(history) returns a thought and an action, or finish . ToolRegistry : dispatch(call) runs the tool by name. Formatter : a bad tool or bad args returns an error: string, not a crash. Loop : the action turn and its observation go into the history. Go to step 2. Stop : finish , no tool calls, max turns, max tokens or a guardrail trip. Budget : after max_turns the loop returns "budget exhausted". ReWOO: plan, fetch, solve Reflexion trial Actor : actor.act(memory) returns a candidate trajectory. Evaluator : binary_evaluator(attempt, TARGET) returns success and delta. Self-Reflector : writes one line, for example "pick larger values". EpisodicMemory : memory.add stores it. The oldest drops past max_len . Next trial : starts fresh but sees the reflections. A success ends the run. LATS: one MCTS iteration Select : walk from root to a leaf by Q(s, a) + c * sqrt(ln N(s) / N(s, a)) . Expand : generate K children with the policy. Simulate : roll out from a child. Score the leaf with the value function. Backpropagate : add 1 to visits and the reward to value_sum on the path. Range -1 to 1. Ignores length. Cosine distance : . Range 0 to 2. Dot product : ​ a i ​ b i ​ . Equals cosine on unit vectors. L2 : ​ ( a i ​ − b i ​ ) 2 ​ . Smaller is closer. HNSW search Build : put each vector in a multi-layer graph, linked to approximate neighbors. Top layers : sparse, with long links between distant clusters. Bottom layer : dense, holds all vectors with short links. Enter : the query starts at the top layer. Descend : greedy moves to closer nodes, then one layer down. Return : approximate top-k in , not . Cost : typically 95 to 99 percent recall. Milliseconds at 10 million vectors. Choose an index Command What it does IndexFlatIP Exact inner product. Cosine on unit vectors. About 100k vectors IndexFlatL2 Exact L2, no training. Up to about 1M vectors IndexIVFFlat K cells, searches the closest few. Needs training. About 10M IndexIVFPQ IVF plus product quantization. 100M and more IndexHNSW Graph index. Fastest for many queries. Large index LSH Random hash projections. Near-duplicate detection KD-trees, ball trees Exact. Low and medium dimension only Size and compression float32, 1536 dim : 6,144 bytes per vector. 61 GB for 10 million. 3,072 dim : 12 KB per vector at full precision. Binary : 192 bytes per vector, 32x smaller. 5 to 10 percent recall loss. Rescore : binary first pass, then full precision on the top 1000. Matryoshka 256 of 1536 : 6x less storage, about 3 to 5 percent loss. Safe cut : 1,536 to 256 is usually safe. 1,536 to 64 is not. Its code is in Lesson 3.1 's appendix; save it as fake_claude.py . The real thing below runs the same calls on the real Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs . Frameworks hide these APIs, but every framework bug you debug will eventually be a question about what was actually sent to the model and what came back. An hour with the raw request and response pays back for years. Why this came about Models became available to developers as web APIs, first as plain text completion and, from 2023, as chat APIs with roles (system, user, assistant). That design is stateless : each request is complete in itself. Everything else in this course builds on this one call, so understanding exactly what goes in and comes out comes first. The problem: getting a reliable answer out of a model A ShopKart customer asks how long a UPI refund takes. The answer is in ShopKart's policy, and the policy has to reach the model with the question. Then your code has to read the reply correctly, including when it is incomplete. Copy What you should see Copy Everything you send and get back, in one place: In the request What it does model Which model answers. Pin an exact model ID in production, so behavior does not change under you max_tokens The most output tokens you accept. The reply stops there even if it is mid-sentence system Instructions and background for the whole conversation, sent as its own parameter, not as a message messages The conversation so far: alternating user and assistant turns, ending with the new user turn. On the newest Claude models a system message may also appear after a user turn, to add an instruction partway through In the response What it tells you content A list of content blocks . Here one text block; later you will meet tool_use blocks ( Lesson 3.1 ) and others stop_reason Why the model stopped. end_turn means it finished; Lesson 3.2 lists all seven values usage Input and output tokens for this request: what you pay for, and what grows as conversations get longer Read the answer from content , not from a convenience property, and always check stop_reason before trusting it. Predict before you run You make a first call asking "Can I return a phone after 10 days?". Then you make a second call with a fresh messages list containing only "What did I just ask you?". What will the second call answer? (Solution P1.) In plain words first A letter, not a phone call Calling a model API is like sending a letter, not having a phone call: each request must contain everything the model should know (the instructions, the whole conversation so far and the new question), because the model keeps nothing between letters. The reply says how it ended (finished, cut off by the length limit, or asking for a tool) and how many tokens were used. Your code is responsible for keeping the conversation and sending it again next time. Idea 1 · The API remembers nothing The experiment below makes three calls. The first asks a question. The second, sent as a fresh list, asks "What did I just ask you?" and the model cannot say, because nothing from the first call exists for it. The third sends the first question, the first answer and the new question together, and now the model can answer. Nothing changed on the server between the second and third calls; only the list you sent did. The API keeps nothing between calls. Each request must carry the whole conversation so far: your code stores the list, appends the model's reply and the next user message, and sends all of it again. The request grows with every turn, which is why long conversations cost more per turn. Copy What you should see Copy Each call is independent. A "conversation" is a list that your code keeps and sends in full every time: earlier user turns, the model's earlier replies exactly as they came back, and the new question. That has two consequences you will meet in every lesson of this course. Every turn costs more input tokens than the last (here 68 without history, 117 with one earlier exchange). And whatever is not in the list does not exist for the model: no memory of yesterday's chat, no knowledge of the logged-in customer, no access to your systems, unless you put it there. Two provider features let the server hold the history for you. Anthropic's message threads (public beta since 2 November 2026) keep it for a few minutes, so each request sends only new messages. OpenAI's Responses API accepts a previous_response_id . Both are optimizations. The model still reads the whole conversation and you are billed for it, and you still need your own copy for when a stored thread expires. Idea 2 · How a reply ends Every reply carries a field that says why the model stopped writing. There are two ordinary reasons: it finished what it wanted to say, or it reached the max_tokens limit you set and was cut off in the middle of a sentence. The same question is asked twice, with a generous limit and a tiny one, so that you see both: Copy What you should see Copy With max_tokens=10 the reply stops after two words, and stop_reason says max_tokens . Code that only reads the text would show the customer "Let me". Set max_tokens to comfortably more than the longest answer you expect, and treat max_tokens as an incomplete reply, never as an answer. Idea 3 · A small helper that owns the conversation Most applications wrap these rules in a small class, so callers send text and get text back: Copy What you should see Copy The helper sends six messages by the third question, and the total token count keeps climbing. That growth is why long conversations get trimmed or summarized ( Lesson 2.8 ), and why agents, which make several requests per question, feel it first ( Lesson 3.2 ). The real thing The same request through the real SDKs. These ran against the local test server described in Lesson 3.1 , which returns each API's documented response format; with a real key, only the wording and the token counts would change. Lesson 2.5 puts four providers side by side. What changes with a real model: the same question can get different wording on every call ( Lesson 1.3 ), so test the facts in an answer, not its exact text. Responses take hundreds of milliseconds to seconds ( Lesson 1.2 ). And errors are real: rate limits (HTTP 429), overload (529 on Anthropic) and timeouts. The SDKs retry some of these for you, twice by default ( Lesson 3.4 ). The second request contained only the second question, so as far as the model is concerned there was no first question. The API is stateless. Memory is the list you send. Solution P2 · A system message first The stand-in rejects it with a 400 error, as the real Messages API does when a system message is the first entry: Copy The stand-in's wording is its own. The fix is the top-level system parameter. On the newest Claude models (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.1 and others), a system message is accepted later in the conversation, after a user turn, to add an instruction partway through; because it comes after the earlier messages, it does not invalidate their prompt cache later · 2.4 ( Lesson 2.4 ). When you port code between providers, this is one of the first differences to handle: OpenAI's Chat Completions API takes a system (or developer ) message first, its Responses API takes instructions , and Claude takes system . Solution D1 · A new list on every turn say starts with self.messages = [...] , so every call throws the history away and sends only the newest question. Build the list once in __init__ and append to it, as Chat does. The tell-tale sign in a trace: input tokens stay flat from turn to turn, when they should grow. Solution M1 · A window on the history Copy Copy The window cuts tokens and still answers the last question correctly, because it only needed the previous turn. The price is that anything older than the window is gone: a question about the first turn would fail. Lesson 2.8 replaces the hard cut with a summary of what was dropped, which keeps the gist at a fraction of the tokens. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What actually happens in a call to a chat model API? Worked answer. The client sends the model ID, a max_tokens limit, the system prompt and the whole conversation as a list of user and assistant messages. The provider tokenizes all of it, the model reads it (prefill) and generates a reply one token at a time (decode) until it finishes, hits max_tokens or a stop sequence, or asks for a tool. The response contains content blocks, a stop reason and token usage. Nothing is stored between calls unless you opt into a provider feature, so the application keeps the conversation and resends it every time, and the cost of each turn grows with its length. A plausible wrong answer. "The model remembers the conversation on the server." That leads to missing history, wrong answers on follow-up questions, and confusion about why costs grow. Follow-ups. Why does a long system prompt slow the first token down? What is prompt caching for ( Lesson 2.4 )? Debug a failure Users say the assistant "forgets" what they said two messages ago. What do you check? Worked answer. Look at the exact request the application sent for that turn. Is the earlier exchange in messages at all? Common causes are a history list rebuilt on every call, history kept per server process (so a load balancer sends the next turn to a replica that never saw it), and a trimming rule that drops too much. Confirm from the trace by checking input tokens per turn: they should grow. Fix it by storing conversations by ID in shared storage, and test with a multi-turn case that asks about an earlier turn. A plausible wrong answer. "The model's context window is too small." A few turns are nowhere near any modern context limit; the history simply was not sent. Follow-ups. How would you keep the full history but bound its cost? What should never be stored in the history? Defend a design Would you call the provider's SDK directly, or put a model-neutral layer in front of it? Worked answer. For a product that must outlive one model, a thin neutral layer: one internal message format, one adapter per provider, or a library such as LiteLLM or a gateway, so switching models is configuration and every call is logged in one place. I would still go direct to a provider's SDK for a feature the layer does not support yet, behind the same interface. The deciding questions are how many providers you will run, how quickly you need new features, and who owns the layer. A layer that hides important differences, such as stop reasons or error types, is worse than none. A plausible wrong answer. "Always use the raw SDK, abstractions only slow you down." That works until the first model switch, which then touches every file. Follow-ups. Which differences between providers must the layer expose rather than hide? How do you test that a switch did not change behavior? Check yourself From a blank file, call a model, print every field of the response, and explain each one. Keep a multi-turn conversation and show from token counts that the whole history is sent each time. Detect a cut-off reply and handle it. Terms you'll hear Industry term What it means Where it shows up JSON Schema The standard format for describing the shape of JSON data: fields, types and allowed values Idea 1 JSON outputs Claude's structured output feature: a schema in output_config.format constrains the reply Idea 1 Constrained decoding Generating only tokens that keep the output valid for a grammar, here compiled from a schema Idea 1 Pydantic A Python library that defines data shapes as classes and validates data against them Idea 2 Validate-and-repair loop Checking a reply with code and sending the errors back for a corrected reply Idea 3 Mentioned here, taught later 2 LangChain, Tool calling This lesson mentions the ideas below before the lesson that teaches them. The one-line meaning is all you need for now; each is marked later where it first appears. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in LangChain A widely used open-source library of building blocks for model applications: models, prompts, tools and agents Lesson 6.2 Tool calling The model replies with a structured request to run a named function; your code runs it and sends the result back Lesson 3.1 About the model on this page The model on this page is a labeled stand-in FakeAnthropic (code in Lesson 3.1 's appendix) returns responses in the documented shape and enforces the documented schema rules, but chooses values with keyword rules. It is not a language model. The section The real thing runs the same code through the real SDKs . Why this came about Developers first parsed model text with regular expressions and hope, and it broke constantly. Providers responded in 2023 and 2024 with JSON modes and then structured outputs , where the model is constrained to a schema you supply. That turned models into components that code can rely on, which tools and agents depend on. The problem: code cannot read prose ShopKart wants every support ticket routed automatically: which team ( category ), how urgent, and which order. The router is code, so it needs fields, not a paragraph. The obvious first try is to ask for JSON in the prompt: Copy What you should see Copy repr shows the exact text, including the newlines. The model did what it was asked, in its own way: a friendly sentence, a Markdown fence, capitalized keys and free-text values ("Delivery issue", "High"). json.loads fails on the first character. Stripping the fence would get you a dictionary, but with keys and values no router expects. Every one of those is a real failure mode of "reply in JSON" prompts, and it is intermittent with a real model, which is worse: it passes your test and fails on Tuesday. In plain words first A form instead of a free-text box Code cannot reliably read prose. So instead of asking the model to "answer", you give it a form to fill in: a schema saying which fields exist, their types and allowed values. The schema is written in JSON Schema ( Lesson F1.8 ), usually generated from a Pydantic class. The model fills in the form as JSON; your code checks it against the same class, and if a value is wrong, either repairs it or asks the model again with the error. Idea 1 · Give the API a schema A JSON Schema describes the exact shape you want: field names, types, and the allowed values of each. With JSON outputs , you pass it in output_config.format , and the API constrains generation ( constrained decoding ) so the reply is JSON that matches it: Copy What you should see Copy Three things changed. The reply is the JSON and nothing else, so json.loads works. category is one of the five values in the enum , so the router can switch on it. And the API enforces required and additionalProperties: false , so no field is missing and none is invented. Who calls what: your code builds the schema and sends it with the request; the API compiles it into a grammar and uses it while generating; your code still calls json.loads on the text block. The first request with a new schema is slower while the grammar compiles; compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use. Run all four tickets through it: Copy What you should see Copy Every reply parses and every category is valid. But look at the last one: the ticket names no order, and the schema says order_id is a required string, so the reply contains a string anyway: "N/A" . A real model might invent a plausible-looking ID instead. A required field forces an answer. When the input may not contain a value, say so in the schema: Copy What you should see Copy None is something code can check. "N/A" , or an invented "SK-1003" , is not. Idea 2 · Let the SDK write the schema Writing JSON Schema by hand is tedious and easy to get wrong. A Pydantic model describes the same thing as a Python class, and the SDK's messages.parse turns it into a schema, sends it, and validates the reply into an object: Copy What you should see Copy The first line shows something the helper does for you. JSON outputs support only part of JSON Schema: numeric limits such as minimum and maximum , and string lengths, are not supported. The helper moves them into the field's description , where the model can read them, and then checks the original constraints itself when it validates the reply. So urgency=7 would still raise an error in your code instead of reaching the router. Send a hand-written schema with an unsupported keyword straight to the API, and the request fails: Copy What you should see Copy transform_schema does what parse does internally. The fixed schema is accepted: Copy What you should see Copy The constraint is now only a hint, so validate the value yourself, which is the next idea. Idea 3 · Valid shape, wrong value: validate and repair Getting data, not prose. A schema tells the model the shape you need; the reply is parsed and checked three times (is it JSON, does it match the schema, do the values make business sense). A failed check goes back to the model once with the error; if it fails again, your code takes a safe default or hands over to a person. A schema guarantees shape, not truth. The API keeps the HTTP response open and sends server-sent events as the model generates: a start event with input usage, then per content block a start, deltas and a stop, then a final delta with the stop reason and output usage. Why this came about As prompts grew, with long system instructions, tool lists and documents repeated on every call, teams paid again and again to process the same text. In 2024 providers introduced prompt caching , which reuses the work on an unchanged beginning of the prompt and charges much less for it. It turned prompt layout into a cost decision. The problem: the same 1,300 tokens, on every call ShopKart's support prompt carries its whole policy section, about 1,300 tokens, and every question resends it: Copy What you should see Copy Each call pays for the full prompt again, and the model processes it again before writing the first token (prefill, Lesson 1.2 ). For a support desk answering thousands of questions a day, the fixed part of the prompt is most of the bill. Prompt caching lets the provider keep the processed prefix and reuse it. In plain words first Not paying twice for the same opening pages Many requests start with the same long text: the same system prompt , the same tool descriptions, the same reference document. Prompt caching lets the provider keep its work on that unchanged beginning (the prefix) for a few minutes, so later requests that start the same way are cheaper and start answering sooner. It only helps if the start is exactly the same, so stable text goes first and anything that changes, such as the user's question or today's date, goes last. Idea 1 · Automatic caching, and why it misses here The simplest switch is one top-level field: Copy What you should see Copy Every call wrote to the cache, and none read from it. That is the documented behavior, not a bug: a cache entry is written at a breakpoint , and with automatic caching the breakpoint is the request's last block, here the question. Each entry is "the system prompt plus this question". The next request has the same system prompt but a different question, so no earlier entry is a prefix of it. Writing costs more than normal input (1.25 times for the default five-minute cache), so this made every call slightly more expensive. Idea 2 · Put the breakpoint where the shared part ends Prompt caching works on the prefix. The provider stores its work on everything before a breakpoint, and later requests that start with exactly the same text read it at a fraction of the price. Put stable material first and the changing part last: a change anywhere in the prefix means everything after it is processed again at full price. Mark the end of the system prompt instead: Copy What you should see Copy The first call wrote the system prompt to the cache; the next two read it, and only the question was processed normally. The usage fields tell you exactly what happened, and the total input is always their sum: Field Tokens that were Price relative to normal input input_tokens After the last breakpoint, not cached 1 cache_creation_input_tokens Written to the cache 1.25 (5-minute) or 2 (1-hour) cache_read_input_tokens Read from the cache 0.1 on most models; 0.05 on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5; 0.025 on Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 The cache key is the exact content of everything before the breakpoint, in the order tools, then system, then messages . Change one character anywhere in that prefix, including the tool definitions later · 3.1 , and it is a different entry. Measure it: what it saves, and when it saves nothing Caching changes the price of input tokens: writing to the cache costs a little more than normal, and reading from it costs a small fraction. Whether that is a saving depends on how often the same prefix is reused. The arithmetic below prices one thousand calls that share a 1,290-token prefix, with and without caching: Copy What you should see Copy The saving comes from three things: the fixed part is most of each prompt, the reads are cheap, and the requests are frequent enough to keep the entry alive. Too rare : an entry lives five minutes, refreshed each time it is read. Requests further apart than that pay to write again: Copy What you should see Copy The one-hour lifetime ( "ttl": "1h" ) costs twice the normal price to write; it pays off when the gap between requests is between five minutes and an hour. - Nothing shared : if every request differs from the first token, there is nothing to reuse. Caching also cuts time to first token , because the cached prefix is not processed again, which matters most for long prompts. Solutions Solution P1 · Only the system prompt is reused Turn 2 would read the system prompt (about 1,290 tokens) and process the rest normally: turn 1's question and answer plus the new question, a few dozen uncached tokens, with nothing written beyond the system prompt. For a short chat that is nearly as good. For a long conversation or an agent run with large tool results, the uncached history grows every turn, which is why conversations use a moving breakpoint. Solution B1 · Below the minimum The prompt is far below the model's minimum cacheable length, so the API processes it normally and ignores the marker, without an error. You notice only by checking the usage fields: both cache fields are zero. Alert when requests marked for caching report zero written and zero read. Solution D1 · Variable content at the front The time is part of the prefix before the breakpoint, and it changes on every request, so every request is a different cache entry: written, never read. Move variable content after the breakpoint, here into the user message: Copy Copy The general rule: anything that changes per request, such as time, user name, account details or retrieved documents, goes after the last breakpoint, or behind a breakpoint of its own placed after the stable part. Solution M1 · A cost report Copy Copy The hit rate here is the share of cacheable tokens that were read rather than written. Two of three requests hit, so 67%. In production, compute it per prompt version and per customer segment, because a single bad template can hide in an average. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism How does prompt caching work, and what does it save? Worked answer. The provider stores the processed state of a prompt prefix, keyed by its exact content up to a breakpoint, for a short time (five minutes by default on Claude, refreshed on each hit, or an hour). A later request with the same prefix reads it instead of processing it again. Reads cost a small fraction of normal input, between 0.025 and 0.1 times depending on the model, and writes cost a little more than normal. It saves input cost and time to first token for long, stable prefixes that are reused often. Output tokens are unaffected. A plausible wrong answer. "It caches the model's answers." It caches the processed prompt prefix; the answer is generated fresh each time. Follow-ups. Why does the order of tools, system prompt and messages matter? Debug a failure After a release, LLM costs rose 40% with the same traffic. What do you check? Worked answer. The cache hit rate, from cache_read_input_tokens per request, before and after the release. If it fell, something made the prefix vary: a timestamp or user detail moved into the system prompt, tool definitions that are now generated in a different order, a new tool, or a changed tool_choice . Diff two consecutive requests' prefixes to find the first difference, then move variable content after the breakpoint. Also check whether the release made prompts longer, or moved traffic to a model with different pricing. A plausible wrong answer. "The provider raised prices." Possible, but check your own usage fields first; they show exactly which tokens were billed at which rate. Follow-ups. How would you add a test that fails if the cacheable prefix changes between two requests? Defend a design Is prompt caching worth designing for from the start? Worked answer. Yes, when the application sends long, stable context repeatedly, which describes most agents and support systems: tool definitions, instructions and policies are large and identical across requests. Designing for it is mostly ordering (stable first, variable last) and monitoring the hit rate, which costs little. It is not worth contorting a prompt for when prompts are short, traffic is sparse, or every request is unique, and it never replaces making the prompt shorter. A plausible wrong answer. "Always cache everything." Writes cost more than normal input, so caching content that is never reused raises the bill. Follow-ups. When would you pay for the one-hour TTL? All of them take a model ID, instructions, a conversation and an output limit, and return text, a reason the reply ended and token usage. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Tool definition The name, description and JSON Schema the model reads to decide how to call a tool Lesson 3.1 Eval case One test question with a written rule for what a correct answer must and must not contain Lesson 11.9 RAG Retrieval-augmented generation: find the relevant passages in your own documents, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them Lesson 4.1 Tracing Recording every step of a run (model calls, tool calls, timings and tokens) so it can be inspected later.
