Techniques such as clear roles, examples ( few-shot prompting ) and explicit output formats emerged from that period. Reasoning models changed some of the advice, so this lesson covers what still holds. In plain words first Writing a brief for a very literal colleague A prompt is a brief for a colleague who is extremely capable, has no context about your company, and takes every word literally. Good prompts say who the assistant is, what it must achieve, which tools to use when, the rules it must follow and the shape of the answer, in that order, with stable text first. Examples show the format better than descriptions do. Reasoning models need less step-by-step instruction and more clarity about the goal and the constraints. From prompt engineering to context engineering Prompt engineering is writing good instructions. Context engineering is the larger job of deciding everything the model sees at each step: instructions, tool definitions later · 3.1 , retrieved documents, memories, conversation history and tool results. In agents, most failures are context failures: the right fact was missing, buried, or contradicted by something else in the window. Industry practice What the model labs say Anthropic ( Effective context engineering for AI agents ) frames context as a scarce budget: find "the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens" that gets the job done, because quality degrades as context grows ( context rot ). OpenAI 's prompting guides for its GPT-5 models stress being explicit and consistent: contradictory instructions waste reasoning effort as the model tries to reconcile them. Google 's prompt engineering guide recommends showing examples, giving the model a role, and stating the output format precisely. See a prompt change the answer Before the anatomy of a long production prompt, see the effect in its smallest form. This uses the small open model from Lesson F7.2 , running on your own computer, so every output below is real and you can change any line and run it again. (No stand-in is involved here; the first run downloads the model.) The helper sends one conversation to the model. The system prompt goes first, with the role system ; the customer's message goes last, with the role user ( Lesson 2.1 ). Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The customer's question never changed. Only the system prompt did. No system prompt. The model has no idea who it is speaking for. It answers as a general assistant: long, generic, and it runs out of its 60 tokens in the middle of a list. It even reassures the customer that a cracked jar is "not a big deal". Role + length. One sentence, as asked. But look at what it says: "contact the manufacturer". The model was told it works for ShopKart and still sent the customer elsewhere, because nothing in the prompt says what ShopKart does about damaged goods. Role + format. Three numbered steps, as asked. The shape is right and the advice is still improvised. Role + context. One line of policy in the prompt, and the answer changes from "contact the manufacturer" to "request a refund". The model did not get smarter; it was given the fact it needed. That last step is the main lesson of this chapter. Instructions control the shape of an answer. Only context (facts the model cannot know: your policies, your data, the customer's order) makes the answer right . A 360-million-parameter model follows instructions loosely, as you can see from the quotation marks and "I'd say" in the last reply; large hosted models follow them far more closely, but they are just as ignorant of your refund policy until you put it in the prompt. Examples in the prompt: zero-shot and few-shot There are two ways to tell a model what you want: describe it, or show it. A prompt with instructions and no worked examples is called zero-shot . A prompt that includes a few worked examples is called few-shot ("shot" is an old machine-learning word for an example). In a chat API, examples are usually written as earlier turns of the conversation: a user message with the input, then an assistant message with the ideal output. The test below asks the model to sort twelve customer messages into four categories, first with instructions only, then with four examples added. It counts two different things: whether the reply is one of the four allowed words, and whether it is the right one. Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output Zero-shot. The instruction said "reply with exactly one word from this list". The model did that for only 4 of 12 messages. For the rest it started chatting: "I apologize for the inconvenience", "Yes, I sell gift cards". Code that expected one of four words would have broken eight times. Few-shot. With four examples, every one of the 12 replies is a valid label. The examples fixed the format completely, which the instruction alone could not do. This is the most dependable effect of examples, and it holds for large models too. Still only 5 of 12 correct. The examples did not make this small model good at the task. It now answers in the right form and often picks the wrong label ("other" for nearly everything). Format is a prompting problem. Accuracy on a task the model finds hard is a model problem, solved by a stronger model ( Lesson 1.3 ) or by fine-tuning ( Lesson 11.4 , where this same kind of task goes from 15% to 90%). Two habits follow. Measure "is the output usable?" separately from "is it right?", because they have different fixes. And when a model ignores a format instruction, add two or three examples before you add more words. Let code search for a better prompt You have now improved a prompt by hand twice: by adding examples, and by choosing which examples to add. Both were guesses followed by a measurement. A program can make the guesses. Prompt optimization means writing several candidate prompts, scoring each one on a set of questions with known answers, and keeping the best. The score decides, not your opinion of the wording. The code continues from the few-shot experiment above. It tries three versions of the instruction, each with four different sets of examples, on a new development set of twelve tickets. The twelve tickets you used earlier are kept aside as the test set , so that the winner is judged on tickets the search never saw ( Lesson F3.5 's rule, applied to prompts). Copy What you should see Copy Reading this output The search found a prompt you would not have picked. The winning instruction is the plainest of the three, a one-line question. The careful version with a definition for every label scores lower with the same examples (6 against 10). With a small model, shorter often wins, and only the measurement shows it. It holds on tickets the search never saw. On the test set the hand-written prompt gets 5 of 12, as it did earlier in this lesson, and the selected prompt gets 9. If the test score had stayed at 5, the search would only have fitted the development set. The same instruction ranges from 6 to 10. With the "question" instruction, one random set of four examples scores 6 and another set scores 10. Which examples you include matters as much as the wording, which is why the search varies both. Twelve tickets is a small ruler. A difference of one or two tickets is noise at this size. Trust the direction (5 against 9), and use a few hundred labelled cases before you believe a ranking of close candidates ( Lesson 12.11 ). How this connects This loop is what a prompt optimizer runs for you. DSPy ( Lesson 7.8 ) takes a metric and a set of examples and searches instructions and demonstrations in this way. Its newer optimizers also use a model to read the failures and propose the next rewrite, where this code only tried the candidates you wrote. It needs the same three things as every other improvement in this course : a dataset with known answers, a metric, and a held-out set. Lesson 2.9 turns the winning prompt into a versioned asset with tests, so that the next model upgrade can be checked against it. Anatomy of a production system prompt The experiments above used one-line system prompts. A production prompt has the same ingredients, written out in full and kept in order. This is the ShopKart support agent's: The parts of a production system prompt, in the order they are written. Each part answers a different question for the model, and each is wrapped in a tag so that the model, and you, can tell them apart. Copy Part Why it is there Role Sets domain, tone and boundaries in one line Context Facts the model cannot know: policies, units, audience Instructions Numbered rules, each testable. Each rule should exist because an eval case later · 11.9 failed without it. Tool guidance When to use which tool. This is where agents most often go wrong. Output format How the answer will be shown or parsed Examples A few representative cases ( few-shot prompting ). They are the strongest signal you can give, so make them varied and correct. XML-style tags are not magic, but they give the model clear section boundaries and let you refer to sections ("follow the rules in <instructions> "). Claude models are trained to respect them; other models handle them well too. Watch out Prompts are not a security boundary "Never reveal customer data" in a prompt reduces risk but does not enforce anything. Enforce permissions in code, tools and the database ( Lesson 10.2 ). Prompting reasoning models Reasoning models (Lessons F7.3 and 1.5 ) think before they answer, and they are prompted differently from older chat models: Habit from older models With reasoning models "Think step by step" Unnecessary and sometimes harmful; the model already reasons. Set the reasoning effort (low, medium, high) instead Long, prescriptive procedures State the goal, the constraints and what "done" looks like; let the model plan Many few-shot examples Fewer, high-quality examples; too many can over-constrain the plan Prompt asks for the reasoning in the answer Ask for a concise answer; reasoning is returned separately (or summarized) by the API Contradictory rules tolerated Contradictions waste reasoning tokens as the model tries to reconcile them; make rules consistent Dynamic few-shot examples: choose the examples per question You saw above that examples fix the output format. They also steer what the model does, but only when they resemble the question in front of it. Examples are the strongest signal in a prompt, but a fixed set wastes tokens on examples unlike the current question. Dynamic few-shot selection keeps a bank of good examples and picks the few most similar to each input (the same retrieval idea as Chapter 4, applied to examples; the code below uses the TF-IDF similarity of Lesson F5.3 ). Explain why, and fix the example bank. (Solution D1.) Make it your own Add a <refusals> section to SYSTEM listing what the agent must not do (share another customer's data, change prices, give legal advice), each with the reply to give instead, and one example of a refusal. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Similar words, not similar intent The cancellation example ("Cancel order A-1002 please") comes first. The second is whichever example shares the most remaining words, likely the address-change example ("Only before dispatch") through "shipped"/"dispatch" overlap, or the order-status one through "order". Solution B1 · Rules exist because of failures A message asking for a refund above INR 5,000 would now get "your refund is done" instead of a request for approval. A test set with one case per rule, run on every prompt change ( Lesson 2.9 ), catches it: each rule should have at least one eval case that fails without it. Solution D1 · Examples are the strongest signal Models follow examples more closely than instructions, so a wrong example teaches the wrong behavior even when a rule forbids it. Remove or correct the example ("Approach: above INR 5,000, call request_refund and say approval is needed"), review every example against the rules, and add an eval case for the conflict. Examples should demonstrate the rules, never contradict them. Solution M1 · Refusals with replacements Each refusal needs a replacement, or the model improvises: for example "Another customer's order: say you can only discuss orders on this account." Add one example showing a polite refusal and the next step. Then add eval cases for each refusal, including rephrased and Hinglish versions, because refusals fail on paraphrases first. Debug a failure A model ignores one instruction in a long system prompt. What do you try? Worked answer. Check that the instruction does not conflict with an example or another rule, and that it is specific and testable ("never promise a date the tools did not return" rather than "be accurate"). Check where it sits: put critical rules in a clearly labeled section and near related tool guidance. Add an example demonstrating it. Then measure on eval cases before and after, because a fix that helps one case can hurt others. A plausible wrong answer. "Write it in capital letters and repeat it." Emphasis can help a little, but conflicts and vagueness are the usual causes. Follow-ups. When would you move a rule out of the prompt and into code? Defend a design Should business rules live in the prompt or in code? Worked answer. Rules that must always hold, such as approval limits, permissions and refund eligibility, belong in code, as tool validation or middleware (Lessons 3.3 and 6.6 ), with the prompt describing them so the model plans correctly. Rules about tone, wording and how to explain things belong in the prompt. A rule only in the prompt will eventually be broken by a paraphrase or an injection ( Lesson 10.2 ). A plausible wrong answer. "Everything in the prompt, it is easier to change." Easier to change, and easier to bypass. Follow-ups. How would you keep the prompt and the code rules in sync? Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Prompt chaining A fixed sequence of model calls with gates Lesson 3.7 Workflow Fixed arrangements of model calls where your code decides the order: chaining, routing, parallel calls, orchestrator-workers Lesson 3.7 Agent loop Call the model, run requested tools, send results, repeat until it answers or a limit is hit Lesson 3.2 ReAct A loop of thought, one action and observation, repeated until the task is done Lesson 3.8 Tool calling The model replies with a structured request to run a named function; your code runs it and sends the result back Lesson 3.1 Reflexion Retrying a task with notes written after the previous failed attempt Lesson 3.8 Test-time compute Spending more reasoning tokens at inference for accuracy Lesson 11.2 Why this came about Researchers found in 2022 that asking a model to work through intermediate steps ( chain-of-thought ) markedly improved its accuracy on reasoning problems, and variations such as sampling several answers and voting followed. In 2024 reasoning models began doing this internally, trained to think before answering. Knowing both explains when to ask for reasoning and when it only adds cost. In plain words first Showing your working Some problems are answered better when the model works through intermediate steps before the final answer, the way a student shows their working. Techniques such as chain-of-thought , asking for several attempts and voting ( self-consistency ), or breaking a problem into sub-questions trade more tokens and time for accuracy. Reasoning models do much of this internally, so the techniques matter most with standard models and for making reasoning visible and checkable. Reasoning techniques in prompts How this connects Lesson F7.3 explained why thinking longer helps a model, built self-consistency (voting over several sampled answers), and showed how reasoning models are trained to do this by themselves. This lesson is the prompt-writer's side of the same ideas: the named techniques people used to get that behaviour from ordinary models, what each looks like in a prompt, and which are still worth using now that reasoning is built in. Before reasoning models, a family of prompting techniques got models to reason better, and they are still widely discussed and still useful with smaller, non-reasoning models. First, what three of them look like. The customer question is the same each time: "I ordered 3 kettles at ₹1,200 each. One arrived broken. Shipping was ₹150 for the whole order. How much should I be refunded?" (ShopKart refunds the broken item and none of the shipping, so the right answer is ₹1,200.) A direct prompt asks for the answer and nothing else: Copy A model answering in one step has to produce the first digit of the answer before it has worked anything out. Weak models often grab a visible number: ₹3,750 (the whole order) or ₹1,350 (item plus shipping). Chain-of-thought asks the model to write its working first. The zero-shot form is one added sentence: Copy Now the model writes "One kettle costs ₹1,200. One was broken, so one item is refunded. Shipping is not refunded..." and each sentence it has written is in its context when it writes the next one ( Lesson F6.5 : every token is predicted from all the tokens before it). The reasoning is not decoration; it is the scratch paper the answer is computed on. The few-shot form shows one or two solved examples with their working instead of the instruction. Decomposition makes the steps explicit and separate: Copy Split across separate model calls, with a check between them, this becomes prompt chaining later · 3.7 , the first workflow pattern later · 3.7 of Lesson 3.7 . The full family, and whether each is still worth using: Technique What it does Still worth it? Chain-of-thought (CoT) Show worked examples with reasoning steps, or simply add "think step by step" (zero-shot CoT) Yes for non-reasoning models on multi-step problems; reasoning models do this internally Self-consistency Sample several reasoning paths at a non-zero temperature and take the majority answer Yes when answers are short and checkable, such as a label, a number or a choice Least-to-most / decomposition Ask for sub-questions first, then answer them in order Yes; in agents this becomes the planner step ( Lesson 3.8 ) Prompt chaining Split a task into several calls, each with its own prompt and checks Yes; it is the workflow pattern of Lesson 3.7 Tree of Thoughts Explore several partial solutions, score them, and expand the best (a search over reasoning) Rarely by hand; reasoning models and agent loops later · 3.2 cover most of it ReAct later · 3.8 Interleave reasoning with tool calls later · 3.1 and observations It is the agent loop itself (Lessons 3.2 and 3.8 ) Self-refine / Reflexion later · 3.8 Critique the draft, then revise; Reflexion keeps the critique as memory for the next attempt Yes with a concrete checker (tests, a schema, a rubric); weak without one Four ways to get more reasoning out of a model, on one question. Each step to the right spends more tokens. A reasoning model does the middle two internally, which is why its prompts no longer ask for them. Self-consistency is easy to reason about with a little probability, and the result is worth knowing: voting helps only when a single path is right more often than not. Copy What you should see Copy At 75% per path, 15 votes reach 98%. At 40%, voting makes things worse, because the wrong answer wins the majority more often. Self-consistency amplifies a model that is usually right; it cannot rescue one that is usually wrong, and it multiplies cost by the number of samples, so keep it for short, high-value decisions. What to use today Your situation Use Why A reasoning model, or a frontier model with thinking switched on A clear goal, the constraints, and what "done" looks like. Set the reasoning effort ; do not add "think step by step" The model already reasons before answering ( Lesson 2.6 ). Extra procedure can make it worse A small or older model on a multi-step problem Chain-of-thought, with the final answer on a marked last line that code can pick out The working gives the model somewhere to compute A short, checkable answer where mistakes are costly (a label, an amount, yes or no) Self-consistency: three to five samples and a vote Cheap insurance, if one path is right more often than not A long task with distinct stages Decomposition into separate calls with a check after each ( Lesson 3.7 ) Each call is simpler, and a failure is caught where it happens A draft that can be checked by a program (tests, a schema, a calculation) Self-refine: run the check and send the failure back The check, not the model's opinion of itself, drives the improvement A draft with nothing to check it against One careful pass, then human review "Are you sure?" with no new information mostly produces a different answer, not a better one ( Lesson 3.8 ) Watch out Visible reasoning is not a guarantee A written chain of thought can contain a wrong step and still end in the right answer, or look flawless and end in a wrong one. Treat it as a debugging aid. What you trust is the final answer after it has been checked: by code where that is possible, by a second sample or a person where it is not. Check your mental model ✗ "More reasoning always means better answers." ✓ It helps on multi-step problems and adds cost and latency everywhere else. ✗ "The model's written reasoning is exactly how it decided." ✓ It is useful evidence, not a guaranteed account of the computation. ✗ "Self-consistency is free accuracy." ✓ It multiplies cost by the number of samples. Exercises Predict before you run Using majority_vote_accuracy , what is the accuracy of 3 votes when a single path is right 60% of the time? Is it worth three times the cost? (Solution P1.) Break it on purpose Self-consistency on a free-text answer: sample five summaries of a refund policy and take "the most common one". Why does this not work, and what would you do instead? (Solution B1.) Debugging exercise Debugging exercise: voting made it worse A team added 5-vote self-consistency to a hard classification task and accuracy fell from 45% to about 41%. Using the table in this lesson, explain why, and say what to do. (Solution D1.) Make it your own Change majority_vote_accuracy to model wrong answers that scatter across three different wrong labels instead of agreeing, and compare the result for p = 0.4. (Solution M1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Small gains, triple cost majority_vote_accuracy(0.6, 3) is 0.648, about 65%: five points for three times the tokens. Worth it only for a short, high-value decision; for most calls a better prompt, a better model or a checker gives more per rupee. Solution B1 · Votes need comparable answers Free text rarely repeats exactly, so there is no majority. Self-consistency needs short, checkable answers: a label, a number, a choice. For long outputs, use a judge or a checker to pick the best sample, or extract a short claim from each sample and vote on that. Solution D1 · Below 50%, voting amplifies the error At p below 0.5 under the worst case (wrong answers agree), the majority is wrong more often than a single sample, as the 40% row shows. Voting amplifies whatever is most likely. Improve the single-path accuracy first (better prompt, examples, a reasoning model, decomposition), then add voting once a single path is right well over half the time. Solution M1 · Scattered wrong answers Simulate it rather than solving it by hand: for each trial draw n answers, right with probability p, otherwise one of three wrong labels at random, and count how often the right label has the most votes (break ties at random). With p = 0.4 and n = 5, the right answer now wins most of the time, because the wrong votes split. That is the "voting does even better" case in the function's comment, and it is why self-consistency helps more on open questions with many possible wrong answers than on yes/no questions. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What is chain-of-thought prompting, and does it still matter with reasoning models? Worked answer. Chain-of-thought asks a model to write intermediate steps before the answer, through worked examples or an instruction to think step by step, which improves multi-step problems for models that do not reason by default. Reasoning models are trained to reason internally, so explicit chain-of-thought instructions add little and can hurt; with them, give the goal, constraints and success criteria, and set the reasoning effort or budget instead. It still matters for small and non-reasoning models. A plausible wrong answer. "Always add 'think step by step'." For reasoning models that is redundant, and the extra visible reasoning costs tokens. Follow-ups. What is self-consistency, and when does it help? Debug a failure Adding chain-of-thought made a classifier slower and no more accurate. What now? Worked answer. Check whether the task needs reasoning at all; single-label classification with clear categories often does not. Look at the errors: if they come from ambiguous categories, fix the label definitions and examples; if from missing information, add it to the context. Remove the reasoning step if it does not help on the eval set , or keep it only for the low-confidence cases. A plausible wrong answer. "Make the chain longer." More reasoning does not fix unclear labels. Follow-ups. How would you route only hard cases to a slower method? Defend a design Self-consistency or a better model: which would you pay for? Worked answer. It depends on single-path accuracy and cost. Self-consistency multiplies cost by the number of samples and helps only when a single path is right well over half the time; a better model raises single-path accuracy for every call. I would measure both on the eval set and compare accuracy per unit of cost and latency. Often the answer is a better prompt or model first, and voting only for a narrow, high-value decision. A plausible wrong answer. "Voting is always cheaper than a bigger model." Five calls to a small model can cost more than one to a larger one. Follow-ups. A When a single reasoning path is right well over half the time B Always, because more samples are always better C Only when each path is usually wrong D Only for single-label classification Voting amplifies whatever a single path does most often, and it multiplies the cost by the number of samples. A The model is too small B The task does not need multi-step reasoning C Chain-of-thought never works D The temperature was too low Single-label classification with clear categories often needs no reasoning. Look at the errors: unclear label definitions or missing information are the usual causes. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Tool definition The name, description and JSON Schema the model reads to decide how to call a tool Lesson 3.1 Long-term memory What an agent remembers across conversations, stored outside the context window and fetched when needed Lesson 3.10 RAG Retrieval-augmented generation: find the relevant passages in your own documents, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them Lesson 4.1 Subagent An agent that another agent delegates part of a task to, with its own instructions and context Lesson 3.11 Sandbox An isolated environment where an agent's code or actions cannot reach anything important Lesson 10.3 Context poisoning A hallucination or error that enters the context and is reused Lesson 3.12 Indirect prompt injection Instructions hidden in content the agent reads, such as a web page Lesson 10.2 Attack success rate Share of attacks that cause harm Lesson 10.3 LangChain A widely used open-source library of building blocks for model applications: models, prompts, tools and agents Lesson 6.2 Tool calling The model replies with a structured request to run a named function; your code runs it and sends the result back Lesson 3.1 Reranker A second, slower and more accurate model that reorders the top search results Lesson 4.6 Why this came about As applications grew from single prompts into agents with tools, memory and retrieved documents, teams found that most failures came from what the model was given at each step, not from the wording of the instructions. By 2025 this was called context engineering : deliberately deciding what goes into each call. In plain words first Packing a suitcase with a weight limit The context window is a suitcase with a weight limit, and every call you decide what goes in: instructions, tool descriptions, the relevant part of the conversation, retrieved documents, memories. Context engineering is packing it on purpose: put in what this step needs, leave out what it does not, compress what is too big, and keep the stable items at the front so caching works. Most agent failures are packing failures: something missing, too much noise, or conflicting instructions. Assembling context A useful order for each model call, top to bottom: A context window is a budget: everything the model sees on one call competes for the same tokens, and the parts that change most should come last so the stable prefix can be cached. System prompt (stable) Tool definitions later · 3.1 (stable) Long reference material: documents, schemas (stable within a session) Long-term memories later · 3.10 relevant to this user (changes slowly) Conversation history, trimmed or summarized Retrieved passages for this question The current question, and any per-turn facts such as today's date This order serves two goals at once: it maximizes prompt-cache hits (stable first), and it puts the most relevant material near the question, where models attend best (the lost in the middle effect). The four moves of context engineering. Each row names tools taught later in the course; here you only need the move itself: Move Meaning Examples Write Save information outside the window for later Scratchpad files, memory stores, to-do lists Select Bring in only what is relevant RAG later · 4.1 , memory search, tool selection Compress Fewer tokens, same essence Summarizing history, clearing old tool results Isolate Split work so contexts stay clean Subagents later · 3.11 , separate state fields, sandboxes later · 10.3 In production How context goes wrong, and the fix for each Drew Breunig's widely cited catalog names four failure modes. Context poisoning later · 3.12 : a hallucination or a wrong tool result gets into the context and is reused as fact; fix by validating tool results and letting the model see errors explicitly. Context distraction : a long history makes the model repeat past actions instead of reasoning; fix with summaries and clearing old tool results. Context confusion : irrelevant tools and documents pull the model off course; fix by selecting tools and documents per step. Context clash : contradictory information from different sources; fix by stating which source wins (live tool data over memory, newest policy over older). When an agent degrades as conversations get longer, check these four before changing the model. A runnable sketch of a context budget, the kind of logic every framework hides: Copy What you should see Copy Real systems count tokens instead of words and summarize dropped turns instead of discarding them, but the priority logic is the same. Untrusted content: delimit and mark it Retrieved documents, emails, web pages and tool results are untrusted : they may contain instructions aimed at your agent ( indirect prompt injection later · 10.2 , Lesson 10.2 ). You cannot make a prompt immune, but you can make the boundary between instructions and data unmistakable. Microsoft's research calls this spotlighting : wrap untrusted text in a delimiter the attacker cannot guess, and tell the model that nothing inside it is an instruction. Copy What you should see Copy (The tag changes every run.) Spotlighting lowers attack success rates later · 10.3 but does not eliminate them; pair it with screening ( Lesson 10.1 ) and with permissions that make a successful injection harmless ( Lesson 10.3 ). Compaction: keep long conversations inside the budget Agents accumulate history and tool results until the window fills and quality drops ( context rot ). Three standard compaction moves, cheapest first: Clear old tool results : keep the fact that a tool was called, drop its bulky output. Summarize old turns into a running summary. Drop what is still over budget, oldest first. Copy What you should see Copy At a generous budget nothing changes; at 600 tokens clearing old tool results is enough; at 300 the old turns collapse into one summary. Anthropic's API offers server-side tool-result clearing and compaction, and LangChain later · 6.2 and the agent SDKs ship summarization middleware; they apply the same logic. Order documents for attention Models use information at the start and end of a long context more reliably than information in the middle ( lost in the middle , Liu and colleagues, 2023). Long-context models have reduced the effect but not removed it. When you put several retrieved passages in a prompt, place the best ones at the edges: Copy What you should see Copy LangChain calls this LongContextReorder . It is a cheap change worth testing on your own eval set ; the gain depends on the model. How this connects Where context engineering continues This lesson covered one model call: what goes into the window, in what order, how to mark untrusted text and how to stay inside a budget. Three later lessons build on it, and you do not need them yet. Retrieval (Chapter 4) is the "select" move done properly: finding the right passages among thousands. Agent memory (Lessons 3.9 and 3.10 ) is the "write" move: what an agent saves outside the window and brings back later. Long-running agents ( Lesson 3.12 ) face the hardest version, because their context grows with every step. That lesson has the field lessons from teams that run such agents: keeping the prompt cache warm, using files as memory, and reciting the plan. Check your mental model ✗ "Putting everything in the context is safest." ✓ Irrelevant text costs money, slows the model and distracts it. ✗ "The model reads every part of a long context equally well." ✓ Information in the middle of a long context is used less reliably. ✗ "Context engineering is the same as prompt engineering ." ✓ Prompting is the instructions; context engineering is everything assembled around them at each step. What does the model see, and why is spotlighting a mitigation, not a defense? (Solution B1.) Solutions Solution P1 · Never split a tool call from its result If the cut falls between the tool call and its result, the kept history starts with a result whose call was summarized away, which providers reject ( Lesson 3.1 ). Compaction must cut at turn boundaries, keeping tool calls and results together; LangChain's trimming and summarization do this (Lessons 6.6 and 6.14 ). Solution B1 · Marking is not enforcement Without the delimiter and the note that the text is untrusted data, the instruction sits in the context with the same weight as real instructions, and some models will follow it. Spotlighting lowers that risk, but a model can still be persuaded, so the refund limit must be enforced in code: tool validation and approval (Lessons 3.3 , 6.6 and 10.3 ). Solution D1 · Lost in the middle Models attend most to the beginning and end of a long context, so a key document in the middle of twelve is more likely to be missed. Retrieve fewer, better documents ( rerank later · 4.6 , Lesson 4.6 ), and order them with the strongest at the edges (the edges_first function above). Then check the case in your RAG eval set. Log the counts per request: a context that is mostly history or mostly documents tells you which lever to pull. Check your understanding Explain the mechanism What is context engineering, and how is it different from prompt engineering? Worked answer. Prompt engineering is writing the instructions. Context engineering is deciding everything the model sees on each call: instructions, examples, retrieved documents, tool results, memory and history, within a token budget, in a good order, with untrusted content marked. For agents that run many steps, most failures come from context: missing information, stale or conflicting information, or a context so long the key facts get lost. A plausible wrong answer. "It is a new name for the same thing." The difference is scope: the whole input, assembled per call, not one static prompt. Follow-ups. How do you decide what to drop when the context is over budget? Debug a failure A long-running agent gets worse after about twenty turns. What do you check? Worked answer. The context at turn twenty: how long it is, what share is old tool output, whether the instructions are still there and still first, and whether summaries dropped facts the agent needs. Fixes: compaction or summarization that keeps decisions and open tasks, clearing old tool results, moving durable facts to memory ( Lesson 3.9 ), and a token budget per part. A plausible wrong answer. "The model gets tired." Models have no fatigue; the input changed. Follow-ups. How would you evaluate a compaction strategy? Defend a design Long context window, or careful context assembly? Worked answer. Careful assembly, even with a large window. Every token costs money and latency, attention to the middle of long inputs is weaker, and irrelevant text can mislead. A large window is valuable for genuinely long inputs, such as a contract or a codebase, and as headroom. For agents and RAG, I would budget each part, retrieve and rank precisely, and cache the stable prefix ( Lesson 2.4 ). A plausible wrong answer. "Put everything in; the window is big enough." It fits, but it costs more and usually answers worse. Follow-ups. When is long context better than RAG ( Lesson 4.10 )? Teams began treating prompts as software artifacts, with version control, registries, evaluation sets and gradual rollout, borrowing practices from software release management. In plain words first Prompts are code that happens to be in English A prompt change can break an application as surely as a code change, so prompts get the same treatment as code: stored in version control or a prompt registry , given versions, reviewed, tested against a fixed set of examples before release, and rolled out gradually. Each answer should be traceable to the prompt version that produced it. Prompts as managed assets Version prompts like code: a registry ( LangSmith later · 6.8 , Langfuse, MLflow Prompt Registry, Azure and Vertex prompt management) or plain files in git, with the version recorded on every trace. Change one thing at a time , and run the eval set before and after ( Lesson 12.11 ). Keep prompts model-specific. A prompt tuned for one model family may underperform on another. When you switch models, re-tune. What a prompt registry gives you: every version of a prompt is kept, and any two can be compared word by word, as here in MLflow. A changed prompt becomes something you can review, test and roll back. Figure: MLflow project , Apache 2.0 . Step by step: from a string to a managed, tested prompt The rest of this lesson builds the prompt machinery that production teams end up writing, one piece at a time. Every block runs offline. Step 1 · Templates with strict variables and versions A prompt in production is a template with variables (today's date, the customer's tier, the language), stored under a version so every trace can say exactly which prompt produced it. A strict template engine fails loudly on a missing variable instead of sending the model a prompt with a hole in it. Copy What you should see Copy The hash identifies the exact template text, so a trace can prove which wording ran. Production stays pinned to version 1 through the alias until version 2 passes the eval set; promoting it is a one-line alias change, and rolling back is the same line. Step 2 · Test prompts like code Prompt changes break things silently, so put the rendered prompt under tests that run in CI, before any model call: required sections present, no unfilled variables, a token budget, today's date injected, and the examples valid. Copy What you should see Copy Static checks catch broken prompts; behavioural checks (does the agent now follow rule 3?) belong in the eval set of Lesson 12.11 . Run both on every prompt change. Industry practice How prompt work is organized in mature teams Prompts live in version control or a registry, are reviewed like code, and are deployed by alias, never edited live in production. Every rule in a system prompt points to the eval case later · 11.9 that made it necessary; rules with no failing case are candidates for deletion. Domain experts edit prompts through a playground connected to the eval set (Hamel Husain's advice), so changes are judged by evidence. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Structured output Getting a model's reply as data in a fixed shape, usually JSON that matches a schema, instead of free text Lesson 2.2 Reasoning effort A setting that controls how much a reasoning model thinks before answering Lesson 2.6 Prompt caching Paying much less for a prompt prefix the provider has already processed recently Lesson 2.4 Tool calling The model replies with a structured request to run a named function; your code runs it and sends the result back Lesson 3.1 Constrained decoding Generating only tokens that keep the output valid for a grammar, here compiled from a schema Lesson 2.2 System prompt The instructions given to the model before the conversation, which set its role and rules Lesson 2.1 Why this came about A model does not compute one fixed answer; it produces probabilities for every possible next token and picks one. That design, inherited from language modeling, is what makes outputs varied and sometimes creative, and also what makes them unpredictable. Settings such as temperature exist to control that randomness, and choosing a model became a trade between quality, speed and cost as the number of available models exploded. In plain words first Rolling weighted dice for each word At every step the model produces a score for every possible next token, turns the scores into probabilities, and then samples : it picks one at random, weighted by those probabilities. Temperature stretches or flattens the weights: low temperature almost always picks the top choice, high temperature takes more chances. Because of that sampling, and because providers' servers are not perfectly deterministic, the same prompt can give different answers. Code that depends on a model must therefore check its outputs rather than expect exact text. Sampling: why the same prompt gives different answers How this connects You have seen this before Lesson F2.3 introduced softmax and temperature, and Lesson F6.5 built greedy, top-k and top-p decoding on a real model. This lesson does not re-teach them. It takes the engineering consequence, that the same prompt can give different answers , and shows what to do about it. The short code section further down is a recap you can skim. At each step the model produces a probability for every possible next token, then samples one. Temperature reshapes the same scores: low temperature almost always picks the top token; high temperature spreads probability to unlikely tokens. Temperature flattens (higher) or sharpens (lower) those probabilities. Use low values for extraction and classification. Top-p ( nucleus sampling ) samples only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. Even at temperature 0, outputs are not guaranteed identical: batching and hardware make tiny numeric differences. Many reasoning models ignore or forbid temperature settings. Design for non-determinism : validate outputs, run evals several times, and never rely on exact wording. In plain words first What an "eval" is, since the word appears from here on An eval (short for evaluation) is a repeatable test for a model or a system built on one. In its simplest form it is a list of inputs, each with a note of what a good answer must contain, and a small program that runs every input and counts how many answers pass. For example: 30 real customer questions, the correct order status for each, and a check that the reply contains that status. The list is called an evaluation set (or eval set, or golden set). Evals matter more with language models than with ordinary code, for two reasons you have just met: the output varies from run to run, and a change that fixes one case can quietly break another. So you run the whole set after every change, and you run each case several times. The score pass^k ("pass to the k") is the share of cases that pass on all of k runs: a case that passes two times out of three does not count. You will build evals in stages: tests for prompts in Lesson 2.9 , an evaluation set for retrieval in Lesson 4.7 , and the full method in Lessons 12.11 and 12.12 . Until then, read "your evals" as "your own list of test cases with a pass or fail check". In production Non-determinism in production The symptoms: a test that passes on Monday fails on Tuesday with no change; two customers asking the same question get different answers; a regex that parses the model's output breaks once a week. The fixes are structural, not "set temperature to 0": structured outputs later · 2.2 instead of parsing prose, fixed workflows for paths that must be identical every time, evals run several times per case and reported as pass^k, and caching answers where the same question should always get the same reply. Sampling: temperature, top-k and top-p At every step the model outputs a score (a logit ) for each token in its vocabulary. Softmax turns scores into probabilities; temperature divides the logits first (low temperature sharpens, high flattens); top-k and top-p cut off the unlikely tail before sampling. Copy What you should see Copy This is why the same prompt can say "shipped" one time and "delivered" the next, and why extraction and classification use low temperatures. Top-p removed "delayed", "lost" and "banana" entirely, which is how nucleus sampling avoids rare nonsense while keeping variety. Choosing a model with a scoring matrix How this connects How this builds on Lesson F7.5 Lesson F7.5 gave a four-step method for picking a model (write down what good looks like, try a strong model, try cheaper ones, check the non-quality needs) and showed how to run models yourself. The two sections below turn that method into something you can keep in code and repeat per step of an agent, and add what to do when a choice stops working. Model choice is a weighted decision over your own eval results, not leaderboard positions. Keep the matrix in code so it is rerun when prices, models or your evals change. Copy What you should see Copy The cheapest model scores best on paper but fails the quality floor, so the choice is frontier-mid . A common production answer combines them: route easy requests to the small model and the rest to the mid model, then prove the router with evals ( Lesson 12.10 ). Choosing a model: a method that lasts Write 30 to 100 real test cases for the step ( Lesson 12.11 shows how). Public leaderboards are a shortlist, not a decision. Shortlist three models across price tiers, including one small model. Measure quality, cost per task, p95 latency and failure modes (refusals, bad JSON , wrong tool). Check the non-functional needs : data residency (for example, an Indian region), context length, tool-calling reliability, rate limits, and whether the model is available on your cloud. Pick per step , not per product. A router on a small model and a planner on a frontier model is normal. Pin the exact version and re-run the tests before any upgrade. Industry practice Start with the best model, then step down OpenAI's A practical guide to building agents recommends building the first prototype with the most capable model to set a quality baseline, then swapping in smaller models step by step where the evals stay green. Anthropic's guidance says the same in other words: get it working, measure, then optimize cost. Idea What it means, in one line Taught in Tool calling The model replies with a structured request to run a named function; your code runs it and sends the result back Lesson 3.1 Prompt caching Paying much less for a prompt prefix the provider has already processed recently Lesson 2.4 Evals and evaluation sets Evals are repeatable tests that measure how well a model or system does a task; an evaluation set is the fixed list of test cases with known good answers. Introduced in Lesson 1.3, first built in Lesson 4.7, and covered in depth in Lessons 12.11 and 12.12 Lesson 1.3 Reasoning effort A setting that controls how much a reasoning model thinks before answering Lesson 2.6 Structured output Getting a model's reply as data in a fixed shape, usually JSON that matches a schema, instead of free text Lesson 2.2 Why this came about Early chat products felt slow because users waited for complete answers. Teams learned that a model's speed has two separate parts, reading the input and writing the output, and that each is tuned differently. As agents began chaining many model calls, those delays added up, so latency became a design concern rather than a detail. In plain words first Reading the question, then writing the answer word by word A model's response time has two parts. First it reads the whole input at once ( prefill ); the longer the input, the longer before anything appears. That wait is the time to first token . Then it writes the answer one token at a time ( decode ); the longer the answer, the longer it takes. So a long prompt makes the start slow, and a long answer makes the whole thing slow. Streaming does not make the model faster; it shows the words as they are written, so the wait feels shorter. Latency: two numbers, not one A model call has two phases, and they behave very differently: Prefill (reading). The model processes your whole prompt in one pass. All prompt tokens go through the network together, in parallel, so this phase is fast: thousands of tokens per second. Decode (writing). The model writes the answer one token at a time. Each new token needs its own pass through the network, so this phase is slow: tens to a few hundred tokens per second. A worked example with round numbers: a 4,000-token prompt at 8,000 tokens per second takes half a second to read. A 400-token answer at 80 tokens per second takes five seconds to write. The answer is a tenth the size of the prompt and takes ten times as long. That asymmetry is the single most useful fact about model latency. How this connects Where the speed difference comes from Decoding is slow because each token depends on all the tokens before it, so the model cannot write them in parallel. It avoids redoing work by storing what it computed for earlier tokens in the KV cache , which Lesson F6.5 builds. You do not need the internals here, only the consequence: reading is cheap, writing is slow. The KV cache: without it, generating token 5 recomputes keys and values for tokens 1 to 4 again; with it, each step computes only the new token's row and reads the rest from memory. Time to first token (TTFT) : how long until the answer starts. It grows with input length and with reasoning. Output speed (tokens per second): how fast the answer streams once it starts. A chat feels fast when TTFT is short and the answer streams. An agent feels slow because it makes several calls in sequence: five calls of 2 seconds each is a 10-second turn before any tool time. Budget latency per step, and remove steps before you optimize them. Output tokens are the expensive part of latency, so ask for concise answers and structured outputs later · 2.2 . A long, repeated prompt is cheap only if it is cached. And agents multiply everything by the number of steps, so the fastest agent is usually the one that needs fewer model calls. The throughput numbers here are illustrative; measure your own model and provider. In plain words first The idea in one line Before anything multimodal, an image has to become a sequence of tokens a transformer can eat. The 2020 ViT paper answered this with 16x16 pixel patches, a linear projection, and a position embedding. Six years later frontier models still begin this way: Claude, for example, reads and bills images as 28×28-pixel patches, up to 2,576 px on the long edge for Claude 4.7 and later. The encoders changed from the original ViT to CLIP, DINOv2, SigLIP 2 and DINOv3, and some added register tokens or 2D-RoPE, but the primitive held. This lesson reads the patch-token pipeline end to end and builds it in Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Patch "16x16 pixel square" A fixed-size non-overlapping region of the input image; becomes one token Patch embedding "Linear projection" A shared learned matrix (or Conv2d with stride=P) mapping flattened patch pixels to D-dim vectors CLS token "Class token" Prepended learnable vector whose final hidden state represents the whole image; optional in 2026 Register token "Sink token" Extra learnable tokens that absorb the high-norm attention artifacts ViTs develop during pretraining Position embedding "Positional info" Per-position vector or rotation making the sequence-order-aware; 2D-RoPE is the modern default Grid "Patch grid" The (H/P) x (W/P) 2D array of patches for a given resolution and patch size NaFlex "Native flexible resolution" SigLIP 2 feature: single model serves multiple aspect ratios and resolutions without retraining Backbone "Vision tower" The pretrained image encoder whose patch-token outputs feed the LLM in a VLM Pooling "Image-level summary" Strategy to turn patch tokens into one vector: CLS, mean, attention pool, or register-based Patch 14 vs 16 "Finer vs coarser grid" Patch 14 produces more tokens per image, better fidelity for OCR, slower; patch 16 is the classic default The problem In plain words first A transformer reads a sequence of vectors, but a photo is a grid of pixels. A Vision Transformer (ViT) cuts the image into small squares called patches, typically 14 or 16 pixels on a side. It turns each patch into one vector with a single shared linear map and adds a position signal, so the model knows where each patch came from. The image is now a sequence of "visual tokens", like words in a sentence. Almost every model that reads images starts this way, from CLIP to today's chat assistants. This lesson builds the patch pipeline, counts tokens, parameters and compute, then measures real vision towers from their published configurations. It also looks inside a real DINOv2 model to see why some ViTs now carry extra "register" tokens. No model is trained. Transformers operate on sequences of vectors. Text is already a sequence (bytes or tokens). An image is a 2D grid of pixels with three color channels — not a sequence. If you flatten every pixel, a 224x224 RGB image becomes 150,528 tokens, and self-attention at that length is a non-starter (quadratic in sequence length). Pre-2020 approaches bolted a CNN feature extractor onto the front: ResNet produces a 7x7 feature map of 2048-dim vectors, feed those 49 tokens to a transformer. This works but inherits the CNN's biases (translation equivariance, local receptive fields) and loses the transformer's appetite for scale. Dosovitskiy et al. (2020) asked the blunt question: what if we skip the CNN? Split the image into fixed-size patches (say 16x16 pixels), linearly project each patch into a vector, add a positional embedding, and feed the sequence to a vanilla transformer. At the time this was heresy — vision without convolutions. With enough data (JFT-300M, then LAION) it beat ResNet on ImageNet and kept improving. By 2026 the ViT primitive is the unquestioned foundation. Every open-weights VLM's vision tower is some descendant (DINOv2, SigLIP 2, CLIP, EVA, InternViT). The question is no longer "should we use patches?" but "what patch size, what resolution schedule, what pretraining objective, what positional encoding." Idea 1 · Patches as tokens Given an image x of shape (H, W, 3) and a patch size P , you carve the image into a grid of (H/P) x (W/P) non-overlapping patches. Each patch is a P x P x 3 cube of pixels. Flatten each cube to a 3 P^2 vector. Apply a shared linear projection W_E of shape (3 P^2, D) to map each patch into the model's hidden dimension D . For the ViT-B/16 canonical config: - Resolution 224, patch size 16 → grid 14x14 → 196 patch tokens. - Each patch is 16 x 16 x 3 = 768 pixel values, projected to D = 768 . - Add a learnable [CLS] token → sequence length 197. The patch projection is mathematically identical to a 2D convolution with kernel size P , stride P , and D output channels. That is how production code actually implements it — nn.Conv2d(3, D, kernel_size=P, stride=P) . The "linear projection" framing is conceptual; the kernel framing is efficient. Idea 2 · Positional embeddings Patches have no inherent order — the transformer sees them as a bag. Early ViTs added a learnable 1D positional embedding (one 768-dim vector per position, 197 of them). Works, but ties the model to the training resolution: at inference you have to interpolate the position table if you change the grid. Many modern vision backbones use 2D-RoPE (the vision encoders of Qwen2-VL and later, DINOv3) or factorized 2D positions. SigLIP 2 keeps a learned position table and resizes it bilinearly to each image's grid (its NaFlex variant). 2D-RoPE rotates the query and key vectors based on the patch's (row, column) index, so the model infers relative 2D position from the rotation angle. No position table. The model handles arbitrary grid sizes at inference. Idea 3 · CLS token, pooled output, and register tokens What is the image-level representation? Three choices coexist: [CLS] token. Prepend a learnable vector to the patch sequence. After all transformer blocks, the CLS token's hidden state is the image representation. Inherited from BERT. Used by original ViT, CLIP. Pool the patches. Average the patch tokens' output hidden states, or let a small learned query attend over them (the "MAP head" attention pooling of SigLIP and SigLIP 2). DINOv2's linear probes use the CLS token together with the mean of the patch tokens. Register tokens. Darcet et al. (2023) observed that ViTs trained without an explicit sink token develop high-norm "artifact" patches that hijack self-attention. Adding 4–16 learnable register tokens absorbs this load and improves dense-prediction quality (segmentation, depth). DINOv2 has variants with 4 registers (measured below), and DINOv3 uses 4 registers from the start; SigLIP 2 does not use them. The choice matters for downstream tasks. CLS is fine for classification. For VLMs that feed patch tokens into an LLM, you skip pooling entirely — every patch becomes an LLM input token. Registers get discarded before handoff (they are scaffolding, not content). The same idea as a formula Patching. Predict before you run In a DINOv2 ViT-B/14 trained without registers, how much of the [CLS] token's last-layer attention will land on just 4 of the 256 patches? And in the variant trained with 4 registers? (Solution P1.) For each model: the norm of the patch tokens at the last block, the number of patches with a norm far above the rest, and where the [CLS] token's last-layer attention goes. Inference only. About half a minute on CPU. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Without registers, [CLS] stares at a few patches. In the last layer, 30% of the [CLS] token's attention lands on just 4 of the 256 patches. Those patches are not the important parts of the photo. Darcet et al. showed that such patches usually sit in plain background and stop carrying local information. The model has repurposed them as scratch space for global information. Their norms show it: the largest patch norm is 4.3 times the median, and two of the eight photos have a patch more than 3 times the median. With registers, the sink moves to the registers. The variant trained with 4 extra learnable tokens sends 27% of [CLS] attention to the registers and only 8% to its top 4 patches. Patch norms are even: the largest is 1.3 times the median, and no patch stands out. The patch tokens are left to describe their own patch, which is what dense tasks (segmentation, depth) and VLMs that read every patch want. A note on this measurement. Eight photos and one model size are a small sample; artifacts are stronger in larger models trained longer (the paper's ViT-L and ViT-g). The norms here are taken before the final LayerNorm, because the LayerNorm hides the outliers. Idea 4 · Pretraining: supervised, contrastive, masked, self-distilled The 2020 ViT was pretrained with supervised classification on JFT-300M. Quickly supplanted by: CLIP (2021): contrastive image-text on 400M pairs. Lesson 12.02. MAE (2021, He et al.): mask 75% of patches, reconstruct pixels. Self-supervised, works on pure images. DINO (2021) / DINOv2 (2023): self-distillation with student-teacher, no labels, no captions. The 2023 DINOv2 ViT-g/14 is the strongest purely-visual backbone and the default for "dense features" use cases. SigLIP / SigLIP 2 (2023, 2025): CLIP with a sigmoid loss and NaFlex for native aspect ratio. A common vision tower in open VLMs (Idefics2, LLaVA-OneVision, PaliGemma 2, Gemma 3); others, such as Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL, train their own ViTs. Your choice of pretraining determines what the backbone is good for: CLIP/SigLIP for semantic matching with text, DINOv2 for dense visual features, MAE as a starting point for downstream finetuning. Idea 5 · Scaling laws ViT scaling (Zhai et al. 2022) established that a ViT's quality obeys predictable laws in model size, data size, and compute. At fixed compute: - Bigger model + more data → better quality. - Patch size is a lever on sequence length vs fidelity. Patch 14 (typical for DINOv2/SigLIP SO400m) gives more tokens per image than patch 16; better for OCR and dense tasks, worse for speed. - Resolution is the other big lever. Going from 224 to 384 to 512 almost always helps, at quadratic cost in FLOPs. DINOv2 ViT-g/14 (1.1B parameters, 256 tokens at 224 px) is the strongest purely visual backbone of its family. SigLIP So400m/14 (about 430M parameters with its pooling head, 729 tokens at 384 px) is one of the most common towers in open VLMs. Both are measured below. The backbone size sets your VRAM floor in any downstream VLM. ViT-B/16 at 224 px makes 196 tokens. CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336 px makes 576, and SigLIP So400m/14 at 384 px makes 729 (27 × 27; the last 6 pixels do not fill a patch). In a VLM each of those tokens becomes an LLM input token, so the vision tower's grid decides a large part of the prompt length. Compute grows faster than parameters. DINOv2 ViT-g has 2.7 times SigLIP's parameters (1,136M against 428M) but needs less compute per image (598 against 690 GFLOPs), because it sees 256 tokens instead of 729. For a vision tower, resolution is usually the bigger cost lever. SigLIP and SigLIP 2 have the same shape. Both So400m/14 towers have 27 layers of width 1,152 and 428M parameters. SigLIP 2 changed the training (extra captioning and self-distillation losses, more languages, NaFlex), not the architecture. So it can replace SigLIP in an existing VLM recipe. The patch embedding is a convolution. Unfolding the image into 196 flat patches and multiplying by the convolution's weights gives the convolution's output to within 3e-06, which is float32 rounding. Idea 7 · 2026 production config A common encoder in open VLMs is SigLIP or SigLIP 2 So400m/14. It has: - About 400M parameters (428M in the transformers implementation, which counts the attention-pooling head). - Patch size 14. At 384 px the grid is 27 × 27 = 729 patch tokens (whole patches cover 378 px; the remaining 6 px are dropped). - Attention pooling (the MAP head) for one image-level embedding. For visual question answering, all 729 patch tokens flow into the LLM instead, usually through a projector that may merge neighbouring patches (Lesson 12.6). - No register tokens. - Learned position embeddings. The NaFlex variant resizes them to each image's own grid, so the aspect ratio is kept. Hosted models follow the same arithmetic. Claude counts ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ visual tokens per image, so a 1920×1080 screenshot costs 2,691 input tokens on Claude 4.7 and later models. What goes wrong, and what is the usual fix? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) SigLIP 2 (February 2025): sigmoid contrastive pretraining plus captioning and self-distillation losses, sizes from 86M to 1B, and a NaFlex variant for native aspect ratios. It is widely used as the vision tower of open VLMs. DINOv3 (August 2025): self-supervised ViT-7B/16 with RoPE and 4 register tokens, plus distilled smaller models, for dense features. Native-resolution encoders in VLMs : Qwen2.5-VL and later and InternVL train their own ViTs with 2D-RoPE, taking images at their own size and merging neighbouring patches before the LLM. Hosted pricing follows patches : Claude counts 28×28-pixel visual tokens per image, with a higher resolution limit (2,576 px, 4,784 tokens) on Claude 4.7 and later. Sources: SigLIP 2 (arXiv 2502.14786) , DINOv3 ViT-7B model card , Vision Transformers Need Registers (arXiv 2309.16588) , Claude vision documentation , Hugging Face SigLIP 2 documentation . Recap What to keep from this lesson Patches of P × P pixels become tokens through one shared linear map (a strided convolution). Tokens = (H/P)(W/P): resolution is the main cost lever, and attention grows faster still. Position comes from learned tables (resized when the grid changes) or 2D-RoPE. Image-level summaries: CLS, mean or attention pooling; VLMs pass all patch tokens on. Registers absorb the attention sink that ViTs otherwise build out of a few patches. Solutions Solution P1 · About a third, and much less with registers About 30%: without registers, the [CLS] token's last-layer attention puts 30% of its weight on 4 of the 256 patches, and the largest patch norm is 4.3 times the median. With 4 registers, the top 4 patches get only 8%, while the registers take 27%. The model still needs a place to store global information; registers give it one that is not a patch of the image. Solution B1 · The position table no longer fits At 448 px the grid is 28 × 28 = 784 patches, plus [CLS] = 785 positions, but the learned table has 197 rows. Adding a 785-row sequence to a 197-row table is a shape error. Hugging Face's ViT raises one unless you pass interpolate_pos_encoding=True . The usual fix is that flag: treat the 14 × 14 table (without [CLS]) as a small image, resize it to 28 × 28 with bicubic interpolation, and use that. It works, but the model has never seen those interpolated positions, so quality usually drops a little until it is fine-tuned at the new resolution. This is why "train at low resolution, fine-tune briefly at high resolution" is standard. It is also why encoders built for many resolutions use 2D-RoPE, or resize the table on every input, as NaFlex does. In plain words first The idea in one line OpenAI's CLIP (2021) proved a single idea big enough to power the next five years: align an image encoder and a text encoder in the same vector space using only noisy web image-caption pairs and a contrastive loss. Zero supervised labels. 400M pairs. The resulting embedding space does zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, and plugs into every 2026 VLM as its vision tower. SigLIP 2 (2025) replaced softmax with sigmoid and scaled past CLIP at lower cost. This lesson walks the math from InfoNCE to sigmoid pairwise loss and builds the Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means InfoNCE "Contrastive loss" Cross-entropy over a batch's similarity matrix; each item's positive is its paired item, negatives are everything else Sigmoid loss "SigLIP loss" Per-pair binary cross-entropy; no softmax, no all-gather, scales cheaply in distributed training Temperature "tau" Scalar that scales logits before softmax/sigmoid; controls sharpness of the distribution Zero-shot "no-finetune classification" Use text prompts to construct class embeddings and classify by cosine similarity; no training on target classes Prompt template "a photo of a ..." Text scaffold around a class name; affects zero-shot accuracy by 1-5 points Dual encoder "Two-tower" One image encoder + one text encoder, outputs in shared D-dim space Hard negative "Tough distractor" A negative similar enough to the positive that the model has to work to separate them Linear probe "Frozen + one layer" Train only a linear classifier on top of frozen features; measures feature quality NaFlex "Native flexible resolution" SigLIP 2 capability to ingest images at any aspect ratio and resolution without resizing Temperature scaling "log-parametrized tau" CLIP parametrizes log(1/tau) so gradients behave; clips to prevent collapse to near-zero tau The problem In plain words first CLIP learns to put a picture and a sentence that describes it at the same point in one shared space. It has two encoders, one for images and one for text, each producing a vector. Training shows the model a batch of images with their captions and rewards it when every image's vector is closest to its own caption's vector rather than to the other captions'. That needs no labels, only image–caption pairs from the web. Once trained, the space can classify images it was never trained on: write "a photo of a dog", "a photo of a cat", and pick the caption closest to the image. This lesson derives the two training losses (CLIP's softmax and SigLIP's sigmoid), then uses the real CLIP ViT-B/32 to classify photos zero-shot and to compute both losses on real vectors. No model is trained. Pre-CLIP vision was supervised. Collect labeled datasets (ImageNet: 1.2M images, 1000 classes), train a CNN, ship it. Labels are expensive, labels bias to what labelers can agree on, and labels do not transfer to new tasks without finetuning. The image-caption web has one billion-plus loosely-labeled pairs for free. A picture of a golden retriever with alt text "my dog Max in the park" carries a supervisory signal — the text describes the image. The question: can you turn this into useful training? CLIP's answer: treat image-caption pairs as a matching task. Given a batch of N images and N captions, learn to match each image to its own caption against N-1 distractors. The supervision is "these two things belong together; these N-1 do not." No class labels. No human annotation. Just a contrastive loss. The resulting embedding space does more than CLIP was trained for. ImageNet zero-shot works because "a photo of a cat" embeds near pictures of cats that were never explicitly labeled cats. This is the bet that spawned every 2026 VLM. Idea 1 · The dual encoder CLIP has two towers: Image encoder f : ViT or ResNet, outputs a D-dim vector per image. Text encoder g : small transformer, outputs a D-dim vector per caption. Both towers normalize their outputs to unit length. Similarity is cos(f(x), g(y)) = f(x)^T g(y) since both are unit-norm. For a batch of (image, caption) pairs, build the similarity matrix S of shape (N, N) : ​ ) , g ( y j ​ )) / τ where tau is a learned temperature (CLIP initializes to 0.07; learned in log-space). Idea 2 · InfoNCE loss CLIP uses a symmetric cross-entropy over rows and columns: Copy This is InfoNCE. The softmax in CE forces each image to match its caption more than every other caption in the batch. The "negatives" are all other batch items. Bigger batches = more negatives = stronger signal. CLIP trained at batch 32k; scale matters. Idea 3 · Temperature tau controls the sharpness of the softmax. Low → sharp distribution, hard negative mining effect. High → soft, all samples contribute. Idea 4 · Why sigmoid scales better (SigLIP) Softmax needs the whole similarity matrix in sync. In distributed training you must all-gather every embedding to every replica, then do the softmax. This is quadratic in world size for communication. SigLIP replaces softmax with element-wise sigmoid: for each pair (i, j) , the loss is a binary classification of "are these the matching pair?" positive class labels are the diagonal, everything else is negative. Each pair's loss is independent, so no normalisation over the whole batch is needed. SigLIP's paper exploits this with a chunked implementation: each device scores its local images against its local texts, then passes its text embeddings to the next device in a ring and repeats, so no device ever holds the full matrix. That makes very large batches cheap in memory; the SigLIP paper also found that gains level off around a batch of 32k. On a clean batch of 10 pairs, InfoNCE with 1/τ = 1 is 2.193, barely below chance (ln 10 = 2.30), although the model ranks every pair correctly. At 1/τ = 100 the same vectors give 0.044. A loss stuck near ln N at the start of training is often a temperature problem, not a model problem. The sigmoid loss needs its bias. Each of the 100 pairs is a yes/no question, and 90 of them are "no". At SigLIP's starting point (t = 10, b = −10) every pair is a confident "no": wrong pairs are right, true pairs wrong, loss 7.2. With t = 100 and no bias, every pair looks like a match (loss 145.8). A bias of −25 puts the decision boundary between the cosines of matching (about 0.3) and non-matching (about 0.2) pairs: true pairs get 0.83, wrong pairs 0.01, loss 0.548. In training, b and t are learned for exactly this reason. Repeated captions become false negatives. In a batch of 64 photos from 10 classes, 10% of the off-diagonal pairs show a photo and a caption of the same class. InfoNCE scores them as negatives, so even this well-trained model is charged 3.099. That is closer to chance (4.16) than to zero, and the gradient would push matching pairs apart. Counting every same-class caption as a positive drops the loss to 1.987. Web captions rarely repeat exactly, which is why CLIP works; curated datasets with few distinct captions need deduplicated batches or multi-positive losses. Solutions Solution P1 · Nearly perfect, so the templates had nothing left to add 99.3% with the bare class names, and the 5-template ensemble added nothing (99.0%). The ten Imagenette classes are so distinct that CLIP gets almost every photo right without help, so prompt templates have no errors left to fix. On harder label sets, such as fine-grained species or ambiguous names, the CLIP paper found templates and ensembles worth several points. Test them where the errors are. Solution B1 · Most negatives are positives in disguise With 20 categories and a batch of 256, each caption appears about 13 times in a batch. For any image, about 12 of the 255 "negatives" carry exactly its own caption. InfoNCE asks the model to rank its own caption above identical copies of itself, which is impossible, so the loss cannot fall much below ln 13 ≈ 2.6. Part of every gradient pushes an image away from correct descriptions. The run above shows the effect at a smaller scale: 10% false negatives lifted the loss from near zero to 3.1. Fixes: sample batches with at most one item per category; use a multi-positive target that counts all same-category pairs as matches (as in supervised contrastive learning); or, best, write captions that actually differ per item (colour, brand, style), so that the contrastive task carries information. With only 20 categories, a plain classifier or a linear probe on frozen CLIP features may simply be the better tool.
