In plain words first The idea in one line CLIP aligns image and text but cannot generate captions, answer questions, or hold a conversation. BLIP-2 (Salesforce, 2023) solved that with a small trainable bridge: 32 learnable query vectors attend over a frozen ViT's features via cross-attention, then slot directly into a frozen LLM's input stream. 188M parameters of bridge connected a ViT-g/14 to frozen LLMs as large as the 11B Flan-T5-XXL. Every adapter-based VLM through 2026 — MiniGPT-4, InstructBLIP, LLaVA's cousins — is a descendant. This lesson reads the Q-Former's architecture, Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Q-Former "Querying transformer" Small transformer with 32 learnable query vectors that cross-attend to frozen ViT features Learnable queries "Soft prompt for vision" A fixed set of parameters that serve as the query side of cross-attention; learned per model, shared across all inputs Cross-attention "Q from here, K/V from there" Attention where query, key, and value come from different sources; how the queries pull from ViT patches ITC "Image-text contrastive" CLIP-style loss applied to Q-Former pooled queries vs text CLS ITM "Image-text matching" Binary classifier on hard-negative-mined pairs; forces the queries to discriminate fine-grained mismatches ITG "Image-grounded text generation" Causal LM loss where text is generated conditioned on queries; forces queries to encode text-decodable content Two-stage pretraining "Representation then generative" Stage 1 trains Q-Former alone (ITC/ITM/ITG); Stage 2 attaches frozen LLM and trains only the projection + Q-Former Frozen backbone "Do not finetune" The vision encoder and LLM weights are fixed; only the bridge trains Projection head "Linear to LLM dim" Final linear layer mapping Q-Former output to the LLM's embedding dimension Perceiver resampler "Flamingo's version" Similar learnable-query cross-attention; Flamingo runs it once per image to make fixed latents, then reads them through gated cross-attention at every LLM layer The problem In plain words first CLIP can tell which caption fits a picture, but it cannot write one. To make a language model talk about images, you have to feed it the image as something it can read: vectors in its own input space. BLIP-2 does this with a small trainable bridge called the Q-Former. 32 learned "query" vectors look at the frozen image encoder's patch features through cross-attention. They come out as 32 summary vectors, which a linear layer maps into the frozen language model's embedding space, in front of the text prompt. Only the bridge is trained, so the cost is a few percent of the full model. This lesson walks through the Q-Former and its two-stage training, counts the real BLIP-2 and LLaVA models part by part, and measures what each visual token costs a real language model. No model is trained. You have a frozen ViT that produces 256 patch tokens of dim 1408 per image. You have a frozen 7B LLM that expects token embeddings of dim 4096. The obvious bridge — a linear layer from 1408 to 4096 — works, but feeding all 256 patch tokens into the LLM's context costs 256 extra tokens per image. Over a batch of 32 images that is 8192 tokens consumed by the visual modality alone. The BLIP-2 question: can you compress the 256-token image representation into far fewer tokens (say 32) while preserving enough information for the LLM to caption, answer questions, and reason about the image? And can you train this bridge without touching the frozen backbones, keeping the training cost at just the bridge's parameters? The answer: a Q-Former. 32 learnable "query" vectors that cross-attend to the ViT's patch tokens, producing a 32-token visual summary that the LLM consumes. 188M parameters total. Trained with contrastive, matching, and generative objectives before ever touching the LLM. Idea 1 · Learnable queries The Q-Former's core trick: instead of letting the LLM's text tokens attend to image patches, introduce a new set of 32 learnable query vectors Q and let them attend to image patches. The queries are parameters of the model — they are learned during training and the same 32 queries are used for every image. After cross-attention, each query holds a compressed summary of the image — "describe the main object", "describe the background", "count the objects", etc. The queries do not literally specialize on semantic labels; they learn whatever encoding makes downstream losses drop. Idea 2 · Architecture The Q-Former is a small transformer (12 layers of width 768, initialised from BERT-base; cross-attention in every other layer) with two paths: Query path: 32 query vectors flow through self-attention (among themselves), then cross-attention over the frozen ViT's patch tokens, then FFN. Text path: a BERT-like text encoder shares the self-attention and FFN weights with the query path. Cross-attention is disabled for the text path. At training time both paths run. The queries and text interact through shared self-attention, which means the queries can condition on text for tasks that need it (ITM, ITG). At inference time for VLM handoff, only the queries flow through, yielding 32 visual tokens. Idea 3 · Two-stage training BLIP-2 pretrains in two stages: Stage 1: representation learning (no LLM). Three losses: - ITC (image-text contrastive): CLIP-style contrastive between pooled query tokens and text CLS token. - ITM (image-text matching): binary classifier — is this image-text pair a match? Hard-negative-mined. - ITG (image-grounded text generation): causal LM head on text, conditioned on the queries. Forces queries to encode text-generatable content. Only the Q-Former trains. The ViT is frozen. No LLM involved. Stage 2: generative learning. Attach a frozen LLM (OPT-2.7B or Flan-T5-XL, etc.). Project the 32 query outputs to the LLM's embedding dim via a small linear layer. Prepend them to the text prompt. Train only the linear projection and the Q-Former on LM loss over the concatenated prompt + image + caption sequence. After stage 2, the Q-Former + projection is the full visual adapter. At inference: image → ViT → Q-Former → linear proj → prepended to text → frozen LLM emits output. Idea 4 · Parameter economics BLIP-2 with EVA-CLIP ViT-g/14 (about 1B, frozen) + OPT-6.7B (frozen) + Q-Former (trained) is about 7.8B parameters, of which only the bridge is trained. The paper counts the Q-Former as 188M, because stage 1 also uses its text path (a BERT-base text encoder). The released inference model keeps only the query path: 105M plus a 3M projection, 1.4% of the stack (measured below). Training cost reflects this: the paper's largest model trained in under 9 days on 16 A100 GPUs. Quality: BLIP-2 beat Flamingo-80B by 8.7 points on zero-shot VQAv2 with 54 times fewer trainable parameters. The bridge works. Worked example Five images in one prompt LLaVA-1.5 passes all patch tokens per image; five images are 2,880 tokens before any text. BLIP-2 passes 32 per image: 160 tokens for five images, 18 times fewer. For a 7B model with full multi-head attention ( , 32 heads of 128, bf16), the KV cache is bytes per token: about 1.5 GB for 2,880 visual tokens, 84 MB for 160. The price of compression: 32 vectors must carry everything about the image. Fine detail (small text, counts, positions) is what gets lost first. Why not 188M, as the paper says? The paper's count includes the Q-Former's text path and the heads used only in stage 1 (contrastive, matching and generation losses). The released model for generation keeps just the query path: 12 layers of width 768 with cross-attention to the image in every other layer. LLaVA-1.5's bridge is smaller still, but sends more tokens. Its projector is a 2-layer MLP of 21M parameters. Instead of compressing, it forwards every one of the 576 patch tokens (a 24 × 24 grid from CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336 px), 18 times BLIP-2's 32. The parameter budget of the bridge says little about cost. The number of tokens it hands to the LLM says a lot, as the next run shows. Prefill time rises with the number of visual tokens: 32 Q-Former tokens are cheap, 576 LLaVA tokens cost several times as much, and five LLaVA images (2,880 tokens) cost far more again. The growth is slightly faster than linear, because attention grows with the square of the sequence. Exact timings vary between runs on a shared CPU; the ordering and the rough ratios do not. Memory follows the same count. The KV cache grows linearly: under 1 MB for the 32-token image, about 36 MB for five LLaVA images on this small model (12 KB per token). For a 7B model with full multi-head attention it is 524 KB per token, so the five-image prompt holds about 1.5 GB of cache per request. That limits how many users a GPU can serve at once. The trade-off BLIP-2 made. Compressing to 32 tokens makes every image cheap, and is why Q-Former-style compressors still appear where many images or long videos must fit. LLaVA's choice of passing all 576 tokens costs more, but keeps detail, and with good instruction data it won on quality. Most current models sit in between, merging neighbouring patches (2 × 2 merging turns 576 tokens into 144). Idea 5 · InstructBLIP and the instruction-aware Q-Former InstructBLIP (2023) extends the Q-Former with an extra input: the instruction text itself. At cross-attention time, the queries now have access to both the image patches and the instruction. The queries can specialize per-instruction ("count the cars", "describe the mood") rather than learning a single fixed summary. Benchmark gains on held-out tasks. Idea 6 · MiniGPT-4 and the projector-only approach MiniGPT-4 kept the Q-Former but trained only the output linear projection while freezing everything else. Cheap, but cost is quality — the queries were BLIP-2's, not yours. Good for rapid iteration, not the best architecture. Idea 7 · Why LLaVA went simpler LLaVA (2023, Lesson 12.05) replaced the Q-Former with a plain 2-layer MLP that projects every ViT patch token into LLM space — 576 tokens per image for a 24x24 grid, all fed to the LLM. Worse compression but lets the LLM attend over raw patches. At the time this was controversial; by late 2023 it was dominant because visual instruction data (LLaVA-Instruct-150k) proved that the MLP could be trained to preserve enough signal. The tradeoff: LLaVA's context fills faster, but it scales naturally to multi-image and video. By 2026 the MLP projector, with patch merging when tokens are scarce, has become the default. Learned-query compressors survive where token budget matters most, such as long video and many images. Idea 8 · Gated cross-attention: Flamingo, the ancestor Flamingo (Lesson 12.04) predated BLIP-2 and used the same cross-attention idea but inside the frozen LLM, through gated cross-attention layers inserted between its blocks, not as a single bridge at the input. BLIP-2 showed you can compress at the input only and still work. The first Idefics (2023) was an open Flamingo-style model; Idefics2 and later moved to input tokens produced by a perceiver resampler. Idea 9 · The 2026 descendants Q-Former: BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, MiniGPT-4, and some early video-language models (Video-LLaMA) for token budget reasons. Perceiver resampler: Flamingo's variant (Lesson 12.04); Idefics2 compresses each image to 64 tokens with one (Idefics3 later switched to pixel shuffle). MLP projector: LLaVA, LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-OneVision, Cambrian-1, and most 2024–2026 open VLMs. They usually merge neighbouring patches before the MLP to save tokens (2×2 merging in Qwen2-VL and later, pixel shuffle in InternVL). Linear projection of every patch: PaliGemma. All four are valid. The deciding question is whether you are constrained on token budget or on quality-per-token. Run scaled-dot-product cross-attention (Q from queries, K/V from patches). Project to LLM-dim (512) via a linear layer. Output the 32 LLM-ready visual tokens. All math in pure Python (nested loops over vectors). Toy but correct shape. The attention-weight matrix is printed so you can see which patches each query pulled from. What did the BLIP-2 paper find happens, and why? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) MLP projectors with token merging are the common bridge in open VLMs: Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL merge 2×2 patches, InternVL uses pixel shuffle, LLaVA-OneVision keeps an MLP with resolution-dependent pooling. Learned-query compressors live on where tokens are scarce: perceiver resamplers (Idefics2) and query-based compression in long-video models. Freeze, then unfreeze : most 2024–2026 recipes train the projector first with the encoder and LLM frozen, then unfreeze the LLM (and often the encoder) for instruction tuning; the fully frozen BLIP-2 setup is now mainly a low-cost option. Visual tokens dominate multimodal prompts : providers bill images per patch-token (Lesson 12.1), so token-saving bridges matter in production as well as in training. Solutions Solution P1 · About 1%, and several times the prefill 108M of 7.75B, about 1.4%: the Q-Former (105M with its 32 queries) and a 3M projection; the 986M vision encoder and the 6.66B OPT model are frozen. On Qwen2.5-0.5B, prefilling 576 visual tokens plus a 40-token question took several times as long as 32 visual tokens (about 4 times when this page was built; it varies between runs), and five LLaVA images about 30 times as long. A short request has a fixed overhead, so the ratio grows with the number of tokens. Solution B1 · Without stage 1, the bridge learns much less The BLIP-2 paper tested exactly this (its Figure 5): without the stage-1 representation learning, zero-shot VQA accuracy dropped sharply for both OPT and Flan-T5, and the OPT model suffered catastrophic forgetting during stage 2. Stage 1 teaches the queries what to extract: the contrastive loss aligns them with text, the matching loss forces fine-grained comparison, and the generation loss makes them carry the information a caption needs. Skip it, and the queries start from random vectors. The language-modelling loss then has to discover visual features through a frozen LLM, which gives a weak, indirect signal. On a small dataset the bridge settles for whatever helps predict common caption words. Pretrain the bridge on image–text alignment first, or start from a released Q-Former checkpoint. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Weigh a trade-off You are choosing the bridge between a frozen vision encoder and a language model that stays frozen, for a new product. One architect wants a query-based transformer that compresses each image to a fixed set of tokens. Another wants a plain MLP that passes every patch through. How do you decide? Level 2 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Decide on the token budget, not on quality in the abstract. At a fixed number of visual tokens, the ablation studies find the connector architecture a wash, within about a point between an MLP on mean-pooled patches, a query bridge and a resampler; a full-patch MLP spends more tokens, so it sits at a different budget. The query bridge caps an image at 32 tokens whatever its resolution and costs 188M parameters plus a two-stage pretraining of its own; the MLP emits every patch, 576 for a 336-pixel image, with about 22M parameters and one language-modeling loss. Pick the compressing bridge when context binds, as with long video or many images; pick the MLP when quality per token and simplicity matter and the context is long enough. The two bridges. Query bridge MLP Visual tokens per image 32, fixed 576 at 336 pixels, about 2880 with tiling Trainable parameters, language model frozen 188M about 22M Pretraining a representation stage with contrastive, matching and generation losses, then a generative stage the language-modeling loss throughout Swap the language model retrain the bridge retrain a small head Many images and video awkward, but cheap in tokens natural concatenation, expensive in tokens What the ablations say. Several controlled studies reached one result. At a fixed visual-token count, the connector explains about 5 percent of the variance in benchmark scores, the per-image token count about 60 percent, and the encoder about 20. An MLP on pooled patches lands within 1 point of a 32-query bridge at the same budget. So the question is how many tokens you can afford, and which encoder you use. Why the field split. The compressing bridge wins where the token budget binds: long video, many images in one prompt, small contexts. The MLP won the single-image case once contexts grew to 32k and beyond, because every patch stays visible to the language model and the recipe has no stage-one losses to tune. Token budgets from the ablations: 64 per image is too few for reading text, 576 to 1024 is the sweet spot for most tasks, and 2048 and above pays only for documents and charts. Hidden costs of the query bridge. Its queries learn an intermediate representation that the language model must then decode, so information is lost in the bottleneck. Change the language model or the encoder, and you retrain it. An instruction-aware variant feeds the instruction into the queries so that they can specialize per question, which recovers some of the loss. A decision rule. Count the tokens per image at your resolution and multiply by the images per prompt. If it fits the context with room for text, use the MLP and spend the effort on the encoder and the data. If it does not, use a compressing bridge, and accept the retraining cost when parts change. Plausible wrong answers. "The query bridge is more advanced, so it gives better answers." At the same token count the two are within about a point; its advantage is compression, not quality. "The MLP is always better because it keeps every patch." Keeping every patch costs tokens; with many images or video the context runs out before quality matters. "Pick the bridge first and the encoder later." The encoder and the token count explain most of the variance; the bridge is the last knob to turn. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the query bridge need a pretraining stage of its own? Expected: its queries start random and must learn to pull text-relevant content from the patches before the language model can use them; the MLP starts from patches that already carry the image. (level 2) What do the three stage-one losses do? Expected: contrastive alignment of pooled queries with text, a matching classifier with hard negatives, and image-grounded text generation that forces the queries to encode what text needs. (level 3) A team picked the MLP and now serves ten-minute videos. What do they hit first? Expected: the context; tokens per frame times frames exceeds any window, so they need heavy frame sampling or a compressing bridge after all. (level 3) If the connector barely matters, where does the quality come from? Expected: the encoder, the token count, the data mix and the resolution schedule; the recipes lesson's decomposition puts the connector last. Where it is taught. In plain words first The idea in one line DeepMind's Flamingo (2022) did two things before anyone else. It showed a single model could process arbitrarily interleaved sequences of images, videos, and text. And it showed VLMs could learn in-context — give a few-shot prompt with three example (image, caption) pairs and the model captions a new image without any gradient step. The mechanism: gated cross-attention layers, inserted between the frozen LLM's existing layers, with a learned tanh gate that starts at zero so the LLM's text capability is preserved at initialization. This Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Perceiver resampler "Fixed-latent cross-attention" Module that produces K fixed tokens from a variable number of input patches Gated cross-attention "Tanh-gated bridge" Residual layer y = tanh(alpha)*cross + x , learnable alpha, init 0 Interleaved input "Mixed sequence" Prompt format with images and text mixed freely in reading order Frozen LLM "No LLM gradients" The text LLM's weights do not update; only resampler + cross-attn layers train Few-shot "In-context examples" Give a few (image, answer) pairs in the prompt; model generalizes without finetuning OBELICS "Interleaved web corpus" Open dataset of 141M web pages with images and text in reading order Chinchilla "70B frozen base" Flamingo's frozen text LLM, from DeepMind's Chinchilla paper Gate schedule "How alpha moves" The rate at which the cross-attention gate opens during training Cross-attn frequency "Every M layers" How often a gated cross-attention block is inserted; Flamingo uses , 4 and 7 for its 3B, 9B and 80B models OpenFlamingo "Open reproduction" MosaicML/LAION open checkpoint at 3-9B; architecture-identical to Flamingo The problem In plain words first Flamingo (DeepMind, 2022) gives a frozen language model eyes without changing what it already knows. It leaves the text stream untouched and inserts new layers between the existing ones. In these, the text tokens look at image features through cross-attention. Each new layer's contribution is multiplied by a gate, tanh(α), and α starts at zero, so on day one the model is exactly the original language model. Training opens the gates gradually. A Perceiver resampler squeezes each image to a fixed 64 tokens, and a mask makes every word look only at the most recent image, so prompts can interleave many images and texts. This lesson explains the design, then inserts zero-gated cross-attention into a real frozen 0.5B language model to show that nothing changes until the gates open. No model is trained. BLIP-2 feeds 32 visual tokens into a frozen LLM's input layer. Works for one image per prompt. But what if you want to feed many images interleaved with text, as in "here is image A, caption it; here is image B, caption it; now here is image C, caption it"? The LLM's self-attention would need to handle image tokens and text tokens in a single stream, and the question of which positions can attend to which images gets fussy. Flamingo's answer: do not change the LLM's input stream at all. Insert extra cross-attention layers between existing LLM blocks. Text tokens still flow through the LLM's causal self-attention as always. Between every few LLM blocks, text tokens also cross-attend to image features via a new gated layer. The gate (initialized to zero) means at step zero the new layers are no-ops — the model behaves exactly like the pretrained LLM. As training progresses the gate opens and visual information starts flowing. The second question Flamingo answered: how do you handle a variable number of images (0, 1, or many) per prompt? A Perceiver resampler — a small cross-attention module that takes whatever number of patches you have and produces a fixed number of visual latent tokens per image. The total grows with the image count, but each text token reads only one image's latents, so what any single text token sees in cross-attention has the same shape regardless of how many images are in the prompt. Idea 1 · The frozen LLM Flamingo starts with a frozen Chinchilla 70B LLM. All 70B weights untouched. The existing text self-attention and FFN operate normally. Idea 2 · Perceiver resampler For each image in the prompt, the ViT produces patch tokens. The Perceiver resampler has fixed learnable latents (Flamingo uses ). Each resampler block is two sub-steps: Cross-attention: the latents attend over the patch tokens (Q from latents, K/V from patches). Self-attention + FFN within the latents. After 6 resampler blocks, the output is visual tokens of dim 1024, regardless of how many patches the ViT produced. A 224x224 image (196 patches) and a 480x480 image (900 patches) both exit as 64 resampler tokens. For video, the resampler is applied temporally: each frame's patches produce 64 latents, and a temporal positional encoding lets the model distinguish from . The full video becomes visual tokens. Idea 3 · Gated cross-attention Between every layers of the frozen LLM, insert a new gated cross-attention block. Flamingo-3B uses (a block before every layer), Flamingo-9B , and Flamingo-80B , trading visual capacity against added parameters: Copy alpha is a learnable scalar initialized to zero. tanh(0) = 0 , so at init the gated branch contributes zero. As alpha moves away from zero, the cross-attention contribution grows smoothly. The residual connection means even a fully-open gate does not overwrite the LLM's text representation; it just adds visual information on top. This is the single most important design choice in Flamingo: visual conditioning is additive, gated, and zero at initialization. A Flamingo at step 0 is a perfect Chinchilla 70B on text-only inputs. Idea 4 · Masked cross-attention for interleaved inputs In a prompt like " caption A caption B ?", each text token should only see images that came before it in the sequence. The cross-attention mask enforces: text token at position t attends only to the resampler tokens of image i_t , where i_t is the most recent image before position t ; tokens from every other image are masked. "Sees only the last preceding image" or "sees all preceding images" are both valid choices; Flamingo chose the former. With every gate at tanh(α) = 0, how much do the logits change? And at tanh(α) ≈ 0.96, what happens to the perplexity of an ordinary English sentence? (Solution P1.) See it drawn Zero-gated cross-attention in a real frozen LLM Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, frozen, with 6 Flamingo-style blocks (gated cross-attention plus gated feed-forward), one after every 4 of its 24 layers, attached with forward hooks. The "visual" input is 64 random latents standing in for one image's resampler output. For gate values from 0 to 0.96: the largest change in any logit, and the perplexity of a fixed English sentence. Nothing is trained. About 20 seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output At a closed gate nothing changes, exactly. With 6 new blocks inserted and 58M new random parameters (12% of the 494M frozen LLM), the logits differ from the original model by 0.0000 and the sentence's perplexity is still 3.91. This is not "almost the same": multiplying by tanh(0) = 0 removes the new branch entirely. Training can start from the pretrained language model with no damage, which is the point of Flamingo's design. Opening the gate injects whatever the branch carries. At tanh(α) = 0.01 the logits move by up to 0.16 and perplexity is unchanged at two decimals (3.92). At 0.1 they move by 1.6 and perplexity rises to 4.05. At 0.46 it is 5.47, and at 0.96 it is 17.58: the untrained branch, fed random "visual" latents, is now overwriting the language model's computation. What training does. The gate gives the optimiser a dial for how much of the visual branch to let in. The gradient on α is non-zero even at 0, so as the cross-attention learns to extract useful image information, opening the gate lowers the loss and α grows. The Flamingo paper reports that the learned gates open to different degrees at different depths. Where the blocks go. Here one block follows every 4th layer, as in Flamingo-9B. More blocks give the image more influence and add more parameters. With 70B frozen parameters, Flamingo-80B's blocks add about 10B. See it drawn The interleaving mask, token by token The prompt "⟨image⟩ A photo of a cat. ⟨image⟩ A photo of a dog. ⟨image⟩ A photo of a" in the Qwen tokenizer, with 64 latents per image. The table shows which image each text token may cross-attend to under Flamingo's rule, and how much more the "all preceding images" variant would read. Instant. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Each caption reads only its own image. The tokens of "A photo of a cat." cross-attend to image 1's 64 latents, "A photo of a dog." to image 2's, and the final unfinished "A photo of a" to image 3's. Self-attention in the LLM still lets every token read all earlier text. So when the model completes the third caption, it can copy the pattern of the first two from the text, while its visual evidence comes only from image 3. That combination is what makes Flamingo's few-shot prompting work. The mask is sparse. Only 33% of the cross-attention entries are allowed. The variant where each token sees all preceding images would allow 61%, and the last token would read 192 latents instead of 64. Flamingo chose the simpler rule: it performed better in the paper's ablations than seeing all previous images, and the LLM's self-attention still carries information about earlier images forward through the text. Text before the first image (not in this prompt) has no image to see. Flamingo handles it by letting the gated block contribute nothing for those positions. Idea 5 · In-context few-shot learning A Flamingo prompt looks like: Copy The model sees the completion pattern and outputs "bird" (or whatever image3 shows). No gradient steps. The frozen LLM's in-context learning capability carries through the gated cross-attention — this is the punchline of the paper and why it matters. Idea 6 · Training data Flamingo trained on three datasets: MultiModal MassiveWeb (M3W): 43M web pages with interleaved images and text, reconstructing reading order. Image-Text Pairs: ALIGN (1.8B pairs) plus LTIP (312M pairs), about 2.1B pairs in total. Video-Text Pairs (VTP): 27M short video clips. OBELICS (2023) is an open reproduction of the interleaved web corpus, which Idefics, Idefics2, and most open "Flamingo-like" models train on. Idea 7 · OpenFlamingo and Otter OpenFlamingo (2023) is the open reproduction. Architecture identical (Perceiver resampler + gated cross-attention on frozen LLaMA or MPT). Checkpoints at 3B, 4B, 9B. Quality lags Flamingo due to smaller base LLM and less data. Otter (2023) builds on OpenFlamingo with instruction tuning on MIMIC-IT (a dataset of multimodal instructions), showing gated cross-attention works for instruction following too. Idea 8 · The descendants Idefics / Idefics2 / Idefics3: Hugging Face's line. Idefics (2023) was an open Flamingo-style model with gated cross-attention. Idefics2 dropped the cross-attention layers and fed 64 perceiver-resampler tokens per image into the LLM's input. Idefics3 replaced the resampler with pixel shuffle. Flamingo-to-Chameleon transition: by 2024 many teams moved to early-fusion (Lesson 12.11); Flamingo-style gated cross-attention remains in production where backbone freezing is required. Gemini's interleaved input: conceptually inherits Flamingo's interleaved-format flexibility, though the exact mechanism is proprietary. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Input-token fusion won for most models : since 2024 most open VLMs (LLaVA family, Qwen-VL, InternVL, Idefics2/3) place projected visual tokens in the LLM's input instead of adding cross-attention layers. Solutions Solution P1 · Exactly nothing, then a large loss of fluency At tanh(α) = 0 the logits change by exactly 0.0000 and the perplexity stays 3.91, the frozen model's own value, even though 58M random parameters were inserted. At tanh(α) ≈ 0.96 the untrained branch dominates: the perplexity of the same English sentence rises to 17.58, more than four times worse. The gate decides how much of the new branch reaches the language model, so starting it closed protects the pretrained model completely. Solution B1 · The model starts damaged At α = 1 the gate is tanh(1) ≈ 0.76 open from the first step, so the randomly initialised cross-attention and feed-forward branches add large, meaningless updates in every block. The run above shows the effect: at a gate of 0.46 the perplexity of plain English had already risen from 3.91 to 5.47, and at 0.96 to 17.58. The frozen LLM cannot adapt. All repair must come from the new layers: they first have to learn to cancel their own noise, or the gates have to close again, before they can learn anything useful about images. Training is slower and less stable, and the early gradients through a damaged language model are poor. Zero-initialised gates avoid all of this. Read the code A teammate's vision-language decoder trains well, but at inference the captions are wrong from the second token on, and a test with an image of 197 tokens crashes with a shape error. Read the block and the decode loop and find the problems. python def causal_mask(n): return torch.tril(torch.ones(n, n, dtype=torch.bool)) class DecoderBlock(nn.Module): def forward(self, text, image, mask): text = text + self.self_attn(self.ln1(text), mask=None) text = text + self.cross_attn(self.ln2(text), image, mask=mask) text = text + self.ffn(self.ln3(text)) return text def generate(model, image, prompt_ids, steps): ids = prompt_ids for _ in range(steps): memory = model.encode_image(image) mask = causal_mask(ids.shape[1]) logits = model.decode(ids, memory, mask) ids = torch.cat([ids, logits[:, -1].argmax(-1, keepdim=True)], dim=1) return ids Level 2 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The masks are swapped. Self-attention over the text runs with no mask, so every position sees the future during training, and the model learns to copy the next token instead of predicting it, which breaks as soon as it must generate. Cross-attention gets the causal text mask, which is square over the text length and cannot apply to scores that span text by image, hence the shape error with 197 image tokens. The decode loop also re-encodes the image on every step; encode once, cache the image keys and values, and reuse them. The mask discipline. Attention Query Key Mask Self-attention over text text, length Nt text, length Nt causal, lower-triangular Nt by Nt Cross-attention into the image text, length Nt image, length Nv none Text may not look ahead during autoregression. The image is fully observed before any text exists, and its patches have no order, so every text position may attend to every patch. Bug 1: no mask on self-attention. With mask=None , position i attends to the positions after it. Under teacher forcing the target of position i is the token at i plus one, which is now visible, so the loss falls fast and the model learns to look it up. At inference the future does not exist, and from the second token the captions fall apart. That is the symptom in the report. Bug 2: the causal mask on cross-attention. The scores of cross-attention have the shape Nt by Nv. A causal mask of shape Nt by Nt fits only when Nv equals Nt, and then it silently hides part of the image from the early text tokens. With a 197-token image memory and a shorter text, the shapes do not broadcast and the forward pass raises. The capstone adds one shape-validation function, so that this mistake raises a clear error instead of corrupting a loss curve. Observation 3: no key and value cache. The image does not change during decoding. Encoding it on every step and projecting its keys and values again multiplies the cost of the heavy encoder by the number of generated tokens. Encode once, project once, store the keys and values, and pass them to every step. The capstone tests that the cached and the uncached paths give identical logits. The fixed block. Copy Plausible wrong answers. "Use the causal mask on both attentions to be safe." Cross-attention scores are text by image, so a square text mask either raises or hides part of the image; the image needs no mask. "The captions are wrong because the image encoder is weak." A model that is right on the first token and wrong from the second leaked the future in training; the mask is the cause. "Recomputing the image each step is fine, the encoder is small." The encoder is the heaviest part per call, and the image never changes; the cache is what makes captioning fast. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the training loss look fine with the first bug? Expected: teacher forcing puts the target token in the input one position later, and an unmasked attention can read it; the loss measures a lookup, not a prediction. (level 2) When does cross-attention need a mask? Expected: with several images and text segments interleaved, where a segment may see only the images before it; for one image and one caption, none. (level 3) What does the gate from the Flamingo design add to this block, and why? Expected: a learned scalar through a hyperbolic tangent on the cross-attention residual, starting at zero, so that a frozen language model keeps its text behavior at initialization and mixes the image in gradually. (level 3) How do you test the cache path? Expected: run the same prompt with and without the cache and assert that the logits match to float tolerance; the capstone ships that test. Where it is taught. The cross-attention fusion capstone sets the mask shapes and the key and value cache, and the Flamingo lesson adds the gate and the interleaved mask. Debug a failure You fine-tune a model built like Flamingo, with a gated cross-attention block after every few layers of a frozen language model, on a small captioning dataset. Captions improve, but text-only quality degrades: the model rambles on plain prompts and loses facts it knew. What is the likely cause, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The gates opened too wide too fast. Each gated layer adds the hyperbolic tangent of a learned scalar times the cross-attention output to the residual stream; at zero the layer is a no-op and the model is the pretrained text model. A high learning rate on the gates, or no regularization, lets visual noise flood the residual stream even when the prompt has no image. Confirm it by reading the gate values per layer against the base and by running a text-only eval with the gates forced to zero; fix it with a lower rate or a schedule on the gates, a text-only data mix, and a check that the layers add nothing when no image is present. The mechanism. Copy At initialization alpha is zero, so the model is exactly the frozen language model. As alpha grows, visual information is added on top of the text representation. The residual means that even a fully open gate does not erase the text path, but a large gate adds a large term at every fourth block. If the cross-attention output is noise, that noise reaches the output. Why a fine-tune breaks it. The gates are the cheapest parameters to move, so a learning rate chosen for the cross-attention weights pushes them fast. A caption-only dataset never shows a text-only prompt, so nothing penalizes gates that add visual terms when there is no image to attend to. With few images per prompt, the masked cross-attention has little to read, and an open gate still adds its output. Confirm. Log the gate value per layer. Compare it with the base checkpoint and with the step at which text quality fell. Run the text-only eval with the gates forced to zero. If the quality returns, the gates are the cause. Send a text-only prompt through the model and measure the norm of the gated term per layer. It should be near zero when no image is present. Fix. A lower learning rate or a warm-up schedule for the gate scalars, so that they open over the run rather than in the first steps. A text-only mix in the fine-tuning data, so that the loss covers the case the product sees. A regularizer on the gates, or a cap on their magnitude. A mask check: text tokens with no preceding image must attend to nothing, and the gated term must add nothing. Fewer gated layers, if the task does not need one every fourth block. Why the design is still right. The gate is what let the original work keep a frozen 70B language model intact while it learned to read images. The failure here is in the schedule, not in the architecture. Plausible wrong answers. "The captioning data is too small; add more images." More caption data with no text-only prompts pushes the gates further the same way; the fix is the gate schedule and the data mix. "Unfreeze the language model so that it can adapt to the visual input." That trades a schedule problem for catastrophic forgetting of the text model, which the frozen design exists to prevent. "Replace gated cross-attention with the simpler concatenation design." The symptom is a schedule problem; the gate is the mechanism that protects the text model, and the simpler design has no such protection. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) What does the residual connection buy once the gate is open? Expected: the text representation is never overwritten, only added to; even a fully open gate leaves the text path intact, which is why the fix is the schedule and not a redesign. (level 3) How would you spot the same damage in a model that concatenates image tokens instead? Expected: there is no gate to read; the damage shows as a shift in the language model weights, so compare the text-only eval before and after, and freeze the language model or limit it to adapters. (level 4) Design a unit test that catches this before training. Expected: build the block with alpha at zero and assert that the output equals the block output exactly for a text-only input, then set a large alpha and assert that a text-only input with an empty mask still equals the block output. (level 4) How do you decide how many gated layers to keep? Expected: ablate the insertion frequency against caption quality and text-only quality on one eval; every fourth block is the reference, and fewer layers mean fewer places for noise to enter. Where it is taught. The Flamingo lesson explains why the gate starts at zero and names an over-fast gate as the cause of degraded text performance, and the cross-attention fusion capstone builds the block and the gate exercise. Explain the mechanism A model must take a prompt with any number of images, some small and some large, interleaved with text, and then caption the last image from a few in-context examples. Explain the module that makes the number and the size of the images manageable, and how a text token knows which image to look at. Level 2 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A resampler with a fixed set of learned latent vectors turns the patch tokens of each image into a fixed number of visual tokens. In the reference design, 64 latents attend over however many patches the encoder produced, 196 for a small image or 900 for a large one, through six blocks of cross-attention and self-attention, and every image exits as 64 tokens of one width. Text tokens then read those tokens through gated cross-attention layers inserted between the frozen language model blocks, and a mask lets each text token attend only to the latents of the most recent image before it in the sequence. The resampler. Each block does two things. The K latents cross-attend to the N patch tokens, with queries from the latents and keys and values from the patches; then the latents run self-attention and a feed-forward layer among themselves. After six blocks the output is K tokens of width 1024, whatever N was. For video the resampler runs on each frame, with a temporal position encoding, so the frame count times 64 is the token count of the clip. Why fixed matters. Interleaved prompts have zero, one or many images. With a fixed count per image, what any one text token sees in cross-attention has the same shape whatever the prompt. The total grows with the image count, but each text token reads one image's latents. The gated bridge. Between every fourth block of the frozen language model sits a new cross-attention layer with a residual gate: the output equals the block output plus the hyperbolic tangent of a learned scalar times the cross-attention. The scalar starts at zero, so at initialization the new layers do nothing, and the model is exactly the pretrained text model. The mask. In a sequence like image A, caption A, image B, caption B, image C, question, a text token attends only to the resampler tokens of the most recent image before it; the other images are masked. Attending to all preceding images is a valid alternative; the reference design chose the most recent one. In-context few-shot. Three image and caption pairs followed by a new image form a prompt that the frozen language model already knows how to complete. The gated layers feed it image content, and its in-context learning carries over without a gradient step. That is the point of keeping the language model frozen and the gate at zero. Against the single-input bridge. The query-based bridge from the earlier lesson also uses learned queries, but once, at the input layer, with 32 queries. The resampler plus gated cross-attention reads the latents every few layers, which costs more parameters and compute and buys interleaving and few-shot behavior. Plausible wrong answers. "Pad every image to the same number of patches." Padding wastes compute on large images and loses detail on small ones; the resampler gives a fixed count without either. "Let the text tokens attend to all image patches directly." The count then varies per image and per prompt, and a prompt with many images floods the attention; the latents keep it fixed. "Initialize the gate open so that the model learns faster." An open gate at step zero destroys the frozen language model's text behavior; a start at zero is what preserves it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the latent side supply the query vectors and the patch side the rest, not the other way around? Expected: the output has one row per query, so queries from the latents give a fixed number of rows; the reverse would give one row per patch again. (level 2) What does the temporal encoding do for video? Expected: each frame gives the same 64 latents, so without a time signal the model cannot tell the first frame from the last; the encoding marks the frame index. (level 3) Why mask to the most recent image instead of all preceding images? Expected: it keeps the shape each text token sees constant and matches the interleaved reading order, where a caption describes the image before it; seeing all images is the alternative with a different trade-off. (level 3) A fine-tune of a model like this lost text-only quality. Where do you look? Expected: the gate; if it opened too wide too fast, visual noise overwrote the text residual stream, so compare the gate values by layer with the base. Where it is taught. The Flamingo lesson walks the resampler, the gated layers and the interleaved mask, and the BLIP-2 lesson gives the query bridge that it is compared with. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 02 (CLIP), Phase 11 (LLM Engineering — instruction tuning) Type : Build. Time : about 180 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, projector + instruction-template builder). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line LLaVA (April 2023) is the most copied multimodal architecture on the planet. It replaced BLIP-2's Q-Former with a single linear projection, replaced Flamingo's gated cross-attention with plain token concatenation, and trained on 158k visual-instruction samples generated by GPT-4 from text-only captions. Any practitioner who built a VLM between 2023 and 2026 built some variant of LLaVA. LLaVA-1.5 swapped in an MLP projector and a 336px encoder. LLaVA-NeXT added AnyRes tiling for high-resolution input. LLaVA-OneVision unified image, multi-image, and video in one recipe. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Projector "MLP bridge" 2-layer MLP with GELU mapping ViT dim to LLM dim Image token " placeholder" Prompt marker replaced by N projected visual tokens before inference Visual instruction tuning "LLaVA stage 2" Training on GPT-4-generated (image, instruction, response) triplets Stage 1 alignment "Projector pretraining" Freeze ViT and LLM, train projector with LM loss on captions AnyRes "Multi-crop tiling" Split high-res image into a tile grid and concatenate each tile's visual tokens LLaVA-Instruct "GPT-4-generated" 158k instruction-response pairs synthesized from COCO captions + GPT-4 Vision encoder freeze "Backbone locked" CLIP weights do not update in stage 1, sometimes not in stage 2 either ShareGPT4V "Better captions" 1M dense captions generated by GPT-4V, used for higher-quality alignment VQA "Visual question answering" Task of answering a free-form question about an image Prismatic VLMs "Design-space paper" Karamcheti 2024 ablation systematically testing projector and data choices The problem In plain words first LLaVA is the simplest way to make a chat model see. A frozen image encoder (CLIP ViT-L/14) turns a photo into 576 patch vectors. A small two-layer network, the projector, maps each one to the width of the language model's word embeddings. The prompt has one placeholder, <image> , and those 576 vectors are pasted where it stands, so the language model reads the picture as 576 extra "words" before the question. Training happens in two steps: first only the projector learns, on image captions; then the language model is tuned on visual question-and-answer conversations. This lesson follows the recipe and runs the real pipeline, from placeholder to generated tokens, on a tiny test model with LLaVA-1.5's exact shapes. Only the code is being checked, so its random weights are fine. No model is trained. BLIP-2's Q-Former (Lesson 12.03) compresses an image to 32 tokens. Clean, efficient, good for benchmarks. But it has two problems. First, the Q-Former is trainable but its loss is not the final task. Stage 1 trains ITC+ITM+ITG. Stage 2 trains LM loss. The queries learn some intermediate representation that the LLM then has to decode. Information is lost in the bottleneck. Second, the Q-Former takes 188M params, and at LLaVA's 2023 scale you had to co-design it with your target LLM. Change the LLM, retrain the Q-Former. Change the vision encoder, retrain. Every combination was a separate R&D project. The LLaVA answer was embarrassing in its simplicity: take the ViT's 576 patch tokens, pass each through a 2-layer MLP ( 1024 → 4096 → 4096 ), and dump all 576 into the LLM's input sequence. No bottleneck. No stage 1 pretraining on weird objectives. Just train the MLP on a direct LM loss. Where does the data come from? LLaVA's second insight: use GPT-4 (text-only) to generate instruction data. Feed GPT-4 the COCO caption and bounding-box data for an image, ask it to produce conversations, descriptions, and complex reasoning questions. 158k instruction-response turns for free. No human annotation. The result: a VLM that ran on 8 A100s for one day, beat Flamingo on MMMU, and shipped an open checkpoint the community could extend. By late 2023 it had spawned 50+ forks. Idea 1 · The architecture LLaVA-1.5 at 7B: - Vision encoder: CLIP ViT-L/14 @ 336 (frozen during stage 1, optionally unfrozen stage 2). - Projector: 2-layer MLP with GELU activation, 1024 → 4096 → 4096 . - LLM: Vicuna-7B v1.5 (a 13B variant uses Vicuna-13B; later forks moved to Llama-3.1-8B). Forward pass on an image + text prompt: Copy The image occupies 576 tokens of the LLM context. At 2048 context, that leaves 1472 tokens for text. At 32k context, it is a rounding error. Idea 2 · Stage 1: projector alignment Freeze ViT. Freeze LLM. Train only the 2-layer MLP. Dataset: 558k image-caption pairs (LAION-CC-SBU). Loss: language modeling on the caption, conditioned on the projected image tokens. In a single epoch at batch 128 this is done in a few hours. The projector learns to map ViT-space to LLM-space. No task-specific supervision. Idea 3 · Stage 2: visual instruction tuning Keep the projector trainable. Unfreeze the LLM (usually fully, sometimes LoRA). The original LLaVA trained on 158k visual-instruction samples; LLaVA-1.5 used a 665k mixture that adds academic VQA data and ShareGPT text conversations. The instruction data is the trick. Liu et al. generated it by: 1. Take a COCO image. 2. Extract the text description (5 human captions + bounding-box list). 3. Send to GPT-4 with three prompt templates: - Conversation: "Generate a back-and-forth dialogue between a user and assistant about this image." - Detailed description: "Give a rich, detailed description of the image." - Complex reasoning: "Ask a question that requires reasoning about the image, then answer it." 4. Parse GPT-4's output into (instruction, response) pairs. None of this touches the image directly — only the text description. GPT-4 hallucinates plausible image content. Some noise, but it worked: 158k turns was enough to unlock dialogue. The same idea as a formula The projector. Prompt text is often predictable boilerplate, and including it would dilute the signal from the answer. The two stages touch very different amounts of the model. Only the 0.3B vision tower stays frozen. This is where the GPU cost and the risk of damaging the language model's text skills lie, which is why many fine-tuning projects use LoRA in stage 2. Idea 4 · Why the community copied this No stage-1-specific losses to tune. LM loss throughout. Projector trains in hours, not days. LLM can be swapped (LLaVA-Llama2, LLaVA-Mistral, LLaVA-Llama3) by retraining just the projector. Visual-instruction data pipeline uses GPT-4 and is cheap to regenerate for a new domain. Idea 5 · LLaVA-1.5 and LLaVA-NeXT LLaVA-1.5 (October 2023) added: - Academic-task data (VQA, OKVQA, RefCOCO) mixed into instruction tuning. - Better system prompt. - A 2-layer MLP projector in place of the original single linear layer, and CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336px (576 tokens) in place of 224px (256 tokens). Training sequences stayed at 2048 tokens. - A grid-splitting HD variant in the paper, which LLaVA-NeXT later shipped as AnyRes. LLaVA-NeXT (January 2024) added: - AnyRes: split high-res images into a 2x2 or 1x3 grid of 336x336 crops, plus one global low-res thumbnail. Each crop becomes 576 tokens. A 2x2 grid plus the thumbnail gives about 2880 visual tokens per image. A 1x3 grid has fewer crops, so it costs fewer tokens. OCR and chart tasks jumped. - Better instruction data mixture with ShareGPT4V (high-quality GPT-4V captions). - Stronger base LLMs (Mistral-7B, Yi-34B). Trainable in stage 1: 21M (0.3%); in stage 2: 6.76B (95.7%), everything except the vision tower (measured below). Training cost: the LLaVA-1.5 paper reports about one day on a single 8×A100 node for the full two-stage recipe. One day, one node, reproducible. That is why LLaVA spread. What changes in training and in the finished model? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) LLaVA's shape is the default open-VLM shape : vision encoder → MLP projector (with patch merging) → LLM, in Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL, InternVL, LLaVA-OneVision, Gemma 3 and SmolVLM. Encoders and LLMs are usually unfrozen in later stages : current recipes train the projector first, then tune everything (often including the vision encoder) on large instruction mixtures. Instruction data comes from strong VLMs, not text-only GPT-4 : ShareGPT4V-style captions, synthetic OCR, chart and document data, and curated mixtures such as The Cauldron and LLaVA-OneVision's data. Training libraries support this out of the box : Hugging Face TRL's SFT trainer handles vision-language models and masks prompts. Sources: LLaVA (arXiv 2304.08485) , LLaVA-1.5 (arXiv 2310.03744) , LLaVA-OneVision (arXiv 2408.03326) , Hugging Face LLaVA documentation , TRL SFT trainer . Recap What to keep from this lesson LLaVA = frozen ViT + MLP projector + LLM; image patches become 576 input vectors. The <image> placeholder is replaced by projected patch features before the LLM runs. Stage 1 trains only the projector on captions; stage 2 tunes the LLM on instructions. Loss is computed on answer tokens only. Simplicity won: swap the LLM, retrain a 21M projector, and you have a new VLM. Solution B1 · The model learns to predict its own prompts The loss now also rewards predicting the system prompt and the user's question. Those are the same few templates in every sample, so they are easy to learn and quickly reach a low loss. They then make up a large share of the gradient, while the answers, the part you care about, get a smaller share. The finished model can drift into generating user-style text: continuing with "USER: …" turns, repeating the template, or asking itself questions. Its loss curve also looks better than its answers are. Mask everything except the assistant's tokens (labels −100), as the run above does. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Estimate it A product manager asks how much of the context window one image uses in a LLaVA-style model with a 336-pixel encoder. Give the number, say where it comes from, and say how it changes with high-resolution tiling or with a query-based bridge. Level 1 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. One image costs 576 tokens: the encoder cuts the 336-pixel image into 14-pixel patches, a 24 by 24 grid, and the projector passes every patch token through. In a 2048-token context that leaves 1472 tokens for text; at 32k or 128k it is a small share. Tiling multiplies it: a 2 by 2 grid of 336-pixel crops plus one global thumbnail gives about 2880 tokens per image, and a 1 by 3 grid plus the thumbnail gives fewer, because it has one crop less. A query-based bridge compresses any image to a fixed 32 tokens, and a resampler to 64. Where the count comes from. Copy The earlier 224-pixel encoder gave 256 tokens. The move to 336 pixels raised the count to 576, and the training sequences stayed at 2048 tokens. What it costs in context. Context One image 2048 576 tokens, leaving 1472 for text 32k a small share 128k a rounding error Tiling for high resolution. Documents and charts need more pixels. The tiling scheme splits the image into a 2 by 2 or 1 by 3 grid of 336-pixel crops, adds one low-resolution global view, and concatenates the tokens of every crop: about 2880 visual tokens per image for the 2 by 2 grid, and fewer for the 1 by 3 grid, which has one crop less. Reading and chart scores jumped with it. The compressing bridges. A query-based bridge uses a fixed set of 32 learned query vectors that cross-attend to the patch tokens, so any image becomes 32 tokens. A resampler with 64 latents does the same at 64. The price is a bottleneck: the language model never sees the raw patches. How many tokens you need. The ablations in the recipes lesson put the sweet spot for most tasks at 576 to 1024 visual tokens per image, 64 as too few for reading text, and 2048 or more as useful only for documents and charts. The token count explains more of the variance in benchmark scores than the connector architecture does. Plausible wrong answers. "An image costs one token, the placeholder." The placeholder is replaced by one embedding per patch token before the forward pass; the encoder grid sets the count. "Higher resolution is free because the encoder is fixed." More patches means more visual tokens in the language model's sequence, and the language model's compute grows with them. "The connector decides the quality, so pick the bridge first." At a fixed token count the connector barely matters; the token count and the encoder matter more. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why does a higher input resolution raise the token count? Expected: the patch size is fixed, so more pixels per side means more patches per side, and the count grows with the square of the side. (level 2) Which tasks justify the tiling cost? Expected: text in images, charts and documents; general scene questions gain little from it. (level 2) When does the 32-token bridge win? Expected: when the token budget binds, as with long video or many images per prompt; for one image in a long context the compression buys little. (level 3) How do you size the budget for video? Expected: tokens per frame times frames, so a compressing bridge or heavy frame sampling is the only way to fit minutes of video; count the tokens before you pick the bridge. Where it is taught. The LLaVA lesson counts the tokens per image and per tiled image, the BLIP-2 lesson explains the fixed-count bridge, and the recipes lesson gives the token budget ablations. Take-home Take-home. You get a frozen vision encoder that emits 197 tokens of width 768 per image and a frozen text embedding table of width 512. Build the smallest module that lets the two talk, train it on paired samples, and ship tests that prove it works. Describe the design, the loss, how you train it, and the tests. Level 2 of 4 · about 30 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Pool the 197 image tokens to one vector, pass it through a two-layer MLP, 768 to 1024 to 512 with a GELU between, and compare it with the mean-pooled caption embedding through a cosine alignment loss, one minus the cosine. Train only the MLP, about 1.3M parameters, with the encoder and the table frozen, for a few hundred steps over a few dozen pairs. The tests: the output shape equals the text width, the frozen parts have no trainable parameters, the loss is zero on identical vectors and two on opposite vectors, a gradient reaches the projector after one backward pass, and the loss at the last step is lower than at the first. Design. Copy Pooling: the first token is the simplest choice; a mean over the 196 patch tokens is the alternative, and the exercise compares them. Two layers, because one linear map cannot bend the space; the GELU gives the one bend that aligns the two bases. Parameters. Layer Shape Parameters first linear 768 by 1024 768 times 1024, plus 1024 GELU 0 second linear 1024 by 512 1024 times 512, plus 512 About 1.3M in total, next to an encoder of 86M. Both big parts have requires_grad=False on every parameter. Training loop. Build 32 synthetic pairs from a seed when no dataset is allowed, and cycle them. One optimizer over the projector parameters only. Run 200 steps and print the loss every 25 steps. The capstone's run falls from about 1.07 to about 0.80. Print the final cosine per pair. Tests. The projector output shape matches the configured output width. The frozen text table and the frozen vision encoder have zero parameters that require a gradient. The cosine loss is 0 on identical vectors and 2 on anti-parallel vectors. A gradient reaches the projector weights after one backward pass. The loss at step 200 is lower than at step 0. What you ship. The projector weights are the only new artifact. At inference the encoder still runs its forward pass, then the projector, and the output lands in the text space. The same shape appears in every open adapter model: pool, project, train alone. The next step, for the discussion. The per-pair cosine aligns direction; a contrastive batch loss would also push each image away from the other captions in the batch. For a decoder that grounds each word, cross-attention from text queries into the 197 image tokens replaces the pooled vector; that is the following capstone. Plausible wrong answers. "Fine-tune the encoder as well; it is only 86M parameters." The take-home gives frozen parts for a reason: a few dozen pairs cannot teach the encoder anything, and the test that checks the frozen table would fail. "Use a single linear layer; it is enough for a rotation." The two bases differ by more than a rotation; the non-linearity is what lets one bend close the gap. "Skip the tests; the loss went down." The loss can fall through a shape bug or a leak into the frozen parts; the tests pin the contract that the loss alone cannot. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why cosine and not mean squared error? Expected: alignment means the same direction in the joint space, not equal vectors; cosine is scale-invariant, so the projector is not punished for a norm the text table happens to have. (level 2) What does a learned temperature on the cosine change? Expected: a sharper or flatter loss surface; too small gives noisy gradients and too large plateaus high, as the exercise shows. (level 3) The capstone's run stops near 0.80 after 200 steps. Is that a floor? Expected: no; it is the loss of one run at 200 steps. The projector has 1024 hidden units for 32 pairs, so more steps or a different rate can push the loss lower; on natural pairs, the encoder features set how far the alignment can go. (level 3) How does this module relate to a query-based bridge? Expected: that bridge ends in the same kind of projection to the text width; the difference is that it first compresses the tokens through learned queries instead of pooling. Where it is taught. The projection capstone specifies the module, the loss, the loop and the five tests, and the cross-attention fusion capstone is the step after it. Explain the mechanism In the first training stage of most open vision-language models, both the vision encoder and the decoder are frozen, and only the small projector learns. A junior engineer asks why anyone would train the smallest part first instead of the parts that matter. Answer them. Level 1 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The two big parts already work: the encoder represents images, and the language model writes text. What is missing is a translation between their two vector spaces, and that translation is small. Training only the bridge costs a few hundred steps on one GPU, cannot damage either pretrained part, and gives the language model inputs it can read before anyone unfreezes it. Unfreezing the language model comes in the second stage, once the bridge produces tokens that look like language. What the projector is. A two-layer MLP: linear, GELU, linear. The capstone's head maps 768 to 1024 to 512 and holds about 1.3M parameters next to an encoder of 86M. The reference open recipe's head maps 1024 to 4096 to 4096, about 22M parameters next to a 303M encoder and a 7B language model. Why the frozen big parts are the point. Stability. Gradients from a few thousand noisy pairs would overwrite features that the encoder learned from hundreds of millions of images. Cost. The alignment stage of the reference recipe trains on 558k caption pairs in a few hours at a batch of 128. The capstone's version drives its loss from about 1.07 to about 0.80 in 200 steps. A clean signal. With both big parts fixed, the loss moves only through the bridge, so you can read whether the two spaces align. Swappability. Change the language model and retrain the bridge; the encoder stays. What the loss is. The reference recipe uses the language-modeling loss on the caption, conditioned on the projected image tokens. The capstone uses a per-pair cosine alignment loss, one minus the cosine between a pooled image vector and a mean-pooled caption embedding, so that the dynamics stay visible; a contrastive batch version is the next lesson. What comes after. Stage two unfreezes the language model, fully or through adapters, keeps the bridge trainable, and trains on instruction data. A bridge that was never aligned first gives the language model noise at the start of that stage. The other kind of bridge. A query-based bridge with a fixed set of learned vectors compresses the image to a fixed token count. It is larger, 188M parameters in the original, and it still trains with the backbones frozen; the principle is the same. Plausible wrong answers. "Train the encoder; it is the part that sees." It already sees, and a small dataset cannot teach it more than it loses by overwriting features; the missing part is the translation. "The projector is too small to carry an image." It does not carry the image; it maps tokens that already encode the image into the space the language model reads. "Freezing is only a memory trick." Memory is one gain; the larger ones are stability, a clean training signal, and the ability to swap the language model. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What does a frozen parameter mean in code? Expected: requires_grad=False , so the optimizer never sees it, and no memory goes to its gradient or optimizer state. (level 2) Why pool the image tokens before the cosine loss in the capstone? Expected: the caption side is one vector, so the image side needs one vector too; the first token or the mean over all tokens are the usual choices. (level 2) One linear layer would be smaller still. Why two? Expected: a single linear map can rotate and rescale but cannot bend; the GELU between two layers gives the one non-linear bend that aligns contrastive vision features to language embeddings. (level 3) What breaks if you skip the alignment stage and start with instruction tuning with everything unfrozen? Expected: the language model receives unaligned inputs, and its gradients on a small set damage its text ability; the two stages exist to give it readable inputs first. Where it is taught. The projection capstone trains the bridge alone with a cosine loss, the LLaVA lesson gives the two-stage recipe and its parameter counts, and the BLIP-2 lesson explains the frozen-backbone economics. Explain the mechanism Draw the standard architecture of a vision-language model that answers questions about an image. Name its three parts, say what each one contributes, and say which part you would expect to train when a team fine-tunes on a few thousand labelled images. Level 1 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A vision encoder, a projector and a language model. The encoder, a pretrained vision transformer, turns the image into patch tokens. The projector, a small two- to four-layer MLP or a query-based bridge, maps those tokens into the language model's embedding space, where they replace a placeholder token in the prompt. The decoder language model reads image tokens and text tokens as one sequence and writes the answer; in most fine-tunes the encoder and the language model stay frozen or get adapters, and the projector is where the training happens. The three parts. Vision encoder. A pretrained vision transformer, contrastively trained or self-supervised, produces one token per patch. With a 336-pixel input and a 14-pixel patch, the reference model gets 576 tokens of width 1024. Projector. A two-layer MLP with a GELU between the layers, from the encoder width to the language model width, 1024 to 4096 to 4096 in the reference model. The capstone's toy head, 768 to 1024 to 512, has about 1.3M parameters. Language model. A decoder-only model that receives the projected image tokens in place of an image placeholder and the text tokens after them, then generates text. How the pieces meet. The prompt holds a placeholder image token. Before the forward pass, the embeddings at those positions are overwritten with the projected vision tokens, and the batch is padded so that every sample has the same count. The language model sees one sequence; nothing else about it changes. Who trains. Stage one, alignment: freeze the encoder and the language model, and train the projector on image and caption pairs with the language-modeling loss on the caption. The capstone's version uses a cosine alignment loss between a pooled image vector and a caption vector, and that loss falls from about 1.07 to about 0.80 in 200 steps with only the projector moving. Stage two, instruction tuning: unfreeze the language model, often through adapters, keep the projector trainable, and train on image, question and answer triples. Large pretraining on interleaved image and text data sits between them in frontier recipes and is out of reach for a small team. Why the projector is enough. The encoder already represents the image, and the language model already reasons in words. The projector's job is to express one in the vocabulary of the other, which a small bend of the space can do. The capstone's encoder has 86M parameters and its projector about 1.3M; training only the projector means a few hundred steps on one GPU. Plausible wrong answers. "The language model looks at pixels through cross-attention into the image." In this pattern the image enters as tokens in the input sequence; cross-attention bridges are a different family. "Fine-tune the vision encoder first; it is the part that sees." The encoder is pretrained and frozen in stage one; the projector is where a small team's training budget goes. "The projector must be a large network to carry the image." It is a two-layer MLP far smaller than the encoder in the capstone, and it trains in minutes. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why does the projector need two layers and not one? Expected: one linear layer rotates and scales; the non-linearity between two layers lets the map bend, which is enough to align contrastive vision features to a language model's embeddings. (level 2) What does the language model see where the image was? Expected: a run of embeddings, one per projected patch token, in place of the placeholder; the model treats them as tokens with no special handling. (level 2) What does a bridge with a fixed set of learned queries change? Expected: it compresses the patch tokens to a fixed count, which saves context at the cost of a bottleneck; the MLP keeps every patch. (level 3) Which part sets the ceiling on reasoning quality? Expected: the language model; the encoder can only feed it, so a larger language model lifts the benchmarks more than a cleverer bridge. Where it is taught. The vision-language models lesson lays out the pattern and its three training stages, the projection capstone trains the bridge alone, and the LLaVA lesson gives the reference recipe.
