Pick between AnyRes tiling (LLaVA-NeXT), NaFlex (SigLIP 2), and M-RoPE (Qwen2-VL) for a given task. Compute token budgets for OCR, charts, and photography without resizing. Name the three failure modes of square-resize: squished text, cropped content, wasted tokens on padding. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 01 (ViT patches), Phase 12 · 05 (LLaVA) Type : Build. Time : about 120 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, patch packer + block-diagonal mask). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Real images are not 224x224 squares. A receipt is 1:3, a chart is 16:9, a medical scan might be 4096x4096, a mobile screenshot is 9:19.5. The pre-2024 VLM answer — resize everything to a fixed square — threw away the signal that makes OCR, document understanding, and high-resolution scene parsing work. NaViT (Google, 2023) showed you could pack variable-resolution patches into a single transformer batch with block-diagonal masking. Qwen2-VL's M-RoPE (2024) dropped absolute positional tables entirely. LLaVA-NeXT's AnyRes tiled high-resolution Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Patch-n'-pack "NaViT-style packing" Concatenate variable-length patch sequences from different images into one batch dimension Block-diagonal mask "Packing mask" Attention mask that confines each image's patches to attend only to themselves, not neighbors in the pack AnyRes "LLaVA-NeXT tiling" Split a high-res image into a grid of fixed-size tiles plus a global thumbnail; encode every tile with a fixed encoder NaFlex "SigLIP 2 native-flex" Single SigLIP 2 checkpoint that serves 256/729/1024-token budgets at inference without retraining M-RoPE "Multimodal RoPE" 3D rotary position encoding (time, row, column) that handles arbitrary H, W, T without position tables cu_seqlens "FlashAttention packing" Cumulative-length tensor the FlashAttention varlen path uses instead of a dense block-diagonal mask min_pixels / max_pixels "Resolution bounds" Qwen2.5-VL per-request knobs capping token count on very small or very large inputs Visual token budget "How many tokens per image" Rough count of patch tokens emitted per image; sets the LLM's prompt budget and attention cost The problem In plain words first A vision transformer trained on 224 × 224 squares sees every image as a 224 × 224 square. A tall receipt gets squashed, small chart labels blur away, and padding a wide image wastes compute. There are three ways around this. Tiling (AnyRes) cuts a large image into encoder-sized crops plus a small overview. Native resolution (Qwen2-VL's approach, SigLIP 2's NaFlex) feeds each image at its own aspect ratio and tells the model where every patch sits. Patch-n'-pack puts several such images into one sequence, with an attention mask that keeps them apart. This lesson compares the three and counts their token costs. It runs real LLaVA-NeXT tiling code on a tiny test model to see how many tokens each image shape costs, and checks that a packed, masked batch gives exactly the same result as encoding each image alone. No model is trained. Transformers expect a sequence. A batch is a stack of sequences the same length. If your images are 224x224, you get 196 patch tokens every time, padding not required, job done. Train on 224, infer on 224, never think about resolution again. The world does not cooperate. Documents are portrait (8.5x11 inches, 2:3-ish). Chart screenshots are landscape (16:9). Receipts are tall and thin (1:3). Medical imaging ships at 2048x2048 or larger. Mobile device screenshots are 1170x2532 (0.46:1). Three pre-2024 options and why each fails: Resize to a fixed square (224x224 or 336x336). The squish distorts text and faces. The downscale destroys chart labels and OCR content. Standard practice until LLaVA-1.5. Crop to a fixed aspect ratio. You throw away most of the image, and picking the crop location is its own vision problem. Pad to the longest side. Fixes distortion but wastes 50%+ of tokens on padding for portrait images. Quadratic attention cost on all those pad tokens. The 2024-2025 answer: let the transformer eat patches at the image's native resolution, and figure out how to pack a heterogeneous batch into one sequence without wasted compute. Idea 1 · NaViT and patch-n'-pack NaViT (Dehghani et al., 2023) was the paper that showed this works at scale. The idea is mechanical: For each image in the batch, compute its native patch grid at a chosen patch size (say 14). Flatten each image's patches into its own variable-length sequence. Concatenate all images' patches into one long sequence for the batch. Build a block-diagonal attention mask so image A's patches only attend within image A. Carry per-patch position information (2D RoPE or fractional position embeddings). A batch of three images at 336x336 (576 tokens), 224x224 (256 tokens), and 448x336 (768 tokens) becomes one 1600-token sequence with a 1600x1600 block-diagonal mask. No padding. No wasted compute. The transformer handles arbitrary aspect ratios. NaViT also introduced random token dropping during training: drop a share of each image's patches (up to about half), which both regularises and speeds training. Idea 2 · AnyRes (LLaVA-NeXT) LLaVA-NeXT's AnyRes is the pragmatic alternative. Given a high-resolution image and a fixed encoder (CLIP or SigLIP at 336), tile the image: Pick a grid layout from a predefined set — (1x1), (1x2), (2x1), (1x3), (3x1), (2x2), etc. — that best fits the image's aspect ratio. Tile the full image into the grid; each tile becomes a 336x336 crop. Also produce a thumbnail: the whole image resized to 336x336 as a global-context token. Encode every tile through the frozen 336-encoder. Concatenate the tile tokens + thumbnail tokens. For a 672x672 image the 2x2 grid gives 4 × 576 = 2,304 tile tokens plus 576 for the thumbnail, 2,880 in all. The Hugging Face implementation also adds one "newline" token at the end of each row of the tile grid (48 rows here), so it hands the LLM 2,928 (measured below). Expensive but effective — the LLM sees both local detail and global context. AnyRes is the route of choice when your encoder is frozen and only supports one resolution. It explodes token count for large images (a 1344x1344 image at 4x4 grid is 9216 + 576 ≈ 9800 tokens, which overflows an 8k LLM context before any text arrives). Idea 3 · M-RoPE (Qwen2-VL) Qwen2-VL introduced Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding. Instead of NaViT's fractional positions or AnyRes's tile-and-thumbnail, each patch carries a 3D position (temporal, height, width). The query/key rotations handle arbitrary H, W, and temporal length. This gives native dynamic resolution. At inference you feed any H×W image (rounded to multiples of 28); the vision encoder, which uses 2D-RoPE, produces H/14 × W/14 patches, and each 2×2 group is merged into one token, so the LLM receives H/28 × W/28 visual tokens. In the LLM each visual token gets a (t, row, column) position and M-RoPE rotates attention accordingly. Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL continue this. InternVL3's V2PE is related: it gives visual tokens smaller, variable position increments than text tokens. Unlike AnyRes, M-RoPE is ) tokens at native resolution — no multiplicative tile overhead. Qwen2-VL's vision encoder also batches images of different sizes NaViT-style: their patches are concatenated and attention is restricted to each image with cumulative sequence lengths (cu_seqlens). Idea 4 · NaFlex (SigLIP 2) NaFlex is the SigLIP 2 checkpoint's native-flex mode. A single model serves several sequence lengths at inference (the paper trains on 128 to 1,024 patches per image). Each image is resized to keep its aspect ratio within the chosen patch budget, and the learned position-embedding table is resized to the image's grid. The selling point: one checkpoint, pick your token budget at inference based on the task. For a semantic task (classification, retrieval), 256 tokens. For OCR or chart understanding, 1024 tokens. No retraining. Idea 5 · The packing mask The block-diagonal mask is where most implementations stumble. For a packed sequence of length N_total covering images i=0..B-1 with lengths n_i , the mask M of shape (N_total, N_total) is 1 if both indices fall in the same image's block, else 0. You can build it from a cumulative length list: Copy This is one line in PyTorch with torch.block_diag or an explicit gather. FlashAttention's variable-length path ( cu_seqlens ) skips the mask entirely and attends within sequences using the cumulative-length tensor directly, so it never computes the masked-out scores; the saving grows with the number of images packed together. SigLIP 2 NaFlex at 1024, or AnyRes 3x3 + thumbnail. Charts and UI: 729-1024 tokens at 384-448 native. Qwen2.5-VL dynamic resolution with max pixels cap. Natural photos: 256-576 tokens is fine. The downstream LLM sees enough. Pay for tokens where content density is high. Video: 64-128 tokens per frame after spatial pooling, 2-8 FPS. Lesson 12.17 covers this. The 2026 production rule: pick a per-task max-pixels cap, encode at native aspect ratio up to that cap, pack the batch, and skip padding. Qwen2.5-VL exposes min_pixels and max_pixels for exactly this knob. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Native resolution with pixel caps is the default in open VLMs: Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL take min_pixels / max_pixels , InternVL uses dynamic tiling with a maximum tile count, and both merge patches before the LLM. Packed variable-length attention (FlashAttention varlen, PyTorch's FlexAttention and nested tensors) is standard for training on mixed resolutions. SigLIP 2 NaFlex gives one encoder that serves several token budgets with aspect ratio preserved. Hosted models bill by resolution : Claude counts 28×28-pixel visual tokens with a long-edge limit (2,576 px on Claude 4.7 and later), so resizing before upload controls cost (Lesson 12.1). Sources: NaViT (arXiv 2307.06304) , LLaVA-NeXT blog , Qwen2-VL (arXiv 2409.12191) , SigLIP 2 (arXiv 2502.14786) , Hugging Face LLaVA-NeXT documentation , Claude vision documentation . Recap What to keep from this lesson Square resizing distorts aspect ratio and loses fine detail. AnyRes tiles an image into encoder-sized crops plus a thumbnail; cost jumps by whole tiles. Native resolution (2D-RoPE, M-RoPE, NaFlex) keeps the aspect ratio; tokens grow with pixels. Patch-n'-pack concatenates images and masks attention per image: no padding, same result. Set a pixel cap per task: OCR and charts need more tokens than photos. Build the block-diagonal mask for a batch of four images with lengths 256, 576, 729, 1024. Verify the attention matrix is 2585x2585 and has exactly 256^2 + 576^2 + 729^2 + 1024^2 non-zero entries. Solutions Solution P1 · 1,176 for a small square, 2,928 for a big photo A 336 × 336 image costs 1,176 visual tokens, about two tiles, because LLaVA-NeXT's smallest grid is 336 × 672; the unused half is removed after encoding. A 2000 × 2000 photo costs 2,928, the same as 672 × 672: it is downscaled into the largest 2×2 grid, plus the thumbnail and 48 row-newline tokens. AnyRes cost rises in steps and stops at the largest grid, so huge images lose detail rather than costing more. Solution B1 · Images leak into each other Every patch attends to the patches of the other images in the pack. Each image's representation now depends on whichever images happened to share its batch, so features change with batch composition, and the model can learn to use the leaked information. That can even make the loss go down. At inference, a single image, or a different set of companions, gives the model an input it never saw in training, and accuracy drops in ways that are hard to trace. In the run above, removing the mask changed outputs by up to 1.30 with no error raised. Always check a packed forward pass against separate ones, as the run does, and make the mask or cu_seqlens come from the same per-image lengths used to pack the sequence. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 05 (LLaVA baseline) Type : Learn + lab. Time : about 180 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, ablation table parser + recipe picker). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The 2024-2026 open-weight VLM literature is a forest of ablation tables. Apple's MM1 ablated image encoders, connectors and data mixes. Allen AI's Molmo proved detailed human captions beat GPT-4V distillation. Cambrian-1 ran 20+ encoder comparisons. Idefics2 formalized the five-axis design space. Prismatic VLMs varied one design choice at a time on a controlled benchmark suite. Out of all that noise, a small set of results holds across papers: image encoder matters more than connector architecture, data mixture matters more than either, an Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Ablation "Turning one knob" Training multiple runs that differ in exactly one design-space axis, holding everything else constant Connector "Bridge" / "projector" Trainable module that maps vision encoder output into the LLM's token space (MLP, Q-Former, Perceiver) Detailed human caption "Dense caption" A multi-sentence human-written description (typically 80-300 tokens) richer than a web alt text Distillation "GPT-4V captions" Training data generated by a stronger proprietary VLM; convenient but prone to inherited hallucination AnyRes / dynamic res "High-res path" Strategy to feed images larger than the encoder's native resolution via tiling or M-RoPE Resolution ramp "Curriculum" Training schedule that starts low-resolution and increases, speeding alignment learning Vision-centric bench "CV-Bench / BLINK" Evaluation that stresses fine-grained visual perception rather than language-heavy reasoning PixMo "Molmo's data" Allen AI's 712K densely-captioned image dataset; human speech transcribed into dense captions The problem In plain words first Building a vision-language model means making five choices: the image encoder, the connector that hands its output to the language model, the language model itself, the training data, and the image resolution. Between 2024 and 2026 several research groups ran careful experiments that change one choice at a time. They agree on a short list of rules: the encoder, the resolution and the number of visual tokens matter most; the connector design matters little; the language model sets the reasoning ceiling; and dense human-written descriptions are better training data than captions copied from another model. This lesson walks through those findings and checks one of them against real models: where the parameters of six current open VLMs actually sit. No model is trained or downloaded. Hundreds of open-weight VLMs exist. Most of the gap between "good" and "state-of-the-art" is not architecture. It is data, resolution schedule, and encoder choice. Knowing which knob to turn first when your model underperforms saves you a 5-million-GPU-hour mistake. The 2023 wave (LLaVA-1.5, InstructBLIP, MiniGPT-4) ran on caption-pair pretraining + LLaVA-Instruct-150k. Good baseline. Topped out around MMMU 35%. The 2024 wave (MM1, Idefics2, Molmo, Cambrian-1, Prismatic VLMs) ran exhaustive ablations. Results were surprising and practical. Idea 1 · The five-axis design space Idefics2 (Laurençon et al., 2024) named the axes: Image encoder. CLIP ViT-L/14, SigLIP SO400m/14, DINOv2 ViT-g/14, InternViT-6B. Encoders differ in patch size, resolution, and pretraining objective. Connector. MLP (2-4 layers), Q-Former (32 queries + cross-attn), Perceiver Resampler (64 queries), C-Abstractor (convolutional + bilinear pooling). Language model. Llama-3 8B / 70B, Mistral 7B, Phi-3, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5. LLM size is the dominant param cost. Training data. Caption pairs (CC3M, LAION), interleaved (OBELICS, MMC4), instruction (LLaVA-Instruct, ShareGPT4V, PixMo, Cauldron). Resolution schedule. Fixed 224/336/448, AnyRes, native dynamic. Ramped during training or constant. Every production VLM makes a choice on each axis. The ablation papers agree that the encoder, the image resolution and token count, and the data matter far more than which connector you pick. Idea 2 · Axis 1: encoder > connector MM1 concluded that "the image encoder together with image resolution and the image token count has substantial impact, while the vision-language connector design is of comparatively negligible importance." Idefics2 found the same direction: a SigLIP So400m encoder beat a larger CLIP ViT-H, and a perceiver resampler with 64 tokens per image cost little quality while saving many tokens. Cambrian-1 (Tong et al., 2024) compared about 20 vision encoders inside the same VLM recipe and introduced a vision-centric benchmark (CV-Bench). Language-supervised encoders (SigLIP, CLIP) were strongest overall; among self-supervised encoders DINOv2 was best, and it helped most on vision-centric tasks. Combining encoders helped further. A common default encoder for open VLMs is SigLIP or SigLIP 2 So400m/14, sometimes combined with DINOv2 features for spatial and dense tasks (Cambrian's "Spatial Vision Aggregator" does this). Several model families (Qwen-VL, InternVL) train their own ViTs instead. Idea 3 · Axis 2: connector design is a wash MM1 and Idefics2 reached the same conclusion: at a fixed visual-token count, connector architecture matters much less than the encoder, resolution and data. The run below shows why it is also cheap: in current open VLMs the connector is usually under 2% of the parameters. What does matter is the token count. More visual tokens = more LLM compute = better performance up to a point, then diminishing returns. 64 tokens per image is too few for OCR. 576-1024 tokens is the sweet spot for most open VLMs. 2048+ helps only for documents and charts. Q-Former vs MLP is a cost question, not a quality question: Q-Former caps tokens at 32-64 regardless of image resolution; MLP emits all patch tokens. For high-res inputs, Q-Former saves LLM context; for low-res, the difference is noise. The same idea as a formula Where the parameters sit. Worked example A 7B VLM, priced per image LLaVA-OneVision-7B (measured below): encoder 398M, connector 17M, LLM 7.62B. At 729 visual tokens per image: TFLOPs in the LLM, against TFLOPs in the encoder and about 0.02 TFLOPs in the connector. Halving the visual tokens to 364 saves about 5.5 TFLOPs per image. Replacing the MLP connector with anything else changes a rounding error. So the first questions are which encoder, how many tokens, and which data; the connector is a detail. Check your mental model ✗ "A better connector is the easiest way to a better VLM." ✓ Controlled studies found the connector matters little at a fixed token count; encoder, resolution, tokens and data matter more. ✗ "More visual tokens are free once the encoder has run." ✓ Every visual token is processed by the whole language model, the largest part of the cost. ✗ "Distilling captions from a strong proprietary model is the best data." ✓ Molmo's human-described images beat distilled data and avoid copying another model's errors. Predict before you run In six current open VLMs, from SmolVLM-256M to Qwen3-VL-8B, what share of all parameters does the connector between encoder and LLM take? Which model will be the exception? (Solution P1.) See it drawn Where the parameters sit in real open VLMs Six open VLMs are built from their published configurations on PyTorch's meta device, so no weights are downloaded. Parameters are grouped into vision encoder, connector (projector, merger or resampler) and language model. A few seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The connector is tiny almost everywhere. LLaVA-OneVision-7B's MLP projector is 17M parameters, 0.2% of the model. InternVL3-8B's is 28M (0.4%), and Qwen2.5-VL-7B's patch merger is 45M (0.5%). Qwen3-VL's is larger, 160M, because it also feeds features from several encoder depths into the LLM, but it is still under 2%. This is the parameter side of "connector design is a wash": there is little there to optimise. Idefics2 is the exception, by design. Its connector is a Perceiver resampler with a modality projection, 743M parameters, larger than its own 418M SigLIP encoder. It buys token savings: 64 tokens per image instead of hundreds. The language model dominates. In every 7–8B model the LLM is 86% to 95% of the parameters. Since every visual token passes through it, it also dominates inference cost. The encoders range from 304M (InternVL3's InternViT-300M) to 632M (Qwen2.5-VL's ViT). Small models are shaped differently. SmolVLM-256M spends 86M on vision and only 0.16B on its language model. At that size the encoder is a third of the model, which is why small VLMs compress visual tokens aggressively. Idea 4 · Axis 3: LLM size sets the ceiling Larger language models consistently score higher on multimodal reasoning benchmarks within each model family (for example Qwen2.5-VL 3B, 7B and 72B). The VLM's multimodal reasoning ceiling is largely the LLM's text reasoning ceiling — the visual encoder can only feed it, not reason for it. This is why the largest open and hosted models lead on reasoning-heavy benchmarks such as MMMU-Pro. A 7B VLM cannot substitute for a 70B VLM through clever connector design. Idea 5 · Axis 4: data — detailed human captions beat distillation Molmo + PixMo (Deitke et al., 2024) is the 2024 result everyone should read. Allen AI had annotators describe images aloud for about a minute each, then transcribed the speech: about 712K densely captioned images. All PixMo data was collected "without the use of external VLMs." Molmo-72B outperformed larger proprietary models including Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro on the paper's academic benchmarks and human evaluation, second only to GPT-4o. The difference is not architecture — it is caption quality: detailed human descriptions carry far more information per image than short web captions and avoid inheriting another model's hallucinations. ShareGPT4V (Chen et al., 2023) and Cauldron (Idefics2) followed the same playbook with mixed human + GPT-4V captions. The trend is clear: for the 2026 frontier, caption density > caption quantity > distillation convenience. Idea 6 · Axis 5: resolution and its schedule Idefics2's ablations found that splitting images into sub-images (feeding higher effective resolution) mainly helps text-heavy tasks such as OCR and document questions, at a large cost in tokens. Many recipes also raise the resolution over training: start low for speed, finish high for detail. Resolution and token count trade off at fixed compute: more tokens at lower resolution help general scene understanding less than higher resolution helps reading small text. The 2026 production recipe: train Stage 1 at 384 fixed, Stage 2 with dynamic resolution up to 1280 for OCR-heavy tasks. Idea 7 · The Prismatic controlled comparison Prismatic VLMs (Karamcheti et al., 2024) is the paper that controlled the axes: a family of 7B–13B VLMs, the same evaluation suite, one design choice varied at a time. Its main findings: The separate projector-alignment stage of LLaVA-1.5 can be skipped: training everything in one stage worked as well and was cheaper. Fusing DINOv2 and SigLIP features beat either encoder alone, especially on localisation tasks. Base language models did about as well as instruction-tuned ones. Training longer and on more data helped. It gives no single ranking of axes, but it is the cleanest controlled study of what to ablate first. Idea 8 · A picker for 2026 Given the evidence, the default open-VLM recipe for a new project in 2026: Encoder: SigLIP 2 So400m/14 at native resolution with NaFlex (or a model family's own ViT), combined with DINOv2 features if you need segmentation or grounding. Connector: 2-layer MLP on patch tokens. Skip Q-Former unless you are token-constrained. LLM: a current open model family (Qwen3, Gemma 3, Llama 3.1), 7–8B for cost, 70B-class for quality, picked by target latency. Data: PixMo + ShareGPT4V + Cauldron, topped up with task-specific instruction data. Resolution: dynamic (min 256, max 1280 pixels per long side). Schedule: Stage 1 alignment (projector-only), Stage 2 full fine-tune, Stage 3 task-specific fine-tune. Every one of those defaults traces back to a measured ablation in the papers cited at the end of this lesson. "If I swap SigLIP for CLIP on a 7B Llama, what is the expected MMMU delta?" "Which axis should I ablate first for an 80% confidence answer?" Break it on purpose To speed up a VLM project, you compare published scores and conclude "model A's Perceiver connector beats model B's MLP by 4 points", although A also uses a different encoder, LLM and data. What went wrong in that reasoning, and how would you test the connector claim properly? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Open VLM families with published recipes : Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL, InternVL3, Gemma 3, Molmo, SmolVLM and LLaVA-OneVision; their technical reports are the current ablation literature. Fully open data and weights : Molmo/PixMo and similar projects release data, code and weights, so results can be reproduced and audited. Native resolution plus patch merging has replaced fixed square inputs in most recipes (Lesson 12.6). Small VLMs (SmolVLM at 256M–2B, Qwen-VL and InternVL 1–4B sizes) make on-device and low-cost inference practical. Sources: MM1 (arXiv 2403.09611) , Idefics2 (arXiv 2405.02246) , Prismatic VLMs (arXiv 2402.07865) , Cambrian-1 (arXiv 2406.16860) , Molmo and PixMo (arXiv 2409.17146) . Solutions Solution P1 · Under 2%, except Idefics2 Under 2% in five of the six models: 0.2% (LLaVA-OneVision-7B), 0.4% (InternVL3-8B), 0.5% (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), 1.8% (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 2.8% (SmolVLM-256M, where everything else is small). Solution B1 · Too many things changed at once The two models differ on at least four axes at once: encoder, language model, data and connector. A 4-point gap could come from any of them, and the ablation literature says the connector is the least likely cause. Published scores also differ in evaluation details: prompts, image resolution, answer parsing and test-set versions. To test the connector claim, hold everything else fixed: same encoder, same LLM, same data and schedule, same number of visual tokens. Swap only the connector, train both, and evaluate both with the same harness, ideally with a few seeds to see the noise. That is exactly what MM1, Idefics2 and Prismatic did, and why their conclusions are more trustworthy than leaderboard comparisons. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Weigh a trade-off You can spend your data budget on one of two things: have a strong proprietary model write captions for two million images, or pay people to describe seven hundred thousand images in detail by speaking for a minute or more about each one. Which do you choose for a new vision-language model, and what is the evidence? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Pay the people. The reference result is a model trained on 712K densely captioned images and no distilled captions that beat a much larger model on 11 of 11 benchmarks. Dense human captions carry 5 to 10 times the information of a short web caption and stay grounded in the image, while distilled captions inherit the hallucinations of the model that wrote them; about 12 percent of crawled pairs already describe things that are not in the image. Caption density beats caption quantity, which beats distillation convenience. The evidence. The dense-caption recipe: annotators described each image for one to three minutes in speech, transcribed to text, which gave 712K densely captioned images. The 72B model trained on them beat a 90B competitor on every one of 11 benchmarks. The difference was not architecture. Two other datasets followed the same path with mixed human and synthetic captions, and the trend across them is that density wins. The first visual instruction set was written by a text-only model from captions and boxes without seeing the image, 158k turns; it worked to unlock dialogue, with noise. Why density beats volume. A dense caption of 80 to 300 tokens names objects, counts, relations, text in the image and context; a web alt text names one thing. For alignment and instruction tuning the model learns from what the caption says about the image, so the information per image is the currency, not the image count. Why distillation is risky. The writing model does not see what it does not see. It hallucinates plausible content, and the student learns to hallucinate with the same confidence. A benchmark built from similar data does not punish it; production users do. When distillation still has a place. Bootstrapping a new domain fast, before human data arrives. Generating questions and answers from a human-written caption, which keeps the grounding in the caption. Filtered: score each synthetic caption against the image with a contrastive checker and drop the ungrounded tail. What to do with the budget. Dense human captions for the alignment and instruction stages, task-specific instruction data on top, and synthetic data only where a human caption anchors it. Measure grounding on a held-out human-labelled set, not only benchmark accuracy. Plausible wrong answers. "Two million captions beat seven hundred thousand; more data wins." The reference result beat a larger model with fewer, denser, grounded captions; volume of thin or hallucinated captions is no substitute. "The strong model's captions are better than what annotators write." They are longer than web captions but not grounded; the model describes what it expects, and the student learns the same habit. "Caption quality only matters for captioning tasks." The reference model gained on every benchmark, reasoning and reading included, because the alignment stage learned more about each image. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why did the speech-based collection matter? Expected: people say far more in a minute than they type, so the captions are long and specific at a cost that scales. (level 3) How do you check that a synthetic caption is grounded? Expected: embed the image and the caption with a contrastive checker and flag low similarity, then read a sample; drop or rewrite the tail. (level 4) How would you prove to a skeptic that the gain is data and not model size? Expected: the reference comparison beat a larger model; replicate at one size with two data mixes and the same encoder, connector and schedule. (level 4) Where in the three-stage pipeline do dense captions pay most? Expected: alignment and the first instruction stage, where the projector and the language model learn what an image contains; task-specific data pays in the last stage. Where it is taught. The open-weight recipes lesson gives the dense-caption result and the data axis, the vision-language models lesson quantifies the ungrounded pairs, and the LLaVA lesson shows the generated instruction data that started the field. Explain the mechanism Your 7B vision-language model trails a competitor on a multimodal reasoning benchmark by several points. The team's plan is a new connector design. Argue for or against, using what the ablation literature says about where the score comes from. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Against. Across the controlled studies, swapping the connector moved a reasoning benchmark by less than a point at a fixed token count, while swapping the encoder moved it by three or more, and doubling the language model from 7B to 13B added two to four points. The reasoning ceiling of such a model is the text reasoning ceiling of its language model; the visual side can only feed it. Spend the effort on the language model size, the encoder, the token count and the data before the connector. The decomposition. The one study that held every axis fixed but one found that the per-image visual-token count explained about 60 percent of the variance in scores, the encoder about 20 percent, the connector about 5 percent, and everything else about 15 percent. The language model sets the ceiling. Going from a 7B to a 13B language model reliably added 2 to 4 points on the flagship reasoning benchmark across the papers in the lesson, and at 70B most benchmarks saturate. The reason is structural: the encoder produces features and the connector translates them, but the reasoning happens in the language model. A 7B model cannot stand in for a 70B model through a cleverer connector. The encoder is the second lever. Swapping the common contrastive encoder for a stronger one added 3 or more points on the reasoning benchmark in one study, and self-supervised encoders led a vision-centric benchmark by about 5 to 7 points over the common contrastive one. The 2026 default pairs a strong contrastive encoder with a self-supervised one for dense features when grounding matters. The connector is a wash. At a fixed token count, an MLP, a query bridge and a resampler landed within about 1 point of each other in several independent studies. The connector is a cost question about tokens, not a quality question. What to do instead. Check the token count per image; more visual tokens up to the sweet spot helps more than any connector. Check the encoder and the resolution schedule. Check the data: detailed human captions beat distilled synthetic captions at the same token count. If the gap is in reasoning, the honest fix is a larger language model, and the budget question follows. Plausible wrong answers. "The connector is where the modalities meet, so it must matter most." Its measured share is about 5 percent of the variance; the token count and the encoder dominate. "A better connector lets a small language model reason like a large one." The reasoning ceiling is the language model's; no bridge adds reasoning the language model does not have. "More visual tokens always help." They help up to the sweet spot and then give diminishing returns at a growing compute cost; the gain is in the token count, not in the architecture that emits them. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does a bigger language model help a visual task? Expected: the benchmark asks for reasoning over what the encoder saw, and the reasoning happens in the language model; the visual side sets what it knows, not how well it thinks. (level 2) When would a connector change still be the right move? Expected: when the token budget binds, because then the connector decides how many tokens you can afford, which is the axis that matters most. (level 3) Which benchmarks move with the encoder and which do not? Expected: vision-centric benchmarks, counting and grounding, move with a self-supervised encoder, by about 5 to 7 points in one study; the reasoning benchmark also moves, by 3 or more points for a stronger contrastive encoder, so the encoder matters for both kinds. (level 3) Design the smallest ablation that settles this for your model. Expected: hold the data, the encoder, the token count, the resolution schedule and the training schedule fixed, swap the language model size in one run and the connector in another, and compare both with the baseline on the same eval. Where it is taught. The open-weight recipes lesson decomposes the variance across the five design axes, and the vision-language models lesson lays out the pattern the axes belong to. Defend a design Design a vision-language model for an on-device mobile assistant that reads the phone screen and taps, types and scrolls. Keep the language model at about 2B parameters. Choose the encoder, the bridge, the resolution plan and the data mix, justify each choice with the ablation evidence, and name the capability you would guard against over-promising. Level 4 of 4 · about 20 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Encoder: the stronger contrastive encoder at native resolution, with a self-supervised encoder's features concatenated for a dense spatial signal, because the encoder explains about 20 percent of the variance and self-supervised features lead vision-centric tests. Bridge: a two-layer MLP, since the connector explains about 5 percent, with features from several encoder depths stacked so that fine position reaches the language model. Resolution: a ramp from low to high, with dynamic resolution up to about 1280 pixels on the long side, because screens are text-dense and reading gains most from pixels. Data: dense human descriptions of screens plus grounded action traces, not distilled captions; and guard the promise on spatial relations, where general models score 50 to 60 percent and the agent must hit the right element every time. Constraints first. A 2B language model sets a low reasoning ceiling: a larger language model adds points on reasoning benchmarks, and this design cannot grow it. So every other axis must carry more, and the task must be framed as perception plus short actions, not long reasoning. Encoder. Choice Why The strong contrastive encoder at native resolution adds 3 or more points over the common one in the ablations; native resolution keeps screen text legible Concatenated self-supervised features lead vision-centric benchmarks by 5 to 7 points over the contrastive one; UI grounding is vision-centric Features from several encoder depths deep layers carry semantics and shallow layers carry fine position; stacking both tightens grounding, which an agent that taps needs Bridge. A two-layer MLP. The connector explains about 5 percent of the variance at a fixed token count, and the MLP is the simplest to retrain when the encoder or the language model changes. The token count is the knob that matters: screens are documents, so budget toward the upper end of the 576 to 1024 sweet spot, and above it for dense screens. Resolution schedule. Start low and ramp. Flat low-resolution training plateaus; a ramp trains faster and ends higher. Dynamic resolution with a minimum of 256 and a maximum near 1280 pixels on the long side handles the range of screen densities, and the document-reading gains of 3 to 5 points from splitting apply to screens. Data mix. Dense human descriptions of screens: what is on the screen, where, and what is interactive. Dense human captions beat distillation across the board in the reference comparison. Grounded action traces: screenshot, instruction, the element and the action, with coordinates. The visual-agent benchmark that frontier models lead has this shape. Task-specific instruction data for the app families you ship to. Synthetic data only where a human description anchors it, filtered for grounding. The capability to guard. Spatial relations. General models score 50 to 60 percent on above, below, left, right and counting, and an agent that taps the wrong element fails the task. Build the eval from real screens with the exact element-selection questions, measure it before any promise, and keep a verification step in the agent loop: read the screen back after the action and check the state. Serving on the device. A 2B language model and a strong encoder at a high resolution still need the visual token budget counted per screen; measure the latency per step at your resolution before you set the schedule. Plausible wrong answers. "Use a query-based bridge to save tokens on the device." It caps the tokens at a count too low for dense screen text, and the ablations put 64 tokens as too few for reading; spend tokens here and save elsewhere. "Generate the screen descriptions with a strong proprietary model." Distilled descriptions inherit hallucinations, and an agent that taps a hallucinated element fails; dense human descriptions won the reference comparison. "A 2B model with a great encoder matches a 70B agent." The language model sets the reasoning ceiling; frame the task as perception plus short actions and verify each step, instead of promising long reasoning. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why stack shallow and deep encoder layers for an agent and not for a captioner? Expected: a captioner needs semantics; an agent needs where exactly, which the shallow layers carry and the last layer blurs. (level 4) The language model is fixed at 2B. Which axis do you lean on hardest, and what is its limit? Expected: resolution and token count, because screens are text-dense; the limit is the latency per step on the device, which the token count sets. (level 4) How do you make the agent robust to being wrong about an element? Expected: a read-back after each action that compares the new screen with the expected state, and a stop when they do not match; the model's own confidence is not a safe signal. (level 4) What does the ablation evidence not tell you about this design? Expected: it comes from general benchmarks on datacenter GPUs; the device latency, the UI domain and the action format need your own ablation, one axis per run. Where it is taught. The open-weight recipes lesson supplies the ablation evidence for each axis and sets this exercise, and the vision-language models lesson covers multi-level features, visual agents and the spatial reasoning limit. Weigh a trade-off You lead a small team training an open vision-language model. The first run lands well below the open-weight models of its size on a general benchmark and on a document-reading benchmark. You can afford three more full runs. Which three changes do you make, in what order, and what do you expect each to move? Level 3 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Order the runs by the variance each axis explains. First, the resolution schedule and the token count: ramp from a low resolution to a high one and add image splitting for the document benchmark, where moving from 448 to 980 pixels added 3 to 5 points in the ablations. Second, the encoder: swap the common contrastive encoder for the stronger one, which added 3 or more points on the general benchmark, and concatenate a self-supervised encoder if grounding matters. Third, the data: replace distilled synthetic captions with dense human-written ones, which beat the distilled set on every benchmark in the reference comparison; leave the connector alone, because at a fixed token count it moves scores by about a point. The evidence behind the order. Axis What the ablations found Expected move Visual tokens and resolution about 60 percent of the variance; 384 to 448 adds 1 to 2 points; 448 to 980 with splitting adds 3 to 5 on reading tasks the document benchmark Encoder about 20 percent; a stronger contrastive encoder adds 3 or more; self-supervised features lead vision-centric tests by 5 to 7 the general benchmark, counting and grounding Data dense human captions beat distillation on 11 of 11 benchmarks in the reference comparison both benchmarks, grounded detail most Connector about 5 percent; within 1 point at a fixed token count nothing worth a run Language model 7B to 13B adds 2 to 4 points both, if the budget allows a larger model Run 1: resolution and tokens. Flat low-resolution training plateaus at medium accuracy. Ramp from 224 to 448 or native, then add splitting for reading tasks up to about 1280 pixels on the long side. The token count explains the most variance, and documents need pixels. Run 2: encoder. Swap to the stronger contrastive encoder at native resolution. If the benchmark includes counting or spatial questions, concatenate a self-supervised encoder's features, as the vision-centric recipes do. Retrain the projector; the language model keeps its adapters. Run 3: data. Replace distilled captions with dense human captions where you can get them, and top up with task-specific instruction data for the document questions. The reference result: a model trained on 712K densely captioned images with no distilled data beat a much larger competitor on every benchmark listed. Caption density beats caption quantity, which beats distillation convenience. What you do not run. A connector ablation. Several controlled studies put it within a point at a fixed token count; the token count is the knob, and run 1 already turned it. How to keep the runs comparable. One axis per run, the same eval, the same seed where the framework allows it, and a record of the data mix and the resolution schedule for each. A run that changed two things cannot be credited to either. Plausible wrong answers. "Start with the connector; it is the cheapest to retrain." Cheap and useless: at a fixed token count it moves scores by about a point in every controlled study. "Generate more captions with a stronger proprietary model." Distilled captions inherit hallucinations; the reference comparison shows dense human captions beating distillation across the board. "Train longer at the same settings." The ablations put the gap in resolution, encoder and data, not in steps; more steps at a flat low resolution plateau. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the document benchmark respond to resolution and the general one less? Expected: reading needs pixels per character; general questions need semantics that the encoder already carries at a low resolution. (level 3) What does a resolution ramp buy over a flat high resolution? Expected: faster alignment early and a higher end point; the ablations show that flat schedules plateau at medium accuracy. (level 4) You cannot get human captions in time. What is the next best data move? Expected: filter the distilled captions for grounding against the image with a contrastive checker and drop the ungrounded tail; density matters, but ungrounded density teaches hallucination. (level 4) If a fourth run appears, is it the connector or the language model? Expected: the language model, if memory allows a larger one; it lifts reasoning by points, where the connector moves a fraction of one. Where it is taught. The open-weight recipes lesson gives the five-axis design space and the ablation tables, and the LLaVA lesson shows the tiling scheme that the resolution run adds. Order a training curriculum that transfers skills from single-image to video without catastrophic forgetting. Explain why a single model beats specialists at the same parameter count when curriculum is done right. Name the three emergent capabilities reported by LLaVA-OneVision: multi-camera reasoning, set-of-mark prompting, iPhone-screenshot agent. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 05 (LLaVA), Phase 12 · 06 (any-resolution) Type : Build. Time : about 180 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, token budget solver + curriculum planner). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Before LLaVA-OneVision (Li et al., August 2024) the open-VLM world had separate lineages: LLaVA-1.5 for single images, multi-image models like Mantis and VILA, video models like Video-LLaVA and Video-LLaMA. Each won its benchmark and failed at the others. LLaVA-OneVision argued a single curriculum could train one model to dominate all three scenarios, and that the emergent task-transfer effects (single-image skills exported to video, multi-image reasoning exported to single-image) beat the sum of specialists. The recipe is dec Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means OneVision scenario "Single-image, multi-image, or video" One of three input shapes the unified VLM handles; the budget stays balanced across Token budget "How many tokens per sample" Total visual tokens the LLM sees per training / inference sample, about 6k to 9k at most in LLaVA-OneVision Curriculum "Training order" Stage ordering (single-image → multi-image → video) chosen for emergent transfer Bilinear pooling "Token shrink" Applying bilinear interpolation to the patch grid (2D) to reduce token count while preserving locality Emergent skill "Not trained, still works" Capability that appears at inference without matching training data, due to curriculum composition AnyRes-k "k-tile setup" k sub-tiles of fixed resolution plus one thumbnail, typical $k \in \lbrace 4, 9 \rbrace$ Task transfer "Cross-scenario generalization" Skills learned on single-image that apply to video (and vice versa) via shared backbone The problem In plain words first Early open vision-language models specialised: one handled single photos, another compared several images, a third watched videos. LLaVA-OneVision trains one model for all three. It keeps the language model's input roughly the same size in every case: one image is cut into high-resolution tiles, several images get one view each, and video frames are pooled down to fewer tokens. Training starts with single images to build perception, then mixes in multi-image and video data. This lesson explains the token budget and the curriculum. It then runs LLaVA-OneVision's real preprocessing code (configuration and tokenizer files only, no weights) to count how many visual tokens each kind of input actually costs. No model is trained. Image, multi-image, and video each stress a model differently. Single-image wants high-resolution tokens (AnyRes, ~2880 visual tokens) to catch OCR and fine detail. Budget per sample: one image, 2880 tokens. Multi-image wants several images at moderate resolution (~576 tokens each) so reasoning across images fits in context. Budget per sample: 4-8 images, 576 each, 2300-4600 tokens. Video wants many frames at low resolution (~196 tokens per frame after pooling) to capture temporal dynamics. Budget per sample: 8-32 frames, 196 each, 1600-6200 tokens. If you train separate models, you pick one budget. If you train one model, you need the budget to scale sensibly across scenarios without blowing context. Pre-OneVision, the default answer was "train one scenario, ignore the others." Video-LLaVA retrofitted video onto an image model with extra training stages. LLaVA-NeXT added multi-image support with tiling. None handled all three cleanly. Idea 1 · The OneVision token budget LLaVA-OneVision does not fix one exact token count. It balances the maximum visual-token count per sample so the three scenarios land in the same range, roughly 6,000 to 9,000 tokens, allocated differently per scenario: Single image: AnyRes-Max-9 (up to 9 tiles + one base view), each 384x384 view giving 729 tokens from SigLIP SO400M. Maximum: 729 * (1 + 9) = 7290 tokens. Multi-image: each image at 384 with no tiling, 729 tokens with no pooling. Up to 12 images → 8748 tokens. Video: up to 32 frames at 384 with 2x2 bilinear pooling → 196 tokens per frame. Total: 32 * 196 = 6272 tokens. The allocation keeps the maximum totals in the same band, so no scenario dominates the context or the gradient. The encoder produces different geometry per scenario, but the LLM consumes a similar budget. The code/main.py planner below uses a smaller toy budget of 4096 to show the same balancing logic. Idea 2 · The three-stage curriculum LLaVA-OneVision trains in stages: Alignment (stage 1). Only the projector trains, on 558K image–caption pairs, as in LLaVA-1.5. High-quality knowledge (stage 1.5). The whole model trains on about 4M high-quality, mostly synthetic, detailed captions and documents. Single-image instruction tuning (stage 2, part 1). About 3.2M single-image samples at high resolution (AnyRes). This builds perception, OCR and fine-grained understanding. OneVision instruction tuning (stage 2, part 2). About 1.6M samples mixing single images, multiple images and video, continuing from the single-image model. The order is deliberate: the paper builds strong single-image skills first and then transfers them to multi-image and video data, which is much scarcer. Idea 3 · Why curriculum works Single-image training builds the perceptual base. Patch tokens carry fine-grained visual features; the LLM learns to integrate them with text. Multi-image and video introduce structural challenges (which image is which, what happened first) that are hard to learn without a strong perceptual base. A plausible reason: if all scenarios are mixed from the start, single-image data is a smaller share of each batch, so perception may be learned less thoroughly while the model fits the structure of multi-image and video prompts. The curriculum aims for perception strength from the single-image stage, then compositional and temporal reasoning from the OneVision stage, without losing either. Idea 4 · Emergent cross-scenario skills The LLaVA-OneVision paper reports three emergent capabilities: Multi-camera reasoning. Trained on multi-image + video separately; at inference, asked to reason about a multi-camera driving scene. The model correctly integrates the views despite never seeing that exact format in training. Set-of-mark prompting. User annotates objects in an image with numbered marks; the model reasons about "what is mark 3 doing relative to mark 7." Trained on neither marks nor annotation; learned from the combination of spatial grounding + multi-image reference. Screenshot agent. Given an iPhone screenshot, the model describes the screen and plans the next tap, a GUI-agent task it was not specifically trained for. The paper presents these as emergent: combinations of skills learned from different scenarios, shown as qualitative examples rather than benchmark results. Idea 5 · Visual-token pooling The token budget requires pooling. OneVision uses bilinear interpolation on the 2D patch grid: SigLIP's 27x27 = 729 patches per 384-px frame become 14x14 = 196 (2x factor), which is the video setting. Pooling is done in patch-grid space, not token space, to preserve locality. The choice of pooling factor per scenario is itself a hyperparameter. Less pooling = more tokens = richer representation. More pooling = fewer tokens = more frames / images fit. The same idea as a formula One view from SigLIP at 384 px with 14-px patches: = 2 7 2 = 729 tokens. Single image, AnyRes with a grid of tiles (at most 9 in the paper's AnyRes-Max-9) plus a base view: ​ ≈ 729 ( g + 1 ) ( + one newline token per row of the tile grid ) . Video : each frame's grid is pooled bilinearly by 2 to = 1 4 2 = 196 tokens, so frames cost ​ = 196 T ( + 1 ) . Budget rule : choose , the number of images and so that each scenario's maximum stays in a similar range (about 6,000–9,000 tokens in the paper). Worked example Three requests, similar budgets One large photo with a 3×3 grid: tokens, plus 81 row-newline tokens in the Hugging Face implementation: 7,371. Video, 32 frames: , plus one newline: 6,273. Twelve images at one 729-token view each, the paper's multi-image setting: . The three maxima are within about 1.4× of each other, so no scenario dominates the context during training. Check your mental model ✗ "OneVision gives every image the same number of tokens." ✓ A single image gets high-resolution tiles, multiple images get fewer tokens each, and video frames are pooled. ✗ "Pooling video frames throws away the frames." ✓ It keeps every sampled frame but averages neighbouring patches, trading spatial detail for temporal coverage. ✗ "The library always follows the paper's budget." ✓ Check the processor: the Hugging Face implementation tiles every image, even in multi-image prompts (measured below). Idea 6 · LLaVA-OneVision-1.5 The 2025 follow-up (LLaVA-OneVision-1.5, arXiv 2509.23661) is "fully open" in training data, model weights, and code. It keeps the ViT–MLP–LLM design but changes the parts: a RICE-ViT encoder, a projector that merges 2×2 neighbouring patches, Qwen3 language models, an 85M-pair mid-training set and a 22M-sample instruction set. The 8B model outperforms Qwen2.5-VL-7B on 18 of 27 benchmarks. Idea 7 · Contrast with Qwen2.5-VL Qwen2.5-VL (Lesson 12.09) makes different choices. It uses M-RoPE and dynamic FPS instead of fixed pooling. Its budget scales with input — a 1-minute video uses more tokens than a 5-second video. LLaVA-OneVision fixes the budget and scales the pooling. Both work; they trade configurability for predictability. Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py is a curriculum and budget planner for a OneVision-style VLM. Given a token budget per sample and a target scenario mix (say 40% single-image, 30% multi-image, 30% video), it: Allocates resolution, pooling factor, and frames per scenario. Checks that every scenario fits within the shared budget. Reports expected token count, LLM FLOPs, and which scenarios are under-tokenized. Prints a stage-by-stage training schedule. Use it to plan a OneVision fine-tune or to sanity-check a VLM deployment's per-request cost. Break it on purpose Serve LLaVA-OneVision for an app where users upload 10 phone photos (4032×3024) and ask what changed between them, passing the photos straight to the processor. What happens to the prompt length, and what should the app do instead? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) One model for images, multiple images and video is now the norm: Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL, InternVL3, Gemma 3 and LLaVA-OneVision-1.5 all handle the three scenarios. Fully open recipes : LLaVA-OneVision-1.5 releases data, code and weights; its 8B model beats Qwen2.5-VL-7B on 18 of 27 benchmarks. Token budgets per request are explicit knobs in production: maximum pixels per image, frames per second, maximum frames, and pooling or merging factors. Video tokens are compressed aggressively : 2×2 pooling or merging per frame is common, with frame sampling set by fps (Lesson 12.9). Wire a Qwen2.5-VL-style JSON agent output format and parse structured tool calls from a VLM response. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 06 (patch-n'-pack) Type : Learn. Time : about 120 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, M-RoPE encoder + dynamic-FPS sampler). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The Qwen-VL family — Qwen-VL (2023), Qwen2-VL (2024), Qwen2.5-VL (2025), Qwen3-VL (2025) — is the most influential open vision-language model lineage in 2026. Each generation made a single decisive architectural bet that the rest of the open ecosystem copied within twelve months: native dynamic resolution via M-RoPE, dynamic-FPS sampling with absolute time alignment, window attention in the ViT, and structured agent output formats. By Qwen3-VL, the recipe had stabilized: a 2D-RoPE-ViT encoder with native-aspect-ratio inputs, an MLP projector into a lar Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means M-RoPE "Multimodal RoPE" 3D rotary position embedding with temporal, height, and width bands in the hidden dim Dynamic FPS "Smart sampling" Frame sampling rate chosen per video based on motion, duration, and token budget Absolute time encoding "Time-aligned M-RoPE" Temporal position IDs set from each frame's timestamp, so the model sees actual seconds, not frame index, with no extra tokens Window attention "Local attention" Spatial self-attention restricted to small windows for speed; global attention added periodically Structured agent output "JSON mode" Training data supervision teaching the VLM to emit parseable JSON with coords and tool names min_pixels / max_pixels "Resolution bounds" Per-request Qwen2.5-VL controls bounding total pixel count and therefore token count Grounding "Point-at-it" Outputting bounding-box coordinates as text tokens; used since Qwen-VL v1 The problem In plain words first Qwen-VL is Alibaba's family of open vision-language models, and the most widely used open line in 2025–2026. Its designs answer two practical questions. First, how to read an image of any shape without squashing or tiling it: cut it into 14-pixel patches at close to its real size, merge each 2×2 group into one token, and give every token its row and column through a 3D position code called M-RoPE. Second, how to know when something happened in a video: sample frames at a chosen rate and attach each frame's real time, first inside the position code (Qwen2.5-VL), later as plain text like "<3.2 seconds>" (Qwen3-VL). This lesson follows the four generations, then runs the real Qwen preprocessing code (configuration and tokenizer files only, no weights) to count tokens and inspect the time encoding. No model is trained or downloaded. Qwen-VL shipped in August 2023 as a direct response to LLaVA-1.5 and BLIP-2. The gap the Qwen team targeted was threefold: resolution, video, and structured output. Resolution: LLaVA-1.5 ran at 336x336. Fine for photos, useless for a Chinese-language invoice or a dense spreadsheet screenshot. Qwen-VL's first innovation was 448x448 and grounded bounding-box output, letting the model point at things. Video: Video-LLaMA stacked per-frame encoders and fed them to the LLM. It worked for short clips, not for multi-minute videos where the temporal axis is the signal. The Qwen team wanted a single encoder that understood time. Structured output: LLaVA emitted free-form text. An agent needs JSON. Qwen-VL trained on explicit JSON output formats including bounding-box coordinates as text. Every Qwen-VL generation extends one of these three axes. Idea 1 · Qwen-VL (August 2023) The first generation: a ViT of about 1.9B parameters initialised from OpenCLIP ViT-bigG/14, a single cross-attention layer with 256 learnable queries that compresses each image to 256 tokens (about 0.08B parameters, similar in spirit to a Q-Former), and Qwen-7B as the language model; about 9.6B parameters in all. Contributions: 448x448 resolution (then SOTA for an open VLM). Grounding: trained on image-text pairs with explicit coordinate-token output. "The cat is at (112, 204), (280, 344) ". Chinese + English multilingual training from the start. The grounding supervision was the real headline: boxes written as plain text with coordinates normalised to [0, 1000), between <box> tags, so no new vocabulary was needed. Idea 2 · Qwen2-VL (September 2024) — M-RoPE and native resolution Qwen2-VL replaced the fixed-resolution + Q-Former stack with a natively dynamic-resolution ViT encoder. Key changes: Native dynamic resolution. Each image is resized only slightly, to multiples of 28 pixels within a minimum and maximum pixel count (patch 14 with 2x2 spatial merge). An image at 1120x672 (40x24 merged patches) produces 960 visual tokens. No tiling, no thumbnail. M-RoPE (Multimodal RoPE). Each token carries a 3D position (t, h, w) instead of 1D. For images t=0, for video t = frame_index. RoPE rotates query/key vectors by a frequency per axis. No positional embedding table. MLP projector. Drop the Q-Former; use a 2-layer MLP on the merged patch tokens. Video with dynamic FPS. Video sampled at 1-2 FPS by default, but the model accepts arbitrary frame counts. Result: Qwen2-VL-7B reached 94.5 on DocVQA, and the 72B model was competitive with GPT-4o on many multimodal benchmarks. The architecture change was the decisive move. Idea 3 · Qwen2.5-VL (February 2025) — dynamic FPS + absolute time Qwen2.5-VL's big shift was video. Dynamic FPS is not just "sample more frames when needed." The paper formalized: Absolute time in the position IDs. Instead of frame indices (frame 0, 1, 2...), the temporal axis of M-RoPE follows actual timestamps, so the gap between two frames' IDs tracks the seconds between them. "At 0:04, the cat jumps." No extra text tokens carry the time, so the encoding adds no sequence length. Dynamic FPS. Sample at 1 FPS for slow footage, 4+ FPS for action. The user or trainer chooses; M-RoPE adapts. Window attention in ViT. Spatial attention is windowed (local within blocks) for throughput; global attention every few layers. Structured outputs for grounding and agents. Boxes and points are emitted as JSON with absolute pixel coordinates of the resized image (Qwen2-VL used coordinates normalised to 0–1000), and the model was trained on agent and tool-use trajectories. Efficient training and inference at scale: the vision encoder was retrained with window attention, RMSNorm and SwiGLU, so large images and long videos stay affordable. Benchmarks: the Qwen2.5-VL report places the 72B model level with GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet on many document, video and agent benchmarks, and well ahead on some document and GUI-grounding tasks. Idea 4 · Qwen3-VL (November 2025) Qwen3-VL (models from September 2025, technical report November 2025) comes in dense 2B, 4B, 8B and 32B sizes and as 30B-A3B and 235B-A22B mixture-of-experts models, with a native 256K-token context. Three architectural changes: interleaved MRoPE (the t, h and w frequencies are interleaved across the dimension instead of split into blocks), DeepStack (features from several ViT layers are fed into the LLM, not just the last one), and text-based timestamps: instead of encoding time in the position ids, each group of frames is preceded by a text marker such as <1.2 seconds> (measured below). The lineage takeaway: by 2025 the basic recipe (native-resolution ViT, 2x2 merge, MLP, LLM) had stabilized. Later generations change how position and time are encoded and scale data and compute. Idea 5 · M-RoPE mathematically Classical RoPE rotates a query q of dimension d by position m using paired coordinates: ​ [ 2 i ] q rot ​ [ 2 i + 1 ] θ i ​ ​ = q [ 2 i ] cos ( m θ i ​ ) − q [ 2 i + 1 ] sin ( m θ i ​ ) = q [ 2 i ] sin ( m θ i ​ ) + q [ 2 i + 1 ] cos ( m θ i ​ ) = 1000 0 − 2 i / d ​ M-RoPE splits the hidden dim into three bands. Say d = 96 . Assign 32 dims to temporal, 32 to height, 32 to width. Each band rotates by its own axis position. A patch at (t=5, h=10, w=20) gets rotations R_t(5) , R_h(10) , R_w(20) applied to its three bands. Text tokens use the same value on all three axes, t = h = w = text_index , so for pure text M-RoPE reduces to ordinary 1D RoPE. Image tokens share one t and take their row and column as h and w; video tokens take t from the frame time. Positions after an image or video continue from the largest id used so far. The benefit: one position encoding handles text, image, and video without branching code or different position tables. Idea 6 · Dynamic-FPS sampling logic Given a video of duration T seconds and a target-tokens budget B : Compute the maximum FPS you can afford: fps_max = B / (T * tokens_per_frame) . Pick a target FPS from {1, 2, 4, 8} that satisfies fps <= fps_max . If motion is high (optical-flow heuristic or explicit user request), pick higher FPS. If motion is low, pick lower. Sample uniformly at the chosen FPS; set each frame's M-RoPE temporal ID from its timestamp in seconds. Qwen2.5-VL trains this logic implicitly; at inference the user controls via fps parameter. A 60-second action sequence at 4 FPS with 81 tokens per frame = 19440 tokens, manageable in a 32k context. The same idea as a formula Image tokens. Time : about 120 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, training-corpus mixer). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Every open VLM before InternVL3 followed the same three-step recipe: take a text LLM trained on trillions of text tokens, bolt on a vision encoder, then fine-tune the seams. This works but has alignment debt — the text LLM has spent its full pretraining budget on pure text and does not natively understand visual tokens. When you add vision post-hoc, the LLM has to re-learn how to relate visual input to its text reasoning without forgetting the text. InternVL3 (Zhu et al., April 2025) rejects the post-hoc approach: one pretraining run, text and mult Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Native multimodal pretraining "From scratch together" Text + image + video tokens participate in the loss from step 1, not bolted on later Alignment debt "Post-hoc penalty" Measurable regression in text skills and answer consistency that comes from bolting vision onto a frozen LLM V2PE "Variable visual pos encoding" Per-modality learnable position encoding allocation; InternVL3's M-RoPE successor ViR "Resolution router" Small classifier that picks minimum resolution needed per query before encoding, saving inference tokens DvD "Decoupled deployment" Vision encoder on one GPU, LLM on another, with stream handoff; doubles throughput for large VLMs InternVL-U "Unified understanding + generation" 2026 follow-up that adds image-generation heads to the native-pretrain backbone Interleaved corpus "OBELICS / MMC4" Documents with text and images in natural reading order; the raw material for native pretraining The problem In plain words first Most open vision-language models are built in steps: take a finished text model, attach an image encoder, train a small adapter between them, then fine-tune. The text model never saw images while it was learning language, and the later stages can wear away some of its text skills. InternVL3 (April 2025) changes the order. It starts from a pretrained image encoder and a pretrained language model like everyone else, but then trains all their parameters together in one large pretraining stage, on image and text data mixed with plain text. It also introduces V2PE, a way to let image tokens use up fewer position numbers, so long documents with many images fit. Its successor, InternVL3.5, adds deployment tricks for speed. This lesson explains these ideas. It runs InternVL3's real image preprocessing (configuration files only) and checks V2PE's position arithmetic. No model is trained or downloaded. Post-hoc VLM training is the default. LLaVA, BLIP-2, Qwen-VL, Idefics — all take an already-pretrained LLM (Llama, Vicuna, Qwen, Mistral) and add vision. The training stages typically look like: Frozen LLM + frozen vision encoder + trainable projector, trained on caption pairs to align embeddings. Unfreeze LLM, train on instruction data (LLaVA-Instruct, ShareGPT4V). Optional task-specific fine-tune. Three symptoms of alignment debt show up: Catastrophic forgetting. The post-hoc VLM loses some text-only skill: scores on text benchmarks such as math word problems often drop after multimodal fine-tuning, which is why many recipes mix text-only data back in. Answer drift. Small phrasings of the same visual question get different answers. The vision encoder connects to the LLM with weaker bindings than the LLM's own tokens. Visual-text inconsistency. The VLM can describe an image correctly and then answer a question contradicting its own description. Visual tokens do not participate in the LLM's internal consistency checks the same way text does. These symptoms are well-documented. MM1.5 Section 4 quantifies them. LLaVA-OneVision's ablations hint at them. Native pretraining is the answer. Idea 1 · Native multimodal pretraining InternVL3 does not start from nothing: it begins with a pretrained vision encoder (InternViT) and a pretrained language model (Qwen2.5 or InternLM3), joined by an MLP projector. What changes is the next step. Instead of first aligning a frozen LLM and then fine-tuning in stages, InternVL3 trains all parameters in one pretraining stage on a mixture of multimodal data (captions, interleaved documents, OCR, video and more) and text-only corpora. Vision tokens, text tokens and cross-modal interactions all share the same next-token loss from the start of that stage, and the text-only data keeps the language skills from eroding. Training is a single stage for the base model; supervised fine-tuning and preference optimisation follow. Idea 2 · V2PE (variable visual position encoding) Qwen2-VL's M-RoPE gives visual tokens separate time, row and column positions. InternVL3's V2PE (variable visual position encoding) solves a different problem: long multimodal contexts. Text tokens advance the position index by 1, as usual. Visual tokens advance it by a smaller step δ (for example 1/2, 1/4 or 1/16), so hundreds of image tokens use up only a few positions. During training δ is sampled from a set of values; at inference a fixed δ is chosen. The benefit: a document with dozens of images stays within the position range the language model handles well, which helps long-context multimodal tasks. RoPE works with fractional positions, so no new parameters are needed (measured below). The same idea as a formula Tokens per image. InternVL3 cuts an image into up to 12 tiles of 448 × 448 (plus a thumbnail when tiled). Each tile has patches of 14 px, and pixel shuffle with ratio 0.5 merges each 2×2 block: ​ = ( 32 ⋅ 0.5 ) 2 = 256 , n image ​ = 256 × ( tiles + thumbnail ) . V2PE positions. With text step 1 and visual step , a document with ​ text and ​ visual tokens ends at position about ​ ≈ n t ​ + δ n v ​ ( plus one step at each switch ) . RoPE at a fractional position : the rotation angle for frequency ​ is simply ​ , so needs no new parameters. Worked example Forty images in one document 40 images at one tile each: visual tokens; with 41 text blocks of 400 tokens, 16,400 text tokens, 26,640 in all. Plain positions ( ): the last token sits at position 26,639. With : about , plus one extra step at each of the 80 switches: 18,989 (measured below). With : about 17,076. The positions are those of a mostly-text document, a range the language model knows well. Native pretraining changes how these parts are trained together, not where they come from. See it drawn V2PE: positions for a long interleaved document A document of 40 images (256 tokens each) and 41 text blocks (400 tokens each) gets position ids with visual steps δ = 1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/16. Then RoPE angles are computed at a whole and a fractional position. Instant. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Visual tokens stop eating the position range. The document has 26,640 tokens. With ordinary positions (δ = 1) the last token sits at 26,639. With δ = 1/4 it sits at 18,989, and with δ = 1/16 at 17,076.5. That is close to the 16,400 text tokens alone, so 10,240 image tokens cost the position range of fewer than 700 text tokens. For a model whose RoPE works best within its trained length, this keeps long multimodal documents in familiar territory. Fractional positions are ordinary RoPE. The rotation angles at position 3.25 lie between those at 3 and 4 (3.25 against 3.0 for the first frequency, 2.437 against 2.25 for the second). Nothing new is learned: only the step size changes. That is why V2PE could be trained with several δ values and used with a fixed one at inference. The price: image tokens next to each other are now very close in position, so the model distinguishes them less by position and more by content. The InternVL3 paper chose the δ values through ablations. Idea 3 · Visual Resolution Router (ViR) Introduced with InternVL3.5 (August 2025), not InternVL3. Not every image patch needs the same number of tokens: a patch of sky carries less than a patch of small text. ViR is a small trained router that chooses, per image patch, how strongly to compress its visual tokens, keeping more tokens where detail matters. The InternVL3.5 paper reports that ViR roughly halves the visual tokens with almost no loss in accuracy. Idea 4 · Decoupled Vision-Language deployment (DvD) Also from InternVL3.5. When you serve a large VLM, the vision encoder runs once per image but the LLM runs autoregressively for every output token. The two components have different bottlenecks (the encoder is compute-bound on big batches of patches; the LLM decode is bound by memory and KV cache). DvD puts the vision encoder and the language model on different GPUs and streams visual features between them, so each can be batched and scaled on its own. Together, ViR and DvD account for most of the up-to-4.05× inference speedup InternVL3.5 reports over InternVL3. Idea 5 · Single-stage vs multi-stage quality InternVL3's main benchmark claim: InternVL3-78B scores 72.2 on MMMU, a new state of the art among open models at release (April 2025), and its report calls it highly competitive with GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Pro. The smaller models (1B to 38B) lead their size classes on many benchmarks. The paper also reports that the native recipe keeps text performance close to that of the underlying language models, supporting the alignment-debt argument. Idea 6 · InternVL3.5 and InternVL-U InternVL3.5 (August 2025) adds Cascade RL (offline reinforcement learning, then online RL) for reasoning, with up to +16% on reasoning benchmarks over InternVL3, plus ViR and DvD for efficiency. The largest model is a 241B-parameter mixture of experts (InternVL3.5-241B-A28B). InternVL-U (March 2026) is a 4B-parameter unified model: an InternVL-style understanding model with an MMDiT-based image-generation head, for understanding, reasoning, generation and editing in one model (Lesson 12.13 covers unified models). Idea 7 · Trade-offs of native pretraining Native pretraining is not free: Compute. Joint training of all parameters on a large multimodal corpus costs much more than training a projector; it is a pretraining run, not a fine-tune. Data. Interleaved image-text corpora at scale are rare. OBELICS is 141M documents; MMC4 is 571M. Text alone ships at 15T tokens. Multimodal pretraining data scarcity is a hard constraint. Base-LLM reuse. A natively pretrained VLM is tied to the LLM it started from; moving to a newer LLM means repeating the joint pretraining, whereas a post-hoc recipe only retrains the adapter and the fine-tuning stages. The bet InternVL3 makes: the alignment debt is worse than the extra training cost. Post-hoc VLMs will keep existing because they remain cheaper for most projects.
