The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Every VLM we have seen so far keeps images and text separate. Visual tokens come from a vision encoder, flow into a projector, then meet text inside the LLM. The vision and text vocabularies never overlap. Chameleon (Meta, May 2024) asked: what if they did? Train a VQ-VAE that turns an image into a sequence of discrete tokens from a shared vocabulary. Every multimodal document is now one sequence — text tokens and image tokens interleaved, a single autoregressive loss. Side effect: the model can generate mixed-modality outputs — alte Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Early fusion "Unified tokens" Images converted to discrete tokens sharing the transformer's vocabulary from step one VQ-VAE "Image tokenizer" CNN + ViT + codebook that maps images to integer indices the transformer can predict Shared vocabulary "One dictionary" A single token ID space covering text + image + modality separators QK-Norm "Attention stabilizer" LayerNorm applied to query and key before their dot product, prevents norm blowup Mixed-modality generation "Text + image output" Inference that autonomously produces interleaved text and image tokens in one pass Codebook size "K entries" Number of discrete vectors the VQ-VAE can quantize to; trades compression for fidelity Tokenizer ceiling "Reconstruction limit" Best PSNR achievable by decoding VQ tokens; bounds the model's image quality The problem In plain words first The vision-language models so far read images but can only write text. Chameleon (Meta, May 2024) treats an image exactly like text. A separate "image tokenizer" (a VQ-VAE) turns every 512×512 image into 1,024 whole numbers, each picked from a list of 8,192 learned visual patterns. Those numbers get their own IDs in the same vocabulary as words. A single transformer then reads and writes one stream of tokens, words and image codes mixed, with one next-token loss. To make an image, the model writes image codes and a decoder turns them back into pixels. This lesson covers the tokenizer, the shared vocabulary, mixed generation and the training tricks that kept Chameleon stable. It runs the real tokenizer code (random weights, real shapes) to turn a photo into 1,024 codes, and measures why QK-Norm was needed. No model is trained. Adapter-based VLMs (LLaVA, BLIP-2, Qwen-VL) treat text and image as two different things. A text token goes through embed(text_token) ; an image goes through visual_encoder(image) → projector → ... pseudo_tokens . The model has two input paths that merge partway in. Three consequences: The LLM can only consume images, not emit them. Output is text only. Mixed-modality documents (alternating paragraphs and images, as in an article) are awkward — you either parse the multimodal input outside the model or chain generations. Distributional mismatch. Visual tokens and text tokens live in different regions of the hidden space, creating subtle alignment issues. Chameleon rejects the premise: images are just sequences of discrete tokens from a shared vocabulary. Train the model on interleaved documents, one loss, one autoregressive decoder, and you unlock mixed-modality generation for free. Idea 1 · VQ-VAE as image tokenizer The tokenizer is a vector-quantized variational autoencoder. The architecture: Encoder: a convolutional network (VQGAN-style, following Gafni et al.'s Make-A-Scene tokenizer) that maps a 512x512 image to a 32x32 feature map of dimension 256 (16x downsampling). Codebook: a learned vocabulary of K vectors (Chameleon uses 8192), also dim 256. Quantization: for each spatial feature, look up the nearest codebook entry by L2 distance. Replace the continuous feature with the integer index. Decoder: CNN that takes quantized features back to pixels. Training: VAE reconstruction loss + commitment loss + codebook loss. The codebook indices form a discrete alphabet for images. For Chameleon: one image becomes 32*32 = 1024 tokens drawn from a vocabulary of 8192. Put those image IDs in the same ID space as the text BPE tokens. Chameleon's single tokenizer has 65,536 entries, and that count already includes the 8192 image codes and the special tokens such as the image separators. The transformer sees one sequence, one loss. Idea 2 · The shared vocabulary Chameleon's vocabulary combines text tokens, image tokens, and modality separators. Each token has a single ID. The input embedding layer maps every ID to a D-dim hidden vector. The output projection maps hidden back to vocab logits. Softmax picks the next token, whatever modality. Separators matter: <image> and </image> tags bracket the image-token sequence. At generation time, if the model emits <image> , downstream software knows the next 1024 tokens are VQ indices to send to the decoder for pixel rendering. Idea 3 · Mixed-modality generation Inference is next-token prediction in the shared vocabulary. Example prompt: "Draw a cat and describe it." Chameleon emits: Copy The model picks the order autonomously — it may produce image then text, text then image, or interleave. Same decoder, same loss. Compare to adapter VLMs where generation is text-only. Chameleon reopens the question of model output modalities. Idea 4 · Training stability — QK-Norm, dropout, LayerNorm ordering Early-fusion training is unstable at scale. Chameleon's paper documents three tricks: QK-Norm. Apply LayerNorm to the query and key projections inside attention, before the dot product. This bounds the attention logits when activations grow (measured below). Used by many post-2024 large models. z-loss. A small penalty on , the log of the softmax normaliser of the output logits, which stops the logits drifting to very large values. Dropout and norm reordering. Chameleon-7B also needed dropout after attention and feed-forward layers. For Chameleon-34B, the paper moved the normalisation inside the residual branch, applied to the output of attention and feed-forward (as in Swin Transformer v2), so the residual stream cannot grow without bound. The paper traces the instability to the softmax and to norm growth when images and text share one model: without these changes, its training-loss curves diverge late in training. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Without QK-Norm, logits grow with the square of the activations. At scale 1 the largest logit is about 5 and attention is spread out (top weight 0.015, close to uniform over 1,024 tokens). At scale 4 the largest logit is 82 and the top token already takes 84% of the attention; at 16 it is 1,309 and 99%. Attention has collapsed onto single tokens, and gradients through the softmax vanish for everything else. In a deep model trained on mixed images and text, activation norms do grow like this. The Chameleon paper traced its divergences to exactly this effect. With QK-Norm nothing changes. Because q and k are normalised before the dot product, the largest logit stays at 4.7 and the top weight at 0.014 at every scale. The model can still learn sharp attention, but only through its weights, not through runaway activations. z-loss keeps output logits centred. Logits that have drifted up by 40 give the same probabilities as centred ones (softmax ignores a constant shift). The z-loss is still 13 times larger (0.031 against 0.002), so training pushes them back. Unbounded logit growth is a common start of numerical trouble in bf16. Idea 5 · The tokenizer's reconstruction ceiling VQ-VAE is lossy. 1,024 codes from an 8,192-entry codebook store 13 bits each: 13,312 bits for a 512x512 image, about 470 times less than raw 24-bit pixels (measured below). Fine detail cannot survive that compression. The Chameleon paper names one visible weakness: images with a lot of text are reconstructed poorly. The tokenizer is the bottleneck. Better tokenizers (MAGVIT-v2, IBQ and others) raise the ceiling. Emu3 (Lesson 12.12) reports image generation that beats SDXL in human and automatic evaluations with next-token prediction alone, using its own, stronger tokenizer and much more data. Idea 6 · Chameleon vs BLIP-2 / LLaVA Chameleon (early fusion, shared vocab): - One loss, one decoder. - Generates mixed-modality output. - Tokenizer is the quality ceiling. - Expensive: VQ-VAE decoder per generated image on inference path. BLIP-2 / LLaVA (late fusion, separate towers): - Vision in, text out only. - Reuses pretrained LLM. - No tokenizer bottleneck for understanding. - Cheap: single forward pass. Pick by task. If you need image generation, Chameleon family. If you only need understanding, adapter-VLM is simpler and reuses more pretrained compute. Idea 7 · Fuyu and AnyGPT Fuyu (Adept, 2023) is a related approach: skip the separate vision encoder entirely, feed raw image patches through the LLM's input projection as if they were tokens, no tokenizer. Simpler than Chameleon, loses the shared-vocab output generation. AnyGPT (Zhan et al., 2024) extends the idea to four modalities: text, image, speech, music. Each modality gets its own discrete tokenizer (images, speech and music each have a dedicated one), and one shared transformer models all the tokens. Any-to-any generation. Debug a failure You pretrain an early-fusion model on interleaved text and image codes. The small runs are fine, but the large run's loss spikes and diverges after a while, and the attention scores climb from layer to layer. What is happening, and what did the published recipe change to make such a run converge? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Early-fusion training at scale is unstable because image codes and text tokens share one softmax and one residual stream, and their gradients and norms differ; the attention logits grow with depth until the softmax saturates and the loss blows up. The published recipe at 34B parameters diverged at several checkpoints without three changes: normalization of the query and key projections before the dot product, dropout after every residual addition rather than only after attention and the MLP, and pre-normalization on the residual branch plus an extra normalization on the skip connection of the last block. The training recipe is as much of the contribution as the architecture. The signature. Norm growth. The query and key vectors grow in magnitude through the layers, the attention logits grow with them, the softmax turns into a near one-hot, and the gradients become spiky. Small runs do not reach the depth or the step count where this compounds; the large run does. Why early fusion makes it worse. A shared vocabulary of 65,536 entries holds the text tokens and 8192 image codes, and one image is 1024 codes in a row. Long runs of image codes carry gradients on a different scale from text, and they can dominate an update. The two modalities also occupy different regions of the hidden space, which pushes the norms apart. The three changes. QK-Norm. Apply layer normalization to the query and key projections inside attention, before the dot product. It bounds the logit magnitude at every depth, and several large models after this adopted it. Dropout placement. Dropout after every residual addition, not only after attention and after the MLP. More regularization where image-code gradients can dominate. Normalization ordering. Pre-normalization on the residual branch, which is standard, plus an extra normalization on the skip connection of the last block, which stabilizes the gradient flow at the final layer. How you would confirm it on your run. Log the norm of the queries and keys and the maximum attention logit per layer over training; the divergence should follow growth in the deep layers. Log the gradient norm split by the modality of the token; a dominance of image-code gradients points at the second change. Restart from a checkpoint before the spike with QK-Norm on, and compare the logit curves. The alternative family. A continuous design that trains a diffusion loss on image patches next to the text loss avoids the shared softmax over image codes, but it has a balance problem of its own: the two losses live on different scales, and the weights between them are a search of their own. Plausible wrong answers. "Early fusion is unstable by nature; use smaller models." The published recipe converged at 34B with the three changes; the instability is a recipe problem. "Clip the gradients harder." Clipping bounds the update, not the logit growth that causes the saturation; the norms keep drifting under a clip. "Use post-normalization everywhere; it is more stable." The recipe kept pre-normalization on the residual branch and added normalization where the norms grew: the queries, the keys, and the skip of the last block. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does normalizing the queries and keys bound the logits? Expected: the dot product of two normalized vectors is bounded by their scale, so the logits cannot grow without limit as the residual stream grows. (level 3) Why not lower the learning rate instead? Expected: a lower rate slows the growth but does not remove the mechanism; the norms still drift with depth, and the run pays in steps for a problem that normalization removes. (level 4) What did the paper report at 34B without the changes? Expected: repeated divergence at several checkpoints, driven by growth of the attention logits, a norm explosion, which the three changes removed. (level 4) How does the two-loss continuous design trade this problem for another? Expected: it removes the shared softmax over image codes but introduces two losses of different magnitude, where one head can dominate without careful loss weights and schedules. Where it is taught. The Chameleon lesson documents the three stability changes and the divergence at scale, and the Transfusion lesson gives the continuous alternative and its own balance problem. Weigh a trade-off A product needs a model that reads screenshots and answers questions today, and might need to draw diagrams later. Two designs are on the table: an adapter model, where a vision encoder feeds projected tokens into a text-only decoder, and a model that turns images into discrete codes in the same vocabulary as text and trains one next-token loss over interleaved sequences. Compare them and pick for this product. Level 2 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The adapter design is late fusion: images enter as projected continuous tokens or through cross-attention, the decoder reuses all its text pretraining, and the output is text only. The shared-vocabulary design is early fusion: a quantizer maps an image to discrete codes, the transformer trains one loss over text and image codes, and it can emit image codes, so it generates pictures. For a product that must read screenshots now, pick the adapter: it reuses more pretrained compute, has no quantizer ceiling for understanding, and is cheaper to serve; add the early-fusion model only when drawing becomes a real requirement, because its image quality is capped by the quantizer and each generated image costs a decoder pass over a thousand or more codes. Two paths into the model. Late fusion, adapter Early fusion, shared vocabulary Image input encoder features projected into the embedding space, or read through cross-attention discrete codes from a learned quantizer, looked up like text tokens Loss language-modeling loss on text a single next-token loss on text and image codes together Output text only text and images, interleaved as the model chooses Reuse of the pretrained LLM full the model trains on the mixed stream from the start Ceiling for understanding the encoder the quantizer's reconstruction Serving cost per answer one decoder step per generated text token one decoder step per generated text token, plus 1024 sequential decoding steps per generated image, one per code, then a decoder pass for the pixels What early fusion buys. One sequence, one loss, and mixed-modality output. The reference model's quantizer maps a 512 by 512 image to 1024 codes from a codebook of 8192, inside a single vocabulary of 65,536 entries that also holds the text tokens and the separators. When the model emits the image-start separator, the next 1024 codes go to the decoder for pixels. What it costs. A quality ceiling. The quantizer is lossy; at that codebook and code count the reconstruction peaks around 26 to 28 dB, below the 32 and more of continuous latent diffusion. A better quantizer lifts the ceiling, but the ceiling is the quantizer. Training stability. Early-fusion training at scale diverged without normalization of the attention queries and keys, dropout after every residual, and an extra normalization on the last block. Compute. Every generated image is a decoder pass over its codes. What late fusion buys. It bolts onto any pretrained decoder, keeps the text stream clean so that text ability survives, and computes the image once; with cross-attention the image keys and values are cached across decode steps. It cannot emit images. The pick. Reading screenshots is understanding, and the adapter is the simpler and stronger tool for it today. When drawing arrives, measure whether a separate generation model behind a tool call meets the need before you move the whole stack to early fusion. Plausible wrong answers. "Early fusion is the future, so start there." For understanding alone it reuses less pretrained compute and caps quality at the quantizer; the adapter is the simpler, stronger choice until generation is required. "The adapter can draw if you add a decoder head." Its images never exist as predictable tokens; drawing needs either image codes in the vocabulary or a separate generation model. "The quantizer is a detail; the transformer does the work." In the early-fusion family the quantizer sets the ceiling on every image the model produces. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why can the adapter model not generate an image? Expected: its output head covers the text vocabulary only; images enter as embeddings and never exist as tokens it could predict. (level 2) What is the shared vocabulary made of? Expected: text tokens, image codes and modality separators in one id space, so one embedding table and one output projection cover all of them. (level 3) Where does the quality ceiling of the early-fusion model come from, and what moves it? Expected: the quantizer's reconstruction; a larger codebook and more codes per image raise it, as the next generation of tokenizers showed. (level 3) A hybrid keeps images continuous and trains a diffusion loss on patches next to the text loss. What does it trade? Expected: no quantizer and higher image fidelity, against two losses on different scales to balance and a diffusion sampling loop at generation time. Where it is taught. The Chameleon lesson sets out the early-fusion thesis and its costs, the cross-attention fusion capstone builds the late-fusion path, and the Emu3 lesson shows what a better quantizer changes. Explain the mechanism In the unified-generation family, the quality of a generated image is said to be capped by the tokenizer, not by the transformer. Explain why, show what moved the cap between two generations of models, and say which design avoids the cap entirely and at what cost. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A discrete image tokenizer is lossy: the decoder can only render what the codes carry, so the best image the model can ever produce is the tokenizer's own reconstruction of a real image. The first shared-vocabulary model used 1024 codes per 512 by 512 image from a codebook of 8192 and reconstructed at about 26 to 28 dB; the next generation used four times the codes, 4096, and a codebook four times larger, 32768, and reached 30.5 dB, close to the 32 dB of continuous latent diffusion. The design that avoids the cap keeps image patches continuous and trains a diffusion loss on them next to the text loss in one transformer; it drops the quantizer and gains fidelity, and pays with two losses on different scales to balance and a sampling loop at generation time. Why the cap exists. The transformer predicts codes. The decoder turns codes into pixels with no other input. Whatever detail the quantizer threw away at encoding time cannot come back: a perfect transformer that predicts the exact codes of a real image renders the tokenizer's reconstruction of that image, nothing better. The reconstruction quality is therefore an upper bound on fidelity to a real image, which is what the dB figures below measure. Distribution metrics measure a different property and do not share this bound. What moved the cap. Model generation Codes per 512 by 512 image Codebook Reconstruction the first shared-vocabulary model 1024 8192 about 26 to 28 dB the next-token generation model 4096 32768 30.5 dB continuous latent diffusion, for reference continuous none about 32 dB Four times the codes carry four times the spatial detail, and a codebook four times larger carries finer values per code. The newer model's main contribution is a better tokenizer, and with it next-token prediction matched a diffusion model on an image generation benchmark. The cost of more codes. Each code is one decode pass in plain next-token generation, so four times the codes is four times the generation time. Masked parallel decoding keeps discrete codes and predicts all masked positions at once in about 16 passes, which pays back the cost of the larger grid. The design without a cap. Keep the image continuous. Project patches with a linear layer, as a vision transformer does at its input, and train one transformer with two losses: cross-entropy on text tokens and a flow-matching loss on noisy image patches. There is no quantizer to bound the detail. The paper reports a better image score than a same-size discrete model by 3 to 5 points. The price: two losses of different magnitude whose weights need tuning, a block-triangular attention mask, and a denoising loop of a few dozen steps per image at generation time. Which to pick. Discrete codes when one next-token stack must handle understanding and the generation of images and video with one loss, and you accept the tokenizer's ceiling. Continuous patches when image fidelity is the priority and the two-loss plumbing is acceptable. Plausible wrong answers. "Scale the transformer and the images get sharper." The transformer predicts codes; sharpness beyond the tokenizer's reconstruction does not exist in the codes to predict. "A bigger codebook is enough." The code count sets the spatial detail and the codebook sets the value detail; the newer tokenizer raised both, and the quantizer design decides whether a large codebook is used. "Continuous patches are strictly better, so discrete codes are obsolete." Continuous patches cost two losses to balance and a denoising loop per image; the discrete family keeps one loss and one decoder for every modality, which is why both survive. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is the reconstruction score of the tokenizer the right number to read before you train the transformer? Expected: it is the ceiling; no amount of transformer scale lifts a generated image above what the decoder can render from the codes. (level 3) What else besides the codebook and the code count lifts a tokenizer? Expected: the quantizer design; the newer models use an inverse-bottleneck quantizer family that uses the larger codebook well, where a naive larger codebook leaves codes unused. (level 4) How does the attention mask differ in the continuous design? Expected: causal over text tokens, bidirectional among the patches of one image, text attends to images that closed before it, and image patches attend to the preceding text; a block-triangular mask. (level 4) Which side of this trade-off does the masked discrete design sit on? Expected: discrete, with the tokenizer ceiling, but with parallel decoding in a few passes; it trades the fidelity of continuous diffusion for simpler training and fast sampling. Where it is taught. The Chameleon lesson names the tokenizer as the reconstruction ceiling, the Emu3 lesson shows how a better tokenizer moved it, and the Transfusion lesson gives the continuous design and its costs. Describe the 3D video tokenizer: what a spatiotemporal VQ codebook looks like, why patches span time. Compare Emu3 vs Stable Diffusion XL on (training compute, inference cost, quality ceiling). Name Emu3's released checkpoints: Emu3-Stage1 (pretrained), Emu3-Gen (post-trained for generation), Emu3-Chat (post-trained for understanding), and the vision tokenizer. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 11 (Chameleon) Type : Learn. Time : about 120 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, 3D video tokenizer math + autoregressive sampler skeleton). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line BAAI's Emu3 (Wang et al., September 2024) is the 2024 result that should have ended the diffusion-versus-autoregressive debate. A single Llama-style decoder-only transformer, trained only on the next-token-prediction objective, across a unified vocabulary of text + VQ image tokens + 3D VQ video tokens, matches or beats SDXL on most image-generation benchmarks and trades wins with LLaVA-1.6 on perception. No CLIP loss. No diffusion schedule. Classifier-free guidance is used at inference for quality, but the core training objective is next-token prediction with teacher forcin Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Next-token prediction "NTP" Standard autoregressive loss: predict token[i+1] given token[0..i]; works for every modality when tokenized SBER-MoVQGAN "The tokenizer base" A VQGAN-family image tokenizer; Emu3 extends it with 3D convolutions for video and a 32,768-entry codebook 3D VQ "Spatiotemporal quantizer" Codebook indexed by (time, row, col); one token covers 4 frames x 8x8 pixels Classifier-free guidance "CFG" Mix conditional and unconditional logits with weight gamma; boosts image quality at inference Unified vocabulary "Shared tokens" Text + image + video all draw from the same integer space; model predicts whichever modality comes next GenEval "Image gen benchmark" Object-focused prompts checked by a detector (counts, colours, positions); Emu3 0.54, SDXL 0.55 The problem In plain words first Chameleon showed that images can be tokens in a language model's vocabulary. Emu3 (BAAI, September 2024) pushes the idea to its limit: one 8B transformer, trained with nothing but next-token prediction, that writes text, generates images and generates short videos. There is no diffusion model and no separate image encoder for understanding. Its quality comes from a stronger image tokenizer: 4,096 codes from a 32,768-entry codebook for a 512×512 image, and a 3D version for video. It also borrows one trick from diffusion: classifier-free guidance, which runs the model with and without the prompt and exaggerates the difference. This lesson covers the tokenizer, the single loss, guidance and the honest benchmark picture. It runs the real Emu3 tokenizer code (random weights) and classifier-free guidance on a small local model. No model is trained. The conventional wisdom through 2024: image generation needs diffusion. The argument: discrete image tokens lose too much information to reconstruct detail, and autoregressive sampling accumulates error across thousands of tokens. Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 3, Imagen, Midjourney all use some form of diffusion. Chameleon (Lesson 12.11) partially disproved this at small scale but did not match SDXL on quality. Emu3 attacked the argument head-on. The claim: better visual tokenizer + enough scale + next-token loss = diffusion-beating image generation in the same model that also does perception. The bet was controversial when it published. Two years on, the open-source unified-generation family (Emu3, Show-o, Janus-Pro, Transfusion) is the default path for research; production frontier models appear to use some variant. Idea 1 · The Emu3 tokenizer The key ingredient is the visual tokenizer. Emu3 trains its own tokenizer on top of SBER-MoVQGAN (270M parameters), adding 3D convolutions for video. It compresses 8×8 in space and 4× in time: a 512x512 image becomes 64x64 = 4096 tokens from a codebook of 32,768. This is larger than Chameleon's 1024 tokens per 512x512 at K=8192 on both axes: four times the tokens and a codebook four times as large. The extra capacity buys reconstruction quality and finer detail, at four times the sequence length. For video: the same tokenizer encodes a spatiotemporal block (4 frames x 8x8 pixels) to one integer, so a 4×512×512 clip is also 4,096 tokens. A 4 s clip at 8 FPS has 32 frames; at 256x256 the token count is (256/8) * (256/8) * (32/4) = 32 * 32 * 8 = 8,192 tokens. Emu3 natively generates 5-second clips at 24 FPS, and its video training stage used a context of 131,072 tokens. Tokenizer quality is the ceiling. Emu3's contribution is partly "we trained a very good tokenizer." Idea 2 · Single-loss training Emu3 uses one objective: next-token prediction on a shared vocabulary across text tokens, image tokens and video tokens. The loss function is identical for every token; the data mixture decides what the model learns to produce. Train on a mix of: - Image gen: <text caption> <image> image_tokens </image> - Image perception: <image> image_tokens </image> <question> text_tokens - Video gen: <text caption> <video> video_tokens </video> - Video perception: analogous. - Text only: standard NTP. The model learns when to emit image tokens vs text tokens from the data distribution. Generation emerges from the model predicting image tokens after the <image> tag. Idea 3 · Classifier-free guidance and temperature Autoregressive image generation gets much better with classifier-free guidance (CFG) at inference. Emu3 uses it: run the model with the prompt and with a negative or empty prompt, and push the logits away from the unconditional ones by a guidance weight. The paper evaluates with a scale of 5.0 to 5.5; the released Emu3-Gen example uses 3.0. This is the same CFG trick diffusion uses, borrowed to the autoregressive setting (measured below on a small text model). Sampling matters: the released example samples with top-k 2048 rather than greedy decoding, since greedy image tokens tend to give flat, repetitive images. The same idea as a formula Tokens per image or clip with 8×8 spatial and 4× temporal compression: F ​ ⌉ ⋅ 8 H ​ ⋅ 8 W ​ ( F = 1 for an image ) . Classifier-free guidance on logits. Cost. Each generated token needs both ​ and ​ : two forward passes (or a batch of two) per token, so a 4,096-token image costs about 8,192 token evaluations. With guidance, each step evaluates the model twice, so the batch is doubled; the wall-clock time stays similar if the GPU has spare capacity. Five seconds of 512×512 video at 24 FPS: temporal steps × 4,096 = 122,880 tokens, which is why the video stage needed a 131,072-token context. That is part of every generated image's cost: the decoder must run once to draw the pixels. 8 × 8 pixels per code. The 256 × 256 photo becomes a 32 × 32 grid of 1,024 codes. On a GPU this is milliseconds, but it shows that the tokenizer is a real network, not a lookup. Video shares the budget. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Without the caption (w = 0), the model guesses. "red" gets 5.5%, behind "a" and "black", and the distribution is wide (entropy 4.84 nats). Plain conditioning (w = 1) helps but stays loose. "red" rises to 38% and becomes the top token, but much probability is still spread over continuations like "a" and "dark". Moderate guidance (w = 3 to 5) makes the prompt decisive. "red" reaches 93% and then 95%, and the entropy falls below 0.5. This is why autoregressive image models use guidance: each image token sticks closely to what the caption implies, and the image follows the prompt. Too much guidance distorts. At w = 10, "red" falls back to 83%, and "sea" and "blood" climb into the top three. Extreme guidance amplifies every difference between the two contexts, including irrelevant ones such as the word "sea" in the caption. In images this shows up as oversaturated colours and artefacts. The paper's scales of 5.0–5.5 and the release's 3.0 sit in the useful range for Emu3. The cost is two passes. Every token needs the conditional and the unconditional logits. Idea 4 · Three roles, one model Emu3 is released as several checkpoints that share one architecture and one pretraining run: Emu3-Stage1. The pretrained model: captions images and generates 512x512 images. Emu3-Gen. Post-trained for image and video generation (quality fine-tuning and DPO). Emu3-Chat. Post-trained for vision-language understanding. Emu3-VisionTokenizer. Encodes and decodes images and video frames. No task-specific heads: the architecture is the same, and only the post-training data differs. Idea 5 · Benchmarks From Emu3 paper (September 2024): Image generation: GenEval overall 0.54 against SDXL's 0.55 (0.66 with a prompt rewriter); DPG-Bench 80.6 against 74.65 (81.6 after DPO); ahead of SDXL on T2I-CompBench colour, shape and texture when prompts are rewritten. Image perception: trails LLaVA-1.6 on VQAv2 (75.1 vs 81.8) and MMMU (31.6 vs 35.1), but beats it on SEED-Bench, OCRBench, and ChartQA. Video generation: 5-second clips at 24 FPS, compared in the paper against video diffusion models on VBench. The numbers are not always winning — Emu3 trades a point here for a point there — but the claim "next-token prediction is all you need" is defensible across modalities. Idea 6 · Compute cost Emu3 is an 8B-parameter model. The paper does not publish a GPU-hour total; for scale, Llama-2-7B pretraining used about 184k A100 GPU-hours, roughly 21 GPU-years. Diffusion models like Stable Diffusion 3 train in similar budgets but need separate text encoders and more complex pipelines. At inference, Emu3 is slower than SDXL per image: 4096 image tokens at 30 tok/s is ~2 minutes per 512x512 image, vs 2-5 seconds for SDXL. Speculative decoding and KV-cache optimization narrow the gap but do not close it. Autoregressive image gen is compute-heavy; this is the standing trade-off. Idea 7 · Why it matters Emu3's deep contribution is conceptual. If next-token prediction scales to match diffusion on image generation, the unified-model path (one loss, one backbone, any modality) is viable. Future models do not need separate text encoders, separate diffusion schedulers, separate VAEs. One transformer, one tokenizer per modality, scale. Show-o, Janus-Pro, and InternVL-U all build on or challenge this thesis, several of them by adding diffusion back for image quality (Lessons 12.13–12.15). Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py builds two toy pieces: A 2D vs 3D VQ tokenizer count calculator: given (resolution, patch, clip_length, FPS), compute token counts for image vs video. An autoregressive image-token sampler with classifier-free guidance at temperature. The CFG implementation matches Emu3's recipe — mix conditional and unconditional logits with a guidance weight. Break it on purpose To speed up Emu3-style generation you drop classifier-free guidance (w = 1) and switch to greedy decoding. What do the images look like, and why? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Autoregressive image generation keeps improving : Janus-Pro (Lesson 12.15), Lumina-mGPT, Infinity and next-scale methods (VAR) cut the token count or the number of sequential steps. Emu3.5 (BAAI, 2025) extends the line to world modelling over long interleaved vision-language sequences, with a faster parallel decoding scheme for images. Hybrids dominate quality leaderboards : transformers that predict text autoregressively and images with diffusion or flow matching (Transfusion, Lesson 12.13; BAGEL; InternVL-U). Laptop reality : Emu3's 8B model needs about 16 GB in bf16 and minutes per image; on an 8 GB GPU it needs 4-bit quantization and is slow. Small diffusion models remain the practical local choice for image generation. Solutions Solution P1 · Sharper up to a point, then strange P(red) goes from 5.5% with no caption (w = 0) to 38% with plain conditioning (w = 1), 93% at w = 3 and 95% at w = 5. At w = 10 it drops back to 83%, and odd tokens ("sea", "blood") enter the top three. Guidance amplifies what the caption changes, the useful parts and the incidental ones alike. Past a sweet spot it distorts the distribution instead of sharpening it. Solution B1 · Flat, repetitive, off-prompt images Without guidance, each image token is sampled from the plain conditional distribution. The run above shows how loose that is: the caption's most important attribute got only 38%. Over 4,096 tokens the image drifts from the prompt: wrong colours, missing objects, weak composition. Greedy decoding makes it worse in a different way. Always taking the single most likely code favours the most common, smooth textures, so images come out flat, blurry and repetitive, with large uniform regions and repeated patches. It is the image version of a language model repeating itself under greedy decoding. Emu3's release samples with top-k 2048 and uses a guidance scale of 3. To speed up generation, cut tokens (lower resolution) or use faster decoding methods instead of removing guidance and sampling. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Estimate it A unified next-token model generates a 512 by 512 image as a sequence of discrete codes. Estimate how long one image takes at a typical decode speed, compare it with a diffusion model, and say what a four-second video clip at low resolution costs in codes. Then name the levers that change the answer. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The reference model's tokenizer reduces 8 by 8 pixels to one code, so a 512 by 512 image is 4096 codes; at about 30 codes per second that is about 2 minutes per image, against 2 to 5 seconds for a diffusion model of the same quality tier. A 4-second clip at 8 frames per second is 32 frames; with the same 8 times spatial reduction and a 4-frame temporal reduction, a 256 by 256 clip is 32 times 32 times 8, which is 8,192 codes. The levers are the codes per image, the decode speed through speculative decoding or the KV cache, and a different decoding scheme such as masked parallel decoding, which needs about 16 passes instead of one pass per code. The image. Copy A diffusion model samples a continuous latent in a few dozen steps and finishes in 2 to 5 seconds. Autoregressive image generation is compute-heavy by construction: one pass per code. The video. The video tokenizer is three-dimensional: one code covers 4 frames by 8 by 8 pixels. Copy Why the model pays this price. The same weights do image generation, image understanding and video with one next-token loss, no diffusion schedule and no separate text encoder. The tokenizer's quality is the ceiling: the reference reports a reconstruction of 30.5 dB against about 32 for a continuous latent space, with four times the codes and four times the codebook of the earlier early-fusion model. The inference knobs. Classifier-free guidance: generate with and without the caption and mix the logits with a weight, typically 3.0 to 7.0; it doubles the forward passes per code. Temperature: 0.8 for image generation and 1.0 for understanding in the reference recipe. Speculative decoding narrows the gap to diffusion, and so does the KV cache, but neither closes it. A different decoding scheme. Masked parallel decoding keeps discrete codes but predicts all masked positions at once and commits the most confident ones, in about 16 passes for an image, against about 20 for continuous diffusion and one pass per code for plain next-token generation. Plausible wrong answers. "An image is a few hundred tokens, like a VLM input." Those are projected encoder tokens for understanding; generation needs discrete codes at the tokenizer's density, 4096 for this image size. "Diffusion is slower because it iterates." Diffusion takes a few dozen passes over all pixels at once; next-token generation takes one pass per code, thousands per image. "A larger codebook makes generation faster." It raises the reconstruction quality; the pass count is set by the number of codes, not by the codebook size. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does guidance double the cost? Expected: each step needs a conditional and an unconditional forward pass to mix. (level 2) What happens to the per-image time at 1024 by 1024? Expected: four times the codes at the same reduction, so about four times the decode time; the lesson's exercise asks for that count. (level 3) Where does the quality ceiling of this model sit, and what moved it up from the first shared-vocabulary model? Expected: in the tokenizer's reconstruction; four times the codes per image and a four times larger codebook lifted it to 30.5 dB. (level 3) When do you still pick this over a diffusion model? Expected: when one model must understand and generate across image, video and text with one loss, and the latency budget allows minutes per image or a batch pipeline. Where it is taught. Explain why bidirectional attention across image patches plus causal attention over text tokens is the right mask choice. Compare Transfusion-style (continuous images, diffusion loss) to Chameleon-style (discrete images, NTP) on compute, quality, and code complexity. Name MMDiT's contribution: modality-specific weights at each block, joint attention at the residual stream. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 11 (Chameleon), Phase 8 (Generative AI) Type : Build. Time : about 180 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, two-loss trainer on MNIST-scale toy). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Chameleon and Emu3 bet everything on discrete tokens. They work, but the quantization bottleneck is visible — the image quality plateaus below continuous-space diffusion models. Transfusion (Meta, Zhou et al., August 2024) takes the opposite bet: keep images continuous, drop the discrete codebook, and train one transformer with two losses. Text tokens get next-token-prediction. Image patches get a diffusion loss. Both objectives optimize the same weights. The architecture underlying Stable Diffusion 3 (MMD Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Two-loss training "NTP + diffusion" A single transformer optimizes both cross-entropy on text tokens and MSE on continuous image patches in the same gradient step Flow matching "Rectified flow" Diffusion variant that predicts a velocity field from noise to clean data; simpler math than DDPM MMDiT "Multimodal DiT" Stable Diffusion 3's architecture: joint attention, modality-specific MLPs and norms Block-triangular mask "Causal text + bidirectional image" Attention mask that is causal across text but bidirectional within image regions Continuous image representation "No VQ" Image patches as real-valued vectors, not integer codebook indices Velocity prediction "v-parameterization" Network output is the velocity field between noise and data, not the noise itself The problem In plain words first Chameleon and Emu3 turn images into discrete codes, and the codebook limits how good the images can be. Transfusion (Meta, August 2024) keeps images continuous. A pretrained autoencoder (VAE) compresses each image into a small grid of numbers, and one transformer reads text and image patches in the same sequence. It is trained with two losses at once: next-token prediction on the text, and a diffusion loss on the image patches. The diffusion loss means: add noise to the image, then learn to predict the noise. A special attention mask lets the patches of one image see each other in both directions, while text stays left-to-right. This lesson explains the mask, the two losses, the comparison with SD3's MMDiT and the measured advantage over Chameleon. It runs a miniature Transfusion forward pass with both losses and checks the diffusion arithmetic. No model is trained. The discrete vs continuous image tokens debate is older than LLMs. Continuous representations (raw pixels, VAE latents) preserve detail. Discrete tokens (VQ indices) fit the transformer's native vocabulary but lose detail at the quantization step. Chameleon / Emu3 went discrete: one loss, one architecture, but image fidelity capped by tokenizer quality. Diffusion models went continuous: exceptional image quality, but a separate model from the LLM, complex noise-schedule engineering, and no clean integration with text generation. Transfusion asks: can we have both? Keep images continuous, still train one model, use two losses stitched into one gradient step. Idea 1 · The two-loss architecture A single decoder-only transformer processes a sequence that contains: Text tokens (discrete, from BPE vocab). Image patches (continuous). Each image is first encoded by a pretrained VAE (86M parameters) into a latent grid: a 256x256 image becomes 32x32 latent positions with 8 channels. Groups of 2x2 latent positions (16x16 pixels) are embedded by a linear layer, or larger groups by U-Net down-blocks. <image> and </image> tags marking where continuous patches live. Forward pass runs once. The loss picks one of two heads per token: For text tokens: standard cross-entropy on the vocab-logits head. For image patches: diffusion loss on continuous patches — predict the noise that was added to each patch. The gradient flows through the shared transformer body. Both losses improve the shared weights simultaneously. Idea 2 · Attention mask: causal text + bidirectional image Text tokens must be causal — you cannot let a text token attend to future text, or teacher forcing breaks. Image patches, however, represent one snapshot; they should attend to each other bidirectionally within the same image block. The mask: Copy Implemented as a block-triangular mask at training and inference. Transfusion uses noise (ε) prediction with a cosine noise schedule over 1,000 timesteps. Idea 4 · MMDiT: Stable Diffusion 3's variant Stable Diffusion 3 (Esser et al., March 2024) shipped MMDiT (Multimodal Diffusion Transformer) around the same time as Transfusion. The architectures are siblings. MMDiT's key differences: Modality-specific weights per block. Each transformer block has separate Q, K, V, and MLP weights for text tokens vs image patches. Attention is joint (cross-modality); everything else is modality-specific. Rectified flow training. A specific flow-matching variant with known sampling and simpler math than DDPM. Scale. MMDiT is the backbone for SD3 (2B and 8B param variants). Transfusion's paper scales to 7B. Both converge on the same core idea: one transformer runs NTP on text and diffusion on continuous image representations. Idea 5 · Why this beats Chameleon-style The quality gap between continuous diffusion and discrete next-token prediction is measurable. The Transfusion paper's controlled comparison against a Chameleon-style model trained on the same data reports: FID parity with Chameleon at about 34 times less compute; at 7B, FID 16.8 against Chameleon's 29.6. It also reaches Chameleon's image-captioning quality with about a fifth of the compute. No discrete tokenizer: images stay as continuous VAE latents, embedded by a linear layer or small U-Net blocks. With U-Net blocks an image can be compressed to just 16 patches with relatively small quality loss. Inference can parallelize image patch denoising, unlike autoregressive image tokens. Downside: Transfusion is a dual-loss model, making training dynamics trickier. Loss weights need tuning. Schedule mismatch between NTP and diffusion can cause one head to dominate. Idea 6 · What sits downstream Janus-Pro (Lesson 12.15) takes a different route: it decouples the vision encoder for understanding (SigLIP) from the one for generation (a VQ tokenizer) while sharing the transformer body, and generates images autoregressively. Show-o (Lesson 12.14) swaps diffusion for discrete diffusion (masked prediction). The unified-generation family branches rapidly after Transfusion. Closed production models that emit images natively may use some descendant of this family, but their architectures are not published, so treat any such claim as a guess. Images are 4x4 grids of bytes. A pair of shared-weight linear projections acts as the transformer stand-in; NTP loss on text, MSE loss on noisy patches. Training loop alternates the two losses, attention mask is explicit. A mask demo prints the block-triangular attention pattern for a text, image, text sequence. Generation is not run: a real sampler would decode text token by token, then denoise the image patches over many steps, as the exercises below count. The transformer is a toy. The two-loss plumbing, attention mask construction, and inference loop are the real artifacts. Flow matching replaced DDPM in most new image generators (SD3, FLUX), including diffusion heads on LLMs. Few-step sampling : distillation and consistency methods cut 250 steps to a handful, which matters more for unified models than for text. Laptop reality : these models are 7B and up; on an 8 GB GPU, run small diffusion models (SD 1.5/SDXL-class with optimisations) or quantized unified models, and expect seconds to minutes per image. Solution B1 · Images stop improving while text looks fine With λ = 0.05 the diffusion term is 100 times weaker than in the paper. The image patches still flow through the model, but the shared weights are tuned almost entirely for text. Text perplexity looks healthy, perhaps slightly better. Image quality stalls: samples stay blurry or off-prompt, and FID barely moves as training continues. You would notice it in the loss curves: the diffusion loss flattens early while the LM loss keeps falling. Explain the mechanism Explain how a single transformer can train the text objective of next-token prediction together with a denoising loss on images in one gradient step. Cover the input representation, the attention mask, how the loss is routed per position, and the balance problem that follows. Then say what a sibling architecture changed. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Text enters as discrete tokens through the embedding table; images enter as continuous 16 by 16 pixel patches through a linear projection, bracketed by image start and end tags. One forward pass runs over the mixed sequence, and the loss is picked per position: cross-entropy on the vocabulary head for text positions, and a flow-matching regression for image patches, which predicts the velocity from a noised patch toward the clean one at a sampled time. The mask is block-triangular, causal over text and bidirectional among the patches of one image, with text attending to images that closed before it and patches attending to the preceding text. Both losses backpropagate through the same weights, so their relative magnitude must be balanced by hand; the sibling architecture keeps the joint attention but gives text and image their own weights in every block. The input. Two kinds of positions in one sequence. A text position holds a token id and goes through the embedding table. An image position holds a real-valued patch vector, projected into the hidden size by a linear layer, the way a vision transformer embeds its input. Tags mark where an image starts and ends. The mask. Copy Teacher forcing on text requires the causal part. An image is one snapshot, so its patches may all see each other. The loss per position. Text: the cross-entropy of the vocabulary head against the next token. Image: sample a time t, interpolate between the clean patch and noise with weight t, feed the noisy patch, and regress the velocity, the noise minus the clean patch, with a mean squared error. Both terms add into one loss and one backward pass; the shared body receives both gradients. Generation. Text decodes token by token. When the model emits the image start tag, generation switches to a denoising loop over the image patches, conditioned on the text so far, for a few dozen steps, then returns to text. The balancing problem. The two losses live on different scales. The lesson's exercise poses a mix of 70 percent text and 30 percent image positions where the image loss is about ten times the text loss in magnitude; without weights, one head dominates the shared gradient. The weights, and any mismatch in schedules between the two objectives, are a search of their own, which is the price of avoiding a quantizer. The reward is image quality above a discrete model of the same size, by 3 to 5 points on the standard image score in the paper. The sibling. The multimodal diffusion transformer behind a well-known image generator keeps the joint attention across modalities but gives text and image their own query, key, value and MLP weights in every block, trains with rectified flow, and ships in 2B and 8B parameter variants. Separate weights remove some of the balancing pressure at the cost of more parameters. Where it sits. Discrete-code designs trade this plumbing for one loss and a tokenizer ceiling; the masked discrete design keeps one loss and parallel decoding. This design is the pick when fidelity is paramount and the two-loss recipe is acceptable. Plausible wrong answers. "One transformer can only have one loss." The loss is a function of the outputs per position; routing a different loss to different positions is one summed objective with one backward pass. "Use a causal mask everywhere for simplicity." Causal attention inside an image hides part of each image from its own patches and hurts generation; the mask must be bidirectional inside an image block. "The two losses balance themselves because they share the weights." Shared weights are the problem: the larger loss dominates the shared gradient until you weight them. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why may image patches attend bidirectionally when text may not? Expected: text is generated left to right under teacher forcing, so a token must not see its target; an image is produced as one snapshot, and its patches have no order. (level 4) How would you set the loss weights? Expected: measure the magnitude and the gradient norm of each loss on a held-out batch, scale them to comparable contributions, and tune from there against a text eval and an image eval together, because one can improve while the other regresses. (level 4) What does the sampled time t do in the training loss? Expected: it picks how much noise the patch carries, so the model learns the whole path from noise to clean; at generation each step moves along that path. (level 4) What does the sibling's per-modality weight set cost and buy? Expected: more parameters per block; it buys separate capacity for two very different input statistics and eases the balance, while the joint attention still lets the modalities condition each other. Where it is taught. The Transfusion lesson builds the two-loss trainer and the mask and names its sibling design, and the Show-o lesson places it against the discrete designs. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Transfusion mixes continuous and discrete representations. Show-o (Xie et al., August 2024) goes the other way: text tokens use causal next-token prediction, image tokens use masked discrete diffusion in the spirit of MaskGIT. Both sit inside one transformer with a hybrid attention mask. The result unifies VQA, text-to-image, inpainting, and mixed-modality generation on one backbone, one tokenizer per modality, one loss formulation (next-token extended to masked prediction). This lesson walks the Show-o design — why masked discrete diffusion is Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Masked discrete diffusion "MaskGIT-style" Training to predict masked tokens; at inference, iteratively unmask the most-confident predictions Cosine schedule "Unmask schedule" Decay of mask ratio over inference steps; concentrates confidence growth at mid-range Parallel decoding "All tokens at once" Every step predicts the full sequence of masked tokens in one forward pass, then commits top-K Hybrid attention "Causal + bidirectional" Mask that is causal over text tokens and bidirectional within image blocks Inpainting "Fill-in generation" Condition on an image with some tokens masked, predict the missing ones; free from the training objective Commitment rate "Top-K per step" How many tokens are declared "done" per iteration; controls inference vs quality trade-off The problem In plain words first Generating an image one code at a time, as Chameleon does, takes hundreds or thousands of steps. Show-o (August 2024) borrows a faster trick from MaskGIT. Start with an image made entirely of "blank" [MASK] tokens. Predict every blank at once, keep the predictions the model is most sure about, blank the rest again, and repeat. A 256-code image is done in about 16 rounds instead of 256. Show-o does this inside one transformer that also reads and writes text normally, left to right. The attention mask lets image tokens see each other in every direction while text stays causal. One model then answers questions about images, generates images, and fills in masked regions (inpainting). This lesson explains masked prediction, the mask, the two losses and the sampling schedule. It checks a working sampler loop and a miniature training step. No model is trained. Transfusion's two-loss training works but has trickier dynamics — the continuous diffusion loss lives on a different numerical scale from the discrete NTP loss. Balancing loss weights is a hyperparameter search. The architecture is effective but complex. Show-o's answer: keep both modalities discrete (like Chameleon), but generate images in parallel via masked discrete diffusion instead of sequentially. The training objective becomes a single masked-token-prediction that generalizes next-token-prediction naturally. Idea 1 · Masked discrete diffusion (MaskGIT) The original Chang et al. (2022) MaskGIT trick is elegant. Start from a fully-masked image (every token is the special <MASK> id). At each step, predict all masked tokens in parallel, then keep the top-K most confident predictions and re-mask the rest. After ~8-16 iterations, all tokens are filled in. The schedule of how many tokens to unmask per step is tuned — cosine schedules work well. Training is simple: draw a masking ratio from the cosine schedule (so every level from a few masked tokens to all of them is seen), apply it to the image's VQ tokens, and train the transformer to recover the masked ones. Exactly what BERT did for text, scaled to image generation. Idea 2 · Show-o: one transformer, hybrid mask Show-o puts MaskGIT inside a causal-language-model transformer. The attention mask is: Text tokens: causal (standard LLM). Image tokens: full bidirectional within the image block (so the masked tokens can see every other image token during prediction). Text-to-image: text attends to prior images, image attends to prior text. Training alternates between: 1. Standard NTP on text sequences. 2. T2I samples: text → image with masked image tokens, masked-token-prediction loss. 3. VQA samples: image → text with masked text tokens (really just NTP). Show-o uses two cross-entropy losses over one vocabulary: mask token prediction (MTP) on the masked image tokens, and next token prediction (NTP) on text, combined as ​ + α L NTP ​ . The base model is Phi-1.5 (1.3B), and images are tokenized MAGVIT-v2-style with a lookup-free quantizer: a 256×256 image becomes 16×16 = 256 codes from 8,192. Idea 3 · Parallel sampling Show-o generates an image in a small number of parallel steps instead of one step per token. The paper shows samples at 2, 8 and 16 steps (quality rises with steps), against 256 sequential steps for an autoregressive model at the same resolution. At each step, predict all masked tokens in parallel; commit the most confident; repeat. Compare: - Chameleon / Emu3 (autoregressive over tokens): N_tokens forward passes, typically 1024-4096 per image. - Transfusion (continuous diffusion): 250 denoising steps in the paper (fewer with modern samplers), each a full transformer pass over all patches. - Show-o (masked discrete diffusion): a handful to a few dozen steps (16 in the paper's examples), each a full transformer pass. Show-o needs far fewer forward passes than Chameleon-style decoding at the same resolution (the paper claims roughly 20 times fewer steps). Its images stay limited by the discrete tokenizer, while continuous diffusion can reach higher quality. Idea 4 · Tasks in one checkpoint Show-o supports four tasks at inference, selected by prompt format: Text generation: standard autoregressive text output. VQA: image in, text out. T2I: text in, image out via masked discrete diffusion. Inpainting: image with some tokens masked, fill in. The inpainting capability comes for free from the masked-prediction training. Mask a region of the VQ-token grid, feed the rest plus a text prompt, predict the masked tokens. Idea 5 · Masking schedule The schedule of how many tokens to unmask per step shapes quality. Show-o recommends cosine: π t ​ ) t = 0 , … , T At step 0, all tokens masked (ratio 1.0). At step , none masked. Cosine concentrates mass on mid-range ratios where prediction is most informative. Linear schedules also work but plateau faster. The same idea as a formula Cosine schedule. After step of , the number of image tokens still masked out of is ​ = ⌊ N cos ( 2 π ​ ⋅ T s ​ ) ⌋ , m 0 ​ = N , m T ​ = 0. Few tokens are committed early (when the model knows little) and many late. Confidence selection. At each step, every masked position gets a prediction and a confidence ​ = max k ​ p ( k ∣ visible tokens ) ; the ​ least confident are masked again. With 16 steps the sampler fixes 2, 3, 7, … tokens at first and about 25 per step at the end; with 4 steps, 20, 55, 84 and 97. Early on almost nothing is visible, so the model's guesses are weakest. Committing only a few lets later steps condition on them. Every run ends with no masked tokens left, so the loop always finishes. Confidence ranking does the work. The stand-in predictor is right 75% of the time on average, but more often when confident. Because the sampler keeps the most confident guesses, the final image agrees with the target on 88–90% of tokens, better than the predictor's average. A real model gains more from extra steps, since each step's predictions condition on the tokens committed before. That is why Show-o's samples improve from 2 to 8 to 16 steps. 16 passes instead of 256. Each step is one full forward pass over the whole grid, so a 256-code image costs 16 passes instead of 256 for token-by-token decoding. A step is a little more expensive (the whole grid is processed), but it is far fewer passes in total. Idea 6 · Show-o2 Show-o2 (June 2025, arXiv 2506.15564) changes the recipe rather than only scaling it: images and videos live in a 3D causal VAE latent space (continuous, not discrete codes), text keeps autoregressive prediction on a language head, and images and video are generated by flow matching on a separate flow head. It is built on Qwen2.5 language models (1.5B and 7B). Idea 7 · Where Show-o sits In the 2026 taxonomy: Discrete tokens + NTP: Chameleon, Emu3, LlamaGen, Janus-Pro. Simple but slow inference. Discrete tokens + masked diffusion: Show-o, MaskGIT, Muse. Parallel sampling, still lossy by tokenizer. Continuous + diffusion: Transfusion, MMDiT, DiT. Highest quality, more complex training. Continuous + flow matching in a VLM: JanusFlow, Show-o2, BAGEL, InternVL-U. Newest. Pick by task: Show-o when you want T2I + inpainting + VQA in one open model with reasonable speed; Transfusion when quality is paramount and you can afford the two-loss plumbing. Which is more balanced? A 512x512 Show-o image is 1024 tokens. At vocab , the model emits ​ ( 16384 ) = 14 , 336 bits (~1.75 KiB) of data. Stable Diffusion outputs 512 512 24 bits = 6,291,456 bits (~768 KiB) of raw pixels. What is the compression ratio and what quality does it buy? Read LlamaGen (arXiv:2406.06525). How is LlamaGen's class-conditional autoregressive image model different from Show-o's masked approach? Solutions Solution P1 · 2 tokens first, about 25 at the end 2 tokens in the first step and about 25 in the last. With and , positions stay masked after step 1. In the last steps the curve is steep, and the run committed 23 to 25 tokens per step. The model commits the bulk of the image only when most of it is already visible. Solution B1 · Early guesses lock in and the image falls apart If most tokens are committed in the first step, they are chosen when the model sees nothing but the caption. Each guess is made independently, with no neighbours to agree with, so committed tokens contradict each other: a sky patch next to a grass patch next to half a face. Committed tokens are never revisited, so these mistakes are locked in. The few remaining steps cannot repair a scene whose layout was decided by guesses that ignored each other. The result is incoherent or noisy images, even from a good model. The cosine schedule does the opposite. It commits a few high-confidence tokens first (often the global layout), then fills in more and more, each step conditioned on what is already fixed. This is also why very small step counts (2 steps) give poor images. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design A design tool wants to ship, with open weights it can host, one model that answers questions about a user's image, edits a region of it on request, and generates a new image from text. The latency per image must stay in seconds, not minutes. Lay out the families you would consider, pick one, and state the test that would make you change the pick. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Three open families cover understanding and generation in one model: next-token prediction over discrete codes, which does everything with one loss but spends one pass per code and minutes per image; continuous patches with a diffusion loss next to the text loss, which gives the best fidelity in about 20 passes but trains two losses; and masked discrete decoding, which keeps one loss, fills an image in about 16 passes, and gets region editing free from its masking objective. For a tool that needs editing and a seconds-level latency with open weights, start with the masked discrete family. Change the pick if a fidelity eval on your own prompts shows the quantizer ceiling hurting, or if the latency budget cannot afford sixteen full passes; the continuous two-loss family then takes over, with editing done through conditioned denoising of the region. The requirements, mapped. Requirement Next-token over codes Continuous two-loss Masked discrete Visual question answering yes yes yes Region edit possible, slow: regenerate codes possible through conditioned denoising native: mask the region's codes Text to image yes, minutes per image yes, about 20 passes yes, about 16 passes Training one loss two losses to balance one cross-entropy on masked positions Fidelity ceiling the quantizer, at 30.5 dB in the best reference no quantizer, about 32 dB and above the quantizer Open weights to host yes yes yes Why masked discrete first. Editing is the feature that distinguishes the product, and the masked objective is editing: mask a region, keep the rest, add the prompt, predict. A latency in the low tens of passes fits a seconds budget. One loss means one training recipe to operate. The reference open model ships text generation, question answering, text-to-image and inpainting from one checkpoint. Why not the other two first. Next-token over codes spends thousands of passes per image; the reference puts a 512 by 512 image at about 2 minutes at a typical decode rate, and a region edit means regenerating codes in sequence. The continuous design has the best fidelity and no quantizer ceiling, but two losses on different scales need a weight search, and editing needs a conditioned denoising sampler that you build yourself. The eval that decides. Fidelity: your own prompt set, judged against the continuous reference at matched passes; if the quantizer ceiling shows, as lost fine texture or unreadable text in images, the pick changes. Edit quality: masked region edits judged for seam quality and prompt adherence. Latency at your resolution and pass count on your hardware; sixteen full passes of a large transformer can still exceed a budget. Understanding: the question-answering eval you already run, because the unified model must not fall behind the adapter model it replaces. Operational notes. Keep the tokenizer fixed and version it with the model; a tokenizer change invalidates every stored code. Log the mask schedule and the pass count as deployment parameters, because they trade latency for quality at serve time without retraining. Plausible wrong answers. "Ship the next-token model; one loss, one stack, no compromise." Minutes per image at the reference decode rate breaks the latency requirement, and a region edit regenerates codes in sequence. "Fidelity decides, so take the continuous design." Fidelity is one requirement; editing and operational simplicity favor the masked design until an eval shows the ceiling hurting. "Pick the model with the best benchmark score." The product needs three tasks, an edit path and a latency budget; a benchmark covers one of those at best. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which of the three tasks does the masked objective give for free, and why? Expected: region editing; training predicts masked codes from the rest, which is what an edit asks for. (level 4) How do you do a region edit in the continuous design? Expected: keep the patches outside the region fixed across the denoising steps and denoise only the region, conditioned on the text and the context; it works, but it is a sampler you write, not a training objective. (level 4) Why does the pass count become a serving parameter in the masked design? Expected: more passes commit fewer codes each and raise quality, fewer passes cut latency; the schedule is set at inference, so the product can trade them per request. (level 4) What single measurement tells you that the quantizer is the bottleneck? Expected: the tokenizer's reconstruction of your real images; if the reconstruction already loses the detail your users care about, no generator on those codes can recover it. Where it is taught. The Show-o lesson places the three families and names the tasks one checkpoint covers, the Transfusion lesson gives the continuous design, and the Emu3 lesson gives the per-code cost of next-token generation. Weigh a trade-off Your team needs one open model for answering questions about images, text-to-image generation and inpainting, with a usable generation latency. One candidate generates images one code at a time; another denoises continuous patches; a third stays with discrete codes and fills them in parallel over a few passes. Compare the three on passes, training complexity and what comes for free. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Next-token generation over codes needs one pass per code, 1024 to 4096 passes per image, with one simple loss. Continuous diffusion in a shared transformer needs about 20 passes, but it trains two losses on different scales. Masked discrete decoding keeps codes and one cross-entropy loss, predicts all masked positions at once and commits the most confident ones each pass, so an image takes about 16 passes; inpainting is free, because the training objective is to fill masked codes from the rest. For a product that wants all three tasks in one open model at a usable latency, the masked discrete design is the fit, and the continuous design is the pick when fidelity is paramount. How masked discrete decoding works. Training samples a masking ratio uniformly, masks that share of an image's codes, and trains the transformer to recover them. That generalizes next-token prediction: for text only the last position is masked, for an image a random subset is. At inference, start from a fully masked grid, predict every masked position in parallel, keep the most confident predictions, re-mask the rest, and repeat on a schedule. A cosine schedule, the mask ratio as the cosine of pi times the step over twice the total steps, concentrates the work at mid-range ratios where predictions are most informative. The attention mask. Text tokens are causal. Image codes attend to every other code of the same image, so a masked position can see all of its neighbors. Text attends to prior images, and image codes attend to prior text. The comparison. Design Passes per image Losses Free extras Next-token over codes one per code, 1024 to 4096 one cross-entropy video with a 3D tokenizer; one stack for everything Continuous diffusion in the transformer about 20 cross-entropy plus a diffusion loss on patches the highest fidelity, no quantizer Masked discrete decoding about 16 one cross-entropy on masked positions inpainting; one checkpoint for answering, writing and generating Per pass, the masked design is cheaper than continuous diffusion, because it emits discrete logits rather than a continuous regression at every patch. What the masked design pays. It keeps the tokenizer ceiling of every discrete design: the image can be no better than the quantizer's reconstruction. Unmasking everything in one pass fails, because the codes are predicted independently and the result is incoherent; the schedule exists so that committed codes condition the rest. Inpainting for free. Mask the codes of a region, feed the rest plus a text prompt, and predict the masked ones. No new objective and no new head: the training task was exactly this. Plausible wrong answers. "Masked decoding is diffusion, so it needs a noise schedule." It is discrete: positions are masked, not noised, and the schedule sets how many codes to commit per pass. "Next-token generation is the fastest because each pass is small." Each pass is a full transformer pass over the sequence, and there are thousands of them per image. "Inpainting needs a separate model." The masked objective is inpainting; masking a region at inference is the task the model trained on. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why can the model not unmask everything in one pass? Expected: each masked position is predicted from a marginal that ignores the others, so the sampled codes do not agree; committing the confident ones first gives the rest conditioning. (level 3) Why does a cosine schedule beat a linear one? Expected: it spends more steps at the mid-range ratios where each prediction is most informative, while a linear schedule plateaus earlier. (level 4) Where does the per-step cost differ between masked discrete and continuous diffusion? Expected: both are full transformer passes, but the discrete head emits logits over the codebook while the continuous head regresses a velocity for every patch; the discrete pass is cheaper per step. (level 4) What would make you give up the one-model simplicity for a specialist? Expected: a fidelity requirement above the tokenizer ceiling, or a latency budget that even sixteen full passes cannot meet, where a dedicated continuous generator wins. Where it is taught. The Show-o lesson walks the masked decoding, the schedule and the task list, the Emu3 lesson gives the per-code cost, and the Transfusion lesson gives the continuous alternative.
