Describe Janus-Pro's routing: SigLIP features on the input side for understanding, VQ tokens on both input and output for generation. Trace the data-mix scaling that makes Janus-Pro succeed where Janus did not. Compare decoupled (Janus-Pro), coupled-continuous (Transfusion), and coupled-discrete (Show-o) architectures. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 13 (Transfusion), Phase 12 · 14 (Show-o) Type : Build. Time : about 120 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, dual-encoder routing + shared-body signal). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Unified multimodal models have an unavoidable tension. Understanding wants semantic features — SigLIP or DINOv2 output vectors rich with concept-level information. Generation wants reconstruction-friendly codes — VQ tokens that compose back into crisp pixels. The two goals are not compatible in a single encoder. Janus (DeepSeek, October 2024) and Janus-Pro (DeepSeek, January 2025) argue the fix is to stop trying: decouple the two encoders. Share the transformer body between tasks, but route understanding through SigLIP and genera Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Decoupled encoding "Two visual encoders" Separate tokenizer or encoder per direction: semantic for understanding, reconstruction for generation Shared body "One transformer" Single transformer processes either encoder's output; no modality-specific weights SigLIP for understanding "Semantic features" CLIP-family vision tower providing rich conceptual features but poor reconstruction VQ for generation "Reconstruction codes" Vector-quantized tokens that decode cleanly back to pixels JanusFlow "Rectified-flow variant" Janus-Pro with a continuous flow-matching generation head instead of VQ Path selection "Which encoder" The task picks the path: understood images go through SigLIP, generated images come out as VQ codes from the image head The problem In plain words first A model that both understands and generates images needs two different things from its image encoder. Understanding wants features that capture meaning ("a dog on a sofa"), the kind CLIP-style encoders produce. Generation wants codes that rebuild exact pixels, the kind a VQ tokenizer produces. One encoder is not good at both. Janus (October 2024) and Janus-Pro (January 2025) from DeepSeek use two. A SigLIP encoder reads images for understanding, a VQ tokenizer writes images as codes for generation, and one shared language model sits in the middle. Janus-Pro scales the data and model to 7B and beats DALL-E 3 on the GenEval benchmark. This lesson explains the split and the scaling, and builds the real Janus-Pro 1B and 7B models from their configurations to see where the parameters sit. No model is trained or downloaded. Unified models share a transformer body across understanding and generation. Previous attempts (Chameleon, Show-o, Transfusion) all use one visual tokenizer for both directions. The tokenizer is a compromise: Optimized for reconstruction (generation): VQ-VAE captures fine-grained pixel detail but produces tokens with weak semantic coherence. Optimized for semantics (understanding): SigLIP embeddings group "cat" images near "cat" tokens but do not permit good reconstruction. Show-o and Transfusion pay for this with a visible quality tax on one direction. Janus-Pro asks: why require one tokenizer when the tasks have different needs? Idea 1 · Decoupled visual encoding Janus-Pro's architecture separates the two encoders: Understanding path. Input image → SigLIP-Large (patch 16, 384 px) → 2-layer MLP → transformer body. Generation path. Input image (if conditioning on an existing image) → VQ tokenizer → token IDs → transformer body. Output generation. Image tokens predicted by the transformer → VQ decoder → pixels. The transformer body is shared. Everything upstream and downstream of the body is task-specific. The task decides the path: images given to be understood go through SigLIP and the understanding adaptor; images to be generated are produced as VQ codes (a 16,384-entry codebook, 16× downsampling, 576 codes per 384-px image) by a separate image head, after a begin-of-image marker in the sequence. Idea 2 · Why this works Understanding loss gets SigLIP features, which CLIP-style pretraining has tuned for semantic similarity. The model's perception benchmarks improve over Show-o / Transfusion because the input features are better for the task. Generation loss gets VQ tokens, which a tokenizer has tuned for reconstruction. Image quality improves over Show-o because VQ codes compose back to pixels cleanly. The shared transformer body sees two input distributions (SigLIP and VQ) and learns to work with both. The claim: enough data + enough parameters, the body absorbs the switching. Idea 3 · Data scaling — Janus vs Janus-Pro Janus (original, arXiv 2410.13848) introduced the decoupling but at small scale (1.3B params, limited data). Janus-Pro (arXiv 2501.17811) scaled: Model size: 1B and 7B (DeepSeek-LLM 1.5B and 7B bases) instead of 1.3B. Training: a longer stage 1 on ImageNet, which was enough to learn pixel dependencies with the LLM frozen; stage 2 drops ImageNet for real text-to-image data; the stage-3 data ratio (multimodal : text : text-to-image) moves from 7:3:10 to 5:1:4. Understanding data: about 90M more samples (captions, documents, charts, tables). Generation data: about 72M synthetic aesthetic images, bringing the real-to-synthetic ratio to 1:1. The upshot: Janus-Pro-7B scores 79.2 on MMBench (Janus: 69.4) and 0.80 on GenEval, ahead of DALL-E 3 (0.67) and SD3-Medium (0.74). Its reasoning is still limited by its size: MMMU is 41.0, far below large understanding-only VLMs. One open model, competitive on generation and solid on everyday understanding. Parameters are grouped into the understanding input path (SigLIP and adaptor), the generation path (VQ tokenizer, code embeddings, adaptor and image head) and the shared language model. The token counts per image follow. A few seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Most of Janus-Pro is the language model. In the 7B model the shared DeepSeek-LLM is 6.49B parameters, 93% of 6.99B. Both visual paths together are under 0.5B. Decoupling the encoders makes the architecture more complex but barely changes its size. The understanding path is the larger of the two. SigLIP-Large is 304M parameters plus a 21M adaptor. The generation path is the VQ tokenizer (72M, encoder and decoder), a tiny code embedding, a 17M adaptor and an 84M image head that predicts one of 16,384 codes. The 1B model is shaped differently. With a 1.44B language model, the visual paths are 23% of the total, and SigLIP alone is 16%. Small unified models spend a larger share on vision, as small VLMs do (Lesson 12.7). Both paths see the same 576-token grid. A 384-px image gives 576 SigLIP features in and 576 VQ codes out (24 × 24 at 16 px each). Idea 4 · JanusFlow — the rectified flow variant JanusFlow (arXiv 2411.07975) swaps the VQ generation path for a rectified-flow generation path (continuous). The split becomes SigLIP-for-understanding + rectified-flow-for-generation. Quality ceilings lift further. The architecture remains decoupled-encoders-shared-body. Idea 5 · The shared body's job The transformer body processes a unified sequence but with two input distributions. Its job is to: For understanding: consume SigLIP features + text tokens → emit text autoregressively. For generation: consume text tokens + (optional image VQ tokens) → emit image VQ tokens autoregressively. The body has no modality-specific weights per block. It is the text-style transformer you'd expect to find inside Qwen or Llama, plus the two input adapters. Interestingly, this means Janus-Pro's body can be initialized from a pretrained LLM, and it is: DeepSeek-LLM (1.5B and 7B). That choice matters: the LLM contributes language and reasoning ability that from-scratch unified models struggle to reach. Idea 6 · Compared to InternVL-U InternVL-U (Lesson 12.10, March 2026) is a 4B unified model that pairs an InternVL-style understanding model with an MMDiT-based diffusion head for generation and editing. It keeps the same principle: separate representations for understanding and for generation, one shared language backbone. The idea of using different visual representations for understanding and generation is now common in unified models (BAGEL, for example, uses a ViT for understanding and a VAE for generation). Idea 7 · Limitations Decoupled encoders add architectural complexity. Two tokenizers to train, two input paths to maintain, two sets of fail modes. For products that do not need generation, Janus-Pro is over-engineered — pick a LLaVA-family understanding model. For products that do not need understanding, Janus-Pro is overqualified — pick a Stable Diffusion 3 / Flux model. For products that need both, Janus-Pro is a useful open reference architecture; newer unified models usually add a diffusion or flow head for image quality. Solutions Solution P1 · About 7%, and understanding is larger About 7%: 0.33B for understanding (SigLIP-Large and its adaptor) and 0.17B for generation (VQ tokenizer, code embeddings, adaptor and image head), out of 6.99B. Solution B1 · Meaning without pixels SigLIP vectors encode what an image means, not what it looks like. They are trained to match captions, so two different photos of "a red car" map to similar vectors, and the details that distinguish them (exact shape, lighting, background texture) are mostly discarded. There is no decoder that turns them back into pixels, because SigLIP was never trained to reconstruct. A decoder trained after the fact gets images that are semantically right but blurry, generic and inconsistent in detail. This is the tension Janus resolves: use SigLIP where meaning matters, and a reconstruction-trained tokenizer (VQ codes, or a VAE latent in JanusFlow and BAGEL) where pixels must come out. Some newer work does generate from semantic features by training a dedicated diffusion decoder on them, but that is a second model, not SigLIP itself. Compare SEED-Tokenizer (images) and SpeechTokenizer residual-VQ (speech) on compression + reconstruction trade-offs. Explain the four-stage curriculum that builds up any-to-any generation. Name the three open any-to-any recipes and their main trade-offs: MIO, AnyGPT, Unified-IO 2. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 11 (Chameleon), Phase 6 (Speech and Audio) Type : Learn. Time : about 120 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, four-modality token allocator + streaming decode loop). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line GPT-4o ships a product most open models cannot replicate: an agent that hears voice, sees video, and speaks back in real time. The open-ecosystem answer by late 2024 was MIO (Wang et al., September 2024). MIO tokenizes text, image, speech, and music, trains one causal transformer over the interleaved sequences, and generates any modality to any modality. AnyGPT (Zhan et al., February 2024) was the proof of concept; MIO is the scale-up; Unified-IO 2 (Allen AI, December 2023) is the cousin with vision + action grounding. This lesson reads the a Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Any-to-any "Multimodal in/out" A single model that accepts and emits text, image, speech, and music in any direction Residual-VQ "Speech tokenizer stack" Multi-codebook tokenization where each layer adds information; base layer is content, later layers are prosody SEED-Tokenizer "Image codes" Discrete image tokenizer with an 8192-entry codebook and 32 tokens per image, used by MIO Chain-of-visual-thought "Visual scratchpad" The model generates an intermediate image as a reasoning step before its final answer Time-to-first-audio-byte "TTFAB" Latency from user voice to first audio output; <500ms for conversational feel Four-stage curriculum "Training recipe" Alignment -> interleaved -> speech-enhanced -> SFT, in that order The problem In plain words first An "any-to-any" model takes any mix of text, images and speech as input and can answer in any of them. MIO (September 2024) builds one by turning everything into tokens. Text uses its normal tokenizer. Each image becomes 32 codes from an image tokenizer, and speech becomes codes from a speech tokenizer that stacks several codebooks, coarse to fine (residual vector quantisation). All these codes get their own number ranges in one shared vocabulary, and one transformer, initialised from the Yi-6B language model, is trained to predict the next token whatever it is. This lesson covers the tokenizers, the training curriculum, streaming speech and the latency budget a voice product must meet. It measures residual quantisation on a real audio codec, EnCodec (93 MB), and computes MIO's token budgets. No model is trained. A unified multimodal model is easy to claim and hard to build at scale. Most "any-to-any" systems until 2024 were pipelined: vision model → text representation → speech model → audio. Each hop loses information, adds latency, and complicates training. GPT-4o's demo video showed a single-model alternative with subsecond response; open systems trailed by months. The engineering challenges: Tokenizers must exist for every modality, compress losslessly-enough for reconstruction, and produce tokens at rates the transformer can consume. A single vocabulary must allocate space for text (32k+), image (8k+), speech (4k+), music (8k+). Fifty-thousand-plus entries minimum. Training data must cover every input-output pair (text→image, image→speech, speech→image, etc.) or the model must compose. Inference must stream output tokens fast enough for conversational latency (<500ms time-to-first-audio-byte). Idea 1 · Four tokenizers for four modalities MIO's tokenizer stack: Text: the BPE tokenizer of its base model, Yi-6B (64,000 entries). The toy below uses a 32,000-entry text range. Image: SEED-Tokenizer (2023), a discrete image tokenizer with an 8192-entry codebook that emits 32 tokens per 224x224 image. Speech: SpeechTokenizer residual-VQ (2023), which encodes speech into 8 hierarchical codebooks at 50 frames per second; the first level is coarse content, later levels add prosody and speaker identity. MIO keeps the content level plus the first three timbre levels, 1024 codes each, so 4096 speech IDs and 200 speech tokens per second. Music: similar residual-VQ (Meta's MusicGen / Encodec family), 4-8 codebooks. MIO itself does not ship a music tokenizer (its fourth modality is video, as frames through the image tokenizer); this lesson's toy adds music to show how a new modality claims an ID range. Each modality produces integer tokens. The tokens get disjoint ID ranges in the shared vocabulary: Copy Total: ~52k vocabulary. The input embedding and output projection span all of it. Idea 2 · Streaming decode Speech generation uses residual-VQ. The transformer predicts speech tokens for all kept levels (in MIO, interleaved in the sequence; in designs like Moshi, a small extra transformer predicts the deeper levels for each frame). Each frame is 20 ms of audio at 50 frames per second. The MIO paper makes no streaming or latency claims; the pattern below is how speech LLMs are made to stream in general. The streaming pattern: User speaks into mic; real-time audio tokenizer emits speech tokens every 50ms. MIO consumes tokens as they arrive (prompt prefill + incremental forward). Output tokens stream out as generated; a parallel speech decoder converts them to audio samples with ~50-150ms latency. Time-to-first-audio-byte: the MIO paper reports no latency number. The budget below is an estimate for this design, against GPT-4o's reported 232 ms minimum and 320 ms average response time to audio. Mini-Omni (arXiv:2408.16725), GLM-4-Voice (arXiv:2412.02612), and Moshi (arXiv:2410.00037) are complementary streaming speech-LLM designs. Moshi reports a theoretical latency of 160 ms and about 200 ms in practice on a single GPU. The same idea as a formula Residual vector quantisation. This coarse-to-fine structure is why MIO can keep SpeechTokenizer's first 4 of 8 levels: the content and much of the voice are in the early ones. What the codes look like. That gap is why streaming speech models predict the deeper levels in parallel, use lower frame rates, and start speaking after a few frames. These numbers are assumptions for illustration, not MIO measurements. Idea 3 · Four-stage curriculum MIO's training curriculum: Stage 1 — alignment. Large-scale modality-pair corpora: text-image, text-speech (and video frames with text). Trains the new vocabulary entries. Stage 2 — interleaved. Multi-modality interleaved documents (blogs with images + video, podcasts with transcripts, etc.). Trains cross-modality context. Stage 3 — speech-enhanced. Speech's share of training tokens rises across the three pretraining stages, from 12.5% to 37.5% to 75%, to lift speech quality without losing text capability. Stage 4 — SFT. Instruction tuning across modalities: VQA, captioning, narration, speech-to-speech dialogue. Missing a stage degrades specific capabilities: skip stage 2 and the model loses cross-modality context; skip stage 3 and speech is poor. Idea 4 · Chain-of-visual-thought MIO introduces chain-of-visual-thought: the model emits intermediate image tokens as a reasoning step. For "is the cat climbing a tree?" the model: Emits <image> tokens rendering the scene (from the input image or a sketch). Emits text analyzing the sketch. Emits the final answer. The rendered intermediate image serves as a scratchpad. The MIO paper presents this as an emergent ability with qualitative examples, not benchmark results. The idea mirrors chain-of-thought for text reasoning. Idea 5 · Competitors in any-to-any AnyGPT (arXiv:2402.12226): 4 modalities (text, image, speech, music), similar design. Unified-IO 2 (arXiv:2312.17172): adds vision action outputs, depth, normals. More task diversity, smaller scale. NExT-GPT (arXiv:2309.05519): LLM + modality-specific diffusion decoders. Not a single-model approach. CoDi (arXiv:2305.11846): composable diffusion; any-to-any via shared latent. MIO is the closest to pure-token any-to-any. AnyGPT is its conceptual ancestor. Idea 6 · Latency budget For a conversational product, every component's latency matters: Mic to audio tokens: ~50ms. Prefill (audio tokens + history): ~100ms on an 8B model. First output token: ~50ms. Parallel residual-VQ + speech decoder: ~100-150ms. Total time-to-first-audio-byte: roughly 300 ms at best for this design. GPT-4o reports as little as 232 ms (320 ms on average); Moshi 160 ms in theory, about 200 ms in practice. Neither MIO nor AnyGPT publishes a measured figure, so treat this budget as an estimate, not a benchmark. Idea 7 · Why any-to-any stays hard Even in 2026, open any-to-any models trail closed ones on two axes: Speech quality. The residual-VQ tokenizer is lossy; conversational speech sounds robotic compared to ElevenLabs-class voices. Cross-modality reasoning. Asking the model "sing about what you see" still fails more often than pure-vision tasks. These are open research problems. Qwen3-Omni (Lesson 12.20) is the most advanced open attempt in 2025. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Open omni models moved to "thinker–talker" designs : Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni (Lesson 12.20) separate text reasoning from streaming speech generation. Full-duplex speech models : Moshi listens and speaks at the same time with about 200 ms latency; GLM-4-Voice and Mini-Omni stream speech tokens from an LLM. Audio codecs as tokenizers : EnCodec, DAC, Mimi (Moshi) and SpeechTokenizer turn audio into RVQ tokens; lower frame rates (12.5 Hz for Mimi) cut token counts. Laptop reality : MIO is 7B (Yi-6B base) and needs 4-bit quantization on an 8 GB GPU; codecs like EnCodec run easily on a laptop CPU. Solutions Solution P1 · Tokens double, quality rises by diminishing steps Tokens double with each doubling of levels: 450, 900, 1,800, 3,600 and 7,200 for 3 seconds. Quality rises, but by smaller steps: 7.0, 10.0, 14.3, 18.7 and 21.8 dB of signal-to-noise. The first levels capture most of the signal, and each later level refines a smaller leftover error. Solution B1 · The voice falls behind real time The token rate doubles from 200 to 400 tokens per second of speech. If tokens are generated one at a time at about 12 ms each, the 8 levels of one 20 ms frame take about 96 ms, five times slower than real time. The voice starts late, stutters, and falls behind more with every sentence. The context also fills twice as fast: a 5-minute conversation becomes 120,000 tokens. The quality gain is small, since the later levels add the finest detail (the EnCodec run shows shrinking gains per level). Keep fewer levels in the main model and predict the rest with a small parallel decoder (as Moshi does), or use a codec with a lower frame rate. Measure the real-time factor, generation time divided by audio duration, which must stay well below 1. In plain words first The idea in one line Video is not a stack of photos. A 5-second clip has causal ordering, action verbs, and event timing that an image model cannot represent. Video-LLaMA (Zhang et al., June 2023) shipped the first open video-LLM with audio-visual grounding. VideoChat and Video-LLaVA scaled the pattern. By 2025 Qwen2.5-VL's time-aligned M-RoPE, and Qwen3-VL's text timestamps, made second-level grounding a standard open-model skill. Each system solved temporal tokens differently — Q-former per clip, concat-pool per frame, time-aligned M-RoPE per token. This lesson reads the patterns, builds a unifo Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Temporal grounding "Time-localized answers" VLM outputs a specific timestamp range for when an event happens Time-aligned M-RoPE "TMRoPE" 3D rotary position whose temporal axis follows absolute timestamps; Qwen2.5-VL uses it for video, and Qwen2.5-Omni names its audio and video form TMRoPE Dynamic FPS "Motion-aware sampling" Sample more frames in high-motion segments, fewer in static ones Frame pooling "Spatial compress per frame" Reduce patches per frame with bilinear interpolation before the LLM Video Q-former "Clip compressor" Cross-attention bottleneck mapping N frames to K learned queries VideoMME "Video bench" Comprehensive short/medium/long video benchmark, 2500+ samples The problem In plain words first A video model has to understand order and timing as well as what is in each frame: what happened before what, and at which second. Early video LLMs (Video-LLaMA, Video-LLaVA) squeezed a short, fixed number of frames into the language model and could only say "early in the clip". Newer models attach each frame's real time: Qwen2.5-VL through its position code, Qwen3-VL as written timestamps. They can then answer "at 4.2 seconds". Two practical questions decide quality and cost: which frames you sample, and how many tokens each frame gets. This lesson covers the architectures, frame sampling, per-frame pooling, benchmarks and answer formats. It checks a frame sampler that finds a brief event that uniform sampling misses, and scores grounding answers with temporal IoU. No model is trained. A 1-minute video at 30 FPS is 1800 frames. At 196 visual tokens per frame (ViT-B at 224), that is 352k tokens — larger than any 2024-era LLM context. Three reduction strategies exist: Subsample frames (1-8 FPS depending on content). Pool each frame's patch tokens aggressively (3x3 or 4x4 bilinear pool). Compress via a Q-former that takes a 16-frame clip and outputs 64 tokens. Each trade-off is different. Subsampling loses temporal detail. Pooling loses spatial detail. Q-former loses both a little but saves tokens. Temporal position encoding is the other axis: how does the model know frame 5 came before frame 6? Options include simple 1D temporal RoPE (Video-LLaMA), learned temporal embeddings (Video-LLaVA), and time-aligned M-RoPE (Qwen2.5-VL, full 3D). Idea 1 · Video-LLaMA: Q-former per clip + audio branch Video-LLaMA (2023) was the first open video-LLM. Architecture: A short clip with a fixed, small number of frames (8 in its default setup), so long videos are heavily subsampled. Per-frame ViT features -> Video Q-former that cross-attends over all 16 frames -> 32 learned queries -> LLM. Parallel audio branch: waveform -> ImageBind audio encoder -> Audio Q-former -> 32 queries -> LLM. Strength: audio-visual joint reasoning. Weakness: fixed clip length, no arbitrary time grounding. Idea 2 · VideoChat and Video-LLaVA VideoChat kept the Video-LLaMA idea but dropped audio and simplified. Video-LLaVA (Lin et al., 2023) trained a single visual encoder on both images and video frames ("alignment before projection"), giving a unified representation. Both are frozen-CLIP-encoder + MLP + LLM. Neither handles long video. Both are 8-16 frame systems. Idea 3 · Qwen2.5-VL and time-aligned M-RoPE Qwen2.5-VL keeps Qwen2-VL's M-RoPE (Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding) and aligns its temporal axis with absolute time. Each patch token carries a (t, h, w) position where t follows the actual timestamp (not frame index). Qwen2.5-Omni (Lesson 12.20) later named its audio and video version of the same idea TMRoPE, Time-aligned Multimodal RoPE. Key differences from simple temporal embedding: Absolute time, not index. The model sees "at 4.2 seconds" not "at frame 15." Per-token rotation, not per-clip. Each visual token rotates independently by its timestamp. Compatible with dynamic FPS. If you sample at 2 FPS here and 4 FPS there, time-aligned M-RoPE handles the uneven spacing natively. Time-aligned M-RoPE enables "at what second does the cat jump?" queries. The model can output "at 4.2 seconds." Video-LLaMA could only say "early in the clip." Idea 4 · Frame sampling strategies Uniform: sample N frames evenly over duration. Simple, loses motion peaks. Motion-adaptive: sample more densely where frames change most, using optical flow or frame differencing (measured below). Note that Qwen2.5-VL's "dynamic FPS" is different: it trains on videos sampled at varying frame rates and encodes absolute time, so you can choose the rate per request; it does not pick frames by motion. Event-driven: run a lightweight detector, sample more where action happens. Used by VideoAgent. Keyframe + context: sample at shot boundaries + a few adjacent frames. Used for cinematic content. Idea 5 · Pooling per frame At 1 FPS and 576 tokens per frame, a 5-minute clip is 172,800 tokens. That overflows Qwen2.5-VL-72B's 128k context, so you must drop the frame rate or pool tokens per frame first. 3x3 bilinear pool reduces to 64 tokens per frame -> 19,200 tokens for 5 minutes. Sweet spot for most tasks. Pool more aggressively (6x6 -> 16 tokens per frame) for agent workflows where spatial detail matters less. Idea 6 · The four video benchmarks VideoMME: comprehensive video understanding, short + medium + long. TempCompass: fine-grained temporal reasoning, "before" / "after" questions. EgoSchema: long-horizon first-person video. Video-MMMU: multimodal multi-discipline video questions. A full video-VLM evaluation hits all four. They stress different axes — TempCompass is all about ordering, EgoSchema is about 3+ minute reasoning, VideoMME spans durations. Idea 7 · Grounding output formats Output formats for temporal grounding: Free text: "The cat jumps around the 4-second mark." Easy to parse but imprecise. Structured JSON: {"event": "jump", "start": 4.1, "end": 4.3} . Qwen2.5-VL can localise events to the second and answer in text or JSON when asked. Timestamp tokens in the sequence: Qwen3-VL writes each frame group's time into the input as text ( <4.2 seconds> , Lesson 12.9), so the model reads and repeats times as ordinary tokens; other video models use special time tokens. Qwen2.5-VL instead encodes time in its M-RoPE position IDs and answers in text or JSON. Whatever the format, parse it strictly and score it with temporal IoU against labelled intervals (measured below); a vague answer like "early in the clip" scores zero. Idea 8 · 2026 best practice For video VLMs in 2026: Model: a native-resolution video VLM with explicit time (Qwen2.5-VL's time-aligned M-RoPE or Qwen3-VL's text timestamps). Frame sampling: dynamic FPS (1-4 depending on motion) with max-frame cap. Per-frame pooling: 3x3 bilinear. Output: structured JSON with time + event fields. Benchmarks: VideoMME + TempCompass for general; EgoSchema for long-horizon. Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py includes: Uniform and dynamic-FPS frame samplers. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Time-aware video VLMs : Qwen2.5-VL (time-aligned M-RoPE) and Qwen3-VL (text timestamps, 256K context), InternVL3.5 and Gemini-class hosted models localise events to the second. Benchmarks : Video-MME, TempCompass, EgoSchema, Video-MMMU and grounding sets like Charades-STA (scored with R@tIoU) remain the standard suite. Solutions Solution P1 · Only 8 frames, by luck; motion sampling every time Only the 8-frame grid catches it, with one frame at 4.28 s. The 12- and 16-frame grids put samples just before and after the jump (3.6 and 4.5 s; 4.0 and 4.6 s) and miss it, though they use more frames. Motion-weighted sampling lands a frame inside the jump (4.20 or 4.28 s) at all three budgets, because the frames where motion changes get the most weight. Solution B1 · A loose metric hides imprecise answers "Start within 2 seconds" ignores the end of the interval and allows large errors. On a 10-second clip, a ±2 s window covers 40% of the video, so even random guesses would often pass. A model that always answers "from 3 to 9 seconds" could score highly and still be useless for finding the moment. The number says little about precision, and it cannot be compared with published results, which use temporal IoU (for example R@0.5 and R@0.7 on Charades-STA). Score with tIoU on parsed intervals at several thresholds. Check how a trivial baseline scores (a fixed interval, or the middle of the clip), and look at errors in seconds by clip length. Explain the four scaling paths: brute context (Gemini 1.5), ring attention (LWM), token compression (LongVILA / Video-XL), agentic retrieval (VideoAgent). Compare raw-context video VLMs vs agentic-retrieval video VLMs (VideoAgent) on accuracy and latency. Design a needle-in-a-haystack test for a 30-minute video and measure recall at a specific minute. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 17 (video temporal tokens) Type : Build. Time : about 180 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, needle-in-haystack simulator + agentic-retrieval router), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A 1-hour 4K video at 24 FPS, patched and embedded, produces on the order of 60 million tokens. A 2-hour podcast episode transcribed is 30,000 tokens. A full Blu-ray feature film, even compressed with aggressive pooling, is hundreds of thousands of tokens. Google's Gemini 1.5 (March 2024) opened this era: 1 million tokens of context in production (2 million soon after) and recall tested up to 10 million tokens in research, doing reliable needle-in-a-haystack recall over hour-long videos. LWM (Liu et al., February 2024) showed ring attention's scaling path. LongVILA and Video-XL scaled ingestion further. VideoAgent swapped raw Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Brute context "Just more tokens" Scale LLM context to millions of tokens; process everything in one pass Ring attention "LWM-style parallel" Distributed attention pattern where each device holds a chunk and rotates Token compression "Summary tokens" Reduce per-clip tokens via a learned compressor before the LLM Needle-in-haystack "NIH test" Insert a unique marker at a random point, ask model to recall it at test time Agentic retrieval "LLM as query planner" LLM asks a retrieval tool for relevant clips, reads them via a VLM, composes answer VideoAgent "Retrieval pattern for video" Canonical agentic-retrieval design: question -> tool -> clip -> answer The problem In plain words first An hour of video is far more data than any model can read whole. Even at one frame per second with heavy compression it is hundreds of thousands of tokens. There are four ways around it. Use a model with an enormous context window (Gemini's approach). Spread a long sequence over many GPUs with ring attention, so each holds only a slice. Compress each clip into very few tokens before the language model sees it. Or treat the video like a database: describe each clip once, search the descriptions, and read only the clips the question needs (an "agentic" approach such as VideoAgent). This lesson explains the four paths and how to choose. It runs a working clip-retrieval step on a 2-hour video's descriptions and checks that ring attention's block-by-block computation gives exactly the same result as full attention. No model is trained. A single frame of Qwen2.5-VL-sized patches at 384 native resolution is ~729 tokens. At 3x3 pooling that's 81 tokens per frame. A 30-minute clip at 1 FPS = 1800 frames = 145,800 tokens. Doable by 2025 open VLMs, tight. At 2 FPS, 291,600 tokens — only the biggest contexts fit. A 2-hour movie at 1 FPS is 583k tokens. Beyond most 2026 open models; requires Gemini 2.5 Pro or pooling more aggressively. Four scaling paths emerged. Idea 1 · Path 1: Brute context (Gemini 1.5, Claude Opus) Throw hardware at the problem. Scale context to millions of tokens, process everything in one forward pass. (Claude does not take video input directly; with Claude you send sampled frames as images, which is Path 3 or 4.) Gemini 1.5 Pro launched with 1M tokens and later 2M. Its report (arXiv:2403.05530) shows near-perfect needle-in-a-haystack recall (above 99%) for text, audio and video up to millions of tokens, tested up to 10M tokens on text. Later Gemini generations keep long video as a headline feature. Engineering: Gemini 1.5 is a sparse mixture-of-experts transformer; how its attention scales to millions of tokens is not published. Not open-source. Idea 2 · Path 2: Ring attention (LWM, LongVILA) Ring attention distributes long sequences across devices in a "ring" where each device holds a chunk. Attention across the full sequence happens by each device sending its chunk to the next in a ring pattern, computing partial attention, and aggregating. LWM (Liu et al., 2024) trained a 1M-token context model this way. Per-device memory scales with the chunk each device holds, so adding devices extends the context roughly linearly. Total attention compute is still quadratic in context; the ring splits that work across devices and overlaps the key/value passing with compute. LongVILA (arXiv:2408.10188) adapted the pattern to VLMs. 1400-frame videos at 192 tokens per frame = 268k context, trained with ring attention across 8-way parallelism. Idea 3 · Path 3: Token compression (Video-XL, LongVA) Cheaper than brute context: compress aggressively before the LLM sees the sequence. Video-XL (arXiv:2409.14485) uses a visual summary token: each clip of N frames produces a single "summary" token that attends over the N. At inference, the LLM sees one summary token per clip, drastically shrinking the context. LongVA (arXiv:2406.16852) uses "long context transfer": extend the language model's context on long text first (to about 224K tokens), then add vision. Without long-video training, it processes over 2,000 frames, more than 200K visual tokens. Token compression trades off recall at specific timestamps for scalability. The model knows generally what happened but sometimes misses exact frames. Idea 4 · Path 4: Agentic retrieval (VideoAgent) Do not feed the full video to the LLM. Instead, treat the video as a database and use an LLM to query it. VideoAgent (arXiv:2403.10517): LLM reads the question. LLM asks a retrieval tool for relevant clips ("show me segments with a cat"). Tool returns matching clip timestamps. LLM reads those clips via a VLM. LLM composes the answer or asks follow-up queries. This is the LLM-as-agent pattern applied to long video. Cheaper inference (only relevant clips encoded), harder engineering (retrieval quality becomes the bottleneck). The same idea as a formula Token count of a long video at frames per second, tokens per frame, duration seconds: . Blockwise attention (ring attention's core). Split keys and values into blocks . Memory per device holds one N ​ × B N ​ block instead of ; total compute is unchanged. Retrieval cost. Reading of clips costs of the full video's tokens, plus one embedding lookup per query. Worked example A 2-hour video, four ways Brute context at 1 fps with 72 tokens per second (Lesson 12.9's 448 × 252 setting): tokens. Ring attention over 8 devices: each holds 64,800 tokens of the sequence; the largest score block per step is 64 times smaller than the full matrix. Compression to one summary token per second of video: 7,200 tokens. Retrieval of 3 one-minute clips: tokens, 2.5% of the full video, provided the right clips are found. Check your mental model ✗ "Ring attention reduces the compute of long attention." ✓ It splits memory and work across devices; total compute stays quadratic. ✗ "Retrieval is always cheaper and just as good." ✓ It is far cheaper, but a missed clip means a wrong answer, and similar descriptions confuse the search. ✗ "A 1M-token context means the model uses all of it equally well." ✓ Recall depends on position, length and distractors; measure at your own lengths. Predict before you run A 2-hour cooking video is indexed as 120 one-minute clip descriptions, with one unusual moment at minute 83 (the chef drops a red spatula). Will a small embedding model retrieve minute 83 for "When does the chef drop something?" and for "What colour is the spatula?" (Solution P1.) See it drawn Agentic retrieval over a long video 120 one-minute clip descriptions stand in for what a VLM would write while indexing a 2-hour video. They are embedded with bge-small-en-v1.5, and three questions retrieve their top-3 clips by cosine similarity. The run then compares the tokens needed to read the whole video with those for the retrieved clips. A few seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output One question finds the needle, the other misses it. "What colour is the spatula?" retrieves minute 83 first (score 0.582), because "spatula" appears in that description. "When does the chef drop something?" does not: the top three are "plating dessert" clips (about 0.70). The small embedding model matches the general cooking phrasing better than the rarer verb "drops". A retrieval-only agent would answer this question confidently and wrongly. Repeated content crowds the results. "When is bread baked?" returns three different "baking bread" minutes. The video has several, so the top 3 cannot cover every occurrence. Real agents need time-ordered results, deduplication or a larger k for "when" questions. The saving is large. Reading the whole 2-hour video at 1 fps costs about 518,400 tokens; reading three retrieved one-minute clips costs 12,960, 2.5%. That is why retrieval is the practical path for very long videos, provided you improve recall. Index richer descriptions (actions as well as topics), combine text and image embeddings, query with several rephrasings, and let the agent ask follow-up searches. See it drawn Ring attention's block-by-block computation, verified Attention over 4,096 tokens computed as if split across 8 devices: each device's queries see the key/value blocks one at a time, as they would arrive around a ring, with an online softmax. The run compares the result with full attention and the memory needed. Instant. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Blockwise attention is exact. Splitting the 4,096 keys and values into 8 blocks and accumulating them one at a time with an online softmax gives the same output as full attention to within 1.9e-16, float64 rounding. Nothing is approximated, which is why ring attention can train long-context models without changing what they compute. Memory is what shrinks. Full attention needs a 16.8-million-entry score matrix. Each device here only ever holds a 512 × 512 block, 64 times smaller, and passes its keys and values on around the ring. Adding devices lets the sequence grow proportionally. Compute does not shrink. The 64 blocks add up to the same 16.8 million scores. Ring attention spreads quadratic work over more hardware and overlaps it with communication; it does not make long attention cheaper. That is why compression and retrieval still matter. Idea 5 · Needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks The standard long-context test: insert a unique visual or textual marker at a random point in the video, then ask a query that requires recalling it. Metric: Recall@k across video length and marker position. Long-context frontier models report near-perfect video needle recall at hour scale; open models generally degrade sooner as videos get longer, and results depend heavily on how many frames and tokens per frame they are given. Treat published numbers as setup-specific and test at your own lengths. Agentic retrieval can match or beat raw-context models on very long videos, but only when the retrieval step finds the right clips; when it misses, the answer is wrong however strong the VLM is (measured below). Idea 6 · Which path to pick For a 15-minute clip: an open long-context VLM with native video input usually works (Qwen3-VL has a 256K native context, for example). For 30-minute to 1-hour content: long-context open models with reduced fps and pooling, or token-compression models such as Video-XL; hosted long-context models when quality matters most. For 2+ hour content: VideoAgent or similar retrieval patterns. Alternatively, summarize to smaller chunks and feed hierarchical summaries. Idea 7 · 2026 production pattern In practice, production long-video pipelines are hybrid: Run dynamic-FPS sampling + aggressive pooling on the entire video (get a 100k-token global representation). Pass it to a long-context VLM for a global summary and per-segment descriptions. If user asks detailed questions, run agentic retrieval using the summary as an index. This combines brute-context for global understanding and retrieval for local detail. Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py : Computes token budgets for videos from 1 minute to 3 hours at varying FPS + pooling. Simulates a needle-in-a-haystack run: inject a marker at a random timestamp, ask a question, score recall. Includes an agentic-retrieval router simulator that picks specific clips to feed to a downstream VLM. Run the budget table and feel the scale gap. Break it on purpose You build a long-video assistant on retrieval only: clips are indexed by their speech transcripts, never by what is on screen. A user asks "when does the red car appear?" What happens, and how do you fix the index? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Hosted long-context video : Gemini models accept long videos directly; for Claude, send sampled frames as images (Lesson 12.1's token costs apply per image). Open long-context VLMs : Qwen3-VL (256K native context), InternVL3.5 and LongVILA-style systems handle long videos with reduced fps and per-frame merging. Sequence parallelism (ring attention, Ulysses, context parallelism in Megatron and DeepSpeed) is standard for long-context training. Agentic video pipelines : index clips with VLM descriptions plus speech transcripts, retrieve by text and by image embeddings, then read only the retrieved clips; this is the practical path on a laptop GPU. Sources: Gemini 1.5 report (arXiv 2403.05530) , Ring Attention (arXiv 2310.01889) , LWM (arXiv 2402.08268) , LongVILA (arXiv 2408.10188) , LongVA (arXiv 2406.16852) , Video-XL (arXiv 2409.14485) , VideoAgent (arXiv 2403.10517) . Recap What to keep from this lesson Long video is hundreds of thousands of tokens even at 1 fps. Four paths: huge context, ring attention, compression, agentic retrieval. Ring attention is exact blockwise attention across devices; memory splits, compute does not shrink. Retrieval reads a few percent of the tokens but fails when the search misses. Production pipelines mix them: a compressed global pass plus retrieval for detail. a1219: Course home / Phase 12 · Multimodal AI Audio-Language Models: the Whisper to Audio Flamingo 3 Arc Lesson 12.19 180 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Compute a log-Mel spectrogram from a waveform: windowing, FFT, filter banks, log transform. Compare encoder options: Whisper encoder, BEATs, AF-Whisper hybrid. When each wins. Build an audio Q-former: N learnable queries cross-attending to spectrogram patches. Explain cascaded (Whisper-then-LLM) vs end-to-end audio-LLM training: why end-to-end scales better for reasoning. Before you start Needs : Phase 6 (Speech and Audio), Phase 12 · 03 (Q-Former) Type : Build. Time : about 180 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, log-Mel spectrogram + audio Q-former skeleton), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Whisper (Radford et al., December 2022) settled speech recognition — 680k hours of weakly-supervised multilingual speech, a simple encoder-decoder transformer, a benchmark that made every subsequent ASR release cite it. But recognition is not reasoning. Asking "what instruments are in this recording" or "what emotion is the speaker expressing" or "what happened at minute 3" requires audio understanding, not transcription. Qwen-Audio, SALMONN, LTU, and NVIDIA's Audio Flamingo 3 (AF3, July 2025) progressively built that stack: keep Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Log-Mel spectrogram "Mel features" 2D (time, frequency) array of log-magnitude values after Mel filter banks Audio Q-former "Audio Perceiver" Cross-attention bottleneck from audio encoder output to fixed-length queries feeding the LLM Cascaded "ASR-then-LLM" Pipeline where Whisper transcribes and a text LLM reasons; loses acoustic information End-to-end "Audio-LLM" Audio features enter the LLM directly via Q-former; preserves acoustic signal BEATs "Audio AudioSet encoder" SSL transformer trained on AudioSet; strong on music + environmental sounds MMAU "Audio reasoning bench" 10k QA pairs across speech, music, environment; 2024 eval standard On-demand thinking "Audio CoT" Model can optionally emit reasoning tokens before final answer, lifts accuracy 3-5 pts The problem In plain words first Whisper (OpenAI, 2022) made speech-to-text reliable, but turning audio into words throws away everything that is not words: the music, the mood, who is speaking, when the door slammed. Audio language models keep that information. An audio encoder (usually Whisper's, sometimes trained further on music and sounds) turns a spectrogram into vectors. A small adaptor maps them into a language model, which answers questions about the sound itself. The line runs from SALMONN and Qwen-Audio to Audio Flamingo 3 (2025). This lesson covers the spectrogram, the encoder, the adaptor, the model lineage, when a simple transcribe-then-reason pipeline is enough, and the MMAU benchmark. It runs Whisper's real feature extractor and encoder shapes, and computes the token cost of audio. No model is trained or downloaded. Speech recognition was solved by Whisper. OCR-of-audio is a commodity. But "commodity" stops at transcription. If the model cannot reason over what it heard — timing, speakers, emotion, music structure, environmental sounds — transcription alone cannot drive product features. Three obvious routes: Cascade: Whisper transcribes, LLM reasons over the transcript. Works for pure-speech scenarios. Fails for music, environmental audio, multi-speaker overlap, emotion. End-to-end audio-LLM: an audio encoder feeds audio tokens directly into an LLM, skipping transcription. Preserves acoustic information (emotion, speaker, environment). Needs new training data. Hybrid: audio encoder + text decoder that can both transcribe and reason. Qwen-Audio and Audio Flamingo pick this route. Idea 1 · Log-Mel spectrogram: the input feature Every audio encoder starts with the same feature: a log-Mel spectrogram. Resample to 16 kHz. Short-time Fourier transform with 25ms windows, 10ms hop. Take magnitude of the FFT result. Apply Mel filter banks (typically 80 filters log-spaced 0-8000 Hz) to warp to perceptual frequency. Log compress for dynamic range (Whisper takes ​ of the clamped power, limits the range to 8 below the maximum, and rescales). Result: a 2D array of shape (T, 80) where T is the number of time frames. For a 30-second clip at 100 Hz frame rate: (3000, 80). Idea 2 · Whisper's encoder Whisper's encoder is a transformer over time frames: two 1D convolutions (the second with stride 2) turn the 3,000 spectrogram frames of a 30-second window into 1,500 vectors, one per 20 ms, followed by 4 to 32 transformer layers depending on model size (measured below). Large-v3 uses 128 Mel bins instead of 80. Output: one hidden-state vector per 20 ms. For ASR, Whisper's decoder is a cross-attention transformer that generates text tokens conditioned on the encoder output. Standard encoder-decoder. For ALMs (audio-LLMs), you want the encoder output as input to a different LLM. The pattern: Whisper encoder frozen, Q-former trainable, LLM frozen or tuned. The same idea as a formula Log-Mel spectrogram. For window (25 ms) and hop (10 ms) at 16 kHz, the short-time Fourier transform is pooled by Mel filters ​ ( f ) : ​ max ( ϵ , f ∑ ​ M m ​ ( f ) ∣ X ( τ , f ) ∣ 2 ) , τ = 1 , … , 100 per second , m = 1 , … , 80. Encoder frames. A stride-2 convolution halves the frame rate: vectors per second; a 30-second window gives 1,500. Tokens for the LLM. With pooling factor (AF3: ), a clip of seconds becomes audio tokens: 25 per second, 1,500 per minute. Worked example A 10-minute meeting recording Whisper encoder output: vectors, processed in twenty 30-second windows. As audio-LLM input at 25 tokens per second: 15,000 tokens. Transcribed instead: about 150 words per minute × 10 ≈ 1,500 words ≈ 2,000 tokens, 7.5 times fewer. So: if the question is about what was said, transcribe and reason over text; if it is about how it was said (tone, speakers, sounds), the audio tokens are worth their cost. Check your mental model ✗ "Whisper works on raw waveforms." ✓ It works on 80- (or 128-) bin log-Mel spectrograms in 30-second windows. ✗ "A transcript contains everything an audio question needs." ✓ Mood, music, speaker identity and sound events are lost in text. ✗ "Audio-LLMs have reached human level on audio reasoning." ✓ On MMAU, humans score about 82%; the best open models reached the low-to-high 70s during 2025. Predict before you run A 3-second clip goes through Whisper's feature extractor and a Whisper-tiny-shaped encoder. What shapes come out of each, and how many tokens would one minute of audio cost an audio LLM that pools to 25 per second? (Solution P1.) See it drawn Whisper's input and encoder, measured Whisper's real feature extractor (default settings) turns 3 seconds of a two-tone test signal into a log-Mel spectrogram. A Whisper-tiny-shaped encoder (random weights) maps it to frame vectors, and the encoders of all five Whisper sizes are built on the meta device to count parameters. Then the run compares the token cost of audio and of its transcript. A few seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The spectrogram shows the sound. Whisper's extractor turns 3 seconds of audio into an 80 × 3,000 array: 80 Mel frequency bins by 100 frames per second, padded to the fixed 30-second window. The loudest bin is 5 while the 220 Hz tone plays and 23 after the switch to 880 Hz: higher pitch, higher bin. Everything after 3 s is the padding value (−0.69). Whisper always processes 30-second windows, so short clips cost as much encoder compute as long ones. The encoder halves the time resolution. The stride-2 convolution turns 3,000 frames into 1,500 vectors, one per 20 ms, which the transformer layers then process. Random weights do not matter here: the shapes are what an audio LLM receives. Encoder size grows quickly. From 8M parameters (tiny, 4 layers) to 637M (large-v3, 32 layers at width 1,280). AF3's AF-Whisper starts from the large-v3 encoder, so its audio encoder alone is larger than many whole small language models. Audio is expensive in tokens. At 25 tokens per second, a minute of audio is 1,500 tokens, against about 195 for its transcript, almost 8 times more. Ten minutes is 15,000 tokens. Use audio tokens when the question needs the sound, not just the words. Idea 3 · BEATs and audio-specific encoders Whisper was trained on speech-dominant data. It is weaker for music and environmental audio. BEATs (Chen et al., 2022) is a self-supervised transformer trained on AudioSet. Captures music and environmental sounds better than Whisper at the same parameter count. AF-Whisper (Audio Flamingo 3's encoder): start from the Whisper-large-v3 encoder and keep training it on speech, sound, and music together, so one encoder carries both the linguistic and the acoustic signal. Earlier systems like SALMONN got the same coverage by concatenating Whisper and BEATs features. Idea 4 · Audio Q-former Same pattern as BLIP-2's visual Q-former. A fixed number of learnable queries (often 32 or 64) cross-attend over the audio encoder's output frames. The queries become audio tokens consumed by the LLM. Training alignment stage: Q-former alone, contrastive + captioning losses on audio-text pairs (AudioCaps, Clotho). Instruction stage: end-to-end, unfreeze LLM, train on instruction data. Idea 5 · The arc — SALMONN, Qwen-Audio, AF3 SALMONN (Tang et al., 2023): Whisper + BEATs + a window-level Q-former + Vicuna. One of the first open audio-LLMs aimed at general audio reasoning. On MMAU it scores 32.8% (test), showing how hard the benchmark is. Qwen-Audio (Chu et al., 2023) and Qwen2-Audio (2024): a Whisper-initialised encoder feeding a Qwen LLM, trained on much richer data and tuned for dialogue. Qwen2-Audio-Instruct scores 52.5% on MMAU (test), the best open end-to-end model in the MMAU paper. LTU — Listen, Think, Understand (Gong et al., 2023): explicit reasoning data, focus on chain-of-thought over audio clips. Smaller but more focused. Audio Flamingo 3 (Goel et al., July 2025): a fully open state of the art at release. Qwen2.5-7B backbone, an AF-Whisper encoder initialised from Whisper-large-v3 (50 Hz features pooled to 25 Hz), small adaptor layers into the LLM, and training on about 8M audio QA pairs (AudioSkills-XL) plus long-audio, thinking and chat data. It handles audio up to 10 minutes and reports 72.4% on MMAU. AF3 also introduces on-demand thinking for audio: a special suffix on the prompt makes the model write a short reasoning prefix (about 40 words on average in its training data) before the answer; with thinking, its MMAU scores rise to about 73–74%. It also ships a streaming text-to-speech module for voice-to-voice chat. Idea 6 · Cascaded vs end-to-end Cascaded pipeline: Whisper transcribes audio → text. LLM reasons over text. Works perfectly for "summarize this podcast." Fails for: - "What's the mood of this song?" — mood is in the sound, not words. - "Who is speaking, Alice or Bob?" — requires speaker identification. - "At what second does the explosion happen?" — temporal grounding lost in text. - "Is this real or generated audio?" — deepfake detection needs acoustic features. End-to-end preserves acoustic signal. Qwen-Audio and AF3 handle music, environment, and emotion natively. Idea 7 · 2026 production recipe For a new audio-understanding product: Cascaded if: transcription is the goal, no music, no emotion inference. AF3 / Qwen-Audio-family if: music, emotion, multi-speaker, or complex audio reasoning. Cascaded is cheaper and simpler. End-to-end is more capable. Idea 8 · MMAU — the audio reasoning benchmark MMAU (Massive Multimodal Audio Understanding) is the 2024-2025 audio reasoning benchmark: 10,000 audio clips (about 10 seconds each) with multiple-choice questions, across speech, music and environmental sounds, covering 27 skills; a 1,000-question test-mini and a 9,000-question test split. Covers classification, temporal reasoning, causal reasoning, open-ended QA. Tests what cascaded pipelines systematically miss. In the MMAU paper (October 2024), humans scored 82% on test-mini, the best system was a cascade (GPT-4o on strong audio captions) at about 59%, and the best end-to-end model, Qwen2-Audio-Instruct, 52.5%. By mid-2025 AF3 and Qwen2.5-Omni reached the low 70s, and Qwen3-Omni (September 2025) reports 77.5%, level with Gemini 2.5 Pro. Audio LLMs improved fast, but still trail humans on reasoning-heavy questions. Solutions Solution P1 · 80 × 3,000 in, 1,500 × 384 out, 1,500 tokens a minute The feature extractor gives an 80 × 3,000 log-Mel spectrogram (padded to 30 s), and the Whisper-tiny-shaped encoder turns it into 1,500 vectors of width 384, one per 20 ms. At 25 tokens per second after pooling, one minute of audio costs an audio LLM 1,500 tokens, against about 195 tokens for a transcript of the same minute. Solution B1 · Frustration is in the voice, not the words The transcript keeps the words and drops the voice. A customer who says "fine, I'll wait" through gritted teeth, sighs, raises their voice or speaks over the agent produces a calm-looking transcript, so the LLM rates them low on frustration. The tool misses the calls that matter most. Long silences, interruptions and the agent's own tone are invisible too. Feed the audio to an audio LLM (or add an acoustic emotion model) for the frustration score. Keep the cascade for content questions like topics and resolutions, where it is cheaper. Describe TMRoPE's time-aligned position encoding across vision, audio, and text within the Thinker. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 19 (audio-LLMs), Phase 12 · 16 (any-to-any) Type : Build. Time : about 180 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, streaming pipeline latency simulator + VAD loop), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line GPT-4o's product demo in May 2024 was disruptive not because of the underlying model but because of the product shape — a voice interface where you talk, the model sees what the camera sees, and it talks back in about a third of a second (OpenAI reported as little as 232 ms, 320 ms on average). The open ecosystem spent the rest of 2024 and 2025 racing to reach that product surface. Qwen2.5-Omni (March 2025) is the reference open design: a Thinker (large text-generating transformer) plus a Talker (parallel speech-generating transformer), linked by streaming speech tokens. Mini-Omni simplified it, Moshi ma Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Thinker "Reasoning brain" Large text-generating transformer producing what to say Talker "Speech-generating mouth" Small transformer producing discrete speech tokens from Thinker's text TTFAB "Latency budget" Time-to-first-audio-byte: from user speech end to first audio sample out TMRoPE "Time-aligned RoPE" Position encoding using absolute timestamps across vision, audio, text Half-duplex "Turn-taking" User and model alternate; VAD silence detects user-done Full-duplex "Simultaneous" Model can speak and listen at the same time; backchannel capable Inner monologue "Moshi separation" Single-model design where thinking-stream and speaking-stream interleave The problem In plain words first A voice assistant that sees and talks, like GPT-4o's voice mode, must answer within about a third of a second, and keep talking smoothly while it thinks. Omni models split the job in two. A large "Thinker" model reads text, images, audio and video and decides what to say. A smaller "Talker" model turns that into speech codes as the words come out, and a fast decoder turns the codes into sound. Qwen2.5-Omni (March 2025) and Qwen3-Omni (September 2025) are the main open versions. They also line up sound and video by real time (TMRoPE), so the model knows that a wave and a "hello" happened together. This lesson covers the split, time alignment, streaming speech, turn-taking and latency budgets. It simulates a thinker–talker pipeline to see what sets the time to first audio, and builds a time-aligned token sequence. No model is trained or downloaded. A real-time voice assistant has to do a lot, fast: Hear the user. Real-time speech tokenization, voice activity detection (VAD) to know when they're done speaking. Optionally see. Camera input at 2-4 FPS, streamed into the Thinker alongside audio. Think. Compose a response conditioned on the conversation history. Speak. Synthesize audio tokens, decode to waveform, stream to the user's speakers. Each step adds latency. Conversational-feel requires total round-trip < 500ms — below that, the user stops noticing the lag. GPT-4o claims ~250ms. Moshi ~160ms. Qwen2.5-Omni ~350-500ms. Every component needs to stream. Nothing can be "batch everything then decode." Idea 1 · Thinker and Talker Qwen2.5-Omni's decomposition: Thinker: the large text-generating transformer (initialised from Qwen2.5-7B in Qwen2.5-Omni-7B). It consumes interleaved text, image, audio and video tokens through a vision encoder (about 675M parameters) and a Whisper-large-v3-initialised audio encoder, and outputs text tokens. Talker: a dual-track autoregressive transformer that reads the Thinker's hidden states and the text tokens it samples, and outputs discrete speech codec tokens. Feeding it hidden states, not just text, lets it pick up tone and emotion before the words are final. Speech decoder: a flow-matching DiT with sliding-window block attention turns codec tokens into a mel-spectrogram, and a modified BigVGAN vocoder turns that into audio, chunk by chunk, so speech can start before the reply is finished. The separation matters. Thinker has to be big for good reasoning. Talker can be small because its job is local — convert text to speech tokens. Bigger Talker is not more expressive; it's slower. Running both in parallel: Thinker emits text token ​ . Talker consumes ​ (via streaming) and emits speech tokens ​ , s i + 1 ​ , … , s i + k ​ . Speech decoder consumes speech tokens as they come and emits audio samples. By the time Thinker is at text token ​ , Talker has already streamed audio for ​ , … , t i + 2 ​ . Idea 2 · TMRoPE — time-aligned multimodal positions Thinker needs to integrate image frames, audio frames (one encoder frame per 40 ms) and text from conversation history. A naive sequence order (all images, then all audio, then text) loses temporal alignment. TMRoPE gives every token a temporal position id in units of 40 ms of real time: audio advances one id per 40 ms, and video frames take the id of their actual timestamp. The input is also cut into 2-second chunks, with each chunk's video tokens first and its audio tokens after, so the frame and the sound of the same moment sit close together and share temporal ids (measured below). This is the infrastructure for "he waved while saying hello" to work — the model sees the video frame and the audio at the same conceptual moment. Idea 3 · Streaming speech synthesis Speech tokens must stream. Mini-Omni (Xie & Wu, 2024) introduced "language models can hear, talk while thinking in streaming": Thinker output tokens and Talker output tokens interleave in the same sequence. Talker fires as soon as Thinker commits the next text token. No batch boundaries. Moshi (Défossez et al., October 2024) is a leading open full-duplex design: 160 ms theoretical and about 200 ms practical latency on one GPU. Architecture: a 7B language model (Helium) predicts text and speech tokens together, with an "inner monologue" of time-aligned text tokens, and a small depth transformer predicts each frame's residual codebooks from Mimi, a 12.5 Hz codec. This is effectively Thinker + Talker fused into one model with careful training. The same idea as a formula Time to first audio. With prefill time ​ , thinker time per text token ​ , talker time per speech frame ​ , frames per text token and a first playback chunk of frames: ​ ≈ T p ​ + t θ ​ + c t τ ​ + T vocoder ​ . Keeping up. Each audio frame lasts ms (here 80); speech plays smoothly only if the pipeline produces frames faster than they play: production time ​ < 1 , in steady state RTF ≈ max ( Δ t τ ​ ​ , f Δ t θ ​ ​ ) . TMRoPE time ids. A token at real time seconds gets temporal id ; audio advances one id per 40 ms, video frames take the id of their timestamp. Worked example Two talkers, one thinker Thinker: 150 ms prefill, 25 ms per text token. Each text token becomes 3 speech frames of 80 ms (240 ms of audio). Small talker at 8 ms per frame: first 4-frame chunk ready at about ms; RTF . 7B-class talker at 90 ms per frame: first audio about 555 ms, and , so it falls behind: every frame after the first few arrives late. A 900 ms prefill (a long video context) pushes first audio near one second even with a fast talker: context size costs latency directly. Check your mental model ✗ "The Talker just reads the Thinker's text aloud." ✓ In Qwen2.5-Omni it also reads the Thinker's hidden states, which carry tone and emphasis. ✗ "A bigger Talker sounds better." ✓ Past a point it only adds latency; it must produce frames faster than they play. ✗ "Time alignment needs the video and audio tokens side by side." ✓ TMRoPE gives co-occurring tokens the same temporal id wherever they sit in the sequence. With a 150 ms prefill, a thinker at 25 ms per text token and a small talker at 8 ms per frame, the first 4-frame chunk is ready after about 228 ms. Then speech is produced ten times faster than it plays (real-time factor 0.10), with no stalls. A slower thinker costs little. Rotary positions with the same temporal id make "what was heard while this was seen" easy for attention to find. Idea 4 · VAD and turn-taking Voice activity detection runs on the input side. Two patterns: Half-duplex: user speaks, model listens. Model speaks, user listens. Clear handoff via VAD silence detection (~200ms). Full-duplex: both can speak simultaneously. Model can backchannel ("uh-huh") or interrupt. Much harder. Moshi supports this. Qwen2.5-Omni streams its input and output in chunks but works turn by turn; turn-taking is handled by the application (for example, voice activity detection with a silence threshold). Full-duplex behaviour requires application-layer handling or a model trained for it, like Moshi. Idea 5 · Qwen3-Omni (November 2025) The successor (technical report September 2025). Thinker: a mixture-of-experts model, 30B parameters with about 3B active; Talker: also mixture-of-experts (3B, about 0.3B active). The Talker predicts each frame's first codebook, a small multi-token-prediction module (about 80M) predicts the rest, and a lightweight causal ConvNet (Code2Wav, about 200M) replaces the DiT vocoder. A new audio encoder (AuT) is trained from scratch on about 20 million hours. Reported theoretical first-packet latency: 234 ms for audio. It supports 119 text languages, 19 for speech input and 10 for speech output. It reports open-source state of the art on 32 of 36 audio and audio-visual benchmarks, close to or ahead of Gemini 2.5 Pro on several (MMAU 77.5). Idea 6 · Production latency budget For a typical streaming interaction: Mic -> audio tokens: 40-80ms. Prefill (prompt + history): 100-200ms at 7B, much more at 70B. First Thinker text token: 40ms. Talker processes first text token: 20ms. First speech tokens commit: 40ms. Residual-VQ decode: 30ms. Speech waveform decode: 50-80ms. Total TTFAB: 320-490ms at 7B, 600-900ms at 70B. Frontier quality usually means 70B+; hence the frontier latency gap. Idea 7 · Token-rate math At 50 speech frames per second, the Talker must produce at least 50 frames per second of output to keep up, every frame, for the whole reply. A small Talker does this easily; a 7B Talker generating every frame token by token would fall behind (simulated below). Lower frame rates (12.5 Hz in Moshi's Mimi codec) and predicting the extra codebooks in parallel make the budget easier. This is why small dedicated Talker models exist rather than "just use the main model." Full-duplex speech : Moshi listens and speaks at once (about 200 ms); hosted voice modes (GPT-4o-class realtime APIs, Gemini Live) set the product bar. Codec design drives latency : low frame rates (Mimi at 12.5 Hz) and parallel prediction of residual codebooks keep the talker ahead of real time. A thinker 2.4 times slower only moves first audio from 228 to 298 ms and keeps a real-time factor of 0.25, because each text token produces 240 ms of speech. Solution B1 · Every turn re-reads twenty minutes Twenty minutes of camera frames and audio is tens of thousands of tokens at least: audio alone at 25 tokens per second is 30,000, before any frames. Memory for the KV cache grows too, and quality can drop as the relevant moment is buried in a long context (Lesson 11.5). Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 05 (LLaVA), Phase 15 (Autonomous Systems, referenced) Type : Learn. Time : about 180 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, action tokenizer + VLA inference skeleton), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line RT-2 (Google DeepMind, July 2023) was the first widely known model to show that a vision-language model trained on web data can be turned into a robot controller. RT-2 discretized actions as text tokens, co-fine-tuned a VLM on web data plus robot-action data, and proved that web-scale vision-language knowledge transfers to robotic control. OpenVLA (June 2024) shipped the open 7B reference. Physical Intelligence's π0 series (2024-2025) added flow-matching action experts. NVIDIA's GR00T N1 (March 2025) released an open dual-system (System 1 / System 2) model for humanoid robots. The V Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means VLA "Vision-language-action" Model that takes image + instruction and outputs action commands Action tokenization "Discrete bins" Quantize each continuous action value (end-effector move, gripper) into 256 bins per dimension, each a vocabulary ID FAST tokenizer "Frequency action tokens" DCT per dimension, round, then BPE: about 30 tokens per arm per one-second chunk Co-fine-tune "Mix web + robot" Train on web VQA data alongside robot demos to preserve general knowledge Flow-matching action head "π0 continuous output" A 300M action expert inside π0 that turns noise into a 50-step action chunk in 10 integration steps System 1 / System 2 "Dual-system control" Large VLM plans slowly, small action head acts quickly; GR00T pattern Open X-Embodiment "RT-X dataset" Over 1M trajectories from 22 robot types and 21 institutions; the usual pretraining corpus The problem In plain words first A vision-language-action model (VLA) is a vision-language model whose answer is a movement instead of a sentence. It looks at the camera image, reads an instruction like "put the apple in the bowl", and outputs what the robot arm should do next: how far to move the gripper, how to turn it, whether to close it. The hard part is turning continuous movements into something a language model can produce, fast enough for a robot that needs new commands 5 to 120 times a second. RT-2 and OpenVLA write each number as a token from 256 bins. FAST compresses a whole second of motion into a few dozen tokens. π0 and GR00T add a small "action expert" that produces a whole chunk of smooth motion at once by flow matching. This lesson explains the four designs and their data, then tokenizes synthetic robot trajectories both ways and times each output style on a small random model. No model is trained, and no robot model is downloaded. A robot that does chores from natural language instructions has been a research target since the 1970s. The 2020s answer: a vision-language-action (VLA) model. Same VLM architecture used for VQA, but output is actions (joint torques, end-effector poses, discrete commands) instead of text. Challenges specific to VLAs: Action spaces are continuous and fast. A typical single-arm action is 7 numbers (a 6-DoF end-effector move plus the gripper), sent 5 to 50 times a second; a two-arm robot like ALOHA has 14, and a humanoid dozens. Robot-specific training data is scarce. Open X-Embodiment has about 1M trajectories; web image–text datasets have billions of pairs (LAION-5B has 5.85B). Control frequency matters. 30 Hz control loop means 33ms budget per action. Safety. A wrong action damages hardware, humans, or property. Idea 1 · Action tokenization (RT-2) RT-2's trick: write the action as text. Its action is 8 numbers: a 6-DoF change in end-effector position and rotation, the gripper extension, and a "terminate" flag. Each continuous number is discretized into 256 uniform bins, and each bin is a vocabulary token: for PaLI-X the bins are simply its number tokens, for PaLM-E the 256 least-used tokens are overwritten. One action is 8 tokens at each control step. Co-fine-tune a VLM (PaLI-X at 5B and 55B, or PaLM-E at 12B) on a mixture: Web image-text pairs (captioning, VQA). Robot demonstrations, action as tokens: about half of the mixture for RT-2-PaLI-X and two thirds for RT-2-PaLM-E. The model sees an image and an instruction and outputs the action tokens. Web pretraining carries over: RT-2 followed instructions such as "move apple to 3" and "move coke can to person with glasses", whose concepts never appeared in its robot data. On unseen objects, backgrounds and environments it averaged 62% success against RT-1's 32%. Inference: about 1–3 Hz for the 55B model and about 5 Hz for the 5B model, served from a multi-TPU cloud service that the robot queries over the network. Idea 2 · OpenVLA — the open 7B reference OpenVLA (Kim et al., June 2024) is the open-weights RT-2 equivalent. It is built on the Prismatic-7B VLM: a Llama 2 7B language model, SigLIP and DINOv2 vision encoders whose patch features are concatenated (about 600M parameters together), and a 2-layer MLP projector. Each of the 7 action dimensions is cut into 256 bins spanning the 1st to 99th percentile of the training actions, so outliers do not stretch the bins, and the 256 least-used Llama tokens are overwritten as action tokens. The loss is cross-entropy on the action tokens only. Trained on about 970k episodes from Open X-Embodiment (a 27-dataset mixture with weights taken from Octo) for 14 days on 64 A100 GPUs, with robot data only: no web data is mixed in. It beat the 55B RT-2-X by 16.5 points absolute across 29 tasks. LoRA at rank 32 trains 1.4% of the weights (97.6M) and nearly matched full fine-tuning (68.2% against 69.7%). Inference: about 6 Hz on one RTX 4090 in bf16, using about 15 GB of GPU memory. 4-bit quantization brings memory to 7.0 GB with the same success rate (71.9% against 71.3%). One action per call is fast enough for slow manipulation, not for high-frequency control. OpenVLA-OFT (February 2025) fixed the speed with action chunks decoded in parallel as continuous values: about 26 times the throughput. Idea 3 · FAST tokenizer — faster action decode Pertsch et al. (January 2025) showed that per-step bin tokens break down at high control rates: consecutive tokens become nearly identical, so the model can reach a low loss by copying the previous token, and learns little. FAST (Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization) normalises each dimension (1st–99th percentile to [−1, 1]), applies a discrete cosine transform (DCT) to each dimension over a one-second chunk, scales and rounds the coefficients, flattens them lowest frequencies first, and compresses the integer sequence with byte-pair encoding (BPE) into a 1,024-token vocabulary. Smooth chunks have few large coefficients, so the compression grows with the control rate. The paper reports 35 → 20 tokens per chunk for BridgeV2 (5 Hz), 140 → 28 for table bussing (20 Hz) and 700 → 53 for two-arm T-shirt folding (50 Hz): about 30 tokens per arm, whatever the rate. The gain is in training: π0-FAST matched diffusion π0 with about 5 times fewer GPU hours. Inference is slower, because 30–60 tokens are decoded one by one with the 2B backbone: about 750 ms per chunk against about 100 ms for π0 on an RTX 4090. Idea 4 · π0 and flow-matching actions Physical Intelligence's π0 (Black et al., October 2024) replaces discrete action tokens with a flow-matching action expert: A 300M-parameter action expert, a second set of transformer weights inside the same model, processes the robot state and action tokens. Through shared attention, these tokens read the VLM's tokens (PaliGemma, 3B), for about 3.3B in total. The output is a continuous 50-step action chunk, produced by flow matching. Training uses a flow-matching loss on the actions. The VLM starts from PaliGemma and is trained along with the expert on over 10,000 hours of robot data: 68 tasks on 7 of Physical Intelligence's own robot configurations, plus about 9% open data (OXE, Bridge, DROID). Inference: 10 Euler integration steps from noise. The observation's keys and values are cached, so each step reruns only the 50 action tokens. Control runs at up to 50 Hz. π0 beat OpenVLA and Octo out of the box on all five evaluation tasks; the paper attributes OpenVLA's weakness to its lack of action chunking. Continuous chunks keep motion smooth, which per-step discretisation struggles with at high rates. π0-FAST (January 2025) is the same backbone trained on FAST tokens and decoded autoregressively, without flow matching. π0.5 (April 2025) co-trains on web data (captioning, VQA, object detection), high-level subtask labels and robot data from several robots. It first predicts a text subtask, then the action chunk by flow matching, and it cleaned kitchens and bedrooms in homes it had never seen. Weights for π0, π0-FAST and π0.5 are open in Physical Intelligence's openpi repository. The same idea as a formula Bin tokens (RT-2, OpenVLA).
