Idea 5 · GR00T N1 — dual-system for humanoids NVIDIA's GR00T N1 (March 2025) is an open model for humanoid robots and other embodiments. GR00T-N1-2B has 2.2B parameters: System 2: an Eagle-2 VLM (1.34B, built from SmolLM2 and SigLIP 2) reads the camera images (64 tokens per 224-pixel frame) and the instruction, at 10 Hz on an L40 GPU. Its 12th-layer (middle) embeddings are passed on, not text subgoals. System 1: a diffusion transformer trained with flow matching cross-attends to those embeddings and produces 16-action chunks in 4 denoising steps (about 64 ms), for closed-loop motor actions at 120 Hz. Small per-embodiment encoders and decoders handle different state and action sizes. The split maps to Kahneman's fast-and-slow thinking: System 2 plans, System 1 acts. Benefits: slow VLM-sized planning does not block fast control; System 1 stays small for latency. Later releases (N1.5, N1.6, and N1.7 at about 3B) keep the design. N1.7 switches the VLM to Cosmos-Reason2-2B (a Qwen3-VL model), lengthens the action chunk from 16 to 40 and adds 20k hours of human video. The training data form a pyramid: human videos with inferred latent actions at the base, 780k simulated trajectories and generated videos in the middle, and real robot teleoperation at the top. Idea 6 · Open X-Embodiment The training data. The Open X-Embodiment collaboration (October 2023) pooled existing robot datasets from 21 institutions: over 1M trajectories from 22 robot types, demonstrating 527 skills. RT-1-X and RT-2-X, trained on it, beat models trained on each robot's own data. It keeps growing (over 2M trajectories in 70+ datasets by mid-2024) and is the usual starting corpus: Bridge V2, Google's RT-1 data, Language Table, bimanual ALOHA sets and, since 2024, DROID. Each sample: (robot state, camera views, instruction, action sequence). Training hygiene: unify action space, normalize joint ranges, resize cameras. OpenVLA trains on it, and π0 uses a subset as about 9% of its mixture. The gap to a specific robot is closed by fine-tuning on that robot's demonstrations; OpenVLA's experiments used 10–150 per task. Idea 7 · Co-fine-tuning vs robot-only Co-fine-tuning mixes web VQA data with robot trajectories. The ratio matters: too much VQA and the model forgets actions; too much robot data and the model loses general knowledge. RT-2's mixture is about half robot data (PaLI-X) or two thirds (PaLM-E). OpenVLA and π0 use no web data during robot training and rely on what the VLM learned before; π0.5 and GR00T mix web and other non-robot data back in. The ratio is a hyperparameter to tune. Models trained from scratch on robot data alone fail more often on unfamiliar objects and instructions: RT-2 roughly doubled RT-1's success in unseen conditions (62% against 32%). Web knowledge is what lets a model follow a novel phrasing like "move coke can to person with glasses". Idea 8 · Safety and action limits A deployed VLA should sit inside checks like these: Hard joint limits (can't torque past spec). Velocity limits (soft clipping). Workspace bounds (end-effector cannot leave the table). Human-in-the-loop approval for novel tasks. These sit outside the VLA as control-layer checks. The VLA's output is a suggestion, not a command. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) π0 and π0.5 are the most used open VLAs : Physical Intelligence's openpi repository has base and fine-tuned checkpoints for π0, π0-FAST and π0.5 (released September 2025), in JAX and PyTorch, and they are also in Hugging Face LeRobot. It runs on a CPU or a consumer GPU such as an 8 GB laptop card, and its asynchronous inference finished tasks about 30% faster. OpenVLA in 4-bit (7.0 GB) only just fits in 8 GB. Faster autoregressive VLAs : OpenVLA-OFT fine-tunes OpenVLA to decode continuous action chunks in parallel, with about 26 times the throughput and 97.1% average success on the LIBERO benchmark. Recap What to keep from this lesson A VLA is a VLM whose output is robot actions: usually a 7-number end-effector move plus gripper, many times a second. RT-2 and OpenVLA write each value as one of 256 bin tokens; simple, but slow and poor at high rates. FAST compresses a one-second chunk with a DCT, rounding and BPE: about 30 tokens per arm at any rate. π0 and GR00T add a flow-matching action expert that outputs a whole chunk in a few parallel passes. Open X-Embodiment is the shared training corpus; fine-tuning on a robot's own demos closes the gap. Safety limits live in the controller, outside the model. Solutions Solution P1 · About 41 tokens, and it pays for the drumming About 41 tokens at 50 Hz against 350 bin tokens (8.5 times fewer), and about 16 at 5 Hz against 35. The count grows much more slowly than the rate, because a smooth second of motion has the same few low-frequency coefficients however finely it is sampled. The paper's real datasets show the same thing: about 30 tokens per arm per chunk. Drumming does not get lost. FAST keeps every DCT coefficient, rounded, so an 8 Hz component appears as non-zero coefficients near index 8 in every dimension. The count rises to about 108 tokens and the error stays at about 0.022. The trade is more tokens, not less accuracy. What would lose the drumming is truncating to the first few coefficients, a different (and worse) compressor. Solution B1 · Stop, go, and a second without looking The robot moves for one second, stops for about 100 ms while the next chunk is computed, then lurches into the next one. It is jerky, and for every one-second chunk it acts blind. If the object slips or a person reaches in after the image was taken, the policy cannot react until the chunk is finished. Real systems overlap planning and acting: Execute only part of each chunk. For example, run the first 25 of 50 actions, then re-plan from a new image. Fewer steps run blind, at the cost of more calls. openpi and GR00T expose this as a setting (GR00T calls it the execution horizon). Compute the next chunk while the current one runs (asynchronous inference). SmolVLA's async mode finished tasks about 30% faster with the same success. Smooth the hand-over between overlapping chunks, for example by averaging the predictions for the same time step (temporal ensembling, from the ACT policy), so the arm does not jump when a new chunk starts. The latency budget decides how much of this is possible. π0's 100 ms per 50-action chunk leaves room to re-plan every 0.2 to 0.5 s; π0-FAST's 750 ms does not. In plain words first The idea in one line Documents are not photos. A PDF, scientific paper, invoice, or handwritten form has layout, tables, diagrams, footnotes, headers, and semantic structure that plain image understanding cannot capture. The pre-VLM stack was a pipeline: Tesseract OCR + LayoutLMv3 + table-extraction heuristics. The VLM wave replaced that with OCR-free models — Donut (2022) and Nougat (2023) — that emit structured markup directly, while layout-aware models such as LayoutLMv3 and DocLLM kept the OCR step and added the page geometry. By 2026 the common approach is to feed the page image to a VLM at high resolution (Claude 4.7 and later accept up to 2,576 pixels on the long edge) and ask for structured markup, or to run a small dedicated document-parsing VLM Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means OCR pipeline "Tesseract-style" Stage-wise stack: detect -> OCR -> layout -> rules; deterministic, fragile OCR-free "Donut-style" Image-to-output transformer that skips explicit OCR; single model Layout-aware "LayoutLM" Input includes per-token bounding boxes; LayoutLMv3 also reads image patches, masks text and patches, and aligns words with patches VLM-native "Frontier VLM" Feed page image directly to Claude/GPT/Qwen VLM at high resolution; no pipeline DocVQA "Doc benchmark" Questions about scanned document images, scored with ANLS (a string-similarity accuracy); the most-cited document score Markup output "LaTeX / MD" Structured output format instead of free-form text; enables downstream automation The problem In plain words first A document is more than its words. On an invoice, "$1,022.40" means "the total" because of where it sits: on the row that says Total, at the bottom right. Document AI is about reading text together with that layout, plus tables, formulas and handwriting. It went through three eras. First came pipelines: OCR finds the words and their boxes, then rules or layout-aware models such as LayoutLMv3 pick out the fields. Then came OCR-free models such as Donut and Nougat, which turn the page image straight into structured text. Now vision-language models read the page image at high resolution and answer or convert it directly. This lesson runs a real OCR engine on a rendered invoice, builds LayoutLMv3's three inputs with its real processor, and counts what one page costs each kind of model. No model is trained, and no model weights are downloaded. "Understand this PDF" is deceptively hard. The information sits in: Text content (most of the signal). Layout (headers, footnotes, sidebars, two-column format). Tables (rows, columns, merged cells). Figures and diagrams. Handwritten annotations. Fonts and typography (title vs body). Raw OCR dumps the text and loses the rest. A system that cares about invoices needs to know "Total: $1,245" came from the bottom-right, not from a footnote. Idea 1 · Era 1 — OCR pipeline (pre-2021) The classic stack: PDF → image per page. Tesseract (or commercial OCR) extracts text with per-word bounding boxes. Layout analyzer identifies blocks (header, table, paragraph). Table structure recognizer parses tables. Domain rules + regex extract fields. Works for clean printed text. Breaks on handwriting, skewed scans, complex tables, non-English scripts. Every failure mode requires a custom exception path. Idea 2 · TrOCR (2021) TrOCR (Li et al., arXiv:2109.10282) replaced the usual CNN-plus-recurrent text recognizer with a pure transformer: an image encoder initialised from BEiT or DeiT reads a cropped text line, and a text decoder initialised from RoBERTa or MiniLM writes it out. It was pretrained on about 684M text lines cut from digital PDFs, then on synthetic and task data; TrOCR-Large reached a 2.89% character error rate on IAM handwriting and 96.6 F1 on SROIE receipts. Clean win on handwritten and printed text. Still a pipeline (a detector finds the lines, TrOCR reads them, layout comes after), but the OCR step improved dramatically. Idea 3 · Era 2 — OCR-free (2022-2023) The first OCR-free models said: skip detection entirely, map image pixels to structured output directly. Donut (Kim et al., arXiv:2111.15664): - Encoder-decoder transformer: a Swin-B encoder reading the page at up to 2560×1920 and a 4-layer BART decoder, about 143M parameters. - Output is a token sequence that converts to JSON: fields for forms and receipts, a class for document classification, an answer for DocVQA (67.5 ANLS, against 78.1 for LayoutLMv2 with OCR). - Pretraining is "pseudo-OCR": read all the text in order, on 11M scanned pages (IIT-CDIP) plus about 2M synthetic pages in four languages (SynthDoG). - No OCR, no layout, no detection. Nougat (Blecher et al., arXiv:2308.13418): - Trained specifically on scientific papers: about 8.2M pages, over 90% of them from arXiv. - Output is Markdown with LaTeX math (Mathpix Markdown), about 1,400 tokens per page. - Handles equations, multi-column layout, figures. - Swin encoder at 896×672 and a 10-layer mBART decoder, 350M parameters. On about 1.5% of test pages it falls into a repetition loop, more often out of domain. These are specialists, not generalists. Donut on a scientific paper fails; Nougat on an invoice fails. Idea 4 · LayoutLMv3 (2022) A different track. LayoutLMv3 (Huang et al., arXiv:2204.08387) keeps OCR but adds layout understanding: Three input streams: OCR text tokens, per-token 2D bounding boxes, image patches. Pretraining: masked language modelling on the text, masked image modelling on the patches (targets from an image tokenizer), and word-patch alignment (is this word's image patch masked?). Downstream: classification, entity extraction, table QA. LayoutLMv3 is the peak of OCR-based document understanding. Strong on forms and invoices: FUNSD form F1 92.1 (large). Requires OCR upstream: with Microsoft's Read OCR it reached DocVQA ANLS 78.8 (base, 133M) and 83.4 (large, 368M). The same idea as a formula Layout as numbers. LayoutLM-style models put each word's box on a 0–1000 grid, whatever the page size : = ⌊ 1000 ⋅ W x ​ ⌋ , y ~ ​ = ⌊ 1000 ⋅ H y ​ ⌋ . Every subword token of a word gets that word's box. LayoutLMv3's image stream is a page cut into patches: = 196 patch tokens. What a page costs a VLM. And how much skew, blur, noise or lost resolution can the OCR take before it stops reading? (Solution P1.) See it drawn An Era-1 pipeline on a rendered invoice A two-column invoice is drawn with Pillow at about 150 dpi and read by Tesseract 5, an open-source OCR engine (via pytesseract ; install the tesseract program first). The output shows the words with their boxes, then the total found two ways: a regex on the text alone, and a rule that uses the boxes. Last, it measures how many of the words survive skew, blur, noise and lower resolution. About 5 seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output On a clean page, OCR is nearly free and exact. Tesseract finds 58 words, each with a pixel box and a confidence of 90 or more, and its text matches what was drawn. This is step 2 of the Era-1 pipeline, and on clean printed pages it is hard to beat for cost. Text alone loses the meaning. A regex for the first dollar amount returns $189.00, the unit price of the drill. The total is the amount on the same row as "Total", to the right of it: one comparison of box coordinates finds $1,022.40. Real pipelines are many such rules, one per field and layout, which is why they are fragile. OCR degrades, then falls off a cliff. A 3-degree skew costs 5% of the words, a 1.5-pixel blur 2%, and skew, blur and moderate noise together 7%. With stronger noise (standard deviation 40 instead of 25), recall drops to 0%: the page no longer segments into text lines, so nothing is read. Resolution behaves the same way: at 75 dpi (body-text x-height about 5 pixels) 93% survives; at 50 dpi (about 4 pixels) only 7%. Each failure needs its own fix (deskewing, denoising, upscaling), the "custom exception paths" of Era 1. See it drawn LayoutLMv3's three streams, and what a page costs Tesseract reads a small form; LayoutLMv3's real processor ( microsoft/layoutlmv3-base , tokenizer and image settings only) turns the words, boxes and image into its three inputs, and the model is built on PyTorch's meta device to count its parameters. Then one A4 page is sized for each kind of model: visual tokens and how tall 10-point text ends up in pixels. Qwen2.5-VL uses its real resizing function; the Claude row approximates its documented limits. A few seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Three streams, aligned by position. 9 OCR words become 28 text tokens, because the RoBERTa-style tokenizer splits "Invoice" into "ĠInv" + "oice" and the invoice number into 7 pieces. Every piece carries its word's box on the 0–1000 grid, so the model knows that all of "INV-2026-0042" sits at the same place. The image adds 196 patches from a 224×224 copy of the page. The base model has 125M parameters as built here (the paper's 133M counts slightly differently). LayoutLMv3's own image cannot read. Shrunk to 224 pixels, 10-point text is 1.3 pixels tall. The patches tell the model where blocks, lines and tables are; the words themselves must come from OCR. That is why it is an Era-1 model with a better back end, not an OCR-free one. OCR-free models pay for legibility in tokens. Nougat's 896-pixel page leaves an x-height of 5.3 pixels for 588 tokens, enough for clean printed papers. Donut's 2560-pixel page gives 15.2 pixels but 4,800 tokens. DeepSeek-OCR's Small mode (100 tokens) leaves 3.8 pixels: below what Tesseract could read in the last run, so its compact modes rely on a decoder trained to read very small text. A VLM's cost follows the resolution you send. Qwen2.5-VL takes the page as given: 1,260 tokens at 100 dpi, 2,772 at 150 and 11,125 at 300, four times the tokens for twice the resolution. Claude's limits cap the cost at about 4,800 tokens; a 300-dpi page is scaled down to an x-height of about 14 pixels. Around 150 dpi (10 pixels) is usually plenty for body text; small print and dense tables are the reason to go higher. Idea 5 · DocLLM (2023) DocLLM (Wang et al., JPMorgan AI Research, arXiv:2401.00908, submitted 31 December 2023, so the ID carries a January 2024 prefix) is LayoutLM's generative sibling. It has no image encoder at all: it reads OCR text plus bounding boxes. The boxes get their own embeddings, and attention gets four terms (text-text, text-box, box-text, box-box). It is pretrained by filling in masked text blocks and built on Falcon-1B and Llama 2 7B. Better for QA on documents; still depends on OCR input. Idea 6 · Era 3 — VLM-native (2024+) 2024 VLMs became good enough to replace the pipeline entirely. Feed the full page image at high resolution to a VLM, ask the question, get an answer. LLaVA-NeXT 336-tile AnyRes works for small documents. Qwen2.5-VL reads the page at native resolution, one token per 28×28 pixels (Lesson 12.9). Claude 4.7 and later accept images up to 2,576 pixels on the long edge (at most about 4,784 visual tokens). PaliGemma 2 (December 2024) added transfer results on text detection and recognition, table structure, molecular structures and music scores, at up to 896 pixels. The gap between VLM-native and OCR-pipeline closed rapidly. By 2026, VLM-native wins on: Scene text (hand-written + printed, mixed scripts). Complex tables with merged cells. Math equations embedded in text. Figures with text annotations. OCR pipelines still win on: Pure-scan workloads at massive scale where per-page latency matters. Pipeline reliability (deterministic failures vs VLM hallucinations). Regulated environments requiring auditable OCR output. Idea 7 · The Claude 4.7 / GPT-5 frontier At high resolution, frontier VLMs read documents very well, near the top of the standard benchmarks. Vendors publish their current scores on their model pages. Open reference points: DocVQA (ANLS): Qwen2.5-VL-72B 96.4 (validation set), LayoutLMv3-Large with OCR 83.4, Donut 67.5. ChartQA: Qwen2.5-VL-72B 89.5. OmniDocBench v1.5 (whole-page parsing into text, tables and formulas), as reported by PaddleOCR-VL's authors: PaddleOCR-VL (0.9B) 92.6, MinerU2.5 (1.2B) 90.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro 88.0, GPT-4o 75.0. DocVQA is close to saturated. For whole-page conversion, small specialised open models now match or beat general frontier models, because they are trained on exactly that output format. Idea 8 · Math equations and LaTeX output Scientific papers need exact LaTeX output for equations. Nougat was trained on this, and its successors among document parsers (MinerU, PaddleOCR-VL, olmOCR and others) produce usable LaTeX for formulas. Without explicit LaTeX training, VLMs produce readable but imprecise transcriptions. A common scientific-paper pipeline in 2026: a document parser for the whole PDF, then a larger VLM on the pages it flags as hard (dense formulas, complex figures). Idea 9 · Handwriting Still the hardest sub-task. Mixed printed + handwritten (doctors' notes, filled forms) is where OCR pipelines with a handwriting recognizer can still win on cost. General VLMs have improved fast on handwriting; test on your own documents, since public benchmarks rarely match a specific hand or form. Idea 10 · 2026 recipe For a new document-AI project: Pure-printed invoices at scale: LayoutLMv3 + rules, cost-efficient. Mixed documents (scientific + handwritten + forms): VLM-native, either a document parser (PaddleOCR-VL, MinerU, Docling) or a general VLM (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL). Full arXiv ingestion: a parser with LaTeX output for text and math, a VLM for figures. Regulatory: OCR pipeline + VLM validator for cross-check. Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py : A toy layout-aware tokenizer: given (text, bbox) pairs, produces the LayoutLMv3-style input. A Donut-style task schema generator: JSON template for forms. A comparison of token budgets per page across OCR-pipeline, Donut, Nougat, and VLM-native. Break it on purpose To save tokens, a team sends every scanned A4 page to a VLM at 640 pixels on the long side (a few hundred tokens) and asks for the invoice total. On a test set of clean, large-print invoices it scores well. What happens on real invoices, and how would you find out before production does? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Small open document parsers convert pages to Markdown, JSON or HTML with tables and formulas: PaddleOCR-VL (0.9B, October 2025, 109 languages; a layout model then a VLM per element), MinerU2.5 (1.2B), IBM's Granite-Docling (258M, September 2025, used inside the Docling toolkit, Apache 2.0) and olmOCR 2 (a Qwen2.5-VL-7B fine-tune from AI2, trained with unit-test rewards). The sub-1B ones run on a laptop GPU or a CPU; a 7B model needs 4-bit on an 8 GB card. Fewer tokens per page : DeepSeek-OCR (October 2025) encodes a page in 64 to 400 visual tokens and reports about 97% decoding precision at up to 10× compression, about 60% at 20×. General VLMs on page images : Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL (2B to 8B sizes fit a laptop in 4-bit) and hosted models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, which accept PDFs or page images directly. Check each vendor's page for its current document scores. Classic OCR still runs at scale : Tesseract, PaddleOCR and the cloud OCR services (Azure Document Intelligence, Google Document AI, Amazon Textract) remain the cheap, auditable first stage for high-volume printed documents. Sources: PaddleOCR-VL (arXiv 2510.14528) , DeepSeek-OCR (arXiv 2510.18234) , Granite-Docling announcement , olmOCR 2 , LayoutLMv3 (arXiv 2204.08387) , Donut (arXiv 2111.15664) , Nougat (arXiv 2308.13418) , Qwen2.5-VL technical report (arXiv 2502.13923) . Recap What to keep from this lesson Documents carry meaning in layout, tables and formulas, not just words. Era 1: OCR gives words and boxes; rules or LayoutLMv3 use the boxes to find fields. Era 2: Donut and Nougat map pixels straight to structured text, as specialists. Era 3: VLMs read the page image at high resolution; small parsers convert whole pages. Resolution decides legibility, and tokens grow with its square: size pages on purpose. ANLS rewards near-misses; check extracted numbers exactly. Solutions Solution P1 · The regex finds the wrong amount; OCR fails at cliffs No. The first dollar amount in the text is $189.00, the drill's unit price. Plain OCR text has no notion of "the number next to Total"; you need the boxes (or a model that sees the layout). A one-line rule on the coordinates finds $1,022.40. OCR held up well to each problem on its own: 95% of words after a 3-degree skew, 98% after a 1.5-pixel blur, 93% at 75 dpi. But it failed abruptly: skew, blur and heavier noise together dropped recall to 0%, and 50 dpi dropped it to 7%. The lesson for production is to measure on degraded samples of your real documents, because the failure is a cliff, not a slope. Solution B1 · The small print disappears first At 640 pixels on the long side, an A4 page is about 55 pixels per inch. Body text at 10 points then has an x-height of about 4 pixels, and 7-point footnotes and small table figures under 3: about where OCR stopped reading at 50 dpi in the first run. Large-print headings survive, so a clean test set with big totals looks fine. On real invoices the model cannot read small figures, and a VLM, unlike OCR, does not return nothing: it produces a plausible-looking number. Wrong totals with high confidence are worse than a visible failure. How to catch it before production: Compute the legibility first : smallest font on your documents, page size, and the resolution you send give the x-height in pixels (the formula above). Under about 5 pixels, expect errors. Test on real, varied pages , including small print, scans and photos, and score extracted fields exactly (or with arithmetic checks such as subtotal + tax = total), not with ANLS. Spend tokens where they matter : send the page at a readable resolution, or crop the region with the totals at full resolution, or use a parser that keeps resolution per element. Describe ColBERT's MaxSim operation and how ColPali generalizes it from text tokens to image patches. Build a tiny ColPali-like indexer: page → patch embeddings → MaxSim over query-term embeddings → top-k pages. Compare ColPali + Qwen2.5-VL generator vs text-RAG + GPT-4 on an invoices / financial reports use case. Before you start Needs : Phase 11 (LLM Engineering — RAG basics), Phase 12 · 05 (LLaVA) Type : Build. Time : about 180 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, multi-vector indexer + MaxSim scorer), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Traditional RAG parses PDFs into text, splits into chunks, embeds chunks, stores vectors. Every step loses signal: OCR drops chart data, chunking breaks table rows, text embeddings ignore figures. ColPali (Faysse et al., July 2024) asked the simpler question: why extract text at all? Embed the page image directly via PaliGemma, use ColBERT-style late interaction for retrieval, and keep all the layout, figures, fonts, and formatting signal the document carries. On its own benchmark, ViDoRe, ColPali scored 81.3 nDCG@5 against 67.0 for the best text pipeline; VisRAG, a related design, reported 20–40% better end-to-end answers than text RAG Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Late interaction "ColBERT-style" Retrieval using per-token or per-patch embeddings + MaxSim, not a single doc vector MaxSim "Max-over-patches" For each query token, pick the highest-similarity document token; sum across query Bi-encoder "Single-vector" One vector per document; faster but loses granularity Multi-vector "Many-vectors-per-doc" Store $N_p$ vectors per document / page; storage cost grows but recall improves Patch embedding "Page feature" One vector per image patch from a VLM encoder, cached per page ViDoRe "Vision doc bench" ColPali's benchmark suite for visual document retrieval PQ quantization "Product quantization" Split each vector into sub-vectors and store a codebook index for each; shrinks storage many times at some cost in accuracy The problem In plain words first The usual way to search PDFs (text RAG) first turns each page into text with OCR, cuts the text into chunks and stores one vector per chunk. Charts, table layout and badly scanned pages get lost on the way. ColPali skips the text step: a vision-language model looks at the page image and produces many small vectors, one per patch of the page. A question is also turned into one vector per word piece. Each word piece then finds its best-matching patch, and the page's score is the sum of those best matches. This is called late interaction, or MaxSim, from ColBERT. The price is storage, because each page has about a thousand vectors instead of one. This lesson explains ColBERT, ColPali and their relatives. It then runs a real 256M-parameter ColPali-family model (ColSmol) against OCR plus a text embedder on rendered pages, and measures how much pooling and binary quantization shrink the index. No model is trained. Text-RAG on PDFs throws away most of the document. A financial report's Q3 revenue growth is usually in a chart; a medical report's findings are in annotated images; a legal contract's signature block is a layout fact, not a text fact. The text-RAG pipeline: PDF → text via OCR / pdftotext. Text → 300-500 token chunks. Chunk → bi-encoder embedding (one vector). User query → embedding → cosine similarity → top-k chunks. Chunks + query → LLM. Five lossy steps. Charts not captured. Tables broken across chunks. Multi-column layout flattens. Figure annotations disappear. ColPali's fix: skip OCR, embed the page image directly. Use ColBERT-style late interaction for retrieval so the model can attend to fine-grained patches at query time. Idea 1 · ColBERT (2020) ColBERT (Khattab & Zaharia, arXiv:2004.12832) is a text retrieval method. Instead of one vector per document, it produces one vector per token. At query time: Query tokens get their own embeddings ( ​ vectors). Document tokens get embeddings ( ​ vectors, typically cached). Score = sum over query tokens of max over document tokens of cosine similarity: ​ max j ​ cos ( q i ​ , d j ​ ) . This is the MaxSim operation. Each query token "picks" its best-matching document token. The final score is the sum. Pros: strong recall, handles term-level semantics. Cons: ​ vectors per document, storage expensive. Idea 2 · ColPali ColPali (Faysse et al., arXiv:2407.01449) applies the ColBERT pattern to images. Each page is encoded by PaliGemma-3B at 448×448 pixels: SigLIP's 1,024 patch embeddings pass through the language model together with a short text prompt, and a linear layer projects every output to 128 dimensions. That is about 1,030 vectors per page ( ​ ). Each user query (text) is encoded into query-token embeddings: ​ vectors. Score = ​ max j ​ cos ( q i ​ , p j ​ ) , i.e., MaxSim over query-text-tokens and page-image-patches. Retrieve top-k pages by total score. At document-ingestion time: embed every page with PaliGemma, store all patch embeddings. At query time: embed the query tokens, compute MaxSim against all stored page embeddings, return top-k pages. Pros: on ViDoRe, 81.3 nDCG@5 against 67.0 for the best text pipeline (OCR plus image captions, embedded with BGE-M3), and indexing needs no OCR or layout step. Each patch vector captures local layout and content. Cons: storage. 1,030 vectors × 128 dimensions × 2 bytes is about 256 KB per page, against about 1.5 KB for one 768-dimensional vector in 16 bits. Mitigated by token pooling (merging similar vectors), quantization (int8 or binary) and compressed multi-vector indexes such as ColBERTv2's PLAID. Check your mental model ✗ "ColPali runs OCR and embeds the text." ✓ It embeds the page image; there is no OCR step anywhere. ✗ "MaxSim averages the similarity of all patches." ✓ Each query vector takes only its single best patch; the page score is the sum of those maxima. ✗ "Shrinking a multi-vector index needs a new model." ✓ Token pooling and binary quantization are applied at indexing time, to the same vectors. ✗ "Vision retrieval replaces the generator." ✓ It returns pages; a VLM still has to read them to answer. Predict before you run Ten rendered pages, four of them look-alike distractors, and six questions. One of the right pages is a bad scan on which OCR finds no words. Which retriever finds that page: OCR plus a text embedder, or ColSmol on the image? And does either fall for the distractors? (Solution P1.) See it drawn Vision retrieval against OCR plus text retrieval Ten pages are rendered with Pillow: a bar chart, tables, notices, invoices, a roadmap and four look-alike distractors. One page is degraded like a bad scan. Text RAG reads each page with Tesseract and embeds the text with bge-small (one vector per page). Vision RAG embeds each page image with ColSmol-256M ( vidore/colSmol-256M , about 0.5 GB, loaded with Sentence Transformers' MultiVectorEncoder ) and scores with MaxSim. About a minute and a half on a 2-core CPU. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Each page becomes 1,135 vectors. ColSmol turns every 850×1100 page into 1,135 vectors of 128 dimensions (image tiles plus a short prompt), and a short question into about 20. Indexing 10 pages took a little over a minute on a 2-core CPU, so a laptop can index a few thousand pages an hour; a GPU is much faster. OCR reads nothing from the bad scan. Tesseract finds 8 to 23 words on each clean page and 0 on the degraded fire-evacuation page. Text RAG cannot retrieve a page whose text it never saw. Its top pick for the fire question is page 7, the clean "Fire extinguisher inspection log", which shares the word "fire". The right page comes third. The image retriever still finds it. ColSmol ranks the degraded page first: blurred, rotated and noisy text is still recognisable as an evacuation notice to a model that looks at the pixels. Neither fell for the other distractors. "How many engineers do we have now" picked the current headcount over the 2027 plan, and the Northwind invoice over the Contoso one, in both systems. Clean, short pages are easy for text RAG too; the gap opens where text extraction fails. Ten pages prove the mechanism, not the size of the gain. Use a benchmark such as ViDoRe, or better your own pages and questions, to measure how much vision retrieval helps. See it drawn Shrinking the index without retraining This block continues from the one above and reuses its page and query vectors. It stores the real ColSmol vectors in float32, bf16 and binary form, and pools them by Ward clustering at factors 2, 3 and 4. For each version it checks whether the right pages still rank first and how closely the scores follow the uncompressed ones. Then it scales the storage to a million pages. A few seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Binary vectors keep the ranking. Storing only the sign of each dimension cuts a page from 290,560 bytes (bf16) to 18,160, 16 times less. All six right pages still rank first, and the scores correlate 0.956 with the full ones. Pooling barely moves the scores. Merging similar vectors by Ward clustering keeps the correlation at 0.999 or more even at factor 4 (283 vectors per page). Neighbouring patches of a page, such as blank margin or a run of text, carry nearly the same vector, so their mean loses little. Together: 48 times smaller. Binary plus pooling at factor 3 stores a page in 6,048 bytes, with correlation 0.948 and every right page still first. On a small, easy set every method ranks perfectly; on a real corpus, measure the recall loss before choosing a setting. At a million pages, storage and compute decide the design. bf16 ColSmol vectors need about 290 GB, binary 18 GB, binary and pooled 6 GB, against 1.5 GB for one bge-small vector per page. Brute-force MaxSim over a million pages is about 5.8 trillion operations per query, roughly a minute on a laptop CPU. So large systems first find a few hundred candidate pages cheaply, then score only those with MaxSim. Idea 3 · ColQwen2 and ColSmol ColQwen2 (illuin-tech, 2024) swaps PaliGemma for Qwen2-VL-2B with dynamic resolution, so the number of vectors follows the page's size and shape; it scores higher on ViDoRe. ColQwen2.5 followed in 2025. ColSmol is the smaller-scale variant for local / edge use: built on SmolVLM-256M or -500M with LoRA adapters, trained on the same 127k query-page pairs. The 256M version runs on a laptop CPU (measured below). Idea 4 · VisRAG VisRAG (Yu et al., arXiv:2410.10594) is a different variant: it pools each page into a single 2,304-dimensional vector (about 4.5 KB) from MiniCPM-V 2.0, by position-weighted mean pooling, and retrieves with ordinary cosine search. Its paper reports in-domain MRR@10 of 77.9 against 76.5 for ColPali, and 20–40% better end-to-end answers than text-based RAG. The trade-off: many vectors per page for fine-grained matching, one vector per page for cheap search at scale. Which one wins on quality depends on the documents and the queries; test both on your own pages. Idea 5 · M3DocRAG M3DocRAG (Cho et al., arXiv:2411.04952) extends multi-modal retrieval to multi-page multi-document reasoning. ColPali retrieves pages across documents (its M3DocVQA benchmark has 3,368 PDFs with 41,005 pages), and Qwen2-VL 7B answers from up to 4 retrieved page images. An inverted-file index (Faiss IVF) cut retrieval from 21 s to 1.8 s per query over those 40k pages. Idea 6 · ViDoRe — the benchmark ColPali's companion benchmark. Visual Document Retrieval Evaluation. Its tasks reuse academic visual QA sets (DocVQA, InfoVQA, TAT-DQA, ArxivQA, TabFQuAD) and add practical topics (energy, government reports, healthcare, AI, sustainability). Metric: nDCG@5. ColPali scored 81.3 average nDCG@5 on ViDoRe; the best text pipeline scored 67.0, and OCR with BM25 65.5. ViDoRe V2 (2025) added longer, harder queries over larger document sets, on which all scores are much lower. Idea 7 · The end-to-end RAG pipeline For a vision-native RAG: Ingest: PDF → page images → PaliGemma encoding → store all patch embeddings. Query: user text → query-token embeddings → MaxSim against all indexed pages → top-k pages. Generate: top-k page images + query → VLM (Qwen2.5-VL or Claude) → answer. No OCR anywhere. Figures, charts, fonts, layout all flow into the answer. Idea 8 · Storage math A 50-page financial report with ColPali's 1,030 vectors per page and 128-dim embeddings: ColPali: 50 × 1,030 × 128 × 2 bytes (bf16) ≈ 13 MB; with binary quantization (1 bit per dimension) about 0.8 MB. Text-RAG: 50 chunks * 768-dim * 4 bytes = ~150 kB. ColPali in bf16 takes about 86 times the storage of the float32 text vectors. Binary quantization plus token pooling at factor 3 brings it to under 2 times (measured on real ColSmol vectors below), usually tolerable. Idea 9 · When text-RAG still wins Pure-text documents with no layout signal (wiki articles, chat logs). Text-RAG is simpler and storage-cheaper. Multi-million-page archives where storage dominates cost. Strict regulatory requirements demanding extractable OCR text alongside the retrieval. For visually rich documents (financial reports, scientific papers, slides, manuals, scanned forms), vision-native retrieval tends to win in 2026; measure it on your own pages. Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py : Toy patch encoder: maps a "page" (small grid of feature vectors) to an array of patch embeddings. MaxSim scorer: computes the ColBERT-style score between a query token embedding set and a page patch set. Indexes 5 toy pages, runs 3 queries, returns top-k with scores. Break it on purpose A team indexes one million pages with a ColPali-family model, stores every vector in bf16 and scores each query with brute-force MaxSim over all pages. What happens to memory and latency, and how do production systems avoid it? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) ColPali-family retrievers are used in production document search: ColQwen2 (2B, fits an 8 GB laptop GPU in bf16) and ColQwen2.5 (3B, more comfortable in 8-bit on such a card) for quality, ColSmol (256M and 500M) for CPUs and edge devices. They load through the colpali-engine library or Sentence Transformers' MultiVectorEncoder , as above. Vector databases with multi-vector fields : Vespa, Qdrant and Weaviate can store several vectors per document and score them with MaxSim, usually as a reranking stage after a cheaper first search. Index compression : token pooling (about a third of the vectors at factor 3, no retraining) and binary quantization are standard ways to cut multi-vector storage. Single-vector alternatives : VisRAG-style pooled page vectors and hosted multimodal embedding APIs (such as Cohere Embed v4 and Voyage's multimodal models) embed a page image as one vector, at a fraction of the storage. Harder benchmarks : ViDoRe V2 (2025) uses longer, more realistic queries over larger document sets; retrieval scores there are far below V1's. Sources: ColPali (arXiv 2407.01449) , VisRAG (arXiv 2410.10594) , M3DocRAG (arXiv 2411.04952) , token pooling (Answer.AI) , ViDoRe V2 , colSmol-256M model card , illuin-tech/colpali . Recap What to keep from this lesson Text RAG loses charts, layout and badly scanned pages before retrieval even starts. ColPali embeds the page image as about a thousand patch vectors; no OCR. MaxSim: each query vector takes its best patch; the page score is the sum. Multi-vector indexes are large; pooling and binary quantization shrink them a lot. Single-vector page embeddings (VisRAG) trade fine matching for cheap search. Retrieval finds pages; a VLM reads them to answer. What does this sum capture that a simple mean similarity does not? ColPali indexes pages as patch sets. What changes if we instead index at the word level (as ColBERT does)? Trade-offs? Design the end-to-end pipeline for a 1M-page corpus with a latency budget of 500ms per query. Pick ColQwen2 / VisRAG and justify. Read M3DocRAG (arXiv:2411.04952). How does it retrieve across thousands of PDFs quickly, and how many retrieved pages can its generator see at once? Solutions Solution P1 · Only the image retriever finds the bad scan Only ColSmol. Tesseract read 0 words from the bad scan, so the text retriever had nothing to match and put the clean "Fire extinguisher inspection log" first; the right page came third. ColSmol, which embeds the pixels, ranked the scanned page first. Neither fell for the other distractors: the current headcount beat the 2027 plan and the Northwind invoice beat the Contoso one in both systems. Clean, short text pages are easy for text RAG too. The gap appears where text extraction fails: bad scans, charts with no text values, layout that carries meaning. That is ColPali's argument, and why you should measure on your own documents before choosing. Solution B1 · Hundreds of gigabytes and a minute per query Memory: at about 1,135 vectors per page, 128 dimensions and 2 bytes, a million pages need about 290 GB of vectors (ColPali's 1,030 vectors: about 260 GB). That does not fit in RAM on one ordinary server, let alone a laptop. Latency: brute-force MaxSim compares every query vector with every page vector, about 5.8 trillion operations for a 20-vector query, around a minute on a CPU and still noticeable on a GPU. Every query also has to stream the whole index through memory. Production systems split the work: Shrink the index : binary quantization (16 times smaller) and token pooling (about 3 times at factor 3) cut 290 GB to about 6 GB, with little loss in this lesson's run; check recall on your data. Retrieve candidates cheaply, then rerank : a first stage finds a few hundred likely pages with an approximate index (inverted-file clustering as in M3DocRAG, which cut 21 s to 1.8 s per query over 40k pages; PLAID-style centroid search; or one pooled vector per page). Full MaxSim scores only those candidates. Use a database built for it : Vespa, Qdrant and Weaviate store multi-vector fields and run MaxSim as a reranking step. a1224: Course home / Phase 12 · Multimodal AI Multimodal RAG and Cross-Modal Retrieval Lesson 12.24 180 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Design cross-modal retrieval: text → image, image → text, audio → video, etc. Compare three fusion strategies: score fusion, attention-based fusion, MoE fusion. Explain generation grounding: what "cite your sources" looks like when sources are a mix of modalities. Name the three canonical multimodal RAG surveys of 2025 and their sub-problem taxonomy. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 23 (ColPali), Phase 11 (RAG basics) Type : Build. Time : about 180 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, cross-modal retriever with fusion + grounded generator), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Vision-native document RAG is one slice. Production multimodal RAG goes wider — retrieving across text, images, audio, and video for workflows like trip planning ("find me a quiet vegan brunch with natural light"), medical triage ("what injury matches this photo + these notes"), e-commerce ("outfits similar to this selfie, in my size"), and field service ("diagnose this engine sound plus photo of the part"). Three 2025 surveys — Abootorabi et al., Mei et al., Zheng et al. — codified the sub-problems: cross-modal retrieval, retrieval fusion, generati Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Cross-modal retrieval "Query one modality, retrieve another" Text query retrieves images; image query retrieves text; requires a shared space or translator Score fusion "Combine scores" Weighted sum of per-modality retrieval scores; simplest fusion MoE fusion "Modality-routed experts" Gating network picks which modality's scores to trust per query Grounded generation "Cite your sources" Each claim in the answer tagged with the source index MuRAG "First multimodal RAG" 2022 paper that established the multimodal RAG pattern Agentic multi-hop "Reformulate and retry" LLM re-queries retrievers when first-pass confidence is low The problem In plain words first Many collections hold more than text: product photos with short descriptions, posts with pictures, videos with transcripts, recordings with notes. Multimodal RAG searches all of these together and hands what it finds to a model that writes an answer with sources. Three questions come up. How does a text question find a photo (a shared space such as CLIP's)? How do you combine results from separate retrievers whose scores are on different scales (fusion)? And how does the answer say which photo or passage each claim came from (grounding)? This lesson covers the patterns from the 2025 surveys, then builds a small two-retriever search over 200 real photos with captions. It compares fusion methods, tunes their weights and handles posts that have no photo. No model is trained. Single-modality RAG is a solved pattern: embed query, embed chunks, retrieve, stuff into LLM. Multimodal RAG requires: Multiple retrieval heads (each modality needs embeddings in a compatible space). Fusion of retrieval results across modalities. Generation grounding that cites sources across modalities. Evaluation metrics that cover cross-modal signal. The 2025 surveys all arrive at the same taxonomy. Idea 1 · Cross-modal retrieval Retrieve documents of modality B given a query of modality A. Three patterns: Shared embedding space. CLIP and CLAP produce text + image / text + audio embeddings in a shared space. Cosine similarity across modalities works directly. Limited to CLIP-trained pairs. Per-modality encoder + translation. Separate text and image encoders plus a small learned module that maps one space into the other, much as BLIP-2's Q-Former bridges an image encoder and an LLM (Lesson 12.3). Flexible but adds a component to train. VLM as encoder. Use a VLM's hidden states as the retrieval representation. Any modality the VLM supports works. Higher quality, more expensive. Choice: CLIP / SigLIP 2 for text+image; CLAP for text+audio; VLM-hidden-states for cross-modal at frontier quality. Idea 2 · Fusion strategies You retrieved 10 results: 5 images, 3 text passages, 2 audio clips. How do you merge? Score fusion (cheapest). Each modality has its own retriever, each returns scores. Normalize scores within-modality then sum. Simple, often works. Attention-based fusion. Concatenate all retrieved items, let a small attention network weight them. Needs training. MoE fusion. Gating network routes to modality-specific experts. Different query types route differently — a visual question weights images higher. Production default: score fusion after normalising each retriever's scores per query (min-max or z-score), or reciprocal rank fusion when scores cannot be compared; tune the weights on labelled queries (measured below). Upgrade to a learned gate (MoE-style) only if an A/B test shows clear wins on your domain. The same idea as a formula Per-query normalisation. Check your mental model ✗ "Cosine scores from two models can simply be added." ✓ Each model has its own scale; the one whose scores vary more decides the ranking. ✗ "Reciprocal rank fusion is always the safe choice." ✓ It throws away confidence, so a retriever that is guessing gets as much say as one that knows. ✗ "Multimodal RAG needs one model trained on every pair of modalities." ✓ Separate retrievers plus fusion work; a shared space is needed only where a query in one modality must find items in another. ✗ "If the prompt asks for citations, the answer's sources are right." ✓ Check them in code: every cited label must exist among the retrieved items. Predict before you run 200 posts, each a real photo with a caption. Most captions are vague ("Weekend vibes"), and almost half the photos are tiny and blurred. A caption retriever and a photo retriever each answer 10 queries. Which one does better alone, and does fusing them beat both? Which fusion method wins? (Solution P1.) See it drawn Two retrievers and three ways to fuse them 200 Imagenette photos (10 classes, 20 each) become community posts. About 4 in 10 captions name what is in the photo; the rest are vague. About half the photos are shrunk to 8×8 pixels and scaled back up. bge-small searches the captions; CLIP ViT-B/32 searches the photos from the text query (cross-modal). The table shows R-precision for each retriever alone and for three fusion methods. About half a minute on CPU. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Each retriever alone sees only part of the collection. Captions find 36% of the right posts in each query's top 20: only 72 of the 200 captions say what the photo shows. CLIP finds 62% from the photos, even though 88 of them are blurred to 8×8 pixels; a clear photo is a strong signal, and some blurred ones keep enough colour and shape. A raw sum is worse than the photos alone. Adding the two cosines gives 61%. Caption scores spread from 0.32 to 0.80 and photo scores only from 0.07 to 0.36, so the weaker caption retriever decides most of the ranking. Normalising first helps. Min-max scaling per query, then equal weights, reaches 65%, above both retrievers alone. Reciprocal rank fusion falls behind. RRF gives 55%. It uses only ranks, and for the many vague captions the caption ranks are noise ("Weekend vibes" is as close to "skydiving" as to anything else). RRF counts that noise as much as the photo ranks. The ceiling is 70%. Only 70% of the posts have either a clear photo or an informative caption; no fusion can find the rest, because neither modality says what they are. See it drawn Tuning the fusion, and posts with no photo This block continues from the one above and reuses its scores. It sweeps the photo weight, tries a per-query weight taken from each retriever's confidence, and removes the photo from 30% of the posts to compare three ways of scoring a missing modality. Instant. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The best fixed weight reaches the ceiling. R-precision rises from 36% (captions only) to 70% at a photo weight of 0.75, then falls to 62% with photos only. 70% is the ceiling from the first run. But that weight was chosen on the same 10 queries it is scored on, so the number is optimistic: tune weights on one set of labelled queries and report on another. Confidence-based weights did not help here. Measuring how far each retriever's top scores stand out gave weights close to 0.5 for every query, and the result (65%) equals plain equal weights. Both retrievers looked equally "sure" on these queries, even though one was usually guessing. A gate that works needs labelled data to learn from, which is what MoE-style fusion trains. A missing photo must be handled on purpose. Scoring a missing photo as 0 drops R-precision to 53%, because every post without a photo sinks. Using the query's median photo score gives 59%, and using the caption score alone gives 58%. Even then, posts without photos make up 19% of the top results against 28% of the collection: they are still under-ranked, so check the share of each kind of item in your results. Idea 3 · Generation grounding The LLM should cite which retrieved item drove each claim. For multi-modal: Text source: standard citation [1] . Image source: [img 3] with a short caption. Audio: [audio 2 at 0:34] . Frontier VLMs cite reliably when the prompt numbers each source and asks for those labels; fine-tuning on answers tagged with source indices helps smaller models. Either way, check citations in code: every label in the answer must exist among the retrieved items, and a claim with no label is unsupported. Idea 4 · The 2025 surveys Abootorabi et al. (arXiv:2502.08826, "Ask in Any Modality"): taxonomy for multimodal RAG. Covers retrieval, fusion, generation. Broadest coverage. Mei et al. (arXiv:2504.08748, "A Survey on Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation"): organises the field in stages, from converting everything to captions, to keeping native images and video, to document screenshots with search planning. Covers parsing, search planning, retrieval, generation, datasets and evaluation. Useful for evaluation design. Zheng et al. (arXiv:2503.18016, "Retrieval Augmented Generation and Understanding in Vision"): vision-focused survey covering visual understanding (including document understanding), visual generation and embodied AI. Reading all three gives you the state of the art as of spring 2025. Most of the sub-problems are still open. Idea 5 · MuRAG — the foundational paper MuRAG (Chen et al., Google, 2022) described itself as the first multimodal retrieval-augmented transformer: a ViT plus T5 model (527M parameters) that retrieves images and text from a memory and generates answers, 10–20 points better than earlier models on WebQA and MultimodalQA. Showed feasibility before the VLM wave. Modern systems (VisRAG, M3DocRAG) follow the same retrieve-then-generate pattern with VLMs. Idea 6 · A production trip-planner example Query: "find me a quiet vegan brunch with natural light." Pipeline: Decompose query. "quiet" → audio/review keyword; "vegan brunch" → menu item; "natural light" → image feature. Retrieve per modality: - Text retrieval on reviews: "vegan brunch, quiet ambiance." - Image retrieval on restaurant photos: "natural light, airy." - Audio retrieval on ambient-sound clips: "low decibel, no music." Fuse scores. Each restaurant has a composite score. Top-k restaurants → VLM generator with all evidence → answer with citations. This is well beyond text-RAG. Each modality adds signal that text alone misses. Idea 7 · Agentic multimodal RAG Multi-hop: if the first retrieval does not return high-confidence answers, the LLM reformulates and retrieves again. Agentic RAG patterns from Phase 14 apply here. Examples: Retrieve initial top-10 → LLM asks "too noisy, filter for <40 dB" → re-retrieve. Retrieve images → LLM sees one has a menu → retrieve the menu text → answer. Adds complexity but handles queries that single-shot retrieval cannot. Idea 8 · Evaluation Cross-modal evaluation is still immature. Common proxies: Recall@k per modality. Fused top-k accuracy. Human-judged end-to-end satisfaction. Task-specific (bookings completed, purchases made). No standard benchmark spans all modalities. Most papers evaluate on domain-specific tasks. Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py : Three mock retrievers (text, image, audio) operating on a shared corpus of restaurants. Score fusion that combines modality scores with configurable weights. A generator stub that emits a final answer with citations. A simple agentic loop that reformulates the query if confidence is low. Break it on purpose A team adds a third retriever, over audio clips, to a text-and-image search and sums the raw cosine scores. The audio model's cosines all sit between 0.85 and 0.95, while text scores spread from 0.3 to 0.8. What does the audio retriever contribute to the ranking, and what goes wrong if they "fix" it by min-max scaling every retriever and weighting them equally? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Hybrid search with built-in fusion is standard in search engines and vector databases: Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Qdrant and Weaviate offer reciprocal rank fusion and score-based fusion of several retrievers in one query. Shared text–image spaces : SigLIP 2 and OpenCLIP models for self-hosted search (CLIP B/32 and SigLIP 2 base run on a laptop CPU); hosted multimodal embedding APIs such as Cohere Embed v4 and Voyage's multimodal models embed text and images in one space. Captions as a bridge : many production systems caption or transcribe images, audio and video with a VLM or speech model at indexing time and search the text, keeping the original media for the generator. The Mei et al. survey calls this the first stage of multimodal RAG. VLM generators with numbered sources : Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL (2B–8B fit a laptop GPU, larger ones in 4-bit) or hosted VLMs read the retrieved images and text, and cite them by label; the application checks the labels. Sources: Abootorabi et al. (arXiv 2502.08826) , Mei et al. (arXiv 2504.08748) , Zheng et al. (arXiv 2503.18016) , MuRAG (arXiv 2210.02928) , CLIP (arXiv 2103.00020) , SigLIP 2 (arXiv 2502.14786) . Recap What to keep from this lesson Multimodal RAG = retrievers per modality (or a shared space) + fusion + a generator that cites sources. A shared space (CLIP, CLAP) lets a text query find photos or sounds directly. Never add raw scores from different models; normalise per query first. RRF needs no calibration but ignores confidence; weighted fusion needs labelled queries to tune. Decide explicitly how to score an item that lacks a modality. Check every citation in code. Solutions Solution P1 · Photos win alone; tuned fusion wins overall; RRF disappoints The photo retriever wins alone: 62% R-precision against 36% for captions, because a clear photo shows the object while most captions say nothing about it. Fusion beats both only if the scores are made comparable first: the raw sum (61%) is slightly worse than photos alone, min-max with equal weights reaches 65%, and a tuned photo weight of 0.75 reaches 70%, the ceiling set by posts with neither a clear photo nor a useful caption. Reciprocal rank fusion came last of the fusion methods (55%). It treats the caption retriever's ranks as just as meaningful as the photo ranks, even for vague captions where they are noise. Solution B1 · Spread decides, and equal weights amplify noise With a raw sum, the audio retriever contributes almost nothing to the ranking. Its scores differ by at most 0.1 between clips, while text scores differ by up to 0.5, so text decides the order. The high level of the audio scores does not matter: adding nearly the same amount to every item does not change who is first. If audio is the most useful signal for the query ("engine knocking sound"), it is ignored. Min-max scaling every retriever and weighting them equally overcorrects. Now the audio retriever's tiny differences are stretched to the full 0–1 range, as large as the text differences. When the query has nothing to do with sound, those differences are noise, and the noise gets a third of the vote. What works: normalise per query, then set the weights from labelled queries (held out from the evaluation), per query type if needed. Or learn a gate on those labels, which is what MoE-style fusion does. Measure each retriever alone too: if one never helps, remove it. Before you start Needs : Phase 12 · 05 (LLaVA), Phase 12 · 09 (Qwen-VL JSON), Phase 14 (Agent Engineering) Type : Capstone. Time : about 240 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, action schema + agent loop skeleton), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The 2026 frontier product is a multimodal agent that reads screenshots, clicks buttons, navigates web UIs, fills forms, and completes workflows end-to-end. SeeClick and CogAgent (2024) proved the GUI-grounding primitive. Ferret-UI added mobile. ChartAgent introduced visual tool-use for charts. Benchmarks such as OSWorld (desktop tasks), VisualWebArena (web tasks) and AgentVista (hard visual tool use, 2026) track the progress; on AgentVista the best model in its paper, Gemini 3 Pro, solves only 27%. This capstone pulls together every thread of Phase 12: perception (high-res VLM), reasoning (LL Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means GUI grounding "Click coordinates" Model outputs (x,y) for the target of an instruction on a screenshot Action schema "Tool definitions" JSON description of valid actions (click, type, scroll, drag) Accessibility tree "Structured DOM" Machine-readable UI hierarchy from browser/iOS APIs Hybrid agent "Screenshot + tree" Uses both image and structured info; more reliable than either alone Visual tool use "Zoom/crop/detect" Agent calls external vision tools (OCR, detection) mid-plan Summary-chain "Memory compression" Periodic text summaries replace long screenshot history VisualWebArena "E2E web bench" 2024 benchmark for end-to-end web tasks AgentVista "2026 hard bench" 209 hard visual tool-use tasks; the best model in its paper (Gemini 3 Pro) solves 27% The problem In plain words first A computer-use agent operates software the way a person does. It looks at a screenshot, decides what to do, and outputs an action such as "click at (298, 301)" or "type Tokyo". A harness carries the action out and takes a new screenshot, and the loop repeats until the task is done. This capstone brings Phase 12 together: reading the screen (high-resolution vision), deciding (an LLM with tools), pointing at the right pixel (grounding), remembering earlier steps (memory) and measuring success (benchmarks). The lesson drives a real headless browser through a mock flight booking with a JSON action loop, including a click that goes wrong and is recovered. It then measures how click precision and screenshot size decide whether small buttons get hit, and what a 20-step task costs in context. No model is trained or downloaded; a scripted policy stands in for the VLM. A booking-site workflow: "find me a flight to Tokyo for April 15, aisle seat under $800, book it." A multimodal agent needs to: Take a screenshot of the browser. Parse the screenshot + URL + goal into a plan. Emit a structured action: click (at x,y), type "Tokyo" (at element E), scroll down, select (radio button). Apply the action to the browser. Observe the new state (next screenshot). Repeat until the task is done. Each step is a multimodal VLM call. The VLM output must be parseable JSON. Errors compound across steps, so recovery matters. Idea 1 · GUI grounding — the primitive GUI grounding is: given a screenshot and a natural language instruction, output the (x, y) coordinate to click (or other action). SeeClick (Cheng et al., arXiv:2401.10935) was an early open result at scale: it fine-tunes Qwen-VL on automatically collected web, mobile and desktop GUI data to output click coordinates as plain text tokens, and introduced the ScreenSpot grounding benchmark. Works. CogAgent (arXiv:2312.08914), an 18B model, added a 1120×1120 high-resolution image branch for dense UIs and reported state-of-the-art results at the time on web (Mind2Web) and Android (AITW) navigation. Ferret-UI (Apple, arXiv:2404.05719) focuses on mobile UIs: it splits elongated phone screens into sub-images so small elements stay visible, and is trained on referring and grounding tasks over iOS and Android screens. Output format is usually JSON: Copy The element_desc helps recovery: if coordinates drift between screenshots, the semantic hint lets the system re-ground. Idea 2 · Action schemas A typical action schema has 6-10 action types: click : (x, y) type : (text, x?, y?) scroll : (direction, amount) drag : (x0, y0, x1, y1) select : (option_index) hover : (x, y) navigate : (url) wait : (ms) done : (success, explanation) The agent emits one action per step. The browser wrapper executes and returns the new state. Idea 3 · Screenshot-only vs accessibility-tree Two input modes: Screenshot-only: full image, no structural info. Most general; works on any app. Accessibility tree: structured DOM / iOS accessibility info. Much more reliable for grounding; works where the tree is available. Hybrid: both, with the tree as a reliable grounder for atomic actions and the screenshot for semantic context. Production agents use hybrid when possible. Browser automation (Selenium + accessibility) always has the tree; desktop apps sometimes do. Idea 4 · Long-horizon memory A 20-step workflow generates 20 screenshots. The VLM's context fills up fast. Three compression strategies: Summary-chain: after every 5 steps, summarize what has happened, drop old screenshots. Skip-frame: keep the first, last, and every 3rd screenshot. Tool-recorded log: execute actions, keep a text log of what was done; don't re-look at old screenshots. Anthropic's computer-use documentation suggests a mix: keep the last few screenshots (three, for example) and prune older ones in batches so prompt caching keeps working, while the history of actions stays in the context as text. Predict before you run The agent books a flight in a real headless browser. Between the moment it reads the results page and the moment it clicks "Select", a cookie banner appears at the top and pushes everything down. What happens to the click, and how can the loop notice and recover? (Solution P1.) See it drawn A JSON action loop in a real browser A mock flight-booking site runs in headless Chromium through Playwright. The policy is a fixed plan standing in for the VLM; at each step it finds its target in the accessibility tree (hybrid grounding) and emits a JSON action: click with coordinates, or type. The harness validates the action, executes it, checks that the page changed as expected, and re-grounds by the action's element_desc if not. The agent stops at the review page and asks for confirmation instead of paying. About 2 seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Every action is a small, checkable JSON object. Typing steps carry the text and a description of the field; click steps carry pixel coordinates plus element_desc . The harness rejects anything outside the schema before touching the page, and checks each typed field's value afterwards. Step 5 goes wrong, silently. The agent grounded "Select SF 205" at (298, 190) while the results page was fresh. Then the cookie banner arrived and pushed the content 111 pixels down. The click at (298, 190) landed on empty space: no error, no exception, just no effect. The check catches it, and element_desc fixes it. The harness compares the accessibility tree before and after each click. Nothing changed, so it looks the element up again by its description, finds it at (298, 301), and clicks there. A screenshot-only agent would have to take a new screenshot and ground again, which is the same idea at higher cost. The agent stops before paying. The final tree shows the review page ("SF 205, Aisle seat, total $760") and a "Pay and book" button it did not press. The done action reports what it found and hands the payment decision to the user. Each look at the screen costs 1,334 tokens at 1280 × 800, which is why memory strategy matters (next run). See it drawn How precise must a click be, and what does memory cost? Four targets on a 2560 × 1440 page, from a 16-pixel close icon to a large card. 400 clicks per setting are aimed at each target's centre with Gaussian error, and the browser itself reports what was hit ( elementFromPoint ). The error is applied either to a full-size screenshot or to one sent at half size. Then the context cost of a 20-step task under three memory strategies. About a second. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Small targets need precise pointing. For the 16-pixel close icon, 94% of clicks land with a 4-pixel error, 48% with 8 pixels and 18% with 16. The 140 × 44 button still gets 84% at 16 pixels, and the large card 100% everywhere. The measured numbers match the erf formula above. A half-size screenshot doubles the error. The same model error, made on a 1280 × 720 copy of a 2560 × 1440 screen, becomes twice as many pixels on the real screen: the close icon drops from 94% to 48% at σ = 4, the 32-pixel icon from 92% to 49% at σ = 8. Saving tokens on screenshots costs accuracy on small targets. A zoom action (crop a region and look again at full resolution) gets precision back where it is needed. Keeping every screenshot gets expensive fast. At step 20 the request holds 29,680 tokens, and the 20 requests together send 311,640. Keeping the last 3 screenshots plus a text log cuts the total to about a third (107,538); keeping only the current screenshot plus the log, to under a fifth (58,180). Prompt caching lowers the price of the repeated part, which is why Anthropic suggests pruning in batches rather than every step. Idea 5 · Visual tool use ChartAgent (arXiv:2510.04514) introduces visual tool use for chart understanding: crop, zoom, OCR, call external detection. The agent can output "crop to region (100, 200, 300, 400) then call OCR" as a tool call. The tool returns text; the VLM continues reasoning. This pattern generalizes: set-of-mark prompting, region annotation, and external detection tools all fit the same "output a tool call, receive a structured response" schema. Idea 6 · The 2026 benchmarks ScreenSpot-Pro (2025). GUI grounding in professional desktop software: 1,581 instructions across 23 applications on high-resolution screens, where the average target covers 0.07% of the screen. At release GPT-4o scored 0.8% and the best grounding model 18.9% (OS-Atlas-7B), 48.1% with a planner that zooms in; specialised grounding models have since climbed much higher. VisualWebArena (2024). 910 visually grounded web tasks on classifieds, shopping and Reddit-style sites. At release the best agent (GPT-4V with set-of-marks) succeeded on 16.4% of tasks; humans on 88.7%. AgentVista (arXiv:2602.23166, 2026). 209 hard tasks on real images across 7 categories, solved with web search, image search, page visits and a code interpreter: a visual tool-use benchmark rather than GUI control. Best in its paper: Gemini 3 Pro 27.3%; the best open model, Qwen3-VL-235B, 12.9%. OSWorld (2024). 369 tasks in real desktop operating systems, where humans succeed on about 72% and the best agent at release on about 12%. On its corrected version, OSWorld-Verified, the best reported agents in 2026 exceed 80%. WebArena / WebShop. Earlier web benchmarks over HTML and text, still used for comparison. Idea 7 · Why it's still hard Agent performance bottlenecks: Visual grounding at fine scale. "Click the small X" fails often at mobile resolution. Long-horizon planning. After 10 actions, the agent drifts from the goal. Error recovery. When a click fails (wrong button), detecting + recovering is rarely trained data. Cross-page context. Jumping between tabs or long forms loses state. Research directions: memory architectures, explicit replanning, multimodal verification (screenshot match for action success). Idea 8 · The capstone build-it The capstone task: build a computer-use agent that: Reads the HTML + screenshot of a booking-site mock page. Plans a multi-step sequence: search → select → fill form → submit. Emits JSON actions matching the action schema. Evaluates on a fixed 10-task slice. The lesson provides scaffold code that is easy to extend into a real browser. Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py is the capstone scaffold: Action schema JSON definition (10 actions: the nine listed above plus screenshot_region , a crop + zoom tool). Mock browser state as dict. Agent loop skeleton: receive state, emit action, apply, loop. 10-task mini-benchmark (synthetic pages) to measure end-to-end success rate. Error-recovery hook for when an action fails. Break it on purpose To save tokens, an agent on a 2560 × 1440 screen sends screenshots scaled to 1280 × 720, but the harness executes the model's coordinates as they come, without scaling them back. What does the agent click, and how do you make this class of bug impossible to miss? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Computer-use APIs from the model vendors : Anthropic's computer use tool (screenshot, click, type, scroll, zoom), OpenAI's computer-use model, and Google's Gemini computer use model each take screenshots and return actions for your harness to execute. The vendors recommend modest screen sizes (Anthropic suggests about 1024 × 768 to 1366 × 768), a sandboxed VM, an allowlist of sites and human confirmation for consequential actions. Browser harnesses with accessibility trees : Playwright (used here) and the Playwright MCP server give agents the page's accessibility snapshot alongside or instead of screenshots; open-source libraries such as browser-use build agents on top. Open GUI models : UI-TARS (2B to 72B) and the Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL families ground clicks and run agent loops; the 2B–3B sizes fit an 8 GB laptop GPU, 7B in 4-bit. Prompt injection from the screen : text on a web page can try to give the agent orders. Treat everything on screen as data, confirm consequential steps with the user, and keep credentials away from the model. Sources: Claude computer use tool , OSWorld , VisualWebArena (arXiv 2401.13649) , ScreenSpot-Pro (arXiv 2504.07981) , AgentVista (arXiv 2602.23166) , SeeClick (arXiv 2401.10935) . Recap What to keep from this lesson The loop: screenshot (and tree) → model → JSON action → harness → new screenshot. Validate every action against the schema; verify every effect on the page. Keep an element description with each click so a stale coordinate can be re-grounded. Small targets need precise clicks; downscaled screenshots multiply the error; zoom helps. Keep a text log and only the last few screenshots. Stop and ask before consequential actions; treat on-screen text as data. What tasks benefit? Read AgentVista (arXiv:2602.23166). Which tasks need the most tool calls, and why do frontier models still fail them? Long-horizon memory compression: design a summary-chain with ≤4 screenshots kept live, any number logged. Build an error-recovery hook: on action failure (button not found), what does the agent do next? Compare screenshot-only Claude 4.7 to hybrid screenshot + accessibility-tree Qwen2.5-VL on 10 web tasks. Which wins on which tasks? Solutions Solution P1 · The click hits empty space, and only a check notices The click lands on empty space. The agent computed (298, 190) from the page as it was. The banner then pushed the results 111 pixels down, so the button was now at (298, 301). Clicking empty space raises no error, so an agent that does not check would carry on as if it had selected the flight. The harness noticed because it compares the page's accessibility tree before and after every click: nothing changed. It then re-grounded the same element_desc , "button 'Select SF 205'", in the current tree and clicked the new centre. The check here is "did anything change". If the stale click had landed on "Select SF 101" instead, the page would have changed, to the wrong flight. A stronger check compares the result with what the action was meant to do (the heading should now say SF 205) and, if it is wrong, goes back before continuing. Solution B1 · Every click lands in the top-left quarter The model's coordinates are in the 1280 × 720 image. Executed unscaled on the 2560 × 1440 screen, each click lands at half the intended x and y: every click falls in the top-left quarter of the screen. A "Pay" button the model sees at (1000, 600), really at (2000, 1200), is never pressed; whatever sits at (1000, 600) on the real screen is pressed instead. It may be harmless, or it may be another button, and nothing raises an error. To make this class of bug impossible to miss: One conversion function , used for every action: store the scale factor with each screenshot and map image coordinates to screen coordinates in one place (as Anthropic's documentation does with get_scale_factor ). Bounds checks : reject coordinates outside the image the model was shown. Verify every action's effect (as in the first run), so a click that lands somewhere unexpected stops the loop. A calibration test : click a known element on a test page at both resolutions and assert that the right element was hit. Prefer element references from the accessibility tree where the app has one; coordinates only where it does not.
