a1301: Course home / Phase 13 · Tools & Protocols The Tool Interface — Why Agents Need Structured I/O Lesson 13.1 45 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain why an LLM that can only generate text cannot, on its own, take actions against the real world. Draw the four-step tool-call loop (describe → decide → execute → observe) and name who owns each step. Write a tool definition as four parts: name, description, JSON Schema input, and a deterministic executor function. Distinguish pure and side-effecting tools and state why the split matters for safety. Before you start Needs : Phase 11 (LLM completion APIs) Type : Learn. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, no LLM). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A language model produces tokens. A program takes actions. The gap between those two is the tool interface: a contract that lets the model request an action and the host execute it. Every 2026 stack — function calling on OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini; MCP's tools/call ; A2A's task parts — is a different encoding of the same four-step loop. This lesson names the loop and shows the minimum machinery to run it. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Tool "A thing the model can call" A triple of name + JSON-Schema-typed input + executor function Function calling "Native tool use" Provider-level API support for emitting structured tool calls instead of prose Tool call "The model's request to act" A JSON payload with id , name , arguments emitted by the model Tool result "What the tool returned" The executor's output, wrapped in a tool role message with matching id Parallel tool calls "Many calls at once" Multiple call objects in one model turn, independent and orderable by id Strict mode "Guaranteed JSON" Constrained decoding that forces the model's output to validate against the declared schema Pure tool "Read-only tool" No side effects; safe to re-run Consequential tool "Action tool" Mutates external state; requires gate, audit, or user confirmation Four-step loop "The tool-call cycle" describe → decide → execute → observe Host "Agent runtime" The program that holds the tool registry, calls the model, and runs the executor The problem In plain words first A language model can only write text. To check today's weather or send an email, it needs a program to act for it. A tool interface is the agreement between the two. The program tells the model which tools exist: a name, a description and the shape of the arguments. The model answers either in words or with a request such as "call get_weather with city = Tokyo". The program checks the request, runs the tool, and gives the result back to the model, which then answers or asks for another tool. That four-step loop (describe, decide, execute, observe) is the same in OpenAI's, Anthropic's and Google's APIs and in MCP. This lesson runs the loop with a real 0.5B open model on a laptop CPU, including the ways it goes wrong: a call written as prose, an unnecessary call, and an email that waits for the user's permission. No model is trained. An LLM emits a probability distribution over the next token. That is the entire output surface. If you ask a chat model "what is the weather in Bengaluru right now," it can write a plausible sentence, but it cannot dial into a weather API. The sentence might be right by coincidence or three days stale. Closing that gap is the purpose of the tool interface. The host program — your agent runtime, Claude Desktop, ChatGPT, Cursor, or a custom script — advertises a list of callable tools to the model. The model, when it decides an action is needed, emits a structured payload naming a tool and its arguments. The host parses that payload, runs the tool for real, and feeds the result back. The loop continues until the model decides no more calls are needed. The first version of this contract shipped in June 2023 as OpenAI's "functions" parameter. Anthropic previewed tool use with Claude 2.1 (November 2023) and shipped tool_use content blocks in 2024. Gemini's API launched with functionDeclarations in December 2023. Every provider now exposes the same shape: a JSON-Schema-typed tool list in, a JSON-payload tool call out. The Model Context Protocol (November 2024) generalized the contract so one tool registry serves every model. A2A (announced April 2025, v1.0 in March 2026) layered the same primitive for agent-to-agent delegation. The four-step loop is the invariant underneath all of these. Everything else in Phase 13 is an elaboration. Idea 1 · Step one: describe The host declares each tool to the model with three fields. The fourth part, the executor, stays on the host side and never reaches the model. Name. A stable, machine-readable identifier. get_weather , not "weather thing". Description. A one-paragraph natural-language brief. "Use when the user asks about current conditions for a specific city. Do not use for historical data." Input schema. A JSON Schema object (draft 2020-12) describing the tool's arguments. The model receives the list. Modern providers serialize these declarations into the system prompt using a provider-specific template, so you as the caller only deal with the structured form. Idea 2 · Step two: decide Given the user's message and the available tools, the model chooses one of three behaviors. Answer directly in text. No tool call. Call one or more tools. Emit structured call objects. Parallel calls are on by default on OpenAI ( parallel_tool_calls ), Anthropic (turn off with disable_parallel_tool_use ) and Gemini, so the model can emit several calls in one turn. Refuse. Decline in plain text. OpenAI's structured outputs report a refusal in a separate refusal field, so code can tell it apart from a valid result. A tool call payload has three stable fields: a call id , a tool name , and a JSON arguments object. The id exists so the host can correlate the later result with the specific call, which matters when parallel calls come back out of order. Idea 3 · Step three: execute The host receives the call, validates arguments against the declared schema, and runs the executor. Invalid arguments mean the model hallucinated a field or used the wrong type — a very common failure mode on weak models. Production hosts do one of three things on invalid arguments: fail fast and surface the error to the model, repair the JSON with a constrained parser, or retry the model with the validation error included in the prompt. The executor itself is ordinary code. Python, TypeScript, a shell command, a database query. It produces a result, which is usually a string but can be any JSON value or a structured content block (text, image, or resource reference in MCP). The result must be serializable. Idea 4 · Step four: observe The host appends the tool result to the conversation (as a tool role message with matching id ) and re-invokes the model. The model now has the tool output in context and can produce a final answer or request more calls. This continues until the model stops emitting calls or the host hits a safety limit on iteration count. The same idea as a formula The loop. Let ​ be the conversation at turn and the model. Each turn the model returns either text or a list of calls ​ = ( id i ​ , name i ​ , args i ​ ) : ​ , T ) ∈ { text } ∪ {[ c 1 ​ , … , c k ​ ]} , m t + 1 ​ = m t ​ + [ c 1 ​ , … , c k ​ ] + [ r 1 ​ , … , r k ​ ] , where is the tool list and ​ = run ( c i ​ ) if ​ validates against the tool's schema, or an error message otherwise. The loop stops at the first text answer or at ​ . Errors compound. If each call is well-formed with probability , a task that needs calls gets through with no bad call with probability . With one retry after a validation error, each call fails only if both attempts fail: without retries , ( 1 − ( 1 − p ) 2 ) k with one retry. Describe costs tokens on every request : ​ tokens(name + description + schema) , paid once per model call, so once per turn of the loop. Worked example Ten calls, one retry, and the price of describing , a task with calls: ≈ 0.60 . Four tasks in ten hit at least one bad call. With one retry: each call fails with probability = 0.0025 , so ≈ 0.975 . In the run below, two short tools add 252 prompt tokens to every request. A 4-turn loop pays that 4 times: 1,008 tokens. Twenty tools of about 120 tokens each would add about 2,400 tokens to every turn. A bound of ​ = 5 turns caps the cost of a confused model at 5 model calls, however long it keeps calling tools. Check your mental model ✗ "The model runs the tool." ✓ The model only writes a request; the host validates it, runs the code and reports back. ✗ "The executor's code is sent to the model." ✓ Only the name, description and schema are; the executor stays on the host. ✗ "If the reply contains JSON, the model made a tool call." ✓ A call counts only in the format the host parses (here <tool_call> tags); JSON in prose is a format error to repair. ✗ "A model with tools will use them only when needed." ✓ Small models call tools eagerly; the descriptions and the host's checks have to compensate. Predict before you run A 0.5B open model gets two tools, get_weather and send_email , and four questions: Tokyo's weather, a comparison of two cities, an email to send, and the capital of France. Which ones will it handle correctly? (Solution P1.) See it drawn The four-step loop with a real model Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (about 1 GB, runs on a laptop CPU) receives the tool list through its chat template. The host parses <tool_call> blocks, validates the arguments with jsonschema , refuses to run the consequential send_email without user confirmation, runs the rest, and returns the results as tool messages. Greedy decoding, at most 5 turns. About 40 seconds on CPU. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Tokyo: a correct call with a choice nobody asked for. The model called get_weather with valid arguments, but picked Fahrenheit on its own; the schema allowed it and the description gave no default. The host converted, and the answer (53.6 °F) is right but not what most users want. Descriptions and schema defaults steer these choices. The comparison: a call written as prose. The model explained that it would call get_weather and printed the call as a JSON code block, outside the <tool_call> tags the host parses. The host saw no call, treated the text as the final answer, and the reply ran out at the 120-token limit. This is the "JSON in prose" failure from Idea 7, on the second question. The email: the gate works. The call was well-formed, but send_email is consequential, so the host refused to run it without confirmation and said so. The model passed that on, though it also asked for the address it already had: small models misread tool results too. The capital of France: an unnecessary call. The answer needs no tool, yet the model called get_weather for Paris and added the temperature to a correct answer. Harmless here; with a paid or slow tool it is wasted time and money. One question out of four went exactly right. Frontier models do much better, but every one of these failure kinds occurs in production, which is why the host validates, gates and bounds the loop. See it drawn What "describe" sends, and repairing a format error This block continues from the one above. It prints the prompt text the chat template builds from the two tools and counts its tokens. Then it reruns the comparison question with one change to the host: a reply that contains a call written as prose is sent back with an instruction to use the proper format. About 15 seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Describing tools costs 252 tokens per request. The chat template pastes each tool's JSON into a system message inside <tools> tags, followed by an instruction to answer with <tool_call> blocks. The model has no other knowledge of the tools: wording in the description is all it can go on. The repair fixes the format. After the host's correction ("emit each call inside <tool_call> tags"), the model makes a proper call on the next turn. It does not fix the reasoning. The model fetched only Zurich's temperature and then answered about Zurich alone; the comparison with Bengaluru never happened. Format repair is cheap and worth doing, but it cannot make a small model plan a two-call task. Bigger models, clearer descriptions, or a host that checks whether the question was answered are the next steps. Idea 5 · The trust split Tools come in two flavors that matter for safety. Pure. Read-only, deterministic, no side effects. get_weather , search_docs , get_current_time . Safe to call speculatively. Consequential. Mutates state, spends money, touches user data. send_email , delete_file , execute_trade . Must be gated. Meta's "Agents Rule of Two" (October 2025) says a single agent session should combine at most two of: untrusted input, access to sensitive data or systems, and the ability to change state or communicate externally. The tool interface is where you enforce that rule — by rejecting calls, requiring user confirmation, or escalating scopes. See Phase 13 · 15 for the full security chapter and Phase 14 · 09 for agent-level permission policies. Idea 6 · Where the loop lives Context Who describes Who decides Who executes Single-turn function calling (OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini) App developer LLM App developer MCP MCP server LLM via MCP client MCP server A2A Agent Card publisher Calling agent Called agent Web browser (function-calling agent) Browser extension / WebMCP LLM Browser runtime Everywhere, the same four steps. The column names change; the structure does not. Idea 7 · Why not just prompt the model to emit JSON? "Ask the model to reply in JSON" was the pre-function-calling pattern. It fails often enough to matter, rarely on frontier models and far more on small ones (the 0.5B model below does it on its second question). Failure modes include missing braces, trailing commas, hallucinated fields, wrong types, and JSON wrapped in prose. You then need a JSON repair pass, a retry, or a constrained decoder. Native function calling is better for three reasons. First, the provider trains the model on the exact call shape, so well-formed calls are the norm. Second, the call payload sits in its own protocol slot, not inside free-text — so a tool call never leaks into the user-visible reply. Third, providers can enforce schema compliance with constrained decoding (OpenAI's strict: true , Anthropic's strict tool use, Gemini's response schemas); in strict mode the arguments are guaranteed to validate. Phase 13 · 02 walks the three provider APIs side by side. Phase 13 · 04 goes deep on structured outputs. Idea 8 · Circuit breakers The loop terminates when the model stops emitting calls or the host hits a maximum turn count. Production hosts set such a bound, commonly between 5 and 25 turns; the OpenAI Agents SDK, for example, stops after 10 turns unless you raise max_turns . The alternative — unbounded loops — shows up every six months as "agent spent $400 in API calls overnight" post-mortems. Do not ship without a bound. Phase 14 · 12 covers error recovery and self-healing in depth; Phase 17 covers production rate limits. Idea 9 · Where Phase 13 goes from here Lessons 02 through 05 polish the provider-level tool-call surface. Lessons 06 through 14 generalize the loop into MCP. Lessons 15 through 18 defend the loop against hostile servers, adversarial users, and unauthenticated remote auth surfaces. Lessons 19 through 22 extend the pattern to agent-to-agent collaboration, observability, routing, and packaging. Lesson 13.23 ships a complete ecosystem using every primitive. Every remaining lesson is an elaboration of this four-step loop. Hold it in mind as the invariant. Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py runs the four-step loop without an LLM. A fake "decider" function simulates the model by pattern-matching on the user message; the executor, schema validator, and observe-step harness are real. Run it to see the full request/response choreography with printable intermediate state, then replace the fake decider with any real provider in a later lesson. What to look at: The tool registry holds four fields per tool: name, description, schema, and an executor reference. Only the first three go to the model. The validator is a minimal JSON Schema subset (types, required, enum, min/max) written in stdlib only. Phase 13 · 04 ships a fuller one. The loop bounds iteration count at five. Production agents need exactly this kind of circuit breaker. Break it on purpose Remove the turn limit from the loop and give the model a tool whose result always says "partial result, call again for more". What happens to cost and latency, and what should the host do instead? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) The same loop in every major API : OpenAI (Responses API function tools), Anthropic ( tool_use and tool_result blocks) and Google Gemini ( functionDeclarations ) all take JSON Schema tool lists and return calls with an id, a name and arguments. Strict modes guarantee valid arguments : OpenAI's strict: true and Anthropic's strict tool use constrain decoding so the arguments always match the schema. MCP 2026-07-28 is the current revision of the Model Context Protocol: stateless, with tool lists that one server offers to any MCP-capable client (Lessons 13.6–13.14). Agent SDKs run the loop for you : the OpenAI Agents SDK, the Claude Agent SDK and LangGraph handle parsing, tool execution and turn limits ( max_turns ), and leave confirmation gates to you. Laptop-sized tool calling : Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 models from 0.5B to 4B, and Llama 3.2 1B/3B, support tool calls through their chat templates; expect more format errors than from frontier models, as the run shows. Sources: OpenAI function calling , Anthropic tool use , Claude strict tool use , Gemini function calling , MCP specification 2026-07-28 , Meta: Agents Rule of Two . Validate every call before running it; return errors to the model so it can retry. Gate consequential tools behind user confirmation. Always bound the loop with a turn limit. Solutions Solution P1 · One right, one half-right, one gated, one unnecessary call Only Tokyo went right, and even there the model chose Fahrenheit unasked. The comparison failed on format: the call was written as JSON in prose, which the host does not parse. The email was a correct call that the host correctly refused to run without confirmation. The capital of France got a correct answer plus an unnecessary weather call. The pattern is typical of small models: they know the call format but apply it unreliably, call tools too eagerly, and lose track of multi-step questions. The host's checks (parsing only the official format, schema validation, confirmation gates, a turn limit) are what keep these errors from turning into wrong actions. Solution B1 · The loop never ends on its own Without a turn limit the loop never ends on its own: every result asks for another call, and the model obliges. Cost grows faster than the number of turns, because each turn resends the whole conversation. If each turn adds tokens, turn sends about tokens and turns send about /2 : 100 turns cost about 50 times as much as 10, not 10 times. Latency grows the same way, and the user waits for nothing. What the host should do: A hard turn limit (5 to 25 is typical), after which it stops and reports what it has. A budget in tokens or money per task, checked every turn. Loop detection : the same tool called with the same arguments twice in a row is almost always a loop; stop or return an error that says so. Honest tool results : a paginated tool should return a cursor and say how much is left, so the model (or the host) can decide when enough is enough. Translate one tool declaration across all three provider formats and predict where strict-mode constraints will differ. Use tool_choice in each provider to force, forbid, or auto-pick tool calls. Know the per-provider hard limits (tool count, schema depth, argument length) and the error signatures each one emits when limits are violated. Before you start Needs : Phase 13 · 01 (the tool interface) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, schema translators). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The three frontier providers converged on the same tool-call loop in 2024 and then diverged on everything else. OpenAI uses tools and tool_calls . Anthropic uses tool_use and tool_result blocks. Gemini uses functionDeclarations and unique-id correlation. This lesson diffs the three side by side so code that ships on one provider does not break when you port it. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Function calling "Tool use" Provider-level API for structured tool-call emission Tool declaration "Tool spec" Name + description + JSON Schema input payload tool_choice "Force / forbid" Auto / required / none / specific-name modes Strict mode "Schema enforcement" OpenAI flag that constrains decoding to match schema tool_use block "Anthropic's call shape" Inline content block with id, name, input functionCall part "Gemini's call shape" A parts[] entry containing name, args, and id Arguments-as-string "Stringified JSON" OpenAI returns args as a JSON string, not an object Parallel tool calls "Fan-out in one turn" Multiple tool calls in one assistant message Refusal "Model declines" OpenAI structured outputs return a refusal field instead of schema-valid output OpenAPI 3.0 subset "Gemini schema quirk" Gemini uses a JSON-Schema-like dialect with minor differences The problem In plain words first OpenAI, Anthropic and Google all run the same tool loop from Lesson 13.1, but each spells it differently. The tool list sits in a different wrapper. The model's call comes back in a different place, and OpenAI sends the arguments as a JSON string while the others send an object. The result goes back in a different kind of message, and the switches that force or forbid tool use have different names. Code written for one provider breaks on the next for these reasons alone. This lesson lines the three formats up field by field. It then builds one canonical tool with translators to each format, checks every translated piece against the providers' own Python SDK types, and converts a schema to OpenAI's strict-mode rules. No network calls and no model are needed. The shape of a function-calling request differs by provider. Three concrete examples from 2026 production stacks: OpenAI Chat Completions / Responses API. You pass tools: [{type: "function", function: {name, description, parameters, strict}}] . The model's response contains choices[0].message.tool_calls: [{id, type: "function", function: {name, arguments}}] where arguments is a JSON string you must parse. Strict mode ( strict: true ) enforces schema compliance via constrained decoding. Anthropic Messages API. You pass tools: [{name, description, input_schema}] . The response comes back as content: [{type: "text"}, {type: "tool_use", id, name, input}] . input is already parsed (an object, not a string). You reply with a new user message containing a {type: "tool_result", tool_use_id, content} block. Google Gemini API. In generateContent you pass tools: [{functionDeclarations: [{name, description, parameters}]}] (nested under functionDeclarations ; parametersJsonSchema takes plain JSON Schema). The response arrives as candidates[0].content.parts: [{functionCall: {name, args, id}}] , and you reply with {functionResponse: {name, id, response}} . Google's newer Interactions API names the same two steps function_call and function_result , linked by call_id . Same loop. Different field names, different nesting, different string-vs-object conventions, different correlation mechanisms. A team that writes a weather agent on OpenAI pays a two-day port to Anthropic and another day to Gemini just for the plumbing. This lesson builds a translator that unifies the three formats into one canonical tool declaration and routes at the edge. Phase 13 · 17 generalizes the same pattern into an LLM gateway. Idea 1 · The common structure Every provider needs five things: Tool list. Per-tool name, description, and input schema. Tool choice. Force a specific tool, forbid tools, or let the model decide. Call emission. Structured output naming the tool and arguments. Call id. Correlate the response to the right call (matters for parallel). Result injection. A message or block that ties the result back to the call. Idea 2 · Shape diffs, field by field Aspect OpenAI Anthropic Gemini Declaration envelope {type: "function", function: {...}} {name, description, input_schema} {functionDeclarations: [{...}]} Schema field parameters input_schema parameters Response container tool_calls[] on assistant message content[] of type tool_use parts[] of type functionCall Arguments type stringified JSON parsed object parsed object Id format call_... (OpenAI generates) toolu_... (Anthropic) id on each functionCall Result block role tool , tool_call_id user with tool_result , tool_use_id functionResponse with matching id Force-a-tool tool_choice: {type: "function", function: {name}} tool_choice: {type: "tool", name} function_calling_config: {mode: "ANY", allowed_function_names: [name]} Forbid tools tool_choice: "none" tool_choice: {type: "none"} mode: "NONE" Strict schema strict: true per tool strict: true per tool (opt-in) mode: "VALIDATED" ; responseSchema for plain JSON output Idea 3 · Limits you will actually hit OpenAI. Up to 128 tools per request. Strict mode: every property listed in required , additionalProperties: false on every object, an object at the root (not anyOf ), at most 10 levels of nesting, 5,000 properties and 1,000 enum values in total. $defs / $ref and recursive schemas are supported. Anthropic. No small fixed tool cap is documented, but every definition costs prompt tokens on every call; for large catalogs Anthropic offers a tool search tool that loads definitions on demand. Strict tool use is opt-in with strict: true on the tool definition. Without it, the schema is a contract the model tends to follow, not a guarantee. Gemini. parameters takes an OpenAPI 3.0-style subset of JSON Schema; parametersJsonSchema takes JSON Schema directly. Gemini 3 models also return thought signatures, which must be sent back unchanged with the conversation. Idea 4 · tool_choice behavior Three modes everyone supports, named differently. Auto. Model picks tool or text. Default. Required / Any. Model must call at least one tool. None. Model must not call tools. Plus one mode unique to each provider: OpenAI. Force a specific tool by name. Anthropic. Force a specific tool by name; disable_parallel_tool_use flag separates single vs multi. Gemini. mode: "VALIDATED" lets the model answer in text or call a function, and constrains any call to the declared schema; allowed_function_names restricts which functions may be called. The same idea as a formula Translate, call, parse. For provider , a translator ​ wraps the canonical tool in that provider's envelope, and a parser ​ pulls the canonical call out of the provider's response ​ . Portable code needs ​ ( R p ​ ) = c for every p , with args = json.loads ( ⋅ ) only for OpenAI. Strict mode (OpenAI) as a rewrite rule. For an object schema with properties and required set , strict mode needs . Each optional property of type becomes "Optional" moves from "may be absent" to "always present, may be null". Worked example One tool, three envelopes The weather tool has one required property ( city ) and one optional ( units ). OpenAI strict mode turns units into type ["string", "null"] with null added to its enum, and lists both in required . The model's call get_weather(city="Tokyo") arrives as "{\"city\": \"Tokyo\"}" (a string of 17 characters) from OpenAI and as {"city": "Tokyo"} (an object) from Anthropic and Gemini. Forgetting json.loads on OpenAI, or calling it on the others, is the most common porting bug. Forcing the tool: OpenAI names it in tool_choice , Anthropic uses {"type": "tool", "name": ...} , Gemini combines mode: "ANY" with allowed_function_names . Check your mental model ✗ "All three providers return tool arguments as JSON objects." ✓ OpenAI returns a JSON string you must parse; Anthropic and Gemini return parsed objects. ✗ "Optional fields work the same in strict mode." ✓ OpenAI strict mode requires every field; optional ones become nullable. ✗ " tool_choice: required exists everywhere." ✓ It is required on OpenAI, {"type": "any"} on Anthropic and mode: "ANY" on Gemini. ✗ "The result goes back as a normal user message." ✓ It must carry the call's id: tool_call_id , tool_use_id or the functionResponse id. Predict before you run One canonical get_weather tool is translated to the three formats, and one response of each provider's shape is parsed back. Will the three parsed calls be identical? And which translated piece is most likely to be rejected by a provider SDK's type checks? (Solution P1.) See it drawn Three envelopes, checked by the providers' own SDK types One canonical tool is translated into OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini declarations. Each is validated against the official Python SDKs' type definitions ( openai , anthropic , google-genai ), without any network call. Three hand-written responses are parsed by the SDKs' response models, reduced to one canonical call, and answered with a result message in each provider's format. A couple of seconds. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The three declarations carry identical content. Name, description and schema are the same; only the wrapper differs: OpenAI nests them under function with parameters , Anthropic puts them at the top level with input_schema , and Gemini lists them under function_declarations , here with parameters_json_schema so the JSON Schema passes through unchanged. All three pass the SDKs' own type checks. The parsed calls are identical. Each response keeps its call in a different place: choices[0].message.tool_calls for OpenAI, a tool_use block in content for Anthropic, a function_call part for Gemini. After parsing, all three give get_weather with {"city": "Tokyo"} . Only OpenAI needed json.loads , because its arguments arrive as a string. The ids differ, and they matter. call_abc , toolu_abc and fc_abc each go back with the result: as tool_call_id in a tool message, as tool_use_id in a tool_result block inside a user message, and as id in a Gemini function_response part. Gemini also wraps the result object in a response dict. See it drawn tool_choice mapping, strict mode, and caught mistakes This block continues from the one above. It maps four tool-choice intents to each provider and validates them against the SDK types, rewrites the schema for OpenAI strict mode and checks the documented rules, and shows the SDK types rejecting two common porting mistakes. Instant. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Four intents, three vocabularies. "Must call a tool" is "required" on OpenAI, {"type": "any"} on Anthropic and mode: "ANY" on Gemini. "Call this tool" is a named object on OpenAI and Anthropic, and ANY plus allowed_function_names on Gemini. All of them passed the SDK type checks. Strict mode rewrites optional fields. The original schema fails OpenAI's strict rules because units is not in required . The rewritten version lists both fields, makes units nullable (type ["string", "null"] , with null added to the enum) and passes. The executor must now treat null as "use the default". The SDK types catch porting mistakes before a request is sent. An Anthropic tool declared with OpenAI's parameters field is rejected because input_schema is missing, and an OpenAI tool result without tool_call_id is rejected. Running your translated payloads through these types in a unit test costs nothing and catches the most common porting bugs. Idea 5 · Parallel calls OpenAI's parallel_tool_calls (on by default) emits multiple calls in one assistant message; you run them and reply with one tool message per tool_call_id . Claude also calls tools in parallel by default; disable_parallel_tool_use: true limits it to one call, and all tool_result blocks go back in a single user message. Gemini returns several functionCall parts in one turn, each with an id you echo in the matching functionResponse . Idea 6 · Streaming All three support streamed tool calls. The wire format differs: OpenAI. Delta chunks of tool_calls[i].function.arguments arrive incrementally. You accumulate until finish_reason: "tool_calls" . Anthropic. Block-start / block-delta / block-stop events. input_json_delta chunks carry partial arguments. Gemini. Function calls normally arrive whole in a streamed chunk. Streaming one call's arguments in pieces ( stream_function_call_arguments , returned in partial_args ) is a Vertex AI option; the Gemini API does not support it. Phase 13 · 03 goes deep on parallel + streaming reassembly. This lesson focuses on the declaration and single-call shapes. Idea 7 · Errors and repair Invalid-argument errors look different too. OpenAI (non-strict). Model returns arguments: "{bad json}" , your JSON parse fails, you inject an error message and re-call. OpenAI (strict). Validation happens during decoding; invalid JSON is impossible but refusal can appear. Anthropic (non-strict). input may contain unexpected fields; the schema is advisory. Validate server-side. With strict: true , sampling is constrained to the schema. Gemini. Unless mode: "VALIDATED" is set, arguments are not guaranteed to match the schema; validate them yourself. The harness in code/main.py does exactly this, then round-trips a fake tool call through each provider's response shape. No network required — this lesson teaches the shapes, not the HTTP. Production teams usually let a library do this: LangChain's bind_tools , Pydantic AI's toolsets, LlamaIndex's BaseTool , or LiteLLM, which accepts OpenAI-format tools and translates them for other providers. Phase 13 · 17 ships a gateway that exposes an OpenAI-shaped API in front of any of the three. Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py defines one canonical Tool dataclass and three translators that emit the OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini declaration JSON. It then parses a hand-crafted provider response of each shape into the same canonical call object, demonstrating that the semantics are identical under the skin. Run it and diff the three declarations side by side. What to look at: The three declaration blocks differ only in envelope and field names. The three response blocks differ in where the call lives (top-level tool_calls , content[] block, parts[] entry). One canonical_call() function extracts {id, name, args} from all three response shapes. Break it on purpose Port an OpenAI agent to Anthropic by renaming fields only, and keep the line args = json.loads(call.arguments) as args = json.loads(block.input) . What error do you get, and which other porting step is easy to miss when the model makes two parallel calls? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) OpenAI : the Responses API returns function_call items (with call_id and string arguments ) and takes function_call_output items back; Chat Completions keeps tool_calls . strict: true uses Structured Outputs for arguments. Anthropic : tool_use / tool_result blocks, parallel calls by default, opt-in strict tool use, and a tool search tool for large tool catalogs. Google : generateContent with functionDeclarations (and parametersJsonSchema ), VALIDATED mode, thought signatures on Gemini 3; the newer Interactions API uses function_call / function_result steps. Translation layers in production : LiteLLM, LangChain's bind_tools , Pydantic AI and Vercel's AI SDK accept one tool definition and handle every provider's envelope. MCP removes much of this work for tools that live in servers: the client adapts MCP tool lists to whichever model API it calls (Lesson 13.6). Solutions Solution P1 · Identical calls, once the string is parsed Yes, once OpenAI's argument string is parsed with json.loads : all three give get_weather with {"city": "Tokyo"} . Only the ids differ ( call_abc , toolu_abc , fc_abc ), and each must be echoed in that provider's result message. Both fail the SDK type checks immediately. Solution B1 · A TypeError, then a lost parallel result json.loads(block.input) raises TypeError: the JSON object must be str, bytes or bytearray, not dict . Anthropic's input is already a parsed object; only OpenAI sends a string. The fix is to parse per provider (as canonical_call does), never in shared code. The step that is easy to miss with parallel calls: on OpenAI each result is its own tool message, one per tool_call_id . On Anthropic, all the tool_result blocks for one assistant turn must go back together, in a single user message, each with its tool_use_id . Sending them as two separate user messages, or answering only one call, makes the API reject the request or confuses the model about which result belongs to which call. a1303: Course home / Phase 13 · Tools & Protocols Parallel Tool Calls and Streaming with Tools Lesson 13.3 75 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain why parallel_tool_calls: true exists and when to disable it. Run a three-city weather benchmark that demonstrates sequential vs parallel latency. Before you start Needs : Phase 13 · 02 (function calling deep dive) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, thread pool + streaming harness). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Three independent weather lookups serialized is three round trips. Run them in parallel and total time collapses to the slowest single call. Every frontier provider now emits multiple tool calls in a single turn. The payoff is real; the plumbing is subtle. This lesson walks both halves: the parallel fan-out and the streamed-argument reassembly, with emphasis on the id-correlation trap. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Parallel tool calls "Fan-out in one turn" Model emits multiple tool calls in a single assistant message parallel_tool_calls "OpenAI's flag" Enable or disable multi-call emission disable_parallel_tool_use "Anthropic's inverse" Opt-out flag; default is parallel enabled Tool call id "Correlation handle" Per-call identifier the result message must echo Accumulator "Stream buffer" Per-id string buffer for partial arguments chunks Out-of-order completion "Fastest first" Parallel calls finish in unpredictable order; ids are the glue Dependency graph "Ordering constraints" Tools whose outputs feed into inputs of other tools; cannot parallelize Parse-early trap "JSON.parse exploded" Attempting to parse an incomplete arguments string stream_function_call_arguments "Vertex AI option" Streams one call's arguments in partial_args pieces; not supported in the Gemini API Completion-order reply "Don't wait for all" Reply with results as they arrive, keyed by id The problem In plain words first "What's the weather in Bengaluru, Tokyo and Zurich?" needs three tool calls. If the model asks for them one at a time, the program waits for each answer before the model asks for the next. Modern models can instead ask for all three in one turn (parallel tool calls), and the program runs them at the same time, so the wait is the slowest call, not the sum. Two things then need care. Every result must carry the id of the call it answers, because results come back in any order. And when the model's output streams in, each call's arguments arrive in small pieces that must be put back together before they can be parsed. This lesson streams a real 0.5B model that asks for three calls in one turn, runs each call as soon as it is complete, and reassembles interleaved argument pieces from OpenAI-style and Anthropic-style streams. No model is trained. Without parallel calls, an agent answering "what is the weather in Bengaluru, Tokyo, and Zurich" does this: Copy Three LLM round trips, each of which also pays the executor latency. Roughly 4x the ideal wall-clock time. With parallel calls: Copy One LLM round trip. Executor time is the maximum of the three, not the sum. How much this saves depends on how many calls fan out and how slow they are; with several slow tools, it is most of the wait. The price is correlation complexity. When the three calls complete out of order, your results must carry the matching tool_call_id so the model can line them up. When results stream, you must assemble partial argument fragments into complete JSON before executing. Without ids, two parallel calls to the same tool can only be told apart by their order, which is fragile. Idea 1 · Enabling parallel OpenAI. parallel_tool_calls: true on by default. Set false to force serial. Anthropic. Parallel by default. Set disable_parallel_tool_use: true (inside tool_choice ) for at most one call per turn. Gemini. Always parallel-capable; tool_config.function_calling_config.mode = "AUTO" lets the model decide. Disable parallel when tools have ordering dependencies ( create_file then write_file ), when one call's output informs another's input, or when the rate limiter cannot handle fan-out. Idea 2 · Id correlation Every call the model emits has an id . Every result the host returns must include the same id. Without this, results are ambiguous. OpenAI. tool_call_id on each tool-role message. Anthropic. tool_use_id on each tool_result block. Gemini. id on each functionResponse , matching the id of its functionCall . Open models served without ids (Qwen's chat template, for example) match results to calls by order, which is exactly the fragility ids remove. Idea 3 · Running calls concurrently The host runs each call's executor on its own thread, coroutine, or remote worker. The simplest harness uses a thread pool; production uses asyncio with asyncio.gather or structured concurrency. Order of completion is unpredictable — the id is the identifier. One common bug: reply with results in call-list order instead of completion order. This usually works because the model only cares about tool_call_id , but if a result is dropped or duplicated, a reply list that is reordered away from the order the results arrived in makes the gap harder to find in logs. Prefer to reply in completion order with explicit ids. Idea 4 · Streaming tool calls When the model streams, arguments arrive in pieces. Three separate streams of chunks for three parallel calls interleave on the wire. You need one accumulator per id. Shape by provider: OpenAI. Each chunk is choices[0].delta.tool_calls[i].function.arguments (partial string). The chunk carries index (position in the call list). You accumulate per-index, read id when it first appears, and parse JSON when finish_reason = "tool_calls" . Anthropic. Stream events are message_start , then one content_block_start per block with type tool_use (containing id, name, empty input). content_block_delta events carry input_json_delta chunks. content_block_stop closes each block. Gemini. Each function call normally arrives whole within the stream. Streaming one call's arguments in pieces ( stream_function_call_arguments , returned in partial_args ) is a Vertex AI option that the Gemini API does not support. Idea 5 · Partial JSON and the parse-early trap You cannot parse arguments until it is complete. Partial JSON such as {"city": "Beng is not valid and will raise. The correct gate is the provider's end-of-call signal: OpenAI's finish_reason = "tool_calls" , Anthropic's content_block_stop , or Gemini's stream-end event. Only then attempt json.loads . A more robust approach uses an incremental JSON parser that yields events as structure completes; OpenAI's streaming guide recommends this for UX that shows a live "thinking" indicator. Brace-counting is unreliable as a completeness test (braces inside quoted strings or escaped content cause false positives) and should only be used as an informal debug heuristic. Idea 6 · Out-of-order completion Copy The host reply must still cite the ids: Copy Order in the reply does not matter for correctness on OpenAI or Anthropic. Gemini accepts any order so long as ids match. Idea 7 · Benchmark: sequential vs parallel The harness in code/main.py simulates three executors with 400, 600, and 800 ms latency. Sequential runs it in 1800 ms total. Parallel runs it in max(400, 600, 800) = 800 ms. The difference is constant, not proportional, so the savings grow with tool count. Real-world caveat: parallel calls stress downstream APIs. A 10-way fan-out to a rate-limited service will fail. Phase 13 · 17 covers gateway-level backpressure; retry semantics are planned for a future phase. Idea 8 · Streaming fan-out wall-clock If the model itself streams, you can start executing as soon as one call's arguments are complete, rather than waiting for all calls to finalize. This is an optimization OpenAI documents but not all SDKs expose. The harness in this lesson does it: as soon as the simulated stream yields a complete argument object, the host kicks off that call. The same idea as a formula Let call have executor latency ​ , let one model turn take to generate, and let ​ be the moment call 's arguments are complete in the stream ( ​ ≤ g ). One call per turn (no parallelism), with calls: ​ ≈ ∑ i = 1 n ​ ( g i ​ + e i ​ ) + g final ​ . One turn, calls run in parallel after the stream ends: ​ = g + max i ​ e i ​ + g final ​ . One turn, each call dispatched as soon as it is complete in the stream: ​ = max ( g , i max ​ ( s i ​ + e i ​ ) ) + g final ​ . Completeness test. A prefix of an argument string is safe to parse only after the provider's end-of-call signal; json.loads(b) succeeding earlier, or braces balancing, does not prove the string is finished. Saved: 1.0 s. - Dispatch on completion: in the run, the three calls complete in the stream at about 2.6, 4.7 and 6.9 s. Their results are ready at about 3.0, 5.3 and 7.7 s, so only the last call's 0.8 s extends past the stream. - One call per turn would add two more model turns, each with a prefill and a generated call: with about 2 s per call on this CPU, roughly 4 s or more, plus the tool waits. - So on a slow model, parallel calls save mostly model turns; on a fast model with slow tools, they save mostly tool time. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Parallel calls are on by default in the OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini APIs; each offers a switch to turn them off ( parallel_tool_calls: false , disable_parallel_tool_use: true ). Streamed tool arguments : OpenAI sends function.arguments deltas per call index (and response.function_call_arguments.delta events in the Responses API); Anthropic sends input_json_delta events per content block; the SDKs' stream helpers reassemble them for you. Async executors ( asyncio.gather , task groups) are the usual way to run a fan-out; agent SDKs such as the OpenAI Agents SDK and LangGraph's ToolNode run parallel calls concurrently. Open models on a laptop (Qwen2.5 and Qwen3, Llama 3.2) can emit several calls in one turn through their chat templates, as shown here; serving stacks such as vLLM and llama.cpp parse them into OpenAI-style tool_calls with ids. Streamed arguments arrive in pieces, interleaved by call: one buffer per call. Parse only after the end-of-call signal; brace counting is not a test. Keep dependent or rate-limited tools sequential. Dispatching each as soon as it appeared hid the first two calls' tool time inside the model's own generation, so of the 1.8 s of total tool latency the user waited only for Zurich's 0.8 s, because that call came last in the stream. On this CPU the model's generation (about 2 s per call, about 6 s for the final answer) costs far more than the tools. That is the stronger argument for parallel calls here: one model turn instead of three. Solution B1 · A race on the same file Run in parallel, the two calls race. If write_file runs first, it may fail because the file does not exist yet, or create the file itself and then have create_file truncate or reject it. The outcome depends on thread timing, so it changes from run to run: the worst kind of bug to debug. What to do: Declare the dependency : mark tools that touch the same resource as not parallel-safe, and have the host run calls on the same resource in the order the model wrote them. Turn off parallel calls for such agents : parallel_tool_calls: false on OpenAI, disable_parallel_tool_use: true on Anthropic, so the model issues one call, sees the result, then issues the next. Design better tools : one write_file(path, text, create=True) removes the dependency altogether. In plain words first The idea in one line "Ask the model nicely to return JSON" fails some of the time, and far more often on small models. Structured outputs close that gap with constrained decoding: the model is literally prevented from emitting a token that would violate the schema. OpenAI's strict mode, Anthropic's schema-typed tool use, Gemini's responseSchema , Pydantic AI's output_type , and Zod's .parse are five surface forms of the same idea. This lesson builds the schema validator and the strict-mode contract learners will use for every production Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means JSON Schema 2020-12 "The schema spec" IETF-draft schema dialect every modern provider speaks Strict mode "Guaranteed schema" OpenAI flag that enforces schema via constrained decoding Constrained decoding "Logit masking" Decode-time enforcement that masks invalid next-tokens Refusal "Model declines" Typed outcome when input cannot fit the schema Parse error "Invalid JSON" Output did not parse as JSON; impossible under strict Schema violation "Wrong shape" Parsed but violated types / required / enum / range additionalProperties: false "No extras allowed" Forbids unknown fields; required in OpenAI strict Pydantic BaseModel "Typed output" Python class that emits and validates JSON Schema Zod schema "TypeScript output type" TS runtime schema for provider output validation Grammar enforcement "Open-weights constrained decode" FSM-based logit masking, as in outlines / guidance The problem In plain words first Programs need data in an exact shape: a field called quantity holding a number, priority being one of three words, and nothing else. Asking a model to "reply in JSON" usually works, but sometimes the model adds a sentence, wraps the JSON in code fences, or invents a field. Structured outputs fix the shape at the source. While the model generates, the decoder only allows tokens that keep the output valid for a JSON Schema, so the result always parses and always fits. This is constrained decoding. It guarantees the format, not the truth: the values can still be wrong. This lesson describes schemas, Pydantic models, refusals and retries. It then runs a real 0.5B model with and without a schema constraint on eight emails, and looks inside the constraint to see which tokens it allows at each step. No model is trained. An agent reading a purchase-order email needs to turn free text into {customer, line_items, total_usd} . Three approaches. Approach one: prompt for JSON. "Reply in JSON with fields customer, line_items, total_usd." Works most of the time on frontier models, much less on small ones. Fails in six ways: missing brace, trailing comma, wrong types, hallucinated fields, truncated at token limit, leaked prose or code fences around the JSON (the run below shows the last one on every email). Approach two: validate after generation. Generate freely, parse, validate against schema, retry on failure. Reliable but expensive — you pay for every retry, and truncation bugs cost one extra turn per occurrence. Approach three: constrained decoding. The provider enforces the schema at decode time. Invalid tokens are masked out of the sampling distribution. The output is guaranteed to parse and guaranteed to validate. Failure collapses to one mode: refusal (the model decides the input does not fit the schema). Every 2026 frontier provider ships some form of approach three. OpenAI. response_format: {type: "json_schema", strict: true} plus refusal in the response if the model declines. Anthropic. output_config.format with type: "json_schema" constrains the reply to a schema, and strict: true on a tool constrains its inputs. A declined request ends with stop_reason: "refusal" . Gemini. responseMimeType: "application/json" with responseSchema (or responseJsonSchema for plain JSON Schema) at request level. Pydantic AI. output_type=InvoiceModel makes the run result's .output an InvoiceModel instance, using the provider's structured output or a tool call under the hood. Zod (TypeScript). Runtime parser that validates provider output against a Zod schema; OpenAI's Node SDK turns a Zod schema into a response format with zodResponseFormat and parses the reply with .parse() . The common thread: declare the schema once, enforce it end to end. Idea 1 · JSON Schema 2020-12 — the lingua franca Every provider accepts JSON Schema 2020-12. The constructs you use most: type : one of object , array , string , number , integer , boolean , null . properties : map of field name to subschema. required : list of field names that must appear. enum : closed set of allowed values. minimum / maximum (numbers), minLength / maxLength / pattern (strings). items : subschema applied to every array element. additionalProperties : false forbids extra fields (default varies by mode). OpenAI strict mode adds requirements: every property must be listed in required , additionalProperties: false on every object, and an object (not anyOf ) at the root; $defs and $ref are fine. If you break these, the API returns 400 at request time. Anthropic's structured outputs likewise need additionalProperties: false and do not enforce minimum , maximum , minLength or maxLength ; the SDK helpers move those into descriptions and check them after decoding. Idea 2 · Pydantic, the Python binding Pydantic v2 generates JSON Schema from dataclass-shaped models via model_json_schema() . Pydantic AI wraps this so you write: Copy What you should see Copy Copy and the agent framework translates the schema into OpenAI strict mode, Anthropic input_schema , or Gemini responseSchema at the edge. The model's output comes back as a typed Invoice instance. Validation errors raise ValidationError with typed error paths. Idea 3 · Zod, the TypeScript binding Zod ( z.object({customer: z.string(), ...}) ) is the TS equivalent. OpenAI's Node SDK exposes zodResponseFormat(Invoice) which translates to the API's JSON Schema payload. Idea 4 · Refusals Strict mode cannot force the model to answer. If the request is declined, OpenAI fills a refusal field and Anthropic ends with stop_reason: "refusal" ; your code must handle this as a first-class outcome, not a failure. Note what strict mode does not catch: an input that does not fit the schema ("the email was a poem, not an invoice"). The model will usually produce a well-formed, made-up invoice rather than refuse, so the schema itself must have a way to say "not applicable" (measured below). Idea 5 · Constrained decoding in the open Open-weights implementations use three techniques. Grammar-based decoding ( outlines , guidance , lm-format-enforcer ): build a deterministic finite automaton from the schema; at every step, mask the logits of tokens that would violate the FSM. Logit masking with a JSON parser : run a streaming JSON parser in lockstep with the model; at every step, compute the valid-next-token set. Inference-engine support : vLLM, SGLang and llama.cpp accept a JSON Schema or grammar per request and apply the mask with fast engines such as XGrammar or llguidance. Commercial providers do this behind the scenes. With precomputed token masks the overhead is small (microseconds per token in the run below), and fixed parts of the output, such as key names, can even be emitted without sampling. The same idea as a formula Constrained decoding. Let ​ ) ⊆ V be the set of tokens that keep the output so far a prefix of some string valid under the schema. At each step the model's distribution is renormalised over that set: ( y t ​ ∣ y < t ​ ) = ∑ v ∈ A ( y < t ​ ) ​ p ( v ∣ y < t ​ ) p ( y t ​ ∣ y < t ​ ) 1 [ y t ​ ∈ A ( y < t ​ )] ​ . Every complete output is then valid by construction. In practice the logits of disallowed tokens are set to before sampling. What it does not change. Within , the model's preferences are untouched: if the model puts most weight on a wrong but valid value, that value is chosen. Retries without constraints. If a free-form output is valid with probability , the expected number of attempts until a valid one is , and attempts all fail with probability . Worked example How narrow is the mask? Qwen's vocabulary has 151,936 tokens. At the very start of the output the schema allows 7 of them (the forms of { ), 0.005%. After "priority": " only 13 tokens remain: pieces of low , normal and urgent . A model that would have written "High" cannot. Inside the free-text customer string, 147,137 tokens (96.8%) are allowed: the schema says nothing about what a name contains. Without constraints, with per attempt, 3 attempts all fail with probability = 0.001 , at a cost of about 1.1 attempts on average. With : 2 attempts on average and a 12.5% chance that 3 attempts all fail. Can still happen on non-strict providers. Schema violation. The output parses but violates the schema. Cannot happen under strict mode. Common outside it. Refusal. The model declines. Must be handled as a typed outcome. Idea 7 · Retry strategy When you are outside strict mode (non-strict tools, prompt-only JSON, models without constrained decoding), the recovery pattern is: Copy One retry is usually enough. Three retries catches weak-model flakes. Beyond three is a sign of a bad schema: the model cannot satisfy it for some inputs, and the prompt or the schema needs fixing. Idea 8 · Small-model support Constrained decoding works on small models: it guarantees the shape of the output whatever the model's size. It does not make the values right. In the run below a 0.5B model goes from 0 of 8 parseable outputs to 8 of 8, but still gets a third of the fields wrong and invents orders from emails that contain none. This is the main reason structured outputs matter in production: they turn format failures into content questions you can measure. The mask lets through only tokens that keep the output valid; inside strings it allows almost anything. A valid output is not a correct output: score the values. Identify the one construct it explicitly forbids in strict mode that plain JSON Schema allows. Then design a schema that uses the forbidden construct non-essentially and refactor it to be strict-compatible. Solutions Solution P1 · 0 then 8 parse, and both non-orders become orders Prompt only: 0 of 8 parse, because every reply comes wrapped in a code fence. Stripping the fences rescues all 8. Constrained: 8 of 8 parse and validate as generated. The constrained version does not notice the non-orders. Both get is_order: true and invented quantities (1 for the thank-you note, 5 for the party invitation). The schema demanded an order-shaped object, and constrained decoding made sure the model produced one. Format correctness and content correctness are separate problems. Solution B1 · A made-up order, stored as fact The pipeline stores a made-up order. Every field must be present and non-null, and decoding is constrained to the schema, so the model has to put some customer name, some quantity and some product into the object, whatever the newsletter says. Nothing fails, nothing is flagged, and the bad record looks exactly like a good one. That is worse than a parse error, which at least stops the pipeline. Fixes, in the schema itself: A discriminated union : {"kind": "order", ...} or {"kind": "not_an_order", "reason": ...} , so "nothing here" is a valid answer. Nullable fields ( "type": ["integer", "null"] ) with an instruction to use null when the email does not say. A decision field first , before the details, so the model commits to "is this an order?" before it starts inventing details. Then measure: run known non-orders through the pipeline and count how many come out as orders. In this lesson's run, a 0.5B model still chose "order" for every email even with these options; a larger model, or a separate classification step, is needed for reliable judgement. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design Design the extraction service for purchase-order emails. The input is free text; the output is a typed record with a customer, line items and a total. Cover the schema, the enforcement mode, the retry and refusal handling, and how you prove it works before it touches the accounting system. Level 3 of 4 · about 20 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Write one JSON Schema 2020-12 with the constraints that matter: required fields, enums for closed sets, a minimum of zero on the total, additional properties forbidden, and any reasoning field ahead of any decision field. Run it in the provider's strict schema mode so that a response that finishes cannot have a parse error or a schema violation, check the stop reason so that a response cut at the token limit goes to the error path, and treat a refusal as a typed outcome that goes to a review queue. Prove it with a labeled set of real emails scored per field, a refusal check on inputs that must not extract, and a run beside the human process before any record is written. The schema. type , properties and required for the shape; every property listed as required, with null allowed where the source can lack a value. enum for closed sets such as currency or status; minimum on the total; pattern , minLength and maxLength on identifiers; items for the line items. additionalProperties: false everywhere, which blocks invented fields and which strict mode demands. Field order as logic: any reasoning field before total or status , because the model commits to the first field it writes. In Python, a Pydantic model generates this schema; the service keeps the schema as the contract and the model as its binding. The enforcement mode. Situation Pick A hosted frontier model, a flat schema the provider's strict schema mode Several providers, retries acceptable a retry library over the Pydantic model, which is portable and does not touch logits A local model, validity required a grammar engine, finite state for a flat schema and context-free for a recursive one Strict mode is the default here: a finished output parses and validates by construction. Two failures remain: the refusal, and a response cut at the token limit, which can still fail to parse. Check the stop reason before you read the output, and send an incomplete response to the error path. Retry and refusal. Outside strict mode: generate, parse, validate, inject the typed errors and retry, at most three times. More than three means the schema or the prompt is wrong for some inputs. In every mode: a refusal is a first-class outcome with a reason attached. Log it, return it typed, send it to the review queue, and never retry it, because forcing a record on an input that does not fit produces an invented record. Proof before accounting sees a record. A labeled set of real emails with gold records; the structured outputs lesson uses 50 documents. Report exact match, accuracy per field and type compliance. A refusal check. Construct inputs that must not extract, such as a lyric, a proof or a blank email, and count refusals against invented outputs. A confidence per field from repeated extraction or token probabilities, with low-confidence records routed to a human. A schema version on every record, and a schema diff that separates breaking changes from non-breaking ones before any deploy. A side-by-side run against the human process on the labeled set, with the service writing nothing until the field-level numbers clear the bar you set with finance. Plausible wrong answers. "Prompt for JSON and parse it, the model is good." That works 85 to 95 percent of the time and fails six different ways; accounting needs the contract. "Retry refusals until the model gives a record." A refusal says the input does not fit; forcing a record invents one. "Validation after generation is as good as strict mode." It is reliable but pays for every retry, and a truncated output costs a turn each time. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why forbid additional properties? Expected: it blocks invented fields, and strict mode requires it everywhere. (level 3) You expect to switch providers next year. Which mode do you pick? Expected: a retry library over the Pydantic model for portability, or keep the schema identical across providers so each strict mode receives the same contract. (level 4) How do you version the schema once records exist? Expected: a version field on each record and a schema diff that separates breaking changes from non-breaking ones. Strict mode makes every field required, so an added field is breaking too, because the records written before it do not contain it; removed fields and changed types are breaking, and relaxed constraints are not. (level 4) Which failure can this design not remove, and where does it go? Expected: a wrong value with the right type; it goes to the field-level eval and the confidence flags, and the low-confidence records go to review. Where it is taught. The lesson structured output gives the schema constructs, the strict mode rules, the retry pattern and the refusal handling, the lesson structured outputs sets the labeled eval and the schema diff, and the lesson constrained decoding gives the mode table and the field order rule. Explain the mechanism An extraction service turns purchase-order emails into typed records. Name the ways a structured output call can fail, say which of them disappear under strict schema enforcement, and describe how the code should treat what remains. Level 2 of 4 · about 7 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Three ways: a parse error, where the output is not JSON; a schema violation, where it parses but breaks a type, a required field, an enum or a range; and a refusal, where the model decides the input does not fit the schema. Strict enforcement removes the first two by construction for a response that finishes. The refusal stays, and it must be a typed outcome that the code logs and returns, never a retry. A response cut at the token limit can still fail to parse, so check the stop reason before you read the output. Three approaches, three failure profiles. Prompt for JSON. Works 85 to 95 percent of the time on a frontier model. Fails six ways: a missing brace, a trailing comma, wrong types, invented fields, truncation at the token limit, and leaked prose such as "here is your JSON". Validate after generation. Generate freely, parse, validate against the schema, and on failure inject the error and retry. Reliable but you pay for every retry. Constrained decoding. The provider masks invalid tokens at decode time, so a finished output parses and validates by construction. The model-side failure collapses to one mode, refusal; a response cut at the token limit and a request error still need their own error path. The retry loop, when you are outside strict mode. Copy One retry is usually enough. Three catches weak-model flakes. Beyond three means the schema or the prompt is wrong for some inputs, and the fix is there, not in a fourth attempt. The validator should return a typed error list with a path and a message for each failure, which is the shape the retry prompt needs. The refusal branch. The model declines because the input does not fit, for example the email was a poem and not an order, or because of a safety reason. The refusal carries the reason. Log it, return it typed, and do not retry. The lesson also uses refusals as a safety signal downstream. One schema setting that matters. additionalProperties: false forbids fields the schema did not name, which is how strict mode shuts the door on invented fields. Strict mode requires it everywhere. Plausible wrong answers. "A refusal is a failed call, retry it." It is a first-class outcome with a reason attached; log it and return it typed. "Strict mode removes every failure." It removes parse errors and schema violations for a finished response; refusals, truncated responses and wrong values with the right type remain. "Retry until it validates." Past three retries the cost grows and the schema is the real problem. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) How many retries, and what does needing more tell you? Expected: at most three; one is usually enough, and beyond three the schema or the prompt is wrong for some inputs. (level 2) Why must the refusal branch not retry? Expected: the model declined for a reason, often fit or safety; a retry wastes cost and can push a wrong extraction through. (level 3) What does the retry prompt need from the validator? Expected: a typed error list with a path and a message per failure, so the model knows which field to fix. (level 3) Which schema setting blocks invented fields? Expected: additional properties set to false, which strict mode requires everywhere. Where it is taught. The lesson structured output names the three failure modes, the retry pattern and the refusal branch, and the lesson structured outputs covers validation with error feedback.
