Running that for real adds problems that only show up over time. The authorization server changes its signing keys on a schedule, so the MCP server must fetch the new public keys without restarting and without letting attackers make it fetch endlessly. Some providers issue opaque tokens that the server cannot read, so it has to ask the provider whether each token is still valid (introspection), and any cache of that answer delays revocation. When the identity service is down, the server needs a rule, decided in advance, for which requests may still go through. On every request the server still checks the issuer, the audience, the expiry and the scope. This lesson runs all of this with real RS256 keys and an introspection endpoint on a simulated clock. The Lesson 13.16 simulator runs OAuth 2.1 in memory. Production has three operational gaps that a memory-only simulator does not see. The first gap is enrollment and credential isolation. A real org may run hundreds of MCP servers and thousands of MCP clients. The 2026-07-28 revision prefers a Client ID Metadata Document : the client uses an HTTPS URL with a path that it controls as its identifier, and the authorization server pulls the metadata. RFC 7591 dynamic registration remains only as a deprecated compatibility path. When DCR is unavoidable, the request declares the correct application_type . The client stores registrations under the authorization-server issuer and access tokens under the (issuer, resource) pair. A changed issuer means a new enrollment, and a different resource means a separately audience-bound token. The second gap is key rotation. JWT validation depends on the authorization server's signing keys, published as a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS). The authorization server rotates these on a schedule (often hourly, sometimes faster under incident response). An MCP server that fetches JWKS once at boot validates fine until the rotation window — then every request fails until restart. Production wires JWKS as a cached value with a refresh job that overwrites the cache before the previous keys expire, plus a fall-back fetch on cache miss for the case where a token signed by a key newer than the cache arrives. The third gap is audience binding. Lesson 13.16 introduced RFC 8707 resource indicators. In production, that indicator becomes a hard claim check on every request. The MCP server compares token.aud against its own canonical resource URL and rejects mismatches with HTTP 401. This is the only defense against an upstream MCP server (or a malicious client holding a token meant for one server) replaying that token against another server in the same trust mesh. This lesson maps each gap onto a concrete piece of the surface. The metadata document is an HTTP endpoint. JWKS cache refresh is a scheduled job plus a key-value cache. JWT validation is a routine the resource server runs before dispatching any tool. Keep the three roles separate and each one enforces only the checks it owns: the authorization server issues and rotates keys, the resource server caches and validates, the client discovers and enrolls. Scope: Production Enforcement After Lesson 16 [Lesson 13.16](#a1316): MCP Security with OAuth 2.1 owns the authorization-code state machine, PKCE, protected-resource discovery, resource indicators, and scope decisions. This lesson does not define a second OAuth flow. It starts after those contracts exist and asks how a deployed resource server keeps enforcing them during key rotation, opaque-token validation, revocation, dependency failure, rollout, and incident response. The production boundary is narrower and more operational: A JWT path verifies a pinned issuer, algorithm, signature key, audience, time claims, and scopes on every request while refreshing JWKS safely. An opaque-token path calls the issuer's authenticated introspection endpoint and validates the returned active state, audience or resource, expiry, subject, and scopes. Revocation policy defines how quickly a credential must stop working and which cache can delay that fact. Failure policy decides what happens when discovery, JWKS, introspection, or revocation infrastructure is unavailable. Evidence records which issuer metadata, key set or introspection response, token claims, policy version, and refusal reason drove the result without storing the token. This distinction keeps the lessons composable. Lesson 13.16 proves the flow. Lesson 13.18 proves that a token remains trustworthy, or is refused, after it reaches a real MCP request path. Idea 1 · RFC 8414 — OAuth Authorization Server Metadata A document at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server describes everything a client needs: Copy A client given an MCP resource URL chains discovery: oauth-protected-resource from RFC 9728 (the resource server's document) names the issuer, then oauth-authorization-server (this RFC) names every endpoint. The client never hard-codes an authorization URL. For a resource identifier with a path, insert the well-known segment before that path. For example, https://mcp.example.com/team/server resolves protected-resource metadata at https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/team/server . Appending /.well-known/... after the resource path is incorrect. The contract you verify before trusting an IdP for MCP: code_challenge_methods_supported includes S256 (PKCE per RFC 7636). The spec is explicit: if this field is absent , the authorization server does not support PKCE and the client MUST refuse to proceed. grant_types_supported includes authorization_code and rejects password and implicit . At least one enrollment path is available: client_id_metadata_document_supported: true (CIMD, preferred), a pre-registered client, or registration_endpoint (deprecated RFC 7591 compatibility). If authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported is true, the client requires the returned RFC 9207 iss and compares it exactly with the issuer recorded before redirecting. response_types_supported is exactly ["code"] for OAuth 2.1. If S256 is missing, the MCP server refuses to deploy against this IdP — there is no degraded mode for PKCE. If neither enrollment path is advertised and you have no pre-registered client_id , you also cannot enroll; the deployment manifest is wrong, not the code. Idea 2 · RFC 9728 (recap) — Protected Resource Metadata Lesson 13.16 covered RFC 9728. The delta in production: this document is the only place a client looks to find the authorization servers trusted by this MCP server. A single MCP server may accept tokens from multiple IdPs (one for staff, one for partners). RFC 9728 declares that set; RFC 8414 documents what each IdP supports. Copy Idea 3 · Client ID Metadata Documents (the recommended default) CIMD inverts registration from push to pull . Instead of asking the authorization server to mint a client_id , the client uses an HTTPS URL it controls as its client_id . The URL resolves to a JSON metadata document; the authorization server fetches it on demand during the OAuth flow. Trust is rooted in DNS: if the server operator trusts app.example.com , it trusts the client served from https://app.example.com/client.json . No registration round-trip, no client_id namespace to exhaust, no per-server state to keep in sync. The metadata document the client hosts: Copy The client_id value in the document MUST equal the URL it is served from (the authorization server verifies this; mismatches are rejected). The authorization server advertises support with client_id_metadata_document_supported: true in its RFC 8414 metadata. For the current CIMD contract, client_id , client_name , and a non-empty redirect_uris array are required. The client identifier is an absolute HTTPS URL with a path. application_type may be included, but it is not a mandatory CIMD field. Do not copy the DCR requirement for application_type into the preferred CIMD path. Two security facts the spec is blunt about: SSRF. The authorization server fetches an attacker-supplied URL. It must defend against server-side request forgery (no fetches to internal/admin endpoints). localhost impersonation. CIMD alone cannot stop a local attacker from claiming a legitimate client's metadata URL and binding any localhost redirect. The authorization server MUST clearly display the redirect URI hostname during consent and SHOULD warn on localhost -only redirects. Because CIMD needs no server-side state, there is no registrar to stand up the way DCR requires. The client side is read-only: serve your metadata document from a static HTTPS endpoint and let the authorization server pull it. If the authorization server operator has already provisioned a client identifier, use that issuer-scoped registration before trying automatic enrollment. Otherwise prefer CIMD. Use deprecated DCR only when the issuer cannot use either pre-registration or CIMD. Idea 4 · RFC 7591: deprecated compatibility enrollment DCR is deprecated in the 2026-07-28 revision. Keep it only for authorization servers that cannot consume CIMD and where pre-registration is impractical. A compatibility client posts: Copy The server responds with client_id and a registration_access_token for later updates: Copy application_type is not decorative. A loopback desktop client declares native ; a server-hosted client declares web and uses HTTPS redirect URIs. token_endpoint_auth_method: none is the right default for a public native client. It gets a client_id only, with PKCE providing the proof-of-possession. Three production pitfalls: The registration endpoint must rate-limit by source IP. Without that, a hostile actor scripts millions of fake registrations and exhausts the client_id namespace. Run a rate-limit check before the registrar handles the request. software_statement (a signed JWT vouching for the client) is required by some enterprise IdPs. The lesson's mock skips it; production wires a verification step that rejects unsigned registrations from anything other than localhost redirect URIs. The registration_access_token must be stored as a hash, not plaintext. Theft of this token means the attacker can rewrite the client's redirect URIs. Idea 5 · RFC 8707 (recap) — Resource Indicators Lesson 13.16 established the shape. The production rule: every token request includes resource=<canonical-mcp-url> , and the MCP server verifies token.aud matches its own resource URL on every call. The canonical URI is the most specific identifier for the server: it uses lowercase scheme and host, no fragment, and conventionally no trailing slash. The path component is not stripped by rule — the spec keeps it when it is needed to identify an individual MCP server. https://mcp.example.com , https://mcp.example.com/mcp , https://mcp.example.com:8443 , and https://mcp.example.com/server/mcp are all valid canonical URIs. Pick one per server and pin aud to exactly that. (This lesson's mock uses bare-host audiences like https://notes.example.com for brevity; a deployment that co-hosts several MCP servers under one origin distinguishes them by path.) Idea 6 · RFC 7636 (recap) — PKCE PKCE is mandatory in OAuth 2.1. The lesson's authorization-code flow always carries code_challenge and code_verifier . The server rejects any token request without a verifier or with a verifier that does not hash to the stored challenge. Idea 7 · MCP 2026-07-28 authorization profile The current MCP revision keeps the OAuth resource-server boundary while making MCP transport stateless. There is no protocol session on which to cache an identity decision. The authorization layer therefore validates each request independently: Implement RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata, and provide its location either through the WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="..." header on a 401 or the well-known URI /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource (SEP-985 made the header optional with a well-known fallback). The metadata authorization_servers field MUST name at least one server. Accept tokens only via Authorization: Bearer ... on every request — never in a query string, never validated only at session start. Validate aud , iss , exp , and required scopes per request. The server MUST validate that the token was issued specifically for it (audience); a missing or mismatched aud is rejected, never treated as wildcard. On 401/403, return WWW-Authenticate: Bearer carrying error=... , the resource_metadata="<PRM-URL>" parameter (the URL of the metadata document, not the bare resource), and scope="..." on insufficient_scope (403). Note: the parameter is resource_metadata , a discovery pointer — there is no resource parameter in the challenge. Authorization-server discovery accepts either RFC 8414 OAuth metadata or OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0; clients must try both well-known suffixes in priority order. The client (not the server) defends against mix-up attacks : it records the expected issuer before redirecting and validates the iss value returned in the actual authorization response (RFC 9207) before redeeming the code. PKCE alone does not stop mix-up, because the client hands its code_verifier to whatever token endpoint it was steered to. A client credential belongs to one authorization-server issuer. If discovery resolves to a different issuer, the client re-enrolls instead of presenting the old client_id , registration token, or access token. CIMD is the preferred enrollment mechanism. DCR is deprecated; a compatibility DCR request still declares the correct application_type . The OAuth 2.1 draft is the substrate; RFC 8414/7591/8707/9728/9207 + RFC 7636 + CIMD are the surface; the MCP spec is the profile. Idea 8 · Deployment capability checklist Vendor feature tables become stale quickly. Inspect the metadata returned by the authorization server you will actually deploy instead. The gate is mechanical: Check Required decision Discovered issuer Exact HTTPS issuer expected by policy PKCE S256 advertised; otherwise stop Enrollment CIMD preferred, pre-registration accepted, DCR only as deprecated compatibility Authorization response Validate RFC 9207 iss when present or advertised Resource binding Token request carries resource ; resource server requires the matching aud Credential storage Key client IDs and registration credentials by issuer; key access tokens by issuer plus resource DCR compatibility Declare native or web ; reject redirect URIs that do not fit the declared application type Do not infer support from a product name or pricing tier. Capture the discovered document in deployment evidence and fail closed when a mandatory field is absent. Idea 9 · JWKS refresh pattern (rotate at the AS, refresh at the resource server) Keep two verbs separate, because conflating them is a real production bug: Rotate is what the authorization server does: mint a new signing key, publish it in the JWKS, retire the old one later. The resource server has no part in this and cannot do it — it does not hold the IdP's private keys. Refresh is what the resource server does: re- GET the published JWKS into its cache. That is the only JWKS action a resource server ever performs. The production failure mode is a stale cache. Solve it with a scheduled refresh job plus a key-value cache. The resource server runs a job (cron, timer, whatever your runtime offers) that, on a fixed interval, fetches <issuer>/.well-known/jwks.json and overwrites cache[issuer] = {keys, fetched_at} . The validator reads from that cache. A token whose kid is missing from the cache triggers one synchronous refresh as a fall-back, then re-checks. This handles two cases at once: the scheduled refresh, and key-overlap windows where a token signed by a brand-new key arrives before the next scheduled refresh. The fall-back must be a re-fetch, never a rotate . If you wire the cache-miss path to a rotate-and-mint, two things break: (1) minting a fresh key produces a kid that still does not match the token, so the lookup fails anyway; and (2) an attacker who sprays tokens with random kid values forces an unbounded series of key creations — a self-inflicted DoS. A re-fetch is idempotent, so a bogus kid costs at most one wasted fetch. The cache shape: Copy Two keys at once is the steady state. Authorization servers rotate by introducing the next key ( k_2026_04 ) before retiring the previous ( k_2026_03 ), so tokens issued under the old key remain valid until they expire. The cache holds the union; the validator picks by kid . Idea 10 · The validation routine The MCP server runs validation before dispatching any tool. The shape code/main.py uses: Copy validate decodes the JWT, resolves the signing key from the JWKS cache (refreshing once on a miss), verifies the signature, then checks iss against the allow-list, aud against this server's canonical resource, exp , and the required scope — returning a WWW-Authenticate challenge on the first failure. Keeping it a single routine on the resource server means every entry point (every tool call, every transport) goes through the same checks; there is no path that reaches a tool without validating first. Idea 11 · Opaque tokens use introspection, not guesswork Not every access token is a JWT. If the issuer documents an opaque token, the resource server cannot decode it into trustworthy claims. It sends the token to the issuer's RFC 7662 introspection endpoint over an authenticated backchannel and requires active: true , the expected issuer context, the exact MCP audience or resource, unexpired time claims, and the scopes required by the concrete tool. Cache introspection by issuer, a one-way token digest, and MCP resource. Never use the clear token as a log or cache label. Bound a positive cache entry by the earliest of token expiry, issuer cache guidance, and the deployment's revocation freshness objective. Keep negative caching short enough that a newly issued token does not remain falsely inactive. A result for one resource cannot authorize another resource even when the opaque token string is identical. Do not choose validation mode from attacker-controlled token contents. Pin JWT versus introspection behavior to validated issuer metadata and deployment configuration. On the JWT path, pin accepted algorithms and trusted jwks_uri ; never follow a key URL or algorithm selected only by the token header. Idea 12 · Revocation is a freshness contract RFC 7009 lets a client ask an authorization server to revoke a token. That request does not erase copies already cached by every resource server. Define the maximum acceptable revocation delay and make every cache honor it. Opaque-token deployments can achieve tighter revocation by introspecting on each high-risk call or using a short positive cache. Self-contained JWT deployments usually combine short access-token lifetimes with refresh-token revocation, key retirement for issuer-wide incidents, and an optional subject, session, or token-id denylist for emergency local refusal. A signed JWT remains cryptographically valid until expiry unless the resource server has current external revocation evidence. Logout, account disablement, consent withdrawal, and incident response are different triggers but must converge on one measurable statement: after at most the declared revocation window, every replica refuses the credential. Test that statement through the load balancer, not only against one warm process. Idea 13 · Dependency failure needs a declared decision Never improvise availability policy inside an exception handler. Failure Safe production behavior Scheduled JWKS refresh fails, known kid remains in a still-valid bounded cache Continue only within the declared stale-on-error window and emit degraded health evidence Token has an unknown kid and the one allowed refresh fails Reject; never accept an unverifiable signature Introspection is unavailable Fail closed for protected calls; do not convert network failure into active: true Protected-resource or issuer metadata changes unexpectedly Stop new enrollment and token acquisition; keep only explicitly pinned, unexpired configuration under a bounded incident policy Revocation endpoint is unavailable Report logout or revocation as incomplete, retain the credential locally as unusable when possible, and do not claim global revocation succeeded Clock source or claim type is invalid Reject rather than widening skew until the token passes Classify failures separately from invalid credentials. A dependency outage is an operational error with health and retry policy. A bad signature, issuer, audience, expiry, or scope is an authorization refusal. Neither reaches the tool handler, and neither should leak token contents into audit evidence. Idea 14 · Audience-replay walkthrough (access-token privilege restriction) Server A ( notes.example.com ) and Server B ( tasks.example.com ) both register against the same authorization server. Server A is compromised. The attacker takes a user's notes token and replays it against Server B. Server B's validator: Decode JWT, fetch JWKS by kid , verify signature. Check iss against its protected-resource metadata's authorization_servers . (Pass — same IdP.) Check aud == "https://tasks.example.com" . (Fail — token's aud is https://notes.example.com .) Return 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="audience mismatch", resource_metadata="https://tasks.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource" . The audience claim is the only defense against this attack at the protocol layer. Skipping it for performance is the most common production mistake; the validator must run on every request, not just at session start. The spec calls this access-token privilege restriction : an MCP server MUST reject any token that does not name it in the audience. Naming note. The spec reserves the term confused deputy for a related-but-distinct problem: an MCP server acting as an OAuth proxy to a third-party API, using a static client ID, that forwards a token without obtaining per-client user consent. Audience binding fixes the replay above; the confused-deputy fix is per-client consent plus never passing the inbound token through to upstream APIs (the MCP server MUST get its own separate upstream token). Idea 15 · Mix-up attacks (a client-side defense the server cannot provide) A client talks to many authorization servers over its life. A malicious AS can try to make the client redeem an honest AS's authorization code at the attacker's token endpoint. Audience binding does not help here — the attack happens before any token exists. The defense lives in the client (RFC 9207): Before redirecting, the client records the expected issuer from the validated AS metadata. On the authorization response, the client compares the returned iss parameter against that recorded issuer (simple string comparison, no normalization) before sending the code anywhere. Mismatch (or iss absent when the AS advertised authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported ) → reject, and do not even display the error fields. PKCE alone does not stop mix-up, because the client hands its code_verifier to whatever token endpoint it was steered to. This is why the spec records the issuer per-request alongside the PKCE verifier and state . Idea 16 · Failure modes Stale JWKS. The validator rejects valid tokens after the AS rotates a key. The fix is the cron-refresh + cache-miss-refetch pattern above. Never cache JWKS without a refresh job. Rotate-as-fall-back. Wiring the cache-miss path to a rotate-and-mint instead of a re-fetch is a real bug: it never produces the missing kid , and it turns attacker-controlled kid values into a key-creation DoS. The fall-back must be the idempotent refresh-jwks . Missing aud claim. Some IdPs default to omitting aud unless resource is present in the token request. The validator must reject tokens with missing aud , not treat absence as wildcard. Mix-up via missing iss check. A client that does not validate the RFC 9207 iss authorization-response parameter against the issuer it recorded before redirecting can be steered into redeeming an honest AS's code at an attacker's token endpoint. This is a client-side failure; the resource server cannot compensate for it. Scope upgrade race. Two concurrent step-up flows for the same user can both succeed and produce two access tokens with different scopes. The validator must use the token presented on the request, not look up "the user's current scope" — that creates a TOCTOU window. Registration token theft. A leaked registration_access_token lets the attacker rewrite redirect URIs. Hash these at rest; require the client to present the cleartext on every update; rotate on suspicion. iss not pinned. A validator that accepts any iss lets an attacker stand up their own authorization server, register a client for the target audience, and issue tokens. The protected-resource metadata's authorization_servers list is the allow-list; enforce it. Credential or token cache collision. A client that keys registrations only by resource can present one authorization server's identity to another. A client that keys access tokens only by issuer can replay a token at the wrong audience. Key registrations by validated issuer, key access tokens by (issuer, resource) , and re-enroll whenever the issuer changes. The same idea as a formula Key rotation without downtime. Let keys live for and let the authorization server publish the old and the new key together for an overlap . A resource server that refreshes its JWKS every never rejects a valid token if ​ ≤ O , where ​ is the longest token lifetime signed by the retiring key. A cache miss on an unknown kid triggers at most one extra fetch per interval , so the fetch rate is at most , whatever an attacker sends. Revocation freshness. With introspection results cached for seconds, a token revoked at time ​ is refused no later than ​ + C . For self-contained JWTs without introspection the bound is the token's remaining lifetime, ​ . Short lifetimes and short caches are the same trade-off: freshness against load on the identity service. The flow: From the repository root, run: Copy The first command prints the issuer-bound enrollment and token-validation transcript. The second reports eighteen passing checks. Neither command opens a network listener or writes credentials. Authorization server publishes RFC 8414 metadata at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server . MCP client calls the metadata endpoint and checks its enrollment options ( client_id_metadata_document_supported for CIMD, registration_endpoint for DCR) and S256 PKCE support. The client checks for an issuer-scoped pre-registration, otherwise enrolls with its HTTPS Client ID Metadata Document. Deprecated DCR remains a separately testable compatibility method. The client records the validated issuer, creates an S256 challenge, receives a one-time authorization code plus iss , validates that returned issuer, and redeems the code with the original verifier and RFC 8707 resource indicator. MCP client calls a tool on the MCP server with Authorization: Bearer ... . MCP server runs validate , resolving the signing key from the JWKS cache. The IdP rotates a key; the scheduled refresh re-pulls the JWKS into the cache. The next call validates against the refreshed keys without restart, and the previous token still validates during the overlap window. An audience-replay attempt against a different MCP resource gets 401 with audience mismatch and a resource_metadata pointer. The JWT here uses HS256 with a shared secret (so the lesson runs on stdlib only). Production uses RS256 or EdDSA with the JWKS pattern above; the validation logic is otherwise identical. Because the IdP and resource server live in one process, refresh_jwks reads the authorization server's key list directly; over the wire it is an HTTP GET to jwks_uri . Break it on purpose A team wires the JWKS cache-miss path to "ask the authorization server to rotate and mint a new key" instead of "re-fetch the JWKS", and it has no rate limit. What happens when attackers send tokens with random kid values? (Solution B1.) Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) MCP 2026-07-28 authorization : Client ID Metadata Documents preferred, DCR deprecated (with application_type required when used), RFC 9207 iss checked by clients, credentials keyed by issuer and tokens by issuer plus resource, audience checked on every request. Libraries used in production : PyJWT's PyJWKClient (JWKS fetch with a key cache), jose / jwcrypto , Authlib in Python; jose in Node; Spring Security and ASP.NET JWT bearer handlers. Each caches the JWKS and supports refresh on an unknown kid . Identity providers : Auth0, Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Keycloak and WorkOS all publish JWKS and RFC 8414 or OpenID discovery metadata; key rotation with an overlap window is the normal operating mode. Opaque tokens use RFC 7662 introspection; many gateways (Kong, Envoy, API Gateway authorizers) cache introspection results, which is exactly the revocation delay shown here. On your laptop : everything runs on the CPU in about a second. Sources: MCP authorization , RFC 8414 , RFC 7662 , RFC 8707 , RFC 9207 , PyJWT . Opaque tokens need introspection; the cache TTL is your revocation delay. Decide in advance what each operation class does when identity services fail. Add a rate-limit check to register_client that runs before the registrar accepts a request. Use a token-bucket per source IP held in a small dict keyed by IP. Read RFC 7591 and identify two fields the lesson's /register handler does not validate. Add the validation. (Hint: software_statement and redirect_uris URI scheme.) Add a second authorization server. Confirm the client stores a separate issuer-keyed enrollment and refuses to reuse the first issuer's token or client_id . Prove the DoS fix. Send the validator a token with a random kid and confirm refresh_jwks runs at most once and the authorization server's key count does not grow. Then deliberately re-wire the fall-back to a rotate-and-mint and watch the key count climb per bogus token — restore the re-fetch afterward. Exercise deprecated DCR with both native and web clients. Confirm a web client with an HTTP redirect URI and a native client without an exact loopback redirect are rejected. Solutions Solution P1 · Two fetches, then none Two fetches in total for everything. The genuine new key causes one re-fetch when the first token signed with it arrives, and that fetch finds k3 . The 100 made-up kid values each miss the cache, but the re-fetch is rate-limited to once per 30 seconds, so they cause at most one more fetch together, and none of them validates. Without the rate limit, each of them would cost a network call to the authorization server. Solution B1 · Every bad kid mints a key Every unknown kid creates a new key at the authorization server. The attacker controls the kid header, so each request with a new value mints and publishes another key: the JWKS grows without limit, every resource server fetches ever-larger key sets, and the authorization server spends CPU on key generation. This is a denial of service on the identity system. It also never helps: a newly minted key has a new kid , never the one the token named, so the token still fails. The fix: the miss path is the same idempotent "refresh the JWKS" as the scheduled job, rate-limited (for example at most once per 30 seconds), and a kid that is still unknown after that refresh is a plain 401. Key creation happens only on the authorization server's own rotation schedule. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, Agent Card + Task harness). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line MCP is agent-to-tool. A2A (Agent2Agent) is agent-to-agent — an open protocol for letting opaque agents built on different frameworks collaborate. Released by Google in April 2025, donated to the Linux Foundation in June 2025, reaching v1.0 in March 2026, with 150+ supporters by April 2026 including AWS, Cisco, Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP, and ServiceNow. It absorbed IBM's ACP and added the AP2 payments extension. This lesson walks the Agent Card, Task lifecycle, and the three protocol bindings, using the A2A 1.0.1 wire names. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means A2A "Agent-to-Agent protocol" Open protocol for opaque agent collaboration Agent Card " /.well-known/agent-card.json " Published metadata describing an agent's skills and supportedInterfaces Skill "A callable unit" A named operation the agent supports (analog to MCP tool) Task "Unit of delegation" A work item with a lifecycle and final artifact Message "Task input" Carries Parts ( text , raw , url , data ) Part "Typed chunk" Exactly one of text / raw / url / data , plus optional mediaType ; no kind field Artifact "Task output" Named, typed output returned on completion AP2 "Agent Payments Protocol" Payments extension built on A2A; card signing is core A2A ( signatures ) Opacity "Black-box collaboration" Called agent's internals are hidden from caller TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED "Task pause" Interrupted state when the agent needs more info The problem In plain words first MCP lets an agent call a tool: the agent sees exactly what goes in and what comes out. Sometimes you want something different: hand a whole job to another agent, perhaps built by another team with another framework, and get the result back without knowing how it did the work. A2A (Agent2Agent) is the open protocol for that. Each agent publishes an Agent Card, a small JSON file at a well-known URL that says what it can do and how to reach it. The caller sends a message; the other agent turns it into a Task that moves through states (working, needs input, completed) and finally returns Artifacts, the outputs. Cards can be signed so a caller can tell a real card from a fake one. This lesson serves a real agent with the official A2A Python SDK, talks to it over the JSON-RPC wire, and signs and verifies its card. A customer-service agent needs to delegate report-writing to a specialized writer agent. Options pre-A2A: Custom REST API. Works but every pairing is a one-off. Shared codebase. Requires the two agents to run the same framework. MCP. Doesn't fit: MCP is for calling tools, not for two agents collaborating while preserving each agent's opaque internal reasoning. A2A fills the gap. It models the interaction as one agent sending a Task to another, with a lifecycle, messages, and artifacts. The called agent's internal state stays opaque — the caller sees only task state transitions and eventual outputs. A2A is the "let agents across frameworks talk to each other" protocol. It does not replace MCP; the two are complementary. Idea 1 · Agent Card Every A2A-compliant agent publishes a card at /.well-known/agent-card.json : Copy Discovery is URL-based: fetch the card, pick the first supportedInterfaces entry whose protocolBinding your client speaks, and enumerate skills. Input and output modes are media types. Idea 2 · Signed Agent Cards A card can carry a signatures array. Each entry is a JWS (RFC 7515) computed over the card's RFC 8785 canonical JSON, with the signatures field left out. Consumers canonicalize the card the same way and verify. Prevents impersonation. Idea 3 · Task lifecycle Copy Clients initiate with SendMessage , and the server creates the Task. The called agent transitions through states; clients poll with GetTask or stream over SSE with SendStreamingMessage and SubscribeToTask . A stream carries statusUpdate and artifactUpdate events and closes when the task reaches a terminal state. There is no final flag. Idea 4 · Messages and Parts A message has a messageId , a role ( ROLE_USER or ROLE_AGENT ), and one or more Parts. Each Part holds exactly one content field, and that field name is the type. There is no kind field. text : plain content. raw : file bytes, base64 in JSON, usually with filename and mediaType . url : a link to file content. data : structured JSON payload (structured input for the called agent). Example: Copy Idea 5 · Artifacts Outputs are Artifacts, not raw strings. An Artifact is a named, typed output: Copy Artifacts can be streamed as chunks. Each artifactUpdate event carries the artifact plus append and lastChunk . The caller accumulates. Idea 6 · Three protocol bindings JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP ( JSONRPC ). POST for requests, SSE for streaming. Methods are PascalCase: SendMessage , SendStreamingMessage , GetTask , ListTasks , CancelTask , SubscribeToTask , CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig , GetTaskPushNotificationConfig , ListTaskPushNotificationConfigs , DeleteTaskPushNotificationConfig , and GetExtendedAgentCard . gRPC ( GRPC ). For enterprise environments where gRPC is native. Same method names. HTTP+JSON/REST ( HTTP+JSON ). Resource URLs such as POST /message:send and GET /tasks/{id} . All three bindings carry the same data model. Each supportedInterfaces entry names one binding and its protocolVersion . Clients send the header A2A-Version: 1.0 on every request, because a server reads a request without it as version 0.3. Copy Idea 7 · Opacity preservation A key design principle: the called agent's internal state is opaque. The caller sees task state and artifacts. The called agent's chain-of-thought, its tool calls, its sub-agent delegation — all invisible. This is different from MCP, where tool calls are transparent. Rationale: A2A enables competitors to collaborate without revealing internals. A2A can be "call this customer-service agent" without the caller learning how that agent implements the service. AP2 extension (Agent Payments) ships. 2026-03. v1.0, the first stable specification, released. 2026-04. One-year announcement: 150+ supporting organizations, SDKs in five languages. Worked example One delegated report The research agent fetches https://writer.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json , sees the JSONRPC interface and the skill draft_report . Solutions Solution P1 · Input required, same task id SendMessage returns a Task in TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED , with the writer's question ("How long should the report be?") as the status message. The task is not finished and not failed; it is waiting. The caller continues it by sending another SendMessage whose message carries the same taskId (and contextId ) and the answer. The writer then resumes, produces its artifact and moves the task to TASK_STATE_COMPLETED . Starting a new task instead would lose the first request's context. Solution B1 · The attacker brings the key Only their own key pair. The attacker edits the card (for example, points the interface at their server), signs it with their own private key, sets jku in the protected header to a URL they control that serves the matching public key, and the verifier dutifully fetches that key and finds the signature valid. Verification then proves only that the card is consistent with itself. Accepting any algorithm adds a second hole: a header saying alg: none , or an HMAC algorithm with a public key used as the secret, are classic JWS confusion attacks. The fix is the pattern in the block above: the key provider returns keys only from a trust store you control (pinned keys, or a JWKS URL you configured for that publisher, not one taken from the card), and the verifier passes a fixed list of algorithms such as ["ES256"] . Build a trace hierarchy that covers agent loop, LLM call, tool call, and MCP client dispatch. Decide what content to capture (opt-in) vs redact (defaults). Emit spans to a local collector (Jaeger, Langfuse) without rewriting tool code. Before you start Needs : Phase 13 · 07 (MCP server), Phase 13 · 08 (MCP client) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, OTel span emitter), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line An agent calls five tools, three MCP servers, and two sub-agents. You need one trace across all of it. The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (still at Development status; since v1.42 in June 2026 they live in their own semantic-conventions-genai repository) are the 2026 standard, natively supported by Datadog, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, OpenLLMetry, and AgentOps. This lesson names the required attributes, walks the span hierarchy (agent → LLM → tool), and ships a stdlib span emitter you can plug into any OTel exporter. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means OTel "OpenTelemetry" Open standard for traces, metrics, logs GenAI semconv "GenAI semantic conventions" Stable attribute names for LLM / tool / agent spans gen_ai.* "The attribute namespace" All GenAI attributes share this prefix Span "Timed operation" A unit of work with a start, end, and attributes Trace "Cross-span ancestry" Tree of spans sharing a trace id SpanKind "CLIENT / SERVER / INTERNAL" Hints about span direction OTLP "OpenTelemetry Protocol" Wire format for exporters Opt-in content "Prompt / completion capture" Off by default; env var to enable traceparent "W3C header" Propagates trace context across services Exporter "Backend-specific shipper" Component that sends spans to Jaeger / Datadog / etc. The problem In plain words first When an agent is slow or wrong, you need to see what happened inside one run: which model calls it made, how many tokens each used, which tools it called, and how long each MCP server took. Tracing gives you that. A trace is a tree of timed steps called spans, all sharing one trace id. OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the open standard for traces and metrics, and its GenAI conventions fix the names: a model call is a chat span with attributes such as gen_ai.usage.input_tokens , a tool call is an execute_tool span, an agent run is an invoke_agent span. When the agent calls an MCP server in another process, the trace id travels inside the request so the server's span joins the same tree. Prompts and answers are not recorded unless you switch that on, because they may hold private data. This lesson traces a real Qwen tool call across two processes with the OTel SDK. A debug from February 2026: user reports "my agent sometimes takes 30 seconds to respond; other times 3 seconds." No traces. Logs show the LLM call, but not the tool dispatch, not the MCP server round-trip, not the sub-agent. You guess. Eventually you find: one MCP server occasionally hangs on a cold-start. Without end-to-end tracing, you cannot find this. OTel GenAI fixes it. The conventions settled in 2025-2026 under the OpenTelemetry semantic-conventions group. They define shared attribute names so Datadog, Langfuse, Phoenix, OpenLLMetry, and AgentOps all parse the same spans. Instrument once; ship to any backend. Idea 1 · Span hierarchy Copy The whole thing nests under one trace id. Span ids link the parent-child relationships. Idea 2 · Required attributes Per the 2025-2026 semconv: gen_ai.operation.name — "chat" , "text_completion" , "embeddings" , "execute_tool" , "invoke_agent" . gen_ai.provider.name — "openai" , "anthropic" , "google" , "azure_openai" . gen_ai.request.model — requested model string (e.g. "gpt-4o-2024-08-06" ). gen_ai.response.model — the model actually served. gen_ai.usage.input_tokens / gen_ai.usage.output_tokens . gen_ai.response.id — provider response id for correlation. For tool spans: gen_ai.tool.name — tool identifier. gen_ai.tool.call.id — the specific call id. gen_ai.tool.description — tool description (optional). For agent spans: gen_ai.agent.name / gen_ai.agent.id / gen_ai.agent.description . Idea 3 · Span kinds SpanKind.CLIENT for calls crossing a process boundary (LLM provider, MCP server). SpanKind.INTERNAL for the agent's own loop steps and tool execution. Idea 4 · Opt-in content capture By default, spans carry metrics and timing — not prompts or completions. Large payloads and PII are off by default. Instrumentations turn content on with a switch such as OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT=true (the exact name and values vary by library), and many use OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=gen_ai_latest_experimental to emit the newest attribute shapes. Review carefully before enabling in prod. Idea 5 · Events on spans When content capture is on, it is recorded on the gen_ai.client.inference.operation.details event (older drafts used gen_ai.content.prompt and gen_ai.content.completion events, now replaced): gen_ai.input.messages : the messages sent, as structured role/parts JSON. gen_ai.output.messages : the messages the model returned, including tool calls. gen_ai.system_instructions : the system prompt, kept separate. A separate gen_ai.evaluation.result event records evaluation scores. Events are time-ordered within a span for detailed replay. Idea 6 · Exporters OTel spans export to: Jaeger / Tempo. OSS, on-prem. Langfuse. LLM-observability-specific; visualizes token usage. Arize Phoenix. Evals + tracing combined. Datadog. Commercial; natively parses gen_ai.* attributes. Honeycomb. Column-oriented; query-friendly. All speak OTLP, the wire format. Your code does not care. Idea 7 · Propagation across MCP When an MCP client calls a server, it puts the W3C trace context in the request's params._meta under the unprefixed keys traceparent , tracestate and baggage . This works the same on stdio and Streamable HTTP. The convention comes from the OTel MCP semantic conventions and is documented in the MCP specification by SEP-414 (Final). The official Python SDK 2.x injects it on the client and extracts it on the server automatically; the server span becomes a child of the client span. Idea 8 · Metrics Alongside spans, the GenAI semconv defines metrics: gen_ai.client.token.usage — histogram. gen_ai.client.operation.duration — histogram. gen_ai.execute_tool.duration — histogram. gen_ai.client.operation.time_to_first_chunk , gen_ai.invoke_agent.duration and, for self-hosted inference, gen_ai.server.time_to_first_token and gen_ai.server.time_per_output_token . MCP adds mcp.client.operation.duration and mcp.server.operation.duration . Use these for dashboards that do not need per-call detail. Idea 9 · AgentOps layer AgentOps (founded 2024) specializes in GenAI observability. It wraps popular frameworks (LangGraph, Pydantic AI, CrewAI) to emit OTel spans automatically. Useful if your stack uses a supported framework; use manual instrumentation otherwise. The same idea as a formula A trace is a tree. Every span has a trace id , its own id and a parent id . For one agent run, ∑ ​ duration ( c ) (for children that run one after another) . The gap between a span and its children is time spent in the span's own code: in an execute_tool span, it is the host's work around the MCP call. Token usage adds up across spans. For the chat spans of one run, ∑ ​ gen_ai.usage.input_tokens ( c ) , and each later call usually re-sends the whole conversation, so input tokens grow with each turn even when the new text is short. Solutions Solution P1 · Same trace, under the tool span Yes. The SDK client puts the current trace context into the request's params._meta as traceparent , and the server, in its own process, starts its tools/call search_notes SERVER span with that context as its parent. So the server span appears in the same trace, under the client span MCP send tools/call search_notes , which is itself under execute_tool search_notes . Most of the time goes to the two chat spans: generating tokens with a 0.5B model on a CPU takes seconds, while the MCP round trip takes a few milliseconds. Solution B1 · Debug switches become data leaks Prompts and answers now flow into a system built for operational data, not for personal or secret data. Every user's messages, including emails, account numbers or pasted API keys, are stored for 90 days and visible to every engineer, which may break privacy law, contracts and the company's own data rules. Traces are also exported and copied (to vendors, to test environments), so the data spreads. Instead: Turn content capture on only for a short window, a small sample, or specific test accounts, and turn it off again. Redact at the source (emails, keys, numbers) before the event is recorded, as in the block above. Send content to a separate, access-controlled store with short retention, and keep only ids and metrics in the general backend. Prefer reproducing the problem with an evaluation set over capturing real user content. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Weigh a trade-off Your trace backend can store the full prompt and completion on every model span. The support team wants it on, because they debug tickets from traces. The security team wants it off. What do you decide, and how do you still give support what they need? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Keep content capture off, which is the default the conventions recommend. Store prompts and completions in your own store, with access control and a retention period, and record a reference id on the span. Support follows the id from the trace to the content, and the trace backend never holds customer data. What the default is. By default a span carries timing and metrics, not prompts or completions. Content capture is opt-in through the stability opt-in variable and separate content variables. When it is on, the content lands in gen_ai.input.messages , gen_ai.output.messages and gen_ai.system_instructions , or in the content events on the span. What goes wrong when it is on. Prompts carry personal data, secrets and customer documents. Operators read traces, and the trace backend sets its own retention. The conventions lesson lists "capturing full prompts in spans" as the first way the pattern fails. A trace backend is also an attractive target, because it holds everything in one place. The pattern that works. Store the content outside the trace: in your log store or object store, under your own access control, audit log and retention. Put a reference id on the span. The lesson calls this the external-reference pattern, and it is also the defense against content poisoning, because the poisoned text never enters the telemetry store. What support gets. The same debugging path with one extra step: trace, span, reference id, content store. The store can redact known patterns on write and log every read. Most tickets do not need the content at all, because the span already shows the model, the tokens, the latency, the tool calls and the status. What you give up. A one-click view of the prompt inside the trace UI. That is the price, and it is small next to a trace backend full of customer data. Plausible wrong answers. "Turn it on, the trace backend is internal." Internal operators read traces, and the backend's retention is not your policy. "Store a hash of the prompt on the span." A hash shows a repeat but gives support nothing to read. A reference id into a controlled store does both. "Keep the content on the span and strip personal data with a regex." Patterns miss, and the span is still the wrong store with the wrong retention. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which spans may carry raw content when capture is on? Expected: none in production. Keep one rule, references only, so nobody has to decide per span. (level 3) A developer turns capture on in staging for a day. What is the risk? Expected: staging often replays production prompts, and the backend keeps them for its retention period. Use synthetic prompts or scrub before export. (level 3) How do you keep the content store from becoming the same leak? Expected: access by role, an audit log of reads, a retention period, and redaction of known patterns before the write. Where it is taught. The conventions lesson sets the opt-in rule and the pattern of storing content outside the span, and the OpenTelemetry GenAI lesson names the content events. The customer's card number is ..." } } Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The span marks a model call as INTERNAL, has no parent, and uses an old attribute name for the input tokens. It omits the provider, the output tokens, the response model and the response id, and it writes the prompt text, with a card number in it, into the trace. Fix the kind and the parent link, use the current attribute names, add the missing attributes, and move the content out of the span. The problems, in order of damage. Line Problem Fix parentSpanId: "" an orphan span; no backend can show which agent step made the call pass the parent context from the invoke_agent span kind: INTERNAL a model call crosses a process boundary CLIENT gen_ai.content.prompt prompt text with customer data in a store that operators read capture off by default; store content outside and put a reference id on the span gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens the attribute was renamed; backends read gen_ai.usage.input_tokens use the current name and add gen_ai.usage.output_tokens no gen_ai.provider.name cost and error dashboards cannot split by provider set it on every model span no gen_ai.response.model with routing, the served model can differ from the requested alias record what the provider returned no gen_ai.response.id no way to match the span to the provider's own log record the response id Why the content line is the one to fight over. The conventions say instrumentations should not capture inputs and outputs by default. Capture is opt-in through an environment variable, and the production pattern stores content in your own log store and records a pointer on the span. A prompt with a card number in a trace backend is a data leak with a retention policy you did not choose. Why the renamed attribute will come back. The GenAI conventions are still marked as in development, and they have renamed attributes before. Pin the conventions version you emit, set the stability opt-in, and test the attribute names of emitted spans, or the next SDK upgrade reopens this review. Plausible wrong answers. "It has a trace id and a model name, so it is fine." A trace id alone does not link the span to its parent, and a model name without a provider cannot be attributed. "Keep the prompt in the span, it is useful." Prompts carry personal data and secrets into a store that operators read. The default is off, and production stores content outside the span. "The two token names are synonyms." Backends read the current name. The old one lands in an unknown attribute, and the token dashboard shows nothing. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the empty parent matter more than the wrong kind? Expected: with no parent the span is an orphan, the trace is no longer a tree, and you cannot see which step made the call. (level 3) The team needs the prompt text to debug failures. What do you offer? Expected: store prompts in a separate store with access control and put a reference id on the span, which is the pattern the conventions recommend for production. (level 4) How do you keep the old attribute name from returning after an upgrade? Expected: pin the conventions version, set the stability opt-in variable, and add a test that asserts the attribute names on emitted spans. Where it is taught. The OpenTelemetry GenAI lesson lists the required attributes, the conventions lesson gives the content-capture rule, and the capstone traces lesson notes the renamed token attribute. Explain the mechanism You add tracing to an agent. In one run it calls a model API twice, runs two tools inside its own process and sends one request to a tool server on another machine. Which of these operations get a CLIENT span, which get an INTERNAL span, and why does anyone care? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A call that leaves the process gets a CLIENT span: the two model API calls and the request to the remote tool server. The agent loop step and a tool that runs in your own process get INTERNAL spans. The kind tells a backend the direction of each call, so it can show which operations left the process and which did not. The tree for this run. Copy Every span shares one trace id. Each child carries the id of its parent. That is what makes the run one tree instead of six loose records. The rule. CLIENT marks a call across a process boundary: a model provider, a tool server, a hosted agent service. INTERNAL marks the agent's own loop steps and any tool that runs in the same process. The conventions apply the same rule to the agent span itself: an agent that runs as a remote service is CLIENT from the caller, and an in-process agent framework is INTERNAL. The attributes that go with each kind. Span Attributes model call gen_ai.operation.name , gen_ai.provider.name , gen_ai.request.model , gen_ai.response.model , gen_ai.usage.input_tokens , gen_ai.usage.output_tokens , gen_ai.response.id tool call gen_ai.tool.name , gen_ai.tool.call.id agent run gen_ai.agent.name , gen_ai.agent.id Why it matters. Backends draw a waterfall from the kinds and the parent links. A CLIENT span with no response id cannot be matched to the provider log. A tool span with no parent is an orphan, and you can no longer see which agent step caused the call. Plausible wrong answers. "Every tool call is a CLIENT span." A tool that runs in your process is INTERNAL. Only the call that leaves the process is CLIENT. "The kind is decoration." Backends read the kind to show direction, and the conventions set it per span category. "Start a new trace for each tool call, for isolation." Separate traces lose the parent link, so you cannot see which step caused the call. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What joins the spans into one tree? Expected: one shared trace id, and a parent span id on every child. (level 2) The agent calls a hosted agent service instead of a local one. What kind is that span? Expected: CLIENT, because the agent runs in another process. (level 2) Which attribute lets a dashboard split cost by provider? Expected: gen_ai.provider.name , and multi-provider dashboards break when it is missing. (level 3) A sub-agent runs inside the same process. Does it start a new trace? Expected: no. It is a child span under the parent agent span, so the whole run stays in one trace. Where it is taught. The OpenTelemetry GenAI lesson draws the span hierarchy, and the conventions lesson names the span categories and their kinds. Defend a design Your agent uses three tool servers over the MCP protocol. Two of them speak streamable HTTP, and one runs as a local subprocess over stdio. Design how a single trace id reaches all three, and say what each server has to do when it arrives. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. For the HTTP servers, inject the W3C traceparent header into every request, as any traced HTTP client does. The stdio transport has no headers, so put the same value into the _meta field of each JSON-RPC request until the protocol adds a standard field for it. Each server reads the value, opens its own span as a child of that context, writes the trace id into its logs, and passes the context on if it calls anything else. Why this is worth the work. The lesson opens with a report from production: the agent sometimes answers in 3 seconds and sometimes in 30. The logs show the model calls and nothing else. The cause was one tool server that hung during its cold start, and nothing short of an end-to-end trace could show it. The HTTP servers. Streamable HTTP carries standard headers. The client injects traceparent , and the server starts a span under that parent. On the client side the call is a CLIENT span under the execute_tool span. On the server side the work is a child of the same trace. The gap between the two is the transport time. The stdio server. Stdio carries no HTTP headers. The protocol roadmap discusses a _meta.traceparent field on JSON-RPC calls. Until it ships, include the traceparent value in _meta on every request yourself, and have the server read it from there. The server logs the trace id so that a log line and a span can be joined later. What every server does with the context. Parse the context from the header or from _meta . Start a span as a child of that context, not a new trace. Write the trace id into every log line of the request. Propagate the context to anything it calls in turn. What you can see afterwards. One waterfall: the agent step, the tool call, the server's work. A hang appears as one long server span under a long client span. Beside the spans, emit the tool execution duration histogram per tool, which answers the dashboard questions without a trace. Plausible wrong answers. "Log a request id and join the logs later." A request id has no parent-child structure and no timing. A trace has both. "The stdio server is local, so it does not need tracing." The hang in the lesson was in a local server's cold start. Local does not mean fast. "Put the trace id into the prompt so the model carries it." The model is not a transport, and a changing value in the prompt also breaks the prefix cache. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) A server ignores the _meta field. What do you see in the trace? Expected: the server's work shows up as a separate trace or not at all, and the client span shows the duration but not where the time went. (level 3) Which span records the hang, the client span or the server span? Expected: both. The client span shows the wait from the agent's side, the server span shows what the server did, and the gap between them is the transport. (level 4) Another team operates one tool server. What do you ask them to commit to? Expected: accept the context from headers or _meta , continue the trace instead of starting one, log the trace id, and export spans to a backend that both teams can read. Where it is taught. a1321: Course home / Phase 13 · Tools & Protocols LLM Routing Layer — LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey Lesson 13.21 45 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Distinguish self-hosted, managed, and production-grade routing options. Implement a fallback chain that retries on provider failures in a defined priority order. Track per-request cost and token usage across providers. Decide between LiteLLM, OpenRouter, and Portkey for a given production constraint. Before you start Needs : Phase 13 · 02 (function calling), Phase 13 · 17 (gateways) Type : Learn. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, routing + failover + cost tracker), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Provider lock-in is expensive. Different tool-calling workloads suit different models. Routing gateways give one API surface, retries, failover, cost tracking, and guardrails. Three archetypes dominate 2026: LiteLLM (open-source self-hosted), OpenRouter (managed SaaS), Portkey (production-grade, open-sourced in March 2026). This lesson names the decision criteria and walks a stdlib routing gateway. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Routing gateway "LLM proxy" One-API-surface layer in front of many providers OpenAI-compatible "Speaks the OpenAI schema" Accepts /v1/chat/completions shape, translates to any backend Model alias "our_smart_model" Name in your code that the gateway maps to a concrete model Fallback chain "Retry list" Ordered list of providers attempted on failure Semantic caching "Prompt-embedding cache" Key is embedding of the prompt; near-duplicates share a cache hit Guardrails "Input/output filters" Redact PII, reject policy violations Per-key rate limit "Team budget" Quota scoped to an API key Cost tracking "Per-request spend" Aggregate token usage x price per model LiteLLM "The open proxy" Self-hostable OSS routing gateway OpenRouter "The managed SaaS" Hosted gateway with credit-based billing Portkey "The production option" Open-source + managed with guardrails built in The problem In plain words first Applications rarely talk to one model provider directly for long. A routing layer is a small service that sits between your code and the providers. Your code asks for a name such as smart or fast ; the router maps that name to real models, tries another provider when the first one fails, spreads load, counts tokens and money per team, can answer repeated questions from a cache, and can remove private data before a prompt leaves your network. LiteLLM is the common open-source choice you run yourself, OpenRouter is a hosted service with one bill for many providers, and Portkey offers both. This lesson runs LiteLLM's real Router with a failing provider and simulated responses (no paid calls), then adds a semantic cache, a privacy filter and a team budget, including the case where the cache gives a wrong answer. Scenarios where provider routing matters: Cost. Claude Sonnet costs 3x what Haiku costs. For a triage task, Haiku is enough; for a synthesis task, Sonnet is worth it. Route per-request. Failover. OpenAI has a bad hour. Every request fails. You want automatic fallback to Anthropic without redeploying. Latency. A live chat UI needs fast time-to-first-token. A batch summarizer does not. Route by latency SLA. Compliance. EU users must stay in EU regions. Route by region. Experimentation. A/B two models on the same workload. Route by test bucket. Hand-coding all of this per integration is repetitive. A routing gateway gives one OpenAI-compatible API and handles the rest. Idea 1 · OpenAI-compatible proxy shape Everyone speaks OpenAI-shape. The routing gateway exposes /v1/chat/completions , accepts the OpenAI schema, and internally proxies to Anthropic / Gemini / Cohere / Ollama / anything. The client does not care. Idea 2 · Model aliases Instead of a pinned snapshot id, your code says our_smart_model . The gateway maps aliases to real models. When a provider ships a new generation, you change the alias server-side; your code does not touch a thing. Idea 3 · Fallback chains Copy Gateways define this in a config. Retries count against a budget so fallback cascades do not explode cost. Idea 4 · Semantic caching Identical-or-near-identical prompts hit a cache instead of the provider. Savings depend entirely on how repetitive the traffic is. Keys are embedding-based, so near-identical prompts share a cache slot, and so can prompts that look alike but mean different things (see the run below). Idea 5 · Guardrails Gateway-level: PII redaction. Regex or ML-based pass before sending prompts. Policy violations. Reject prompts with prohibited content. Output filters. Scrub completions for leaks. Portkey and Kong both ship opinionated guardrails. LiteLLM leaves them optional. Idea 6 · Per-key rate limits One API key = one team. Per-key budgets prevent one team from consuming the shared quota. Most gateways support this. Idea 7 · Self-hosted vs managed trade-offs Factor LiteLLM (self-hosted) OpenRouter (managed) Portkey (production) Code Open source, Python Managed SaaS Open source (Mar 2026) + managed Setup Deploy a proxy Sign up Either Providers 100+ 300+ 100+ Billing Your own keys OpenRouter credits Your own keys Observability OpenTelemetry Dashboard Full OTel + PII redaction Best for Teams that want full control Rapid prototyping Production with compliance LiteLLM wins when you have an SRE team and want data sovereignty. OpenRouter wins when you want a single subscription and no infra. Portkey wins when you need guardrails and compliance out of the box. Idea 8 · Cost tracking Every request carries provider , model , input_tokens , output_tokens . Multiply by per-model per-token prices (pulled from a pricing sheet the gateway maintains). Per-user / per-team / per-project aggregation. Idea 9 · MCP plus routing A gateway can route both LLM calls AND MCP sampling requests. When a sampling request's modelPreferences prefer a specific model, the gateway translates to the right backend. This is where Phase 13 · 17 (MCP gateway) and this lesson's routing gateway sometimes merge into one service. Idea 10 · Routing strategies Static priority. First in list; fall back on error. Load balancing. Round-robin or weighted. Cost-aware. Pick the cheapest model meeting latency / quality. Latency-aware. Pick the fastest model in the last N minutes. Task-aware. Prompt classifier routes coding to one model, summarization to another. The same idea as a formula Cost of one call. Check your mental model ✗ "With a router, my code never needs to know about providers." ✓ Mostly true for chat calls; provider-specific features (caching controls, structured-output limits, tool quirks) still leak through. ✗ "A semantic cache is a free win." ✓ It can return a confidently wrong answer for a prompt that looks similar but means something else. ✗ "Fallback only changes which provider answers." ✓ It can change quality, cost, latency, data residency and tool-call format; test the whole chain. ✗ "A budget check before each call stops spending exactly at the limit." ✓ It can overshoot by the calls in flight; reserve an estimate before calling if that matters. Predict before you run The smart alias points at an OpenAI deployment whose endpoint refuses connections, with smart-backup (Claude Sonnet) as its fallback. Which model will answer, and how many failed attempts will the logger record? Over 40 calls with weights 3:1, roughly how many go to each fast deployment? (Solution P1.) The call to smart first went to gpt-5 , whose endpoint refused the connection. The logger saw one failed attempt (LiteLLM reports it as an InternalServerError , a server-side class of error that triggers fallback), and the router moved to smart-backup . The caller got an answer from claude-sonnet-4-5 and did not have to change any code. Every response carries its cost. LiteLLM priced the backup call at US$0.00033 from its bundled price map, the same number as the worked example. That is near the expected 30 and 10; the exact split changes from run to run without the fixed seed. Cheaper is not always cheaper per task. gpt-5-mini is far cheaper per token than Haiku here; whether it is good enough for the task is a quality question the router cannot answer for you. Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The first question is a miss, the paraphrase a hit. what's the refund policy for orders above $100 scores 0.980 against the cached question and reuses its answer: a call saved. Solution B1 · A slow, expensive, non-compliant outage Latency explodes. If the primary hangs rather than refusing, each attempt waits up to 60 seconds, and 3 retries mean up to 4 minutes before the first fallback is even tried, then possibly another 4 minutes on the second step. Users time out long before an answer arrives. Use short connect timeouts, a small total deadline for the whole chain, and a circuit breaker that skips a provider known to be down. Cost can double. A timeout after generation started may still be billed, and every retry of a long prompt is paid again. Retries should apply only to errors that are safe and cheap to retry. Compliance breaks quietly. The last step sends user data to another country. If the data must stay in a region, the fallback is a violation, and it only happens during outages, when nobody is watching. Each fallback target must satisfy the same data rules as the primary, or the chain must stop and return an error. Behaviour changes. Defend a design The CTO wants every product-critical model call to survive a full outage of one provider, with no redeploy and without doubling the bill. Design the setup: where the second provider sits, how a request moves between the two, what has to be identical on both sides, and what the design costs. Level 4 of 4 · about 18 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Put a gateway in front of the application with one model alias per use case, a priority list of two providers behind each alias, and a fallback rule on server errors and rate limits with a bounded retry budget. Keep the cacheable prefix layout, the tool order and the output schema identical on both providers, so that a failed-over request can hit the second provider's cache once that prefix is cached there, and still parses. The steady-state uplift is small, because the gateway sends traffic to the preferred provider most of the time, and the real price is paid in evals and prompt tests that run twice. Why two. The lesson on managed platforms argues that locking into one platform locks you out of most of the frontier, because the strongest model moves between vendors every few months, and that a single platform's regional outage is a product outage. Its policy is a two-provider minimum for any product-critical call. The cost uplift is negligible because the gateway routes to the better option in normal operation, and the availability gain during an outage is decisive. The gateway in front. The lesson on the routing layer gives the shape. Everyone speaks one API schema, so the gateway exposes one endpoint and translates behind it. Your code names an alias such as our_smart_model , and the gateway maps the alias to a concrete model on a concrete provider. Behind each alias sits a priority list: the primary, then the second provider on a server error or a rate limit, then refuse. Retries count against a budget, so that a failing primary cannot multiply the cost. The gateways lesson adds the rest of what the layer owns: rate limits per tenant, credentials pulled from a vault at runtime, observability and guardrails. What the two sides share. The cacheable prefix layout. The rule for cross-provider fallback in the lesson on prompt caching is to keep the layout identical, so that any hit works on either side. Stable parts first, the user message last. The tool serialization order. A reshuffled tool list breaks the cache on every request. The output schema and the parser. A failover that returns a shape the application cannot parse is still an outage. The eval set. Both providers run the same regression suite on every prompt change, or the fallback path drifts without anyone noticing. What it costs. Two sets of evals and prompt regressions per release. Cold caches on the second provider when the outage begins. The first requests pay the write premium, and the minimum cacheable block has to be met on both sides. The gateway's own latency, from a few milliseconds to tens, depending on its class. A log line per call that names the provider that served it, so that the bill splits and the failover rate is visible. Prove it before the outage. Inject rate-limit errors from the primary in staging and watch the traffic move. Measure the time to the first successful response on the second provider, and compare the first-token time and the cache reads during the failover with the steady state. Plausible wrong answers. "Two providers double the bill." The second provider carries traffic only during failures. The gateway routes to the preferred one the rest of the time. "Tune a separate prompt per provider." Then every change ships twice and the fallback path drifts. Keep one layout and one eval set for both. "Fail over on any error." A guardrail block or a schema error repeats on the second provider and doubles the cost of a request that should fail fast. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the second provider cost little in steady state? Expected: the gateway sends most traffic to the preferred provider. The second one carries traffic only during failures and drills. (level 4) What breaks first on a failover without the identical prefix layout? Expected: the cache on the second provider misses on every request, so the outage hour costs full price and the first-token time jumps. (level 4) Which failures trigger the failover, and which do not? Expected: server errors, rate limits and timeouts on the primary. Not a guardrail block or a malformed response, which would fail the same way on the second provider. Where it is taught. The managed platforms lesson sets the two-provider policy, the routing layer lesson gives aliases and fallback chains, the AI gateways lesson lists the gateway features, and the prompt caching lesson keeps the cacheable layout identical across providers. In plain words first The idea in one line A skill is not a long prompt with a better filename. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Agent skill "A saved prompt" A discoverable directory of procedural instructions and optional resources Portable core "Fields every runtime shares" The contract defined by the Agent Skills specification Runtime extension "Extra frontmatter" Host-specific configuration whose behavior requires a compatible adapter Activation "The skill ran" The skill body entered model-visible context; execution may come later Skill dependency "Import another skill" A runtime-mediated invocation edge with availability and policy checks Tool contract "A function schema" Inputs, outputs, permissions, side effects, errors, and evidence for a capability Ten-Minute First Success In plain words first A skill is a folder that teaches an agent how to do one kind of task. Its entry file, SKILL.md , starts with a short header holding a name and a description , followed by the instructions in plain Markdown; the folder can also hold reference notes, scripts and templates. The agent first sees only the name and description of every installed skill. It opens a skill's full instructions only when a task matches, and reads the extra files only when a step needs them. Skills are not the same as tools: an MCP tool gives the agent a new capability, a skill tells it how to approach a job, and other pieces (repository instructions, hooks, subagents) do other jobs. This lesson checks skill packages with the lesson's validator and with the specification's reference validator, measures what the catalog costs in tokens, and maps jobs to the right piece.
