In plain words first The idea in one line A registry entry tells you what a publisher declared. Production admission proves what you fetched, what you observed, what you approved, and what you can safely restore. The problem In plain words first The official MCP Registry is a public list of MCP servers: who published them, which version, and where the code or endpoint lives. It checks that a publisher owns its name, but it is not a security review, and it does not decide what your company may run. Admitting a server safely means joining several pieces of evidence: the name really belongs to the verified publisher; the downloaded package is exactly the declared one (same digest); the live server exposes exactly the tools you reviewed; the record is still active. After admission the work continues: if a running server's tools change, it is quarantined; if a version goes bad, you roll back to an earlier approved one; and every decision goes into a log that shows if anyone edits it. This lesson queries the live Registry and PyPI, then runs the lesson's admission controller against real SDK servers. You find com.example/inventory in a registry. Its description looks right. Its package exists. The server answers server/discover . That is not one fact. It is a chain of facts from different authorities: A publisher authenticated for a namespace submitted a record. A package registry served an artifact with a specific identity and digest. A running endpoint reported a protocol version, capabilities, tools, and diagnostic server information. Your organization decided that this exact combination was allowed. Collapsing those facts into “it is in the registry, so trust it” creates a supply chain blind spot. A valid publication can still be deprecated. A package tag can point at an unexpected artifact if you do not pin its digest. A server can add a destructive tool after review. A rollback can silently choose a version that was never admitted. The fix is an admission controller with evidence at every boundary. The Registry Is an Index, Not Your Approval System The official MCP Registry stores server metadata. Its server.json record names a server version and declares one or more packages or remote endpoints. Publication rules add namespace authentication, package ownership checks, restricted registry rules, and a narrow publisher metadata location. Those controls answer publication questions. Your production policy still answers deployment questions: Boundary Question Evidence owner Namespace Was the publisher allowed to use this name? Registry authentication plus your verified namespace input Record What did the publisher declare for this version? Immutable server.json digest Execution source Which package or remote endpoint will execute? Declared source fields, verified ownership result, transport, and trusted digest Runtime What does the endpoint expose now? server/discover and tool descriptors Admission Did your policy approve this exact set? Local pin and ledger entry Operations Is it still safe, and what can replace it? Drift checks, status sync, health, and rollback route The Registry schema version and the MCP protocol version are independent. A record may use the published 2025-12-11 server schema while the live server supports MCP 2026-07-28 . Never infer one from the other. Seven Controls in One Admission Decision 1. Namespace verification Official Registry names use authenticated namespaces. A verified domain can map to a reversed domain prefix. For example, control of example.com can establish com.example/* . Do not accept a string prefix check: Copy That also accepts com.exampleevil/tool . Split the name at / , require a non-empty slug, and compare the namespace segment exactly. More importantly, pass the verified namespace into admission from the authentication result. Do not derive trust from the untrusted record. GitHub-backed namespaces and domain-backed namespaces use different authentication paths. Normalize either path into one admission input: the exact verified namespace string. 2. Provenance join For a package record, the declaration and fetched artifact must join on explicit fields: package registry type package identifier package version verified ownership result downloaded artifact digest Also validate the declared package transport. A record with only a remote endpoint is valid and must not be rejected for lacking a package. For a remote source, join the declared URL and transport type to independently verified endpoint ownership and a digest of the trusted connection or deployment evidence. The lesson code supports both source kinds and hashes the selected source together with the Registry source, server name, Registry version, record digest, and evidence digest. The resulting provenance digest is a compact pointer to the full evidence set. It is not a substitute for retaining the evidence. Never accept a digest supplied only by the artifact you are trying to verify. Calculate it at a trusted fetch boundary, or receive it from a package service whose verification result you validate. 3. Pin the decision, not only the version Registry versions are unique publication identifiers. Published metadata is immutable. A changed record requires a new version. Semantic versioning is recommended, but the Registry does not require it and does not accept version ranges. This means ^1.4 is not an admission pin. Neither is “latest.” A useful pin contains: Copy Pinning several layers lets you identify which boundary changed. A record digest change under the same Registry version is a Registry integrity failure. A source digest change under the same package coordinate or remote deployment is an execution-source integrity failure. A toolset digest change is runtime drift. 4. Live drift detection Admission should observe the server that will actually receive traffic. Call server/discover , list or otherwise obtain the exposed tool descriptors through your trusted path, and verify: 2026-07-28 is in supportedVersions all locally required capabilities are present every tool descriptor has the required identity and schema surface the normalized descriptor digest matches the admitted pin on later checks The optional result _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo"] value is self-reported display, log, and debugging context. Record it as diagnostic evidence, but never use it to establish namespace, package ownership, endpoint ownership, admission, or any other security decision. A direct serverInfo alias outside _meta is not the contract field and should not be promoted into diagnostic evidence. Normalize only fields whose order has no meaning. The sample sorts the tool list by stable name before hashing, so a harmless list-order change does not cause drift. It does not discard descriptor fields. A new tool, changed schema, changed description, or new annotations changes the pin. The sample treats malformed descriptors and any descriptor digest change as drift, quarantines the pin, removes its active route, and blocks that version as a rollback target. A production policy may allow an editorial change only through a new review, because descriptions influence model tool selection. “Cosmetic” metadata can alter agent behavior. 5. Registry status is live state The Registry API attaches a response-level _meta object beside each server record. Registry-managed fields live under _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol.registry/official"] . Pass the response _meta object to admission and read _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol.registry/official"].status . A direct _meta.status value is not the official wire shape. Do not confuse response metadata with the publication record's own _meta . Status can be: active : returned by default and eligible for local admission deprecated : still discoverable with a warning, but no longer a safe automatic choice deleted : hidden by default while its historical record remains available through deleted or incremental views Sync status after admission. If an active version becomes deprecated or deleted, quarantine its pin and stop routing new work to it. Keep the evidence. Deletion from the default listing is not permission to erase your audit trail. Publisher-provided custom metadata belongs only under _meta.io.modelcontextprotocol.registry/publisher-provided in a publication record. Registry-managed response metadata is separate. Do not let a publisher set its own official status. 6. Rollback means route restoration An immutable publication is not edited during rollback. Rollback selects a previously admitted, currently eligible pin and changes the active route. A safe target must: Have a completed admission record. Still have an active Registry status under your policy. Not be quarantined by runtime or security evidence. Still resolve to the pinned package and live descriptor set. Pass current health checks. The sample focuses on the first three conditions. A real reconciler should re-fetch the package and re-check the live endpoint before activation. 7. Append an admission ledger An admission database says what is active. A ledger explains why. Each sample entry contains a sequence, time, event, server, version, outcome, reasons, evidence, the previous entry hash, and its own hash. Changing an older outcome breaks verification of that entry and every later link. This is tamper-evident, not magically tamper-proof. Anchor periodic ledger heads in a separate trust domain, such as signed release metadata or write-once storage. Restrict who can append. Keep authorization tokens, package credentials, tool arguments, and private endpoint data out of evidence. The same idea as a formula Admission is a conjunction of joins. RegistryAdmissionController.admit() joins publication, provenance, runtime, and policy. check_live() compares a new observation with the pin. observe_registry_status() quarantines versions whose Registry state changes. rollback() activates only a previously admitted eligible target. AdmissionLedger.verify() detects changes to recorded history. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Put the controller between discovery and routing: Copy Use separate identities for these jobs. A Registry sync worker needs read access to metadata. An artifact verifier needs package fetch access. A route reconciler needs permission to activate an approved pin. None of them needs every credential. Make rollout state explicit. “Approved” means the evidence passed policy. “Active” means the route currently selects it. “Quarantined” means it cannot receive new work. “Superseded” means another admitted version is active. Do not encode all four meanings in one Boolean. Run admission before exposing a server in tools/list . Otherwise a client can discover a tool during the gap between publication and policy evaluation. Before you start Needs : Phase 13 · 09 (transports), Phase 13 · 17 (gateways), Phase 13 · 30 (registry admission) Type : Build. Time : about 100 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A server is not conformant because its happy path worked through one SDK. Conformance lives at the wire, at version boundaries, through intermediaries, and during rollback. The problem In plain words first Shipping an MCP server or client safely means proving it speaks the protocol correctly, not just that it works in one demo. The protocol has two eras: the 2026-07-28 stateless style, and the older style that starts with an initialize handshake. Each needs its own strict checks, and a client must never fall back to the older, weaker style just because a reply went missing. The proof is a corpus of recorded transcripts: correct exchanges that must pass, and broken ones that must fail with exactly the right error. Two more kinds of evidence complete it: a comparison between what came over the wire and what an SDK handed to your code, and a capture of what a proxy changed. This lesson records a corpus from the official SDK's HTTP server, checks it with the lesson's harness, and finds two real differences. Your client calls tools/list through an SDK and gets tools. The integration test passes. That result leaves important questions unanswered: Did the request carry modern per-request protocol metadata? Did MCP-Protocol-Version , Mcp-Method , and Mcp-Name match the JSON-RPC body? Did the response contain a valid resultType on the wire, or did the SDK synthesize one? Would the client preserve a future additive field? Would a recognized modern error accidentally trigger a legacy handshake? Did a proxy preserve the origin status and JSON-RPC error? Did the notification serializer emit a forbidden response? Can operations prove why a release was promoted or rolled back without storing secrets? Conformance is a set of observable invariants. Build a harness that captures those invariants before production traffic has to discover them. Start With Version Eras MCP 2026-07-28 uses self-contained per-request metadata. A modern request carries params._meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and params._meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities . The exact namespaced keys matter; bare protocolVersion or clientCapabilities aliases are malformed. When mirrored routing headers are present at the HTTP boundary, their values must agree with the JSON-RPC body. Modern successful results carry resultType . Versions through 2025-11-25 use the earlier initialization era. A legacy result without resultType is interpreted as complete only after the client has selected that earlier era. Do not create one permissive validator that accepts both shapes at once. Use two branches: Branch Entry evidence Missing resultType Initialization Modern Successful server/discover or recognized modern response Invalid Not the default path Legacy Configured allowlist plus a valid legacy initialize result after an inconclusive modern probe Interpreted as complete Required by that era The separation prevents a malformed modern peer from being rewarded with weaker validation. Strict mode Strict mode requires proof of modern behavior. A successful server/discover proves the modern branch. A recognized modern JSON-RPC error also proves it. Correct the request or stop. Never downgrade because the server returned -32020 , -32021 , or -32022 . Fallback mode Fallback mode performs one bounded modern probe. A timeout, empty reply, closed connection, or unrecognized response is inconclusive. It does not prove that the peer is legacy. Only an endpoint explicitly configured or allowlisted for compatibility may then receive a bounded legacy probe, and the client selects the legacy branch only after validating that probe's initialize result and negotiated legacy revision. Fallback is not “try legacy after any error.” A recognized modern error contains useful correction information. Downgrading after it can hide a header mismatch, missing capability declaration, or unsupported version. This prevents an attacker, outage, or filtering proxy from forcing downgrade by dropping the modern response. Record the endpoint policy, inconclusive modern observation, exact positive legacy evidence, and selected era together. Record the selected era beside every transcript. Without that fact, a missing field can look acceptable in one test run and invalid in another. Build a Transcript Corpus A transcript fixture records what crossed the boundary, not only the SDK call: Copy Keep two classes of fixtures. Golden transcripts Golden transcripts prove accepted behavior: modern discovery or method request with matching metadata and headers complete result with required fields input_required result when the method can request more input extension result only after the corresponding capability was advertised legacy result without resultType , but only in the selected legacy era notification processing with no JSON-RPC response A golden transcript is precise, not large. Keep volatile IDs and timestamps deterministic or normalize them before comparison. Negative transcripts Negative transcripts prove refusal behavior: header and body mismatch missing per-request capabilities unsupported matched protocol version missing modern resultType unknown or unadvertised resultType response jsonrpc other than 2.0 or an ID that differs in value or JSON type a response containing both result and error , or neither one an error without an integer code and string message a known protocol error mapped to the wrong HTTP status response emitted for a notification malformed JSON-RPC envelope proxy collapse of a protocol error For each negative case, assert the rejection boundary and stable error code. “The call failed” is too weak. A proxy-generated 500 and an origin -32020 can both look like failure while telling operators completely different stories. The header-mismatch fixture must include the server's actual HTTP 400 JSON-RPC response with the matching request ID and error code -32020 . Enforce that automatically whenever the local validator observes HeaderMismatch ; do not make response verification an optional fixture flag. A case with HTTP 500 and no body fails even when the local rejection code was correct. A harness that stops after its own request validator throws has tested only itself, not the server's wire behavior. The official MCP conformance project is useful as an external suite and versioned reference. Keep your local transcripts too. They capture your proxy, SDK, authentication, extensions, and release path, which a general suite cannot know. Header Values Must Match the RPC Body In modern Streamable HTTP, intermediaries can route or enforce policy using mirrored headers. The JSON-RPC body remains the protocol source of truth. A mismatch is an integrity failure, not a hint to choose one value. Validate in this order: Parse and validate the JSON-RPC envelope and metadata types. Compare MCP-Protocol-Version with params._meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion . Compare Mcp-Method with method . When the method has a routing name, compare Mcp-Name with the corresponding body value. After equality is established, decide whether the matched version and capability set are supported. This order distinguishes mismatch -32020 from unsupported version -32022 . It also stops a gateway from authorizing the header name while the origin executes a different body name. HTTP field names are case-insensitive, while their values remain case-sensitive. Normalize header names before lookup and reject conflicting duplicates. For an unsafe, non-ASCII, or leading-or-trailing-whitespace Mcp-Name , decode the exact =?base64?{Base64EncodedValue}?= UTF-8 sentinel before comparing it with the body. Reject an incomplete sentinel, invalid Base64, invalid UTF-8, or raw unsafe value with -32020 . Raw surrounding whitespace is invalid even when the body contains the same characters because that value required sentinel encoding before transport. An intermediary can reject malformed HTTP before a request reaches the MCP server, so its failure may be an HTTP error without JSON-RPC. Capture whether a rejection came from the intermediary or origin. The origin MCP server should use the protocol error contract when it handled a valid JSON-RPC request. Unknown Fields Are Not Unknown Results Forward compatibility requires two different rules. Additive unknown fields Result objects and _meta maps can gain fields. A validator should preserve or ignore an additive field according to its role, unless the field violates a reserved contract. The sample keeps the full raw result in evidence and accepts futureHint beside a known result. If you are a transparent proxy, preserving an unknown field is usually safer than stripping it. If you are an application client, ignoring it can be valid. Your differential test should still reveal that the SDK omitted it so the behavior is deliberate. Unknown resultType resultType is a discriminator. Core modern results use complete or input_required . An extension can add another value only when its capability was advertised. The Tasks extension, for example, can add task in that negotiated capability context. An unknown or unadvertised discriminator cannot be safely treated as complete. The client does not know the lifecycle it would be discarding. Reject it. The same raw response can therefore contain an acceptable unknown field and an unacceptable unknown result type. Test both cases. The discriminator is only the first layer. Validate the method-specific payload after it. A complete tools/list result needs a tools array whose descriptors have unique non-empty names, useful descriptions, and object-root inputSchema values. A task result is valid only for an eligible tools/call with the Tasks capability and requires taskId , known status, creation and update timestamps, and ttlMs , plus a valid optional polling interval. A complete completion/complete result requires a completion object with no more than 100 string values, an optional non-negative integer total that is not smaller than the returned values, and an optional Boolean hasMore . A well-spelled resultType cannot make a malformed payload conformant. The Notification Invariant A JSON-RPC notification has no id . The receiver must not send a JSON-RPC success or error response. For an accepted HTTP notification shape, the harness expects an HTTP 202 with an empty body. MCP 2026-07-28 defines no core client-to-server notifications over Streamable HTTP. The sample uses a namespaced course extension notification only to test the one-way serializer invariant. Do not present it as a new core method. Test the serializer, not only the handler. A handler may return None while middleware wraps it in a JSON success object. Capture the final egress bytes. Add an SDK Differential SDKs often turn wire objects into convenient language types. That is useful, but a normalized object cannot prove what was received. For every high-risk fixture, capture: Raw status, headers, and response body before SDK decoding. SDK-normalized return value or exception. The expected semantic projection for the selected era. Fields lifted, synthesized, stripped, or changed by the SDK. The sample permits SDK-only removal of known wire bookkeeping such as resultType , _meta , ttlMs , and cacheScope while comparing the application payload. It reports a dropped futureHint because that unknown semantic field disappeared. Do not assume every difference is an SDK bug. The point is to make the transformation visible. Decide whether your component is an application endpoint, which may ignore an additive field, or a transparent intermediary, which should preserve it. Run the differential against every SDK and version you ship. If two SDKs normalize the same transcript differently, release policy should say which behavior is acceptable rather than choosing the most convenient output after the fact. Capture Proxy Evidence Most production MCP failures occur across more than one process. Record three views: View Minimum evidence Ingress request headers, JSON-RPC body, content type, authenticated route, receive time Origin forwarded headers and body digest, origin status, response headers and body Egress client-visible status, headers, body, and send time The sample detects two common transformations: an origin HTTP 400 or 404 JSON-RPC error becomes a generic proxy 500 the egress JSON-RPC body differs from the origin body Add deployment-specific assertions for content type, Accept , compression, request-scoped SSE, cache headers, and trace correlation. Capture both sides of TLS termination when policy permits. Never log credentials just to prove the path. Redact Before Evidence Leaves Memory Redaction is part of conformance operations, not a later cleanup job. Apply it before serialization, hashing, logs, test artifacts, or failure uploads. The sample case-folds key names and removes separators before matching, then recursively replaces values under keys such as Authorization , Cookie , Set-Cookie , X-Api-Key , accessToken , clientSecret , registrationAccessToken , token , password , secret , and api_key . Canonicalization and the denylist must use the same form so camelCase, hyphenated, underscored, and dotted variants cannot bypass one another's policy. A production collector should add method-specific argument policy, because a harmless key like query can still contain personal or regulated data. Hash the redacted evidence bundle. Keep raw captures only in an approved short-lived system when a specific investigation requires them. A digest proves which redacted bundle drove the decision; it does not reveal the removed value. Make Health and Rollback Part of the Gate Protocol conformance is necessary but not sufficient for release. A conformant candidate can still time out, leak memory, or overload a dependency. Define a health window before rollout: minimum sample count maximum error rate maximum latency percentile saturation or resource limits observation duration comparison with the admitted baseline Define rollback evidence before rollout too: exact prior version admission evidence digest SHA-256 artifact and descriptor pins current Registry status current health result route restoration procedure an attestation over those exact fields from a trusted release-controller identity Require that rollback target to be verified and healthy before promotion, not only after the candidate fails. A successful release without a usable recovery path is not production-ready. If a candidate fails and the rollback target lacks that evidence, hold traffic instead of guessing. “Roll back to whatever was there” is not an operational control. Do not reduce readiness to truthiness checks such as a non-empty version, healthy: "yes" , or an arbitrary evidence string. The sample requires exact types, an active status, three SHA-256 digests, a trusted signer, and a valid HMAC-SHA-256 attestation over the complete rollback payload. Its deterministic demo key is a non-secret fixture. Inject a protected key, KMS verification result, or public-key attestation verifier at the release boundary in production. The release gate also refuses empty transcript, SDK differential, or proxy evidence. Each source must carry valid evidence digests. A green health window cannot fill in a boundary that was never observed. The same idea as a formula A corpus as a test of two sets. Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Conformance testing : the MCP project publishes a conformance suite and SDK tiers (official SDKs must pass it), and the MCP Inspector exercises servers interactively. Solutions Solution P1 · No: -32602 No. The SDK answers HTTP 400 with -32602 (invalid params): it treats the missing clientCapabilities field as a malformed request. The lesson's harness maps the same situation to -32021 . The corpus records the disagreement instead of hiding it; the next step is to read the 2026-07-28 error definitions and change whichever side is wrong, then keep the transcript as a regression test. Solution B1 · A downgrade on demand They can force a downgrade at will. By dropping or delaying the server/discover reply (or injecting any error), the attacker makes the client fall back to the legacy era, where results without resultType are accepted, initialization and sessions return, and the newer header-body checks and error codes do not apply. Weaker validation is then used against a server that actually speaks the modern protocol, and real modern errors (a header mismatch, an unsupported version) are hidden by the fallback instead of being corrected. The rule should be: a successful discover or a recognized modern error means modern; correct the request or stop. Only an inconclusive probe (timeout, empty or unrecognized reply) to an endpoint explicitly allowlisted for legacy, followed by a valid legacy initialize reply, may select the legacy era, and the decision and its evidence are logged. In plain words first The idea in one line A compiled program is a set of tables that point at each other. A reader you wrote gives output you can check byte by byte. Before You Start: Authorization and the Law In plain words first A compiled program is a file of tables. One header says what kind of file it is and where the other tables are. Section headers name the pieces: the machine code, the read-only data, the symbol table that names functions and their sizes, and the relocations, notes that say "fill in this address later". Program headers tell the operating system's loader which parts of the file to map into memory and with which permissions. Reverse engineering starts by reading these tables exactly, byte by byte, and it is only done on programs you are allowed to study; in this track that means programs you wrote. This lesson checks the lesson's own small ELF reader against three independent parsers on the same file, then compiles the same C source with this machine's GCC and reads both the objects and a linked executable. Every target in lessons 32 to 36 is a program you wrote and compiled. The source is code/fixtures/ledger.c , four short C functions. You own the source, the compiler command, and the object files it produced. There is no licence to read, no protection to pass, and no third party whose code you open. The track never covers software protections, licence checks, or programs you do not own. The rule exists because the law treats disassembly as copying. In Sega Enterprises Ltd. v. Accolade, Inc. , 977 F.2d 1510 (9th Cir. 1992), the court held that intermediate copies made during disassembly are copies under the Copyright Act. It then held that "where disassembly is the only way to gain access to the ideas and functional elements embodied in a copyrighted computer program and where there is a legitimate reason for seeking such access, disassembly is a fair use of the copyrighted work, as a matter of law." The second case is Sony Computer Entertainment, Inc. v. Connectix Corp. , 203 F.3d 596 (9th Cir. 2000). Connectix copied the PlayStation BIOS while it built an emulator, and the court held those copies fair use. Both cases protected the study. Neither protected copied code in the final product. Two statutes set the limits. 17 U.S.C. 1201(f) lets a person who "has lawfully obtained the right to use a copy of a computer program" circumvent an access control "for the sole purpose of identifying and analyzing those elements of the program that are necessary to achieve interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs". Four limits stack: a lawful copy, the interoperability purpose, elements that were not already "readily available", and analysis that is otherwise non-infringing. Section 1201(f) is an exception to the anti-circumvention rule only. The copying question stays with fair use. In the European Union, Directive 2009/24/EC Article 5(3) covers study. A person with a right to use a copy can "observe, study or test the functioning of the program in order to determine the ideas and principles which underlie any element of the program". The right applies while loading, displaying, running, transmitting, or storing the program. Article 6 permits decompilation without the rightholder's authorisation when it is "indispensable to obtain the information necessary to achieve the interoperability of an independently created computer program". The conditions match 1201(f). A licensee performs the acts, the information was not already readily available, and the acts stay within the parts needed. Article 6(2) bars using the result for any other goal or for a program that is substantially similar in expression. Article 8 makes contract terms contrary to Article 6 or Article 5(3) null and void. When a future target is not yours, obtain written authorization before you open the file and keep the authorization with your evidence. Section 2.1 of the Reverse Engineering 101 manual gives the full citations and the CJEU cases. The problem You compiled ledger.c and ran llvm-objdump -t on the object. The output lists percent_change at value 0000000000000000 with size 0000000000000010 . Which 16 bytes of the 1,768-byte file are that function? The listing also shows R_X86_64_PC32 .rodata+0x10 at offset 0x36 , and the four bytes at that spot in the file are zero. What will they become, and why is the addend 0x10 when the table starts at 0x14 ? rea answers layout questions with inspect_binary_layout , and that tool exists only on Linux x64 with pwntools 4.15.0 behind REA_PWNTOOLS_PYTHON . On this Mac it is absent. address_to_file_offset needs a Ghidra session and a complete copy of the original file bytes with a matching SHA-256. inspect_artifact lists what a container holds by path and content hash. It never opens the tables inside an object file. So you write the reader yourself in about 950 lines of Python with struct.unpack and no dependency. The tests compare every table with llvm-objdump text captured once into the fixtures. The File Is Tables That Point at Tables The System V gABI, chapter 4, Figure 4-1, draws two views of one file. The linking view has an ELF header, an optional program header table, sections, and a required section header table. The execution view has an ELF header, a required program header table, segments, and an optional section header table. The gABI adds one sentence that governs the whole reader: "Only the ELF header has a fixed position in the file". Every other structure is found by an offset stored in another structure. The gABI also fixes the scalar types and says that "ELF uses no bit-fields". Elf64_Addr and Elf64_Off are 8 bytes, Elf64_Half is 2, Elf64_Word is 4, and Elf64_Xword is 8. The x86-64 psABI, section 4.1.1, requires ELFCLASS64 , ELFDATA2LSB , e_machine EM_X86_64 (62), and e_flags 0. Little-endian with fixed widths means struct.unpack with a < prefix reads every record in one call. The first 64 bytes of ledger-x86_64-O1.o : Copy Read them against the gABI "ELF Header" page. e_ident is the 16 bytes 7f 45 4c 46 (the magic), class 2 (64-bit), data 1 (little-endian), version 1, OS ABI 0 (System V), and padding. Then e_type 0x0001 is ET_REL , a relocatable object. e_machine 0x003e is 62, EM_X86_64 . e_entry is zero because an object has no entry point. e_phoff is zero because an object has no program headers. e_shoff is 0x428 , the file offset of the section header table. The last row holds e_ehsize 0x40 , e_phentsize 0, e_phnum 0, e_shentsize 0x40 , e_shnum 0x0b (11 headers), and e_shstrndx 0x0001 . The reader turns that row into one call: Copy The format string is the gABI figure read left to right: two halfwords, a word, three 8-byte values, a word, and six halfwords. The reader refuses a file whose magic, class, or byte order differs, and it refuses e_shentsize or e_phentsize values that are not 64 and 56. A wrong width would make every later offset wrong, so the check sits at the top. Section Headers and Two String Tables Each section header is an Elf64_Shdr of 64 bytes (gABI Figure 4-8): sh_name , sh_type , sh_flags , sh_addr , sh_offset , sh_size , sh_link , sh_info , sh_addralign , and sh_entsize . The format string is <IIQQQQIIQQ . sh_name is an offset into the section whose index is e_shstrndx , and the name ends at the first zero byte. In this object e_shstrndx is 1, and clang named that section .strtab , so one table serves both the section names and the symbol names. The reader prints the 11 headers of the -O1 object: Copy Index 0 is the reserved null header. .text holds 159 bytes of code at file offset 0x40 , right after the header, with flags A (allocated in memory) and X (executable). .rodata holds 80 bytes of read-only data. .rodata.str1.1 holds the five label strings F\0D\0C\0B\0A\0 , 10 bytes, with flags M (mergeable) and S (strings). .comment holds the 47-byte compiler stamp \0Apple clang version 17.0.0 (clang-1700.6.3.2)\0 . .llvm_addrsig has type 0x6fff4c03 , inside the OS-specific range SHT_LOOS to SHT_HIOS that the gABI reserves, and LLVM's ELF.h names it. Its flag E is SHF_EXCLUDE , so a linker drops it. The sh_link and sh_info columns are the pointers between tables. .rela.text has sh_info 2 and sh_link 10: it patches section 2 and takes its symbols from section 10. .symtab has sh_link 1, the string table for symbol names, and sh_info 9, the index of the first non-local symbol. sh_addr is zero in every row because an object has no addresses yet. The linker assigns them. Two gABI rules let the reader draw a complete map of the file. Sections "are contiguous and do not overlap", and a file "may contain inactive space". The reader sorts every structure by offset and fills the holes: Copy The three gaps total 10 bytes, and each one is alignment. .rodata has sh_addralign 8, so it starts at 0xe0 rather than 0xdf . .symtab has alignment 8, so seven bytes sit unused after .comment . The section header table itself is aligned to 8. Sections of type SHT_NOBITS occupy no file bytes at all, so the map skips them. Nothing in this object has that type. A .bss in a linked program does, and a reader that trusts sh_size there reads past the file. Symbols: Binding, Type, Section, Value, Size An Elf64_Sym is 24 bytes (gABI Figure 4-18): st_name , st_info , st_other , st_shndx , st_value , st_size , format <IBBHQQ . st_info packs two fields: the binding in the high four bits and the type in the low four. The gABI names the bindings STB_LOCAL 0, STB_GLOBAL 1, STB_WEAK 2, and the types STT_NOTYPE 0, STT_OBJECT 1, STT_FUNC 2, STT_SECTION 3, STT_FILE 4. The low two bits of st_other hold the visibility, STV_DEFAULT 0 here throughout. Copy Index 0 is the reserved undefined symbol. st_shndx names the section that defines the symbol, with three reserved values: SHN_UNDEF 0, SHN_ABS 0xfff1 for the file name, and SHN_COMMON 0xfff2 . Section symbols have an empty name, so llvm-objdump prints the section's own name for them, and the reader does the same. The gABI rule that "all symbols with STB_LOCAL binding precede the weak and global symbols" shows up as the first nine rows, and .symtab recorded 9 in sh_info for that reason. In a relocatable object st_value is an offset inside the symbol's section, because sh_addr is zero. The file offset of a function is therefore sh_offset + st_value - sh_addr , and its length is st_size : Copy For percent_change that is 0x40 + 0 , and the 16 bytes are 85 ff 74 09 29 fe 6b c6 64 99 f7 ff c3 31 c0 c3 . The sizes matter as much as the starts. grade ends at .text offset 0x3e . The two bytes 66 90 that follow are a nop the compiler added so that total starts at 0x40 , a 16-byte boundary. Those two bytes belong to no symbol. Lesson 13.33 uses st_size as the stop condition for a disassembler, and lesson 36 masks them out before it compares a rebuild. Relocations: What the Zero Bytes Mean An Elf64_Rela is 24 bytes (gABI Figure 4-23): r_offset , r_info , and a signed r_addend , format <QQq . The gABI splits r_info with two macros: ELF64_R_SYM(i) is i >> 32 and ELF64_R_TYPE(i) is i & 0xffffffff . In a relocatable file r_offset is an offset inside the section named by the table's sh_info . The type names and formulas come from the x86-64 psABI, Table 4.9. There S is the symbol value, A the addend, P the place being patched, and L the PLT entry. R_X86_64_64 is S + A , R_X86_64_PC32 is S + A - P , and R_X86_64_PLT32 is L + A - P . The -O1 object has eight records: Copy Take the first one apart. Offset 0x36 lies inside grade , which spans 0x10 to 0x3e . The instruction at 0x33 is 48 8d 0d 00 00 00 00 , a lea of a RIP-relative address, and its four-byte displacement sits at 0x36 . The processor adds the displacement to the address of the next instruction, 0x3a . The compiler wants the result to be .rodata + 0x14 , where a five-entry table of 32-bit values 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 begins. So the stored value must be (.rodata + 0x14) - 0x3a . The formula S + A - P with P = 0x36 gives .rodata + A - 0x36 . Setting the two equal gives A = 0x14 - 4 = 0x10 . The addend carries the target offset minus the four bytes between the displacement and the end of the instruction. That table is how clang compiled the switch in grade at -O1. The code computes score / 10 with a multiply by 0x66666667 and two shifts, subtracts 6, compares with 4, and indexes the table. The -O1 ELF object keeps no symbol for the table. The reference is the section symbol .rodata plus an addend, and only the arm64 build of the same source names it l_switch.table.grade . The second record, at 0x84 in grade_label , points at a second table of 8-byte values at .rodata + 0x28 . The third, at 0x93 , points at .rodata + 0x0 , the start of labels.rel . The five .rela.rodata records fill labels.rel . Each entry sits at offset 4i and gets the addend 4i , so S + A - P reduces to the string's address minus the base of the table. grade_label reads an entry with movslq , adds the table base back, and has the pointer. The first record names the section symbol .rodata.str1.1 with addend 0 because the string F is the first byte of that section. The others name .L.str.1 to .L.str.4 , the compiler's local labels for D , C , B , and A . The same source compiles to three different tables at three optimization levels. The reader shows the difference without a disassembler: Build Where labels lives How grade selects How grade_label reaches grade -O0 .data , five 8-byte pointers, five R_X86_64_64 records A jump table in .rodata : five R_X86_64_PC32 records pointing into .text A call with R_X86_64_PLT32 grade-0x4 -O1 .rodata as labels.rel , five 32-bit relative entries A value table at .rodata+0x14 , one R_X86_64_PC32 Inlined, no call -O2 Same as -O1 Same as -O1 Inlined, total grows to 140 bytes At -O0 the switch is a real jump table whose five entries point back into .text at +0x91 , +0x8c , +0x87 , +0x82 , and +0x86 . The call to grade carries the same -0x4 addend for the same reason as the lea . At -O1 the optimizer saw that every case returns a constant and replaced the jumps with a table of results. Lesson 13.33 decodes both shapes. Program Headers: The Loader's View A relocatable object has no program headers, so e_phnum is 0. An executable or a shared object has them, and the loader reads nothing else. An Elf64_Phdr is 56 bytes (gABI Figure 5-1): p_type , p_flags , p_offset , p_vaddr , p_paddr , p_filesz , p_memsz , p_align , format <IIQQQQQQ . The gABI fixes three rules for PT_LOAD entries. They appear in ascending p_vaddr order, and a p_memsz larger than p_filesz means zero fill. p_vaddr is congruent to p_offset modulo p_align . Every target in this track is a program you built, and no linker on this Mac produces a Linux executable from ledger.o . So the fixture tiny-x86_64 comes from code/fixtures/build_tiny_elf.py , which writes 736 bytes with struct.pack . The file holds an ELF header, two program headers, a 36-byte _start , a 3-byte .rodata , a symbol table, and six section headers. _start writes ok\n to file descriptor 1 and exits with status 42. On Linux x86-64 it runs. Here it is a fixture for the program header path. Copy The single PT_LOAD maps the whole 736-byte file at 0x400000 . The reader maps an address to a file offset by finding the PT_LOAD that contains it and computing p_offset + (address - p_vaddr) . For the entry point that is 0 + (0x4000b0 - 0x400000) = 0xb0 , the start of .text . This is the computation behind rea's address_to_file_offset . For a Ghidra target, that tool returns {address, file_offset} . The Hopper provider also returns provider_file_offset and image_base_file_offset . The tool needs a complete original copy of the file, and the SHA-256 of that copy must match the target. The documentation of rea's inspect_binary_layout adds a line to keep: "A linked address is not a runtime address". A position-independent executable loads at a base the kernel chooses, and the file offset is the only stable coordinate. Program headers also explain why a stripped executable still runs. A linker can remove the section header table entirely, and e_shoff becomes zero. A tool that walks sections then sees nothing. The loader never looked at them. The Same Ideas in Mach-O Apple publishes no prose specification for Mach-O. The headers in the XNU source are the specification: EXTERNAL_HEADERS/mach-o/loader.h , nlist.h , and reloc.h . The fixture ledger-arm64-O1.o is the same ledger.c built with clang -target arm64-apple-macos -O1 -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables -c . A mach_header_64 is 32 bytes: magic , cputype , cpusubtype , filetype , ncmds , sizeofcmds , flags , reserved . The magic is 0xfeedfacf , MH_MAGIC_64 . cputype is 0x0100000c , CPU_TYPE_ARM64 . filetype is 1, MH_OBJECT . ncmds is 5 and sizeofcmds is 616: the load commands occupy the 616 bytes after the header, and each one starts with {cmd, cmdsize} . The flag 0x2000 is MH_SUBSECTIONS_VIA_SYMBOLS . Copy LC_SEGMENT_64 (0x19) is the Mach-O answer to both ELF tables. Its segment_command_64 has segname , vmaddr , vmsize , fileoff , filesize , maxprot , initprot , nsects , and flags . Then nsects records of type section_64 , 80 bytes each, follow in the same command. The loader.h comment on MH_OBJECT says the sections live "in one unnamed segment with no segment padding". Copy Each section names its parent segment in segname , so two sections called __const are distinct because one is __DATA,__const and the other __TEXT,__const . A 32-bit field follows, packed as r_symbolnum (24 bits), r_pcrel (1), r_length (2), r_extern (1), and r_type (4). The six __text records are three pairs of ARM64_RELOC_PAGE21 and ARM64_RELOC_PAGEOFF12 , one pair per table reference. An arm64 adrp plus add does what one x86-64 lea does, so each reference needs two records. The five __DATA,__const records are ARM64_RELOC_UNSIGNED with r_length 3, so each one patches an 8-byte absolute pointer. LC_SYMTAB (0x2) holds symoff 1240, nsyms 17, stroff 1512, strsize 176, and 1512 plus 176 is 1688, the file size. Each nlist_64 is 16 bytes: n_strx , n_type , n_sect , n_desc , n_value . n_type is a bit field. N_TYPE (mask 0x0e ) equal to N_SECT ( 0xe ) means defined in the section whose 1-based ordinal is n_sect . N_EXT ( 0x01 ) marks an external symbol. nlist_64 has no size field. Check your mental model ✗ "Section headers are what the loader uses." ✓ The loader reads program headers; a stripped file can lack section headers and still run. ✗ "The zero bytes in an object's code are the real values." ✓ They are placeholders a relocation will patch at link time. ✗ "A symbol's value is always an address." ✓ In a relocatable object it is an offset in its section; in an executable, a virtual address. ✗ "Two compilers produce the same tables for the same source." ✓ Section names, sizes and relocation types differ; parse what is there, not what you expect. Solutions Solution P1 · The parsers agree; the compilers do not Yes, the parsers agree: identical section tables, function values and sizes, and relocation records. No, the compilers do not: GCC's -O1 grade is 83 bytes, clang's 46, and GCC adds endbr64 , uses different section names and keeps a PLT call at -O1 . Parsing is deterministic; code generation is a choice each compiler makes. Solution B1 · Release builds move the ground Section headers may be gone. Release builds are often stripped, and a linker or packer can drop the section header table entirely ( e_shoff = 0 ). The loader never needs it, so the program runs, but a section-name lookup finds nothing. Use program headers ( PT_LOAD ) to map addresses to file offsets, as the second block does. st_value is an address, not an offset, in an executable. In a relocatable object, st_value is an offset inside its section and sh_addr is 0, so sh_offset + st_value happens to work. In a linked executable, st_value is a virtual address such as 0x40112e ; the correct formula subtracts the section's (or segment's) address: sh_offset + (st_value - sh_addr) . Read the code From a relocatable object: the symbol grade has st_value 0x10 , st_size 46 , section .text ; .text has sh_offset 0x40 and sh_addr 0 . The relocation table holds one record at offset 0x36 , type R_X86_64_PC32 , symbol .rodata , addend 0x10 , and the instruction at 0x33 is leaq (%rip), %rcx whose last four bytes are zero. Answer three questions: which file bytes are grade , what the zero bytes become, and why the addend is 0x10 when the table of return values starts at .rodata+0x14 . Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The file offset of a function is sh_offset + st_value - sh_addr , here 0x40 + 0x10 , so grade is the 46 bytes at file offset 0x50 , and st_value alone is an offset inside the section, not a place in the file. The zero bytes are the displacement field of a RIP-relative operand; the link editor writes S + A - P into them, the symbol value plus the addend minus the address of the field. The processor adds that field to the address of the next instruction, 0x3a , which is four bytes past the field, so the final target is .rodata + 0x10 + 4 = .rodata + 0x14 ; the addend carries the target offset minus the four bytes between the field and the end of the instruction. Tables that point at tables. Only the ELF header has a fixed position in the file. Every other structure is found by an offset stored in another structure: e_shoff names the section header table, sh_offset names a section's bytes, st_value is an offset inside the section named by st_shndx while sh_addr is zero in an object. Sizes matter as much as starts: grade ends at .text offset 0x3e , and the two bytes 66 90 after it are a nop the compiler added so the next function starts on a 16-byte boundary. They belong to no symbol, a disassembler stops at st_size , and a byte comparison masks them. Three relocation outcomes. Type Formula What the link editor does R_X86_64_PC32 to a defined symbol S + A - P writes the distance and the record is gone R_X86_64_PLT32 to an undefined function L + A - P makes a PLT entry and a GOT slot when the symbol stays preemptible; when the link binds the symbol, writes the direct distance R_X86_64_64 in a position-independent image S + A keeps a relative record for the loader The same compensation appears on every RIP-relative operand in the fixtures: a call to grade carries grade-0x4 for the same reason. The five words at .rodata+0x14 read 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 , which is how the compiler turned the switch into a table of return values at -O1 . The jump table at -O0 uses the same arithmetic. In the unoptimized object every table byte is zero and the targets exist only as five records in .rela.rodata . Apply S + A - P to entry k at offset 4k : the stored value is .text + A - (.rodata + 4k) , the code adds .rodata back, so the target is .text + A - 4k . Entry 0 is 0x91 , entry 1 is 0x8c - 4 = 0x88 , entry 2 is 0x7f , entries 3 and 4 are both 0x76 , the shared case. When the section headers are gone. A linker can remove the section header table and e_shoff becomes zero; a tool that walks sections sees nothing. The loader never looked at them: PT_LOAD maps an address to a file offset with p_offset + (address - p_vaddr) . A linked address is not a runtime address either, since a position-independent executable loads at a base the kernel chooses, and the file offset is the stable coordinate. Plausible wrong answers. " grade is at file offset 0x10 ." That is st_value , an offset inside .text ; the file offset adds sh_offset . "The table starts at 0x10 because the addend says so." The addend compensates for the four bytes to the end of the instruction; the target is 0x14 . "The instruction is lea 0(%rip) ." The zeros are a placeholder the link editor fills; the relocation record names the operand. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What are the two bytes right after grade , and whose are they? Expected: alignment padding, a nop , owned by no symbol; st_size is the stop condition. (level 3) In the -O0 object the jump table bytes are all zero. Where are the targets? Expected: in the five relocation records; target equals the addend minus 4k , and the code adds the table base back. (level 3) The executable is stripped of section headers. How do you find the bytes behind an address? Expected: through the PT_LOAD program header, p_offset + (address - p_vaddr) . (level 4) A decompiler shows the table under a DAT_ name at an absolute address. Reconcile it with .rodata+0x14 . Expected: it placed the object at its own base and applied the relocation; subtract the base it gave .rodata and the offset is 0x14 . Where it is taught. In plain words first The idea in one line A disassembly listing is a claim about which bytes are instructions, and this lesson builds the decoder and graph that check the claim. The problem In plain words first Machine code is just bytes; a disassembler turns them back into instructions. On x86-64 that is hard, because instructions have different lengths (1 to 15 bytes), so starting at the wrong byte gives nonsense. There are two basic strategies. A linear sweep decodes from the start of the code to the end, one instruction after another; it is simple but gets confused when data sits between instructions. Recursive descent starts at a known entry and follows jumps and branches; it skips data but stops at jumps whose target is computed at run time, such as a switch's jump table. Decoded instructions are grouped into basic blocks, the blocks form a control-flow graph, and dominators reveal its loops. This lesson checks the lesson's hand-written decoder against Capstone and its graph algorithms against networkx, and finds one instruction the decoder does not know. You compiled ledger.c at -O0 and asked an agent what grade does. The agent called a disassembler, read the listing, and answered that the function ends in jmpq *%rax with no known target. It then wrote pseudocode with a single return 0 . You open the same object in llvm-objdump -d and see four blocks after the jump that store 4, 3, 2, and 1. The listing had them all along. Nothing in the listing says how execution reaches them, so the tool treated them as dead code. A listing answers one question only: which bytes form which instruction. It does not say which instructions run, in what order, or from where. To answer them you need three more structures: the bytes that control flow can reach, the basic blocks, and the edges between them. rea 6.5.0 has no disassembler of its own. For deep analysis, its README asks you to bring Ghidra, Hopper, or IDA. For offline inspection, rea can also call a GNU objdump or a Rizin that you install. Its call graph stops at unresolved targets: "Callers/callees contain only resolved functions.... Targetless computed flow remains unknown.". This lesson builds the part that produces those facts, so you can judge them when a tool reports them. The Instruction Format Has One Rule Per Field Intel SDM Volume 2, Figure 2-1 gives the byte order of every instruction. First come optional prefixes, then one to three opcode bytes, then an optional ModRM byte and an optional SIB byte. A displacement of 0, 1, 2, or 4 bytes follows, then an immediate of 0, 1, 2, or 4 bytes. The whole instruction is at most 15 bytes (SDM 2.3.11). AMD APM Volume 3, Chapter 1, Sections 1.1 to 1.7 describe the same format in fewer pages and are a good cross-check. Each field decides what the next field means. A decoder is therefore a chain of small decisions, and each decision has a sentence in the manual behind it. Prefixes come in four groups SDM 2.1.1 lists the legacy prefixes. Group 1 holds F0 lock and the repeat prefixes F2 and F3 . Group 2 holds the six segment overrides ( 2E is %cs ) and the branch hints. Group 3 is 66 , the operand-size override. Group 4 is 67 , the address-size override. The manual says one prefix from each group can be used. Compilers emit more. The alignment padding in ledger-x86_64-O0.o at offset 0xf2 reads 66 66 66 66 66 2e 0f 1f 84 00 00 00 00 00 , five copies of 66 in a row. llvm-objdump prints it as nopw %cs:(%rax,%rax) and so does the decoder you build. The decoder collects every prefix byte it sees and asks later which ones mattered. 66 has a second job. For SSE instructions it is a mandatory prefix that selects the opcode, so 66 0f ef c0 is pxor %xmm0, %xmm0 and not a 16-bit anything. F3 0f 6f is movdqu . The decoder first looks up the pair of mandatory prefix and second opcode byte. Only when that pair has no entry does 66 mean a 16-bit operand. REX adds four bits and must sit next to the opcode SDM 2.2.1 defines REX as one byte from 40 to 4F with the shape 0100WRXB . W selects a 64-bit operand. R extends the ModRM reg field. X extends the SIB index field. B extends the ModRM r/m field, the SIB base field, or the register in the opcode byte (Table 2-4). REX must come right before the opcode or the escape bytes, and a REX followed by a legacy prefix is ignored. In 48 89 e5 the byte 48 is REX with W set. The opcode 89 is MOV r/m, r , and ModRM e5 selects %rsp into %rbp . Remove the REX and the same bytes are movl %esp, %ebp . REX changes the names of the byte registers too. With any REX present, encodings 4 to 7 select %spl , %bpl , %sil , and %dil instead of %ah , %ch , %dh , and %bh . The decoder keeps two tables for that reason. Opcodes live in two maps A one-byte opcode is the common case. 0F escapes to the two-byte map, and 0F 38 or 0F 3A escape to three-byte maps that the fixtures never use (SDM 2.1.2). Some opcodes use the ModRM reg field as three more opcode bits, written /digit in the manual. 83 /7 is cmp with an 8-bit immediate, 83 /5 is sub , and FF /4 is the indirect jmp . The decoder in code/main.py covers the opcodes in the four fixture objects plus a few neighbours. The list is the eight arithmetic forms, mov , lea , movslq , movzbl , imul , the shifts, test , and idiv . It continues with push , pop , call , ret , the sixteen conditional jumps, the multi-byte nop , and five SSE2 opcodes. Any other opcode raises DecodeError with the address and the reason. A decoder that guesses is worse than one that stops. ModRM and SIB select the operands SDM 2.1.3 splits ModRM into mod (bits 7:6), reg (5:3), and r/m (2:0). mod = 11 means r/m is a register. mod = 00 , 01 , and 10 mean memory with no displacement, an 8-bit displacement, or a 32-bit displacement. r/m = 100 means a SIB byte follows. SIB splits into scale (7:6), index (5:3), and base (2:0), and an index of 100 means no index register. Two special rows in Table 2-2 matter in 64-bit mode. mod = 00 with r/m = 101 is not (%rbp) . It is a 32-bit displacement relative to the next instruction (SDM 2.2.1.6). mod = 00 with a SIB base of 101 is a 32-bit displacement with no base register. Take 8d 44 08 fa from grade at -O0 . The opcode 8D is lea . ModRM 44 is 01 000 100 : an 8-bit displacement, reg %eax , and a SIB follows. SIB 08 is 00 001 000 : scale 1, index %rcx , base %rax . The displacement byte fa is -6. The AT&T text is leal -0x6(%rax,%rcx), %eax , which computes score / 10 - 6 , the switch index. The displacement is where the link editor writes 48 8d 0d 00 00 00 00 is leaq (%rip), %rcx . The four zero bytes are the displacement field of a RIP-relative operand. In a relocatable object they are placeholders. The entry in .rela.text at offset 0x69 says R_X86_64_PC32.rodata-0x4 . The psABI (Table 4.9) defines R_X86_64_PC32 as S + A - P : the symbol address plus the addend minus the address of the field. The processor adds the field to the address of the next instruction, so the final target is S + A + (end - P) . For this lea the field is the last four bytes, so end - P is 4 and the target is .rodata + (-4) + 4 =.rodata + 0x0 . The addend of -4 compensates for those four bytes in advance. Every RIP-relative operand in the fixtures carries this -4 inside its addend, so .rodata+0x10 on the -O1 lea means .rodata+0x14 . The decoder records the offset of the displacement field inside each instruction. resolve_reference() looks that offset up in the relocation table and reports where the operand will point after linking. That one function is what turns leaq (%rip), %rcx into "the table at .rodata+0x0 ". Immediates are 32 bits at most, with one exception SDM 2.2.1.5 says immediates stay at most 32 bits in 64-bit mode and are sign-extended. The exception is MOV r64, imm64 ( B8+r with REX.W ), which the AT&T syntax calls movabsq . The decoder reads 8-bit immediates as signed for arithmetic ( 83 c1 fa is addl $-0x6, %ecx ) and as unsigned for shift counts and shuffle selectors ( pshufd $0xee ). That split matches what llvm-objdump prints. Near branches, push , and pop default to a 64-bit operand and ignore 66 (SDM 2.2.1.7). That is why the decoder names them pushq , popq , callq , and retq without reading an operand-size prefix. Decode One Instruction by Hand Before you trust the code, decode 48 69 c0 67 66 66 66 from grade on paper. 48 is in 40 to 4F , so it is REX with W = 1 . Operand size is 64 bits. 69 is IMUL r, r/m, imm32 . c0 is ModRM 11 000 000 : register form, reg %rax , r/m %rax . The next four bytes are the immediate, little-endian: 0x66666667 . AT&T order is immediate, source, destination: imulq $0x66666667, %rax, %rax . That is seven bytes, and llvm-objdump prints the same text. The constant is the reciprocal that lets clang divide by 10 with a multiply and the sarq $0x22 that follows, which shifts by 34. You will meet that pair again in lesson 34, where the lifter turns it back into score / 10 . The decoder does these five steps in Decoder.decode() , _State.modrm() , and _State.finish() . Read them in that order and match each branch to the SDM section named in its docstring. Linear Sweep Schwarz, Debray, and Andrews describe linear sweep in Section 3.1 of "Disassembly of Executable Code Revisited" (WCRE 2002). Start at the first byte of the code section, decode one instruction, continue at the byte after it, and stop at the end. objdump works this way, and so does llvm-objdump . Copy The method has one failure mode, and the paper's Figure 1 shows it. Bytes that are data get decoded as instructions, and the decoder then misses the real instruction boundaries for a while. On x86 the decoder usually re-synchronises within a few bytes, which is what makes the error hard to see. Detection happens only on an invalid opcode, and the paper's conclusion is that these algorithms "fail silently". The sweep is also the oracle for this lesson. The decoder must agree with llvm-objdump -d on every instruction of every fixture, and llvm-objdump is itself a linear sweep. The captured text lives in code/fixtures/*.objdump.txt . The test parses each line into address, bytes, and text, drops the comments after # , and compares. The four objects hold 86, 56, 84, and 11 instructions, 237 in total, and the decoder matches all of them. Recursive Descent Section 3.2 of the same paper calls the second method recursive traversal. Start at a known entry point and decode until a control transfer. For a direct jump, continue at the target. For a conditional branch, continue at both the target and the next instruction, and for a call, continue after it, because the callee returns. For a return, stop. Keep a set of visited addresses so the walk ends. Copy The failure mode is the opposite one. An indirect jump has no target in its bytes. The walk stops there, and every block reachable only through the jump stays unknown. The paper's Figure 2 shows a second hazard: a target set derived from relocations that points into the middle of an instruction. The descent in main.py records that case as a conflict and stops that path, so the overlap is visible instead of silently decoded twice. Andriesse and others measured nine disassemblers on 981 compiler-generated binaries (USENIX Security 2016). Inline data and overlapping code were rarer in real compiler output than the literature assumed, and the hard primitive was function boundary recovery. Keep both findings in mind. The trap in the next section is rare in compiler output. The indirect jump in grade is common. Basic Blocks Allen defined the basic block in "Control Flow Analysis" (1970). It is a sequence of instructions that is entered only at its first instruction and left only at its last. Yakdan and others restate it for decompilation in Section II.A.2 of "No More Gotos" (NDSS 2015), with the header node as the function entry. The construction is a two-pass scan over the decoded instructions, sorted by address. The first pass collects leaders. A leader is the entry, a branch or jump target, a table target, or the instruction after any control transfer. The second pass starts a new block at every leader and at every gap in the address sequence. Copy Edges follow from the last instruction of each block. A return has no successor. A jump has one, tagged jump . A conditional branch has two, tagged taken and fallthrough . A plain instruction at the end of a block falls through to the next block, which happens when the next instruction is a branch target. An indirect jump has the targets of its table, tagged table , or none, and the block is recorded in unresolved . Two more facts come out of the same scan. A block that the entry cannot reach is unreachable, and the sweep over grade at -O0 produces five of them. A block whose start address falls inside an instruction of another method's listing is the overlap case from the trap. The Control-Flow Graph of total total at -O1 is 31 bytes and 13 instructions: Copy The leaders are 0x40 (entry), 0x44 (after the jle ), 0x50 (target of the jne ), 0x5b (after the jne ), and 0x5c (target of the jle ). Five blocks, five edges: From To Kind Why 0x40 0x44 fallthrough jle not taken, count is positive 0x40 0x5c taken count is zero or negative, return 0 0x44 0x50 fallthrough the nopw is alignment inside the block, execution passes through it 0x50 0x50 taken jne 0x50 , the loop 0x50 0x5b fallthrough loop exit, return the sum The six-byte nopw at 0x4a is padding so that the loop head at 0x50 sits on a 16-byte boundary. It is reachable, so it belongs to block 0x44 . The one-byte nop at 0x5f after the last retq is also padding, and nothing reaches it. The sweep over the function makes a sixth block for it, and unreachable() lists it. At -O2 the same function is 140 bytes with two loops. The SSE2 body at 0x80 adds eight values per pass with paddd , and the scalar remainder runs at 0xc0 . The CFG has two back edges, 0x80 -> 0x80 and 0xc0 -> 0xc0 , and the test suite checks both. Dominators With the Iterative Algorithm A block d dominates a block b when every path from the entry to b passes through d . The immediate dominator of b is the dominator of b that is closest to b . The notion goes back to Prosser (1959) through Allen (1970), and it is the structure that lesson 34 needs to place if and while correctly. Cooper, Harvey, and Kennedy wrote "A Simple, Fast Dominance Algorithm" (2001). They argue that the data-flow formulation, run in reverse postorder with a compact representation, beats Lengauer-Tarjan (1979) on graphs under about a thousand nodes. Their paper says its purpose is "not to present a new algorithm". It shows that simple algorithms can win in practice and are good teaching tools. A function CFG almost never has a thousand nodes. Copy number holds the reverse postorder position of each block, with the entry at 0. intersect walks two fingers up the current dominator tree until they meet. The paper writes the comparison with postorder numbers and < . This code uses reverse postorder numbers, so the comparison is > . Everything else follows the paper's pseudocode. For total at -O1 the result is idom(0x44) = 0x40 , idom(0x50) = 0x44 , idom(0x5b) = 0x50 , and idom(0x5c) = 0x40 . The edge 0x50 -> 0x50 is a back edge because its target dominates its source, and a back edge marks a loop (Allen 1970). back_edges() returns it. The subl $0x4 followed by ja is a bounds check: indexes above 4 go to the default case at 0x9a , so the table has five entries. The leaq with its relocation puts the table address in %rcx , and the previous section showed that address is .rodata+0x0 . The movslq loads a signed 32-bit entry scaled by 4. The addq adds the table base, so each entry is the distance from the table to its case block. In the object file every table byte is zero. The targets exist only as relocations in .rela.rodata : Copy Apply S + A - P to entry k at offset 4k . The stored value is .text + A - (.rodata + 4k) , and the code adds .rodata + 0 to it, so the target is .text + A - 4k . Entry 0 is 0x91 - 0 = 0x91 , entry 1 is 0x8c - 4 = 0x88 , and entry 2 is 0x87 - 8 = 0x7f . Entries 3 and 4 are 0x82 - 12 = 0x76 and 0x86 - 16 = 0x76 . Solutions Solution P1 · It skips them as undecodable bytes It treats them as undecodable bytes: the decoder has no rule for f3 0f 1e fa , so the sweep records the byte, moves one byte forward, and tries again, four times, until it reaches the next real instruction. The output keeps going, but each function now starts with a gap of "unknown" bytes, and anything that relies on the entry instruction (a recursive descent from the symbol, a prologue matcher) is broken. Capstone, which knows the instruction, reads endbr64 . Solution B1 · Tables decoded as code The table entries are decoded as instructions. Jump-table entries are 4- or 8-byte offsets or addresses, and their bytes decode to plausible-looking but meaningless instructions ( add , adc , odd prefixes). Worse, because x86 instructions vary in length, the sweep can stay misaligned after the table, so the first real instructions of the next function decode wrongly until it happens to resynchronize. The listing then has garbage blocks and false branch targets. Recursive descent starts from known entry points and only decodes what control flow reaches, so it never decodes the table as code. On its own, though, it stops at the jmp *table(,%rax,8) . A resolver recognizes the bounds check, the table base and the entry size, reads the entries as data, and adds them as edges, which is what the lesson's jump_table_resolver does for grade -O0 . Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Disassemblers and decoders in production : Capstone (used by many tools, here in AT&T syntax), Zydis, Intel XED, LLVM's MC layer ( llvm-objdump ), GNU objdump, and the engines inside Ghidra, IDA Pro, Binary Ninja and radare2/rizin. Research : the USENIX Security 2016 study by Andriesse et al. found compiler-generated code mostly well-behaved, with jump tables and function boundaries as the main error sources; this still guides tool design. On your laptop : decoding and CFG building are instant on the CPU; Ghidra needs Java and about 4 GB of RAM, comfortable on 16 GB. Debug a failure A 24-byte function keeps a four-byte table 31 c0 90 48 inside its body and jumps over it with jmp 0x14 . llvm-objdump -d prints xorl %eax, %eax , nop , and addq $0x1, %rax at 0x13 ; every byte decodes and a retq is present. Name the three ways this listing is wrong, say which method gets it right and why the reference tool shares the mistake, and say what agreement between your decoder and that tool does and does not prove. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The listing is wrong three times: the jump at 0xe targets 0x14 and no instruction in the listing starts there; the instruction that runs at 0x14 is a 32-bit addl $0x1, %eax , while the listing shows a 64-bit addq one byte early because the table's last byte 48 was swallowed as a REX prefix; and the four table bytes appear as code. Recursive descent from the symbol follows the jump, decodes six instructions, reads addl at the target and claims no table or padding byte. llvm-objdump is itself a linear sweep, so it inherits the sweep's blind spot: agreement with it checks the decoder on instruction boundaries, and only the descent checks which instructions run. Two methods, opposite failures. A linear sweep starts at the first byte of the code section, decodes one instruction, continues at the byte after it, and stops at the end; data inside code gets decoded as instructions, and on x86 the decoder usually re-synchronises within a few bytes, which is why the error is hard to see and why the method is said to fail silently. Recursive descent starts at a known entry, follows direct jumps and both arms of a conditional, continues after a call, stops at a return, and keeps a visited set. Its failure is the opposite one: an indirect jump has no target in its bytes, so the walk stops there and every block reachable only through it stays unknown, which is what happens at jmpq *%rax in the unoptimized grade . The trap under five tools. The comparison harness reports the sweep with 8 instruction starts in the trap range, with extra starts at 0x10 , 0x12 and 0x13 and a missing start at 0x14 . Three graph builders report 6 starts, 2 blocks and 1 edge, and leave 0x10 to 0x14 unclaimed. One framework also invents a function on the table bytes, two instructions in a four-byte block, so the REX byte at 0x13 belongs to no instruction. The last finding is the useful one: no graph builder decodes 0x10 to 0x14 , so those bytes sit inside a function and are data. What the oracle is for. The decoder must agree with llvm-objdump -d on every instruction of every fixture, and it does, on 86, 56, 84 and 11 instructions, 237 in all. That agreement proves the decoder reads prefixes, opcodes, ModRM, SIB, displacements and immediates the way the manual says. It proves nothing about reachability, because the oracle never asked. A measurement of nine disassemblers on 981 compiler-generated binaries found inline data rarer than the literature assumed and function starts the hard primitive; the trap is rare in compiler output, and the indirect jump is common. Byte accounting. Compare the two methods byte by byte. Bytes that only the sweep claims are padding, data, code behind an indirect jump, or code of a function with no known entry. The sweep decodes the whole section, so these are the bytes to account for. Bytes the descent claims are the ones it reaches from that entry; that is reachability, not proof that they run. Plausible wrong answers. "The reference tool is right because it is the reference." It is a sweep; it is the oracle for decoding, not for reachability. "Use the descent alone." It stops at indirect jumps and leaves reachable code unknown until a table is recovered. "Every byte decoded, so the listing is complete." A listing says which bytes form which instruction, not which instructions run. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Change the last table byte from 48 to e8 and rebuild. What does the sweep print? Expected: a callq that swallows the addl and the retq , with a target outside the section; the function appears to have no return. (level 3) Why does the descent stop at jmpq *%rax in the unoptimized grade , and what fixes it? Expected: no target is in the bytes; the resolver reads the five relocations of the table and pushes four distinct targets. (level 3) What does "fail silently" mean in operational terms? Expected: the decoder re-synchronises within a few bytes and detects nothing unless it hits an invalid opcode, so a wrong listing looks complete. (level 4) How do you classify bytes that the descent does not claim? Expected: padding, data, code behind an indirect jump, or part of a function with no known entry; account for every byte as one of these or as reached by the descent. Where it is taught. The disassembly lesson builds both methods and the trap fixture, and the landscape lesson runs five tools over it and accounts for every byte. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Decompiler output is a claim with a hidden derivation. When you build the derivation yourself, every line of that output becomes a thing you can check. The problem In plain words first A decompiler turns machine code back into something like C. It does this in stages: decode the bytes into instructions, group them into blocks, translate each instruction into a small intermediate language, give every value one name (SSA form), simplify and delete what is unused, guess types from how values are used, and finally rebuild if statements and loops from the graph. Each stage can lose or invent information. The output is a hypothesis about the program, not the program. You trust it only after you check it, ideally by running it against the original. This lesson runs the lesson's own eight-stage lifter on code from a different compiler to see where it stops, then compiles its pseudocode and Ghidra's next to the original object and runs all three on edge cases. Here is percent_change as the oracle prints it: Copy Stage 1: Bytes to Instructions Lesson 13.33 built the decoder. This lesson keeps a small copy so the code runs on its own. The copy covers exactly the opcodes that clang emitted for ledger.c at -O0 and -O1 . For anything else it raises DecodeError with the address and the opcode byte. The decoder follows the byte order of the Intel SDM, Volume 2, section 2.1. Prefixes come first, then the opcode, then ModR/M, then SIB, then the displacement, then the immediate. Section 2.2.1 adds the REX prefix, one byte from 0x40 to 0x4F , which must sit directly before the opcode. REX.W selects a 64-bit operand, REX.R extends the reg field, REX.X extends the SIB index, and REX.B extends r/m or the SIB base. Section 2.1.3 defines the three ModR/M fields mod , reg , and r/m , and the three SIB fields scale , index , and base . In 64-bit mode, mod = 00 with r/m = 101 means a 32-bit displacement relative to the next instruction (section 2.2.1.6).
