Stage 2: Blocks and Dominators A basic block is a sequence of statements with one entry at the top and one exit at the bottom. That is the definition from Allen (1970), and every decompiler paper reuses it. build_blocks() collects leaders: the function entry, every jump target inside the function, and every address after a jump or return. Each block gets successors from its last instruction. A conditional jump has two successors and a jmp has one. A ret has none, and a block that ends in an ordinary instruction falls through to the next leader. total at -O1 has five blocks: Block Instructions Successors 0x40 testl %esi, %esi then jle 0x5c 0x5c , 0x44 0x44 movl %esi, %ecx , xorl %edx, %edx , xorl %eax, %eax , nopw 0x50 0x50 addl (%rdi,%rdx,4), %eax , incq %rdx , cmpq %rdx, %rcx , jne 0x50 0x50 , 0x5b 0x5b retq exit 0x5c xorl %eax, %eax then retq exit immediate_dominators() is the iterative algorithm of Cooper, Harvey, and Kennedy (2001). It walks the blocks in reverse postorder and intersects the dominators of the processed predecessors until nothing changes. On graphs this small it finishes in two passes. For total it says that 0x44 dominates 0x50 . It also says that 0x50 dominates itself through the back edge, which is how stage 8 finds the loop. The same function runs twice more. dominance_frontiers() uses it for SSA in stage 5. post_dominators() runs it on the reversed graph with a virtual exit node to find joins in stage 8. Stage 3: Lifting to a Small IR The IR has six statement kinds: Assign , Store , Branch , Jump , IndirectJump , and Return . Expressions are constants, variables, binary operations with a width, casts ( sext , zext , trunc ), and loads. Five more shapes exist only to be simplified away later: Flags , Cond , Concat , SignFill , and Symbolic . Registers are variables named by their 64-bit family. A write to %eax is an Assign to rax with width 32, and a read of %eax is a read of rax at width 32. In 64-bit mode a 32-bit write zero-extends into the full register, so a later 64-bit read of the same value is a zext . The lifter does not know the reaching definition, so it records the read width and lets SSA insert the cast in stage 5. Instruction IR statements subl %edi, %esi flags = cmp(esi, edi) then esi = esi - edi testl %edi, %edi flags = test(edi, edi) je 0xd if je(flags) goto 0xd else goto 0x4 xorl %eax, %eax eax = 0 cltd edx = signfill(eax) idivl %edi dividend = edx:eax , eax = dividend / edi , edx = dividend % edi movslq %edi, %rax rax = sext64(edi) sarq $0x22, %rcx rcx = rcx >>s 34 shrq $0x3f, %rax rax = rax >>u 63 addl (%rdi,%rdx,4), %eax flags = add(eax, load32(rdi + rdx * 4)) then eax = eax + load32(rdi + rdx * 4) leaq (%rip), %rcx with its relocation rcx = &.rodata+0x14 pushq %rbp , movq %rsp, %rbp , subq $0x10, %rsp , popq %rbp nothing, frame bookkeeping retq return rax Flags are a variable Every instruction that sets the condition codes writes one variable named flags , and every conditional jump reads it. A cmp a, b writes cmp(a, b) , a test a, b writes test(a, b) , and sub writes the same cmp shape as a side effect. A jcc becomes Branch(Cond(cc, flags), target, fallthrough) . The condition code decides the comparison operator when the two meet in stage 6: Code After cmp(a, b) After test(a, a) je a == b a == 0 jne a != b a != 0 jl , jge , jle , jg signed < , >= , <= , > signed compare with 0 jb , jae , jbe , ja unsigned < , >= , <= , > unsigned compare with 0 xorl %eax, %eax is lifted straight to eax = 0 . The flags it sets are written as add style flags that no jump in the fixture reads. The xor idiom matters in grade , where Ghidra lost it. cltd and idiv cltd fills %edx with the sign bit of %eax . idivl %edi divides the 64-bit pair %edx:%eax by %edi , puts the quotient in %eax , and the remainder in %edx . The lifter writes the pair into a temporary named dividend first. The remainder statement then reads the old %eax and not the fresh quotient. In SSA the high half shows up as signfill of the low half. The simplifier reduces the pair to the low half, and the division becomes a 32-bit / . Stack slots at -O0 At -O0 clang keeps every local in the frame. percent_change stores %edi to -0x8(%rbp) and %esi to -0xc(%rbp) , then reads them back for every use. The lifter watches for pushq %rbp followed by movq %rsp, %rbp . After that prologue, a memory operand with base %rbp , no index, and a displacement becomes a variable named local_<hex> . -0x8(%rbp) is local_8 , -0xc(%rbp) is local_c . The frame instructions themselves produce no IR, and neither do subq and addq on %rsp . Any other memory operand stays a Load or Store . Relocations The leaq (%rip), %rcx in grade has displacement zero in the file. The relocation at offset 0x36 says R_X86_64_PC32.rodata+0x10 . The linker will write S + A - P into the field. S is the address of .rodata , A is the addend 0x10 , and P is the address of the field. The instruction then computes next_ip + disp = (P + 4) + S + A - P = S + A + 4 . The lifter applies the same arithmetic without a linker. The target offset is the addend plus the distance from the field to the end of the instruction, 0x10 + 4 = 0x14 . The IR says rcx = &.rodata+0x14 , and the table there holds the five int values 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 . Stage 4: Parameters From the Calling Convention The System V AMD64 psABI, section 3.2.3, passes INTEGER class arguments in %rdi , %rsi , %rdx , %rcx , %r8 , %r9 , in that order. The result returns in %rax and then %rdx . Section 3.2.1 says that %rbp , %rbx , and %r12 through %r15 belong to the caller and must be preserved. Everything else belongs to the callee. collect_params() applies one rule: an argument register that is read before any write in the function is a parameter. The highest such register fixes the count, so a function that reads %rsi and never %rdi still has two parameters. percent_change reads %edi and %esi , so it has param_1 and param_2 . grade reads only %edi . total reads %rdi as a 64-bit base and %esi as a 32-bit count. Now Ghidra's param_3 has an explanation. idivl writes %rdx , and the psABI allows a 128-bit INTEGER return in %rax:%rdx . In an object file there is no caller to say how wide the return value is. Ghidra kept both registers as the return value. On the zero path, xorl %eax, %eax writes only %eax . Ghidra read %rdx there as an input of the function, and that input became param_3 . The instructions are right. The signature is a guess about the parts the instructions leave open. Stage 5: SSA, One Name per Definition After lifting, grade writes rax four times and rcx three times. Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman, and Zadeck (1991) define static single assignment form. Each variable is assigned exactly once, and phi functions at join points select among the definitions that reach them. Their construction has two steps. Section 5.1 places phi functions using dominance frontiers, and section 5.2 renames every definition and use with a walk over the dominator tree. insert_phis() and rename() follow those two sections. The SSA listing of total shows what the construction produces: Copy Version 0 of a register is its value at entry. esi_0 and rdi_0 are the parameters. The loop header 0x50 has two predecessors, the setup block and itself, so every variable with a definition in the loop gets a phi there. The flags_2 phi is dead on arrival. Minimal SSA places it because flags has definitions in both predecessors, and stage 6 removes it because nothing reads it. The renaming step also fixes widths. edx_1 = 0 is a 32-bit definition and rdx_3 = rdx_2 + 1 is 64-bit, so the phi rdx_2 takes the wider width. The read of %rcx in cmpq %rdx, %rcx is 64-bit while its definition ecx_1 = esi_0 is 32-bit, so the use becomes zext64(ecx_1) . Every cast in the final pseudocode comes from this one rule. The "lite" part is the way out of SSA. coalesce_webs() joins each phi with its arguments into one variable, called a web, and gives the web one name. This works for the shapes a compiler emits for these functions. It can break on parallel copies, where two phis at one join exchange values, and the lesson does not handle that case. Cytron's section 7 describes the general exit through coloring. Stage 6: Simplify, Substitute, Remove Dead Code optimize() repeats three passes until nothing changes. The simplifier rewrites expressions bottom up with these rules: Before After Cond(je, cmp(a, b)) a == b , and the same for the other nine codes Cond(jle, test(a, a)) a <= 0 x + (-6) x - 6 trunc32(zext64(x)) where x is 32-bit x trunc32(a + b) on 64-bit operands trunc32(a) + trunc32(b) (signfill(x): x) / d x / d at width 32 load32(base + idx * 4) base[idx] trunc32(p >>s 34) + trunc32(p >>u 63) with p = sext64(x) * 0x66666667 x / 10 Forward substitution moves a definition into its only use. The rule has three conditions. The use is in the same block. The use is a statement and not a phi. When the definition contains a load, no store or call sits between the definition and the use. A constant or a section address is substituted anywhere except into a phi, because a phi argument has to stay a variable for the web. Dead code removal deletes an assignment or a phi whose destination has no use and whose expression has no call. The order of the passes matters. In percent_change the remainder edx_2 = dividend_1 % edi_0 is dead, so it goes first. That leaves edx_1 = signfill(eax_1) with one use, so it is substituted into dividend_1 = edx_1:eax_1 . The pair rule then reduces signfill(eax_1):eax_1 to eax_1 , and the division becomes eax_1 / edi_0 . Now eax_1 = esi_1 * 100 has one use, and esi_1 = esi_0 - edi_0 has one use, and both move into the return statement. The flags definitions have been substituted into the branch conditions and disappear. Four instructions become one line: Copy The 0x66666667 multiply grade divides the score by 10, and clang emits no idiv . It emits imulq $0x66666667, %rax, %rax , then sarq $0x22, %rcx on a copy, then shrq $0x3f, %rax , then adds the two. Granlund and Montgomery, "Division by Invariant Integers using Multiplication" (PLDI 1994), describe the method. The compiler picks a multiplier m and a shift s . For every x in the range, (x * m) >> s must equal x / d . Here m = 0x66666667 = 1717986919 and s = 34 . The arithmetic checks out: 2^34 / 10 = 1717986918.4 , and the ceiling is 1717986919 . The error is m * 10 - 2^34 = 6 . For the identity to hold on every 32-bit x , the error times 2^31 must stay below 2^34 , so the error must be at most 8. Six is at most eight, so (x * m) >> 34 equals floor(x / 10) for every non-negative int . For negative x the floor rounds away from zero while C rounds toward zero. shrq $0x3f extracts the sign bit of the product, which is 1 exactly when x is negative. Adding it corrects the rounding. magic_divisor(m, s) tests a candidate pair. It computes d as the integer quotient of 2^s by m and tries d and d + 1 . It accepts a d only when m equals the ceiling of 2^s / d and the error bound holds. The same multiplier with s = 33 gives d = 5 , which is correct, because 0x66666667 is also the ceiling of 2^33 / 5 . A test checks the identity against c_div(x, 10) on 2,406 values including both ends of the int range. With recognition on, grade reads ecx_1 = param_1 / 10 - 6; . With recognition off, the demo prints the raw form: Copy Both compile and both compute the same values. Keep the switch. When you read code from a compiler you have not studied, the raw form is the honest one. Stage 7: Types From Use Machine code has widths and no types. infer_types() turns three kinds of evidence into C types. A web whose definitions are 32 bits wide is int , and a 64-bit web is long . A web that is the base of an element access base[idx] with 4-byte elements is int * . The pointer type spreads along copies and phis, so local_8 = param_1 at -O0 makes both of them int * . The return type is the width of the value in the return statements. The result for total is int total(int *param_1, int param_2) . Ghidra wrote int total(long param_1,uint param_2) . Both are consistent with the instructions. The lifter used the scaled load as pointer evidence. Ghidra kept the register width and wrote the access as *(int *)(param_1 + uVar2 * 4) . Neither can see const , and neither can tell int * from unsigned * . Lee, Avgerinos, and Brumley (TIE, NDSS 2011) frame type recovery as constraint solving over a lattice. The result is an upper and a lower bound instead of one guess. Noonan, Loginov, and Cok (Retypd, PLDI 2016) add polymorphism and recursion. They report 98 percent recall on const pointer annotations from idioms the compiler leaves behind. This lesson uses the two cheapest rules from that line of work and names what they cannot see. Unsigned arithmetic is kept in the expressions and not in the variable types. ja after cmpl $0x4, %ecx prints as (unsigned int)ecx_1 > 4 , and shrq prints as (unsigned long)rax_1 >> 63 . The variables stay signed so that a reader sees the register value and the one place where the instruction treats it as unsigned. Stage 8: Structuring From the Graph Cifuentes (1994), chapter 6, matches regions of the graph against the shapes of a high-level language. Loops come first (6.6.1), then two-way conditionals (6.6.2), then n-way conditionals (6.6.3). Yakdan, Eschweiler, Gerhards-Padilla, and Smith (NDSS 2015) take the other road. They derive the condition under which each node executes and build the structure from those conditions, with no fixed shapes. Their motivation is a measurement. Hex-Rays on one sample produced 1,571 goto statements in 49,514 lines, one per 32 lines, and their structuring produced none on 1,530 coreutils functions. structure() is a small member of the first family. It needs two facts from stage 2. The immediate post-dominator of a block that ends in a Branch is the join of the conditional. A back edge is an edge to a block that dominates its source. The natural loop is the set of blocks that reach the back edge source without passing the header. For a Branch with join j : If j is the jump target, emit if (!cond) { fallthrough region } and continue at j . If j is the fallthrough, emit if (cond) { target region } and continue at j . If j is the function exit, both arms return. Emit the smaller arm as if (cond) {... } and the other arm after it, without an else . This is the early return in percent_change and total . Otherwise emit if (cond) { target } else { fallthrough } and continue at j . This is percent_change at -O0 , where both arms store local_4 and meet at the epilogue. For a loop header: If the header ends in a Branch with one successor outside the loop, emit while (cond) { body } . total at -O0 has this shape: the header compares local_14 with local_c and leaves on jge . If the header is also the block with the back edge, or the latch exits instead, emit do { body } while (cond); . total at -O1 has this shape: block 0x50 adds, increments, compares, and jumps to itself. An IndirectJump ends a block with no successors. grade at -O0 is a real jump table, jmpq *%rax through five relative offsets at .rodata+0x0 , and lesson 33 resolves those targets. Here the lifter prints a note instead. Four blocks at 0x76 , 0x7f , 0x88 , and 0x91 are reached only through the indirect jump and were not lifted. The practice lab adds the switch . What -O1 did to the switch At -O1 clang did not keep a jump table for grade . It computed score / 10 - 6 and compared the result with 4 as an unsigned number. Then it loaded the return value from a five-entry table of int at .rodata+0x14 . The unsigned compare is one instruction that covers both score / 10 < 6 and score / 10 > 10 . A negative difference is a large unsigned value, so it fails the same check. The table holds 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 for the quotients 6 through 10. The switch with five return statements became an if and an array read. The lifter emits exactly that, and names the table lookup_14 after its section offset. The length of the table is a heuristic. table_values() reads from the table start to the next .rodata offset that any .text relocation references, or to the end of the section. In this object the next referenced offset is 0x28 , the table of grade_label , so lookup_14 has (0x28 - 0x14) / 4 = 5 entries. The unsigned compare against 4 agrees. Ghidra does not know the length either. It wrote *(uint *)(&DAT_001000b4 + (ulong)uVar2 * 4) , a byte address plus an offset, and left the five values for the reader to look up. What the Research Says About Reading Pseudocode LLM4Decompile (EMNLP 2024) measured Ghidra alone at 20.12 percent re-executability on HumanEval-Decompile. About one in five functions recompiled and passed the assertions that come with the benchmark. Refining Ghidra's output with their 6.7B model raised that to 52.74 percent. DecompileBench (Findings of ACL 2025) ran six industrial decompilers and six LLM approaches on 23,400 functions from 130 programs. The LLM outputs read better and had 52.2 percent lower functionality correctness. Liu, Raff, and Micinski (arXiv 2609.05370, September 2026) explain the gap. They used 300 GitHub library functions and 287 CVE-grounded functions. The strongest refinement model raised Ghidra's build rate from 75 to 90 percent while the behavioural match rate fell from 74 to 62 percent. Candidates that passed every test in the benchmark still diverged on fuzzed inputs. That happened in 4.9 percent of cases across eight systems, and in up to 13 percent for one system. Up to one tenth of disclosed vulnerabilities disappeared from the refined code. The cause they trace is simple. Invented fields, types, callees, and guards replaced the visible unknowns that the decompiler had left in the text. Solutions Solution P1 · It stops at stage 1, twice With default flags it stops at stage 1 for every function: Ubuntu's GCC puts endbr64 at each function entry, and the decoder only knows the instructions in its clang fixtures, so it raises DecodeError on the first byte. With -fcf-protection=none there is no endbr64 ; percent_change then lifts correctly, but grade and total stop at a mov $imm32, %edx (opcode ba ) that clang never emitted in the fixture. Nothing is wrong with the lifter's logic; its stage 1 simply has not seen these encodings. Solution B1 · Readable is not equivalent That the rewrite has the same behaviour on all inputs, not just two. The original, compiled from switch (score / 10) with case 10: case 9: , returns 4 for 90 to 109, 0 for 110 and above, and 0 for every negative score (where C's division truncates toward zero). A model that "simplifies" to if (score >= 90) return 4; returns 4 for 110 and for 1000; one that writes score / 10 with unsigned types changes negative scores. Two hand-picked tests miss all of these. Debug a failure From the decompiler's pseudocode, an agent rebuilds percent_change . The pseudocode reads undefined1 [16] percent_change(int param_1, int param_2, ulong param_3) with lVar1 = (long)((param_2 - param_1) * 100) . The rebuild is (int)(((long)after - before) * 100 / before) , and four hand-written tests pass. The listing of the same record reads IMUL EAX, ESI, 0x64 , CDQ , IDIV EDI . What went wrong, and what is the rule? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The 16-byte return and the third parameter are the decompiler's inference, not the program: idiv writes the pair EDX:EAX , the zero path leaves EDX untouched, so the decompiler modelled a 16-byte result and read %rdx as an input. The listing says every operation is 32 bits wide, so the honest rebuild is 100 * (after - before) / before in int ; the long version divides the unwrapped product and fails 26 of the overflow cells while compiling to 26 bytes where the original has 16. The rule is to read the listing before the pseudocode, write the rebuild from the operation widths, and cite the record id it came from. Instruction or guess, line by line. Difference Verdict return type undefined1 [16] against int guess; idivl writes two registers and no caller fixes the width param_3 guess that follows from the first; %rdx is read on the zero path only because the return width was guessed lVar1 / (long)param_1 & 0xffffffff against / param_1 instruction; cltd plus idivl is a sign-extended 32-bit division, and both texts describe it if (param_1 != 0) first instruction order; the branch jumps to the zero return, and either arm may be printed first A difference with an instruction behind it is a presentation choice. A difference with no instruction behind it is a guess, and the guess can be on either side. Why four tests passed. The naive cases avoid every hard class. The wrapped and unwrapped products agree whenever (after - before) * 100 fits in 32 bits, so a test that never crosses that line sees two equal functions. On a grid with overflow cells, the long rebuild fails 26 cells, every one with |before| > 1 ; for before equal to 1 or -1 the 64-bit quotient truncates back to the wrapped value and the two agree by accident. The size told you first. Compiled with the original flags, the long rebuild is 26 bytes: movslq , imulq , cqto and idivq replaced the 32-bit forms. Size is a diagnostic and never an acceptance, and the listing had shown the widths before any compile. What the research says about this pattern. A 2026 study of decompilation systems found candidates that passed every test in a benchmark and still diverged on fuzzed inputs. The strongest refinement model raised the build rate from 75 to 90 percent while the behavioural match rate fell from 74 to 62 percent, and the cause was invented fields, types, callees and guards that replaced the visible unknowns a decompiler leaves in its text. The long rebuild is an invented type. Plausible wrong answers. "The decompiler is broken; ignore its output." Its instructions were right; only the parts the instructions leave open were guessed, and the listing in the same record is the correction. "The & 0xffffffff is a decompiler bug." It describes the truncation of a sign-extended division correctly. "Ten tests pass, ship it." A grid with overflow, negative, rounding and trap cells is the test; the ten cases avoided every hazard. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why did the four tests not catch it? Expected: none of them made the product exceed 32 bits, and the two versions agree everywhere the product fits. (level 3) Which inputs expose the difference, and which hide it by accident? Expected: overflow cells with |before| > 1 fail; before of 1 or -1 agree because the wide quotient truncates to the wrapped value. (level 3) What did the 26-byte size tell you before any run? Expected: wider instruction forms replaced the 32-bit ones, so the candidate computes in a different width than the listing. (level 4) How does the refinement-model finding change how you read clean pseudocode? Expected: a clean signature is right for the wrong reason when it fills an unknown; keep the ugly honest form and record what no instruction supports. Where it is taught. Before you start Needs : Phase 13 · 32 (ELF from scratch), Phase 13 · 33 (disassembly and control flow), Phase 13 · 34 (lifting to pseudocode) Type : Build. Time : about 105 minutes. Code in : Python, C, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A finding about a compiled program is a record with a hash, a confidence, an authority, and a list of what it cannot show. The problem In plain words first In reverse engineering, and especially when an AI agent does it, every statement should say how it is known. "Observed" means a tool read it directly from the file or a run produced it. "Derived" means it was computed from observed facts. "Inferred" means someone, person or model, believes it. Each statement becomes a small record that names the exact file (by its hash, not its path), the tool and its version, the settings, the result and its limits. A record's id is a hash of its content, so any edit makes a new record instead of silently changing the old one. A belief becomes accepted only when observed runs confirm it, and open questions are tracked as records too. This lesson creates fresh records with Capstone and with runs of the shipped object, settles two competing predictions, and then tries to forge a result. You ask an agent what grade in ledger-x86_64-O1.o returns for a score of 55. The agent calls rea, reads the Ghidra pseudocode, and answers 0. A reviewer asks how the agent knows. The agent has a block of text that Ghidra printed. For the default path, that text reads uVar1 = -(param_1 >> 0x1f) ^ (uint)((ulong)((long)param_1 * 0x66666667) >> 0x3f); . The bytes at that point say xor eax, eax . The expression and the instruction both produce 0 for every input. The agent did not know that. It trusted the text because a tool produced it. A 2026 study ran three agents on 24 reverse engineering tasks ( NDSS BAR 2026 ). It named four recurring weaknesses: training bias, over-trust in observations, context limits, and plan persistence. Another 2026 study planted text inside binaries and found that models proposed the planted unsafe action in 35 of 40 cases ( arXiv 2607.12507 ). rea 6.5.0 gives the agent a vocabulary for this. Every successful tool call produces one Evidence record with a confidence of observed , derived , or inferred , an authority , and a list of limitations . The packaged skill tells the agent: "Every conclusion must distinguish observations, inferences, and unknowns. Cite Evidence IDs, preserve limitations and incomplete coverage, and never imply that static analysis observed execution.". Three things rea leaves to you. Its snapshots cache exact query results, not analysis. Its verification passes a claim when a comparison dimension is unchanged, and its own comment says that a pass "does not establish global implementation equivalence.". Its obligation ledger takes candidates only from JavaScript and managed graphs, so a native function never reaches verified through it. This lesson builds the missing piece in plain Python. You write a ledger that stores every fact about the fixture as a record with a content hash. You make predictions about percent_change and grade , mark them inferred, and check them against runs of a test program you compile yourself. You import two real rea records and the snapshot they came from, and your ledger recomputes every hash rea wrote. Three Words for Confidence, Five for Authority confidence is an enum with three values, never a number. authority has five values. When a producer says nothing, rea uses shipped-artifact with observed . Value Meaning on the fixture Records in this lesson observed A fact read from bytes or from a run the ELF reader's section and symbol reads, the two Ghidra records, 17 host runs derived A fact computed from observed records the switch table model, the division model, every unknown mutation inferred An expectation that no observation states yet 18 predictions shipped-artifact The file on disk was the source every read of ledger-x86_64-O1.o controlled-replay A run you controlled produced the fact the host runs of harness.c analyst-inference Your own judgement predictions and unknown mutations historical-reference An older source tree or document none here external-service A service outside the file and the host none here Two confusions cost the most time. The first treats pseudocode as an observation of behaviour. It is an observation of what Ghidra printed. The second treats an empty list as proof of absence. rea's design note is strict: "Missing coverage is unknown, not absence.". The ledger in code/main.py encodes both rules. The Record A record has exactly sixteen fields, and rea 6.5.0 rejects any other field. code/main.py keeps the same names as rea, so a record from either side validates on the other. The sixteenth field, relationship_coverage , says how complete a list of callers or callees is. Its value is complete , partial , or unknown , or null when the operation reports no call relationships. Field What it holds evidence_id ev_ and 64 hex digits, a hash of the content subject name , digest.sha256 , format , architecture , local_path , or null provider id , name , version or null analysis_profile the provider's settings and their digest, or null , always present predicate_type a tag, rea.analysis by default operation , parameters the tool and its input raw_result , normalized_result provider output and the canonical result confidence , authority the enums above environment id , platform , architecture , isolation , or null limitations plain sentences relationship_coverage status complete , partial , or unknown with diagnostics, or null locations address , address-range , artifact-path , file-offset , file-offset-range evidence_links the ev_ ids this record rests on This is the real record rea wrote for grade , cut to the fields that matter here. The full file is code/fixtures/rea-evidence-grade.json , 37,573 bytes. Copy The real parameters object of the profile has 25 keys. The real limitations list has ten sentences. Keep them. A limitation is part of the content, so dropping one changes the id, and your ledger would then reject the record. Note what the record does not say. environment is null because Ghidra read a file and ran nothing. locations is empty because this operation reports addresses inside normalized_result . relationship_coverage has the status complete . Its diagnostic says that only resolved Ghidra call references are returned, and that unresolved computed or indirect calls stay unknown. So the caller and callee lists are complete for resolved calls only. The Id Is a Hash of Content, and the Path Is Not in It rea computes evidence_id as ev_ plus SHA-256 over the RFC 8785 canonical JSON of a projection of the record. The projection keeps the subject's digest , format , and architecture and drops name and local_path . It drops relationship_coverage when its value is null , so a record without call relationships keeps the same id as before the field existed. Everything else, including raw_result and every limitation, is hashed. RFC 8785 sorts object keys, removes whitespace, and fixes the number and string forms. For records whose numbers are integers, Python's standard library produces the same bytes: Copy code/main.py refuses floats before it hashes, because RFC 8785 and Python print some floats differently. Derive the Table, and Say That You Derived It The 46 bytes of grade contain four patterns that lesson 33 decoded: Bytes Instruction Offset in grade 48 69 c0 67 66 66 66 imul rax, rax, 0x66666667 3 48 c1 f9 22 sar rcx, 34 13 83 c1 fa add ecx, -6 23 83 f9 04 77 0c cmp ecx, 4 then ja 28 A multiply by 0x66666667 followed by a shift of 34 is a signed division by 10. The file holds no 10. derive_grade_model() writes that fact as a limitation: "The divisor 10 is a derivation from the multiplier 0x66666667 and the shift 34. The file holds no 10." The add ecx, -6 sets the first case to 6. The cmp ecx, 4 with an unsigned jump admits five cases, 6 to 10. The lea at .text+0x33 carries the relocation with addend 0x10 . A PC32 relocation measures from the end of the 4-byte displacement, so the table starts at .rodata+0x14 . Five little-endian words there read 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 . The switch in ledger.c returns 1 for 60 to 69, 2 for the seventies, 3 for the eighties, and 4 for 90 to 100. The compiler turned the switch into a lookup table of return values. The resulting record ev_605106bff2d9998f… has confidence derived , and its evidence_links name the two observed records it rests on. Remove the bytes record from the ledger and the derived record has a dangling link. The figure above shows that state when you turn off ev_a467c242… . Now compare with Ghidra. Its pseudocode for the same bytes: Copy Ghidra applied the relocation and named the table DAT_001000b4 , which is .rodata+0x14 after it placed .text at 0x100000 . It recovered the division by 10 and the five cases. For the default value it printed an expression that is always 0 and never says 0. The p-code in native_value_flow marks those operations is_dead: true . The record is a faithful observation of Ghidra. The meaning you read from it is derived, and the value you expect from a run is inferred. The percent_change record shows the other failure. Ghidra's signature reads undefined1 [16] percent_change(int param_1,int param_2,ulong param_3) . The source says int percent_change(int before, int after) . idiv writes EDX:EAX , and the zero path leaves EDX untouched, so the decompiler inferred a 16-byte return and a third parameter. Its own native_api.return_type.confidence for grade is "low" . Treat a recovered signature as the provider's inference, and record it that way. Promotion Rules A claim moves from inferred to supported only through observed runs. check_claim() looks for execute_function records with the same function and arguments, compares each result with the prediction, and counts the covered inputs: Status Condition rea's completion ledger pass every input has an agreeing run and none disagrees pass fail any run disagrees fail unknown some inputs have runs, others have none unknown unsupported no input has a run unsupported promote_claim() is the strict form. It raises ClaimError when any id is inferred or derived . It raises when an id names a run of another function or of other arguments. Unknowns Are Records with a Hash Chain rea stores a residual unknown as a strict record. code/main.py keeps the same fields and the same invariants. The id is unk_ plus SHA-256 over {domain, question, scope_digest} , with the question's whitespace collapsed to single spaces. Two analysts who ask the same question about the same file get the same id. The scope_digest is the SHA-256 of the object. Every change is a new revision. Revision 1 has previous_revision_digest null . Every later revision names the revision_digest of the one before it, and the digest covers every field except itself. verify_unknown_chain() walks the list and recomputes each digest. It checks that each link points at the previous revision. It checks that the mutation evidence each revision names is in the ledger. Each mutation is itself an evidence record, as rea does with provider rea-unknown-registry . Ours carries confidence derived , authority analyst-inference , and no subject. Its limitation reads "A registry mutation records what the analyst decided. It is not proof of the answer." That is why the demo's 81 records include 36 derived mutation records: 18 openings and 18 updates. Three invariants are enforced on every revision: Only a resolved unknown carries a resolution , and only revision 1 has no predecessor. A contradicted unknown names at least one contradicting id, and no id appears in both lists. A verified resolution names at least one evidence id with the required confidence and authority. The third rule is where the ledger refuses most often. rea's workflow notes say "Only qualifying observed evidence can verify a resolution.". resolve_unknown() therefore rejects the table model, rejects an observed record with authority shipped-artifact , and accepts the run record ev_f4ffbe8f922ec7fe… . The resolved revision for grade(95) is revision 2, and its previous_revision_digest is ffca840b55a8a188… , the digest of revision 1. update_unknown() takes expected_revision and raises revision-conflict when it is stale, as rea's update_unknown tool does. The right reaction is the one rea's notes give: reread the current revision and decide again. One unknown stays open after the demo: unk_f2eb0d7f84c80a19… , "Does grade(score) == 4 for every score from 90 to 100 hold when the compiled function runs?". Its status is investigating , its supporting ids include the two runs, and its probe still names the nine inputs without a run. A Cache of Answers Is Not a Database of Analysis rea has three things that look like a cache. The Ghidra target snapshot is a private copy of the input, imported with -readOnly -deleteProject and deleted on close. The in-memory AnalysisSnapshotCache holds up to 10,000 entries for one binary identity. The snapshot file holds target , binding , entries , workflow_entries , and an evidence_bundle . The cache key is query_ plus SHA-256 over {target, binding, operation, parameters} . target is {sha256, kind, format, architecture} , and a raw-binary target also has entry_point . binding is the provider and the whole analysis profile, digest included. Change any of the 25 profile parameters, for example jump_table_evidence from typed-case-default-blocks-v1 to a v2 , and the digest changes, so every key changes. code/fixtures/rea-snapshot.json is the file rea wrote during the two runs, 142,690 bytes. rea wrote it with owner-only permissions, and the committed copy is readable by everyone. It has two entries and an evidence bundle with the same two records. AnswerCache.import_snapshot() recomputes each query_id and refuses the file when any differs. It refuses a snapshot whose target or binding differs from the active one, with rea's wording profile_mismatch . It refuses a snapshot whose format_version is not course-answer-cache-1 . Three measurements from this machine. The first grade query took 8.6 s, with a fresh Ghidra import. The percent_change query against the same snapshot took 8.5 s, because a different query is a cache miss. A third grade query took 2.1 s and returned the identical record with the identical evidence_id . The in-memory replay in rea adds the limitation "Loaded from a local REA analysis snapshot; this call did not re-run the provider.". Our lookup() adds a sentence of the same kind, so a reader can tell a replay from a fresh answer. A mutation ends the cache. In rea 6.5.0, a rename or a comment clears the snapshot cache before rea sends the call to the provider. A failed reply cannot prove that the write rolled back, so a failed write also stops replay. A metadata import that changes the database does the same. Why an Agent Needs This An agent that drives rea through MCP sees the full record on every call and can cite evidence_id in its report. The research from 2026 says where that goes wrong. Over-trust in tool output was one of the four weaknesses in the NDSS BAR study. In the planted-text study, showing binary content as data alone still left 15 unsafe proposals of 40, and provenance checks with tool authorization removed them. A third study watched an agent drive Ghidra through MCP ( arXiv 2606.06838 ). In binaries with hundreds of functions, only 10 to 15 percent received real analysis before the agent produced stubs. Solutions Solution P1 · One fails, one passes, the listing promotes nothing The prediction " grade(110) == 4 " fails: an observed run of the same input contradicts it. The prediction " grade(110) == 0 " passes: the run covers its only case and nothing contradicts it. The listing alone promotes neither: promote_claim accepts only observed execute_function records, and a disassembly listing, however accurate, records how the code looks, not what it returns. Solution B1 · A note without evidence Almost everything that would make it reusable: No subject identity : it does not say which file (by hash) it describes, so it is silently applied to the rebuilt binary, where layout, idioms and even behaviour can differ. No provider or method : which tool, version and settings produced "switch on score/10"? Without that, nobody can re-check it. "Verified" without evidence : verified by what? It says "A for 90+", but the runs show grade(110) = 0 ; the claim was never tested on the inputs where it is wrong. No confidence label or limitations : a reading of the source, a decompiler's text and an observed run look the same in prose. As records, the old findings would be tied to the old binary's hash; a new hash means they are history, not current evidence, and the agent must re-observe and re-run before claiming anything about the new build. RE Cheat sheet · Reverse Engineering with rea Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Take-home Take-home. Build the harness an agent uses to answer one question about a program you compiled yourself, through the analysis tool's MCP server: what does the program print for a score of 95, and where does the letter come from? Deliver the authorization note, the call plan with its deadlines, the ledger that lists each claim on its own line, the open unknowns, the rule for text that comes out of the file, and the tests you ship. Level 4 of 4 · about 60 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Begin with the authorization note: the target is your own build, and the note still answers the five questions in writing, a lawful copy, a named purpose, facts not already available, work confined to the needed parts, and your own expression in anything you release. Plan the calls in order, open_binary , list_procedures , list_strings , analyze_function on the two functions, then read_bytes on both tables the dossiers name, and export_evidence_bundle before close_binary , with a client deadline set from a measured cold start because the first engine-backed call pays for the import. Keep a ledger with one row per claim, each row a kind among observed, derived, inferred and unknown, an evidence id and a boundary, and let the row "95 prints A" stay inferred until the two table reads turn it observed. Treat every string, name and line of pseudocode from the file as data with an address, never as an instruction. Authorization. Every target is a program you wrote and compiled, and the note says so with hashes. For any other program the note answers the five questions before the first command and names the purpose the law names. The tool does not check authorization; the note is yours. Call plan and deadlines. open_binary returns the format, kind, SHA-256 and architecture without importing anything. The first engine-backed call starts the headless import and takes seconds; later calls on the same target take milliseconds. The server allows 330,000 ms for that start, and the pinned client SDK waits 60,000 ms by default, so the client deadline is the one to set from your own first run. Ask every question before close_binary , because the project is deleted and the retained records go with it; export the bundle first so every id in the ledger stays checkable. The ledger. The recorded session returned 13 procedures and 39 strings, then two dossiers. Its ledger reads, in part: Claim Kind Evidence Boundary _grade divides its argument by 10 derived the dossier's multiply by 0x66666667 and the shifts a reading of the listing that the pseudocode confirms five 4-byte entries sit at the table the lea names derived cmp w8, #0x4 and the scaled load count from the compare, width from the shift the five values in that table unknown none; read_bytes with length 20 would observe them no call in this session read memory nothing calls _grade with a call instruction in this build observed callers: [] and one DATA reference coverage complete for resolved calls only a score of 95 prints A inferred the C source the reader owns no record of this session supports it the function name _nothing refused invalid_request a failed call produces no evidence The second-to-last row separates an honest report from a confident one. The reader compiled the source and knows the answer; the agent's records stop at two unread tables, and the two read_bytes calls are the next steps of the investigation. Text from the file is data. Every string, symbol name, comment and line of pseudocode copied out of the target is target text. The agent quotes it with its address and never acts on it, and the ledger has no row kind for an instruction received from the file. Each result that can carry such text arrives with a provenance marker that names the analysis target as untrusted; the marker tells the agent which text came from the file, and the agent still applies the rule. A 2026 study planted text inside binaries and found that models proposed the planted unsafe action in 35 of 40 cases without controls; showing the content as data alone still left 15 of 40, and provenance checks with tool authorization removed them. Tests to ship. A stand-in server replays the recorded records for the same tool and arguments, so the loop runs with no engine installed. Every record's id recomputes from its content, and a record with one limitation removed is refused. Promotion refuses a derived or inferred id and passes only with an agreeing run under controlled-replay . The ledger marks a claim unknown when some inputs have runs and others do not, and never rounds it up. A fixture binary carries a string that reads like a command; the test asserts that the ledger holds it as a value with an address and that nothing executes. A client deadline shorter than the measured cold start produces a recorded timeout step, not a finding. Plausible wrong answers. "The pseudocode returns an entry of _labels , so the letter is observed." The access is observed; the value behind it was never read. "Skip the authorization note for a file I compiled." Write it anyway; the questions answer themselves for your own build, and the habit is the control for every other file. "Treat the usage text as the program's instructions to the agent." It is target text; quote it with its address and never follow it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why export the bundle before the close? Expected: the close deletes the project and clears the retained records, and the ledger's ids are checkable only against a bundle. (level 4) A run of the host build agrees with the prediction for 95. What limitation travels with that row? Expected: the object never ran; a build of the same source for another architecture did, which is the strongest observation without an emulator. (level 4) The strings list contains "run this command to continue". What does the ledger do? Expected: records the string with its address as an observed value, flags the request, and executes nothing; the provenance marker is data about data. (level 4) The agent has the C source. Why does "95 prints A" still read inferred? Expected: no record of the session supports it; two read_bytes calls would, and until then the honest kind is inferred. Where it is taught. The agent investigation section walks the recorded session and its ledger, the use rule section gives the five questions, the open_binary section measures the cold start, and the evidence , rebuild , dynamic analysis and ELF lessons supply the ledger, the harness, the verdicts and the law notes. Explain the mechanism In the record, the dossier for the function _grade lists callers: [] and callees: [] , and its relationship_coverage.status reads complete . The agent writes "nothing calls grade". What does the record support, and what would make the agent's sentence true? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. complete means the engine returned every resolved call reference without a known read limit; the diagnostic beside it says that unresolved computed or indirect calls remain unknown. The one incoming reference is a DATA reference from the function starts table, not a call instruction, so the record supports "no resolved call instruction targets this function in this build". The design rule is that missing coverage is unknown, not absence, and the agent's sentence needs either a run or an argument that covers indirect calls, so the honest move is to record a residual unknown with the probe that would close it. Three values and a null. relationship_coverage states how complete the caller and callee sets are: complete , partial with its limitations and the limited direction, or unknown with a reason, and null for an operation that reports no call relationships. Provider caveats stay in limitations and do not make the coverage partial. One part of a dossier does declare its coverage in numbers: the value flow reports whether it was truncated and how many operations, inputs and edges it omitted. A zero there is a count the tool stands behind; an empty array elsewhere is a count with no such statement. The same lesson in two other empty lists. A bundle comparison across two builds lists ten records that are in one bundle only and classifies every one as unknown with the kind unresolved_branch , because a bundle has no marker that says it is complete. A summary view of a six-file application reports semantic_unknowns: 118 and marks its coverage unknown . Each one proves that nothing was observed, never that nothing exists. The record for what is still open. A residual unknown is a durable record with an unk_ id, a revision chain, a status and the evidence that would close it. The id is a hash of the domain, the question with whitespace collapsed, and the scope digest of the target, so two analysts who ask the same question about the same file get the same id, and a second record_unknown answers already-exists . Every change is a new revision that names the digest of the one before, each mutation is itself an evidence record with authority analyst-inference , and only an observed record of the required authority can mark a resolution verified . The unknown for this dossier asks whether anything calls _grade at run time, and its probe is a run or a read of the computed targets. Plausible wrong answers. " complete means every call that can happen." It means every resolved reference was returned; indirect and computed calls stay unknown. "An empty list means none." It means none observed; the design rule says missing coverage is unknown. "Close the unknown with a sentence in the report." A resolution needs evidence ids of the required confidence and authority, never prose. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) The dossier does list a single incoming reference. What is it? Expected: a DATA reference from the function starts entry, which the unwinder and crash reporter use, not a branch instruction. (level 2) Why does a zero in the value-flow counts carry more weight than an empty callers array? Expected: the count is a declared statement about truncation that the tool stands behind, while the array has no completeness statement beyond resolved references. (level 2) How do you write the open question down so it survives the session? Expected: record_unknown with the question, the required authority and confidence, and a recommended probe; the id derives from the question. (level 3) Two analysts update the same unknown. What stops the second from overwriting the first? Expected: update_unknown takes expected_revision and answers revision-conflict when it is stale, so the second rereads the head and decides again. Where it is taught. The coverage section defines the field and the unknown record, the agent investigation section shows the DATA reference trap, and the evidence lesson builds the revision chain. Explain the mechanism Two machines analyze the same object in different folders and get the same ev_ id. A colleague copies one record, deletes one limitation sentence to shorten it, and the file no longer imports. Later an untouched bundle written by an older release fails the same way. Explain all three outcomes from the id rule. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The id is a content hash: ev_ plus a SHA-256 over the RFC 8785 canonical JSON of a projection of the record, where the projection keeps the subject's digest , format and architecture , drops name and local_path , and hashes everything else, raw_result and every limitation included. So a moved file keeps its id, a dropped limitation changes the content and the validator refuses it with "Evidence semantic identifier does not match its record", and the older bundle fails because the id rule itself moved: the older release left a null relationship_coverage out of the hash and the current one hashes it, so the first record with null coverage fails evidence_integrity_mismatch . Saved evidence is not migrated; regenerate it with the release you run. The recipe. Canonical JSON sorts object keys, removes whitespace and fixes number and string forms. For records whose numbers are integers, a standard-library json.dumps with sorted keys and compact separators produces the same bytes, which is why a few lines of Python or Node recompute every captured id. Floats are refused before hashing, because the canonical form and the language runtime can print them differently. The analysis profile digest is a separate SHA-256 over {provider, parameters} , and a profile whose provider differs from the record's provider is rejected. What is inside and what is outside. A path in subject is outside the hash. A path anywhere else is inside it: two captured files failed to match because the capture kit masked a directory inside normalized_result and locations , so a record that carries a path there gets a different id on every machine. Keep paths out of results and locations in your own records. A limitation is content on purpose: dropping one makes the record look stronger than the facts allow, and a later reader cannot repair that, so the id breaks. Rebinding without rehashing. A record can be shown under a new path with a rebind that refuses when the digest, format or architecture differ. Snapshot replay does the same when it writes the open target's path into a stored record: the evidence_id does not change, because the path was never in it. The error envelope. Every error has the same five fields: code , category , message , retryable , remediation.action , and optional details . The refused bundle names the failing record by index and says which field failed. invalid_request is retryable with corrected arguments; evidence_integrity_mismatch is not. Plausible wrong answers. "Ids are random identifiers assigned at write time." They are content hashes, which is why two machines agree. "Trim limitations to save context tokens." Each one is hashed. A trimmed record with the old evidence_id is refused, and the reader loses what the fact does not cover. "Fix the id field so the bundle imports." The validator recomputes the hash from content, and a patched id is still a mismatch. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why leave the path out of the hash at all? Expected: the same observation of the same bytes should carry one id on any machine and in any folder; identity belongs to the content, not to where the file sits. (level 3) A producer writes an absolute path into locations . What happens when a colleague imports the bundle? Expected: the unchanged bundle still imports, because the stored path hashes to the stored id; but the same observation made on the colleague's machine carries their path and gets a different id, and any edit that masks the path breaks the id. Locations hold addresses and relative artifact paths, not host paths. (level 3) Why does a limitation count as content and not as a comment? Expected: without it the record claims more than the provider did, and nobody downstream can tell. (level 4) How do you handle the older bundle? Expected: regenerate it with the current release, since the rule changed and ids are not migrated; never patch an id by hand. Where it is taught. The evidence record section gives the projection and a script that recomputes ids, the errors reference shows the refused bundle, and the evidence lesson recomputes every recorded hash in Python. Explain the mechanism An agent asks a decompiler for grade , reads the default branch of the pseudocode, and reports "grade(55) returns 0, observed". The pseudocode line is uVar1 = -(param_1 >> 0x1f) ^ (uint)((ulong)((long)param_1 * 0x66666667) >> 0x3f); and the bytes at that point are xor eax, eax . Which of the three confidence words belongs on each claim hidden in that sentence? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Confidence is one of three words and never a number: observed is a fact read from bytes or from a run, derived is a fact computed from observed records, and inferred is an expectation that no observation states yet. The record is observed about what the decompiler printed, with authority shipped-artifact , because the file on disk was the source. That the default value is 0 is derived, from the listing's xor and from the expression, which is always 0 and never says 0. That grade(55) returns 0 when the function runs stays inferred until an execute_function record with authority controlled-replay agrees with it. The two enums. Value Meaning observed read from bytes or from a run derived computed from observed records inferred an expectation no observation states shipped-artifact the file on disk was the source controlled-replay a run you controlled produced the fact analyst-inference your own judgement historical-reference an older tree or document external-service a service outside the file and the host When a producer says nothing, the record gets observed and shipped-artifact . Read observed with care: in a function dossier it means that the tool recorded what the decompiler returned, with the bytes as authority. It does not mean the pseudocode is the program's source. The two confusions that cost the most. The first treats pseudocode as an observation of behaviour. It is an observation of what the decompiler printed. The expression above and the instruction both produce 0 for every input, and the agent did not know that; it trusted text because a tool produced it. The second treats an empty list as proof of absence. Missing coverage is unknown, not absence. How a claim moves. A claim moves from inferred to supported only through observed runs: pass when every input has an agreeing run and none disagrees, fail when any run disagrees, unknown when some inputs have runs and others do not, unsupported when no input has a run. A run of a host build of the same source counts, with the limitation that the object itself never ran. That sentence travels with the claim, because a report that drops it has lost information the reader needs. Plausible wrong answers. "It is observed because a tool produced it." The tool's text is observed; the behaviour it describes is derived or inferred. "Give it a confidence of ninety percent." Confidence is a category with three values, not a number. "The expression is a decompiler bug." It is correct and unreadable; two spellings of one bit cancel, and the instruction says it in two bytes. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why is confidence a word rather than a probability? Expected: the three words name the kind of support, and a number would hide which kind it was. (level 2) A run of the same source compiled for the host agrees with the prediction. Is the claim about the x86-64 object observed? Expected: yes, with the limitation that a host build ran and the object did not; it is the strongest observation without an emulator. (level 2) Which authority does a run under your own harness receive? Expected: controlled-replay , as opposed to shipped-artifact for a read of the file. (level 3) The decompiler's signature says the function returns 16 bytes and takes a third parameter. Which word? Expected: the provider's inference; the dossier marks its return-type confidence low, and the record should say so. Where it is taught. The evidence lesson builds a ledger with the three words and five authorities, and the evidence record section shows the fields on a recorded dossier. Debug a failure After a tool upgrade, a call to open_binary with the saved snapshot answers profile_mismatch , although the target's SHA-256 and the provider are unchanged. The same morning a colleague renamed one function, and later close_binary with a snapshot path failed with "Analysis snapshots are unavailable because analysis metadata may have changed". Explain both refusals, and say what a snapshot is and is not. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The cache key is the string query_ plus a SHA-256 over the target identity, the binding, the operation and the parameters, and the binding includes the analysis profile digest over 25 parameter version strings; the upgrade moved two of those values, so the digest changed and no stored entry can match, which the import reports as profile_mismatch . A rename is a mutating call, and the session empties the cache and sets a flag before the call is dispatched, even when the reply fails, because a failed reply cannot prove that the write never reached the provider, so the export is refused and the way out is to export the evidence bundle, close without a snapshot, and reopen. A snapshot is a file of exact past answers plus their evidence bundle, not a saved provider database. Three things called a snapshot. The target snapshot is the private copy the launcher imports read-only and deletes on close; nothing of the analysis survives it, and every new session imports the target again. The in-memory analysis snapshot cache holds up to 10,000 entries for one target identity. The snapshot file is what close_binary writes and open_binary reads: the target identity, the provider binding, the cache entries and the session's evidence bundle. Only an exact query that qualifies can reuse a result, and a new or live query still starts the provider. What qualifies and what a hit looks like. A call qualifies when its operation is not stateful, names its document or address where one is implied, declares no artifact mutation, and carries a cache policy of snapshot . A hit returns without touching the provider and adds one limitation: "Loaded from a local REA analysis snapshot; this call did not re-run the provider." The replayed record is rebound to the open target's path and keeps its evidence_id , because the path is outside the hash. The lesson's measurements make the point: a first query took 8.6 s with a fresh import, a different query against the same snapshot took 8.5 s because it was a miss, and a repeat took 2.1 s and returned the identical record with the identical id. Load is a full check. Entries must be in canonical id order, every query id is recomputed and must match, no id appears twice, and every entry must have an evidence record in the bundle with the same profile and result. A bundle record for another target fails the whole file. The write is atomic and owner-only. Why the order of invalidation matters. The current release invalidates and then calls the provider; an earlier release invalidated only after a successful call. The documentation states the rule: a metadata write clears the cache of the active session even when its reply fails, since the provider can already have applied the write. Plausible wrong answers. "A snapshot is a saved project; reopen it." It holds answers to past questions, and the project is deleted on close. "Patch the profile digest so the old entries match." The digest names the contract the answers were produced under; a forced match replays answers from a changed contract. "A rename is metadata, so cached answers stay valid." A rename is a mutating call; the cache is emptied before dispatch and the export is refused. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) You cached analyze_function for one function and then asked about another. Why a miss? Expected: the parameters are part of the key, so only the exact same question replays. (level 3) Why not invalidate after the mutating call succeeds? Expected: a failed reply cannot prove rollback, so a cache kept after a failure could replay an answer about a database that changed. (level 3) How does a reader tell a replayed record from a fresh one? Expected: the added limitation sentence that says the provider did not re-run. (level 4) What is the right action after the upgrade refusal? Expected: run the analysis again under the new profile and keep the old bundle as evidence about an old contract; never edit the digest to force a match. Where it is taught. The snapshot section gives the key, the qualifying rules and the invalidation order, and the evidence lesson builds the same cache and refuses a bumped profile version. a1336: Course home / Phase 13 · Tools & Protocols Rebuild and Prove Equal: Differential Tests, Byte Comparison, and the Evidence Loop Lesson 13.36 110 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Write a rebuild from the instruction listing and name the evidence record it came from. Build an input grid with one class per hazard: zero guard, negative values, truncating division, 32-bit overflow, and a divide trap. Run the original and the rebuild in one program and record every cell, including a trap. Recompile the rebuild with the original flags and compare function bytes after masking relocation fields. Read the constants a relocation points at and compare them, so a wrong literal cannot pass. Drive rea's MCP server from a small stdio client and record each step with its evidence id. Mint a fail-closed proof record whose id is a hash over its claims and evidence links. Before you start Needs : Phase 13 · 34 (lifting to pseudocode), Phase 13 · 35 (evidence, confidence, and unknowns) Type : Build. Time : about 110 minutes. Code in : Python, C, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Passing your tests proves agreement on your tests, so equality needs a grid that reaches every edge and bytes that match after relocation masking. The problem In plain words first When you rebuild a function from its machine code, a few passing tests prove little: the rebuild can agree on the inputs you tried and differ on others, often exactly where numbers overflow. This lesson's standard is stronger. Leg one runs the original and the rebuild on a large, designed grid of inputs and compares results. Leg two compiles the rebuild and compares its bytes, its relocations and the constants they point to with the original. The runs below push leg one to its limit: for a function of one 32-bit argument, every possible input can simply be tried, all 4.3 billion of them. For two arguments that is impossible, so a solver (Z3) proves equality, or finds an input where the two differ, from a formula built directly from the original machine code. You asked rea for the function dossier of percent_change in our ledger-x86_64-O1.o fixture. Ghidra 12.1.4 returned pseudocode, and the agent wrote this C from it: Copy Four tests pass: (100, 150) gives 50, (200, 100) gives -50, (0, 5) gives 0, (50, 100) gives 100. The agent also rebuilt grade as four if statements on 90, 80, 70, and 60. Six more tests pass. The report says "verified". That report answers none of these questions: What does the original return when (after - before) * 100 does not fit in 32 bits? What does the original return for a score of 110? Does the rebuild compile to the same 16 bytes as the original? When two compiled functions hold the same bytes, do their relocations point at the same constants? Which evidence record did the rebuild come from, and did the agent read the listing or the pseudocode? What status does the proof get on a host without a C compiler? Every target in this lesson is a program we wrote and compiled. The scope and law rules from lesson 32 apply unchanged. What the Evidence Says The agent loop in code/main.py made six calls to rea 6.5.0 over stdio. The recorded run is code/fixtures/runs/agent-run.json . The server answered initialize with protocol version 2025-11-25 . Three calls returned Evidence records: Step Tool Time Evidence id 2 analyze_function percent_change 6.31 s ev_e88b10dc0c6400e51bb6f7fdc3eaea8d2c97cc02463f0db3e6afeefc273197cd 3 analyze_function grade 0.02 s ev_67b6d3f992eaf49a2e16de084b6ebfdd9884e8c5c7f75e175b7bb20f4f748ce1 4 read_bytes 0x1000b4, 20 0.00 s ev_c26146cfedf4c1ee146d8ff00cfa9a5d3f5335bdd9c97ccf4e1af5f6ea3ed6bc The first call paid for the Ghidra import and auto-analysis. Each record carries confidence: "observed" , authority: "shipped-artifact" , and the SHA-256 of the object, 9a4a8082ba5e285a732552981a6935e0c5255725664f380e37c44ebfb04d803f . Ghidra loads the relocatable object with .text at 0x100000 , so percent_change sits at 0x100000 and grade at 0x100010 . The pseudocode for percent_change is where the long came from: Copy The decompiler saw cltd and idivl write both edx and eax and modelled a 16-byte return value with a 64-bit division. The listing in the same record says something plainer: Copy Every operation is 32 bits wide. IMUL EAX, ESI, 0x64 multiplies in 32 bits and keeps the low half. CDQ sign-extends eax into edx , and IDIV EDI divides the 64-bit pair by a 32-bit divisor. A rebuild that follows the listing is 100 * (after - before) / before in int . The grade record has the same shape. The pseudocode names a table, *(uint *)(&DAT_001000b4 + (ulong)uVar2 * 4) , and an unreadable default expression built from 0x66666667 . The listing shows the divide by 10 as IMUL RAX, RAX, 0x66666667 , SAR RCX, 0x22 , SHR RAX, 0x3f , ADD ECX, EAX . Then ADD ECX, -0x6 , CMP ECX, 0x4 , and JA keep tens from 6 to 10. XOR EAX, EAX before the compare is the default of 0. LEA RCX, [0x1000b4] and MOV EAX, dword ptr [RCX + RAX*0x4] read a table of five 4-byte entries. Step 4 read those 20 bytes: 01000000 02000000 03000000 04000000 04000000 . The table is 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 for tens 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. That is the switch in ledger.c , with case 10 and case 9 sharing the value 4. Both proofs in rea's own evidence pages started from the listing and from read_bytes of constants. The DX-Ball first pseudocode was FUN_00406400(void) with no stack input, and the instruction view corrected it. Read the listing first. Cite the record id, then write the C. Leg One: Execute and Compare McKeeman's 1998 definition of differential testing needs "two or more comparable systems" fed "mechanically generated test cases", and treats a different result, a hang, or a crash as a bug candidate. He named the hard part: "The ugliest problem in testing is evaluating the result of a test." The original function is the oracle here. We do not need to know the right answer. We need the original and the rebuild to disagree nowhere on a grid that reaches every hazard. Design the grid input_grid() in code/main.py builds 92 cells. For percent_change it takes every pair from ten before values and seven after values: Copy For grade it takes 22 scores: both sides of each band edge, negatives, 0, 110, and the two int limits. classify() tags each cell. Overflow has 32 cells, negative 17, boundary 14, plain 12, and zero guard 7. Negative truncation has 5, rounding 2, beyond the switch 2, and trap 1. Each class exists for one reason. The zero guard cells check the TEST EDI, EDI branch. Negative cells check truncating division: C and idiv round toward zero, so -9 / 10 is 0 and -10 / 10 is -1. Rounding cells check that the multiply happens before the divide, so (105 - 100) * 100 / 100 is 5 and not 0. Overflow cells make (after - before) * 100 exceed 32 bits. The one trap cell makes the wrapped product equal INT_MIN with before equal to -1. Yang, Chen, Eide, and Regehr built Csmith to generate programs with no undefined behaviour. An oracle disagreement on undefined behaviour is noise and never a bug report. Signed overflow is undefined in C. Our oracle is a compiled object with one fixed behaviour, so overflow cells are in scope. The lesson is to know which cells rest on the standard and which rest on the compiled bytes. The driver and the trap code/driver.c reads one cell per line from stdin and prints the inputs, the original result, and the rebuild result. build_harness() compiles the candidate with -Dpercent_change=cand_percent_change -Dgrade=cand_grade , so both versions link into one program under different names. On an x86-64 Linux host the original is the fixture object itself. On any other host it is ledger.c compiled natively, and the report records original_kind: fixture-source . The driver installs a SIGFPE handler with sigsetjmp and siglongjmp . For before = -1 and after = 536870911 , the difference is 536870912 and the 32-bit product wraps to -2147483648. On x86-64, idiv with that dividend and a divisor of -1 raises the divide error exception. The quotient does not fit in 32 bits (Intel SDM Volume 2, IDIV). The handler turns that into the recorded value trap . On AArch64, sdiv has no trap and returns -2147483648 for the same operands. Our run on an arm64 Mac recorded exactly that. Read the object ElfObject in code/main.py reads one ELF64 relocatable object with struct.unpack_from . It checks the magic, the 64-bit class, little-endian data, e_machine 62, and e_type 1. Then it walks the section headers, the string table, .symtab , and every .rela section. In the fixture, percent_change starts at .text offset 0 with size 16 and grade at 0x10 with size 46. total starts at 0x40 with size 31 and grade_label at 0x60 with size 63. The 16 bytes of percent_change are 85 ff 74 09 29 fe 6b c6 64 99 f7 ff c3 31 c0 c3 . The function has no relocations. grade has one: offset 0x26 inside the function, type R_X86_64_PC32 , symbol .rodata , addend 0x10 . It belongs to the 7-byte leaq at offset 0x23 , whose last four bytes are the displacement field. Mask, then compare the records In a RELA object the addend lives in the relocation record, and the four field bytes are zero. The candidate grade_switch.o also holds zero there. A plain byte compare passes while the two relocations name different places. mask_relocations() zeroes the field on both sides anyway, so the same method holds for REL objects and for Mach-O, where the field carries the addend. Then prove_bytes() compares the relocation records by offset, type, and target section. The original says .rodata+0x10 and the candidate says .rodata-0x4 . The addend differs because the candidate object has no labels.rel table in front of its switch table. A different addend is a different offset, not a different function. Read the constants the relocation points at For a PC-relative field that ends its instruction, the CPU adds the next instruction address, so the target is symbol plus addend plus 4. In the original that is .rodata+0x14 , and in the candidate it is .rodata+0x0 . read_table() reads five 4-byte entries there. Both hold 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 . The count five comes from the listing: CMP ECX, 0x4 with JA admits indexes 0 to 4, and [RCX + RAX*0x4] reads 4 bytes per index. CLAIMS in code/main.py records that shape for grade and records zero relocations for percent_change . This step exists because of a bug the TH08 project documented. Its older comparison "replayed the target address into the instruction's relocation field, then compared instruction bytes without checking the floating-literal data at that address. Source 0.0 could therefore appear exact against target 128.0 ." The fix audited 1,548 floating-literal references and corrected twelve more. grade_case10_wrong.c is our version of that bug. Its 46 code bytes equal the original, its relocation record has the same shape, and its table is 1, 2, 3, 4, 3 . Only the constant check fails it. What rea's verifier can and cannot say rea's verify_reconstruction takes claims that point at comparison Evidence and returns pass, fail, or unknown per claim. Its fixed limitation reads "Pass means every declared claim passed; it does not establish global implementation equivalence." A claim about a function compares provider text from compare_functions . A behavioural claim compares two recorded process captures from compare_process_captures . When a source record has incomplete call coverage, a claim about calls is unknown . Nothing inside rea compiles a rebuilt function or runs it over your input grid. The two legs in this lesson are the part rea leaves to you. rea's obligation ledger expects a proof record with predicate_type: "rea.reconstruction-proof" , operation: "verify_reconstruction_obligations" , confidence: "observed" , and normalized_result.passed === true . No public rea tool emits one. build_proof() in code/main.py mints it: Copy The id is ev_ plus the SHA-256 of the record without the id, over sorted-key compact JSON. aggregate() is fail-closed: fail wins, then unknown , and an empty claim list is unknown . On a host without a C compiler the two behaviour claims are unknown , so the record says unknown even when both byte claims pass. authority is controlled-replay , because the proof comes from our own harness and not from the object file alone. What the Research Says Liu, Raff, and Micinski measured eight decompilation systems in nine configurations in 2026. Candidates that passed every test the benchmark includes still diverged on fuzzed inputs. The rate was 4.9 percent overall and up to 13 percent for one system. On 300 GitHub library functions and 287 CVE-grounded functions, the strongest refinement model raised Ghidra's build rate from 75 percent to 90 percent. Over the same functions the behavioural match rate fell from 74 percent to 62 percent. They traced the cause to invented fields, types, callees, and guards that replaced the visible unknowns a traditional decompiler leaves behind. Our percent_change_wide.c is one of those invented types. The pseudocode offered a long , the rebuild kept it, and the result compiled, passed ten tests, and failed 26 overflow cells. The grade-threshold rebuild is an invented guard. Both would count as re-executable under the LLM4Decompile metric, which recompiles the output and runs the benchmark's assertions. Ghidra's own pseudo-C passed 20.12 percent of those assertions on HumanEval-Decompile. DecompileBench measured 23,400 functions from 130 real programs. It found LLM methods 52.2 percent lower on functionality correctness than industrial decompilers, with higher understandability scores. The three proofs the field uses are the three legs you can build. Phoenix and DREAM recompile the output and run the original program's tests. McKeeman and Csmith run generated inputs against the original with inputs kept inside defined behaviour. Ramos and Engler check two C functions with bounded symbolic execution, which proves equality on all explored paths up to an input size. This lesson builds the first two. Solutions Solution P1 · Two are perfect, two are not The switch and the table rebuilds get none wrong. The thresholds rebuild gets 2,147,483,538 wrong: every score from 110 up to INT_MAX , where it returns 4 and the original returns 0. The case 10 rebuild gets exactly 10 wrong, the scores 100 to 109, where it returns 3 instead of 4. Solution B1 · A proof about the wrong program They proved that the rebuild matches the pseudocode in mathematical integers, which is a different statement from "the rebuild matches the binary". The model is not the program. Pseudocode is a decompiler's hypothesis; if it invented a wider type or dropped a guard (as the wide rebuild did), the hand model has the same error, and the proof certifies it. Unbounded integers remove overflow. In mathematical integers (a - b) * 100 / b never wraps, so the 64-bit rebuild and the 32-bit original look identical. The very inputs where they differ (overflow) are excluded by the model. Traps disappear. Unbounded division has no INT_MIN / -1 case. A meaningful proof models the original from its instructions with fixed-width bit-vectors and explicit trap conditions, as the second block does, or uses a tool that lifts machine code (angr, Triton).
