Industry practice What's current (2024–2026) Equivalence checking tools : SMT solvers (Z3, cvc5, Bitwuzla) for bit-precise reasoning; symbolic executors such as angr, KLEE and Triton lift real machine code instead of a hand model; Alive2 checks LLVM optimizations; CBMC does bounded model checking of C (the "Ramos and Engler" style of checking two functions). Differential testing at scale : libFuzzer and AFL++ run the original and the rebuild side by side; Csmith-style generators keep inputs inside defined behaviour. Decompilation research (2024-2026) shows rebuilt code that passes benchmark tests but diverges on fuzzed inputs; enumeration where the domain is small and proofs where it is not close that gap. On your laptop : the 2^32 sweep takes under a minute on a modern CPU (faster on the ROG than on this 2-core runner); Z3 proofs of small functions take seconds. Neither needs the GPU. For larger domains, prove: build the original's formula from its instructions, with machine-width arithmetic and trap conditions. Defend a design Design the second leg of a rebuild proof: build every candidate under the compiler and flags that produced the original, then compare it with the original function. Eight candidates are on the table, among them a pair of percent_change rebuilds whose source lines are written differently, a grade candidate whose 46 code bytes and relocation shape match the original but whose case 10 returns 3, and candidates whose relocation addend differs from the original. Say what the compare does at each step, which candidate each step stops, and what a pass means. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Three steps in order: mask every relocation field by zeroing its bytes on both sides and compare the code; compare the relocation records by offset, type and target section, not by addend, because the original says .rodata+0x10 and every candidate says .rodata-0x4 and that is a different table position, not a different function; then read the bytes each relocation points at, here five 4-byte words, and compare them. The wrong-constant candidate passes the first two steps and fails only the third, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 against 1, 2, 3, 4, 3 . A pass proves that this compiler with these flags produced the same code and the same referenced data from the candidate; it does not prove that the candidate is the original source text, since the two percent_change rebuilds with different text compile to identical 16 bytes. Why mask when the field is already zero. In a RELA object the addend lives in the record and the four field bytes are zero on both sides, so a plain compare would pass while the two relocations name different places. Masking anyway keeps one method for REL objects and for Mach-O, where the field carries the addend. The addends differ because the original object holds another table in .rodata before the switch table and the candidate object does not. Why read the constants. This step exists because of a documented bug in another reconstruction project: a comparison replayed the target address into the relocation field, compared instruction bytes, and never checked the data at that address, so a source literal of 0.0 appeared exact against a target literal of 128.0 until 1,548 floating-point references were audited. The wrong-constant candidate is this fixture's version of that defect, and the table read is the audit. The count of five comes from the listing: a compare against 4 with an unsigned jump admits indexes 0 to 4, and the load reads 4 bytes per index. What the tool's own compare can see. The comparison tool line-diffs provider text on eight dimensions, and its assembly dimension carries two fixed limitations: exact provider text is compared without address or generated-name normalization, and assembly is opaque provider text with relocation normalization unavailable. An unchanged assembly dimension means equal text from one engine, a changed one means different text, and neither is a statement about bytes. Two copies of the same code at different addresses diff as changed. The byte-level proof is the part the tool leaves to you. Plausible wrong answers. "Equal size means equal function." Size is a diagnostic; a candidate with the right length can differ in hundreds of bytes. "A byte match recovers the source." Different source text can compile to identical bytes; the match is a statement about one compiler and one set of flags. "The comparison tool said unchanged, so the bytes match." It compared decompiler text with addresses inside and says so in its own limitations. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is the addend left out when the two relocation records are matched? Expected: the addend encodes where the table sits in that object's .rodata , which depends on what else the object holds, not on what the function does. (level 3) What does a changed assembly dimension in the comparison tool tell you about the two functions' bytes? Expected: nothing; it is a text diff with addresses inside, and a relocatable object against its linked image diffs as changed. (level 4) Two candidates with different source text pass every byte check. What have you proved? Expected: that this compiler folded both to the same code and data, not that either is the original text; signed overflow being undefined lets the compiler merge the two multiplies. (level 4) A candidate passes bytes and constants. Is behaviour settled? Expected: on the same architecture yes, since code and referenced data are equal; the trap cell still depends on the host that runs the grid, so the proof names it. Where it is taught. The rebuild lesson builds the masking, the record compare and the table read, the proof harness section records the eight candidates, and the comparison section states the assembly limitation. Defend a design Design the proof record for a rebuilt function that an obligation ledger will accept. The analysis tool's own verifier grades declared claims against comparison records, and its fixed limitation reads "Pass means every declared claim passed; it does not establish global implementation equivalence"; its readiness rule says that nothing weaker than pass adds up to pass. Your CI host has no C compiler. Say what your record contains, how its id is formed, which claims it can and cannot carry from the tool, and what status it gets on that host. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Mint one evidence record of your own, since no public tool emits it, and give it predicate_type: rea.reconstruction-proof , operation: verify_reconstruction_obligations , confidence: observed , authority: controlled-replay , and a normalized_result with passed , status and a list of claims, each behavioral or structural-function with its status and the ev_ ids of the function dossiers it rests on, repeated in evidence_links . The id is ev_ plus the SHA-256 of the record without its id over sorted-key compact JSON. Aggregation is fail-closed: fail wins, then unknown , and an empty claim list is unknown . The tool's verifier can only grade a structural-function claim as same provider text on one dimension, so behaviour and bytes come from your own two legs; on a host without a compiler the behavioural claims are unknown , and the record says unknown even when both byte claims pass. Why the tool's pass is not enough. A structural-function claim names one of nine dimensions of a compare_functions record, and the verifier computes its status in a fixed order: any limitation makes it unknown , an observed changed makes it fail , an observed unknown or an open residual unknown makes it unknown , otherwise pass . The recorded run sent four claims and got two passes and two failures. The total claims failed although both builds came from one source line, because -O2 unrolled the loop into 62 instructions where -O1 had 13; different text does not mean different behaviour. The reverse holds too: a rebuild with a wrong constant in a lookup table prints the same assembly text, so a text claim can pass on a wrong function. Nothing in the tool runs a function or compiles one. The two legs you run. Leg one compiles the original and the candidate into one program under different names, runs a grid with one class per hazard, and records every cell, including a trap. Leg two recompiles the candidate with the original flags, masks the relocation fields, compares the relocation records by shape, and reads the constants they point at. Each leg produces one claim per function, and each claim links the dossier records of the function it covers. The behavioural claim without a compiler is unknown , not skipped and not passed. Authority and id. authority is controlled-replay , because the proof comes from a harness you ran and not from the object file alone; shipped-artifact would claim that the file by itself supports equality, which it does not. The id excludes nothing but itself: adding a claim or a run changes the content and the id, so a proof produced later on a host with a compiler is a new record, and both are kept. No public tool emits this record; the obligation ledger expects it, and you mint it. Driving the verifier at all. The tool's verifier is one of 65 MCP tools without a CLI command, so a stdio client sends initialize , the initialized notification and tools/call . Both dossiers and the comparison record must be in the same connection, because the verifier reads the connection's bundle, and a close clears the retained records; export the bundle before you close. The readiness rule, copied. A stage result of fail, unknown, unsupported, truncated or skipped never adds up to pass. That sentence is the aggregation function. Plausible wrong answers. "A pass from the verifier proves the rebuild equals the original." Its own limitation says otherwise; it compared decompiler text on one dimension. "Mark the behavioural claims passed on CI since the bytes matched." Nothing weaker than pass adds up to pass; a missing run is unknown . "Keep the same id after adding the run results." The id is a content hash; a changed record is a new record. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is the authority controlled-replay and not shipped-artifact ? Expected: the fact came from a run and a recompile you controlled; the file alone cannot show that two functions are equal. (level 4) The verifier passed both percent_change claims while the comparison's overall status was unknown . How? Expected: each claim reads its own dimension; the unknown dimension was references , and the residual unknown it opened names only overall and references . (level 4) A compiler appears on the CI host next week. What happens to the record? Expected: the behavioural claims rerun and pass, the content changes, so a new id is minted, and the earlier unknown record is kept as history. Where it is taught. The rebuild lesson mints the record and its fail-closed aggregate, the verification section shows the four graded claims and the readiness rule, and the proof harness section runs the two legs. Estimate it Design the input grid that runs an original and a rebuild of percent_change(int before, int after) and grade(int score) side by side, so that every hazard the listing shows has at least one cell. Estimate how many cells you need and in which classes, and how many cells a rebuild that kept the decompiler's long will fail. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Read the hazards off the listing: a zero guard from TEST EDI, EDI , truncation toward zero for negative operands, multiply-before-divide order for rounding, a 32-bit wrap from IMUL EAX , a divide trap when the wrapped product is INT_MIN and the divisor is -1, and for grade both sides of every band edge plus scores beyond the switch. Ten before values crossed with seven after values give 70 cells, 22 scores add the rest, 92 in all: 32 overflow, 17 negative, 14 boundary, 12 plain, 7 zero guard, 5 negative truncation, 2 beyond the switch, 2 rounding, 1 trap. The long rebuild fails the overflow cells with |before| > 1 , 26 of them, and a threshold rebuild of grade fails the two cells beyond the switch, so the plausible pair fails 28 of 92 while all ten naive cases pass. One class per hazard. Differential testing needs two comparable systems fed mechanically generated cases, and the hard part is evaluating the result. Here the original is the oracle, so the only question is where the two can disagree, and each class answers one such question. The zero guard cells take the early return. Negative cells check that -9 / 10 is 0 and -10 / 10 is -1. Rounding cells check that (105 - 100) * 100 / 100 is 5 and not 0. Overflow cells make (after - before) * 100 exceed 32 bits. The one trap cell makes the wrapped product equal INT_MIN with before equal to -1: the difference is 536870912, which wraps to -2147483648, and the divisor is -1. Why overflow is in scope. Signed overflow is undefined in C, and a program generator that avoids undefined behaviour does so because an oracle disagreement there is noise. This oracle is a compiled object with one fixed behaviour, so the overflow cells are in scope; the lesson is to know which cells rest on the standard and which on the compiled bytes. The listing settles it: the multiply keeps the low 32 bits, and the rebuild must too. The host is part of the result. On x86-64 the trap cell raises the divide error exception, because the quotient does not fit in 32 bits, and the driver turns SIGFPE into the value trap . On AArch64 sdiv has no trap and returns -2147483648. The recorded run on an arm64 host shows that value with match: true , and a run of the same grid on x86-64 records the string trap . The report names the architecture beside every row, and a proof without the host name is incomplete. Model and run stay apart. A Python model of the listing, with a 32-bit wrap and a C-style division, predicts each cell; the run observes it. Zero disagreements means the model and the binary agree on every cell. The model is derived evidence and the run is observed evidence, and the report keeps them in separate fields rather than rounding one into the other. Plausible wrong answers. "Ten hand-written tests cover it." They passed on both wrong rebuilds; none crossed the width or the switch bound. "Fuzz it instead of a grid." Random inputs find divergence but do not name the hazard; a class per instruction tells you what a failure means and what a pass covers. "Skip the divide-by-minus-one cell; nobody does that." It is the one cell whose result depends on the architecture, and the report must name the host. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why include cells whose behaviour is undefined in C? Expected: the oracle is a compiled object with one behaviour, and the listing shows the width, so the rebuild is held to the bytes and not to the standard. (level 3) Of the 32 overflow cells, how many does the long rebuild pass, and why? Expected: six, those with before of 1 or -1, because the 64-bit quotient truncates back to the wrapped value by accident. (level 4) The grid passes on an arm64 host. What stays unproven for x86-64? Expected: the trap cell, whose original result differs by architecture; rerun on x86-64 or mark it with the host. (level 4) Extend the grid to total(const int *values, int count) . Which classes appear? Expected: count 0, a negative count, one element, and sums that wrap at 32 bits, each with the listing instruction that motivates it. Where it is taught. The rebuild lesson builds the grid and the driver, and the proof harness section records the 92 cells, the 28 mismatches and the trap row on an arm64 host. Before you start Needs : Phase 13 · 32 (ELF from scratch), Phase 13 · 33 (disassembly and control flow), Phase 13 · 34 (lifting to pseudocode) Type : Build. Time : about 150 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript, C, x86-64 assembly, Java (one Ghidra script). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Five tools read the same object and give four addresses, three block counts, and two answers for one switch, and this lesson builds the harness that shows which is which. The problem In plain words first Reverse engineering has a long history and many tools: disassemblers such as objdump, interactive tools such as IDA and radare2, and full frameworks with decompilers such as Ghidra, angr and Binary Ninja. Inside, most of them translate machine code into an intermediate language of their own (P-code for Ghidra, VEX for angr, ESIL for radare2, RzIL for rizin), because analysing a small, regular language is easier than analysing x86 directly. They also number addresses differently, and on hard code they disagree. A careful analyst knows which family a tool belongs to, translates its addresses, and checks claims across tools instead of trusting one. This lesson re-captures the lesson's IR fixtures with the lifters installed here and then puts eight tools, five captured and three run live, on a small trap that splits them. You ask an agent to summarise what three reverse engineering tools say about grade in ledger-x86_64-O1.o . The agent runs each tool, reads three listings, and reports that the function sits at 0x08000050 in one tool, 0x400010 in another, and 0x100010 in the third. It concludes that the tools disagree about where the function is. The tools agree. The object is relocatable and has no load address, so each tool chooses one. Subtract the address each tool gave .text and every answer is 0x10 . The agent compared raw addresses because nothing told it what the address meant in each tool. Later the same agent reads grade in the -O0 build and reports 3, 8, 8, and 9 basic blocks from four tools. All four numbers are real. One tool stopped at jmp rax . Two tools read the jump table through its relocations. One tool split a block at the jump to place a label. A block count without the reason behind it is a number without a claim. This lesson is the map you need before you trust any of those numbers. Lessons 32 to 36 built one decoder, one lifter, one evidence record, and one rebuild. The second half of the track puts them next to the tools people use. To do that you need the history of the field, the families the tools fall into, the pipeline every decompiler runs, and a harness that compares what the tools say on objects you compiled yourself. Fifty-Three Years in Dated Steps The field is older than most of its tools. Each date below has a primary source in Further Reading. 1973 to 1991: debuggers first, then disassemblers The first decompilation theses are from 1973. Hollander at Stanford and Housel at Purdue wrote them, and both are known today through citations. The practical tools of the period were debuggers. Maranzano and Bourne wrote the adb tutorial at Bell Labs in 1977, and the debugger shipped with UNIX V7 in 1979. Tim Paterson's DEBUG , with an 8086 disassembler, shipped in PC-DOS 1.00 in August 1981. Richard Stallman's GDB entered distribution in 1986. SoftICE put a kernel debugger under DOS in 1987. Batch disassemblers came next. Sourcer, from V Communications in 1988, ran multiple passes over a DOS program and wrote a commented listing. GNU binutils began with unnumbered snapshots in 1988, and objdump carries a 1990 copyright. Ilfak Guilfanov wrote the first line of IDA in January 1991 and released IDA 0.1 as shareware on 20 May 1991. 1991 to 2009: interactive disassemblers and the first decompilers Cristina Cifuentes finished "Reverse Compilation Techniques" at QUT in July 1994. Her decompiler, dcc , took i80286 DOS programs to C, and her 1995 paper with Gough set the phases that every later decompiler kept. REC followed in 1997 and Boomerang in 2002, the first open-source decompiler, under a BSD licence. IDA became a commercial product at DataRescue in 1996, gained a plugin SDK in 1999, and moved to Hex-Rays, founded in 2005. The Hex-Rays Decompiler 1.0 shipped on 17 September 2007. In the same year Mike Van Emmerik submitted "Static Single Assignment for Decompilation", the thesis that put SSA at the centre of decompiler data flow. Halvar Flake's "Structural Comparison of Executable Objects" (2004) started the diffing family, and BinDiff went on sale in August 2004. radare started in February 2006 as a forensic hex editor with 64-bit offsets. radare2, the modular rewrite under LGPL-3.0, had its first release on 7 March 2009. 2009 to 2019: frameworks and intermediate representations LLDB was announced as an LLVM subproject on 8 June 2010. BAP, the Binary Analysis Platform with its BIL intermediate language, appeared at CAV 2011. Google acquired zynamics, the makers of BinDiff, on 1 March 2011. Hopper appeared on the Mac App Store around the end of 2011. Matt Godbolt started Compiler Explorer in 2012 so that a C++ programmer could see the assembly a compiler produced. angr received its first line of code in August 2013. The Phoenix paper (Schwartz, Lee, Woo, Brumley, USENIX Security 2013) showed semantics-preserving structuring with 40 goto statements across 8,676 functions. DREAM (Yakdan and others, NDSS 2015) removed the goto statements with pattern-independent structuring. Vector 35 was founded on 14 January 2015, and Binary Ninja went on sale on 23 July 2016 with its Low Level IL and a Python API. angr was released publicly in 2015 and placed third at the DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge in August 2016. BinDiff became free of charge in March 2016. Cutter 1.0 gave radare2 a Qt GUI in December 2017. In 2018 Guilfanov presented "Decompiler internals: microcode" at Recon, the first public description of the Hex-Rays IR. 2019 to 2026: open decompilers and the research turn Ghidra 9.0 was released by the NSA at the RSA Conference on 5 March 2019 under Apache-2.0, with full source on GitHub a month later. angr 8.19.2.4 added a preliminary decompiler the same year. Binary Ninja 2.0 shipped its High Level IL decompiler on 20 May 2020. Rizin was announced as a fork of radare2 on 8 December 2020, and the Cutter team moved to it. IDA Freeware 7.6 added a cloud x64 decompiler in May 2021. BinDiff 8 was open-sourced under Apache-2.0 on 25 September 2023. SAILR (Basque and others, USENIX Security 2024) became angr's default structurer and argued that only spurious goto statements should be removed, because Linux 6.1 has 3,754 of them in its source. Binary Ninja 4.0 added a Free edition in February 2024, and IDA 9.0 added idalib for headless use. The learned-decompiler papers run from SLaDe (2023) through LLM4Decompile (2024) to DecompileBench (2025) and two 2026 studies on agent-assisted readability and on decompilers that recompile more and preserve less. The versions this lesson ran are the current ones on 14 October 2026: Ghidra 12.1.4 (21 September 2026), radare2 6.2.4 (5 October 2026), rizin 0.9.1 (29 June 2026), and angr 10.0.3 (10 October 2026). Binary Ninja 6.0 "Krypton" (3 September 2026) and IDA 9.4 (13 July 2026) are the current closed tools. This lesson did not run them. The Tool Families A tool belongs to a family by what it produces. The families overlap in one program, and the overlap is where most confusion starts. Disassemblers A linear sweep decodes from the first byte of a code section to the last. GNU objdump -d and llvm-objdump -d work this way, and neither builds a control-flow graph. GNU objdump treats symbols as instruction boundaries and sweeps between them. binutils 2.47 (26 July 2026) is GPL-3.0-or-later. LLVM 23.1.3 is Apache-2.0 with the LLVM exception. Apple's Command Line Tools ship llvm-objdump as "Apple LLVM version 17.0.0", and that is the copy this lesson captured. An interactive disassembler runs recursive descent from known entries, adds heuristics for function starts, and keeps a database. IDA Pro (processor modules, autoanalysis queues, FLIRT signatures), Ghidra ( Disassembler plus Auto Analysis analyzers), Binary Ninja (recursive descent, then linear sweep over unknown regions), Hopper, radare2 and rizin ( aa , aaa , af ), with Cutter and iaito as GUIs, are all in this family. Andriesse and others (USENIX Security 2016) measured nine of them on compiler-generated binaries. Instruction accuracy was close to 100 percent, and the hard primitive was function starts, with false negative rates of 20 percent or more. Decompilers Commercial decompilers: the Hex-Rays Decompiler (twelve target families from x86 to RISC-V), Binary Ninja's HLIL with its Pseudo C rendering, and Hopper's pseudo-code view. Open decompilers: the Ghidra decompiler, a C++ engine under Apache-2.0 that r2ghidra and rz-ghidra reuse as a plugin and that pypcode reuses as a lifter; the angr decompiler on AIL with SAILR structuring under BSD-2-Clause; r2dec and jsdec in JavaScript; Boomerang and dcc as history. radare2 also has a built-in pdc , "pseudo disassembler output in C-like syntax". rizin has no built-in decompiler. The command pdc does not exist in rizin 0.9.1, and pdg needs the rz-ghidra plugin. Debuggers GDB (1986) with the GEF and pwndbg front-ends, LLDB (2010), WinDbg with Time Travel Debugging (2017), OllyDbg (frozen in 2014), x64dbg (GPL-3.0, 2014), the Ghidra Debugger with its Python connectors, the Binary Ninja debugger, and the built-in debuggers of radare2 and rizin. Lesson 13.42 uses two of them on your own builds. Binary analysis frameworks angr (VEX IR, symbolic execution, CFGFast and CFGEmulated , decompiler), BAP (BIL, OCaml), Dyninst, Jakstab, and ByteWeight are the frameworks that Andriesse named. Ghidra is a library through PyGhidra, Binary Ninja through import binaryninja , and IDA through idalib . Format and engine libraries LIEF 1.0.0 (12 July 2026, Apache-2.0) parses ELF, PE, Mach-O, COFF, and the Android formats. CLE, "CLE Loads Everything", is angr's loader. Capstone 5.0.9 (28 May 2026, BSD-3-Clause) decodes; Keystone 0.9.2 (GPL-2.0) assembles; Unicorn 2.1.4 (GPL-2.0) emulates. radare2 6.2.4 bundles Capstone 5, and rizin 0.9.1 vendors Capstone, Zydis, and tree-sitter. What a loader does with relocations decides what every later stage can see, and you will meet the effect in the -O0 jump table below. Disassembly Lesson 13.33 built both methods. Every tool in the table except llvm-objdump runs recursive descent and then adds a search for function starts. Binary Ninja's documentation names the phases in order: Recursive Descent, Call Target Analysis, CFG Analysis as "linear disassembly of the unknown regions", and Tail Call Analysis. Ghidra runs its analyzers by priority, with "Disassemble Entry Points" and "Function Start Search" early. IDA keeps autoanalysis queues, each with a priority, and FLIRT signatures for library code. angr's CFGFast documents four sources of function starts: symbols, a prologue scan, call targets, and a complete scan of the remaining bytes. That last source is where angr invents functions at padding. CFG recovery Each tool cuts blocks the way lesson 33 did, with one difference you will measure. angr ends a block at a call , because its IRSB is a single-entry, multiple-exit block and a call is an exit. Ghidra, radare2, and rizin run through a call. On grade_label at -O0 , which calls grade , angr reports 2 blocks and the other three report 1. The instructions are the same. Lifting Binary Ninja defines lifting as "translating from a lower level language to an intermediate language considered higher". The IRs differ in what they are for. P-code and VEX were built for analysis and decompilation. ESIL and RzIL were built for emulation, and neither has an SSA stage. Hex-Rays microcode starts as RISC-like code with 72 opcodes and passes through maturity levels from MMAT_GENERATED to MMAT_LVARS . Binary Ninja lifts to Lifted IL, then folds flags into conditions in LLIL, and MLIL "translates registers and memory accesses into variables". The next section puts four of these IRs side by side on one instruction. SSA Van Emmerik's thesis lists what SSA buys a decompiler: expression propagation, parameter and return identification without an ABI assumption, preservation analysis, type analysis as a sparse data-flow problem, and the analysis of indirect jumps and calls. Ghidra calls its SSA construction Heritage and adds two operations that exist only in the graph, MULTIEQUAL for the phi and INDIRECT for side effects. Binary Ninja exposes an SSA form at every IL level. angr has two SSA stages inside Clinic . Hex-Rays does not name an SSA form and does use-def data flow in its global optimisation passes. ESIL and RzIL have none. Data flow and types Ghidra's main simplification loop runs "Eliminate Dead Code", "Propagate Local Types", and "Perform Term Rewriting" until nothing changes, with the rewriting done by a pool of Rule objects. Hex-Rays transforms microcode, detects call arguments at MMAT_CALLS , and allocates local variables at MMAT_LVARS . angr runs CallingConventionAnalysis , VariableRecoveryFast , and Typehoon , an implementation of Noonan, Loginov, and Cok's polymorphic type inference. Lesson 13.41 is about this stage. Structuring Ghidra's CollapseStructure searches for sub-graphs that match a structure, collapses them to one node, and when it gets stuck removes an edge and marks it unstructured. Hex-Rays reduces the CFG to if , while , do , and switch and leaves the rest as goto regions. angr identifies single-entry, single-exit regions and structures them with SAILRStructurer by default, with PhoenixStructurer and DreamStructurer as alternatives. Lesson 13.34 wrote one structurer by hand. Emission Ghidra emits C tokens through PrintC with an Oppen pretty-printer after ActionNameVars and ActionSetCasts . Hex-Rays beautifies and prints the ctree. Binary Ninja renders HLIL as Pseudo C, Pseudo Rust, or Pseudo Python. angr returns codegen.text . radare2 prints pdc , pdd , or pdg . One Instruction in Four IRs Take 48 83 ec 10 , subq $0x10, %rsp . Decode it on paper with the rules from lesson 33. 48 is REX with W = 1 . The operand is 64 bits. 83 is the group-1 arithmetic opcode with an 8-bit immediate. The ModRM reg field picks the operation. ec is ModRM 11 101 100 . mod = 11 is the register form. reg = 101 is /5 , which is sub . r/m = 100 is %rsp . 10 is the immediate, 16. Four lifters were given those four bytes. The fixtures hold the exact commands and the full text. ESIL from radare2 6.2.4 is one comma-separated string of 30 tokens: Copy It is a stack machine. 16,rsp,-= subtracts in place. Every flag is then written with an internal operator: $o overflow, $s sign, $z zero, $p parity, $b borrow. RzIL from rizin 0.9.1 is an S-expression with 14 set effects: Copy Every flag is a boolean expression over bitvectors. The parity flag alone is a four-level let . P-code from the SLEIGH specification x86:LE:64:default through pypcode 4.0.1 is nine operations after the IMARK : Copy Register transfers with temporaries in the unique space. The flags are computed at the instruction, eagerly, and CF and OF are computed before the subtraction overwrites RSP . VEX from pyvex 10.0.3 is seven statements after the IMark : Copy No flag appears. VEX names registers by their offset in the guest state, and offset 48 is rsp . Offsets 144 to 168 are cc_op , cc_dep1 , cc_dep2 , and cc_ndep . The lifter stores the operation code 8, which is the 64-bit subtraction, and the two operands. A later branch that reads a flag computes it from the thunk. That is why pcode.writesFlags is true and vex.computesFlags is false in the harness report, and why VEX is the shortest of the four. The same four lifters on 48 63 c7 , movslq %edi, %rax , the first instruction of grade at -O1 , give 5 ESIL tokens ( 32,edi,~,rax,= ), 1 RzIL set , 1 P-code operation ( RAX = sext(EDI) ), and 4 VEX statements. No lifter writes a flag, because the instruction has none. Ghidra's own listing of that instruction, captured through the headless script, prints the same operation as (register, 0x0, 8) INT_SEXT (register, 0x38, 4) : register offset 0 is RAX , offset 0x38 is RDI , and the sizes are 8 and 4 bytes. 83 f9 04 , cmpl $0x4, %ecx , from the bounds check in grade , gives 30 ESIL tokens, 13 RzIL set effects, 10 P-code operations, and 7 VEX statements with cc_op 7, the 32-bit subtraction. Nothing writes %ecx . The two subtraction widths you will meet in VEX are 7 for 32 bits and 8 for 64 bits, and the translator you build carries that table. A tool that loads a relocatable object at base ​ reports an instruction at section offset as ​ = B t ​ + o . Comparing tools means mapping back: ​ − B t ​ . One x86 instruction can expand into many IR operations because flags are explicit: subq $0x10, %rsp is 1 machine instruction, 9 P-code operations and 7 VEX statements. Worked example The trap, by hand lookup is movslq at 0x0 (3 bytes), leaq at 0x3 (7), movzbl at 0xa (4), jmp 0x14 at 0xe (2), then four data bytes 31 c0 90 48 at 0x10-0x13, then addl $1, %eax at 0x14 (3) and retq at 0x17. So: sweep tools invent 0x10, 0x12, 0x13 and miss 0x14; descent tools are exact; angr's hybrid invents 0x10 and 0x12 but still finds 0x14. Debug a failure An agent runs four tools on one relocatable object and reports that grade sits at 0x08000050 in one, 0x400010 in another and 0x100010 in a third, so the tools disagree about where the function is. On the -O0 object it then reports 3, 8, 8 and 9 basic blocks for the same function. Explain both reports, and say what a block count measures. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The object has no load address, so each tool picks one: 0x08000000 for the file in two tools, which puts .text at 0x08000040 , 0x400000 in a third, 0x100000 in a fourth, and the sweep prints offsets with no base at all. Subtract each tool's .text address and every answer is 0x10 , which is what the symbol table says. The block counts are four answers to how far each tool followed one indirect jump and where it cut: 3 blocks is a tool that stopped at jmp rax and left 36 bytes unreached, 8 with 11 edges is a tool that read the five relocations behind the table and found four distinct targets, 8 with 7 edges is a tool whose case blocks exist but whose transfer at 0x62 goes to an unresolvable node, and 9 with 12 edges is a tool whose switch analysis placed a label on the jump at 0x74 and whose block model starts a new block at a label. Reduce before you compare. The harness reads the base from each capture and compares after reduction. A disagreement on raw addresses is a disagreement about loaders, and the test that every tool places grade at offset 0x10 from its own base is the first thing to fix in place. Loaders also differ on relocations: one processes them on import, one applies them, and one prints a hint that relocations were not applied unless a setting says so. What a loader does with relocations decides what every later stage can see. Compare in order, read the notes. Instruction starts first: in the agreement case all four tools report the same starts in every function, and the four graph builders report 3, 3, 5 and 4 blocks with identical edge sets. Then blocks, then edges, and each tool's own note before judging a count: a switch_op with five cases and four distinct targets, a COMPUTED_JUMP flow with four targets, or an unresolvable target node explains most differences. All four tools decoded the same 33 instructions once they reached them. The lesson-33 graph had 8 blocks and 11 edges, and one tool matches it exactly; the tool with 9 and 12 found the same four targets and split one block at a label. Where tools invent and miss. One framework ends a block at a call , because its IR block is single-entry multiple-exit, so a function that calls another reports 2 blocks where the other three report 1 for the same instructions. The same framework invents functions at padding gaps with no symbol, 9 across the four objects, and one more on the trap table. The sweep decodes padding bytes that no graph builder treats as code. The harness names one missed range in one tool, the 36 case bytes of grade , and no missed function in any tool. What was run and what was read. Two commercial tools were described from documentation only and are marked as not run in the figure and the table. A description is useful evidence of a different kind from a capture, and the report says which is which. Every capture is stored with its command, version and date; a disagreement you cannot re-read is not a finding. Plausible wrong answers. "The tool with the most blocks found the most code." The extra block is a label split; all four decoded the same instructions where they reached them. "Compare the raw addresses; the tools disagree." The object is relocatable, and each tool chose a base; the offset agrees. "The sweep tool is broken because it prints 0x10 ." It prints section offsets with no base, which is the correct answer with the base removed. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) One tool reports 9 blocks and 12 edges, another 8 and 11, for the same control flow. Who is wrong? Expected: neither; a label on the indirect jump started a new block, and both found the same four computed targets. (level 3) On the caller of grade , one tool reports two blocks and the rest one. Explain. Expected: that tool's IR block ends at a call; the instruction set is the same. (level 4) One listing shows the four case blocks as dead code. How do you classify those bytes? Expected: missed by a stopped walk, since three tools reach them through the table; the byte accounting names the range and the tool. (level 4) You could not run two commercial tools. How do they appear in the report? Expected: from their documentation, marked as not run, with no measured number attributed to them. Where it is taught. The landscape lesson reduces the four bases and explains each block count from the tool's own note, and the disassembly lesson builds the graph the counts are compared against. a1338: Course home / Phase 13 · Tools & Protocols Calling Conventions and Stack Frames: System V, Windows x64, and AArch64 Lesson 13.38 140 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Pick the calling convention from the object header: ELF x86-64 is the System V psABI, COFF AMD64 is Microsoft x64, ELF AArch64 is AAPCS64, Mach-O arm64 is Apple's variant. Decode the prologue of one function byte by byte for each ABI and place every saved register, the return address, and the frame pointer at its offset from the entry stack pointer. Infer the parameter registers of a function from the registers it reads before it writes them, and the stack argument slots from the loads above the entry stack pointer. Tell the independent register sequences of System V from the positional slots of Microsoft x64, and both from the NGRN and NSRN counters of AAPCS64. Check every inference against the source signature, the rule in the specification, and the compiler's own unwind data in .pdata , .xdata , and .eh_frame . Compare how Ghidra, IDA, Binary Ninja, radare2, rizin, and angr name and recover the same facts, and record where their output disagrees with the source. Before you start Needs : Phase 13 · 32 (ELF from scratch), Phase 13 · 33 (disassembly and control flow) Type : Build. Time : about 140 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript, C, x86-64 and AArch64 assembly. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A disassembly shows which registers a function reads. Only the ABI says what those registers mean, and the ABI is chosen by the object header, so this lesson reads the header first and then checks every register against the rule that put it there. The problem In plain words first A calling convention is the agreement between a function and its callers about where arguments go, where the result comes back, which registers a function may overwrite, and how the stack is laid out. Without it, a reverse engineer cannot tell which register holds which parameter. Linux and macOS on x86-64 use the System V rules: integers in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9 , floating-point values in xmm0 to xmm7 counted separately, and a 128-byte "red zone" below the stack pointer. Windows uses different rules, and ARM64 has its own. The compiler also writes a second description of each function's stack frame for exception handling and debuggers. This lesson checks the System V predictions on a live process in gdb, then reads GCC's frame description two ways and compares it with the lesson's analysis of clang's build. You compiled convention.c for Linux x86-64 at -O2 and asked radare2 6.2.4 for the arguments of eight_args . It answered with seven: rdi , rsi , rdx , r8 , r9 , rsp+0x8 , and rsp+0x10 . The C source has eight parameters. The bytes read %rcx exactly once, in leaq (%rdx,%rcx), %rax , and the tool's variable recovery did not count a register that only appears inside an address. You then opened the Windows build of the same file in rizin 0.9.1. It reported the convention as amd64 and found r8 , rcx , rdx , and three stack slots. The object is COFF, so the convention is Microsoft x64, the fourth register argument is r9 , and there are four stack slots. The two tools miss different registers in the same source. A listing is a sequence of instructions. A calling convention is a contract that lives outside the listing: which registers carry arguments, which the callee must preserve, where the return address and the stack arguments sit, and what the caller must leave above the stack pointer. Four documents define the contracts that matter here. The System V AMD64 psABI (Version 1.0, build dated 12 March 2025) sections 3.2.1 to 3.2.3. The Microsoft x64 calling convention, stack usage, and prolog and epilog pages (page dates from 2018-12-17 to 2025-03-19). The Arm AAPCS64 release 2025Q4 (23 January 2026) sections 6.1 to 6.9. Apple's arm64 platform notes. This lesson reads those rules, applies them to one C file compiled three ways, and builds the analyzer that turns a listing into a checked list of parameter locations, saved registers, and frame offsets. One Header Picks the Rulebook convention.c has twelve functions: leaf_add , eight_args , mixed , by_value , big_ret , sum_varargs , keeps , and five callers of extern functions with the same shapes. The structs use long long , because long is 4 bytes on the MSVC target and 8 bytes on the others, and a struct that changes size changes convention. Apple clang 17.0.0 compiled it seven times from this machine: -target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu , x86_64-pc-windows-msvc , and aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu at -O0 and -O2 , and arm64-apple-macos at -O2 . No Linux or Windows headers are installed, so the file declares what it needs and includes only clang's own stdarg.h and stddef.h . describe_object() in code/main.py reads the 4-byte magic number and one machine field and names the contract: Header Field Value Rulebook 7f 45 4c 46 ELF e_machine at offset 0x12 62 System V AMD64 psABI 64 86 COFF Machine at offset 0 0x8664 Microsoft x64 7f 45 4c 46 ELF e_machine 183 AAPCS64 cf fa ed fe Mach-O 64 cputype at offset 4 0x0100000c AAPCS64 with Apple differences The three contracts disagree on almost every row of the table that follows. Every value is quoted from the document named in the header row, and every one is checked by a test against the fixtures. Rule System V psABI Microsoft x64 AAPCS64 Integer arguments %rdi %rsi %rdx %rcx %r8 %r9 , next free register RCX RDX R8 R9 , by position x0 to x7 , by NGRN Floating-point arguments %xmm0 to %xmm7 , next free register XMM0 to XMM3 , by position v0 to v7 , by NSRN Integer result %rax , then %rdx RAX x0 , then x1 Floating-point result %xmm0 , then %xmm1 XMM0 v0 Result too large for registers address passed in %rdi "as if it were the first argument", returned in %rax pointer in RCX , arguments shifted right, returned in RAX address in x8 , x0 to x7 untouched Callee-saved %rbp %rbx %r12 to %r15 RBX RBP RDI RSI RSP R12 to R15 , XMM6 to XMM15 r19 to r29 , SP , low 64 bits of v8 to v15 First stack argument on entry 8(%rsp) 40(%rsp) , above a 32-byte shadow store 0(sp) Below the stack pointer 128-byte red zone "considered volatile" no red zone (Apple: 128 bytes) Alignment at the call (%rsp + 8) multiple of 16 on entry 16-byte aligned outside prolog and epilog SP mod 16 = 0 Variadic marker %al holds an upper bound on vector registers used floats duplicated in the integer register none in registers; Apple uses 8-byte stack slots System V: Two Independent Register Sequences and a Red Zone psABI 3.2.3 classifies every eightbyte of every argument as INTEGER, SSE, or MEMORY and then assigns registers from two lists that do not interact. "INTEGER" takes "the next available register of the sequence %rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %rcx, %r8 and %r9". SSE takes %xmm0 to %xmm7 . "If there are no registers available for any eightbyte of an argument, the whole argument is passed on the stack", and memory arguments "are pushed on the stack in reversed (right-to-left) order". eight_args(a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h) at -O2 is 27 bytes: Copy Six registers, then two loads at 8(%rsp) and 16(%rsp) . Figure 3.3 of the psABI puts "memory argument eightbyte 0" at 16(%rbp) when %rbp is the frame base, which is 8(%rsp) on entry before any push. g is at 8, h at 16. mixed(int i, double d, long long l, float f) shows the two lists. The ints take %edi and %rsi , the first and second INTEGER registers. The double and the float take %xmm0 and %xmm1 , the first and second SSE registers. The first instruction is cvtsi2sd %edi, %xmm2 , and %xmm2 is a scratch register that the function writes before it reads. An analyzer that treats the destination of cvtsi2sd as a read invents a third floating-point argument. radare2 did exactly that and reported mixed as (double arg1, double arg2, double arg3) in xmm0 , xmm1 , xmm2 . by_value(struct pair p) passes a 16-byte struct as two INTEGER eightbytes in %rdi and %rsi , and returns it the same way: leaq 0x1(%rdi), %rax; leaq -0x1(%rsi), %rdx; retq . big_ret(long long seed) returns 32 bytes, which is class MEMORY, and the psABI says "the caller provides space for the return value and passes the address of this storage in %rdi as if it were the first argument". seed moves to %rsi , and the function starts with movq %rdi, %rax because "On return %rax will contain the address that has been passed in by the caller in %rdi". The red zone is the other System V signature. psABI 3.2.2: "The 128-byte area beyond the location pointed to by %rsp is considered to be reserved and shall not be modified by signal or interrupt handlers." At -O0 , eight_args is pushq %rbp; movq %rsp, %rbp and then six stores to -0x8(%rbp) through -0x30(%rbp) with no subq . The stores sit 48 bytes below the stack pointer. The -O2 build of sum_varargs allocates 88 bytes with subq $0x58, %rsp and then writes the register save area at -0x58(%rsp) down to -0x80(%rsp) : 128 bytes below the stack pointer, the whole red zone. Build the same file with -mno-red-zone and leaf_add gains a pushq %rax and an addq $0x8, %rsp to hold its 8 bytes of locals above the stack pointer. Variadic calls add one register. "%al is used as hidden argument to specify the number of vector registers used", an upper bound from 0 to 8. call_varargs sets it with xorl %eax, %eax at -O2 and movb $0x0, %al at -O0 . sum_varargs reads it first: testb %al, %al; je skips eight movaps %xmmN saves when no vector register was used. Microsoft x64: Positions, a Shadow Store, and No Red Zone The Microsoft rules are positional. "Integer arguments are passed in registers RCX, RDX, R8, and R9. Floating point arguments are passed in XMM0L, XMM1L, XMM2L, and XMM3L." and "Any floating-point and double-precision arguments in the first four parameters are passed in XMM0 - XMM3, depending on position." The same mixed arrives as %ecx , %xmm1 , %r8 , %xmm3 : slot 0 is an int, so RCX ; slot 1 is a double, so XMM1 ; slot 3 is a float, so XMM3 . XMM0 and XMM2 stay empty. The caller must also leave room. "The caller must always allocate sufficient space to store four register parameters, even if the callee doesn't take that many parameters." The pages call it the shadow store or the home addresses, and the four slots are "effectively owned by the called function". On entry 0(%rsp) is the return address, 8(%rsp) to 39(%rsp) are the four homes, and the first stack argument is at 40(%rsp) . eight_args at -O2 reads 0x28(%rsp) , 0x30(%rsp) , 0x38(%rsp) , 0x40(%rsp) : 40, 48, 56, 64. The caller side shows the arithmetic. call8 at -O2 is subq $0x48, %rsp and then stores of 5, 6, 7, 8 at 0x20(%rsp) to 0x38(%rsp) before movl $1, %ecx and friends. 72 bytes is 32 for the shadow store, 32 for four stack arguments, and 8 so that the return address is on a 16-byte boundary. call_varargs has only register arguments and still allocates subq $0x28, %rsp : 32 for the shadow store and 8 for alignment. keeps pushes three nonvolatile registers (24 bytes) and then subq $0x20, %rsp , so that ext finds its 32-byte shadow store below the return address. Structs follow their own rule. "Any argument that doesn't fit in 8 bytes, or isn't 1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes, must be passed by reference." and "16-byte arguments are passed by reference." by_value therefore receives a pointer to a copy in %rdx , after a hidden result pointer in %rcx : "the caller must allocate memory for the return value and pass a pointer to it as the first argument. The remaining arguments are then shifted one argument to the right." call_pair builds the copy at 0x20(%rsp) with movaps , passes leaq 0x20(%rsp), %rdx , passes the result buffer with leaq 0x38(%rsp), %rcx , and reads .b back from 0x40(%rsp) . There is no red zone. "All memory beyond the current address of RSP is considered volatile: The OS, or a debugger, may overwrite this memory during a user debug session, or an interrupt handler." The -O0 leaf_add needs 8 bytes of locals and gets them with pushq %rax at entry and popq %rcx before retq , two single-byte instructions instead of a subq and an addq . The stack-usage page defines the leaf that may do this: "A leaf function is one that does not require a function table entry. It can't make changes to any nonvolatile registers, including RSP". Variadic callees home their registers. "For vararg or unprototyped functions, any floating point values must be duplicated in the corresponding general-purpose register." sum_varargs at -O2 stores %rdx , %r8 , %r9 to 0x18(%rsp) , 0x20(%rsp) , 0x28(%rsp) after one pushq %rax , which is entry offsets 16, 24, 32: the homes of the second, third, and fourth register parameters. Its va_list is leaq 0x18(%rsp), %rax , the home of %rdx , the first unnamed argument. AAPCS64, and What Apple Changes AAPCS64 6.8.2 walks a list of rules with two counters. C.9: an integral argument "is copied to the least significant bits in x[NGRN]" and NGRN increments. C.1 does the same for floating-point arguments with NSRN. C.12: a composite of at most 8 - NGRN double-words is "copied into consecutive general-purpose registers". C.13 sets "The NGRN is set to 8" once an argument goes to the stack, so nothing returns to registers afterwards. eight_args uses x0 to x7 and never touches the stack. mixed is w0 , d0 , x1 , s1 . by_value is x0 and x1 in and out. 6.9 says a result that would be passed in registers "is returned in the same registers", otherwise "The address of the memory block shall be passed as an additional argument to the function in x8". big_ret writes str x0, [x8] , stur q0, [x8, #0x8] , str x9, [x8, #0x18] and never writes x0 . call_big sets mov x8, sp , and seed stays in x0 , because 6.9 adds "there is no requirement for the callee to preserve the value stored in x8" and x8 is not one of the argument registers. 6.1.1: "A subroutine invocation must preserve the contents of the registers r19-r29 and SP." 6.4.5.2: at a public interface "SP mod 16 = 0". The stack is full-descending and "No thread is permitted to access (for reading or for writing) the inactive region" below it, so the Linux -O0 leaf_add emits sub sp, sp, #0x10 for 8 bytes of locals where System V used the red zone. 6.4.6 defines the frame record: "a frame record of two 64-bit values on the stack ... The lowest addressed double-word shall point to the previous frame record and the highest addressed double-word shall contain the value passed in LR on entry to the current function." and "The location of the frame record within a stack frame is not specified." clang shows both positions in this one file. keeps at -O2 on Linux puts the record at the bottom with stp x29, x30, [sp, #-0x30]!; mov x29, sp . The same function at -O0 puts it at the top with sub sp, sp, #0x20; stp x29, x30, [sp, #0x10]; add x29, sp, #0x10 . Apple's arm64 notes keep the registers and the alignment and change the frame, the red zone, and variadic calls. "The frame pointer register (x29) must always address a valid frame record. Some functions, such as leaf functions or tail calls, may opt not to create an entry in this list." The Apple build of keeps saves x22, x21, x20, x19 first and puts the record on top: stp x29, x30, [sp, #0x20]; add x29, sp, #0x20 . "The platforms reserve register x18. Don't use this register." "The ARM64 red zone consists of the 128 bytes immediately below the stack pointer", and clang still emitted sub sp, sp, #0x10 for the -O0 leaf, so the compiler does not use it by default. Variadic arguments are assigned "to the appropriate number of 8-byte stack slots" and "the type va_list is an alias for char*". call_varargs on Apple stores 10, 20, 30 to [sp] , [sp, #8] , [sp, #0x10] and passes only w0 ; the Linux build passes w1 , w2 , w3 and tail-calls with b extva . The Apple sum_varargs reads add x8, sp, #0x10 , the caller's stack pointer, as its va_list ; the Linux sum_varargs saves x1 to x7 and q0 to q7 into a 224-byte frame and initialises the structure fields __gr_offs to -56 and __vr_offs to -128 with one mov x8, #-0x38; movk x8, #0xff80, lsl #32 . Symbols differ too. Mach-O prefixes every C symbol with _ , so the listing shows _keeps and the first function appears under the private label ltmp0 . The analyzer renames labels through the symbol table. Decode One Prologue by Hand, Three Times keeps(int n) calls ext(i) in a loop and keeps n , i , and acc across the call, so every ABI must save registers. Read the first bytes of the -O2 build for each target. System V, 4 bytes: 55 is push r64 with the register in the low three bits: 50 + 5 , %rbp . Depth 8, %rbp saved at entry offset -8. 41 56 : 41 is REX with B set, 56 is 50 + 6 . REX.B extends 6 to 14: pushq %r14 at -16. 53 is 50 + 3 : pushq %rbx at -24. Three pushes are 24 bytes. The return address adds 8, and 32 is a multiple of 16, so the callq ext inside the loop is aligned without a subq . There is no movq %rsp, %rbp , so this build has no frame pointer. The body uses %rbp as the callee-saved register that holds acc ( xorl %ebp, %ebp , addl %eax, %ebp ). The epilogue is the mirror: 5b 41 5e 5d c3 . Microsoft x64, 7 bytes: 56 is pushq %rsi at -8. 57 is pushq %rdi at -16. 53 is pushq %rbx at -24. All three are nonvolatile here, and RDI and RSI were argument registers under System V. 48 83 ec 20 : REX.W, opcode 83 /5 with an 8-bit immediate, ModRM ec is 11 101 100 : subq $0x20, %rsp . Depth 56. 56 plus the return address is 64, aligned. The 32 bytes are the shadow store that ext is owed. The epilog page allows only "an add RSP,constant or lea RSP,constant[FPReg], followed by a series of zero or more 8-byte register pops and a return or a jmp", and the bytes are 48 83 c4 20 5b 5f 5e c3 . AArch64, 16 bytes in four words, little-endian: a9bd7bfd is stp with pre-index. Bits 31:30 10 select 64-bit registers, bits 25:23 011 select pre-index, bit 22 is 0 for store. imm7 at bits 21:15 is 1111010 , which is -6, scaled by 8: -48. Rt2 at 14:10 is 30, Rn at 9:5 is 31 ( sp ), Rt at 4:0 is 29. stp x29, x30, [sp, #-0x30]! : the stack pointer drops 48, x29 goes to -48 and x30 to -40. f9000bf5 is str with an unsigned 12-bit offset scaled by 8: imm12 at 21:10 is 2, Rn is sp , Rt is 21. str x21, [sp, #0x10] , entry offset -32. 910003fd is add immediate: imm12 is 0, Rn is sp , Rd is 29. mov x29, sp : the frame pointer points at the record at -48. a9024ff4 is stp with a signed offset: imm7 is 4, scaled to 32. Rt2 is 19, Rt is 20. stp x20, x19, [sp, #0x20] : x20 at -16, x19 at -8. The frame is 48 bytes: x29 at 0, x30 at 8, x21 at 16, 8 bytes of padding at 24, x20 at 32, x19 at 40. The lowest word of the record points to the previous record and the next word holds LR, as 6.4.6 requires. cmp w0, #0x1 sits between the first and second store; the scheduler moved it into the prologue, and the analyzer tolerates a compare or an arithmetic instruction between stack operations. The Compiler Wrote the Same Facts Twice A prologue parse is one derivation. The compiler emits a second one for the unwinder, and the two must agree. On Windows the second derivation is .pdata and .xdata . Build the -O2 object without -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables and llvm-objdump -h shows .xdata of 0x34 bytes and .pdata of 0x48 bytes. 0x48 is 72, six RUNTIME_FUNCTION entries of 12 bytes with three IMAGE_REL_AMD64_ADDR32NB relocations each. The six are sum_varargs , keeps , call8 , call_varargs , call_pair , and call_big . The other six functions are leaves, and the exception handling page says "If the search doesn't find a function table entry, the code is assumed to be part of a leaf function, and RSP directly addresses the return pointer." The .xdata bytes for keeps are 01 07 04 00 07 32 03 30 02 70 01 60 . UNWIND_INFO starts with Version in 3 bits and Flags in 5 bits: version 1, no flags. SizeOfProlog is 7, CountOfCodes is 4, FrameRegister and FrameOffset are 0. Each UNWIND_CODE is an offset in the prolog and a byte of opcode and info. 07 32 : at offset 7, op 2 is UWOP_ALLOC_SMALL , info 3 means 3 * 8 + 8 = 32 bytes. 03 30 : op 0 is UWOP_PUSH_NONVOL , register 3 is rbx . 02 70 : rdi . 01 60 : rsi . The codes are stored in reverse order of execution, and they name the same three pushes and the same 32-byte allocation as the bytes 56 57 53 48 83 ec 20 . The sum_varargs entry is 01 01 01 00 01 02 00 00 : a 1-byte prolog with one code, UWOP_ALLOC_SMALL of 8 bytes. That is how the unwinder sees pushq %rax : an allocation, because %rax is volatile and nothing is being saved. On Linux the second derivation is .eh_frame , which psABI 4.2.4 defines and DWARF 5 section 6.4 encodes. llvm-dwarfdump --eh-frame on the relocatable object prints one FDE per function and resolves the R_X86_64_PC32 relocations, so the ranges are usable. For keeps : Copy The CFA is the stack pointer before the call, 8 above the entry stack pointer, so RBP -16 is entry offset -8, R14 -24 is -16, RBX -32 is -24, and the deepest CFA offset of 32 is the 24-byte frame plus the return address. The AArch64 FDE for keeps says DW_CFA_def_cfa: W29 +48 with W29 -48 , W30 -40 , W21 -32 , W20 -16 , W19 -8 . There the CFA is the entry stack pointer itself, so the offsets are the frame offsets without conversion, and the CFA is defined from x29 while the frame record is live. eh_frame_cross_check() runs this comparison for all 12 FDEs of both objects. One entry needed care: call8 under System V pushes two outgoing arguments mid-body, so its deepest CFA offset is 32 while its prologue frame is 8, and the check compares the deepest stack pointer the body reaches, 24, plus 8. What the Tools Call This Every tool in this field has a data structure for the calling convention and a pass that assigns one to a function. The names differ and the gaps differ. The closed tools are described from their documentation; the open ones were run on the fixtures and their output is captured beside the objects. Ghidra 12.1.4 (Apache-2.0). The rules live in compiler specification files, .cspec , next to the SLEIGH language. x86-64-gcc.cspec declares a <default_proto> named __stdcall , "Derived from System V Application Binary Interface AMD64 Architecture Processor Supplement April 2016", with <pentry> lists for XMM0_Qa to XMM7_Qa and RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9 , a stack entry at offset 8, a join_dual_class rule for types up to 16 bytes, outputs XMM0_Qa, XMM1_Qa, RAX, RDX , and hidden_return for the rest. x86-64-win.cspec declares __fastcall with four <group> elements that pair XMM0_Qa with RCX , XMM1_Qa with RDX , and so on, which is the positional rule, a stack entry at offset 40, convert_to_ptr for structs of 3, 5, 6, or 7 bytes with the comment "only structs of size 8,16,32,64 bits can be packed to register", unaffected listing RBX RBP RDI RSI RSP R12 to R15 and XMM6 to XMM15 , and a localrange of stack 8 to 39, which is the shadow store. AARCH64.cspec declares __cdecl whose first entry is x8 with storage="hiddenret" , then q0 to q7 and x0 to x7 , convert_to_ptr for structs of 17 bytes or more, and killedbycall including x8 with the comment "indirect result location register, which is not reflected in the pentry list". Expected shape: Copy Read code/main.py in this order: describe_object() reads the ELF, COFF, or Mach-O header and the symbol table and returns the ABI and the function list. parse_listing() splits the llvm-objdump -d -r text into functions, keeps the relocation target of every call and jump, and strips comments with the marker of the right syntax: # for AT&T, // and ; for AArch64, where # introduces an immediate. effect_x86() and effect_arm() turn one instruction into reads, address reads, writes, loads, stores, and a stack pointer delta. The last AT&T operand is the destination; the first AArch64 operand is the destination except in stores, compares, and branches. lea reads an address and loads nothing. The destination of mov , cvtsi2sd , setcc , and the zero idiom xor r, r is a write only. A call writes the whole volatile set. A pre-indexed store moves sp before the access and a post-indexed load moves it after. analyze_function() walks the body once up to the first ret or tail jump. It tracks the depth of the stack pointer below its entry value, so a memory operand disp(%rsp) is at entry offset disp - depth and disp(%rbp) is at frame_pointer + disp . It records argument-class registers that are read before they are written, loads at or above the first stack argument offset of the ABI, stores of argument registers into the frame, accesses below the current stack pointer, and the depth at every call. _return_registers() keeps a result register when its last access before the exit is a write. A read as a data operand kills the candidate; a read as an address base does not, which is what keeps rax alive in big_ret under Microsoft x64, where movq %rcx, %rax is followed by stores through (%rax) . expected_locations() applies the three rulebooks to a C signature: the two System V lists with eightbyte classes, the Microsoft positional slots with by-reference structs, and the AAPCS64 counters with x8 for results above 16 bytes. run_checks() compares the two and adds the frame rules: callee-saved registers written must be saved, (rsp + 8) % 16 == 0 or sp % 16 == 0 at every call, 32 bytes of shadow at every Microsoft call, no access below the stack pointer under Microsoft and AAPCS64 and at most 128 bytes under System V, and an epilogue that mirrors the prologue with the stack pointer back at its entry value. seh_cross_check() and eh_frame_cross_check() read the unwind data of the objects built without -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables and compare it with the prologue parse. Solutions Solution P1 · rdi, xmm0, rsi, xmm1; rsi; zero In mixed(1, 2.5, 3, 4.5f) : 1 in edi (low half of rdi ), 2.5 in xmm0 , 3 in rsi , 4.5 in the low 32 bits of xmm1 . In big_ret(9) , 9 is in rsi , because rdi carries the hidden pointer to the 32-byte return buffer. In sum_varargs(3, 10, 20, 30) , al is 0: no vector registers carry variable arguments. Solution B1 · Wrong registers on two platforms The Windows DLL uses the Microsoft x64 convention: the first four arguments are in rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 (or xmm0-3 by position). Labelling rdi and rsi as parameters is wrong; on Windows they are callee-saved registers, so the tool will show them being "used" when the function merely saves them, and miss the real arguments. It will also misread the 32-byte shadow store above the return address as locals or arguments. The Linux library uses System V but with two independent sequences: in f(int a, double x, int b) , b is in rsi , and x is in xmm0 . A tool that numbers integer registers by position shifts every argument after the first double , labels rdx as b (it is unused), and never shows x at all. The fix is to choose the convention from the file format and target (PE/COFF versus ELF or Mach-O, and the machine), classify each parameter by type, and keep separate counters where the ABI requires them. In plain words first The idea in one line An optimizing compiler replaces source constructs with cheaper instruction shapes. Each shape has a derivation, and this lesson builds the recognizer that runs the derivation backwards and checks it against the source. The problem In plain words first Optimizing compilers rewrite simple source code into faster, stranger machine code. A division by 10 becomes a multiplication by a large constant and a shift; a switch becomes a table of addresses, a table of values, or a chain of comparisons; a loop may be unrolled, vectorized or replaced by a formula; a branch may become a conditional move. Each of these shapes is an idiom: once you know its derivation, you can read it back to the source. Some security features look like idioms too, such as the stack canary check and the endbr64 marker. This lesson compiles divisions by twelve constants with this machine's GCC and recovers every divisor from the machine code using the lesson's formula, then shows the canary and CET marks and makes a canary fire in a small program of our own. You compiled idioms.c at -O2 and asked an agent what div7u does. The agent read imulq $0x24924925, %rax, %rax and answered that the function multiplies by 613566757, shifts, and adds. Every word is true. The function computes x / 7 . The same object holds a switch with seven cases that has no jump at all, a switch with five cases that is a jump table, a switch with two cases that is a sete and a cmovne , and a loop over n integers that runs eight integers per iteration in two xmm registers and then finishes the rest in a second loop. At -O0 the same source produced divl , seven-entry jump tables, and one scalar loop. At -O1 the seven-case switch became a table of values and the vector loop did not exist yet. These shapes are idioms. A compiler emits each one from a rule you can read in its source, and each one can be decoded back to the construct it came from. The decoding is arithmetic, and arithmetic can be checked. Lesson 13.34 proved one of them, the multiply by 0x66666667 . This lesson builds the recognizer for all of them, runs it over 18 builds of our own code, and verifies all 373 reports against the C source. An Idiom Is a Shape With a Derivation An idiom is a sequence of instructions the compiler emits for one source construct. Three things make it recognizable. It has a fixed shape, the operands carry constants that the derivation predicts, and the shape differs from what a programmer would write by hand. The recognizer in code/main.py works on the text of llvm-objdump -d -r , which lesson 33 established as the oracle for instruction boundaries. It parses each function into instructions with address, bytes, mnemonic, operands, and the relocation line that follows it. It reads the object file for two things only: the bytes of .rodata , where value tables live, and the .rela.rodata entries, where jump-table targets live before linking. Every detection is an Idiom record with a kind , a decoded source form, a list of evidence addresses, a detail dictionary, and a verified flag. The flag comes from the C source. parse_source() reads idioms.c , finds each function, and extracts the divisors after / and % , the multipliers after * , the switch cases and their values, the ? : operators, the for loops, and the callees. A division idiom is verified when its divisor is in the function's division list. A lookup table is verified when its entries match the case values, up to a constant factor. A tail call is verified when the callee is called in the source. The demo report ends with an unverified list, and the test suite asserts that the list is empty for all 18 builds. Decoding needs names. The recognizer runs a small symbolic evaluator over each function's basic blocks, in listing order, with the parameter names from the source in the argument registers of the System V and AAPCS64 conventions from lesson 38. Stack slots are tracked by their operand text so -O0 code reads through its spills. At each block entry the states of the predecessors are merged, and where they differ a name that an earlier idiom assigned wins over a constant. That is how cmovll %edx, %eax in digest reads back as sum % 10 < 5 ? sum % 10 : 5 : the loop idiom named the accumulator sum , the division idiom named its quotient sum / 10 , and the modulo idiom named its result sum % 10 . The source writes rem > 5 ? 5 : rem . Both expressions give the smaller of rem and 5, and they agree at rem == 5 . Division by a Constant Granlund and Montgomery, "Division by Invariant Integers using Multiplication" (PLDI 1994), replace n / d with a multiply and a shift. Pick a shift s and a multiplier m = ceil(2^s / d) . Then floor(n * m / 2^s) equals floor(n / d) for every n in range when the error e = m * d - 2^s is small enough. For unsigned 32-bit n the bound is e <= 2^(s - 32) . For signed n with |n| < 2^31 the bound is e <= 2^(s - 31) , and a sign fix-up adds 1 when n is negative, because the floor rounds the wrong way for negative quotients. magic_numbers(d, bits, signed) in main.py searches s upward from 32 and returns the first pair that satisfies the bound. That search reproduces every constant clang emitted in the fixtures. Unsigned 10 by hand 2^35 / 10 = 3435973836.8 . The ceiling is 3435973837 = 0xCCCCCCCD . The error is 0xCCCCCCCD * 10 - 2^35 = 2 , and the bound at s = 35 is 2^3 = 8 . At s = 34 the error would be 6 against a bound of 4, so 35 is the smallest shift. Check with n = 123 : 123 * 3435973837 = 422624781951 , and 422624781951 >> 35 = 12 . clang emits exactly this for div10u at -O2 on x86-64: Copy 0x23 is 35. The movl %edi, %ecx zero-extends the 32-bit argument into a 64-bit register, which is the unsigned form. The recognizer reads the multiplier from the movl $imm that feeds the two-operand imulq , reads the shift, and calls divisor_from_magic(0xCCCCCCCD, 35) . That function tries 2^35 // m = 10 and 11, and accepts 10 because magic_numbers(10) gives the same multiplier and shift back. On AArch64 the same function is mov w8, #0xcccd; movk w8, #0xcccc, lsl #16; umull x8, w0, w8; lsr x0, x8, #35 . The constant arrives in two 16-bit halves, the multiply is umull , and the shift is written in decimal. The recognizer assembles the halves and reports the same divisor. Unsigned 7 by hand, with the add fix-up 2^35 / 7 = 4908534052.57 . The ceiling is 4908534053 = 0x124924925 , which needs 33 bits. The error is 3 against a bound of 8, so the shift is 35, and no smaller shift works. A 32-bit multiply cannot hold the multiplier, so the compiler multiplies by the low 32 bits 0x24924925 and adds the dividend back in a fixed sequence: Copy Read it as t = (n * 0x24924925) >> 32 , then q = (((n - t) >> 1) + t) >> 2 . The total shift is 32 + 1 + 2 = 35 . With n = 100 : t = 14 , (100 - 14) >> 1 = 43 , 43 + 14 = 57 , 57 >> 2 = 14 . The recognizer detects the sub , shr , add , shr tail after a 32-bit shift, adds 2^32 back to the multiplier, and recovers 7. evaluate_division() runs this exact sequence and the test checks it against n // 7 on the 32-bit edge values. The AArch64 form is sub w9, w0, w8; add w8, w8, w9, lsr #1; lsr w0, w8, #2 , one instruction shorter because the shifted add is one instruction. Signed 3 by hand 2^32 / 3 = 1431655765.33 , ceiling 1431655766 = 0x55555556 , error 2, and the signed bound at s = 32 is 2^1 = 2 . The bound holds with no room to spare, so the shift is 32 and clang uses shrq $0x20 . With n = -7 : the product is -10021590362 , the arithmetic shift by 32 gives -3 , the sign bit is set, so the fix-up adds 1 and the result is -2 , which is -7 / 3 in C. The signed fixtures div10s and div3s both carry the fix-up as shrq $0x3f on a copy of the product followed by addl . What the constants are not The multiplier alone names no divisor. 0x66666667 with shift 34 is 10. The same multiplier with shift 33 is 5, as lesson 34 showed. The recognizer therefore always pairs the multiplier with the total shift, and the clangMatchesAlgorithm field records that the pair is the one the search produces. Powers of two never use the multiply. magic_numbers() refuses them, because the compiler emits a shift with a sign bias instead, and mod8s in the next section shows that shape. The idiom belongs to the instruction selector At -O0 , div10u is movl $0xa, %ecx; xorl %edx, %edx; divl %ecx . div10s is cltd; idivl %ecx . In the same object, digest divides its loop sum by 10 with imulq $0x66666667 . One flag explains the difference. The fixture idioms-x86_64-nofastisel-O0.o was built with -O0 -mllvm -fast-isel=false , and in it every division is the multiply, including div10u with movl $0xcccccccd, %ecx; imulq %rcx, %rax; shrq $0x23 . The hardware divide is the fast instruction selector's choice at -O0 . The multiply is SelectionDAG's lowering, which is what LLVM's UnsignedDivisionByConstantInfo and SignedDivisionByConstantInfo produce. The digest block that holds the division also holds a switch , and that block went to SelectionDAG. The recognizer reports both forms, hardware idivl and magic multiply , and the figure shows the mixed -O0 function. Modulo Follows the Quotient x % d is x - (x / d) * d . The compiler computes the quotient with the idiom above, multiplies it back, and subtracts. On x86-64 the multiply back by 10 is addl %ecx, %ecx; leal (%rcx,%rcx,4), %ecx , which is 2 * q * 5 . On AArch64 it is one instruction, msub w0, w8, w9, w0 , which computes w0 - w8 * w9 with w9 = 10 . The recognizer follows the quotient register through copies, tracks the accumulated factor through add , lea , shl , and imul , and accepts a sub when the factor equals the divisor. When the same quotient also feeds another expression, both idioms stay in the report. At -O1 the compiler computes sum / 10 once in digest and uses it for the switch index and for the modulo. On x86-64 it even combines the quotient twice, leal (%rax,%rsi), %edi for the modulo and addl %esi, %eax for the switch. The recognizer reports one division and one modulo and marks the quotient as shared. A report that lost the division here would make the switch index unreadable. Signed modulo by a power of two has its own shape, because the quotient is never computed: Copy For a negative x the code biases by 7 before masking, so that the truncation rounds toward zero as C requires. The masked value is x rounded to a multiple of 8, and the subtraction leaves x % 8 . AArch64 does it with negs w8, w0; and w9, w0, #0x7; and w8, w8, #0x7; csneg w0, w9, w8, mi : mask both x and -x , then pick and negate by the sign. Ghidra names its rule for this RuleSignMod2nOpt , with the brief "Convert INT_SREM forms: (V + (sign >> (64-n)) & (2^n-1)) - (sign >> (64-n)) => V s% 2^n ". At -O0 AArch64 writes modulo as sdiv w9, w8, w10; mul w9, w9, w10; subs w0, w8, w9 . The recognizer accepts that form too and reports hardware sdiv + mul + subs . Five Ways to Lower a switch LLVM decides the shape of a switch in two places. SimplifyCFG::simplifySwitchLookup runs at -O1 and above and turns a switch whose cases all produce constants into a table of values, when there are at least three cases and the target can build lookup tables. Its table kinds are SingleValueKind , LinearMapKind , BitMapKind , and ArrayKind . The -O0 pipeline never runs this pass. The remaining switches reach SwitchLowering::findJumpTables in instruction selection, which builds a jump table when the cluster has at least min-jump-table-entries entries, 4 by default, and is dense enough: NumCases * 100 >= Range * MinDensity with jump-table-density 10 for normal functions and 40 under -Os . What is left becomes a binary search over the case constants, with splitWorkItem choosing the pivot. The fixtures hold one function per outcome. Two flags move these boundaries. -fno-jump-tables turns table_switch , call_switch , and the digest switch into comparison trees on x86-64, with pivots 2 and 4 for the seven-case function.
