The fixture idioms-arm64-jt4-O2.o records that run. GCC puts both decisions in tree-switch-conversion.cc , with the classes jump_table_cluster , bit_test_cluster , switch_decision_tree , and switch_conversion . Its -ftree-switch-conversion is on at -O2 , -fjump-tables and -fbit-tests at -O1 , and the jump table threshold comes from case-values-threshold , whose default is the machine's value. No GCC is installed on this machine, so those names come from the GCC source and manual, and Compiler Explorer is where you check them. Loops: Vectorized, Unrolled, or Replaced LLVM's loop vectorizer is on at -O2 , -O3 , and -Os , and off at -O0 and -O1 , a rule that dates to LLVM 3.4 in January 2014. sum_n at -O2 shows every part of the shape: Copy The guard cmpl $7; ja sends trip counts below 8 to the scalar loop. The mask andl $0x7ffffff8 rounds the trip count down to a multiple of 8. The body loads 32 bytes per iteration into two xmm accumulators, four 32-bit lanes each, so the vectorization factor is 4 and the interleave factor is 2. After the loop, paddd , two pshufd , two more paddd , and movd reduce the eight lanes to one integer. The loop at 0x270 is the scalar remainder for the last 0 to 7 elements. The recognizer finds the loop from its back edge, sees the SIMD registers, reads the lane count from paddd , counts distinct accumulators, divides the step 0x20 by 4, and reports 4 lanes x 2 accumulators = 8 elements per iteration , with the mask, the guard, the reduction, and the remainder loop as fields. AArch64 does the same with ldp q2, q3 , two add v.4s , addv s0, v0.4s , and fmov w8, s0 . A fixed trip count removes the loop. sum4 is one movdqu , the reduction, and movd , with no back edge. poly8 cannot vectorize, because each iteration depends on the previous accumulator, so the compiler unrolls it eight times: eight loads at offsets 0 through 0x1c from %rdi , each followed by a shift by 5 and a subtract that compute acc * 31 . The recognizer counts the loads at consecutive offsets from one base and reports loop unrolled by 8, no back edge . On AArch64 the same loads arrive as four ldp pairs. Turn the vectorizer off with -fno-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize and sum_n becomes a scalar loop unrolled by 8, with eight addl k(%rdi,%rdx,4), %eax and addq $8 , plus a remainder loop. sum4 becomes four adds. The recognizer reports unrolled loop with copies: 8 and indexStep: 8 for the first and copies: 4 for the second. Lesson 13.33 found two back edges in total at -O2 and called them two loops. This lesson names them: one vector body and one scalar remainder of the same source loop. A back edge is a loop only when its target can reach it again. is_loop() checks that, because digest on AArch64 contains backward branches to a shared default block that are not loops, and the first version of the recognizer counted them as vector loops. Loops that become library calls LoopIdiomRecognize turns a loop that stores zero into every byte into a call to memset , from -O1 upward. fill at -O2 is testl %esi, %esi; jle; movl %esi, %edx; xorl %esi, %esi; jmp memset@PLT . The call is a tail jump with the relocation R_X86_64_PLT32 memset-0x4 , and the function's retq is only on the empty path. The recognizer reports store loop recognized as memset(...) and verifies it against the source loop, because the source never names memset . copy16 calls memcpy with a constant 16, and the x86 backend expands it inline as movups (%rsi), %xmm0; movups %xmm0, (%rdi) , within its limit of 8 stores per memcpy . At -O0 the same call is two 8-byte movq pairs. With -fno-builtin the call stays a call, jmp memcpy@PLT with movl $0x10, %edx , and fill keeps its loop, which the vectorizer then turns into a loop of two 16-byte movups stores per iteration. The recognizer reports vectorized store loop: 2 x 16-byte stores = 32 bytes per iteration for that build. Calls That Disappear or Become Jumps tail_caller returns tail_target(x + 1) . At -O0 it is addl $0x1, %edi; callq tail_target@PLT; addq $0x10, %rsp; popq %rbp; retq . At -O2 it is incl %edi; jmp tail_target@PLT and nothing else. The caller's frame is gone and the callee returns to the caller's caller. On AArch64 the jump is b tail_target with R_AARCH64_JUMP26 . The recognizer treats a jmp or b that carries a call relocation as a tail call. Lesson 13.33 's recursive descent must treat it as a function exit, because the target is outside the function. twice_sum calls leaf_add . At -O0 the call is there, callq leaf_add@PLT . From -O1 the body of leaf_add , leal (%rdi,%rsi), %eax , appears inside twice_sum and no call remains. At -O0 clang marks every function optnone and noinline and runs only the always-inliner. The recognizer knows from the source that twice_sum calls leaf_add , finds no call or tail jump to it, and then looks for the callee's body shape in the caller: the mnemonic and source operands with the destination removed, so add w8, w1, w0 in the AArch64 caller matches add w0, w1, w0 in the callee. One match is the evidence. dispatch combines both: a 16-entry jump table whose every case is movl %esi, %edi; jmp fN@PLT . The recognizer reports one switch and 16 tail calls, all verified against the 16 calls in the source. Branches That Became Data Moves clamp_max is movl %esi, %eax; cmpl %esi, %edi; cmovgl %edi, %eax . The evaluator names %edi as a and %esi as b , records the compare, and reads the cmovg as a > b ? a : b , which is the source text. abs_int is movl %edi, %eax; negl %eax; cmovsl %edi, %eax and reads as -x < 0 ? x : -x ; AArch64 writes it as cmp w0, #0; cneg w0, w0, mi and reads as x < 0 ? -x : x . is_pos is xorl %eax, %eax; testl %edi, %edi; setg %al , which reads as (x > 0) . These are -fif-conversion in GCC's words and cmov selection in LLVM's. LLVM's X86CmovConversion pass can turn a cmov back into branches when it judges that profitable, which is why the same source can show either shape in a loop. At -O0 none of these exist. clamp_max is a compare, a jle , two stores to the same slot, and a load. The recognizer reports nothing for it at -O0 and branchless select from -O1 , which is one of the facts the figure makes visible. mul9 is one leal (%rdi,%rdi,8), %eax , and the recognizer reports strength reduction with x * 9 , because the source multiplies by 9. It only does so when the source has the factor; a lea that scales a table index is not a multiplication. Two Hardening Features That Look Like Idioms The stack protector is a compiler feature, and it leaves a shape that an agent will otherwise read as program logic. canary.c compiled with -fstack-protector-strong for x86-64 Linux gives: Copy %fs:0x28 is stack_guard in glibc's tcbhead_t , at byte offset 40, and LLVM's getIRStackGuard names that slot for glibc, bionic, and Fuchsia. The prologue copies the guard above the buffer, the epilogue compares, and the failure path calls __stack_chk_fail . On AArch64 Linux the guard comes from the global __stack_chk_guard through the GOT with adrp and ldr , and the failure is bl __stack_chk_fail . The recognizer reports the guard source, the slot, the compare, and the fail call. plain_leaf , which has no array, has no canary under strong , which protects functions with arrays, alloca , or address-taken locals. The research notes also record the MSVC form under /GS , a cookie mixed with %rsp and checked by __security_check_cookie ; no MSVC linker exists on this machine, so that shape is described from the compiler's assembly output only. -fcf-protection=full puts endbr64 , bytes f3 0f 1e fa , as the first instruction of every function. It is a landing pad for indirect branches on processors with control-flow enforcement, and it executes as a nop elsewhere. Ghidra's x86-64 function-start patterns include the endbr64 prefixed variants of push rbp; mov rbp, rsp for this reason. The recognizer reports it as cet landing pad , so a function that starts with four unusual bytes is not mistaken for data. What the Decompilers Fold Every decompiler in lesson 37 runs some of these derivations as rewrite rules. Ghidra's decompiler names them in ruleaction.cc . RuleDivOpt is "Convert INT_MULT and shift forms into INT_DIV or INT_SDIV", with the forms sub( (zext(V)*c), d) >> e => V / (2^n/(c-1)) where n = d*8 + e and the signed variant with sext and s>> . RuleModOpt is "Simplify expressions that optimize INT_REM and INT_SREM". RuleDivTermAdd handles the add fix-up, RuleSignDiv2 turns (V + -1*(V s>> 31)) s>> 1 into V s/ 2 , and RulePositiveDiv turns a signed division of values with clear sign bits into the unsigned one. Lesson 13.37 captured Ghidra 12.1.4 on lesson 33's grade at -O1 , and the output reads uVar2 = param_1 / 10 - 6; . The division is folded. The input to those rules is visible without Java. The venv's pypcode 4.0.1 lifts with the same SLEIGH specification Ghidra uses, and code/fixtures/idioms-x86_64-O2.lifts.json holds the raw P-code for div10s : 112 entries for seven instructions, of which 7 are the IMARK markers that open each instruction, among them RAX = RAX * unique[95a00:8] after unique[95a00:8] = sext(0x66666667) , RCX = RCX >> unique[d1a00:4] , and RAX = RAX s>> unique[c5c00:4] . The shrq carries 41 operations and the sarq carries 40, and most of them compute the flags. RuleDivOpt matches the multiply and the two shifts in this stream, and dead-code elimination removes the flags that nothing reads. angr 10.0.3 ran on our -O2 object, and idioms-x86_64-O2.angr.json holds its decompiler output for 20 functions. It folds the unsigned form: div10u is return a0 / 10; . It does not fold the signed form: div10s is v1 = a0 * 1717986919; return ((long long)(v1) >> 0x22) + (v1 >> 63); and mod10s is a0 - (...) * 2 * 5 . For div7u it prints (a0 / 7 + ((a0 * 6 / 7 & 0xffffffff) >> 1 & 0xffffffff) & 0xffffffff) >> 2 , where the fix-up terms survive as arithmetic. It folds mul9 to a0 * 9 , linear_switch to (a0 < 7 ? a0 * 10 + 10 : 0xffffffff) , clamp_max to ((int)a1 < (int)a0 ? a0 : a1) , is_pos to a0 > 0 , and fill to return memset(a0, 0, a1); . It prints table_switch as a load *(int *)(4 * a0 + 4195400) without the values, sum_n with _mm_add_epi32 and _mm_shuffle_epi32 intrinsics, and tail_caller as tail_target(); return; with the argument lost. In plain words first The idea in one line A linked program calls functions it does not contain. This lesson reads the tables the link editor wrote for those calls in three formats, follows one call to the slot the loader fills, and finds the functions of a build after its names are gone. The problem In plain words first A compiled object file is not yet a program. The linker joins objects, fills in the addresses that relocations left blank, and, for code that uses shared libraries such as the C library, sets up indirection: calls go through a small stub (the PLT) that jumps via a table of addresses (the GOT), which the dynamic loader fills in when the program starts or the first time each function is called. Windows (PE) and macOS (Mach-O) do the same job with different tables. Shipped programs are often stripped of their symbol names, so a reverse engineer has to find functions from other evidence and name them by matching known code. This lesson builds a program over ledger.c on this machine, reads its dynamic tables with the lesson's reader, watches a GOT slot change in gdb, and then finds the functions of the stripped program three ways. You linked main.c against libledger.dylib and asked an agent which function main calls at 0x1000005a0 . The agent disassembled the instruction and read bl 0x100000694 . That address holds twelve bytes: adrp x16 , ldr x16, [x16, #0x38] , br x16 . The agent followed the load to 0x100004038 , read the eight bytes 00 00 00 00 00 00 10 80 , and reported a call through a corrupt pointer into kernel space. Then you stripped the static build of the same program and asked how many functions it has. The agent ran nm , saw one name, __mh_execute_header , and answered one. Both answers read the file as if it were the running process. The word at 0x100004038 is a chained fixup. Bit 63 says bind, twelve bits say where the next fixup is, and the low bits say which import to bind. dyld replaces the word with the address of _puts before main runs. The stripped file lost its symbol table and kept LC_FUNCTION_STARTS , which lists all five function starts in nine bytes. This lesson builds five readers in standard-library Python. A COFF reader for our own objects and a PE32+ reader for the import, export, and base relocation directories. A Mach-O reader for load commands, stubs, the indirect symbol table, the chained fixup chain, and the exports trie, checked word for word against dyld_info . An ELF reader for the dynamic section, the PLT, and the GOT, plus a planner that says what a PIE link of our objects would create. A function finder for a stripped build with four methods and a score for each. A signature builder in the shape of FLIRT, with wildcarded relocation bytes and a CRC16 of the tail. Only Mach-O links on this machine. The arm64 executables and the dylib were linked, stripped, and run. The ELF and COFF objects compiled here with clang -target , and no ELF or PE link editor is installed, so the two linked images in those formats were written byte by byte from the specifications by two Python scripts in the fixtures folder. llvm-objdump reads them, and so does the library probe. They were not run, and the text says so where it matters. What the Link Editor Does With a Relocation Lesson 13.32 read relocation records and lesson 33 applied S + A - P to a lea . A record names a place P , a type, a symbol S , and an addend A . The x86-64 psABI Table 4.9 gives one formula per type, with L for the place of the symbol's PLT entry, G for its GOT offset, GOT for the GOT address, and B for the load base of the image. Three outcomes cover our objects. The link editor writes the value into the field and the record is gone. R_X86_64_PC32 against a symbol defined in the inputs is this case. The distance between two bytes of one image never changes, whatever the load address. The link editor makes a PLT entry and a GOT slot. R_X86_64_PLT32 against an undefined function is this case. The call gets L + A - P , the distance to the entry. The entry jumps through the slot. A R_X86_64_JUMP_SLOT record in .rela.plt tells the dynamic linker to fill the slot. The link editor keeps a relocation for the loader. R_X86_64_64 is an eight-byte absolute address, and a position-independent executable does not know its address until it loads. The record becomes R_X86_64_RELATIVE with formula B + A in .rela.dyn . main-x86_64-O1.o has 18 records: 14 in .text , 2 in .data.rel.ro , and 2 in .rodata . plan_dynamic_link() in code/main.py applies the three rules to them together with ledger-x86_64-O1.o : Record Count Decision Why R_X86_64_PC32 to .rodata , .L.str , fns , the table in .rodata 16 in place the symbol is defined in the inputs R_X86_64_PLT32 to percent_change , grade , total , grade_label 4 direct, no PLT defined in ledger-x86_64-O1.o , so the link editor reduces PLT32 to PC32 R_X86_64_PLT32 to puts twice and printf twice 4 PLT entry and GOT slot undefined, provided by a shared library R_X86_64_64 to grade in fns[] 2 R_X86_64_RELATIVE an absolute field in a PIE Two imports give a .plt of 48 bytes (PLT0 plus two entries of 16), a .got.plt of 40 bytes (three reserved slots plus two), and a .rela.plt of 48 bytes. The two relative records give a .rela.dyn of 48 bytes. These numbers come from the spec applied to our records. The hand-built tiny-dyn-x86_64 implements the PLT part of this plan for the same two imports, and its sizes match the plan. The compiler writes PLT32 on every call, defined or undefined, since binutils 2.31 (H.J. Lu, 2018-02-13) and LLVM 7.0.0 (D43383, 2018-02-20). The link editor decides. A PLT32 in an object therefore says "a call", and says nothing about whether a PLT entry will exist. Two more types appear in other builds. R_X86_64_GOTPCRELX and R_X86_64_REX_GOTPCRELX ( G + GOT + A - P ) ask for a GOT slot without a PLT, which -fno-plt produces and which the link editor may relax to a direct lea or call when the symbol is local (psABI Appendix B). R_X86_64_32 and R_X86_64_32S cannot hold an address in a PIE and the link fails. Neither kind occurs in our two objects. The Dynamic Section, the PLT, and the GOT The gABI chapter 5 says that an executable that takes part in dynamic linking has one PT_INTERP program header, which must precede any loadable segment, and one PT_DYNAMIC , which covers the .dynamic section. The section is an array of Elf64_Dyn pairs, a signed tag and a value, ended by DT_NULL . tiny-dyn-x86_64 is 5,184 bytes written by build_tiny_dyn_elf.py from the gABI and the psABI. Its dynamic section holds twelve pairs at 0x1000 : Tag Number Value Meaning DT_NEEDED 1 libc.so.6 a string table offset, 0xb , the library to load DT_HASH 4 0x1a0 the SysV hash table DT_STRTAB 5 0x188 .dynstr DT_SYMTAB 6 0x140 .dynsym , 24 bytes per entry DT_STRSZ 10 0x15 21 bytes of strings DT_SYMENT 11 0x18 24 DT_PLTGOT 3 0x10c0 .got.plt DT_PLTRELSZ 2 0x30 two 24-byte records DT_PLTREL 20 7 the records are DT_RELA DT_JMPREL 23 0x1b8 .rela.plt DT_FLAGS_1 0x6ffffffb 0x08000000 DF_1_PIE , a GNU tag DT_NULL 0 0 end The gABI says why DT_JMPREL is separate: it "holds the address of relocation entries associated solely with the procedure linkage table. Separating these relocation entries lets the dynamic linker ignore them during process initialization, if lazy binding is enabled." DF_BIND_NOW in DT_FLAGS , DF_1_NOW in DT_FLAGS_1 , or LD_BIND_NOW in the environment turn lazy binding off and the dynamic linker processes them at startup. PLT0 and the entry for puts psABI section 5.2 gives the two shapes in Figure 5.2. Here are the bytes of our file: Copy Do the arithmetic once. The RIP-relative displacement is relative to the next instruction. 0x1f6 + 0xed2 = 0x10c8 , which is .got.plt + 8 . 0x1fc + 0xed4 = 0x10d0 , which is .got.plt + 16 . 0x206 + 0xed2 = 0x10d8 , the fourth slot. 0x210 - 0x20 = 0x1f0 , PLT0. Every entry is 16 bytes, so the entry for exit starts at 0x210 , pushes $0x1 , and reads 0x10e0 . The GOT reserves three slots. psABI 5.2: entry zero holds the address of _DYNAMIC , and "entries one and two in the global offset table also are reserved". Our .got.plt reads 0x1000, 0, 0, 0x206, 0x216 . glibc fills slot one with its struct link_map and slot two with _dl_runtime_resolve when it loads the file. Slot three holds 0x206 in the file, which is the pushq inside puts@plt . psABI: the slot "initially ... holds the address of the following pushq instruction". So the first call runs call 0x200 , jmpq *0x10d8 lands on pushq $0 , jmp 0x1f0 pushes GOT+8 and jumps through GOT+16 into the resolver, which reads record 0 of DT_JMPREL , R_X86_64_JUMP_SLOT puts , looks puts up in libc.so.6 , writes its address into 0x10d8 , and jumps there. The second call runs call , jmpq *0x10d8 , and arrives. Drepper writes that "the overhead for all but the first call is therefore 'only' one indirect jump". The psABI footnote on %r11 explains one register choice in lesson 38: it is a scratch register so "code in the PLT need not spill any registers". The call site in .text reads e8 d4 ff ff ff at 0x227 , and 0x22c - 0x2c = 0x200 . llvm-objdump prints callq 0x200 <puts@plt> for it and names the entry from the .rela.plt record, which is how plt_entries() names it too. What the file does not have The file has no PT_GNU_RELRO . Jakub Jelinek proposed RELRO on the binutils list on 2004-01-06: move the sections written only during relocation to the start of the writable segment, so the dynamic linker can mprotect them read-only afterwards. GNU ld's default script puts .init_array , .fini_array , .data.rel.ro , .dynamic , and .got inside, and keeps only the three reserved slots of .got.plt inside, 24 bytes, because the other slots are written lazily. That is partial RELRO. -z now sets DF_BIND_NOW and moves the whole .got.plt inside, full RELRO, because nothing is written after startup. glibc's _dl_protect_relro calls mprotect(start, end - start, PROT_READ) on the page-aligned range. -fno-plt goes one step further on the compiler side: calls go through jmpq *name@GOTPCREL(%rip) , lazy binding is impossible, and GCC's manual says that "all external symbols are resolved at load time". The file has no version sections either. A real link against libc.so.6 adds .gnu.version , one Elfxx_Half per .dynsym entry, and .gnu.version_r , a Verneed for each library with Vernaux records for each version name. printf@GLIBC_2.2.5 means: the entry of printf in .gnu.version holds an index, the Vernaux whose vna_other equals that index has vna_name "GLIBC_2.2.5", under the Verneed whose vn_file is "libc.so.6". Index 0 is local, 1 is global, and bit 15 ( VERSYM_HIDDEN , 0x8000 ) hides a version from the link editor. The hash table is a SysV DT_HASH with one bucket and a three-entry chain, 24 bytes. It has no impact on performance." GNU strip --strip-all removes .symtab , .strtab , .debug_* , and .comment . The PE Format page defines the object: a 20-byte file header, no optional header, a section table of 40-byte entries, a symbol table of 18-byte records, and 10-byte relocation records per section. CoffObject in code/main.py reads all four. The file header says machine 0x8664 , 10 sections, 37 symbol records, SizeOfOptionalHeader 0. The section table names .text , .data , .bss , six sections called .rdata , and /16 . A name that starts with / is a decimal offset into the string table, which begins with its own four-byte size; /16 resolves to .llvm_addrsig , which is the name llvm-objdump -h prints. The 37 records include auxiliary records. A section symbol (storage class 3) carries one that holds the section length, the relocation count, a checksum, and a COMDAT selection. Five of the .rdata sections have selection 2, "any", and hold one string literal each under an MSVC-mangled name: ??_C@_04JDDJEAHN@even?$AA@ is the string "even". The link editor keeps one copy of each. The last record is .file with the auxiliary record "main.c". llvm-objdump -t prints these as [ 0] , AUX scnlen ... , [ 2] , and so on, skipping the auxiliary indexes, and the test compares our index and name pairs with that text. The relocations: 14 IMAGE_REL_AMD64_REL32 in .text and 4 IMAGE_REL_AMD64_ADDR64 in .rdata . REL32 is "the 32-bit relative address from the byte following the relocation". That is R_X86_64_PC32 with the -4 built in: the ELF record carries addend -4 because the record has an addend field, and the COFF record has none. ledger-x86_64.obj has three REL32 at 0x36 , 0x84 , and 0x93 , and lesson 32's ledger-x86_64-O1.o has its three R_X86_64_PC32 at the same three offsets. The code is the same, and the formats differ only in where the four is written. Walk the headers. The MS-DOS stub starts with MZ and at offset 0x3c holds e_lfanew , 0x40 . At 0x40 the signature PE\0\0 . Then the COFF file header: machine 0x8664 , 4 sections, SizeOfOptionalHeader 240, characteristics 0x22 (executable image, large address aware). The optional header starts with the Magic field, 0x20b , which means PE32+. AddressOfEntryPoint is 0x1000 , ImageBase is 0x140000000 , SectionAlignment 0x1000 , FileAlignment 0x200 , SizeOfImage 0x5000 , Subsystem 3 (console). DllCharacteristics 0x8160 decodes to HIGH_ENTROPY_VA 0x0020 , DYNAMIC_BASE 0x0040 , NX_COMPAT 0x0100 , and TERMINAL_SERVER_AWARE 0x8000 . Then 16 data directories of RVA and size. Four are set: Export at 0x2080 size 0x4d , Import at 0x2000 size 0x28 , Base Relocation at 0x4000 size 0xc , IAT at 0x2040 size 0x18 . Addresses in an image are RVAs, offsets from the load base. The section table maps them to file offsets: .text RVA 0x1000 at file 0x200 , .rdata RVA 0x2000 at 0x400 , .data RVA 0x3000 at 0x600 , .reloc RVA 0x4000 at 0x800 . PeImage.rva_to_offset() is that table. The import directory At RVA 0x2000 sits an array of 20-byte import descriptors ended by a zero descriptor. Ours has one: Import Lookup Table 0x2028 , timestamp 0, forwarder chain 0, name 0x2068 , Import Address Table 0x2040 . The name RVA points at "msvcrt.dll". The lookup table holds 64-bit entries ended by zero. Bit 63 set means import by ordinal, with the ordinal in bits 15 to 0. Bit 63 clear means bits 30 to 0 are the RVA of a hint/name entry: a 16-bit hint, "an index into the export name pointer table", then the ASCII name. Ours are 0x2058 (hint 0, "puts") and 0x2060 (hint 0, "exit"). The spec says the IAT is "identical to the contents of the import lookup table until the image is bound". Our IAT at 0x2040 holds the same two RVAs, and the test checks that the 24 bytes at 0x2028 equal the 24 bytes at 0x2040 . "During binding, the entries in the import address table are overwritten with the 32-bit (for PE32) or 64-bit (for PE32+) addresses of the symbols that are being imported." The Windows loader does that before the entry point runs. There is no lazy binding and no stub. The code reaches the slot directly: Copy FF /2 is the indirect near call. The two instructions have the same bytes because each one sits eight bytes after the other and reads a slot eight bytes after the other. iat_calls() scans the code section for ff 15 , adds six and the displacement, and names the slot from the import directory. The export directory At RVA 0x2080 the 40-byte export directory table: flags, timestamp, version, a name RVA pointing at "tiny-x86_64.exe", ordinal base 1, 1 address table entry, 1 name pointer. Three tables follow. The Export Address Table at 0x20a8 holds one RVA, 0x1000 . The Export Name Pointer Table at 0x20ac holds one RVA to the string "tiny_entry". The Export Ordinal Table at 0x20b0 holds one 16-bit unbiased index, 0. Name k maps to address entry ordinals[k] , and the exported ordinal is ordinals[k] + ordinal base . The spec adds a rule we do not use: an address entry that points inside the export section is a forwarder string such as MYDLL.expfunc , and the name pointer table is "ordered lexically to allow binary searches". Base relocations .reloc holds blocks. Each block starts with a page RVA and a block size, then 16-bit entries with the type in the top four bits and a page offset in the low twelve. Our one block: page 0x3000 , size 12, entry 0xa000 , type 10, IMAGE_REL_BASED_DIR64 , offset 0, and a padding entry of type 0, IMAGE_REL_BASED_ABSOLUTE . The eight bytes at RVA 0x3000 hold 0x1400020d0 , the image base plus the RVA of the string "linked by hand". If the loader places the image anywhere else, it adds the difference to that field. The spec: "Image files do not contain COFF relocations ... An image contains relocation information in the form of base relocations in the .reloc section (unless the image has the IMAGE_FILE_RELOCS_STRIPPED attribute)." /DYNAMICBASE is on by default in current link.exe, so images carry .reloc and DYNAMIC_BASE . A PE image has no symbol table to strip. The file header's PointerToSymbolTable "should be zero for an image because COFF debugging information is deprecated", and the names live in a separate PDB. What survives in every image is the import directory, the export directory, and, for 64-bit code, .pdata , whose RUNTIME_FUNCTION entries name the start and end of every function that allocates stack or calls another function. Leaf functions are absent from it. A FLIRT-Shaped Signature Hex-Rays describes FLIRT in its documentation: a pattern is "first 32 bytes of a function where all variant bytes are marked", the variant bytes come from fixups and external references, patterns live in a tree, and beyond the pattern "we calculate the CRC16 of the bytes starting from position 33 until the first variant byte" and store that length. Two functions with the same pattern and CRC are told apart by a tail byte at a position where they differ, then by the names they reference. A collision that nothing separates is "solved by natural intelligence". Every relocation_info record covers one four-byte word, and those bytes become variant. What the tools do with the same idea IDA Pro 9.4 ships FLIRT signatures per processor and the sigmake tool to build them; IDA Free covers x86 and x86-64 only and is for non-commercial use. Lumina is a server that keys function metadata by an md5 of the function and skips functions under 32 bytes. Ghidra 12.1.4 (Apache-2.0) has Function ID: a full hash over mnemonics and addressing modes that is "robust against changes due to linking" and a specific hash that adds constant operands, scored per matched instruction, with parent and child functions as tie-breakers; its shipped databases cover Visual Studio libraries only, and you populate your own from your own binaries. Binary Ninja 6.0 Krypton (commercial, with a Free edition) uses WARP (Apache-2.0): the function GUID is a UUIDv5 over the basic block GUIDs, each a UUIDv5 over block bytes after zeroing "all relocatable instructions" and dropping NOPs, with called, caller, and adjacent functions as constraints. BinDiff 8 (Apache-2.0) matches functions between two binaries with a fixed order of steps, from hash matching through flow graph MD indexes to call sequence matching, and weights the similarity from matched edges, blocks, instructions, and the flow graph MD index. Diaphora 3.4.3 (AGPL-3.0, IDA only) adds the small primes product, where each mnemonic maps to a prime and a function is the product, an order-free multiset fingerprint. radare2 6.2.4 (LGPL-3.0) has zignatures ( zg , z/ , zb ) and reads FLIRT .sig files with zfs ; rizin 0.9.1 (LGPL-3.0) creates .pat or .sig from an open binary with Fc and applies one with Fs . Worked example Following `puts` through the classic PLT The lazy build's .rela.plt says the GOT slot for puts is at link address 0x4000 ; its PLT entry is at 0x1030 . First call: jmp *GOT[puts] lands on puts@plt + 6 , which pushes the relocation index and jumps to PLT0, which calls the resolver. The resolver writes puts 's libc address into the slot. Recap What to keep from this lesson The linker resolves relocations; the dynamic loader fills the GOT through the PLT. Lazy binding fills slots on first use; bind-now fills them at start-up and allows a read-only GOT. PE and Mach-O solve the same problem with imports, stubs and fixups. Solutions Solution P1 · libc already, a PLT address, and nine of ten In the Ubuntu-default build, the slot already holds puts 's address in libc when main starts, because bind-now makes the loader resolve every PLT slot before running the program. In the lazy build it holds puts@plt + 6 , a PLT address, until the first call. After stripping, no single method finds all ten .text functions; combining .eh_frame , endbr64 and call targets finds nine, missing only the CRT helper register_tm_clones . Solution B1 · Almost nothing Almost nothing. GCC at -O2 omits the frame pointer by default ( -fomit-frame-pointer ), so most functions never execute push %rbp; mov %rsp,%rbp ; and with Ubuntu's -fcf-protection , the first instruction is endbr64 , so even functions that do set up a frame do not start with that pattern. The finder reports very few functions, possibly some in the middle of code where the bytes happen to match. Use the evidence the build actually leaves: .eh_frame FDEs (present for every compiled function unless explicitly disabled), endbr64 markers, direct call targets, entry points and exported dynamic symbols, and the gaps between known functions; then confirm by disassembling from each candidate. Weigh a trade-off A stripped arm64 executable holds five functions, and nm lists one name. Compare four ways to recover the function starts, score each against the unstripped twin at -O0 and -O2 , and say how you name the functions afterwards and where that naming collides. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The link editor's own table wins: LC_FUNCTION_STARTS is nine bytes of uleb128 deltas that list all five starts at both levels, and strip does not touch it. A prologue scan for the pre-indexed frame store finds 0 of 5, because the compiler emits sub sp, sp, #N first; a mask for that sub finds 5 of 5 at -O0 and 1 of 5 at -O2 , where four leaf functions have no frame at all. Call targets plus the entry point find 5 of 5, since a bl into the middle of a function is something a compiler does not emit for C. Names come from signatures built from your own objects, a 32-byte pattern with relocation bytes wildcarded and a CRC16 of the tail; at -O2 two functions share their first 36 bytes because one inlined the other, and the tail byte at 44 and the lengths 60 against 72 split the collision. The four finders. Method What it reads -O0 -O2 Why LC_FUNCTION_STARTS uleb128 deltas in __LINKEDIT 5 of 5 5 of 5 written for the unwinder and crash reporter; survives strip frame-store prologue stp x29, x30, [sp, #-0x10]! 0 of 5 0 of 5 the compiler stores the pair at a positive offset after sub sp sub sp mask (word & 0xff0003ff) == 0xd10003ff 5 of 5 1 of 5 leaf functions at -O2 allocate no frame; one starts with cbz call targets every bl inside __text , plus the LC_MAIN entry 5 of 5 5 of 5 nothing calls main , so the entry is added by hand No false positives appeared here because the program is small. One-byte patterns such as the x86-64 push rbp byte hit inside other instructions, which is why real pattern files pair a start pattern with a byte that must end the previous function. Prefer the tables the link editor wrote, then call targets to fill gaps, and scan for bytes last. What strip leaves per format. The names the loader binds survive everywhere: imports and exports in the dynamic symbol table, the import and export directories of a PE image, the chained imports table and the exports trie of a Mach-O. Function starts survive as unwind data ( .eh_frame unless built without unwind tables), as .pdata entries for non-leaf functions in a PE image, and as LC_FUNCTION_STARTS . The static symbol table and the debug sections go. A fully stripped library whose symbol table holds zero records still links, because the link editor reads the exports trie. Signatures and the collision. A signature is the first 32 bytes of a function with every relocated byte marked variant, a CRC16 over the bytes after the pattern up to the first variant byte, and the names the function references. Built from the unstripped objects and applied at every recovered start, the signatures name all five functions at both levels. At -O2 the two colliding functions produce identical pattern and CRC lines; the report records both candidates and the byte that decided them. A collision that nothing separates stays an unknown. The premise is checked too: every non-variant byte of each object function equals the byte at the same offset in the linked file, so the link editor changed only the relocated words. Plausible wrong answers. " nm shows one function, so there is one." It shows the symbol table; the link editor's starts table lists five. "Scan for the standard prologue." At -O2 four of five functions have no frame; the scan reports what the compiler chose to emit. "A matching CRC proves the name." Two functions shared pattern and CRC; the tail byte and the lengths decided, and the record says so. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the frame-store scan find nothing even at -O0 ? Expected: the compiler emits sub sp first and stores the frame record at a positive offset, so the pre-indexed form never occurs. (level 3) Why can strip not remove the function starts table? Expected: the unwinder and the crash reporter read it, the link editor writes it into __LINKEDIT , and only the symbol table is the debugger's. (level 3) Two signatures match at the same start. What do you record? Expected: both candidates, the tail byte and the lengths that split them, and an unknown when nothing does. (level 4) Which table plays this role in a PE image, and whom does it omit? Expected: .pdata with its RUNTIME_FUNCTION entries, which omit leaf functions that allocate no stack and call nothing. In plain words first The idea in one line A decompiler prints a->balance when it has a type table and *(int *)(param_1 + 4) when it does not. This lesson builds the table from the accesses, reads the real one from DWARF 5, and shows where the two agree. The problem In plain words first Machine code has no types. A struct field shows up only as an offset added to a pointer, such as 4(%rdi) for a 4-byte member 4 bytes into the struct. To recover the struct, you collect every access through the same pointer, note each offset and width, and apply the platform's layout rules (alignment and padding) to fill the gaps. When the program was built with debug information, DWARF describes the types exactly, which gives you something to check against. C++ adds hidden data: a pointer to a virtual-method table (vtable) at the start of each object, and type information for dynamic_cast and exceptions. This lesson checks one struct three ways (the lesson's DWARF reader, pyelftools on GCC's DWARF, and the compiler's own offsetof ), then reads C++ vtables from clang's and g++'s objects and from a live process in gdb. You compiled account.c without -g and asked an agent what bump does. The agent sent the object to Ghidra 12.1.4 and got this back: Copy The same source compiled with -g gives this from the same decompiler: Copy The instructions are identical in both objects. The difference is a type table. With the table the decompiler knows that the first parameter points at a 32-byte structure whose field at offset 4 is a 4-byte int named balance . Without it the decompiler knows only that something 8 bytes wide arrived in %rdi and that 4 bytes at +4 were read and written. Everything in that table has a source. The offset 4 comes from the displacement byte of addl 0x4(%rax), %ecx . The width 4 comes from the l suffix. The name comes from a DW_TAG_member entry in .debug_info . This lesson builds both halves: a pass that recovers what the instructions prove, and a reader that decodes what the compiler recorded. The gap between them is what a type name costs. A Member Access Is a Displacement Intel SDM Volume 1, section 3.7.5, defines the effective address as Offset = Base + (Index * Scale) + Displacement , with a scale of 1, 2, 4, or 8 and a displacement of 8, 16, or 32 bits. Section 3.7.5.1 adds the 64-bit mode form RIP + Displacement . A struct member access uses the first form with no index: the base register holds the address of the object and the displacement is the member offset. An array access adds the index term, and the scale or a separate multiply carries the element size. Take bump at -O0 . The listing from llvm-objdump -d -r reads: Copy Decode 03 48 04 with the rules from lesson 33. 03 is ADD r32, r/m32 . ModRM 48 is 01 001 000 : mod = 01 means a memory operand with an 8-bit displacement, reg = 001 is %ecx , r/m = 000 is %rax . The displacement byte is 04 . The instruction reads 4 bytes at %rax + 4 and adds them into %ecx . The l suffix that llvm-objdump prints is the operand size, so the field is 4 bytes wide. The %rax came from the frame slot at -0x8(%rbp) , and that slot received %rdi , the first integer argument under the System V calling convention. Three facts follow: the first parameter is a pointer, the object it points at has a 4-byte field at offset 4, and bump reads and writes that field. Nothing in these bytes says int , balance , or struct account . Nothing says how big the object is. The remaining 28 bytes of the struct are invisible to bump . The System V Layout Rules The x86-64 psABI, section 3.1.2, gives three rules for aggregates. "Structures and unions assume the alignment of their most strictly aligned component. Each member is assigned to the lowest available offset with the appropriate alignment. The size of any object is always a multiple of the object's alignment." Figure 3.1 of the same document gives the scalar sizes and alignments: char 1 and 1, short 2 and 2, int 4 and 4, double 8 and 8, any pointer 8 and 8. Apply the rules to the struct in account.c : Copy Member Size Alignment Lowest offset that fits Padding before kind 1 1 0 0 balance 4 4 4 3 (bytes 1 to 3) code 2 2 8 0 rate 8 8 16 6 (bytes 10 to 15) label 8 8 24 0 The last member ends at 32. The strictest alignment is 8, and 32 is a multiple of 8, so the size is 32 with no tail padding. Nine bytes of the 32 are padding, and the psABI says "The contents of any padding is undefined". The order of the members decides the size. The same five members as double, pointer, int, short, char fill offsets 0, 8, 16, 20, 22 and end at 23, which rounds up to 24. sysv_layout() in code/main.py applies the three rules and produces both results. Python's ctypes module applies the same rules through the host compiler's convention, and ctypes.sizeof , ctypes.alignment , and the .offset of each field give 32, 8, and 0, 4, 8, 16, 24 for the same struct. The Arm AAPCS64 states the same aggregate rules in its section 5.10.1, and Apple's arm64 document keeps these five scalar sizes, so the numbers agree across the two targets. The Pass trace_function() in code/main.py walks one function's instructions in address order and keeps a small abstract state. A holder is a 64-bit register or a frame slot such as -0x8(%rbp) . Each holder has one of three values. A Pointer is a root plus a constant offset plus a set of strides, where a stride records that an unknown multiple of that many bytes was added. An Index is an integer of unknown value that is a multiple of a scale. Anything else is nothing. The state starts with the six System V argument registers holding Pointer("param0", 0) through Pointer("param5", 0) . Then each instruction applies one rule: A movq between a 64-bit register and a frame slot copies the value. A 32-bit or narrower write to a register makes it an Index with scale 1. A leaq with a pointer base produces a pointer with the displacement added, and with an index register it adds scale * index_scale to the strides. A leaq whose base is %rbp or %rsp names a frame object, which is how main passes rows . shlq $n on an Index multiplies its scale by 2^n , and imulq $k multiplies by k . addq of a pointer and an index keeps the pointer and adds the index scale to the strides. addq $k to a pointer moves its offset and is also recorded as an increment of that register. A call makes every caller-saved register unknown, and the argument registers that hold pointers are recorded as a call site. Any memory operand whose base register holds a pointer becomes an Access with the pointer's root and offset, the width and kind from the mnemonic, and a store flag. Width and kind come from the mnemonic alone. access_width() maps the b , w , l , and q suffixes to 1, 2, 4, and 8 bytes, movsbl and movswl to signed narrow loads, movzbl to unsigned, the sd and ss scalar SSE instructions to 8-byte and 4-byte floats, cvtsi2sdl to a signed 4-byte integer source, and the 16-byte movaps family to a vector. leaq and the nop forms are not accesses. Copy A load of 8 bytes through a pointer produces a new pointer whose root names the field it came from, such as param0->0x18 . When that value is later used as a base, or advanced with leaq , the field it came from is marked as a proven pointer. That is the rule that turns offset 24 from "8 bytes" into "pointer". Four kinds of stride evidence infer_layout() merges the accesses of every witness function and collects the stride from four sources, each with the instruction that produced it. Kind Where it comes from Build that shows it scale an Index with scale above 1 reached a pointer, from shlq $0x5 or imulq -O0 , shlq $0x5, %rcx at 0x59 loop-step a 64-bit increment of the base or index register inside a loop that also contains the access -O1 , addq $0x20, %rdx at 0x24 offset-delta same-width accesses through one base register inside one loop, at offsets a constant apart -O2 , eight loads 32 apart call-site the offsets at which one frame object is passed to the witness functions -O0 , main passes rows , rows+0x20 , rows+0x40 A loop is a backward jmp or conditional branch, and an increment counts only when the loop range contains both the increment and the access. That rule excludes the addl $0x1, %eax that advances i at -O0 , because it is a 32-bit add and because the access does not go through %eax . The final stride is the greatest common divisor of every value found. The size is the stride when the stride is at least as large as the end of the last field. The vectorised loop at -O2 At -O2 clang vectorises sum_balances . The loop body from 0x50 to 0xaa reads eight elements per pass: Copy %rax starts at list + 0xe4 . The eight displacements place the loads at offsets 0x04, 0x24, 0x44, 0x64, 0x84, 0xa4, 0xc4, 0xe4 from list , which are 4, 36, 68, 100, 132, 164, 196, 228 . The increment is 0x100 , which is 256. Inside one loop, take the same-width accesses through one base register. Their offsets are d apart, here 32. If the loop step is k * d and there are exactly k distinct offsets, the loop was unrolled k times, and every access is the same element access at offset (offset - lowest) mod d . Here 256 = 8 * 32 with eight offsets, so all eight loads fold onto offset 4, and the stride evidence records offset-delta 32 , unrolled 32 , and loop-step 256 . C++ Objects shapes.cpp defines Shape with a virtual destructor, a pure virtual area() , and a virtual name() , and Rect , which derives from Shape and adds two int members. The Itanium C++ ABI governs how clang lays these out on x86-64 Linux. Mangled names Section 5.1.2 of the ABI says "a name is mangled by prefixing _Z to an encoding of its name". The object has 19 such symbols. _ZNK4Rect4areaEv reads as _Z , then N for a nested name, K for a const member function, 4Rect and 4area as length-prefixed source names, E to close the nested name, and v for an empty parameter list. llvm-cxxfilt prints Rect::area() const . _Z8describeRK5Shapei is describe(Shape const&, int) : R is a reference, K is const, 5Shape is the class, i is int . The special names in section 5.1.4 are _ZTV for a vtable, _ZTI for typeinfo, and _ZTS for the typeinfo name string. Constructors and destructors are C1 , C2 , D0 , D1 , and D2 , so _ZN4RectD0Ev and _ZN4RectD2Ev both print as Rect::~Rect() : the deleting destructor and the base-object destructor share a source name. Demangler in code/main.py covers that subset plus the builtin type codes of section 5.1.5.2 and the S_ substitutions of section 5.1.10. The test runs it on all 19 names and compares with the captured llvm-cxxfilt --no-strip-underscore output. The flag matters on macOS, where the tool strips one leading underscore by default and then fails to recognise Z8describe... . The vtable from its relocations Section 2.5.2 of the ABI lists the components of a virtual table in order: virtual call offsets, virtual base offsets, offset to top, the typeinfo pointer, and then the virtual function pointers. The address point, the value an object's vptr holds, is the address of the first function pointer (section 2.6.2). Rect has no virtual bases, so its table is offset to top, typeinfo, and functions. The symbol _ZTV4Rect is 0x30 bytes, six 8-byte slots. In the object every byte is zero. The contents are in .rela.data.rel.ro._ZTV4Rect : Copy Slot 0 holds the offset to top, which is 0 and needs no relocation. Slot 1 is the typeinfo. The address point is at +16 . From there, slot 0 is the complete-object destructor, slot 1 the deleting destructor, slot 2 area , slot 3 name . read_vtable() reads the symbol size, the relocations in its range, and the zero at offset 0. Shape 's table has the same shape with __cxa_pure_virtual in slot 2, which is the runtime function that a pure virtual call reaches. RTTI Section 2.9.4 describes std::type_info as a vptr followed by a pointer to the mangled type name, and lists the derived classes. _ZTI4Rect has three relocations: _ZTVN10__cxxabiv120__si_class_type_infoE+0x10 , _ZTS4Rect , and _ZTI5Shape . The first is the vtable of __si_class_type_info , the class the ABI uses for a type with a single public non-virtual base at offset zero, and the +0x10 is that vtable's address point. The second points at the string 4Rect , which is the mangled type name, and name() on a type_info returns exactly that string. The third is the base. _ZTI5Shape uses __class_type_info and has no base pointer. read_typeinfo() returns these three facts. The virtual call describe at -O0 makes one virtual call: Copy The first movq loads the object pointer. The second reads 8 bytes at offset 0 of the object, which is the vptr, because the ABI places it first in a class with virtual functions. The callq goes through 0x10 past the vptr, and 0x10 / 8 is slot 2. find_virtual_calls() matches the pattern and reports both candidates: Rect::area() const from _ZTV4Rect and __cxa_pure_virtual from _ZTV5Shape . Which one runs depends on the object, which is why the call is indirect. DWARF records the same slot. The DW_TAG_subprogram entries for area in both classes carry DW_AT_vtable_elem_location (DW_OP_constu 0x2) , name carries slot 3, and the destructors carry slot 0. Rect is a DW_TAG_structure_type of 16 bytes with a DW_TAG_inheritance entry for Shape at offset 0 and members w at 8 and h at 12. Shape is 8 bytes with one artificial member _vptr$Shape . Two independent derivations give slot 2 for area : the relocation table and the debug entries. At -O1 the object has no vtable at all. main constructs Rect as a local, so the compiler resolved r.name() and describe(r, 2) at compile time and inlined them. Nothing takes the address of the table, so the table is not emitted. describe still contains movq (%rdi), %rax and callq *0x10(%rax) , because its parameter can be any Shape . A missing vtable is a fact about one object file, and the test test_the_optimised_object_keeps_the_call_pattern_but_drops_the_vtables checks both halves. The Microsoft ABI differs in every one of these details. Decorated names start with ? and encode the calling convention, so void test(void) compiled as C++ __cdecl is ?test@@ZAXXZ . The RTTI locator sits at vfptr[-1] as a _RTTICompleteObjectLocator , and the symbols are ??_7 for a vftable and ??_R4 for the locator. Microsoft's own documentation says there are "no standards for C++ naming between compiler vendors". This lesson's fixtures are Itanium only. Type Inference Research The pass here is the constraint-generation half of a type inference system, restricted to one struct reached from a parameter. The field has gone further. TIE (Lee, Avgerinos, Brumley, NDSS 2011) framed type reconstruction as constraint generation and solving over a binary IR, measured conservativeness and precision, and compared against a commercial decompiler on 87 coreutils programs. Retypd (Noonan, Loginov, Cok, PLDI 2016) added subtyping, polymorphism, and recursive types, and reported reconstruction of pointer const annotations with 98% recall. An open-source implementation exists under GrammaTech's name. OSPREY (Zhang and others, IEEE S&P 2021) treats each memory location as a random variable and infers the most probable types. DIRTY (Chen and others, USENIX Security 2022) and ReSym (Xie and others, CCS 2024) post-process decompiler output with learned models, and ReSym reports 72.9% precision on full struct layouts. RecStruct (Chen and others, USENIX Security 2026) recovers nested structs without a decompiler, with flow-insensitive symbolic execution and union-find over stack slots. Solutions Solution P1 · Three agree; the reader fails on GCC Yes, the three agree on every offset and on the size of 32. No, the lesson's reader stops on GCC's object with a TypeError : GCC encodes names with DW_FORM_strp , which the reader reads but does not resolve through .debug_str , so a name arrives as a number. Solution B1 · Declaring before collecting The analyst declared the struct after seeing three accesses, instead of collecting every access through that pointer type across the whole program first. The later accesses reveal a 2-byte member at 8 ( short code ) and an 8-byte member at 24 ( label ), so the struct is at least 32 bytes and has five members. They also skipped the layout rules: with char at 0, int at 4 and double at 16, bytes 8-15 are not necessarily padding; an 8-byte-aligned double after an int ending at 8 would be at 8, not 16, so the gap at 8-15 was itself a sign of a missing member. And with no evidence for the struct's size (a loop stride, an allocation size, a memcpy length), they could not know where it ends. Method: gather accesses (offset, width, signedness, float or integer) from every function, use strides and allocation sizes for sizeof , apply the ABI's alignment rules to explain each gap, and leave unknown bytes marked unknown rather than inventing fields. In plain words first The idea in one line A breakpoint hit is an observation about one run of one build. This lesson builds the harness that turns those observations into confirmed, refuted, and not-observed verdicts on the claims the static lessons made. The problem In plain words first Static analysis reads code; dynamic analysis watches it run. A debugger can stop a program at an instruction (a breakpoint, made by temporarily replacing an instruction byte), stop when a memory location changes (a watchpoint, done by the CPU's debug registers, of which there are only four), show registers and memory, and save the whole process to a core file for later study. A tracer such as strace shows every request the program makes to the operating system. One run proves what happened on that run, for those inputs, and nothing about others. Optimization changes what a debugger can see: a function that was inlined or computed at compile time has nothing to stop at. This lesson runs the lesson's debugging plan with gdb on GCC builds at -O0 and -O2 , traces the system calls, and reads a core file without the process. Lesson 13.41 read struct account from DWARF and said balance sits at offset 4. Lesson 13.33 built the control-flow graph of classify and said the first branch goes to the return -1 block when the balance is negative. Lesson 13.32 said the first two arguments arrive in x0 and x1 . Every one of those sentences was derived from bytes. None of them was observed. An agent then reads the same program and reports "main calls bump , classify , and sum_balances ". The symbol table lists all three, so the sentence looks safe. You build the program at -O2 , set a breakpoint on each function, and run it. The process prints its four lines and exits. Every breakpoint reports hit count = 0 . The agent was not wrong about the source. It was wrong about the build it was asked about. The compiler inlined all three calls and folded sum_balances(rows, 3) into the constant 315. The only way to know that for this binary on this machine is to run it under a debugger and look. This lesson builds a harness that does the looking. It compiles account.c , reads the listing, plans one lldb session, runs it, and grades each static claim against what the stops show. The grading has three outcomes. confirmed means a stop showed the claim to be true for this run. refuted means a stop showed it to be false. not-observed means no stop could test it, and the record says why. Lesson 13.35 then stores each verdict as an observed record with authority controlled-replay . A Debugger Is Three System Services and a Table A debugger does four things to a process it does not own the code of. It stops the process, reads and writes its registers, reads and writes its memory, and gets told when the process stops again. The kernel provides each of these as a service, and the services differ by operating system. On Linux the service is ptrace(2) . The manual page says it "provides a means by which one process (the tracer) may observe and control the execution of another process". PTRACE_TRACEME lets a child announce that its parent will trace it, PTRACE_ATTACH takes an unrelated process, PTRACE_PEEKDATA reads "a word at the address addr in the tracee's memory", PTRACE_GETREGS reads the registers, and PTRACE_SINGLESTEP runs one instruction. The Yama module limits attach: /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope at its default of 1 means "the target process must be a descendant of the caller", 2 means only an administrator may attach, and 3 means nobody may. On macOS ptrace is a smaller interface. Apple's manual lists PT_TRACE_ME , PT_ATTACHEXC , PT_STEP , PT_CONTINUE , and PT_KILL , and says that with PT_ATTACHEXC "Signals from the child go to the parent as Mach exceptions". Memory and registers do not go through ptrace at all. lldb's debugserver calls task_for_pid() to get a Mach task port for the process, then task_set_exception_ports() so that breakpoints arrive as exception messages. The system daemon taskgated decides who may call task_for_pid . You can see the cost of that design in a transcript this lesson keeps. The session's shell runs under a Seatbelt sandbox. The same plan that produces eleven stops outside the sandbox produces this inside it: Copy The process was created and then could not be adopted. The error is about the debugger's rights, and it says nothing about the program. The harness records it as a launch failure, with zero stops and no verdicts. The table is the breakpoint table. The debugger remembers which instruction byte it replaced at which address, so it can put the original back when you continue, and it counts hits per location. breakpoint list prints that table, and the harness reads it at the end of every run. Breakpoints: One Byte or One Word Replaced A software breakpoint is an instruction the processor traps on, written over the first bytes of the instruction you want to stop at. On x86-64 that is INT3 , opcode CC , one byte long, which the Intel manual describes as "intended for calling the debug exception handler". On arm64 it is BRK #imm16 , a four-byte instruction whose exception "records the exception in ESR_ELx, using the EC value 0x3C". The Arm manual adds that the preferred return address is the BRK instruction itself, which is why a stop reports the address of the replaced instruction and not the one after it. lldb sets breakpoints by name, by file and line, or by address. By name it skips the prologue: Copy bump + 12 is the fourth instruction. The three before it are sub sp, sp, #0x10 , str x0, [sp, #0x8] , and str w1, [sp, #0x4] , the frame setup that the DWARF line table attributes to the function's opening line. At the stop, x0 and x1 still hold the arguments, because the prologue only copied them. By address, lldb needs to know which module the address belongs to. A bare breakpoint set -a 0x100000504 before the process exists is a load address with no section behind it, and in a first test it stayed unresolved through the whole run with hit count = 0 . The form the harness uses names the module: Copy With -s the number is a file address inside account-O0 , lldb adds the load slide, and after the run the location reads resolved, hit count = 2 . The lesson 33 listing gives file addresses, so this is the form that connects a static listing to a dynamic stop. Decode the branch by hand The first conditional branch in classify at -O0 is the word 36f800a8 at 0x1000004f0 , which llvm-objdump prints as tbz w8, #0x1f, 0x100000504 . Decode it from the Arm A64 encoding of TBZ . Bit 31 is b5 , the high bit of the bit number. It is 0. Bits 30 to 25 are 011011 , the test-and-branch group. Bit 24 is 0, which selects TBZ and not TBNZ . Bits 23 to 19 are b40 , the low five bits of the bit number: 11111 = 31. With b5 = 0 the tested bit is 31, the sign bit of a 32-bit value. Bits 18 to 5 are imm14 : 00000000000101 = 5. The branch offset is imm14 * 4 = 20 = 0x14 , so the target is 0x1000004f0 + 0x14 = 0x100000504 . Bits 4 to 0 are Rt : 01000 = 8, so the register is w8 . w8 was loaded one instruction earlier by ldr w8, [x8, #0x4] , which is a->balance at offset 4. TBZ branches when the bit is zero. The branch is taken when the sign bit is clear, which is balance >= 0 . The source wrote if (a->balance < 0) return -1; , so the compiler inverted the condition: the taken edge skips the return -1 block, and the fall-through at 0x1000004f4 enters it. The static claim the harness carries is therefore an edge claim with a predicate: taken when a->balance >= 0 , fall-through otherwise. The lift of the second branch works the same way. subs w8, w8, #0xc8 computes balance - 200 and b.le 0x100000524 is taken when that is at most zero, which is balance <= 200 . Watchpoints Are Hardware and Few A watchpoint stops the process when memory at an address is accessed. It cannot be a replaced instruction, because any instruction anywhere might do the access. Processors therefore carry a small set of address comparators. On x86-64 they are the debug registers: DR0 through DR3 hold "the addresses of up to 4 breakpoints", and DR7 enables each one and sets its condition (execute, write, or read-write) and its length (1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes). On arm64 the pairs are DBGWVR<n>_EL1 , which "holds the data virtual address used for watchpoint matching", and DBGWCR<n>_EL1 for the controls, and the Arm manual says "An implementation can include between 2-64 watchpoints". lldb reports the number it was given: Copy Four on this machine. The watched address 0x16fdfe00c is x0 + 4 : the struct pointer at the bump stop plus the DWARF offset of balance . size = 4 is the int . type = m means modify. When the slots run out lldb refuses the next watchpoint, and because a region that is not aligned or not a power of two can take two slots, the number of watchpoints you may set can be smaller than four. Data watchpoints report after the access. The Intel manual says "an instruction that writes memory overwrites the original data before the debug exception generated by a data breakpoint is generated", and lldb keeps the old value in its own cache to print both: Copy The stop is at 0x1000004d0 , the instruction after str w8, [x9, #0x4] at 0x1000004cc . One quirk is worth knowing before you parse the output. Right after watchpoint set , lldb prints Watchpoint 1 hit: with an empty old value and new value: 250 . That is the initial read, and the harness ignores a hit without an old value. Stepping, Stop Hooks, and Batch Mode lldb's command grammar is <noun> <verb> [-options] [arguments] . The stepping verbs are thread step-in ( s ), thread step-over ( n ), thread step-inst ( si ), thread step-inst-over ( ni ), and thread step-out ( finish ). thread until 12 runs to a line. thread return <expr> returns early with a value. The harness does not step. It stops at planned addresses and lets a stop hook do the reading: Copy -o may be repeated, and the commands run in order at every stop. register read names the two argument registers and the program counter. memory read -s4 -fx -c24 $x0 prints 24 four-byte words in hex from the address in x0 , which is 96 bytes, three struct account rows. frame variable -P 1 prints the arguments and locals and expands pointers one level, so a shows its five fields. Batch mode is lldb -b . The manual says --batch runs the commands from -s , -S , -o , and -O and then quits, and that if a command stopped "due to a signal or crash, the debugger will return to the interactive prompt". The harness writes the plan to a file and passes it with -s . One setting matters: settings set interpreter.stop-command-source-on-error false . Without it, the first continue after the process has exited ends the whole file, and breakpoint list never runs. With it, lldb prints error: Process must be launched. and goes on. Two facts about the output shape decide how the parser works. First, hook output is printed as the hook runs, and the Process N stopped block with its frame #0 line is printed afterwards. The parser therefore collects register, memory, and variable lines into a pending chunk and attaches the chunk to the next frame #0 line it sees. A chunk whose program counter is in dyld at _dyld_start is the entry stop before the program runs, and no frame #0 ever claims it. Second, a breakpoint with --auto-continue does not report its stop at all, and a stop hook does not run for it. A first version of this harness used auto-continue and recorded nothing. The plan uses plain breakpoints and a fixed budget of continue commands instead. The hook printed this before the stop block: Copy Read the eight words of the first row against the DWARF offsets. Word 0 at offset 0 is 0x73 , which is 's' , the kind byte, followed by three padding bytes. Word 1 at offset 4 is 0xfa = 250, balance . Word 2 at offset 8 is 0x9 , code , a short in the low half with two padding bytes above it. Word 3 at offset 12 is padding before the 8-byte-aligned double . Words 4 and 5 at offset 16 are 0x3ff4000000000000 , which is the IEEE-754 encoding of 1.25. Words 6 and 7 at offset 24 are 0x100000719 , the label pointer into __TEXT . The next eight words start with 0x6c = 'l' and 0xffffffd8 = -40: the third row, loan , 32 bytes later. Apple's core(5) says "A small number of signals which cause abnormal termination of a process also cause a record of the process's in-core state to be written to disk", into /cores/core.pid , "provided the terminated process had write permission in the directory, and the directory existed". No kernel core is written until you raise the limit with ulimit -c unlimited , or system-wide with launchctl limit core unlimited . lldb writes a core on demand without a crash. What One Run Proves One run proves one input on one build. The C standard defines undefined behaviour as "behavior, upon use of a nonportable or erroneous program construct or of erroneous data, for which this document imposes no requirements", so a program that overflows a signed int may legitimately print different results at -O0 and -O2 . Lesson 13.36 met this with the percent_change overflow cells. UBSan turns the question into a stop: -fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow -fsanitize-trap=undefined makes the overflow "execute a trap instruction", which lands in lldb as a stop with a reason. Optimized code also moves what you want to watch. GDB's manual says "the optimizer has rearranged your code; the debugger shows you what is really there" and that a variable optimized out of existence is one "GDB never sees". GDB prints such a value as <optimized out> , and its source separates that from <unavailable> : optimized out "does not actually exist in the program", unavailable "exists in the program (at the machine level), but GDB has no means to get to it". lldb prints <variable not available> when the program counter is outside every range of the variable's DWARF location list. A watchpoint on a local that lives in a register never fires, because a register is not memory. The -O2 run above shows the extreme case: the whole function was folded away, and the silence of a watchpoint that was never set proves nothing. The harness therefore writes three kinds of record and never a fourth. A stop that tested the claim and agreed is confirmed . A stop that tested it and disagreed is refuted . A claim no stop could test is not-observed , with the reason, and the breakpoint hit counts are part of that reason. Lesson 13.35 's ledger accepts the first two as observed records with authority controlled-replay , and keeps the third as an open unknown. Xcode injects it into debug builds, strips it on export, and notarization rejects a binary that still has it. Apple's engineers state the rule for the refusal: the task port is denied when the target has the hardened runtime enabled and does not have get-task-allow . Recap What to keep from this lesson Breakpoints replace a byte with int3 ; watchpoints use four hardware registers. Plan stops from the listing; the binary, not the source, decides what can be hit. Optimized builds may inline or fold code so nothing stops; that is not evidence of dead code. strace shows the requests to the kernel; core files freeze a process for later study. One run proves one run. Solutions Solution P1 · Five, then zero Five at -O0 (one bump , three classify , one sum_balances ), and zero at -O2 . At -O2 , GCC inlines the three functions into main and folds the results into constants, so main calls only printf ; the out-of-line functions are never entered. The watchpoint never fires at -O2 because it is armed only after the first stop, and there is none. Solution B1 · Not hit is not dead "Not hit" only means no call to the out-of-line copy happened on that run of that build. At -O2 , classify was inlined into main and its result computed at compile time; its logic still determines the program's output ( class 0 1 -1 ). Deleting it from the source changes the program. And one run covers only one input; other inputs could reach code this run skipped. The right steps: read the release build's listing to see whether the function was inlined or folded; set breakpoints on the inlined locations (with -g , gdb can break on inlined call sites), or debug an -O0 build to observe the logic; and use coverage across many inputs, plus the call graph, before claiming any code is dead. Debug a failure An agent reports "main calls bump , classify and sum_balances ". You build the program at -O2 , set a breakpoint on each name, and run it under the debugger. The program prints its four lines and exits with status 0, and breakpoint list shows every breakpoint resolved with hit count = 0 . Grade the agent's claim and the seven other static claims in the plan, and name the harness mistake that would have produced a transcript with no stops on a build where the calls do happen. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Each breakpoint resolved, so the symbol exists and a trap was written at its address; a hit count of zero after a full run with exit status 0 means no instruction fetch reached it, so for this build the call-edge claim is refuted, and only that one, because the compiler inlined all three calls and folded the sum into the constant 315. The output claim is confirmed by the four lines and the exit status, and the argument-register, field-offset, store and stride claims are not-observed, because no stop could test them, with the hit counts as the reason. The harness mistake is --auto-continue : such a breakpoint reports no stop and the stop hook never runs, so a first version of the harness recorded nothing even on the unoptimized build where every call happens; plain breakpoints, a stop hook and a fixed budget of continue commands fix it. Three verdicts and never a fourth. A stop that tested a claim and agreed is confirmed ; a stop that tested it and disagreed is refuted ; a claim no stop could test is not-observed , with the reason. The ledger accepts the first two as observed records with authority controlled-replay and keeps the third as an open unknown. A resolved breakpoint never stands in for a run. What the refutation does and does not say. The claim was that main calls the three functions in this program. For this build and this run it does not, and the harness checked that the run completed, since a hit count of zero before exit would mean only that the run had not reached the call yet. The claim did not say the functions are dead code, and the run does not say that either: nm still lists them because they are external and another object could call them, and the debug information for the optimized build has four subprograms and zero inlined-subroutine entries, so even it does not record the inlining. The struct still has balance at offset 4 in this build; no stop read memory to show it, and not-observed keeps that distinction. The unoptimized run for contrast. The same plan on the -O0 build produced eleven stops: hit counts 1, 3, 1 for the three names and 2, 1, 1, 1 for the four edge breakpoints placed at the target and fall-through of two conditional branches. The watchpoint on a->balance fired once with old value 250 and new value 255, which is one write of by equal to 5, and the first row of memory read at the entry stop decoded word by word against the DWARF offsets. All eight claims ended confirmed there. Two more transcript traps. An address breakpoint set without naming the module stays unresolved with hit count = 0 for the whole run, because a bare number before the process exists has no section behind it; the form that connects a listing address to a load address names the module. And the first continue after the process has exited ends the whole command file unless interpreter.stop-command-source-on-error is false, so breakpoint list never runs and the transcript has no hit counts to read. Plausible wrong answers. "Hit count zero means the functions are dead code." It means no fetch reached them in this run of this build; they are exported and other callers are possible. " nm lists them, so they are called." The symbol table lists exported functions; the debug information shows four subprograms and no inlined entries. "Use auto-continue so the transcript stays clean." An auto-continue breakpoint reports no stop and the hook never runs; the clean transcript is empty evidence. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the run refute the call edges without making the functions dead code? Expected: the claim was about this program's main ; the functions are exported and another object could call them. (level 3) Where does the watchpoint on a->balance go in the optimized run? Expected: nowhere; it is set at the bump stop, which never happens, so the store claim is not-observed; a register-resident local would never fire either. (level 4) The transcript stops before breakpoint list . What happened and what changes? Expected: a continue after exit ended the command file; set the interpreter not to stop sourcing on error so the table prints. (level 4) Why keep the transcript and not only the verdicts? Expected: the verdicts are derived from it, anyone can re-derive them, and its header records the command line and the debugger version. Where it is taught. The dynamic analysis lesson runs both builds and grades every claim, and the evidence lesson stores the verdicts as observed records and the rest as unknowns.
